items.title: Is God Another Addiction?
items.description: “God does not and cannot exist,” Iris Murdoch once wrote, “but what led us to conceive of him does exist, and is constantly experienced and pictured.” You could hang that sentence—epigraph, baleful blessing—over Meghan O’Gieblyn’s memoir, “Will and Attention”
items.author: James Wood
paragraphs: “God does not and cannot exist,” Iris Murdoch once wrote, “but what led us to conceive of him does exist, and is constantly experienced and pictured.” You could hang that sentence—epigraph, baleful blessing—over Meghan O’Gieblyn’s memoir, “Will and Attention” (Doubleday). In some ways, it resembles a conventional addiction memoir: an alcoholic in her twenties, O’Gieblyn got sober, flourished for more than a decade as an essayist and critic, and then started drinking again during the pandemic. She vividly recounts her year of secrecy and collapse, followed by rescue and restoration. The fractions of fall and rise are in order: the book’s existence attests to the recovery.

But “Will and Attention” is more complex and surprising than its form suggests. An anguished engagement with theological and philosophical texts, above all the writings of Simone Weil, it is closer to an unfinished spiritual diary than to the familiar sort of sculpted redemption story. O’Gieblyn was raised in a fundamentalist Christian community on Lake Michigan and intended to enter the ministry. She lost her faith in her early twenties, relatively late for a loyalist. (Losing one’s faith, like discovering an aptitude for music or sports, tends to happen early or not at all.) You may wonder whether she only mislaid it. She certainly does: “I want very much to live a good and virtuous life, without alcohol and drugs, which have made my life miserable. And I still long to believe in God, despite the resounding silence that suggests that he does not exist, or is not interested in us, or in me specifically.” Perhaps her book is really a memoir of her addiction to God. More anguishing, to a God who does not and cannot exist.

A sentence of Weil’s provides the book’s title. On the wall above her desk, O’Gieblyn tells us, is a line from the French thinker’s notebooks, collected in “Gravity and Grace”: “We have to try to cure our faults by attention and not by will.” O’Gieblyn is in pained and plaintive agreement with Weil, who goads her throughout the book. She shares Weil’s suspicion of the will, but has doubts when it comes to her own powers of attention. Her account opens with an acute examination of the paradoxes of willing (an example of how boldly this memoir follows its philosophical interests). Experience has taught her that you cannot will yourself out of addiction, or into religious faith. At twenty-eight, she started treatment for alcoholism, but only when she had reached the very bottom—she was living out of her car, having “lost basically everything and having refused the interventions of everyone who’d previously tried to help.” This turn to sobriety felt less like determination than like surrender, a failure of will. She notes that “will” means both desire (to want something, to will it) and the faculty used to control or cancel desire (will power). So “the will is both the problem and the solution to the problem.” O’Gieblyn considers her alcoholism and her loss of faith to be failures of will, yet she grew up hearing worshippers testify that their conversion to evangelical Christianity came through a surrendering of the will, a submission to God’s grace. At the wooden tabernacle where congregants gathered on summer evenings beside Lake Michigan, the pulpit bore a sign that read “LET GO AND LET GOD.” She remains “fascinated with this idea, despite having no metaphysical beliefs to support it.”

If O’Gieblyn’s self-diagnosis is right, the collapse of will that led to her loss of faith is awkwardly close to a collapse of will that might lead to her return to faith. A failure of will is not quite a surrender of will; a voluntary submission might be seen as some noble version of willing, a willing away of will. Nevertheless, we seem to be in a strange twilight realm in which religious success may resemble secular failure.

In 2018, this former evangelical Protestant, who had studied at the Moody Bible Institute, in Chicago, found herself wandering into the Catholic St. Mary’s, “a large and beautiful church on our side of town.” (O’Gieblyn lives in the Midwest but does not name the town.) She is winningly honest about classic conversion narratives that somehow fail to persuade, and modest about her ability to account for her own urgings. So she cannot say exactly why she started attending Mass, except that she remembers being “overcome one spring with an inarticulate but decisive need to worship something.” The nature of the object wasn’t especially important; she simply wanted to kneel before something beautiful, to lose herself in it. The large Catholic church was drowned in golden light, and she was transfixed by the priestly mummery (her word is “pageantry”—a moment when the author and a certain kind of reader may diverge at supersonic speed), by “the senseless, hexlike redundancy of the Nicene Creed.” This worship began to take on the shape and the dynamic of her former alcoholism: she kept the visits secret, as if they were shameful, from her husband and her closest friends. By the fall, these services became “the most intensely sensuous experience” of her week; “there was nothing more desirable, more perfect, than to lose myself in a trance of senseless movement.” There’s a deliberate hint here, I think, of Emma Bovary’s secret raptures, her own wayward Catholic sensuousness.

As O’Gieblyn started going to church, she stopped going to the recovery meetings that had sustained her for years. She collapsed back into religion and then into drinking. When she eventually tells her husband, Barrett, that she has started drinking again, he calls her secrecy a kind of “infidelity.” Attending Mass had been the first infidelity. The “success” of religion led to the “failure” of alcohol. She now sees that the return to church “was just a veiled desire for intoxication, that the experiment with Catholicism served as a gateway back into drinking.” She was returning to “the things that had ruined my life before: alcohol and institutional religion.”

As in “Madame Bovary,” the priests are a mite disappointing, even if the cloaks and swirling stoles enchant. O’Gieblyn starts talking to the church’s pastor, whom she calls Father Aaron. He is intelligent, well read, respectful of the writer’s doubts. Shrewd, too: he gently parries her desire to become “a Catholic atheist,” and asks, “Why would you have a desire for something that doesn’t exist?”—the very question that O’Gieblyn can’t stop asking herself. It’s a version of C. S. Lewis’s insistence that an unappeasable yearning points to the existence of something beyond this world. O’Gieblyn concedes that this “shapeless longing for nothing I could locate, which I took to be a yearning for God,” has intermittently possessed her all her life—“and religion has never cured it.” Nor does religion offer a cure at St. Mary’s. She and Father Aaron get bogged down in orthodoxies both doctrinal and political (he asks her about the Catholic sacraments, and why she hasn’t had children), and the fever slowly cools. She confesses her secret churchgoing to Barrett, who calls it “addict behavior.”

This particular “addict behavior” is a heart murmur against the turbulent pulse of the actual addict behavior. Unappeased by religion, O’Gieblyn’s “shapeless longing” restlessly seeks its familiar object, its proper location, its old home. Soon, the pandemic brings its own kind of turbulence, vitally evoked here in bold Didion-like strokes: “I remember thinking that we were all slowly losing our minds. I remember the day that the heat broke and the entire city was loosed into the streets . . . . The evening when all the businesses downtown simultaneously boarded up their storefronts and tacked BLM posters to their doors, as though it were calf’s blood, hoping to be passed over.” In 2021, she publishes a book, resumes travelling, gives talks and readings. Airport bars, foreign cities, lonely hotel rooms: the sour reek of temptation. In Helsinki, she falters; at the Nashville airport she goes under and drinks three white wines, followed by vodka at O’Hare. The degradation is shameful, and shamefully compelling to read about. O’Gieblyn falls back into old tricks that come as easily as “riding a bicycle.” Drinking at home, she knows how to disguise her flushed cheeks and the smell of booze before Barrett returns: she takes a hot bath. One night, while he is sleeping, she slips out of the house to find another drink—or thinks she did, because the next morning she can remember only standing at the door, about to leave. But Barrett heard her, and he asks what’s going on. The culminating scene of confession and forgiveness is at once domestic and utterly religious. She’s on the threshing floor, saved and abased: “It is the only moment in my life when I have felt loved so completely, loved in the depth of my wretchedness and failure.”

One fascination of this brave book—brave in its disclosures but more so in its demands, its spiritual rigor, and its ardent intellectualism—lies in watching the eloquent, intelligent sufferer steadily entrapping herself. I don’t mean the obvious entrapment by her twin poisons, alcohol and institutional religion. I mean something more fundamental and less fathomable: her theology of alcoholism. The association of intoxication with religious ecstasy has a long history; its terrible force here comes from O’Gieblyn’s sense that the substance that has ruined her life also grants the surrender she was unable to achieve through worship. When she was young, she writes, she could never relax into God’s presence. The bustling ego, the barging will, always got in the way. “Alcohol is the only thing that has ever allowed me to rest happily in the presence of God,” she writes. Her drinking days in her twenties, and their morning hangovers, “were the closest I have come to the experience of enlightenment.” Her recent relapse, despite the secrecies and shame, was also a time of bliss. Alcohol offers her mystical release. Drinking, she can annihilate the self as the ancient mystics did, and as a modern one, Simone Weil, commands. The will recedes, peace and freedom suffuse her soul, and she glimpses the “nothing”—the God, the absent God—that her “shapeless longing” is always seeking. She experiences not the warm secular blur that most of us feel but “a bolt of religious rapture that makes you want to sell all your possessions and hole up in a cave with your one precious pearl.” In this theology, alcoholism represents not just fallen addiction but also religious application; she reminds us that “addiction” descends etymologically from the Latin verb addicere, to devote.

On this point, O’Gieblyn is movingly, almost repetitively, adamant. I should say that I’m largely immune to seeing alcohol or drugs as vehicles of religious insight: I think spilt religion should be cleaned up. Shouldn’t we avoid trading in substitutes, in transferences? But, as someone who, like O’Gieblyn, grew up in and came through an evangelical upbringing, I comprehend the longing that compels her to seek a godly non-God, a presence that may be an absence.

Still, the cost of persistently naming these experiences as religious would seem to be very high. If you can encounter God only by drinking to oblivion, every religious success is an abject secular failure. So is drinking O’Gieblyn’s problem, or is God? Which intoxication comes first? O’Gieblyn recognizes this dilemma (though she wouldn’t put it exactly like this) but remains in thrall to the longing that sustains it. Although she presents herself as having lost her faith, she can’t help wanting to return to it. Just when she thinks she’s out, God pulls her back in.

There is a telling moment when she considers her religious youth and ruefully wonders whether she ever had any true faith “in a heavenly Father.” “I had not been born again,” she wittily decides. “I had only been born.” But, a page later, she writes, “A friend of mine who left the church says that every liberatory deconversion narrative obscures a tragedy about failing to believe.” Does it? Can’t it just be liberatory? Surely O’Gieblyn sees that her friend is ruling out what we might call good-faith faithlessness. It’s as if we catch her revising her jest: I had not been born again, but it’s a tragedy that I wasn’t.

A tormenting syllogism seems to grip the author: she longs to encounter God; to do so, she must escape her will; to escape her will, she must drink. Therefore she drinks. Or she drank: this beautifully sober book describes her release from that prison. But her tradition does appear to have bequeathed her a powerful suspicion of the will. As she concedes, Christianity has reasons to denigrate human will, making it the source of disobedience and an explanation for much of the world’s evil. Salvation comes instead through God’s grace, the unearned gift that saves us from ourselves. Assigning responsibility for evil to human will also helps to absolve God. Yet understanding this religious inheritance, as O’Gieblyn so lucidly does, offers little assurance that one can escape its hold.

In practice, she treats the will, even the ego, as a sly old enemy to be outwitted or annihilated: “What I drank for was the peace and freedom from my own will.” Weil offers an extreme version of this hostility to the self. She was a daring mystic, but her pursuit of selflessness assumed the punitive intensity of a kind of ego-starvation: literally and theologically, the self was always too large. “Gravity and Grace” presents an exacting vision of kenosis, or self-emptying, in which an ideally voided ego will learn how to worship an ideally voided God. “To empty ourselves of the world,” Weil writes. “To take the form of a slave. To reduce ourselves to the point we occupy in space and time—that is to say, to nothing.”

O’Gieblyn’s memoir ends with a glimpse of serenity in freedom and something like redemption—a renewed sobriety, rooted in attending to the good, to the beautiful, to the world. (She uses Iris Murdoch’s writing about the good to soften some of Weil’s religious ferocity.) “Attention” replaces the feeble or malevolent “will,” as Weil says it should. For O’Gieblyn, “the good” also seems to replace “God.” On holiday in Italy, swimming regularly, alert to herself and to the beauty of her surroundings, she hopes that she is “no longer trying to obliterate my ego,” and begins to doubt “whether this was really the goal of spiritual life.” The reader who has journeyed this far with O’Gieblyn hopes that it is indeed a release and not merely a reprieve, that the old grinding syllogism will not return. Yet this reader can’t help noting that O’Gieblyn’s “attention,” which she and Weil offer as the alternative to will, sounds an awful lot like willed attention: “I was attuning my mind to the good. I was teaching myself, through daily acts of attention, to want it.” It’s one of the many ways that this remarkably honest spiritual journal seems alarmingly open and unfinished. ♦

items.title: You’ve Got to Go to This Place for Vacation
items.description: We have to tell you about this place we went on vacation. We just got back, and, trust me, it’s unlike any place you’ve been. Going to this place was life-changing. I’m glad we went before it’s ruined by tourists.
items.author: Sue D Gelber
paragraphs: We have to tell you about this place we went on vacation. We just got back, and, trust me, it’s unlike any place you’ve been. Going to this place was life-changing. I’m glad we went before it’s ruined by tourists.
What’s that, honey? No, I’m not going to bore them with stories. I just want to tell them how great and unique and authentic our trip was!

We were on a five-day tour, so we really got to know this place. And our guide was born there, so we’re kind of like locals now. He shared so much interesting information! Yes, honey, I know he gets paid to do that, but you could tell he really liked us. He even said that I should consider becoming a tour guide!

Our bus drove by all the important sites, including a museum and a church and a statue. I learned so much! Honey, I hate to disagree with you, but I definitely could name three things this place is famous for. Yes, I’m certain I could find it on a map. Please stop interrupting me when I’m telling them about our vacation!

We stayed in this great area. It was near the site of a famous battle where local residents fought off an invading army and thousands of people died, causing the soil to turn red with blood. I took a selfie there to show my zest for travel and my reverence for history. Plus, the glow from the red soil was super flattering.

This place was so charming, full of small streets and alleys. And a river ran right through the center of town! True, honey, a lot of towns have rivers, but I could tell that this place was unique and really embraced its maritime heritage.

The people were so friendly and happy! I really loved the life style of this place. I wish we could move there. Granted, I say that after every vacation, but this time I mean it! This place reminded me of a simpler time—when children played in the dirt with sticks and rocks. Like when our grandparents were young. But without the polio.

The food was so fresh! We went to a market where they sold amazing produce, but there were also local artisans selling unique items like bangle bracelets and T-shirts. No, honey, it’s not “just like” the Saturday market here at home. It was very authentic and Old World. I could almost imagine the locals handcrafting refrigerator magnets by the light of an open fire!

The music scene was incredible. There was this musician playing on a street corner, and people tossed coins into his guitar case. But it wasn’t like someone playing on the street here at home, because this street was lined with cobblestones, which everyone knows is the best kind of street material.

The weather was great. It was warm during the day, and, when the sun went down, it got cooler. Isn’t that amazing? Yes, honey, I know that’s “how the sun works,” but the change in temperature was in Celsius, not Fahrenheit, so it was more dramatic. Yes, I’m sure about that.

We were really lucky to be there during this annual event where they do this thing that’s really important to their culture. People come from all over to see it. We met an old man who lived hours away from this place, but he wanted to see this event before he died. And he did! He died right there in front of us. It was beautiful.
No, honey, he didn’t just fall asleep. Yes, I’m sure! Please let me tell the story my way. I know he was dead because I could see that he was finally at peace. Which is more than I can say.

Anyway, we had a great time. Well, except for the fight we had that day we toured the town square and I wanted to kill you—remember, honey? I wanted to display your severed head on the post in the middle of the square! But apparently they don’t do that anymore, which is too bad.
Vacationing in this place was so peaceful and authentic and unlike anyplace else on earth. Trust me, you have to go.
Well, next year we’re going to this other place. We can’t wait to tell you about it! ♦

items.title: Why I Am Not Like Other Tourists
items.description: I’m very quiet, so you hardly know I’m there until you see my bright-yellow safety vest, my walking stick, and my traveller’s badge, which features an image of binoculars and reads “World Explorer: Official.” To blend in, I wear khaki shorts with deep pockets,
items.author: Kerry Elson
paragraphs: I’m very quiet, so you hardly know I’m there until you see my bright-yellow safety vest, my walking stick, and my traveller’s badge, which features an image of binoculars and reads “World Explorer: Official.” To blend in, I wear khaki shorts with deep pockets, like a local.
I study the region’s language. For example, in many languages, I know how to say, “Hello,” “Do you have lite mayonnaise?,” and, “What is the Wi-Fi password?”
I wear my sandals with socks to prevent chafing. My socks are a heathered oatmeal color, and I feel that they lend my travel outfits a special warmth and authenticity.
I can go without air-conditioning for a few minutes.

I like to eat how the locals eat. For instance, I know that Maine is famous for its seafood and I have a feeling that people who live there eat fish for breakfast, lunch, and dinner. But, when I was visiting Maine, a resident told me, “Well, I like to go to Denny’s.” I said, “For fish, no doubt.” He said, no, he prefers hash browns, but I imagine that’s highly unusual in Maine.
Sometimes, I get off the beaten path. I like to walk on the grass right next to the path, just to see what that feels like.

Some tourists take a tour bus everywhere. I’ll admit, I do that—I ride to old churches, museums, and historic battlefields. But I don’t just ride the bus—I get off the bus, as well. In fact, I may even check out a nearby fish market, buy a cooler of fresh hake, and bring that on board, so that I can cook it up on a hot plate back at the hotel. It can be a struggle to hold a cooler of hake on your lap, but that’s the thing about travel—it’s not always easy.

If I get lost, I can find my way back to the hotel using my wits, dramatic hand gestures, and smartphone. I used these survival tools when a tour-bus driver left me behind one time at a fish market in Spain, where I had just purchased some cod. I’m sure it was all just a miscommunication about what time I was expected back on the bus—maybe I needed to return by 16:30, not 17:00. That’s how time goes in Spain—it goes into the teens, up to 24 o’clock. I finally got back to the hotel at 19 o’clock, ate some of the cod, and slept like a baby. What a day.

I understand that, when I am travelling, locals might eat dinner at a different hour than I am used to. Dinner is important to me, but I can eat it at 7:30 instead of 7:00 if that is customary for the people of a particular region.

One time, in Spain, someone said, “Actually dinner here is served starting at 21 at night, also known as 9 P.M.,” and I said, “But that’s bedtime.” Then I thought, “Hold on. Maybe at around 18 o’clock, to tide myself over, I can have some smoked mackerel fillets, and then do a little waiting.” And you know what? That fish kept me sated until the big bedtime cena. (For those of you who haven’t been to Spain, that means “dinner.”) Getting out of my comfort zone is what travel is all about.
Next, I’m off to Florence, Italy. I’ll be heading to some lesser-known spots that Rick Steves highlighted on PBS.

If you live in Florence and spot me striding around in my safety vest, take a second to think, That person must be from the area—look at how confidently they stand. Then come on over anyway, introduce yourself, and invite me to join you for a conversation about local things, in a local place for locals that also has powerful air-conditioning and room for my fish cooler. I look forward to meeting you! ♦

items.title: Itinerary for Your First Couples’ Vacation
items.description: You and the love of your life are planning an international holiday together. It’s special! It’s exciting! You’re calling it a “holiday” because it’s more European that way! This guide will help you make the most of your whirlwind adventure.
items.author: Grace Henes
paragraphs: You and the love of your life are planning an international holiday together. It’s special! It’s exciting! You’re calling it a “holiday” because it’s more European that way! This guide will help you make the most of your whirlwind adventure.

Lie extensively about what you enjoy doing on vacation. Say things like “I just love wandering around and taking it all in,” when the activities you really love are getting drunk in the general vicinity of a body of water and reading bad novels about sexy enemies. Book the cheapest ticket you can find on an airline whose baggage policy seems designed for minimalist schoolchildren. Pack eight times the amount of underwear that you will need and zero shoes with arch support.

Upon arrival, check into the rental home, which will be both smaller and darker than the photos online. The toilet will be separated from the bedroom by a wall the width and consistency of a Communion wafer. Consider how long the human body can go without expelling waste. Gaze out the window and indulge in a brief cinematic fantasy about what it would be like to leave everything behind and move to this city with your partner, immediately triggering your preferred attachment disorder.

After spending five full business days curating a list of restaurants, learn that none of them are restaurants your partner is interested in. Be totally fine with that! Try to find a restaurant you both want to eat at that isn’t too touristy, expensive, loud, or busy, but which also exists. Walk to the restaurant your partner decided on, laughing thirty per cent less than usual at their jokes to punish them. Once you sit down, receive a menu that doesn’t believe in I.B.S. Panic-order a dish with a name that you don’t fully understand. When the food arrives, learn that it is a pig’s trotter. You are both vegetarian—fill up on bread.

Go to a famous, cold museum, full of art that is both pretentious and boring. Lie sophisticatedly about how much the art speaks to you. Stare at a painting of a sad, buxom peasant next to a horse, and think about how you once puked during a screening of “Wreck-It Ralph,” and how this moment is much worse than that. Sit on a bench while your partner painstakingly reads every plaque, resenting their childlike sense of wonder, then quietly devour a granola bar in the bathroom because you are still hungry from not eating your expensive hoof.

Attempt the kind of athletic sex that you imagine people have on vacation (uncomfortable, but visually impressive). Accidentally puncture a hole in the wafer wall. Apologize to each other profusely. Realize that you packed the wrong adapter, and now must jerk each other off manually, like it’s the Middle Ages. Take a cursed nap for five hours and miss the romantic candlelit dinner that you booked two full months in advance. Wake up disoriented and spend your evening watching dubbed reruns of “Boy Meets World” while eating the local equivalent of Cheetos.

Pay more than is reasonable to walk through a building that is old, but doesn’t appear to be doing much else. Stand alone in a room where a child tyrant used to do religious persecution and wonder if you would be less anxious if you lived in ancient times and only had to worry about dying of feudal warfare. Wait on another bench while your partner reads another plaque, and get a slow and painful sunburn that you won’t notice until later because it is overcast and you never learn.

The last day is the perfect time to have your breakdown. Walk to the breakfast place that Instagram told you you must visit if you don’t want to be a fucking loser. It will be closed because it is a public holiday, just like every other day in this country. Burst into tears in front of a gelato stand, then have a long conversation about your parents and why it is their fault that you are not able to hold hands in front of a famous statue. Agree never to visit this city together ever again.

Much like a person’s body will trick them into forgetting the pain of childbirth, amnesia will set in as soon as you arrive back home. Post a story of your amazing, romantic vacation, and patiently wait for your high-school nemesis to watch it while you start preliminary research for your next couples holiday—would it be crazy to go to Paris? ♦

items.title: Never Going to Italy
items.description: One of my lifelong ambitions is never to go to Italy. When I was a boy, in Ohio, my parents urged me to wish for something more realistic, such as never going anywhere in Missouri (several states away). Mom and Dad knew that never going to Italy would be unatt
items.author: Ian Frazier
paragraphs: One of my lifelong ambitions is never to go to Italy. When I was a boy, in Ohio, my parents urged me to wish for something more realistic, such as never going anywhere in Missouri (several states away). Mom and Dad knew that never going to Italy would be unattainable for people like us. But I kept dreaming, as I pored over my lists of places in Italy I dreaded to see, foods I hoped not to eat, and famous cathedrals I did not want to go on tours of. After all, a big part of the fun of never travelling somewhere is in the planning. My folks had the wisdom to allow me that, though they knew the disappointment sure to come.

My own inborn artistic temperament created an additional problem, because I happen to be highly susceptible to the visual arts. Much as I try to scrub my brain of all knowledge of painting and sculpture, I can’t. With great effort, I got rid of every word in the art lover’s vocabulary except for one pesky holdout: “provenance.” Even today, if I find myself at a cocktail party and a particular work of art comes up in conversation, out of my mouth always leaps the question “Yes, but what is its provenance?” As it turns out, “provenance” is the only word you need in order to fall into a bottomless pit of art-related discussion that always seems to lead to Italy (usually by way of Vasari). For me, in this direction lies madness.

I also have a strange and regrettable weakness for inventing catchy acronyms for art museums. Even if I firmly resolve to use a museum’s entire name whenever that museum comes up, my natural bent betrays me. For example, I faithfully try to say “the Museum of Modern Art,” but what I blurt out instead is “MOMA” (an acronym I invented some years ago). Similarly, I always want to refer to the Los Angeles County Museum of Art by its full name, and never say “LACMA,” the popular acronym I came up with (though it is, I admit, much shorter and handier). And not many people know that I’m the person who thought of calling the famous Musée du Louvre, in Paris, “MUDULOU” (pronounced “moo-doo-loo”). In these now widely adopted coinages of mine, I discern a vague, threatening spectre somehow inexorably drawing me toward Italy—and I tremble.

I had a close call the other day. I was on an airplane that was diverted from Heathrow to Italy, because of bad weather. Now, I consider Heathrow my second home. As a citizen of the world (except for Italy), I would have preferred that the flight brave the storm so that I could relax in Heathrow’s Citizens of the World (Except for Italy) V.I.P. Lounge. But the pilot of the plane was the rugged type who looks like a male model and therefore seeks the male model’s natural habitat—i.e., Italy. The plane kept on going, Italy bound, while I sweated in my seat. The dream of a lifetime was about to come to an inglorious end. Then, ten minutes before we entered Italian airspace, the weather over London cleared and the plane turned around. My dream still lived! I began to weep quietly. I told myself, “Hold on to your dreams! You will never go to Italy, if only you believe you won’t!”

This near-Italy experience has only made me more determined. Never going to Italy might take a lot of sloth, but I believe I am up to it. First, I’ll need to be in the very worst physical condition. That way, when someone interrogates me about why I haven’t yet gone to Italy, I’ll answer, “Can’t! Too out of shape!” Second, I’ll have to write a book exposing organized crime in every major Italian city. Then the Italian government will not allow me to cross the border, because of the potential costs of heightened police protection. And, third, I’ll lose my passport! The beauty of that strategy is in its simplicity. I’m surprised I’ve never thought of it before.

I can hear the Italy-goers, in their multitudes, telling me that I’m only cheating myself. But look at it this way: I’m also not carrying around a small flag, leading a tour group into one basilica or another and bumping into you as you try to get a better look at that gorgeous-whatever Vasari. In the busiest Italian places, check out the one less-crowded corner. The person helpfully not standing there is me. ♦

items.title: The Strategist Readers’ Choice Award Winners
items.description: Over the course of a decade, we’ve tried a lot of stuff. Our intrepid team of Strategist staffers has spent years testing, researching, consulting experts, and debating with one another about which products within the vast online-shopping landscape, from mattr
items.author: Kitty Guo
paragraphs: Over the course of a decade, we’ve tried a lot of stuff. Our intrepid team of Strategist staffers has spent years testing, researching, consulting experts, and debating with one another about which products within the vast online-shopping landscape, from mattresses to moisturizers, are actually worth your money. The result is a thoroughly vetted compendium of Best in Class nail clippers and underwear; fugly shoes that are comfortable for miles and miles; and the weirdest, most useful doodads money can buy.

But throughout these ten years, our readers have been buying and trying out things right alongside us, and they’ve got thoughts to share. We asked them to decide which of our already cherry-picked favorites should be crowned the absolute crème de la crème. Back in July, we put out a call for responses to our first Readers’ Choice poll, asking participants to choose their favorite products in 47 categories. Thousands of people cast hundreds of thousands of votes, and after we tallied everything up, the products below emerged as the winners. Below, we present the pick of the litter in dozens of categories, including beauty, fashion, kitchen, travel, and more.

paragraphs: This article was featured in New York’s One Great Story newsletter. Sign up here.

The year is 2016. You just added a copy of The Girl on the Train to your Amazon cart and are now three pages deep in white-ankle-sock reviews, completely paralyzed about which to buy. You finally caved and sprang for Prime, so in a miraculous feat of logistics, it’ll only take about two days to arrive. Everyone’s watching a little telekinetic girl named Eleven on Netflix, the Chainsmokers are playing this weekend, and the city is a sea of wide-leg cropped jeans and Stan Smiths. In this world, the Strategist was born as your everything guide to smartly shopping the internet.

A guide really was essential at this point because for the first time, you could buy a bed in a box — just like that! Delivered to your door. But how would you know if it was any good? Then every brand decided to be a disruptor by turning our eyebrows into Boy Brows and selling white T-shirts at whatever price you chose. Still, you couldn’t see or touch a product until you bought it, so you needed someone to tell you if it was all actually worth it.

We thought, Why not take the obsessiveness and mischievousness at the heart of New York Magazine’s years of service journalism and apply that to the Wild West of online shopping? Why not assign actual serious journalists to find out what’s the status soap of the moment or to test 100 pens? Why not commission our favorite writers to tell us about the “products they would do an unpaid infomercial for, but we’d actually pay you” (which was in the email our editors used to send potential contributors)? The early Strategist was filled with tone poems from Molly Young about the shampoo replacement that changed her life and Stephanie Danler on the wonders of Skin Food. It was the precursor to the Strategist of today in which Mary H.K. Choi writes about her desperate hunt to replace a discontinued eyeliner and a staff of several dozen writers and editors have become characters in our readers’ daily lives.

In 2016, discount shopping was still an in-person sport where people left their Thanksgivings early to score a $200 60-inch flat-screen at Best Buy — even if it meant causing bodily harm to other customers. For the past ten years, we’ve published weekly Friday sales roundups and daily Deals of the Day while Black Friday transformed into a fully virtual Cyber Week, Prime Day evolved into a twice-a-year affair, and every brand seemed to commit to a perpetual online sales bin. Price-tracking tools like CamelCamelCamel have gone from an insider trick of the trade to a mainstream shopping hack. Now everyone is what we’ve always affectionately called a deals freak. To keep up, we’ve gotten even better at our deals scouting, covering dozens of discounted items per day in micro-sales and launching a dedicated daily newsletter with even more.

Today, you can’t click on anything on the internet without hitting an affiliate link. With TikTok Shop, shopping-specific Substacks, hordes of influencers, rabbit-hole Reddit threads, and endless scrolls of Temu and Shein, each time you open your phone, someone is trying to sell you something, and there is more to choose from than ever. And here we are, still recommending you use a yacht step as a step stool.

To celebrate these past ten years, we’ve decided on the top-ten products that have defined the Strategist — our Strategist canon — each one chosen because it represents an important moment for our site but also an important moment in online-shopping history, which for us go hand in hand.
The Japanese nail clipper you suddenly didn’t need to go to Japan to buy

A decade ago, with 1,700 yen to blow at the Narita airport, Jason Chen, the former Strategist deputy editor who became a Wirecutter editor in 2019, picked up a pair of Green Bell nail clippers. “The Green Bell slices through nails like a Santoku through a tomato. Makes sense, given that they were made in Seki, the city famed throughout Japan for creating Samurai swords,” he wrote. “The Japanese clippers, as you’d expect from a country that’s always elevated the mundane with powerful design, have a pleasing frosted-Champagne finish and the serious weight of a small stapler.” What was perhaps less expected was the fact that no flight to Tokyo was required to pick up a pair — they were already available on Amazon. “I was super surprised,” says Chen. “I thought they were a Japan-only thing.”

While that discovery might not seem very exciting now, back then, there was a certain rush to finding international products online for the first time. Items you once had to beg your friend to bring back in their carry-on — French moisturizers, Korean sunscreens, Japanese notebooks — were now available to ship from halfway across the world. Chen also discovered a windproof, lopsided Dutch umbrella in Amsterdam that is almost impossible to blow inside out. Then our global finds kept coming. A nifty collapsible Midori pen, tubes of Biafine and Homeoplasmine and A313, our beloved Hobonichi Techo. That little thrill of discovery was like wandering the aisles of a grocery store or beauty-supply shop abroad, and adding a bottle of Nuxe’s dry oil to your late-night toilet-paper order made you feel like a citizen of the world. It also made all of us realize just how small the world was becoming.

“Ten years later, I’m still a devotee,” adds Chen of his nail clippers. “I have three of them now: one in each bathroom and another for my travel dopp.” Because traveling is still fun (even if you don’t need to schlep souvenirs back anymore). —Dominique Pariso, Strategist senior writer
The YogaToes that really are incredible

There is something truly bizarre, a little unsettling even, about an item ending up on this list because my grandma once had two toes amputated. But sometimes life is just like that. You never really know what’s coming — or what exactly you might need to deal with it — until it’s right in front of you.

That’s how it was with my YogaToes, the squishy, ladderlike toe separators that I’d put on at the end of most days in an effort to avoid bunions (a lifelong fear), hammertoes (the ailment behind those amputations), and really any and all podiatric-related issues. I learned about them from my mom, who, the story goes, had one vice — buying shoes — until she gave it all up for comfort and surgery-free feet. The trait was inherited.

I guess I felt comfortable talking about this in my place of work because the Strategist has always respected — revered, really — the unquantifiable doodad. The little unexpected things that come out of nowhere and change your life. Everyone here realized that a lot of other people are probably suffering through your highly particular neuroses, too. (I’ve since learned Kelly Rowland and Simon Rex also can’t live without toe separators). But it’s not just that. There’s a twofold appeal to reading about a doodad: Half of it is about how you learned of the thing (an opera singer’s neck stretcher, Ike Barinholtz’s instant coffee), and the other half is that it ever existed in the first place (AirPod condoms). It’s the TubShroom, the bendy piece of foam that’s actually the best phone stand, a foot sling for planes, a neck hammock for headaches, a doohickey to get rid of chin hairs, and a different doohickey to get rid of mosquito bites. The site has become a compendium of the most useless useful stuff. The not-too-expensive little things that really are incredible. I mean, how else would you ever know they existed?

It wasn’t about how many hours I tested this little jellyish, aqua-blue toe-stretcher or how many scientific studies proved its worth. It was about how it made me feel — both my toes and my mind. The funny thing is that ten years later, my mom now works at a podiatrist’s office, I left and then returned to the Strategist, and we’ve all still got YogaToes in our nightstand drawers. —Lauren Levy, lead editor
The underwear celebrities would’ve never told us about themselves … until they did

In December 2016, I sent a cold email pitch to a website that had existed for about six weeks. I randomly stumbled across it while frantically shopping for a high-quality pair of nail clippers (the above) and knew I’d met my match. That first pitch had three ideas: socks with deliberate holes in them, the velvet hangers that saved my closet, and the underwear I bought for both myself and the actors I dress as a wardrobe stylist for film and television — Commando’s revolutionary no-seam, no-show, buttery-soft underwear. I’ve been here yapping about the life-changing products I’ve stumbled across ever since.

Launched in 2005, Commando’s signature “no VPL” underpants were the solution to a historically grim situation: For years, the only way to not have your skivvies show under tight-fitting clothes was to submit to the torture of a thong. How do I know this? I was boots on the red carpet, giving actors a choice between butt floss and, well, going commando under a premiere gown.

Seamless undergarments are everywhere now, but something easy to lose sight of in the sea of blatant copies and AI-generated recommendations is that Commando really did invent the category. To quote the brand’s founder, Kerry O’Brien, “When people told me that my vision for my first product, underwear without elastic or trim, wasn’t achievable, I didn’t believe them.”

My seamless-underwear article was only the beginning: The Strategist has since become the internet’s go-to place to talk about your underthings. We’ve run the underwear gamut around here, seeking out the very best all-cotton non-granny panties, workout undies, non-shapewear shapewear, and period underwear. Over the years, it’s even become a safe space for a few brave celebrities to share their undergarments with us — like June Squibb and Joanna Goddard’s favorite Jockeys and Lucas Gage’s beloved J.Crew boxer briefs.

But it’s not just underthings — the Strategist invited in the behind-the-scenes experts no one usually talks to to gab about the stuff nobody ever talks about. Wardrobe stylists like me, makeup artists on their low-key drugstore buys, executive assistants on their bosses’ wildest asks, and retail employees on what’s really going on at Anthropologie. One by one, they’ve shared their particular industry’s most useful tips and tricks, insider information, and secrets you’d otherwise never know.

Ten years on, the Strategist has endured because (yes, I’m waving my Strategist foam finger in the air here) the collected experts, writers, and editors are out here doing the dang work. We wear the underwear, find the right sources, and stick our nose in other people’s business. Here’s to ten more years! —Alison Freer, contributing writer
The fugly shoes we’ve walked 10,000 miles in

Long before there was the “freaky shoe” phenomenon and 10,000-step shoe testing on TikTok, there was what we now refer to as the Strategist Fugly Shoe. The Fugly Shoe is the faccia brutta of footwear — orthopedic-y by design but beautiful in its own way. Beloved not just because it looks cool but because it supports your fallen arches and bad ankles.

The first humble pair to grace the site was Merrell Hambleton’s Charleston Shoe Co. Monterey Sandals. “Walk in them. Run in them. Never take a cab again in them — they really do feel like sneakers. You will get compliments on these shoes, and the compliments will be from well-dressed strangers,” she wrote. Apparently, our readers were sold because the South Carolina–based shop later shared that it made $40,000 selling these grannyish sandals on both the Saturday and Sunday after the article appeared.

“I’ll never forget that morning. We all arrived at work only to discover that our website had crashed from an overwhelming amount of traffic,” says Charleston Shoe Co. founder Neely Woodson Powell. “That turned into the biggest day of online sales we’d ever had at that point in our company’s history. We still talk about it all the time.”

One month after came Stephanie Danler’s Danskos. Danler opened her ode thusly: “Two notes about loving ugly things: (1) What is ugly is usually functional, and function is a virtue. (2) You’ll have to repeat that to yourself often because your prettier, richer, more stylish, less functionally minded friends will never stop ridiculing the ugly objects you cherish most.” Danler bought her first pair of Dansko clogs — technically medical shoes initially worn by nurses and doctors before becoming a fixture in professional kitchens — at 15 for a restaurant job, and by now, even Zendaya owns a pair. When I reached out to see if Danler was still a die-hard fan, she told me, “I am not a fair-weather Dansko wearer. The same thing happened with my Tevas, which I have been wearing since high school in Boulder, Colorado. I wore them through the ugly years. Then they were cool again. My fugly shoes and I will live through another few cycles of that.”

There have been many, many more fugly shoes in the years since: Mary-Kate Olsen’s delicately strappy Tevas, Sandy Liang’s bridal Merrells, the Calzuro clogs favored by Italian surgeons, Arcopedico’s woven sock-shoe beloved by both the super-fashionable Misty White Sidell and Portuguese grandmothers.

“I think Strategist readers are, generally speaking, anti-trend. Part of the ethos is testifying on behalf of a product or object that is not cool, per se, but is exceptional,” Danler says. “It gets you off the hamster wheel of Instagram fashion and into cooler, weirder, more personal territory. I don’t care that all the influencer girls are wearing Havaianas. It’s more like, Have you seen Oofos?” —D.P.
Snail mucin from the Google Doc (you know the one)

Like so many Strategist articles, the original Google Doc was born out of personal obsession — one I really thought only my closest friends would find interesting. At the time, I was going through an especially difficult period with my skin: unrelenting cystic, hormonal acne. So I found myself exploring every fix I could find. I went down a deep skin-care rabbit hole and, in the process, became a serious fan of K-beauty. At that time, 2016, the category was really only known among hardcore skin-care and beauty obsessives.

I don’t remember exactly how I discovered CosRx Snail Mucin, though I suspect I found it at my favorite beauty store, Senti Senti in Chinatown. What I do remember is being immediately struck by how beautiful the formula was. It was the first product I’d ever used that seemed to address the many contradictory demands of my finicky, dry, acne-prone skin. I honestly couldn’t tell you how many bottles of snail mucin I’ve gone through over the years.

I compiled everything into what eventually became a master Google Doc of the 16 products that improved my acne — obviously including the snail mucin — and passed it around to my friends simply because it was easier to have it in one place, rather than explaining the whole process over and over.

Somehow, the doc made its way to Katy Schneider, who’s still an editor at New York Magazine (I love you, Katy!), and she asked if I would be interested in adapting it for publication on the Strategist.

It felt truly insane to have something I made out of pure, genuine curiosity and obsession be taken seriously by someone else. The first time someone came up to me to say they’d loved the article, I was standing outside the restaurant Lovely Day on Elizabeth and Spring. I could hardly believe it. People still bring it up to me, and it never stops feeling both surreal and very touching.

Before I started writing for the Strategist, I knew how much I loved skin care, but my experience here showed me just how rewarding it was to help people navigate beauty and, more important, make them feel seen and understood. Having struggled with acne for most of my life, I understood firsthand how overwhelming it could be. I wanted to be the person who could make that experience feel a little less daunting and maybe even a little less lonely.

I’m not exaggerating when I say that one article kind of dictated the course of my career. In the nineish years since, I’ve become a licensed esthetician and started working one-on-one with clients through my skin-care consultation practice. I’ve published a book, Let’s Face It: Secrets of a Skincare Obsessive, and I’ve also had the privilege of consulting with brands on product development and storytelling.
None of this would have been possible without the Strategist taking a chance on a random skin-care-stuffed Google Doc. How has it been ten years? —Rio Viera-Newton, contributing writer
The Amazon coat that took over the Upper East Side — and then the world

In the winter of 2018, every woman on the Upper East Side started wearing an unassuming olive-green coat. It was cheap, made by an unknown Chinese brand called Orolay, and, by March of that year, installed in online-shopping history as “the Amazon Coat” (you can read the full oral history, too).

Like all great legends, its origin is shrouded in mystery. No one knows exactly who bought the first Orolay coat, but by the time it caught the attention of Schneider, then the Strategist’s associate editor, it was all over town. “The coat’s appeal lies in its fashionable-yet-accessible, lightly directional look … and its startling price — the super-stylish women who own it take pleasure in telling curious onlookers that no, their jacket is not Sacai, and, actually, it costs under $100, including shipping if you’re an Amazon Prime member,” wrote Schneider. It had spread the old-fashioned way — by word of mouth among sharply dressed uptown women who saw their friend wearing it, then bought one, then told their friend, who bought one, too, and so on and so on, until uptown sidewalks were a sea of Army green.

Once we published our story, the coat went from an if-you-know-you-know status symbol to a now-everyone-knows viral item. It broke containment from the Upper East Side, to the point that you couldn’t walk down the street or take the subway anywhere without seeing one. Nowadays, products go viral all the time — all it really takes is a single TikTok video or trend piece to catch on before everyone is suddenly wearing the same thing — but at the time, the Amazon Coat was one of the first. Thousands of people bought it, it was covered by countless publications, and it even inspired its own very popular Instagram account.

Of course, the life cycle of any viral product ends the same way: Once everyone has it, no one really wants it anymore. And while the Amazon coat is mostly relegated to the back of people’s closets now, you still see the odd one in the wild every winter. It really is quite warm. —D.P.
The rise and fall of a status plant

“The fiddle-leaf fig has taken us all on a wild ride,” wrote former Strategist staffer (and plant dad) David Notis, despite it being “like the avocado toast of house plants.” He went on to chart its rise: “It went from West Elm catalogue cameos, to boutique-y plant shops like the Sill, to basically being sold out everywhere (even though you could maybe still find one in a matte-white ceramic pot if you were willing to pay $250).”

This ficus became a calling card of the millennial aesthetic, but there were other signifiers: Casper mattresses, Everlane alpaca crew sweaters, terrazzo planters, boob bath mats, Outdoor Voices cloud pants, Veja sneakers, pink velvet chairs with brass legs, Areaware, Coming Soon, Glossier Boy Brow, Boy Smells candles. Bold Helvetica. In the mid-to-late 2010s, this collection of things became the entire cultural moment, the personality of millions. It was an era as much defined by the direct-to-consumer brands that promised to change the world (or at least offer it transparent pricing) as by any actual taste, but we were there to tell you which pair of Everlane high-waisted pants were worth it and which Baggu bag would make the best gift.

After buying his first fiddle-leaf fig, “I was mostly just curious if it would actually work on a logistical level — like if I press this button, is Amazon really going to deliver a plant in a box to my apartment? Really?” says Notis. “Sitting here in 2026, it’s interesting to think about how surreal it felt at the time and how normal it feels now.”

So much else has changed too. Now, Glossier is sold at Sephora, Allbirds has pivoted to AI, and who knows what’s going on with Everlane after selling its soul to Shein. The death of DTC, like the death of millennial optimism, was probably inevitable, propped up by venture capital and cheap advertising that eventually ran dry. But our fiddle-leaf figs, carefully tended over the years, continue to reach toward the light. —D.P.
Amy Sedaris’s pink paper towels

Amy Sedaris’s Greenwich Village apartment is the stuff of legends. When we visited back in 2019, it was packed to the gills with all manner of stuff, including two boxes of googly eyes (“one fancy, one not”), 13 bottles of Comme des Garçons’ Avignon perfume (“just in case they ever stop making it”), and Il Bisonte leather wallets (“my go-to gift for straight and gay guys”), along with 47 other treasures we catalogued — all of which were carefully and relentlessly collected with Sedaris’s extremely keen eye.

In many ways, Sedaris is a bit like the Strategist’s fairy godmother. “Since we launched the Strategist, Amy Sedaris has always been one of our North Stars in terms of someone who embodies the obsessiveness, sense of humor, and exquisite taste that we’re always striving for,” wrote New York Magazine deputy editor Alexis Swerdloff. While we’ve interviewed plenty of celebrities, New York legends, and cool people over the years, none have been baked into the blueprint of the site quite like Amy. During the 2023 holiday season, she graced the site as our deputized gift columnist, counseling somebody to give their wicked stepmother a mushroom-growing log. The following year, she provided another 104 inspired ideas, and her semiannual guest spot has become our favorite Yuletide tradition. So to represent her status as the Strategist’s patron saint, we are including her favorite fuchsia paper towels. Because while everyday life demands buying necessities — even in an apartment as fantastical as Sedaris’s, the kitchen counters still need wiping down — those essentials need not be boring.

When we reached out to Sedaris to revisit the pink paper towels, this is what she had to say: “My brother David turned me on to these Renova paper towels. He would buy them in England at Waitrose grocery store and, like a mule, bring them back to me. They make a terrific gift.” She is the expert, after all. —D.P.
The card game that taught us how to play together again

Being a shopping editor in 2020 would not get your name on any essential-workers lists. But writing about internet shopping when internet shopping was suddenly the only kind of safe shopping a person could do did make it feel a lot more urgent. Thus began the Strategist’s Great Pandemic Pivot.

First, we explained the difference between an N95 and a KN95, tested close to a hundred fabric face masks, and figured out the best masks for kids. Then, as Amazon and other retailers failed to keep up with the demands of the housebound hordes, we tracked down in-stock toilet paper from unlikely sources and found impossible-to-find essentials such as diapers, hand sanitizer, and pet supplies. After that, we directed our efforts toward things that weren’t exactly essential but helped pass the time, including flour for fledging sourdough starters, ankle weights, puzzles, bikes, and, for one memorable summer, inflatable backyard pools and roller skates. We wrote guides on how to do things for ourselves: install a window air conditioner, cut hair, tint brows, groom your dog, groom your husband, do an at-home eye exam, self-monitor a pregnancy, wax, give a tattoo, give a manicure, remove a manicure, and grow a coronavirus victory garden. We asked event planners how to throw weddings and bar mitzvahs and board-game nights and Mother’s Day brunches over Zoom. We figured out how to work out at home and how to work from home, how to protest safely, how to bundle up in unheated dining sheds, where to buy heated furniture for midwinter social-distanced hangs. Our readers bought fancy canned fish and mask chains and comfortable pull-on pants and board games — so many board games.

Even when we started to inch our way back into civilization from our carefully tended quarantine dens, some pandemic habits came with us. When we published this ode to a “divisive (but delightful)” little card game called Dutch Blitz one month before the World Health Organization declared the official end of the COVID-19 global health emergency, it became an immediate reader favorite. “This card game threatens to tear my family apart — but we can’t stop playing it,” warned contributor Laura Guidry. “I’ve brought it to bars and on hikes. I’ve ordered packs to give to friends going through tough times that involve waiting. I’ll persuade my husband to play a few hands between meetings as we both work from home and are slugging through the day.” After years of carefully skirting around each other at a respectable six feet of distance, maybe a competitive hand of cards was exactly what we all needed: a reason to gather, to play, to get up in each other’s faces, if just to shout “Blitz!” —D.P.
The maybe placebo — but also maybe not — spritz putting us all to sleep

I’ve long gone through periods of nervousness about sleeping, knowing there may be hours when I can’t switch off my brain. And then, once I’m worried, it becomes even harder to fall asleep. My mind scampers along to every possible corner to find fuel for that anxiety.

But I don’t like taking pills to fix the problem. My trick, instead, is creating a nightly routine that signals my mind and body to settle down. Salt Lab Magnesium Oil spray became that ritual for me. Two to four spritzes on the soles of my feet had me asleep within 20 minutes — and staying that way. It really worked. To be sure, I used the spray for a full year before I wrote about it.

When my ode to Salt Lab went live, the reaction was immediate. Everyone, it seems, is struggling to get those precious eight hours, and our readers have bought almost 15,000 sprays in the year since. The story’s comments section sparked a sleep-remedy exchange: CBD gummies, magnesium creams, and supplement powders popped up. And all the sharing reminded me of how I’d spritz the feet of my houseguests with Salt Lab so they, too, could sleep like babies.

Because going without sleep is such a life-disrupting cycle, when you find something that works, it feels like a miracle tale you must spread. You become a proselytizer. But there are also a lot of sleep scams out there (as the other half of the Salt Lab commenters forcefully reminded me), and for years, the Strategist has been doing the legwork to weed those out. It’s been a decadelong effort to find what actually works — not just the sleep tinctures, supplements, sprays, and creams but your entire sleep habitat. We’ve slept on dozens of mattresses and pillows, swaddled ourselves in every possible variation of bedsheet (one of the very first categories we devoted ourselves to), tested out silk sleep masks and weighted sleep masks, and put sound machines head-to-head. We’ve found ever-stranger sleep solutions, including water-powered cooling pads for sweaty sleepers, an upright wedge pillow for snorers, and a nifty chin strap for nighttime mouth breathers in an effort to leave no sleep hack behind. And before there was my magnesium spray, there was a better-than-Ambien lavender stick and CBD tinctures. As you read this, the Strategist is investigating whether red light really works for sleep. The quest is eternal. —D.P. and Diksha Basu, contributing writer

items.title: 10 What I Can’t Live Withouts That Defined Celebrity Shopping
items.description: Our “What I Can’t Live Without” series started with a simple question: What are the everyday things that celebrities actually use and like? Not the red-carpet diamonds or the $6,000 cashmere throw blanket, but the mouthwashes, the ankle socks, the personal fan
items.author: Ambar Pardilla
paragraphs: Our “What I Can’t Live Without” series started with a simple question: What are the everyday things that celebrities actually use and like? Not the red-carpet diamonds or the $6,000 cashmere throw blanket, but the mouthwashes, the ankle socks, the personal fans. In 2016, Common’s answer was Frank Ocean’s album Blonde, Billy Crudup’s was a Hammacher Schlemmer sound machine, and Rachel Antonoff’s was Blistex Lip Medex. Getting celebrities to respond wasn’t easy initially. “It was just us trying to convince people to do it in the beginning,” says New York deputy editor Alexis Swerdloff. But some, like Antonoff, were early gets. (“I don’t remember exactly how it was sold to me, but I love a recommendation,” says Antonoff. “I have this interior Rolodex of like, No, this is the best detergent.”)

In the ten years since, we’ve interviewed hundreds of celebrities and notable people, from New York City mayoral candidates and the stars of the Real Housewives to Amy Sedaris and Jennifer Aniston. And the column has grown into one of our flagship series (and led to offshoots like “What I Can’t Cook Without” and “What My Kids Can’t Live Without”). Now, we’re looking back at ten of the most memorable “What I Can’t Live Without” columns by returning to the celebrities and writers who interviewed them.
André Leon Talley, the unexpected UGG wearer

Longtime contributing Vogue editor André Leon Talley, who died in 2022, was known for his high-end taste — he collected monogrammed Louis Vuitton suitcases and Limoges luncheon plates with drawings by Jean Cocteau — but his 2016 “What I Can’t Live Without,” the first in the series, was less the stuff of a Christie’s auction, and decidedly more down to earth. “He’s one of the most glamorous people in the world, and he’s talking about UGGs,” says Swerdloff of his list, which also included cleaning supplies and an electric toothbrush. It was that toothbrush that inspired the text that for years ran at the beginning of every column: If you’re like us, you’ve probably wondered what famous people add to their carts. Not the JAR brooch and Louis XV chair, but the hand sanitizer and the electric toothbrush.

New! You can now save this product for later.
How Aubrey Plaza became our personal “deodorant guru”

If it wasn’t for Aubrey Plaza, we might not know about Real Purity’s natural deodorant. It turns out that Plaza, whose list was published in 2017, heard about it from Judy Greer, who later included it in her “What I Can’t Live Without” in 2022. “I do everything Judy Greer tells me to do,” said Plaza at the time. Strategist editors followed suit: Swerdloff and Strategist deputy editor Simone Kitchens both still use the deodorant. Several other items from Plaza’s list have become Strategist canon, too: Writer Kitty Guo credits the Oribe Dry Texturizing Spray with saving her bad haircut, alongside Lucas Papaw “miracle ointment,” which has appeared in Dido’s, Erin Wasson’s, Selma Blair’s, and Alison Brie’s “What I Can’t Live Withouts” since.
Fifteen minutes with Debi Mazar turned into two hours

Often, we only get a short amount of time to chat with celebrities about their items — but sometimes they can’t help but gab. What was meant to be a tightly scheduled 15-minute phone call between Debi Mazar and former writer Chloe Anello lasted more than two hours. “She knew who she was. She knew what she liked,” Anello says. “As we were talking about one thing, it reminded her of something else that she loved.” When Anello got off the phone, she had about 60-something items, 50 of which we ran in one of our longer columns in the series.

“I’m a person who tries things for people and gives my opinions. I’ve been given a lot of free stuff because of my job. They let me take home things that I discover on the set. I’m always flying through an airport and I’m like, Oh, what’s this?” says Mazar. When the list was published, “Everyone called me, like, ‘Oh, my God. I love this list. I am so ordering that.’” Five years later, she still wears Chanel No. 5 and agua de violetas, washes her dishes with Palmolive, and drinks Café Bustelo.
It turns out Jason Schwartzman is our biggest (celebrity) fan

“I love the Strategist; I need the Strategist. So many of the things in my life I’ve gotten from the Strategist,” Jason Schwartzman told New York on a red carpet at Sundance in 2024. Months later, senior writer Lauren Ro met with him for his “What I Can’t Live Without” interview. Schwartzman showed Ro the phone case he got for his wife after reading Amelia Meath’s “What I Can’t Live Without” and a Pilot Varsity fountain pen he bought after reading Ottessa Moshfegh’s. The interview went on for nearly three hours over the course of two days, and the post became our most-viewed “What I Can’t Live Without” in 2024. Maybe it was thanks to his enthusiasm: for an airbrush he discovered on the set of Fargo, a light meter that was part of his research for Asteroid City, and Boggle Sit & Solve puzzles. “He’s somebody that loves to learn. You can just see that in the way that he has chosen the items and how he talks about them and how he has thought about using them,” says Ro.
New! You can now save this product for later.
People tell Ottessa Moshfegh they have the same pajamas regularly

When we talked to the My Year of Rest and Relaxation author in 2022, she was newly “pajamas obsessed” and sleeping in J.Crew’s End-on-End Cotton Long-Sleeved Pajama Set, a recent acquisition at the time. Moshfegh was wearing the very same pajamas when we called recently: “I didn’t sleep, therefore didn’t sleep in [them], but have been in my pajamas since last night and have not changed because I’m hopeful to sleep more,” she told us. It was the pair that she bought the same year as the interview, and even now, four years later, she still hears from people about them. “I would say every six months or so, somebody tells me that they wear the same pajamas as me,” says Moshfegh.
Samantha Irby: “You need to know what the real shitters use.”

Similar to Debi Mazar’s multi-hour interview, Samantha Irby’s went from a quick hit to a two-hour call. In the first 40 minutes, she chatted about everything from scam texts to The Real Housewives of Miami. Then she got down to her stuff: There was her Owala (which later led to our investigation into the new status water bottle), the oregano oil a hippie recommended to her at a co-op, and the Lectrofan sound machine she credits with keeping her “marriage intact.” When we spoke to Irby again recently, she told us that she still reads the column and bought the incense Katie Crutchfield of Waxahatchee burns. “In the way that I’m curious about people, I assume people would be curious about me,” she says. “What does a person who has diarrhea all the time wipe their ass with? You need to know what the real shitters use.” (Charmin UltraStrong rolls, in Irby’s case.)
John Derian (still) uses nearly everything on his list

We’ve regularly talked to people with particular, exacting, and exceptional taste over the years — and there might be no better example than designer John Derian. He’s consistent, too: We interviewed Derian in 2017 and again in 2023 and learned that he still used every single thing on his original list, including the Zig Memory System Calligraphy Dual Tip Marker and Tom’s of Maine Unscented Deodorant. “I think probably the first time I was just sort of like, I’m so basic,” jokes Derian. Basic or not, it turns out that he’s in good company with his recommendations: Danny Meyer also seasons with Maldon sea-salt flakes; Ana Gastayer wears the same deodorant brand, Schmidt’s; and Kiehl’s Ultra Facial Moisturizer SPF 30 protects Chloe Bailey in the Caribbean sun.

Sally Jessy Raphael hasn’t read your comments

No “What I Can’t Live Without” has the number of comments that 91-year-old former talk-show host Sally Jessy Raphael’s 2025 column does: 112, as of the publication of this article. (That’s even more than the 87 left for Ballerina Farm’s Hannah Neeleman and Diane von Furstenberg’s 71.) As one reader wrote, “This is the apotheosis of the ‘Can’t Live Without’ column.” Others loved her Coke Zero Cherry and Sharpie markers. Not that Raphael is reading the comments: “I don’t ever look and see what anyone thinks. I never watch a show I’ve done. People say, ‘Well, haven’t you seen any movie you’ve been in?’ The answer is no,” says Raphael.
“I think Lena Dunham always knows what the hook is.”

When we talked to Lena Dunham in 2017 for the column, she had just wrapped Girls. Nine years later, as Dunham’s memoir Famesick was about to come out, we checked back in to hear about her eBay and Etsy search terms — which we ran in our Secret Strategist newsletter — and her latest batch of things she can’t live without. Her updated list included the Ozlo Sleepbuds she learned about from Susan Orlean’s “What I Can’t Live Without” (both go to bed listening to true-crime podcasts) and Four Thousand Weeks by Oliver Burkeman for “making choices about what’s important to you.” Readers took Dunham’s recommendations seriously; they were among the most-purchased items on the site this April. “I think Lena Dunham always knows what the hook is,” says Erin Schwartz, who spoke with Dunham over email, phone, and text. “Like the thing about all of her animals wanting to sit on the crystal infrared mat, I thought it was just such an indelible image of this sort of woo-woo mat and the rabbits flustered on it.”

We saw Tracee Ellis Ross’s “What I Can’t Live Without” onstage

“She really in so many ways, was humbly showing off that she has been on the forefront of a trend, with the Free City T-shirts being on Girlfriends and wearing Ruby Woo, for so long,” says senior writer Liza Corsillo of her call with Tracee Ellis Ross for the actress’s 2026 “What I Can’t Live Without.” Not long after, Corsillo got tickets to Tracee Ellis Ross’s Broadway show Every Brilliant Thing and she recognized Ross wearing a few things from her list, like the Levi’s 1950’s 701 jeans and Asics they talked about. Ross also told us she carried Alex Mill’s Perfect Weekend Tote (monogrammed with her initials, TER) to and from the theater as well. “It makes her feel like she’s part of the Strat family,” says Corsillo. (It was featured on the site as the perfect mom bag in 2025.)

items.title: Kara Swisher Says Elon Musk’s Jail Threat Is ‘Toddler Behavior’
items.description: Elon Musk is having quite a month. In addition to being the subject of a “terrifying” new documentary, debuting a new flying car that may not actually be a flying car, and announcing that he is considering a megamerger of Tesla and SpaceX into a rocket-ship/ca
items.author: Intelligencer Staff
paragraphs: Elon Musk is having quite a month. In addition to being the subject of a “terrifying” new documentary, debuting a new flying car that may not actually be a flying car, and announcing that he is considering a megamerger of Tesla and SpaceX into a rocket-ship/car/robot/social-media/payments/satellite-internet/AI/data-center behemoth, he’s once again become a main character in multiple simultaneous scandals. Musk reportedly made the decision to abruptly throttle Ukraine’s access to SpaceX Starshield, severely limiting the country’s combat operations and ability to defend itself against Russia. That has become a full-blown international incident, prompting so much backlash that Musk and President Trump are each blaming the other for the move. In addition, the world’s richest man (Musk) has publicly attacked India’s richest man (Mukesh Ambani), alleging that the latter is blocking Starlink’s growth in the country. And Musk has now sunk more than $445 million into backing Republican candidates ahead of what may be a disastrous midterm election. Per usual, Musk is lashing out and tweeting through the turmoil. That includes attacking journalist and longtime Musk critic Kara Swisher, threatening her with jail time after she pointed out that he will likely face a reckoning when Democrats are back in power. Here’s her response in the latest episode of Pivot with co-host Scott Galloway.

Kara Swisher: Guess what? Elon Musk is pissed at me again. I said on the Bulwark podcast that Elon might need to be worried if the GOP loses the House and the Senate, and he tweeted, “Live by the sword, die by the sword. It sounds like Kara Swisher really wants to go to prison.” I really don’t.
Scott Galloway: Does this stuff bother you, or do you enjoy the attention?

Swisher: No, none of it. I think it’s toddler behavior. It’s kind of ridiculous. He threatened Congress, I think, too. And oddly enough, you were meaner to him this week on our clip. And of course he comes after me.

Galloway: Yeah, but I’m not important enough. It’s like when Trump goes after Jess Tarlov or Musk goes after you; I’m still waiting for my global important person to come after me. How come you and Jess get all the hate?

Swisher: I don’t know. Jessica’s the same way, and Kaitlan Collins. What happened was I gave an interview to Catherine Rampell at the Rampart and I talked to congresspeople and heard they were coming after Elon and it’s called reporting. And I said, in a Kamala Harris administration, all those investigations, there were several criminal things attached to them. So he could have gone to prison, but he got rid of them. I was making a point that he got rid of all the investigations either through his relationship with Trump or through DOGE. And now they’re going to come back. And I said, “And you’re going to see a lot of congressional people saying so.” And they did. The next day, all of them went on the record, not just Elizabeth Warren, but even a Republican was saying, “We need to investigate this Ukraine thing.”

And so I was just pointing out the dead fucking obvious of what’s going to happen if — she was asking me why he was throwing so much money at the midterms. I think it’s $400 million at this point. And I said it’s not because he believes in Trump; he believes in himself and he’s trying to save his own skin. Anyway, he for some reason lost his mind. And by the way, this is something Elon said to Tucker Carlson and his mother said “Don’t joke about it” recently. So it’s not something that he said the word “prison,” but then he just said this thing, “live by the sword, die by the sword.”

I don’t know who he’s talking about, and that I want to go to prison, which is like — I don’t mind being in a prison movie and acting in it. And if the ladies from Hunting Wives were in there, I probably wouldn’t mind prison, but I don’t know. Jess wrote me too. And I was on Kaitlan’s show last night and all of us just get relentless hate by all these really troubled men. And in the case of Jess and Kaitlan, it’s Trump. In the case of me, it’s Elon.

Galloway: Yeah. You get to say what you want. He gets to say what he wants. The difference is when you’re the president of the United States or the wealthiest man in the world and you have this cultlike following, I think you need to be a little bit more mindful of the potential knock-on effects of if you have a couple hundred million people that follow you religiously and have bought into yourself, proclaimed views of yourself as a Jesus-like figure, you have to recognize that there’s a nonzero probability that saying something like that about someone else might result in physical harm to them or their family.

And so you’d like to think that these individuals are a little bit more measured and realize that as you get more powerful, you are going to be subject to more attacks, some fair, some unfair. And I’m not saying your or Jess’s attacks against Musk or the president have been unfair. I don’t think they have been. This is the world we live in now where individuals say an autocrat thinks the following. If I go after these people and exert my power, I will silence my critics. And if you want to see a chorus, he’s about to find out what a real Kara Swisher criticism is on November 4 if the Democrats take the House and the Senate.

The fact that this individual is making geopolitical decisions around the fate of the West on a whim, and he’s blaming the president, the president’s blaming him, you don’t think every — right now, no [Republicans in Congress] want to raise their head above the parapet and piss him off because he might dump $200 million into their competitor’s campaign. On November 4, you are going to see the mother of all subpoenas and requests for him to come testify before Congress.

Swisher: They’ve already said it. They’ve already said save your communications about this Ukraine thing. I think it was a final straw for a lot of people, although it shouldn’t have been the final straw. I mean, DOGE should have been the final straw.

And he’s done this before. He said my heart was seething with hate or filled with hate. I got a few really strange phone calls. I wouldn’t call them death threats. They were not nice. They were not nice. And of course over on Twitter, all the VC stans of his are just losing their minds because they’re just suck-ups and acolytes in a way that’s really unattractive. And it’s just nuts. If you can’t stand the heat, Elon, get the fuck out of the kitchen. I don’t know what else to say.
