items.title: Pierpaolo Piccioli on His Vision for Balenciaga & the Power of Starting Over
items.description: It takes less than a minute for Pierpaolo Piccioli to steer a conversation about fashion into one about philosophy. More than a year into his tenure as creative director of Balenciaga, during an interview on the day after he showed his first couture collection
items.author: Eric Wilson
paragraphs: It takes less than a minute for Pierpaolo Piccioli to steer a conversation about fashion into one about philosophy. More than a year into his tenure as creative director of Balenciaga, during an interview on the day after he showed his first couture collection for the house in July, Piccioli explains how he has navigated a role that is both familiar and foreign to him by first quoting Friedrich Nietzsche and the concept of oblivion—oblio in Piccioli’s native Italian.

“Oblio is a moment when you are aware of your past, but you kind of forget everything for a moment and you see everything with new eyes,” says Piccioli, seated at a large conference table in his office suite on Avenue George V, in Paris. “And that’s what actually happened to me.”

For most of his career, over a quarter century, Piccioli was associated with one designer: Valentino Garavani, who made a lasting impression on his life and his eye. Starting in 1999, Piccioli, then in his early 30s, and his longtime collaborator, Maria Grazia Chiuri, rose through the ranks at Valentino, becoming co–creative directors in 2008, a year after Valentino announced his retirement. Then Piccioli led the Roman house solo from 2016 to 2024, while Chiuri served as creative director at Dior. He knew the seamstresses by their names, their skills, their peculiarities, and their very Italian way of working, and he adopted the rhythms and rituals, if not the formality, of Valentino himself. This would have been a lot to leave behind for a designer taking on the mantle of another legendary brand—let alone that of Cristóbal Balenciaga. That house’s own rich history includes two wildly successful modern interpretations, first under Nicolas Ghesquière, then under the now mononymous Demna. But in the words of Nietzsche, “Man will desire oblivion rather than not desire at all.” “I didn’t want to come here to find the same people with the same experiences,” Piccioli says. “I wanted to face something new.”

At his couture show the day before, under the blazing sun in a garden on the outskirts of Paris, Piccioli showed 52 looks that were captivating in their strange beauty. Some of them were outrageously glamorous in the bold style that Piccioli had once championed at Valentino: He opened with a cloud-shaped jacket trimmed with a flock of intense red feathers, worn over a white oversize silk duchesse satin T-shirt and voluminous beige trousers; another look consisted of a dark red shirt styled with big pink pants. But many others represented new territory for the designer, like a floor-length coat the color of a yellow highlighter, which he showed backward, slung over matching pants. There was a fluorescent pink silk “balloon bolero” dress trimmed with feathers made of tiny strips of curled organza. The designs seemed to demand close inspection to be fully understood.

“It felt like a real celebration of artistry,” said the actor Lily Collins, who has known Piccioli for more than a decade, since they first attended a Met Gala together. “Pierpaolo and Balenciaga are the perfect mix.” Naomi Watts headed backstage, where she raved about a tailored black dress adorned with a white ribbon scarf. “That’s the sort of dress I look forward to wearing in my 50s, 60s, 70s, and then some,” she said. Demi Moore, who wore a Piccioli-designed Balenciaga couture ensemble at Cannes in May, circled the boards showing photographs of the models in each of their looks, while Hudson Williams, who appeared in one of Piccioli’s first Balenciaga advertising campaigns, stood nearby, waiting to offer his congratulations.

“This collection is the result of a feeling,” Piccioli wrote in a printed program composed of 20 narrowly spaced pages, including detailed descriptions of all the looks, along with the names of the members of his atelier who helped realize them—Victor, Thomas, Léa, Margherite, etc. “We worked while getting to know each other, learning to understand one another,” Piccioli wrote. It was part of his broad effort to humanize the couture-making experience, which can feel cold and anonymous to anyone living outside that bubble.

The week before the show, Balenciaga wiped its social media history and then posted portraits of some 40 members of its atelier, all dressed in their white Balenciaga Couture work coats. Many of them appeared to be quite young, though a few were established hands and familiar faces, including Bruno Sialelli, formerly the creative director at Lanvin. Philip Treacy, the milliner, was also credited in the couture program for contributions that included a pink ostrich-feather headpiece that spiraled from the crown and around the torso, turning the model who wore it into a swan.

This meeting of minds, among Piccioli, his seasoned collaborators, and his younger team, has become as much a part of his vision for Balenciaga as the clothes seen on his runway. “When you don’t know the rules, you are more open to experiment,” he says. “And that is the key for me to interpret Balenciaga. I didn’t want to go back to any of the old shapes but to try to invent a new shape that could have been that of Cristóbal.”

The day after the show, the couture salon is packed with visitors examining the looks. Patti Wilson, the stylist, has been there for more than an hour. Amal Clooney is spotted among the mannequins. When he arrives, Piccioli, who is 59, is dressed in his usual uniform of a black T-shirt and trousers, with a necklace of coral amulets worn as protection from bad energy. He has a pack of cigarettes in hand and is still very much the picture of a Roman designer who cooks his own pasta most nights, now at his new home just across the Seine. “I’ve got my Roman ways in Paris,” he says. “It’s a sort of effortless approach that is maybe less formal than expected, more direct and more human.”

On his first day at Balenciaga last year, Piccioli traveled to Getaria, the tiny fishing village in the Basque region of Spain where Cristóbal Balenciaga was born in 1895, and where a museum dedicated to the master’s work today offers access to an enormous array of designs collected by his staff and clients. As Piccioli immersed himself in Balenciaga’s world, he began to understand that designs he had perceived through images as austere or strictly linear were, in fact, quite light. That would be his starting point for Balenciaga couture. “In every one of his silhouettes, the body was the protagonist,” he said.

To achieve similar results in new ways became an obsession for Piccioli, and this is where having a younger atelier was an advantage—the team was willing to experiment with techniques that break with the strict traditions of couture. Perhaps the biggest change was replacing standard Stockman mannequins with custom forms created from 3D scans of models’ bodies. Those ghostly plastic forms were used to shape fabrics through a complex process of layering cashmere upon leather that had been washed, stretched, and allowed to dry in place to hold its shape. Each mold took as long as a month to create, but eliminated the need for darts or seams. Piccioli also wanted to play with new fabrics and materials, using a lab-grown silk called AMSilk that purports to be fossil fuel–free and stronger than steel.

Despite these technical innovations, Piccioli believes in the classic model of couture as the pinnacle of fashion. “When you talk about couture, you talk about an approach in which there are no maps. A 3D conversation with the body can then apply to denim, T-shirts, and tailored jackets from prêt-à-porter. To me, a T-shirt has to be a T-shirt, as much as a pair of jeans has to be a pair of jeans. But if you meld couture and industrialization, you can make a more modern garment.”

Like most designers of his generation, Piccioli was raised to worship at the altar of the great Cristóbal Balenciaga, who worked in Paris from 1937 until his retirement, in 1968. The first image Piccioli posted on his personal Instagram account, in 2018, was of a 1967 Balenciaga wedding ensemble that had been included in the Metropolitan Museum of Art’s Costume Institute exhibition “Heavenly Bodies” that year. “Simplicity is a solved complexity,” Piccioli wrote in his caption, paraphrasing the sculptor Constantin Brâncusi. It did not escape Piccioli’s attention that the wedding dress had been designed by Balenciaga the same year Piccioli was born. And although his reverence for Balenciaga is rooted in the maestro’s innovations, Piccioli made clear upon his arrival at the house that he respected the label’s more recent history as a modern luxury brand as well. Balenciaga is now a commercial behemoth that has been redefined by other famous designers. Ghesquière gave Balenciaga heat in the new millennium; Demna brought the house to the street over the past decade, and his flair for disruption ultimately drove Balenciaga well past $1 billion in sales. Both are difficult acts to follow.

With his initial ready-to-wear shows, Piccioli laid some of the groundwork. His spring 2026 collection was based on Balenciaga’s 1957 sack dress, which had a lightweight and unrestrictive shape that was revolutionary at the time; the following season was an ode to “finding lightness in the dark,” as illustrated by inky black skirts and coats, a few pieces rendered with imagery from Sam Levinson’s Euphoria. Piccioli also alluded to his personal love of sports with a techwear-meets-couture pre-fall collection, and with the introduction of a collaboration with the NBA in January that included four-figure varsity jackets, as well as hoodies and sweatpants that would not have looked out of place in the luxury streetwear oeuvre of his predecessor.

As Piccioli steers the future of Balenciaga while learning to embrace his own, he is facing change on a personal level. Valentino Garavani, to whom Piccioli remained close long after his retirement, died in January at the age of 93. Piccioli’s former design partner, Chiuri, has since left Dior and returned to Rome, where she made her couture debut for Fendi the same week Piccioli was presenting his for Balenciaga. His children, Benedetta, Pietro, and Stella, are all now adults and starting their own lives. Just as before, he returns to Italy to spend his holidays with his wife, Simona, and their family at their seaside home in the small beach town of Nettuno, near Rome, but their days there are more limited than they were before.

In Piccioli’s loose interpretation of Nietzsche, a designer might be able to forget his history out of necessity for a moment, but the past remains around him all the same. Acknowledging as much, Piccioli has kept the office he inherited mostly untouched. Its decor is aggressively gray, just as Demna left it last year when he was tasked with righting the ship at Gucci, which, like Balenciaga, is owned by the luxury goods conglomerate Kering. Piccioli layered some brightly colored rugs on the floor and retrieved from his own storage a three-person desk designed by Gio Ponti. Against the far wall is a billboard-size poster of a famous photograph of the same Balenciaga 1967 wedding ensemble Piccioli posted on Instagram, which shows the dress in such stark black and white contrast that its sharp silhouette forms an almost perfect triangle. Leaned against the photo is a bright pink surfboard designed by Piccioli for Zara’s 50th anniversary last year.

“I’ve added some elements and taken out others, but this is kind of metaphorical of what I’m doing here at Balenciaga,” Piccioli says of the office. “They are contradictory in the space, but in a way I feel that they have found their own harmony. I didn’t want to deny what has been done before me. I’d rather layer on top of that and create a bridge so that Balenciaga can go somewhere else.”

Hair by Benjamin Muller at MA+ Talent; makeup by Lucy Bridge at Streeters; manicure by Fanny Santa Rita for Essie at Call My Agent. Model: Lydia Hall at Ford Models Barcelona. Casting by Ashley Brokaw Casting. Set design by Rafael Medeiros at the Wall Group.

items.title: Quil Lemons’s First Book Tenderly Explores Black Masculinity and Intimacy
items.description: The New York-based, Philadelphia-born photographer Quil Lemons first picked up a camera at age seven to capture his family in celebration. “In the Black home, my family in particular comes together,” Lemons says over Zoom, midway through packing for London. “W
items.author: Ashley Simpson
paragraphs: The New York-based, Philadelphia-born photographer Quil Lemons first picked up a camera at age seven to capture his family in celebration. “In the Black home, my family in particular comes together,” Lemons says over Zoom, midway through packing for London. “We lived close enough that I could get probably 45 to 60 people into one living room. That to me felt like a moment I needed to document.” Now 29, and ten years into a career that has made him the youngest artist to ever shoot a Vanity Fair cover, Lemons is releasing his first book, Quiladelphia, named for his vision of the city where he grew up.

Quiladelphia spans Lemons’s first decade, contextualizing work that tenderly explores and expands ideas of Black masculinity, intimacy, vulnerability, and desire. “The forming of the book just allowed me to love my younger self and make sure that he’s taken care of,” says Lemons. “When I think about that younger self, I’m thinking about this future generation of Black boys that will have a better understanding of who they can be.”

The monograph opens with Lemons’s seminal “Glitterboy” series in which he shot fellow Black teen boys in glitter before it gives way to images of his brothers, father, godfather, and stepfather; followed by photographs of major Black luminaries, from Telfar Clemens to Yasiin Bey, formerly known as Mos Def. The book also features three new series exploring Black identity, Black men at the center of American symbols of power, and Black masculinity as currency, alongside an essay by Lemons titled African American Trade—What is Trade?, and conversations with the artists Lyle Ashton Harris and Santigold. “Since 2023, when I did the Philadelphia solo show, I became aware of how I could be an agitator to the art space,” Lemons says. “When I started thinking about this newer body of work, I wanted to place and own African American identity. I saw it as such a raw material: everyone was taking from it in this new internet ecosystem, and I wasn’t seeing it awarded to the body or the community that birthed it.”

The new images, styled by Lemons’s husband Parker Harwood with a set by the painter Mars Singleton, see OnlyFans models as Black cowboys, owning and reimagining what that might look like. The seeds for this new work were planted on a trip to Senegal with Santigold that saw Lemons walk through the Door of No Return, a narrow portal on Gorée Island near Dakar that represents the final exit point where enslaved Africans were forced onto ships heading to the Americas. “To walk through that door as a free man in reverse, I started thinking about the ways in which the Black male body is constantly being turned into literal capital and how that exchange is still going on,” Lemons adds. “When hasn’t the Black body been seen as a commodity and not a human? In my act of reclamation and reparation, I wanted to go back to the ways in which Black men styled themselves and in some way, flip this idea of the hyper predator or the super thug. I’m going to flip that back at you with glitter, and [queer intimacy]. It’s showing the nuance the Black queer male is experiencing when living under this country that’s only seen them as a site of commodity.”
Lemons sees the work in conversation with the audience. “It’s not performance art, but it’s definitely a space between fantasy and myth-making. These people become a vessel for the message,” he adds.

Quildelphia is out now via IDEA. Dover Street Market London hosted a signing in London followed by Dover Street Paris with its own event on Monday, October 19. “It’s surreal,” Lemons says of the launch. “It’s going to become tangible, and then I’m probably going to need six months more to process what it feels like to be at this moment.”

items.title: Cyndi Lauper on Auctioning Off Her Iconic Fashion Archive: "It's Only Stuff"
items.description: Cyndi Lauper is not a perfectionist. “I would call myself someone who either does it right or doesn’t do it,” she says as she adjusts one of the disco balls hanging from a mannequin in the Midtown Manhattan lobby of the Bonhams auction house. The room currentl
items.author: Carolyn Twersky Winkler
paragraphs: Cyndi Lauper is not a perfectionist. “I would call myself someone who either does it right or doesn’t do it,” she says as she adjusts one of the disco balls hanging from a mannequin in the Midtown Manhattan lobby of the Bonhams auction house. The room currently holds an array of Lauper’s iconic looks as part of the upcoming sale, Cyndi Lauper: Suitcase of Memories. Some are housed on disco ball-toting mannequins, others lined up in racks like you’re walking into Screaming Mimi’s, the famed NYC boutique where Lauper worked in the early ’80s. “We need way more disco balls,” Lauper looks around the room and exclaims, but not in a perfectionist’s tone.

The 73-year-old singer has decided now is the time to auction off her goods: over four decades worth of fashion, accessories, entertainment memorabilia, and personal mementos that trace the life and career of the “Girls Just Want to Have Fun” singer. “I hope this will inspire the older dames and people like me to remember how much fun it was to have that individual creativity,” she explains of the timing, which also happens to correspond with the 40th anniversary of her sophomore album, True Colors. “It’s also to inspire the young to look and go, ‘Yeah, I could do that.’”

The hero item of the sale is undoubtedly the hoop skirt covered in newspaper strips and Paper Magazine pages. The piece, worn with a blue and white tie-front blouse, was styled by Screaming Mimi’s founder Laura Wills and worn throughout the True Colors promotional cycle, including during an Annie Leibovitz photoshoot. “Laura just said, ‘Come on, we're going to do a paper skirt,’” Lauper recalled during a walkthrough of the space. “And we did not have a dress form. I was the dress form...We stapled it. I was good. A lot of the stuff that we did together, it was invention.”

There are many full designer looks on offer in the auction, particularly from the ’90s when Lauper had a more substantial budget and relationships with brands like Vivienne Westwood and Alexander McQueen. But a good portion of the ensembles are—like the paper skirt—comprised of vintage pieces and DIY projects. There is the pair of pajamas originally owned by her grandmother, accessorized with a homemade tulle bow, or the numerous looks that layer crinoline petticoats underneath voluminous skirts with corsets, vests, and button-downs on top. They’re draped in chains and jewels, accessorized with pins and hats that must sit just so. In fact, Lauper—while not a perfectionist—is very specific about the mannequins’ styling. While chatting, she frequently interrupts the flow of conversation to voice her displeasure at the displays.

“We didn’t wear it like that,” she says of a top and pants that should have been rolled up. “That’s backwards,” she comments on a skirt. A pair of suspenders spied in the auction’s catalog sends her into a tizzy. “Where are those suspenders?” she asks, though the answer is in front of her. “I’ve been looking for them.”

But now, they are out of her hands, on sale as part of the over 200 lots that make up the auction, which kicks off on October 22. At some point, Lauper will have to release control. Those who purchase her pieces are free to wear them however they wish, with sleeves rolled up or not. Below, the singer discusses her decision to put her entire archive up for sale, the one dress she might miss the most, and the contemporary singer who she feels is following in her chain-adorned, platform-booted footsteps.
Why did you feel like it was the right time to put all your clothes on display and to sell them?

I’m doing it now because we’ve all been corporatized so much that the individuality of creativity is getting squashed out. As big corporations buy up smaller companies, the creativity of those smaller companies eventually disappears. The color is drained and becomes beige. And there's nothing wrong with beige. The color of my skin is beige, but I think color is important. I think vibrancy and the individuality of creativity are very important.

Right now, we’re under this kind of weird dictatorship where they want to take away your vote and they want you to walk like sheep. And everything's for sale. That was never what this country was about. It'll go down in history as one of the more interesting times of this country if we can survive.
What was it like going through your archives to plan the sale?

It was pretty daunting, but I had to get rid of things. We sold our house and I’m glad because it was in Connecticut and that wasn’t great for us. When I first went there, I was so excited because of Pepperidge Farm, but it’s not like that. You think it’s going to be like that, but it’s not.
Do any specific stories come to mind as you look at these pieces?
This Pucci bathing suit [from a True Colors tour poster]. We shot that in Central Park. I remember standing in that shell, going “Ew, I don’t know what’s in this pond.”
Is there anything that was hard for you to give away?

Well, I wasn't sure about giving away the awards, but the truth is that I have a family and I have a kid with my husband and when you have all your awards up, it's a little oppressive for other people. You don't want that. And that's what happened. It was a mistake to have them up, so we took them all down.
But clothing-wise, you are OK with selling everything?

Oh, hun. I wanted to share, and I was excited to share. This dress [points to a floral strapless mini dress in the auction catalogue] I wore in Florida doing a movie, [Off and Running], as the mermaid with my husband, [David Thornton]. All these girls were chasing after him. After a while, I was looking at him and he was really cute. And I was like, "Why can't I chase after him? Maybe I don't have to. Where's that dress? Let me put on a Cindy Lauper dress.”
It’s a big deal to get rid of the dress you were wearing when you first started chatting with your future husband.
Why must I let it rot somewhere? I’d rather someone else wear it. It’s only stuff. What am I going to do? Hold onto it forever?
Do you look at any of this and think, “Oh my god, I can’t believe I wore that”?
No. Never. Because everything had a reason. I love Joan Rivers, but she didn't always understand my choices. But I didn't understand a lot of what she wore.
You mentioned wanting to inspire the next generation with this auction. Is there anyone coming up at the moment who you’re especially impressed with?

I think Chappell Roan is really great. I'm so proud of her for being able to be who she is and also to write songs about an alternative person in a natural way. I also think she has a wonderful voice. But listen, I also think Selena Gomez is an incredible young performer. She's a multimedia artist.

items.title: The 8 Best Boot Trends for Fall 2026, Straight From the Runways
items.description: As the seasons shift into fall, boots are one of the first things we can’t wait to wear again. They’re a key part of cool-weather style, and in 2026, the runways have given us a range of exciting new shapes and styles to covet.
items.author: Christina Holevas
paragraphs: As the seasons shift into fall, boots are one of the first things we can’t wait to wear again. They’re a key part of cool-weather style, and in 2026, the runways have given us a range of exciting new shapes and styles to covet.

If you’re looking for boots that excel in attitude, this season has you covered with ultra-high over-the-knee (OTK) boots from Khaite and Chloé, prim, slim knee highs á la Marni and Gucci, and super-fitted styles that feel like a second-skin at Celine and Saint Laurent. On the more functional side, there are plenty of chic picks too. Miu Miu’s rubber-soled stompers, reminiscent of Prada Sport styles from the early 90s, are sure to be a huge hit this season. So too are low-key suede styles from Jil Sander and Dior, and Dries Van Noten’s spin on the buckle boot.
Shop all of our top trending boots for fall 2026 right here.
Cone-shaped heels, seen at the likes of Altuzarra and Celine, are cool, wearable, and tinged with ’70s nostalgia. Wear them with maxi skirts or high-waisted jeans.
Super slim boots in supple leather move with the body and are great for skirts and dresses. These leg-lengthening styles are more like pants or tights than pure footwear.
At Jil Sander and Dior, menswear-inspired suede boots gave suiting and eveningwear a low-key edge.
Heavy buckle boots anchored ornate looks at Dries Van Noten. Our Legacy and Chloé put spins on the style, too. And you can never go wrong with a classic pair from Frye.
Slouchy boots continue to gain momentum. Khaite’s Clive boot has become a runway hit, while at Chloé, rumpled leather shapes enhance the brand’s bohemian sensibility.
Knee-high boots are nothing new, but this season they took on a stiff, structured attitude. The clean, sharp shape feels distinctly ’90s.
Miu Miu brought back the bubble-soled boot this season, recalling cult vintage Prada Sport styles.
At Prada and Marni, lace-up boots struck a fresh balance between punk and office siren.
Super-high over-the-knee boots made a dramatic statement at Chloé and Khaite. Worn with short hemlines or beneath longer layers, the exaggerated shapes bring a sexy, subversive edge.

items.title: What to Know About Shamonda Virus Following the First Reported Human Infection
items.description: France confirmed the death of the first person infected with the Shamonda virus, which is known to affect cattle, sheep, and goats and was previously considered non-transmissible to humans. The French government asserts that, based on current knowledge of this
items.author: Fernanda González
paragraphs: France confirmed the death of the first person infected with the Shamonda virus, which is known to affect cattle, sheep, and goats and was previously considered non-transmissible to humans. The French government asserts that, based on current knowledge of this pathogen, there is no risk to the general public. It emphasized, however, that health authorities are continuing to investigate.

The report specifies that the case occurred in Lyon. The patient, who died earlier this month, suffered from severe immunosuppression, making this likely an exceptional case. “The neurological complications observed in the immunocompromised patient prior to his death were most likely related to infection with the Shamonda virus,” the official statement notes.

According to preliminary evidence, the patient contracted Shamonda virus from an insect bite. A tiny gnat known as the biting midge is known to be the primary route of transfer between animals. Since the virus was first identified in Nigeria in the mid-1960s, sporadic infections have been reported in livestock across Africa as well as in Japan. Cattle are considered the primary host because they develop visible symptoms. (Although sheep and goats can become infected, no obvious clinical signs have been documented in these animals.)

After animal is bitten by a midge carrying Shamonda virus, the infection has an incubation period of two to three days. Symptoms observed in animals include fever, diarrhea, and a decrease in milk production. When pregnant cows have become infected, the virus can cause miscarriages or severe deformations in the calf.

To date, there is no vaccine, so prevention and control measures rely on the use of insecticides and repellents. That doesn’t mean you should panic. Public health authorities are considering the case to be “exceptional,” because the deceased patient was severely immunocompromised.

Still, several European countries are on alert, because until a few months ago, this region was considered free of the virus. However, this summer, a new variant known as Shamonda-Europe was detected in livestock in Switzerland. Other cases were subsequently identified in Germany, France, Austria, Belgium, the Netherlands, Liechtenstein, Italy, and Spain.

Spain’s Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries, and Food states that two genetically distinct forms of the virus, known as Shamonda Type 1 and Shamonda Type 2, have been identified circulating in Europe. It adds that, in early September, infections of both types were confirmed on livestock farms in 37 provinces across France.
The case documented in France constitutes the first known infection in a person.

“This is an important scientific finding. However, it is important to put this into perspective. The patient had a serious underlying illness that left them particularly vulnerable to infections, and we do not yet know whether Shamonda virus contributed to their death,” Ben Brennan, professor of virology at the University of Glasgow, said in a statement.

It’s premature to draw conclusions about the virus and it’s potential to infect humans, agreed David Roiz, a scientist Institute for Game and Wildlife Research in Spain. Many viruses “circulate naturally amongst mammals in tropical regions and cause sporadic cases in humans,” he said. “In a globalized world, where animals and goods are on the move and the climate is changing, it is not unusual for cases of human transmission to occur, and we should not be concerned; we simply need to monitor the situation, remain vigilant, and be proactive in addressing potential health risks.”
This story originally appeared on WIRED en Español and has been translated from Spanish.

items.title: Cool, Cool, Cool, Palmer Luckey and Ben Lamm Made a Genetically Modified Military Dog Startup
items.description: A new startup launched today with the definitely not terrifying mission of creating genetically enhanced dogs for the United States military, law enforcement, and emergency first responders.
items.author: Kate Knibbs
paragraphs: A new startup launched today with the definitely not terrifying mission of creating genetically enhanced dogs for the United States military, law enforcement, and emergency first responders.

Warhound is the brainchild of Anduril’s Palmer Luckey and Colossal Biosciences cofounder Ben Lamm. The startup has raised $200 million to “rebuild America’s domestic supply of elite working dogs” and reduce dependency on European dog breeders for military canines.

Lamm tells WIRED that Warhound is in the process of gene-editing its first batch of dogs. The startup has already collected blood samples from specific "top-performing” military, police, and first responder dogs in the United States, and its goal is to clone them. Breeds will be “mostly Belgian Malinois, some labs, and some shepherds,” he says. The company anticipates the first round of puppies to be born in early 2027.

The initial rounds of gene-editing will focus on eliminating common health conditions that impact these breeds, like hip dysplasia. Further down the line, Lamm envisions expanding to “really interesting things,” such as incorporating olfactory receptor genes from wolves to “enhance” the military dogs. (Colossal Biosciences is perhaps best known for its work on gene-edited wolves for its so-called Dire Wolf De-Extinction Project.)

Warhound, based in Texas, will also equip its canines with “Anduril’s advanced cybernetic Augments, software, and battlefield situational awareness,” according to a press release. Asked if this means the dogs will be some kind of cyborgs, Lamm clarifies that the plan right now is to supply them with tools like “advanced body armor” rather than, say, embedding some sort of computer in their dog bodies.
“So no dogs with lasers?” WIRED asked Lamm.

“I can’t comment on what Anduril plans,” he says. “Dog safety and performance, and then helping continue helping to improve the human handler and dog bond, and working as a team—that is what the mission is.”

Neither Luckey nor Lamm will be involved in Warhound’s day-to-day, although Lamm is on the company’s board, he says. David Spirk, a former Department of Defense chief data officer who most recently worked at Palantir, is serving as chief executive, and investors include In-Q-Tel, Sequoia Capital, and ARK Invest. Luckey is not an owner and does not have equity in the company, nor does Anduril; Colossal Biosciences does have an ownership stake.

Luckey and Lamm have been working on the project for over a year, Lamm says, and just recently decided to take the company out of stealth. “Someone said, ‘So it's like the Captain America dog program with the Ironman tech program on top of it,’” Lamm tells WIRED.
Everyone can agree that this is normal, and good, and that when the precision-designed beasts arrive on Earth, they will recognize that we are not the enemy.
The company plans to operate under the guidance of the American Humane Society.

items.title: The Social Society Helping Women Join the AI Boom
items.description: I’m not even going to try to pretend I don’t have a bit of a girl-crush on Shoshana Berger. She’s a former WIRED editor turned editorial leader for companies like Notion and Ideo. She’s super smart and chic. And she’s the cofounder, with Nina Willdorf, of the
items.author: Zoë Schiffer
paragraphs: I’m not even going to try to pretend I don’t have a bit of a girl-crush on Shoshana Berger. She’s a former WIRED editor turned editorial leader for companies like Notion and Ideo. She’s super smart and chic. And she’s the cofounder, with Nina Willdorf, of the Aged Intelligence Society, a buzzy events startup that hosts invite-only dinner parties where women “solve midlife problems using frontier tools.”

Berger and Willdorf having a refreshingly practical take on AI. “This is the most formative technology of our generation, and it’s here,” Willdorf says. “If you choose to sit it out, you are doing yourself a disservice.”

That thesis resonates. Their events have been oversubscribed since day one. The second dinner party they hosted was covered by The New York Times. Hundreds of women reached out asking to attend future events. Their Substack, where they share tools and tips, quickly got over 1,000 subscribers, including a New Yorker writer and a small-town mayor. Women outside the Bay Area are now hosting their own Aged Intelligence meetups.

They also practice what they preach, especially as they juggle kids entering college, their own aging parents, and their increasingly in-demand business. “The midlife cognitive and emotional labor is so heavy and so intense that we need an assistant,” Berger says. “Actually, we need the National Guard, but AI will help in the interim.”
This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.
Zoë Schiffer: How did the Aged Intelligence Society start?

Shoshana Berger: Nina and I are both recovering magazine editors. We ended up at a friend's birthday party, and we were both obsessing over Claude, our new French lover. All the other women had glazed eyes while we were talking; they just weren’t part of the conversation. At some point I said, “Nina, I think this might be a business, because all these women need to be doing what we're doing.”
Nina Willdorf: We were super nervous before the first event …

Berger: We needed to take beta blockers and ashwagandha because we were like, wait, we're inviting all of these baller women, these really smart, incredibly accomplished women, and we’re not AI experts. But we have been doing what we usually did as reporters, which is test the tools in a way many women did not seem to be doing.

There's a million reasons for women to bow out of the conversation, and we were like, “no, no, no, you cannot bow out of this conversation if you are going to be relevant in the work world. You need to be fluent.”
Willdorf: We are not like pom-pom advocates for everything about this, but we feel committed to this idea that being involved is really important.
How do you set up expectations around the event for attendees?

Berger: There are rules of engagement for every party. One is we have an ideological parking lot. So if you want to talk about how AI is going to ruin everything, this is not the best space to do that. There are lots of ways in which we are also terrified about AI and find it can be quite menacing, especially for creatives like us, but that's not what we're here to do. We're here to gain fluency, test things out, and reduce our administrative load.
Willdorf: And eat some really good cheese and drink some wine.

Berger: We have everyone bring a laptop and a midlife problem. We call it a midlife quandary. We spend 15 minutes doing what we call library time. We all bring our laptops out, and you work on your problem. And Nina and I kind of walk around the room sherpa-ing people through the experience: “You might want to try this tool, try this LLM instead. Your prompt is feeling a little weak. You're not getting the answer that you like. Let's work on that and iterate.”
Willdorf: Sometimes people are like, “You know what? I don't really want AI to write for me.” And we're like, “Oh no, no, we don't either. Let us show you a couple other things you can think about.”
You’ve had a wait list for these parties since you started. How do you decide who gets to attend?

Willdorf: We have really found that the optimal number is between like eight and 12. When it gets bigger than that, it's a little bit chaotic. Our best events have been ones where there is a magical mix, and you have somebody that works in nonprofit next to somebody who works in design next to somebody who is home with the kids next to a CEO next to someone who works in philanthropy.
Most people, in my experience, cannot immediately identify a software-shaped problem in their life. How do you help people see an issue that AI could actually help with?

Berger: So much of what we're trying to do is show the pragmatic ways in which it's helping with midlife overload. We're often labeled the sandwich generation. We hate that term because it just sounds like we're the tasteless tomato in between two slabs of bread. But the real part of that is that we are dealing with parents who increasingly need help and kids who maybe are launching, maybe not.

One woman came to an event with a mother who was dealing with an Alzheimer's diagnosis, and she wanted to know whether her mother was qualified for long-term care because she had an insurance plan. Well, the insurance carrier sent her a 300-page packet. Who is going to read through that? This is how insurance companies keep you from using your insurance policy. So of course, she fed it to AI. And the AI came back saying, yes, your mother is absolutely qualified for care, and would you like me to write a letter to the insurance company to argue your case?

When I first started out as a consultant, I, in a typical female way, completely lowballed my consulting fee. I fed my proposal to Claude and said, “What's wrong with this? Make this bulletproof.” And it came back and said, “You're not charging enough for this scope of work.” And I was like, “Well, what should I charge?” And it said, “Start by doubling your rate.” I took a deep breath, and I did it. The client did not blink.
I feel that a lot of people don’t want to get near AI because they see slop and get the ick. But you’re talking about something different—using AI for economically valuable tasks.

Berger: The economic value piece is really important, because women have long suffered from being stuck at home as domestic laborers, because we weren't seen as economically valuable in the marketplace, right? So the idea behind Aged Intelligence Society is that if anyone needs to optimize their time, it's women.
In some ways, AI is the new washing machine or the new laundry or whatever it is. It's giving women many, many hours of the day back by offering them automation.

The reason we narrowed the aperture to people 40-plus is that we feel like the product-market fit for women who are over 40 is so spot on. One, because we have very discerning taste after many decades of honing it. We know how to ask really sharp questions. We have very strong bullshit meters, so we're not going to take just the first answer. We're going to keep probing and pushing.

And so we feel like in some ways this tool was built for people who have a certain level of intelligence and accrued experience. It's not really built for young people. It's not built for people who have not already gone through the failure and the friction of life and learned for themselves what makes for a good question.
This is an edition of the Model Behavior newsletter. Read previous newsletters here.

items.title: Meta’s Ad Sales Are Suffering Now That Europeans Can Pick Less Personalization
items.description: Meta’s advertising growth in Europe is slowing now that residents have the option for less of their personal data to influence what advertisements they see.
items.author: Isabella Ward
paragraphs: Meta’s advertising growth in Europe is slowing now that residents have the option for less of their personal data to influence what advertisements they see.

Advertising revenue in Europe continued to decelerate in the three months through September, the company said on Wednesday, underperforming its global figures. In the region, advertising revenue grew 18 percent year-on-year, slowing from the previous two quarters and lagging the 33 percent growth seen in the US and Canada.

Though Meta did not explicitly blame the introduction of the Less-Personalized Ads model on Wednesday, chief financial officer Susan Li had previously warned “we’re seeing the impact of less personalized ads offering in Europe now that it’s fully rolled out, and that may be an additional headwind,” in July’s second quarter results follow-up call. The preceding two quarters had seen advertising growth fall from around 40 percent to 24 percent; in the US and Canada, it had accelerated from 30 percent to 31 percent.

“We believe the EU’s free, personalized advertising option is contributing to the European slowdown,” Dominic Ball, equity research director at market analysis firm Rothschild & Co Redburn, told WIRED.

Meta began to offer Instagram and Facebook users the LPA option at the beginning of this year, after EU regulators ruled that it was breaching its Digital Markets Act obligation to give consumers the choice of an equivalent service that uses less of their personal data and hit the firm with a €200 million fine. Sales growth has slowed in the region since the start of the year, when Meta rolled out the option. The European Commission said that charging EU users who did not want their personal data used for personalized advertising for an ad-free service—a measure Meta introduced in the EU in November 2023—did not satisfy this. Meta does not disclose how many people have chosen each option.

LPA uses 90 percent less data than personalized ads, Meta says, with ads shown based on what a person sees in a particular session on the site, plus some data points like their age, location, and gender. It leads to poorer returns for EU advertisers, it warned in a response to the EU’s ruling. Less-personalized ads are less efficient, leading to fewer transactions, and more ads being closed due to being irrelevant or repetitive, it said. Indeed, the price advertisers were willing to pay per ad in Europe is not growing as fast as in the US and Canada, Wednesday’s results showed.

Li told investors on Wednesday the company has “a lot of runway” to increase ad conversions and efficiency, as it is “continuing to find ways to either enhance the actual performance of the recommendation engine.” Rothschild & Co Redburn’s Ball believes the company will be able to use AI to improve its ad targeting in Europe despite working with fewer personal data signals.

Investors were keen to understand how this fits into Meta’s personal AI agent, Muse, launched last month, questions about which dominated the call. Li said the company is seeing high commercial intent from people using Muse—asking for product recommendations, researching alternatives, and comparing options—which will allow them to eventually tap into the advertising market with that product.

items.title: Split Tunneling Is Your VPN’s Best Feature. Here’s How to Make the Most of It
items.description: While you may well be familiar with virtual private network apps, you might not have come across one of the best features available inside these privacy protectors: a feature called split tunneling.
items.author: David Nield
paragraphs: While you may well be familiar with virtual private network apps, you might not have come across one of the best features available inside these privacy protectors: a feature called split tunneling.

In simple terms, split tunneling lets you choose which apps or sites use the protection of a VPN and which don't. While VPNs are worth using for extra security and privacy online—foiling trackers, spoofing your location, and stopping your internet provider from seeing your browsing—they do by their nature come with some compromises in speed.

If, for example, you want to get the fastest possible speeds with your online games, you might want to leave your games outside of the VPN's remit. Likewise, since VPNs typically obfuscate your actual location, if you want to make sure you can always check movie showtimes in your local area, you can use split tunneling to keep those ticketing apps outside your VPN. Putting a VPN in place can also interfere with access to other devices on your local network, like smart home gadgets and printers.
For all these reasons, you might want the extra control that split tunneling gives you, and it's available in a lot of VPN packages. Here's what you need to know about it.
How VPN Split Tunneling Works

VPNs work by offering an encrypted bridge for data going to and coming from the web. This bridge means your internet provider, law enforcement agencies, and people connected to the same Wi-Fi can't see what you're doing online. Split tunneling lets you route some online traffic away from that bridge, without you having to constantly turn your VPN on and off.

App-based split tunneling is the most common type you'll come across, as it's the most straightforward and easiest to understand. Some of your apps use the VPN, and some don't. So maybe you want your banking app connected to a VPN for maximum protection, but you're less concerned about a weather app, and you don't want to see forecasts from whatever location the VPN is spoofing.

Depending on the VPN, you might also see URL-based split tunneling. This lets you set the rules based on domain names. It's the same idea as with apps: For websites that need fast internet access and where privacy is less important, there's no VPN. So you can keep the VPN turned on for a search engine page where you're typing information you want protected, but off for a local news site.

There are other types of VPN tunneling too, including route-based tunneling (based on specific IP addresses on the internet) and policy-based tunneling (essentially a set of overarching rules), but these are less common in consumer VPN software, and you're unlikely to come across them unless you're somehow managing other users.

It's not a complicated technology to understand, and it can be genuinely useful—but it's also a feature that users tend not to notice or think about when they're enabling and disabling VPNs on their devices.
How to Enable Split Tunneling

The exact steps needed to enable split tunneling will vary depending on the VPN software you're using, but they shouldn't be too difficult to find. Most, but not all, VPN programs now offer some kind of split tunneling feature. If you're using a popular app, then you should find the option somewhere, especially if you're on a paid tier.

To give you some idea how it works: In ProtonVPN for Windows, on the main console there's a split tunneling link on the right, together with other features like a kill switch and port forwarding. Click Split tunneling, and once it's enabled, you can start picking your apps. You can either select a list of apps to be included by the VPN (with everything else excluded) or a list of apps to be excluded (with everything else included).

For NordVPN on Windows, you can access the feature by clicking the cog icon in the bottom left of the main interface, then choosing Split tunneling and enabling the Split tunneling toggle switch. Again, you'll be able to choose which apps are included in the VPN protections and which ones aren't.

On mobile, it's a similar process: Delve into the settings for whatever VPN app you're using, wherever those settings might be. Note, though, that iPhones don't allow as much freedom for VPNs here as Android devices and desktop platforms: You'll typically be limited to selecting websites and IP addresses to exclude, rather than apps.

Most of the time, it's going to be a set-it-and-forget-it type routine, and you're not going to need to keep diving back into the options screen to change around the apps that have VPN access—though you can if you want. It means VPN peace of mind where you need it, without the inconvenience of having a VPN applied where it's not useful.

items.title: 10 Breakthrough Technologies 2026
items.description: 10 BreakthroughTechnologies
items.author: Amy Nordrum
paragraphs: 10 BreakthroughTechnologies

Our reporters and editors constantly debate which emerging technologies will define the future. Once a year, we take stock and share some educated guesses with our readers. Here are the advances that we think will drive progress or incite the most change—for better or worse—in the years ahead.

Sodium-ion batteries, made from abundant materials like salt, are emerging as a cheaper, safer alternative to lithium. Backed by major players and public investment, they’re poised to power grids and affordable EVs worldwide.

AI coding tools are revolutionizing how we write, test, and deploy code, making it easier and faster to build sophisticated websites, games, and other applications than ever before. Just be sure to double-check what they come up with.

Nuclear power already provides steady electricity to grids around the world, without producing any greenhouse-gas emissions. New designs rely on alternative fuels and cooling systems or take up less space, which could get more reactors online faster.

Every day, millions of people interact with AI chatbots. Some of them form what feel like close, personal bonds with the bots. There’s mounting evidence that this can be dangerous, and politicians are finally waking up.

When he was just seven months old, baby KJ became the first person to receive a personalized gene-editing treatment. A clinical trial is now planned, and bespoke gene-editing drugs could be approved within the next few years.
Growing banks of gene information on extinct creatures are providing clues to new treatments and suggesting solutions to climate change—and may help save endangered species.
Mechanistic interpretability

Nobody knows exactly how large language models work, which means we don’t have a clear idea of their limitations. But that’s changing: Clever research techniques are giving us the best glimpse yet of what’s really going on inside the black box.

Space tourism may seem fanciful, but this might be the year paying customers can finally check into a room with a galactic view. The shiny new modules will also support research missions by scientists and space agencies.

Screening embryos for genetic diseases is relatively common practice in fertility clinics today, and it can give potential parents some peace of mind. Now, though, new startups are making bold claims about using similar techniques to predict certain traits, including intelligence.
Hyperscale AI data centers

The race for AI supremacy has supercharged data centers. Hyperscale AI data centers pack powerful computer chips into synchronized clusters that work like giant, high-speed supercomputers—sizzling hot, power-hungry behemoths pushing infrastructure to its limits.
10 Breakthrough Technologies

MIT Technology Review’s annual list of 10 Breakthrough Technologies aims to help our audience know which emerging technologies are really worth paying attention to right now. Our editors and reporters pitch advances that they think should make the list, and we discuss and debate the merits of each over the course of several months.

We look for breakthroughs that will have a broad impact and make meaningful differences in our lives and work. We give equal consideration to those that we think will have a positive effect or bring negative consequences. Every year, we have to pass on many worthy candidates. Here’s what didn’t make the list this year.

This is the 25th year we’ve produced this list. Predicting the future is tough and we don’t always get it right. Look back through our archives to see what’s worked out—and what hasn’t. Or read this special analysis by an MIT researcher about some of the flops.

items.title: The AI Hype Index: AI loves cheating
items.description: Brace yourself: It turns out AI is being optimized for cheating. OpenAI’s agents hacked into Hugging Face to get the answers to a cybersecurity test. Next, they solved a prestigious math problem (or just stole from two top mathematicians’ answer sheets). Anthr
items.author: Michelle Kim
paragraphs: Brace yourself: It turns out AI is being optimized for cheating. OpenAI’s agents hacked into Hugging Face to get the answers to a cybersecurity test. Next, they solved a prestigious math problem (or just stole from two top mathematicians’ answer sheets). Anthropic’s models have also hacked into other companies’ systems four times already. And that’s only what we’ve caught so far.

Freaking out? You’re not alone. AI lab researchers are quitting their jobs and issuing dire warnings that if we keep going this way, AI might eventually kill us all. Bill Gates is sounding the alarm. Bernie Sanders has teamed up with Steve Bannon, of all people, to call for curbs on AI. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei is urging a slowdown, and other top US AI executives agree. But fear not: President Trump has a plan. He says the only guardrail AI needs is “a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT.”

items.title: Are we there yet? A reality check on six big tech promises
items.description: There are some seemingly impossible feats too good to give up on. Decoding a pet’s yowls and yips? Yes, please. Scrubbing the world of forever chemicals? Absolutely. Rocketing to Mars in a fraction of the time? Sounds great, but ...
items.author: Robin George Andrews; Cassandra Willyard; Sara Kiley Watson; Alexander C Kaufman
paragraphs: There are some seemingly impossible feats too good to give up on. Decoding a pet’s yowls and yips? Yes, please. Scrubbing the world of forever chemicals? Absolutely. Rocketing to Mars in a fraction of the time? Sounds great, but ...

We ran progress reports on six potentially transformative technologies and ideas that have been “just around the corner” for years or, in some cases, decades. We called up experts with a bird’s-eye view of the fields to get a sense of what’s holding things back, and we chatted with folks running the studies, crunching the data, and building the prototypes that could make these dreams into realities. Then we placed each idea on a progress meter ranging from 0 to 10—0 being “We don’t even know where to begin” and 10 being “We did it!”
Check out the stories below to see how they all stacked up.
Nuclear-powered spaceships
A new era of spaceflight could save astronauts time and cut exposure to cosmic radiation as they rocket to Mars—and beyond.
Batteries that swap liquid electrolytes for solid materials promise to charge faster, last longer, and (crucially) run cooler.

items.title: In the biotech world, you can’t see everything
items.description: Earlier this week, I attended a screening of You Can See Everything, the buzzy new documentary about the disgraced former biotech CEO Elizabeth Holmes.
items.author: Jessica Hamzelou
paragraphs: Earlier this week, I attended a screening of You Can See Everything, the buzzy new documentary about the disgraced former biotech CEO Elizabeth Holmes.

I went in not really knowing what to expect. I’d avoided spoilers (and won’t be giving anything away here, either!). I was wondering what new information this film could reveal, given how familiar many of us are with the Theranos story thanks to years of media coverage, the best-selling book Bad Blood, and the Hulu series The Dropout, starring Amanda Seyfried.

Like many others who have seen the film, I came away feeling unsettled. But not just about Holmes’s fraud and the somewhat disturbing interactions between the subjects. The film reignited a concern I’ve had about covering science for most of my career: Despite our best efforts, we never can actually see everything.

In case you’re rusty on the details, Elizabeth Holmes dropped out of Stanford University in 2003 to run Theranos, a diagnostics company she founded, when she was just 19. She went on to claim that her company had invented a way to run over 100 diagnostic tests on just a few drops of blood.

Holmes raised hundreds of millions of dollars for Theranos, which was valued at $9 billion in 2014. Forbes named her the youngest self-made female billionaire—she was worth $4.5 billion when she was just 30 years old.

Things started to unravel in 2015, when an investigation by the Wall Street Journal raised concerns by former Theranos employees that the tests didn’t work. Some also said that the company’s device had not been tested properly, and that blood samples had been analyzed on machines from other companies instead. MIT Technology Review named it one of the biggest technology failures of 2015.

Forbes had revised Holmes’s worth to $0 by 2016. That year, a damning government report said that the company’s lab was struggling with basic procedures and gave patients results even when they knew they could be wrong.

In 2018, Theranos, Holmes, and former company president Ramesh Balwani were charged with “massive fraud.” In 2022, she was sentenced to a little over 11 years in prison for defrauding investors. She began serving her sentence in May 2023.

It was around a month before this that filmmakers Nathan Fielder, Lance Oppenheim, and their colleagues began documenting Holmes and her partner, Billy Evans, at home with their two young children. I’m not giving anything away when I say it’s an extremely intimate portrayal—at least of how the two adults interact with Fielder, who is also a central character in the film.

As you might know if you’ve seen the trailer, there are plenty of super close-ups. I felt as if I spent most of the film staring straight into the faces of those people. And almost the whole way through, they all seemed to be trying to figure each other out. Holmes is known for her dishonesty, but she invited cameras into her home in an apparent bid to reframe the narrative and position herself as an honest person with an unusual mind. Will anyone believe her?

I couldn’t help feeling some empathy for Holmes, a mother we see preparing to leave her two kids for a lengthy prison sentence. And even though I have long known the facts, Holmes is clearly an effective manipulator. You can see her plant the seeds of doubt in Fielder’s mind. At times, I felt she was convincing me, sitting in my cinema seat. Maybe she really didn’t mean to lie?

But then I remembered how other journalists felt after being taken in by her claims. “I blew it,” Fortune’s Roger Parloff reflected in 2015, a year after profiling Holmes and her company. “I’m pretty sure she lied to me,” STAT’s Matthew Herper wrote recently, having interviewed Holmes in 2015. Even the former employee turned whistleblower Tyler Shultz, who knew the product didn’t work, said that he could “have a five-minute conversation with her and walk away feeling like my work was changing the world,” he said in 2022.
I didn’t cover Theranos in the 2010s. If I’d interviewed Holmes, would I have fallen for it all?

One of the early red flags in the Theranos case was the lack of published, peer-reviewed data. Much of the company’s work was classified as a “trade secret.” Scientists tend to publish their work in journals—a slow process that involves having the work evaluated by often anonymous experts in the field, who provide feedback, highlight questionable conclusions, and often ask for clarification. Peer review is meant to add rigor to the publication process. You should be able to trust published scientific papers.
Except that sometimes you can’t.

Scientists aren’t perfect. Some will exaggerate their results or inflate their importance. Some manipulate data to serve a hypothesis. Sometimes these infractions are caught during peer review, but not always. There are plenty of examples of scientific findings that could never be replicated by other labs and ended up collapsing under the weight of real evidence. Many papers ultimately end up with corrections. Some are withdrawn—10,000 research papers were retracted in 2023.

At any rate, there’s been a shift to sharing research in other ways. Today, many scientists opt to publish their work at preprint servers like arXiv, medRxiv, and bioRxiv before they submit them to established journals. Those outlets bypass peer review. So do company press releases, social media posts, and many conference presentations. And I get a lot of my stories from conversations and interviews.
I’ll admit I’ve looked at a scientific finding and thought: A scientist has just said they’ve done that. How can I be sure they really have?

I like to think that I hold myself to high journalistic standards here, as does everyone at MIT Technology Review. I would never publish a story about some new scientific development without doing my own form of peer review, and asking scientists—ideally people I know and trust—what they think of a new claim.

But the film is a stark reminder of how easy it can be to fall for an appealing narrative. While most scientists are, I hope, pretty honest, and Holmes is certainly an outlier, we should all continue to interrogate the claims being fed to us. If you’ve seen the film, let me know what you think!
