items.title: The Chrome Hearts Hustle
items.description: This article was featured in New York’s One Great Story newsletter. Sign up here.
items.author: Ezra Marcus
paragraphs: This article was featured in New York’s One Great Story newsletter. Sign up here.

On a hot afternoon in August, I step off an elevator into a fluorescent-lit showroom on the second floor of an office building in the Financial District. Jack Jiang, the shop’s 19-year-old proprietor, is sitting behind a glass countertop, wearing gray sweatpants and a black hoodie that reads GO FUCK YOURSELF in lime-green cursive. There is no security guard, even though Jiang is surrounded by millions of dollars’ worth of luxury clothes and accessories: a Supreme x Ducati motorbike, a shelf full of Hermès Birkin bags, and racks and racks of Chrome Hearts. The brand’s signature crosses are everywhere: on jeans, biker jackets, and hoodies; on silver handcuffs, a stapler, a hacksaw, and a baseball hat. While giving me a tour of the space, Jiang pulls out a toilet plunger carved from ebony wood and capped with a silver cross, listed for $8,500. “It’s been used!” he tells me.

Jiang moves more than $20 million worth of product a year. Under the username Legos, he posts videos on TikTok of himself tracking down the items he later off-loads to his showroom. In one video, he shows up at a Beverly Hills high-school party. “We gonna finesse all these rich Beverly Hills kids’ Chrome!” he says to the camera. Inside, the attendees scream his name and clamor to sell him the clothes off their bodies. One says the diamond-studded necklace he’s wearing was a gift from his grandmother and he wants at least $2,500 for it; another strips off his Chrome Hearts pants while standing on a table. In another video, Jiang shows off a Chrome Hearts beanbag chair the rapper Bhad Bhabie sold him. He’d later resell it for nearly half a million dollars.

Jiang is not the only one buying and selling Chrome Hearts for exorbitant prices, nor is he the only one posting these interactions online. The brand has become extremely popular over the past few years among the young and wealthy and especially among crypto entrepreneurs fresh off absurd windfalls from meme coins and NFT projects. “A lot of young teenagers, they’re making $10 million, $50 million at the age of 19, 20 — it’s instant, so a lot of them don’t know how to spend it,” Raphael Badalov, a 22-year-old reseller who goes by the handle byraph, tells me recently, fingering his Chrome Hearts Star of David necklace. We are standing in the middle of a massive floor-through space overlooking West 25th Street, soon to be his new showroom. These same kids have spent the past half-decade “seeing their favorite rappers onstage in head-to-toe Chrome Hearts,” another reseller, Vincent Ferraro, says. “They wake up rich overnight. Like, why not live your dream? Get your dream car, get your dream jeans.”

Except they can’t. As with Hermès, according to the resellers and collectors I spoke to, it is impossible to purchase much of anything at a Chrome Hearts store unless you’ve cultivated a yearslong relationship with the brand. “You can go in these stores with a million dollars in cash and you’ll get nothing and then another guy will come in that has a relationship and they’ll offer him a bunch of cool stuff,” says longtime collector Mason Balbier. He would drop by the store and hang out with the salespeople, and eventually, “it just started happening,” he says. (The brand denies their pieces are dispersed based on “status.”) To get your hands on Chrome Hearts as a new buyer, then, your only option is to turn to resellers like Jiang, who charge whatever they feel like — five figures for jeans and leather jackets, higher for rarer pieces. The comment sections of Jiang’s reselling videos are full of people mocking the high prices. “Is it really worth that? I would say it’s not,” Jiang says. “I feel like it’s retarded.” Still, he added, “if there’s someone willing to pay that price, that means there’s logic behind it. There’s a saying in China: It makes sense if it happens.”

Chrome Hearts was founded in 1988 in Los Angeles by a carpenter, Richard Stark, and his two friends, the jeweler Leonard Kamhout and the leather craftsman John Bowman. They sold studded leather pants and custom motorcycle gear to other friends; in the beginning, they designed the costumes for a low-budget horror movie. After a few years, they managed to open a shop on the Upper East Side, which they filled with silver fleurs-de-lis, Gothic-style belt buckles, and handmade chaps. Cher and Lenny Kravitz were early fans, as were members of Guns N’ Roses and Aerosmith. By the mid-’90s, Stark and his wife, Laurie Lynn, had grown the brand into a multimillion-dollar company, opening stores in Tokyo and West Hollywood and collaborating with Rei Kawakubo and Rick Owens. Chrome Hearts continued to operate like a small family business, never releasing collections on a schedule, gifting to celebrities, putting on a runway show, or even expanding production outside its L.A. factory. In the aughts, as other companies began expanding their web presences, Stark and Lynn opted not to sell online.

The Starks’ three children, Jesse Jo, Frankie Belle, and Kristian, became involved in their parents’ company as they got older, roping in friends like Bella Hadid and Young Thug to model for the brand’s magazine and wear the clothes. Lil Uzi Vert’s 2020 album included the song “Chrome Heart Tags”; the YouTuber FaZe Banks got the brand’s cross tattooed on his kneecap. “The family’s ability to market without really marketing is flawless because they’re very, very good at seeding,” Badalov tells me. “They did everything in their power to make sure that wherever you go, you’ll never not see the brand, but you’ll never see the brand directly from the brand.” Eventually, Chrome Hearts became a sort of young-money uniform: Kim Kardashian wore it to the 2025 Met Gala; Timothée Chalamet, another friend of Kristian’s, wore it to a series of NBA games. Limited-edition collaborations only drove up the hype: triple-white Air Force 1’s, a limited-edition drop with Drake at the Aspen store.

The resellers have been swarming the internet since the early 2020s, cashing in on the fact that no one could get any of this stuff. Badalov remembers the moment he decided to go all in on reselling the brand. He was 17, working at a luxury vintage showroom. “One day, a client comes into the showroom I was working at and he brings in a bunch of Chrome Hearts rings,” Badalov says. He watched the man sell the collection for thousands of dollars. “I had an intuition. I’m like, This is going to be the biggest brand of our generation, guaranteed.” He started building his relationship at the Chrome Hearts store and snapping up pieces he knew he’d be able to resell.

The brand responded to the surge of resellers by bolstering efforts to shut them down — banning them from stores, introducing an appointment-only booking system, and training salespeople to look out for suspicious customers. Badalov had been selling for about a year when he was banned, but by that point, he’d established a customer base and a name for himself. Over the next few years, he managed to sell millions of dollars of Chrome Hearts, mostly jeans. On his Instagram, he posts his celebrity clients, including Playboi Carti, Central Cee, and Fabolous. He’s attuned to the absurdity of his life. “I’ve sold jeans for $300,000 before, and you and I are having a regular conversation about it. But let’s not forget that’s fucking insane,” he says. His prices come down to instinct. “There’s one-of-one jeans with Travis Scott’s name tag in them — those jeans you can get half a million for right now,” he says. “If you buy the Chrome Hearts Levi’s with green patches, those are probably worth $30,000 to $35,000. The same pair with crocodile patches is $100,000. It takes one person to buy it secondhand, and as soon as somebody does, word gets out and then boom — we have a market price.”

Jiang started his reselling career as a middle-schooler at a boarding school in Massachusetts. He followed sneaker resellers on TikTok and thought he could make some extra money. He started small, waiting on line at Foot Locker to buy shoes to flip, but quickly moved on to rarer kicks: sought-after editions of sneakers from Jordan, Off-White, and Yeezy. He made his first million at 16. During his sophomore year of high school, his friend offered to trade him a pair of Chrome Hearts jeans for two pairs of rare sneakers; he quickly off-loaded the pants to another reseller for a $4,000 profit. This never would have worked with sneakers, he realized, where the pros are sensitive to margins and obsessively track prices on resale sites like StockX. But with Chrome Hearts, there was a convenient information asymmetry. “You can’t find those details online. People who have Chrome Hearts, a lot of them don’t post it,” he says. “You might see a listing for $25,000, but I’m only selling for $15,000. So what’s the real price? You can’t really determine that.”

Also helpful was the fact that some of the items were produced in extremely low quantities, a core part of Chrome Hearts’ business model: only a handful of exclusive jeans made for a particular store or one-offs created for celebrities like Drake. This meant the resellers could set the market price wherever they wanted. All they had to do was find product. When they posted online that they were on the hunt, people with closets full of items they’d bought decades prior were more than happy to sell their jeans to a high-schooler offering ten times what they’d originally paid. As a teenager, “I would fly around the country,” Jiang says. “If today there’s a 40-year-old guy in Scottsdale, Arizona, who bought $400,000 worth of Chrome Hearts back in 2010 — all one-of-one pieces, gold — the advantage I provided was I would literally pull up to his house, wire ready.” He once spent $2.5 million buying out a single collection. Documenting the search turned him and his fellow Chrome Hearts traders into minor celebrities. In his videos, people scream after him and ask for selfies. Online, “Chrome Hearts reseller” has become yet another recognizable Gen-Z digital hustle, as familiar to the kids as “peptides booster” or “OnlyFans creator.”

Jiang breaks his clients into tiers. “If we’re talking about people spending more than $50,000 per item, then I have, like, 30 to 40,” he says, “mainly overseas buyers in Thailand, China, and Japan. Middle-aged, successful businessmen who love the brand. I’ll get a $100,000 item and it will sell within ten seconds because no one else has it.” Then, he says, he has the “$10,000-to-$50,000 range. Those are the 13-year-olds who can spend $20,000, the crypto kids, and the college athletes who are getting paid through NIL.”

He does whatever he needs to get the rarest items for his customers. In one recent TikTok clip, Jiang can be seen sitting on a couch in a palatial showroom, buying Chrome Hearts from a teenager recently embroiled in a crypto scam. “My boy used to buy Chrome when he was up!” Jiang jokes. The two haggle over the price of a pair of pants; Jiang ultimately buys them for $9,000. Then the boy pulls out a pair of women’s boots. “I found them in my mom’s closet,” he says. Ferraro employs proxies to shop on his behalf, going into stores, developing relationships, and eventually buying items secretly bound for the resale market.

“We all do it,” says Ferraro, chain-smoking out the window of his Soho showroom. He’s 36, a former club manager and relative elder statesman to the younger crop of resellers. “I was always on eBay, hustling like that,” he says. “It was always, like, my passion, whereas I was working nightlife just to pay the bills. Then COVID came and everyone’s getting their checks, so they’re buying more shit. So I was just pumping out more listings, buying stuff in Japan.” Ferraro shows me a parade of rarities: a custom kimono, a green crocodile-leather backpack studded with dagger zippers, a leopard-print beanbag chair, and a floor-length fur coat with a two-foot leather cross down the back listed for $225,000.

There is friendly competition among him and the other top resellers. If you are someone with a rare pair of jeans, “you’re not gonna just text me,” he says. “You’re gonna text Raph. You’re gonna text Legos.” It can be stressful. “People really made this their life. It’s my life. A lot of people live off this now. They quit their jobs, and they do this full time. So if jeans come up, people are fighting over them.”

This past winter, Ferraro got an alert from his security system at 4 a.m. When he opened his phone to check the footage, “I see fucking four guys in here with ski masks, and my heart dropped. And I’m like, ‘Fuck! Call the cops! We gotta get over there now.’” The group had planned the heist meticulously: Dressed as construction workers with vests and gloves, they pulled up to the showroom in a Ford SUV and carried a ladder to the scaffolding outside. “The ladder didn’t work, so they climbed the scaffolding,” Ferraro says. They broke a window and went in with bags ready to go, “just dumping it in. So the alarm is screaming. I think they really wanted to get more, but you can tell they were nervous.” They tossed bags of clothes off the fire escape to their getaway driver. On the way out, they split up and turned off their phones, he says, “because they got pinged by the cops and stuff. Super-thought-out.” They were long gone by the time Ferraro got to the showroom, where he found the floor covered with broken glass. “This was, like, a heartbreaking moment, bro,” he says. “They took over $1.2 million of stuff, which was, like, 60 pairs of jeans.”

Eventually, four people were arrested. One of them, a 21-year-old named Abdallah Diaby, turned out to be an agented model with over 90,000 Instagram followers. He showed up to court wearing thousands of dollars of John Varvatos necklaces and $1,500 Balmain biker jeans. (He has pleaded not guilty.) Ferraro was glad to see them prosecuted but frustrated that his clothing was never recovered, even though his store was insured. “None of the items have ever come up, which is insane because, bro — I’d say I’m the top, original, No. 1 reseller in the world, so everyone comes to me with specialty items. Lenny Kravitz jeans, Drake jeans, they put their name in them.” Even the noncelebrity custom jeans would have been findable given production variance between pairs. “My shit is so one-of-one. It was a bad place to rob. If they robbed a Louis Vuitton, they’re never gonna find it. There’s gonna be too many; that shit’s in rotation. So I don’t know what their plan is with it.” He claimed the cops offered the defendants time off their sentences if they revealed where they stashed or sold the clothes, to no avail. “They’re facing five to seven years, and they’re still saying they don’t know where it is. I’m like, Come on, bro.”

Theft is an increasing problem for the resellers. Recently, a pair of 17-year-olds came into Jiang’s shop trying to sell him goods that, he learned later, were stolen from a different reseller. They also, as it turned out, were casing the joint. A few days later, one of them broke in through a window at night and made off with over a million dollars’ worth of jewelry and pants. Jiang reached out to a resellers group chat and asked members to be on the lookout lest any of his pieces resurface. Sure enough, he soon got a ping from a reseller in Switzerland, where one of the alleged thieves had flown to try to move his items. “They are good,” Jiang says. “They know how to climb walls and stuff. Like, it’s crazy.” Still, he adds, they left fingerprints, and he believes they’ll be arrested. Jiang is planning on moving his showroom to a more secure location.

There’s another less tangible risk for the resellers: If the bubble pops, they will be left holding warehouses full of literal bags. After all, Chrome Hearts is now so overexposed, and the resale market so hot, that the brand is at risk of becoming a parody of itself. Recently, someone on r/MensFashion posted a picture of Chalamet and Kylie Jenner wearing Chrome Hearts jeans with orange crosses captioned “Chrome Hearts is the new Ed Hardy.” A better comparison, though, might be Supreme, whose once-frenzied resale market collapsed under its own weight after its late-2010s peak. “You kind of have to tell when your investment is over,” Gabriel Prensena, a young menswear influencer, tells me. He’s been posting his Chrome Hearts hauls for years and, like many young people, treats his designer-clothing trove as something akin to a basket of stocks to be bought and sold. Now, he’s wondering if the market is looking bearish. He’s begun trimming his Chrome Hearts collection “because I have a scary feeling the value is going to go down sooner than later.” The brand, to him, has started to feel gauche. “It’s one of those things that’s, like, you see the logo and then you automatically correlate it with some sort of money-slash-wealth.”

The resellers know their living depends on decisions being made by a company over which they have no control. “Longevity-wise, I think it all depends on a few factors,” Badalov says. “If they start making more shit, they’ll fuck up the market, obviously. And if there’s more inexperienced people or just money-hungry people selling bullshit, it’s not going to kill the market, but it’ll drive a lot of customers away.” And as with any bubble, even a brief dip in prices could spiral into a full-scale sell-off as spooked resellers try to unload their product ahead of a collapse. At the same time, the scarcity of the items means the market will never really be saturated. In one YouTube video, a Miami-based reseller who goes by the handle Chrome Plug shows off a one-of-one duffle bag he hopes to sell for $100,000. “This is what we’d call blue-chip Chrome. This is your Microsoft. This is your Tesla. This is your eBay and Amazon of Chrome. Your price will only go up,” he says. “It will never go down because there’s people that have spent a lot of money that were all kind of in conglomeration, holding the prices up together and making sure that we’re able to still get the price that we need for items like this.” In other words, at the very top, Chrome Hearts resellers buying from one another is enough to keep the prices elevated.

Badalov is trying to pivot to futureproof his empire. He recently started offering something like concierge services for people new to being rich. “You focus on the experience,” he says. “If you have a guy buying a $100,000 pair of jeans, he’s going to want to buy a $100,000 watch. He’s going to want to go to a cool restaurant. He’s going to want to book a private trip.” He’s had takers. But in the short term, he’s confident in his clothing stock: “People were saying Chrome was going to die two years ago. There’s nothing else to say about that.”

items.title: The Butt Runneth Over
items.description: Three months ago, Dylan, a.k.a. Glute Max Guy, set out on a simple mission: “Glutemaxxing until my butt gets too big for my pants.” He’d been working out for a decade but tended to neglect his lower body. He wasn’t motivated solely by aesthetics, he said, but
items.author: Allison P Davis
paragraphs: Three months ago, Dylan, a.k.a. Glute Max Guy, set out on a simple mission: “Glutemaxxing until my butt gets too big for my pants.” He’d been working out for a decade but tended to neglect his lower body. He wasn’t motivated solely by aesthetics, he said, but “I didn’t want to have the Hank Hill ass that most men seem to be content with. I wanted to look and feel athletic.” He thought posting every day would help him stay consistent.

Dylan is a fairly average guy: brown hair, brown eyes, a beard; he watches reality TV with his wife. He often works out in his condo or a basic gym, and he approaches his glutemaxxing methodically. Six days a week, he posts his workouts: three sets, 12 reps. He eats one gram of protein per pound of body weight (around 200 grams total); he takes ten to 15 grams of creatine a day.

There is nothing even close to thrilling about the pursuit of this ass. Yet the comments under his TikToks and Instagram Reels are full of men lobbing thirsty compliments and women asking for tips. The enthusiasm inspired Dylan to start the Glute Max Club community, sort of like a Patreon, where people chat about their own glute journey and follow along with his. Yes, his ass has gotten bigger, he reports. So has his follower count.

Dylan is but one man moved to action by the ass Zeitgeist. On television, even the most macho, hetero-coded shows, such as Paradise and Reacher, feature long shots of men’s bare cheeks — as did the horniest romance, Heated Rivalry, which turned a quiet appreciation for the male ass into a loud, panting yearning for juicy cakes.

Different eras have had different ideal butts: the square, flat bottom of the ’80s, like Patrick Swayze’s, was followed by the tight little tush of the ’90s. In the 2010s, the focus shifted to a woman’s pliant, movable butt, and the Brazilian butt lift surged in popularity as people tried to achieve it. Heated Rivalry can be said to have had a hand in repopularizing the male butt and informing its current ideal. Now when people say they want a butt, it’s a high, muscular bubble butt, or a “hard football booty,” says Azelion, a New York–based photographer who claims his own gets him a lot of attention on Sniffies and Grindr. It’s the ass of a cheeked-up hockey player, of soccer stars like Jude Bellingham, of tennis juggernauts Frances Tiafoe or Carlos Alcaraz. A cake so firm the cheeks look like they could crush a windpipe, it’s not an ass a Kardashian could call a plastic surgeon to replicate. The people want the bum of an athlete, one that sits atop strong thighs and requires tracking macros to build.

Now that athletes are embracing style — see the pregame fit check in most professional sports — some brand designers are taking notice of their sportier bodies.“People aren’t afraid to show it off,” says Ian Bradley, a stylist and fashion consultant. For Bradley, it’s become easier in the past six years to find pants that fit men with thick thighs and huge asses. “Generations of Black football players struggled to find pants,” he says with a sigh, but now he has a few go-to brands; he points to Thom Browne, who dresses LeBron James, and Zegna, a favorite for formalwear. “There are more options, even in high fashion. Not everyone is just doing a Hedi Slimane cut — no shade.”

Still, high fashion has been slower to evolve. Designers seem to understand that butts are the moment, but few are rushing to send more clappable cheeks down the runway. This past February, Gucci’s artistic director, Demna, dressed men in bum-snuggling pants that drooped so low they would have been pornographic if the models had any sort of ass. Prada’s spring 2027 show had men in pants as tight as Lululemon leggings, yet the cheeks were too microscopic to even fill those out. Emily Dawn Long, an upstart brand, seized on the moment with a butt-crack-centric collection, but the butts wearing it were barely there. Where were the fluffy cinnamon rolls I’ve been lusting after? Fashion is not quite reading the room, because the room is full of people making awooga noises over recent photos of Hudson Williams in Balenciaga pants: The trousers’ draping is best showcased on a firm apple ass. There is a disconnect, in other words, between the kind of butt we desire and the kind of butt designers are willing to dress.

For real men off the runway, it’s actually a hard time to find yourself in a butt deficit. At 39, Tom was pursuing, as he puts it, the typical Fire Island gay body with the help of a trainer. Through bodybuilding, he had sculpted a “pretty nice booty for a white guy,” he says, which became slightly less nice when he had to stop seeing his trainer during COVID. Then came the GLP-1, which he’s been on for years. Now, at 45, his butt is as “flat as a pancake.”

“I catch myself in the mirror sometimes, and I’m like, Oh my God, I have old-man butt,” Tom says. He’s trying to build it back through four-times-a-week workouts with two dedicated leg days. He eats protein. He takes creatine. He does a “million squats and dead lifts and hip thrusts and all these things that are supposed to activate your glutes.” But no matter how many he does, he just has “this sad, deflated whoopee cushion for a butt,” he says woefully. And still he tries.

Seeing your fat ass as an asset isn’t particularly new to women or gay men. What feels most revelatory in this era of ass fetishization is that more straight men have come to understand that a good backside can be as impressive as a well-developed torso.

At a party, I polled a group of straight, married men and their wives about their butts. A woman volunteered that her husband had started going to Pilates. One man lamented how only recently, as women he knew kept talking about the “butts on the hockey show,” did he realize how supremely flat his own ass is. It’s making him insecure.

Another one of the husbands has started developing his naturally big butt. Glute fitness, he notes, has been credited with improving longevity. Still, he’s not totally comfortable with the “nasty little move” he has to do at the end of a squat to ensure glute activation. He demonstrated, suddenly squatting down and popping up with a dramatic clench of his ass cheeks and an audible moan that made him, and everyone else, delighted but uneasy. I worried about him using the gym’s hip-thrust machine.

Azelion, the photographer, has noticed the current booty culture feels very straight. “You have a group of men who are realizing that women and gay men are responding positively to it, so it’s kind of like, ‘Wait, I have something to offer, too,’ ” he says. The proliferation of straight men on TikTok and Instagram pursuing perfect glutes, he says, has “changed the landscape of what it means to have a nice ass (for worse).”

I’ve noticed this too. Glutemaxxing has turned the basic desire for a good ass into an unnecessarily complicated quest to make one’s butt muscles as big, hard, and strong as possible. It can often feel like the erotic instinct for an ass worth lusting after has been sublimated into a whitewashed wellness obsession.

The math should be simple: three muscles (gluteus maximus, medius, and minimus), two firm cheeks, one perfect ass. And yet glutemaxxing requires an astonishing number of Romanian dead lifts, Bulgarian split squats, cable kickbacks, hip thrusts, glute bridges, elevated sumo squats. The number of ways one can fail to fully activate one’s glutes, the calculations of how much protein and fiber and creatine to consume, could lead to a certain kind of mania.

When I scroll Fitness Instagram or TikTok (sometimes for my own gains, other times because, well, butts are nice to look at), I am inundated with male trainers who seem to be the disciples of the original Glute Guy, Bret Contreras, who allegedly invented the hip thrust 20 years ago after watching MMA fighters fling their opponents off with their hips. I’ve screenshotted tips from @thelabootybuilder, a bro who helps women “grow their peach, inch by inch,” and become grotesquely obsessed with @iamnunzi, who has the exact snatched waist to round ass ratio I find to be my personal ideal. I am impressed and repulsed by how he wears the spandex workout shorts that lift and separate your ass cheeks and unsettled by how the conversation is one macro away from sounding like a pro–RFK Jr. fitness regimen.

Something vital gets lost when the goal is a perfect marble-statue butt. It’s beautiful to look at — and look we do — but the life force is gone when optimization enters the conversation. What is the point of a juicy booty if we’ve glutemaxxed the eroticism out of it? Is it still a desired object when its pursuit has been divorced from desire? I sometimes sense that though more straight men want bigger butts, the sexiness of an ass has become secondary to its functionality. You’re building your glutes so can pick up a heavy box at age 60? What about so you’ll have something for someone to grab on to? Straight men’s need to optimize their butts has arguably ruined butts.

Not according to Jacob, 29, who started working out his butt to alleviate hip problems. His glutes were weak, and he wanted to make them strong. He and his friend Yianni started getting into glute workouts. The workouts turned into a friendly competition, which has grown to include some 30 friends participating in something called the Great Cake Competition.

He laid out all the details for me: They took official measurements at the start. He made a Strava-like app that includes 3-D renderings and growth charts. A photographer took glamour shots for before and after pictures. He got custom thongs for all of his friends, and when they do the final measurements in November, the winners will get plaster casts of their own asses.

As a result of growing his ass, Jacob has spent a long time getting really heady about what growing an ass can do for humanity. He’s moved away from the realm of fitness and function and developed a philosophical outlook on the whole thing. He sees the butt as the epicenter of his spiritual power — the root chakra. Unlocking his glutes is an act of self-acceptance and a way to achieve freedom from shame. That shame, he adds, is at the core of a lot of men’s lack of interest in engaging with their glutes.

The longer we talk, the more reasons he lists for the revolutionary potential of building a butt: It’s counter to Ozempic culture (“Everyone should eat as much as they can and make their asses as big as they can!”); it’s a way to ground himself physically — to align himself with the earth. The glutes aren’t just the key to longevity but an antidote to the ills of the manosphere. “The ultimate power comes from restraint and groundedness, which are representative of the ideals of masculinity I think we should be venerating,” Jacob says. If more men did, he thinks, society would move away from fascist applications of power.
And here I thought the men’s butt moment was about sex.

items.title: Drake Is Ready for Christian-Girl Autumn
items.description: Happy 40th-birthday weekend to Drake, who rang in the big four-oh early with a dinner in New York Thursday night. In doing so, the Scorpio debuted a new alter ego: autumnal auntie on a GNO.
items.author: Emma Childs
paragraphs: Happy 40th-birthday weekend to Drake, who rang in the big four-oh early with a dinner in New York Thursday night. In doing so, the Scorpio debuted a new alter ego: autumnal auntie on a GNO.

Drake faced the crisp October nighttime air in black leather pants, a black crewneck sweatshirt, and a Frappuccino-colored suede shawl trimmed with fringe. It’s the type of outerwear you’d find in a Christian-Girl Autumn starter pack — a coat whose owner would throw punches for Rae Dunn at HomeGoods and has pumpkin-spice season marked on the calendar. A video posted on X shows the Toronto rapper walking into the Soho restaurant Mamo holding the buttery fabric tight around his shoulders, “When will my husband return from war?” style.

Naturally, Drake’s choice of outerwear on his birthday outing has made it a fruitful morning on the internet. “I know that’s right pashmina papi,” one Instagram commenter wrote. “Ok Auntie splurged at @kohls with this one!” and “Housewives of Texas I see you,” chimed in others. Here at The Cut, we thought about that Selena Gomez meme and started manifesting for Drake to star in a Nancy Meyers movie. “I see him as the new neighbor who just moved from a big city to a toney enclave and is clueless about homeownership and through that forges a beautiful bond with a group of 60-plus-year-old women on the block,” head of social Lucia Tonelli spitballed.

You know what? I enjoy Drake’s fringed birthday shawl. X sleuths later discovered it’s a vintage Hermès shawl, sourced by stylist Juliet Charlotte. (Because, duh; Champagne Papi is a bougie diva). The man’s a known fashion risk-taker, too — who could forget his denim Chanel lederhosen from Oktoberfest last year? — and I always support one’s journey of self-expression by way of style experimentation. Plus it seems Drake’s just a blanket-coat type of guy: Back in 2014, he layered an off-runway Chanel poncho over a “Hotline Bling”–themed groutfit. It’s his birthday; he’ll shawl if he wants to.

items.title: Your Daily Horoscope by Madame Clairevoyant: October 23, 2026
items.description: This morning, the sun leaves Libra to enter Scorpio. For the next month, you may find yourself placing less value on social harmony and more on candor. Right now, avoiding sensitive subjects or “agreeing to disagree” in the name of good manners will seem deepl
items.author: Claire Comstock-Gay
paragraphs: This morning, the sun leaves Libra to enter Scorpio. For the next month, you may find yourself placing less value on social harmony and more on candor. Right now, avoiding sensitive subjects or “agreeing to disagree” in the name of good manners will seem deeply unsatisfying, if not outright unfair. You’d rather have a conversation that gets heated over one that tiptoes around the important stuff. Your instinct for honesty is a good one, but remember that your interactions don’t have to be contentious to be authentic and interesting. Particularly as Venus aligns with the sun tonight, you have a good chance of finding people who are on your wavelength — and who are willing to go deep with you.

You aren’t generally interested in cultivating an air of mystery. You are who you are, and you’d rather be honest about it: You make it clear what you do (and don’t) bring to the table and then let others decide how they want to proceed. Today, though, consider this: You don’t owe it to anyone to put all your cards on the table right away. Keeping some information to yourself, at least for now, could motivate people to put more effort into getting to know you on a deeper level.

Sometimes, you feel pressured to resolve conflicts as quickly as possible — regardless of whether the outcome is satisfying. But today, refuse to accept solutions that don’t work for you. If you’re going to accept a compromise, make sure it’s one that genuinely feels fair. It might be tempting to agree to a bad deal just because you’re tired of arguing, or because you’re being pushed to relent, but don’t do it. You can’t expect to get everything you want, but you shouldn’t feel bullied or taken advantage of either.

You often feel safest when hiding your opinions behind multiple layers of irony. That way you can always backpedal if you change your mind about something; you’ll have plausible deniability if your words provoke a reaction you don’t like. But today, trying to be cagey or clever won’t get you anywhere. There’s room for humor in your conversations, but it shouldn’t act as a substitute for saying what you really mean. It’s better to be honest — even if you know some people will disagree — than to worry excessively about being liked.

When people express a desire to get to know you better, you have a hard time not feeling suspicious. If it’s not immediately clear why they’re interested in you, you tend to assume they must have some kind of ulterior motive. But today, give yourself a little more credit than that. You have lots to offer; it shouldn’t be surprising that others might want to spend time with you. You don’t have to let your guard down completely, but give people a chance.

Today, you might wonder — even more than usual — why the people around you act the way they do. You’ll want to dig into the deeper feelings and past experiences that motivate them, to understand what’s going on beneath the surface. But be careful not to get too swept up in your own musings. Your theories might sound compelling, and they might even be accurate. But you won’t actually know what’s going on in someone else’s head unless they tell you. So if you’re curious about someone, don’t just study them. Talk to them.

You might feel as though you need to rush through your day today. Especially if other people try to convince you that your usual routines are “inefficient,” and that you should instead do things the way they think is best, you’ll be inclined to believe them. But take a step back and realize you’re allowed to set your own pace. You have no obligation to speed up just because other people are in a hurry. Rushing will only lead to stress and avoidable mistakes, so keep things slow and steady for the time being.

In general, you want to give everyone a fair chance. You always try to hear people out, even when you suspect you won’t agree with them. You do your best to offer grace even when it’s not deserved. But privately, you worry people think you’re a pushover. Today, you’ll have the opportunity to prove them wrong. You know you have deep reserves of conviction and determination, and this could be the time to let others see them. As much as you value kindness, you occasionally need to make it clear that you shouldn’t be underestimated.

More often than you might realize, you hide the parts of your personality you worry might repel people. You want to be successful and liked, and so your strategy is to amplify your most charming qualities and conceal the ones that embarrass you. But this is a stressful — and ultimately lonely — way to live. Today, give yourself permission to relax. Stop working so hard to maintain a polished façade, and just do what feels natural, what feels right. Maybe some people won’t like it, but others will like you more for your honesty.
Sagittarius Daily Horoscope

Generally, you’re willing to change your mind when presented with new information. You’d rather be adaptable than stubborn; you’d rather learn and grow than double down on a wrong idea. But today, don’t automatically assume that everyone else must know more than you do, and therefore you should be the one to fall in line. If you know in your gut that you’re right, then now is the time to be brave and stay true to yourself, regardless of what anyone else has to say.

You’re someone who’s caring but also strategic with your relationships. You understand that sometimes it’s important to maintain positive connections even with people you don’t particularly care for. Being civil and helpful can make everyone’s lives easier — and you never know when you might need a friend. But today, remember that there are some relationships that aren’t worth the stress, frustration, or heartache. If someone is being cruel, difficult, or draining, consider whether it’s best to distance yourself, at least temporarily. There’s no shame in taking care of yourself.

You occasionally convince yourself that if you don’t actively seek attention, you’ll be able to fade into the background. There, you can observe and behave as you wish, unnoticed. Today, though, the people around you are probably paying closer attention than you realize. Don’t assume that no one’s watching just because you haven’t sought the spotlight. Try to carry yourself in a way you can be proud of, because even if it seems like nobody’s got an eye on you, chances are, someone does.

When you’re afraid you won’t like the answers to your questions, you often avoid asking them at all. The less you know, you imagine, the simpler things will be! If you can avoid learning unpleasant or inconvenient facts, then you won’t have to figure out what to do about them. But today, knowledge will only help you. The clearer a picture you have of what you’re dealing with, the more effectively you’ll be able to navigate it. Follow your curiosity where it leads you. You’ll ultimately be glad you did.

items.title: The Royal Family Is Loving Celebrity Traitors
items.description: Prince William appeared on a very special episode of The Graham Norton Show on Friday. The entire couch was filled with guests who had ties to his Earthshot Prize, a global environmental award that, he said, allows people to “talk about urgency and optimism to
items.author: Olivia Craighead
paragraphs: Prince William appeared on a very special episode of The Graham Norton Show on Friday. The entire couch was filled with guests who had ties to his Earthshot Prize, a global environmental award that, he said, allows people to “talk about urgency and optimism together.” That’s wonderful, of course, but not exactly why the episode was so special. The actual big reveal was that William and his family are quite familiar with the Traitors turret.

William said that he and his family have recently been watching the second season of Celebrity Traitors and that they’re all gagging for Maya Jama as a Traitor. Well, sort of. He actually just said that they’re enjoying the program.
“I love it, the family love it,” he told Norton, per People. “Charlotte and Louis are obsessed with it. It’s really good telly.” No word on if George is keeping up with the series while at Eton.

My VPN and I have to agree. Unfortunately, William did not divulge any specifics about his family’s thoughts on the season. Do they also think that James Acaster is not built for the turret? Did Charlotte love it when Richard E. Grant told everyone he was a Traitor in the very first episode? Is Kate finding Michael Sheen to be incredibly charming? Maybe William can come back to the couch next week and we can get some more details.

Celebrity Traitors isn’t the only culture William is taking in. He also shared his affinity for Christopher Nolan movies, specifically The Dark Knight, which he loves because it’s “psychologically dark and deep.” The same could be said for Celebrity Traitors. Maybe that’s why he’s so into it.

items.title: Kristen Bell’s Happy Tears
items.description: Kristen Bell’s Happy Tears
items.author: Rachael Combe
paragraphs: Kristen Bell’s Happy Tears
As the third season of Nobody Wants This hits Netflix, the TV perennial, Frozen superstar, and modern-marriage poster girl reveals her secret sauce.

Kristen Bell appears on my computer screen eating a bowl of yogurt. She is backlit by a gauzy curtain in a corner of her California home, her blond hair in a top knot. She wears a black T-shirt and no visible makeup. She is 46, looks 16, and, almost immediately, is speaking with the wisdom of your coolest 76-year-old aunt.

“We all act like we’re not connected, but that’s the biggest joke. I see the world as a large family that f*cking fights a lot. I like that about myself, and I’m not planning on changing it no matter how much tribalism is presented to me,” she says. It’s a theme she returns to repeatedly in our conversation. “That’s what I love about Nobody Wants This. They’ve learned not just how to love, but how to fight and how to forgive and how to choose each other despite differences. I think that’s something the world could use more of.”

Bell speaks with her hands, fluttering and fanning her tapered pink nails, and expertly deploys eye contact — she’s not taking her eyes off of you, so you can’t take your eyes off of her. “I’m a feeler,” she says, her eyes welling up. “I wish I wasn’t sometimes. But I also know it leads me to a lot of my creative process. And I think creativity is one of the most important things in the world.” She sees her gifts — her ability to communicate emotion, her crystalline singing voice — as almost a moral imperative to improve the lives of those around her. “I do think thoroughly about how, hopefully, [a project] will land,” she says. “I could be in [viewers’] living room at night after they’ve had a hard day, and when they sit down, I could sweep them away into a world that is only imaginary, and for one hour, they forget that their hands and feet hurt.”

The third season of Nobody Wants This, Bell’s hit Netflix comedy, drops Oct. 22. The show, about agnostic, devil-may-care sex podcaster Joanne (Bell) falling in love with a careful, tradition-loving rabbi, Noah (Adam Brody), and the chaos it causes in each of their lives, is rom-com light. But it debuted in 2024 amid heightened antisemitism in the wake of the Oct. 7 attacks in Israel and the war in Gaza. Initially, the show was knocked by some for stereotypical portrayals of Jewish women — but it ended up being a huge win for Netflix, drawing 57 million viewers in its first three months on the platform. And as Joanne and Noah’s love story has developed, the series has blossomed into a surprisingly sweet treatise on tolerance, resilience, and the beauty of Jewish ritual and spirituality.
“Having people be disappointed in me is really hard for me. Like really hard. And with raising kids, that’s like a whole other level.”

Bell has made a career of making you root for other headlong women, rushing into danger (Veronica Mars), into the arms of oversexed rockers (Forgetting Sarah Marshall), into ice storms (Frozen), and into the afterlife (The Good Place). Though there are some Extremely Online People who don’t always manage to connect with Bell’s sense of humor on social media — the brouhaha about her tongue-in-cheek Instagram post to Dax Shepard on her last wedding anniversary comes to mind — she radiates likability even when she’s playing a next-level bitch (see her recurring guest roles in Party Down and Parks and Recreation). As Bell’s husband of 13 years, podcaster and comedian Shepard recently put it, “How on Earth could you hate this woman? She’s so lovely. If you hate this woman, clearly you’re bonkers.”

It’s true that in our stressed-out, maxed-out, polarized, atomized, rage-baited era, Bell is like a half-pint of lemonade: a sweet-tart all-American crowd-pleaser, able to take down the temperature and brighten the spirits of any room. Now that Dolly Parton and Betty White are no longer with us, Bell is probably in the running to take over their roles as America’s Most Beloved. But, as with Parton and White, what is sometimes missed thanks to Bell’s Labubu level of cuteness and killer comedic timing is the weapons-grade intelligence ticking away behind every performance. “People know she’s funny. But I don’t think anyone fully, fully grasps how wicked smart she is,” says Monica Padman, Bell’s longtime business and producing partner and co-host of the podcast Armchair Expert with Shepard. “She’s very quick and witty. Because she has all these other beautiful and shocking qualities … [that] does not really get mentioned.”

Bell has frequently claimed to have no big plan, no ambition for world domination, and yet, let’s face it: With her hit show, three upcoming movies (Violent Night 2, Sonic the Hedgehog 4, and Frozen 3), and a new role as a L'Oréal Paris spokeswoman, she’s dominating. “I’m a busybody. I like doing. I like creating. I like new experiences,” she says. “It’s hard for me to state my goals because my narrative tells me I don’t have them. Perhaps that’s because I would feel too arrogant. My goal is to be happy with the next decision. I go based on my gut. I have very strong gut feelings. Obviously, I wanted to create a life for myself and put food on the table, which is why I wasn’t doing plays in my backyard for free my whole life.”

Community theater in her native Detroit is where Bell caught the acting bug, playing a banana in a play about Raggedy Ann. “My mom had heard me singing all the time around the house,” she says, and took her for voice lessons and to an audition. Though Bell did ultimately get an agent and snag a few professional gigs before heading to New York University’s prestigious Tisch School of the Arts, she’s glad she grew up in the theater and not on set. (She has one pre-college major movie credit, as an extra in Claire Danes’ 1998 Polish Wedding.) “In theater, there is no craft service. There are no PAs. There is no driver. You show up on time or you’re fired, whether you’re the lead or in the chorus. You go sit in your moldy dressing room until your cue is ready, and you better be on stage. There’s more of a collective energy.”

Bell immediately connected with the tolerance in the theater community. “It was a group of people who were a bit weirder than the norm, just like I was. Everything was accepted. You could choose to wear something insane — a huge striped top hat — and you might feel nervous in the grocery store. Is anyone looking at me? You walk into a theater, and they’re like, ‘Oh, baby queen, gorgeous, I love it. Where did you get it? Can I try it?’ There’s such an effusive sense of celebrating everything.”
“I’m a little bit Veronica Mars, a little bit Sarah Marshall. I’m a tiny bit Joanne. But I’m the most like Anna [from Frozen].”

Bell dropped out of Tisch her senior year, in 2001, when she won the part of Becky in a Broadway production of The Adventures of Tom Sawyer. Soon she was scoring guest parts in TV series. Her big break came in 2004 with the titular role in Veronica Mars. She was the first person who auditioned with creator Rob Thomas, who says he saw 100 more actors before realizing Bell had nailed it in that first meeting. Bell went on to dazzle everyone involved with her flawless takes and ability to handle everything from screwball comedy to her character’s devastating rape. She earned the nickname “Money” because of her dependability in every take. Thomas told directors that if they ever had a difference of opinion about a creative choice with Bell, Bell was always right. “She had so much control. So much control,” Thomas says. “When you’re doing the CW shows that I was doing, you’re working with young actors. You see a lot of bad acting. But Kristen was like clockwork, just, like, done.”

Shepard, whom Bell met through mutual friends in 2007, wanders into the room as she is telling the story of their early romance. He was initially attracted to her passion for Bed Bath & Beyond coupons — as a fellow Michigander, he found her thriftiness familiar and hot. “I definitely stole those from my neighbor’s mailbox back in the day. And I’ll say that on the stand,” she says.

But he really fell for her during a game of “running charades” Bell organized at her house. Running charades, for the uninitiated, involves sprinting back and forth for clues before acting them out under a time pressure. Bell tells me she would gather 30 people, “theater folk. We played it full contact. You were allowed to move furniture as an obstacle. You were allowed to push an old dog into a hallway that someone could maybe trip [over]. You were allowed to hip check people.” The one thing Bell would not allow was folding up the clues — too much of a time waster to unfold. Bell had climbed onto her kitchen counter to give a “very harsh speech that if you fold your paper, you will no longer be invited back. I’m done with people folding their paper. This is a time game. If you do it, you’re out.”
She turns to Dax and says, “And then you said later on — right? — you thought that was very attractive.”

“I knew there was trouble ahead,” Shepard calls out from off camera. He describes it as the moment he realized she was “a boss, a force of nature to be reckoned with. I said, ‘Look at this little powerful [person].’”

Over the years, his instinct has been confirmed — “She’s not afraid of the gorilla she lives with,” Shepard jokes. The two got engaged in 2010 but postponed the wedding until after California legalized same-sex marriage. They finally tied the knot — after Bell re-proposed on Twitter and Shepard accepted — in 2013, after the birth of their eldest daughter, Lincoln (now 13). Their second daughter, Delta (now 11), followed in 2014.

Bell describes Lincoln and Delta as the primary factors in her decisions about which projects she accepts. “Is this going to pull me away from my kids too much? Will I still be able to be the mom that I want to be? That’s really the No. 1, to be honest. There’s nothing higher than that,” she says. “I would easily let my whole career and all its legacy and notoriety ‘disapparate’ tomorrow if it meant sacrificing something major in my kids’ lives, or not being there.”

This sounds like it could be a cliché celebrity homily to the sanctity of motherhood: Many mothers who don’t have to worry about their every word being picked apart online will admit that sometimes they wish their job and their kids would “disapparate” simultaneously, at least long enough to take a bath. But Padman says it’s true on an existential level for Bell. “She is a mom first. She is meant to be a mother. She moms outside of just her children, too,” Padman says. “She’s just such a maternal figure in so many people’s lives. People go to her for advice and nurturing. She oozes a maternal quality and she’s very willing to meet that across the board: with her kids, with adult friends, with other people’s children. She’s an open source of that.”
“I am not ashamed to admit I love my algorithm. You know what I did? I crafted it. I don’t pause on negative stories. I don’t pause on clickbait. I don’t pause on train wrecks.”

Which is not to say that Bell is some Pollyanna, twirling through her perfect life. Shepard and Bell have been admirably open about the challenges of marriage and family life. “It’s hard. Do not think because I am on your television that it is easy for me. It’s brutal. I cry weekly,” she says, citing Dr. Becky and Lisa Damour, Ph.D., as expert sources she regularly turns to for guidance. She says she wants to be honest about the strains of family life to make people feel seen. “Oftentimes when you’re in that cyclone of puberty, you could think, My kid is the only one doing this. And that is just simply not a fact.”

But Bell says that openness has become trickier to navigate as her girls have gotten older. “It’s always a debate between Kantianism and utilitarianism,” she says — yes, as in the 18th century German philosopher Immanuel Kant. “For the good of the people, we should share our dirty stories, we should share our shame, we should share our hardships. But for the good of the one? My main job in life is to protect those two. I guess a conclusion we came to at a time in our parenting journey is, like, we can share all the cute things when they’re little, but when they could possibly be exposed to [media] or possibly have a feeling in response to it … well, now, the equation has changed. There’s someone else in the mix, and you have to have enough self-awareness and consideration to consider that person. And that person is my daughter, so she’s No. 1.”
“Do not think because I am on your television that it is easy for me. It’s brutal. I cry weekly.”

The level of thoughtfulness Bell applies to, well, everything she does, does not come without a cost. Over the years, she has shared the work she does to stay on top of clinical depression and anxiety, starting from when she was in college. She wrote an op-ed for Time magazine, made a video for the Child Mind Institute, and was a mental health spokesperson for the telehealth company Hers. She’s advocated for therapy and destigmatizing medication and spoken about her success with eye movement desensitization and reprocessing (EMDR) therapy.

Most recently, she has been touting her work with neuropsychologist Julia DiGangi, Ph.D. “She is a knife through the noise,” Bell says, confessing that she found her while scrolling online. “I am not ashamed to admit I love my algorithm. You know what I did? I crafted it. I took very seriously when [author] Yuval Harari told us to pay attention to what you consume, not just your food. I don’t pause on negative stories. I don’t pause on clickbait. I don’t pause on train wrecks. I keep informed, but when I’m participating in social media, it’s dogs doing funny stuff. It’s knitting. It’s crafts. It’s tiny tidbits that help you get through your day. She popped up.”

She did an online course with DiGangi “to soothe my anxiety” and started seeing “the biggest difference in my life than I have with almost anything I’ve applied.” Soon she was reaching out to DiGangi for individual coaching. “I still struggle with [anxiety] every day. It’s not anything that’s gone away. I think it takes a long time to change your neural pathways from habits you’ve created. Your brain is a pattern detector. That’s the main thing she talks about, and it’s so true. But if I can change my patterns, maybe I can change the amount of anxiety in my body.”

Lately, Bell has been examining her pattern of people-pleasing. On a podcast with psychologist Adam Grant, she blew this reporter’s mind when she said, “I’m accepting the fact that over-explaining is a form of begging.” Juggling the roles of mother, wife, friend, daughter, actor, celebrity, and involved citizen would seem to offer an almost impossible bind for Bell — one that is familiar to many women of her generation. You can’t say yes to everything; you want to show up for every part of your life; time and energy are finite; saying no means disappointing someone.

It is clear as Bell speaks that she compounds the problem by holding herself to exceptionally high standards. “I do things I love and care about... So oftentimes I will work myself to the bone or work till I’m exhausted because I genuinely care about how it lands in the world,” she tells me at one point. And, “Being considered arrogant makes me feel sick because I believe that no person is worth more than another.” She repeatedly checks in with me over the course of our call, hoping I’m getting what I need for this story and apologizes for getting “so philosophical so quick.” She says that “having people be disappointed in me is really hard for me. Like really hard. And you know with raising kids, that’s like a whole other level.”

When we commiserate about the unstoppable detritus and waste of raising growing kids, she admits that thinking so much about every plastic bag and candy bar wrapper that enters her home is exhausting. “My cognitive labor, much like yours, is an absolute burnout. It is always burnt out.” (Bell tip that turns out to be pretty helpful: She recommends the company Ridwell, which takes away otherwise hard-to-recycle items.)

“I’m a busybody. I like doing. I like creating. I like new experiences. It’s hard for me to state my goals because my narrative tells me I don’t have them. My goal is to be happy with the next decision.”

So the question (asking for a friend) is: If she’s no longer overfunctioning and people-pleasing — is she pissing people off? “It’s not causing difficulty. It’s causing a reckoning of my interiority,” she says. “It’s causing me to recognize when my people-pleasing is out of fear, which is about 50% of the time … and when it’s coming out of a genuine commitment to the health and happiness of my stewardship to the world around me. And just the enlightenment that it’s a choice reduces my fear by quite a bit.”

When you’re watching Bell play Joanne from Nobody Wants This, it can feel hard to square Bell’s meticulous caretaking with that more libertine character. Bell’s acting has a quality of being so natural as to seem like she’s always being herself on screen. “I almost never see performances that match her natural tone,” says Padman. “When you know her very well, you’re watching her play all these roles ... and you’re like, ‘Oh, she’s acting, because that’s not her at all.’”

Toward the end of our interview, Bell picks up her computer. “Sorry,” she says. “I’m going outside to get my little dose of sunshine today.” She arranges herself on a lounge chair and tips her head toward the sun as she considers what parts of herself she brings to each role. In sunshine, you can see a delicate earring glinting in her helix. There are a stack of life-size Halloween skeletons on the patio behind her chair, all face-down, like they’re trying to hide from the Zoom camera. “I’m a little bit Veronica Mars, a little bit Sarah Marshall. I’m a tiny bit Joanne,” she says. “But I’m the most like Anna [of Arendelle].”
“Oftentimes I will work myself to the bone or work till I’m exhausted because I genuinely care about how it lands in the world.”

Bell says the process of crafting the Frozen characters with Disney was the most collaborative project she’s ever been a part of. They worked through multiple iterations of the script, using improv and making character tweaks. “They were very open to each and every suggestion I had that rounded her out to be someone that I needed to see when I was a little girl. I needed to see a princess that did not have good posture,” Bell says. “I wanted that out there for the girls who felt a little quirkier, to see some representation.” Anna drooling while sleeping, her clumsiness — those are Bell’s input. She remembers telling writers, “I need her to talk too fast and wear her heart on her sleeve and just try because she wants to, because she cares.”

Some parts of the Frozen story were out of her control — “The Snow Monster will come when the Snow Monster will come,” she says — but as she’s explaining how she and her colleagues were able to influence how their characters reacted and “put words in [their] mouths,” Bell becomes visibly emotional. “It’s been one of the joys of my whole life that,” she says, pausing, her voice rising and growing thinner, “that project has been loved and accepted as it has been because I felt like I was very revealing in it.”

Her emotion is contagious. I tell her that Frozen came out shortly after I gave birth to my second daughter, and how, as a woman without a sister, I was so moved by the film’s ending that I could not stop crying, mostly with joy that my girls would know the sisterhood I had always longed for. “I love that. We are all connected. You may not have a sister,” she tells me, fixing me with her empathetic gaze, “but you can choose anyone to be your sister.” It’s an idea — along with a renewed commitment to recycle my candy wrappers and fix my Instagram algorithm — that stays with me.
