items.title: Can you ever really think what someone else is thinking? | Psyche Ideas
items.description: Most of us have had the experience of looking into someone’s eyes and sensing that we know what’s on their mind. Not much is needed for this sense of knowing what someone is thinking: some words, a gesture, a smile, or just a shared gaze. Friends exchange comm
items.author: Víctor Verdejo
paragraphs: Most of us have had the experience of looking into someone’s eyes and sensing that we know what’s on their mind. Not much is needed for this sense of knowing what someone is thinking: some words, a gesture, a smile, or just a shared gaze. Friends exchange comments about their day and nod affirmatively. Parents utter ‘Oh my God’ as they watch their toddler take a first step. Commuters give each other a weary glance as the train pulls away without them. Encounters like these involve a meeting of minds – we feel that we understand and are understood.

Having the opportunity to connect with others in this way is gratifying. It provides a sense of belonging to a wider sphere, a sphere where your thoughts and your meanings are not just your thoughts and your meanings. Where they are open to another. When communication unfolds successfully – when the click happens, or insofar as the click happens – you and another person can seem to be thinking the same thing.

This idea transpires in the way people talk: we tend to speak as if we literally share thoughts, as though ideas can flow seamlessly from one mind to another. We often say that we ‘think the same’ or ‘know what’s on somebody’s mind’ or ‘get our thoughts across’. These are natural illustrations of how much people unreflectively rely on the idea that thoughts are not only shareable but indeed are ordinarily shared in our communicative exchanges.

This intuitive picture is old and powerful. Yet the notion that people think the very same thought in successful communication has come under increasing scrutiny. Contemporary philosophers argue that what seems like straightforward thought-sharing is more complex, and more interesting, than the familiar metaphors suggest. They both challenge this natural idea and show that understanding each other plausibly involves thinking differently from each other. Realising this can help us see how communication really works.

The idea that communication and understanding are built on shared thoughts has a long history. Plato influentially suggested that ideas involved in our knowledge and talk are in fact unchanging, perfect forms inhabiting a separate realm – a shared eidetic foundation of reality. Augustine of Hippo, in De doctrina Christiana (397-426), expressed the view that signs are used to ‘transmit to another’s mind what is in the mind of the person who gives the sign’. But the basic schema that informs our communicative intuitions nowadays was more clearly proclaimed in the modern period. In the third book of An Essay Concerning Human Understanding (1689), John Locke contended that the purpose of communication via language is the transfer of thoughts or ideas from one person to another:

The chief end of language in communication being to be understood, words serve not well for that end, neither in civil nor philosophical discourse, when any word does not excite in the hearer the same idea which it stands for in the mind of the speaker.

This view persisted from the 19th century to the present, in the work of philosophical giants such as Gottlob Frege, H P Grice and Robert Stalnaker, among others. Frege, for instance, advocated a conception of shareable thoughts that result in a ‘common stock’ consistent with logic and science. Stalnaker developed an influential framework for communicative contexts resting on the notion of a ‘common ground’, or information shared by the speakers in a conversation.

Whereas these and other works clearly align with the idea of thought-sharing, recent developments in thinking about the nature of communication suggest a more nuanced picture. Sometimes, of course, people suffer dramatic misalignment and just miscommunicate; the thought doesn’t get across, and they don’t understand each other. But even when communication succeeds in practical terms, there is often diversity and mismatch in what we’re thinking.
Effective communication is consistent with – and may even require – differences in thought

Suppose that, after a hard day’s work, you tell me, irascibly: ‘I had an awful day at work,’ to which I respond:, ‘I see.’ Here, there is a sense in which I perfectly understand what you said. But there are two ways in which this falls short of thought-sharing in the common sense of the term. First, your thought might be extremely rich – filled with feelings of frustration and details of the whole lot of things that have gone wrong throughout the day. But communication, in this case, doesn’t require us to share all of that. Moreover, even if you were to tell me all the ins and outs, there is some quality of the thought that can hardly be shared: after all, it is your job and your frustration. Even if I sympathise, it can barely affect me and my behaviour in the same way it affects yours.

People rarely, if ever, communicate about things as if from nowhere. Each of us must occupy a distinctive space, a point of view, with our own background knowledge, memories and current experience regarding the matters we talk about. A popular example from John Perry illustrates this cleanly: suppose that you are in the mountains with a hiking partner, and a bear starts to approach them. In fright, they shout: ‘A bear is about to attack me!’ You understand that they are in danger, so you run to get help while your partner defensively curls up into a ball. But if you completely shared your partner’s thought – which would include thought content about an imminent threat to the self, from their perspective – then you would behave in the same way that they do and curl up too.

In this case, as well as in more ordinary cases, effective communication is consistent with – and may even require – differences in thought. Our cognitive lives are, after all, so different. Our beliefs, backgrounds and sensibilities influence the specific content of our thoughts, and they can never really be the same from one thinker to the next.

In the science-fiction trope of the ‘hive mind’ (eg, the Borg of Star Trek, or the virus-induced collective consciousness of the 2025 TV show Pluribus), individual minds in the hive share all thoughts automatically and seamlessly; they are literally of one mind in every respect. If real-life communication consists of thought-sharing, it certainly isn’t like this for us, yet we sometimes talk as if it is. Recognising this is important: it not only avoids a distorted conception of communication, it also helps to calibrate our expectations when we communicate.

In recent philosophical work, there are some who defend a sophisticated version of thought-sharing. They make room for the variability of what people are actually thinking when they understand each other, but retain the idea that you can, in some sense, share a thought. This approach, which I myself favour, reflects that the basic concept of thought-sharing is not only natural, but explanatorily useful. For example, the notion that you can share a thought makes it easy to distinguish between misunderstanding what someone means (‘getting the wrong idea’) from grasping what someone means (‘getting the idea’) and yet disagreeing with it.

In this way of viewing thought-sharing, each person’s version of the shared thought is layered: thought similarity at one level is compatible with a level of disparity that reflects each person’s distinctive points of view. To constitute a ‘shared thought’, some core content or state must be identical, even as some other components of the thought differ. On this view, sharing thoughts is complex because thoughts themselves are complex.
Treating our thoughts as if they are about the same things often suffices for understanding and joint behaviour

But other philosophers explain communication differently: via coordination or informational relations among different thoughts. On these accounts, if I know or somehow track what you are thinking, I don’t actually need to ‘share’ your thought in order to understand what you are saying.

One particularly influential example of this is relationism, the kind of approach originally championed by Kit Fine. According to this perspective, communication is not really a matter of thought identity, but thought coordination. What matters is not the intrinsic properties of two people’s thoughts or the extent to which those are the same. What matters is how those thoughts are related. For instance, treating our thoughts as if they are about the same things often suffices for understanding and joint behaviour. So, if you tell me about your ‘awful day at work’, and elaborate about impending deadlines, an unkind boss and feeling overwhelmed, and I respond sympathetically, we both presuppose or act as if our thoughts are about these same things – even if the thoughts themselves are different – and doing so allows the conversation to serve its function. I may not need to share your experience in order to understand you. It might be enough that our thoughts coordinate – that they stand in an appropriate relation to one another.

The debate continues between proponents of these perspectives. But the richer picture drawn by these trends helps us think about communication and shared understanding without positing (as some would be tempted to) perfect matching in the way people think.

Let us return to our opening thought: the existence of mutual understanding, possibly triggered by words, gestures or even a simple glance. This prospect underwrites the possibility of a common world, and takes us beyond our private experiences. Yet recalcitrant, multifaceted difference is also an undeniable part of the picture. We should not expect mutual understanding in communication necessarily to lead to a common, monolithic thought or experience.

Noting this could prevent unnecessary frustration and overoptimistic expectations when we communicate. Communicating smoothly does bring our thoughts into contact with those of others. But there are important limits on someone else’s access to the full richness of your thoughts and point of view, and vice versa. Knowing this before we speak might inspire more patience in communication, more willingness to restate or elaborate in order to build the shared kernel of our differing thoughts, or a degree of acceptance when someone doesn’t seem to fully ‘get it’. It takes time and effort to share anything more than superficial or abstract thoughts and, even then, it is impossible to share everything we think. But that is exactly as it should be.

It may still seem plausible and useful to suppose that we can think ‘the same thing’. But, often, the connection you have to someone else’s thought is looser than it might appear, and interestingly complex. Whatever perspective you take, the question of whether or how we ever truly ‘share’ thoughts gives us reason to pause and consider what it actually means to connect with someone else – to understand and to be understood.

items.title: Why romantic relationships matter more to men than to women | Psyche Ideas
items.description: For centuries, the self-sufficient man who shuns romance has appeared as a kind of noble figure. ‘He that hath wife and children hath given hostages to fortune,’ wrote Francis Bacon in ‘Of Marriage and the Single Life’ (1625). ‘Certainly the best works, and of
items.author: Iris Wahring
paragraphs: For centuries, the self-sufficient man who shuns romance has appeared as a kind of noble figure. ‘He that hath wife and children hath given hostages to fortune,’ wrote Francis Bacon in ‘Of Marriage and the Single Life’ (1625). ‘Certainly the best works, and of greatest merit for the public, have proceeded from the unmarried or childless men.’ For Bacon, romantic relationships (and family) are impediments to a man becoming his best. Ralph Waldo Emerson devoted an entire essay, ‘Self-Reliance’ (1841), to the conviction that a man should stand apart from the crowd. ‘I shun father and mother and wife and brother, when my genius calls me,’ he wrote. Decades later, Rudyard Kipling reduced the idea to a single line: ‘He travels the fastest who travels alone.’

Such visions of self-sufficient masculinity endure in depictions of silent cowboys, wandering rōnin, desert hermits, elite soldiers, or libertines who treat love as a sport. Powered by their own strength and resilience, these men are domesticated only when circumstances or a determined partner finally insists on it. According to this view of masculinity, love is a welcome addition but never a need.

Women, on the other hand, have often been portrayed as being consumed by their desire for romantic relationships. Consider an often-quoted line from Lord Byron’s epic poem Don Juan (1819-24): love is just one part of a man’s life, Byron writes, but ‘tis woman’s whole existence’. If men can take or leave romance, the logic goes, then women must be the real romantics. They are the ones who fall harder and faster, and the ones who carry the emotional weight of a relationship.

But that’s not how things really work. As a researcher specialising in the psychology of romantic relationships, I have found that the evidence points the other way. In 2023 and 2024, I analysed more than 50 empirical studies and meta-analyses, revealing masculinity to be much more fragile than assumed. At every stage, from the first spark of attraction to the aftermath of a breakup, it is men who depend more on their romantic partners, for their happiness and, in measurable ways, for their survival.

To understand the disproportionate weight love carries for men, we must examine the trajectory of relationships, starting from the time when men are single and searching for a partner. On average, men consider finding a partner more important for their happiness than women do. When single, they are less satisfied with their relationship status and long for a partner more intensely. They also plunge into the feeling of falling in love more often and more quickly, and they experience unrequited love more frequently. Contrary to common expectations, men are typically the first to say ‘I love you’ in heterosexual relationships, according to a 2022 study led by Christopher Watkins from Abertay University in the UK, which surveyed participants across seven countries on three continents.

Once in a relationship, both partners usually benefit. Longitudinal research indicates that entering a romantic relationship itself is typically accompanied by increases in life satisfaction. Accordingly, couples tend to show higher levels of wellbeing, better mental and physical health, and even higher life expectancy than their single counterparts. Yet, all these benefits are more pronounced for men. For example, a 2020 meta-analysis by Yafeng Wang from Wuhan University in China and colleagues, involving data on marital status and mortality risk from 7.9 million individuals and 1.9 million deaths, found that unmarried women had a 22 per cent higher mortality risk than married women, but unmarried men even had a 46 per cent higher mortality risk than married men. So for the average man, being in a committed relationship is more decisive for how long they will live than it is for the average woman.
Following a divorce, the risk of suicide doubles for men

Many romantic relationships, however, end in a breakup and, if they do, this is typically initiated by women: among heterosexual couples, 60 to 70 per cent of breakups and divorces are initiated by women, according to studies in the US, Germany and Netherlands. The remaining 30 to 40 per cent are equally divided between mutual breakups and those initiated by men.

When the split happens, men suffer more. While a breakup is typically painful for women too, men tend to struggle more to find any positive aspects, such as relief or newfound independence, following a split. They are less likely to feel like they have learned something from the breakup. Men also tend to experience a sharper decline in life satisfaction, reporting higher levels of loneliness afterward and more frequently resorting to harmful coping mechanisms, such as alcohol and substance abuse.

Most alarmingly, the end of a relationship can be fatal. Following a divorce, the risk of suicide doubles for men. In a research paper in 2025, the men’s health expert Michael Wilson from the University of Melbourne and colleagues reviewed 75 prior studies on suicidality in men to find ‘the factors underpinning men’s suicidal ideation, suicide attempt, and death by suicide following relationship breakdown’. They found that the risk of suicide was especially high during the separation period itself, nearly twice the odds seen in men who were already divorced (and more than four times as high as married men). For women, the suicide risk after a divorce or separation increases by a far smaller amount, if at all. For a significant number of men, losing a romantic relationship is, quite literally, a matter of life or death.

How did we arrive at a place where the supposedly ‘stronger’ gender longs intensely for a partner, relies more heavily on them for health and wellbeing, is more frequently left behind, and remains emotionally fragile in the face of heartbreak? Multiple factors may play a role here.

Consider, for instance, the unequal distribution of household chores. Women spend substantially more time and effort doing unpaid care work, including both the execution and planning of tasks as part of home organisation. This unequal distribution of duties between heterosexual romantic partners is not without costs and is associated with lower levels of mental and physical health in women. However, after a breakup from a cohabitating partner, women tend to spend less time on household chores than before, leaving them with more time for enjoyable activities. Men, on the other hand, often suddenly lack the person who managed this workload, and may start spending more time on less enjoyable domestic activities.
Men, throughout their lives, are less likely to receive emotional support

A related practical factor that may shape the profound effect that romantic relationships have on the physical health and life expectancy of men is that women are more likely to remind their partners to go to the doctor than vice versa. Accordingly, while both men and women in romantic relationships tend to visit the doctor more often than their single counterparts, the difference between partnered and single individuals is more pronounced among men.

Child custody is another point. It is noteworthy that following a divorce, children tend to stay with their mothers in most cases, regardless of who initiates the breakup. That means fathers who walk away from a relationship not only lose their romantic partner but also risk a substantial reduction in contact with their children. The result is a compounding sense of loss, which mothers in the same position are far less likely to face.

However, the most robust and far-reaching explanation for why the ‘stronger’ gender is so much more emotionally fragile in the face of heartbreak is intimacy: research consistently shows that men, throughout their lives, are less likely to receive emotional support.

All humans possess an innate need for intimacy. We want to confide in others, to feel secure, to be touched and held, and to know someone has our back. A central condition for experiencing emotional intimacy is receiving emotional support. Emotional support involves caring for another person’s wellbeing by understanding and appreciating them. Longitudinal and intervention research has proven that emotional support is a central resource for mental and physical health. The fundamental problem is that men often lack this support outside the boundaries of a romantic relationship. As shown in numerous studies, they tend to receive less emotional support from their friends and family than women do. Instead, men are more likely to view their romantic partners as their primary confidant.

This ‘intimacy deficit’ begins remarkably early. Even boys aged around 10 or 11 report opening up to friends far less than girls do. As they grow older, men are significantly less likely than women to have confidants they can turn to in times of trouble. To fill this gaping void, many men lean almost exclusively on the emotional support of their partners. Consequently, finding a partner represents a massive gain in emotional closeness for a man. And losing that partner can represent the loss of his entire emotional infrastructure.
We have created a paradox: forms of masculinity that forbid vulnerability guarantee an even higher level of vulnerability

The root of this isolation is the traditional male gender role. From early childhood, boys are socialised to view vulnerability as a weakness. Parents subtly enforce this: studies show that when talking to preschool-aged daughters as compared with sons, parents focus more on emotional experiences and react more positively to sadness.

By adolescence, boys have learned the lesson. They expect that opening up to friends will feel ‘weird’. Adult men go on to judge other men harshly when they show vulnerability, seeing it as a violation of traditional masculinity. A comprehensive meta-analysis led by the social psychologist Alice Eagly from Northwestern University in Illinois, including studies spanning from 1946 to 2018, shows that communal traits, like emotionality and nurturance, are still overwhelmingly attributed to women. Both men and women continue to view emotionality as a desirable trait in women, but an undesirable one in men.

Yet, beneath this stoic mask, men experience vulnerable emotions like sadness and fear just as frequently and intensely as women do. We have created a paradox: forms of masculinity that forbid vulnerability guarantee an even higher level of vulnerability. Because deep emotional connection is socially acceptable for men only within the confines of a romantic relationship, they are left utterly defenceless when they are single or when a relationship ends.

While the societal roles and expectations for women have expanded massively in recent decades, the template for masculinity has largely stagnated. We continue to raise boys who become men who are wholly dependent on romantic partners for their basic emotional needs. This is an unfair burden to place on women and is actively impairing the health and life expectancy of millions of men.

Everyone, regardless of gender, should have the capacity to lead a fulfilled, emotionally supported life without a romantic partner. To achieve this, we must rewrite the societal image of masculinity from the ground up. We need to dispel the myth of stoic self-reliance. We need to normalise emotional openness and platonic intimacy among men, to ensure they lead healthy, resilient lives that are no longer existentially dependent on a romantic partner.

This shift must be systemic. It begins with parents, who must be encouraged to raise sons to view emotional openness as a fundamental life skill rather than a weakness. In schools, the importance of emotionally close friendships must be explicitly taught, creating spaces where boys learn that vulnerability is a strength.

Furthermore, we need targeted, community-based programmes for adult men that foster connections beyond romance. A promising model is the ‘Men’s Shed’ movement, which originated in Australia and is now run in several other countries around the world. These community workshops provide a space where men, typically of retirement age, can work on practical projects and talk ‘shoulder to shoulder’ rather than face-to-face. Such informal settings bypass the stigma of traditional therapy, reducing social isolation and increasing wellbeing.

For centuries, men have been told that romantic relationships don’t matter that much and that self-sufficiency is the answer to all problems. The research tells a different story: love, it turns out, is never just a small part of a man’s life.

items.title: Why I wrote mad letters to celebrities on my mother’s behalf | Psyche Turning Points
items.description: My mother paced the patio, working through that week’s crisis aloud. An office mate, she was certain, was a CIA operative sent to spy on her.
items.author: Joe Mullich
paragraphs: My mother paced the patio, working through that week’s crisis aloud. An office mate, she was certain, was a CIA operative sent to spy on her.

I paced back and forth with her, hoping to shift her attention by describing what happened in my third-grade class. When none of my attempts landed, I went to our mailbox to retrieve the monthly issue of Reader’s Digest. At age eight, I was in love with the English language. I tore open the magazine to a feature called ‘It Pays to Increase Your Word Power’, a list of 10 little-used words. The third item stunned me – ‘sesquipedalianism’. I laughed when I read the definition: using a big word when a small one would do.
Before I realised it, my mother was looming behind me, ever-present cigarette dangling from her mouth. Peering at the long, odd, winding word, she nodded with satisfaction.
‘Al Pacino would understand that word,’ she said. ‘We should write a letter to Al Pacino. He will be able to put a stop to this. And be sure to use that seis-qui-whatever word.’
‘You think Al Pacino would know sesquipedalianism?’
‘Without a doubt! He’s an artist. If we use it in the letter, he’ll know how serious we are.’

I ran to my room. It was always a big moment when my mother came out of her walking fits. The next few minutes were critical in how the rest of her day went. I grabbed a handful of the #2 pencils I always kept sharpened and at the ready.

Initially, my mother simply had me proofread the letters she sent to celebrities asking them to intervene in the vast and ever-expanding conspiracy that was orchestrated against her. We wrote to Neil Armstrong, Walter Cronkite, Sean Connery and many people I did not recognise. Over time, my edits to her letters became so extensive that she decided to just dictate her thoughts and let me compose the missives.
When I came back, she was sitting at the breakfast nook, hands clamped at the edges of the table so tightly her knuckles turned white. I sat across from her.
My mother’s ramblings seemed like radio static while she spoke, and I understood her paranoia only when I translated it onto the page

She took a deep drag from a cigarette. When she looked down at the notebook, with my crisply sharpened #2 pencil hovering over it, her eyes turned into slits. She contemplated how to describe the full array of the injustices against her. In such moments, I would wait silently, sometimes for a few seconds, sometimes for 15 minutes, until the dam burst. At some point, words and thoughts would tumble out of her in turbulent currents. Sometimes the thoughts would contradict and bounce off each other, which only increased the frenzy of her telling.
When she finished, her eyes would be glassy but then focus. ‘You think we have it?’ she asked.
She took a deep drag on her cigarette and then snuffed it out. ‘I need to go lay down. Let me know when it’s done.’

I never took actual notes when she spoke. I just doodled on the notebook. I had learned that my mother’s meaning was never in the words themselves but in-between the words, in the tone, in the pauses, in the way her voice raised and lowered. Random and wild thoughts would fly by me like objects swirling in a tornado.

Her word salad never made sense when she was speaking. However, when I paused to put the jumble into a letter, one stray fact would jump out to me, and immediately lead me to another stray fact, forging a connection I had not noticed until then. My mother’s ramblings seemed like radio static while she spoke, and I understood her paranoia only when I translated it onto the page. In the middle of the tornado that was her mind lurked an eerily calm coherence – one I could reach only by listening and writing my way to its centre.

When I finished the letter, I called to her. She came out of the bedroom and plopped herself on the Naugahyde seats, looking both fascinated and sceptical at the paper I held in my hands. Then I read it aloud:

Only you can help me! This is a FEDERAL matter. They plot against me. I am a single MOTHER with 3 small children. No one is on my side. The father (mama’s boy) does nothing. Please use your connections. I am begging you. All I want is what everyone wants, to be left in peace.
PS You are very handsome! (wink, wink)

Stripped of the frantic energy in her voice, her plea made a kind of sense. She was always complaining about how her co-workers at the US Postal Service were ‘getting in her business’ and how her supervisors would ignore her complaints. I added the underlines, capitalisation and exclamation points because I knew from past letters that she particularly liked how they looked on the page.
‘How did you know all that?’ she asked.
She was not one for affectionate hugs, although she would occasionally goose me or my brothers

She took the yellow legal paper and held it as though it was a Gideon Bible. I had the sense that my mother didn’t really understand what she thought until I wrote it down. When it was read back to her, the magnitude of the situation would awe her. At this moment, we had the deepest connection – perhaps the only true connection – we would have in my lifetime. She stared at the letter in amazement that her pain and suffering could be made comprehensible.
‘You understand!’ she said.
‘It’s really not complicated when you get to the heart of it.’

She tipped her cigarette to me in a kind of salute and gave my hand a squeeze, a gesture that shocked me. She was not one for affectionate hugs, although she would occasionally goose me or my brothers, jabbing a middle finger into our blue jeans as we passed by. ‘Better watch out,’ she would direct. We were all very careful before entering any long, cramped hallway to make sure she wasn’t on the other side.
‘This is an excellent letter,’ she said. ‘I can’t imagine how Al Pacino won’t want to get involved. We need to get him this letter asap!’

She chuckled at the foolishness of my question. ‘Oh, if Al Pacino wants to help, he can help, believe you me. The government isn’t afraid of the little people, like you and me. They piss on the little people. But if the Godfather speaks, they’ll listen.’

I dragged my chair to the closet where we kept the brooms and mops. I stood on the chair to reach the upper shelf, which held a stack of phone directories. I opened up to the P section. There was a long string of Pacinos: A. Pacino, Alberto Pacino, Albert Pacino. I picked one at random.
When I wrote ‘Mr Al Pacino’ on the envelope, she said: ‘No. Make it ‘Senor Al Pacino.’ And put a little wavy thing over the N.’

She wrote ‘personal and confidential’ at the bottom of the letter, added three exclamation points, and circled it twice. She never put her return address on the envelope – ‘for security reasons’. Mrs Bottomfield, the neighbour my mother frequently threatened to kill for spying on her, was watering her lawn. She froze in terror at the sight of my mother. However, my mother was in such a happy mood that she let out a boisterous ‘Good afternoon, Beverly!’ and waved at her nemesis. Mrs Bottomfield waved back warily and slowly backed into her house, peering at us through the screen door until we were a safe distance away.
We walked to the mailbox three streets over. My mother believed it was safer to use ‘anonymous mailboxes’.
After depositing the letter, my mother said: ‘Al Pacino is going to lose it when he gets that letter. All hell is going to break loose. They won’t know what hit them. Let’s go get some ice cream.’
I was in the bubble of her madness, but my notebook – my words – shielded me from becoming consumed
‘Thrifty?’ I said excitedly, referencing the nearby drugstore where they would let you sample several flavours of ice cream before choosing one.
‘You bet! Don’t mention any of this to your brothers. They wouldn’t understand like you do. Let’s keep it just between us.’
Another day, another secret.

When I wrote the letters for my mother, it was the only time I felt we occupied the same plane of reality. I was in the bubble of her madness, but my notebook – my words – shielded me from becoming consumed. I cared about her, but I watched from a distance, and that distance made her trust me, if only for a few minutes since trust was not something she could extend to anyone for a long period. When I started to write a letter from her perspective, everything she said made perfect sense, and it made me sorry for what she was going through.

My mother always made Don Quixote relatable to me. If you saw windmills as hulking giants out to destroy you, tilting at them with a lance was survival, not folly. Everything makes sense if you find the proper angle to view it from.

I had always been a quiet child, who liked to keep to the edges of a room or sit under a table and listen to adults talk at a party. But sitting across from my mother in that breakfast nook, I understood for the first time what I actually was: a translator. My gift was being able to listen to people and understand what they said and what they actually meant. That was the moment I found my calling.

items.title: Why a world without friction is a world without progress | Aeon Essays
items.description: In conversations, few words catch my attention faster than ‘friction’ – and especially talk of making things frictionless. From the workplace to grocery shopping, our societies seem to be striving to remove friction from everything. The motivation appears to b
items.author: Jennifer R Vail
paragraphs: In conversations, few words catch my attention faster than ‘friction’ – and especially talk of making things frictionless. From the workplace to grocery shopping, our societies seem to be striving to remove friction from everything. The motivation appears to be that decreasing resistance makes life easier and smoother.

Having spent a career as a tribologist, studying friction, wear and lubrication scientifically, I have some opinions on this. I’ll confess that, in most of my career, I too have sought to reduce friction, developing new materials, designs or even instrumentation in order to lower friction in a jet engine or reduce emissions from your car. However, I’ve also found myself trying to figure out how to increase friction to remove plaque on teeth.

The reality is that friction, despite seeming so antagonistic, is necessary and even productive. The force that resists motion has, since humans first struck a spark from a stone, been the very thing that propels us forward. And this paradox offers a lens through which to reread humanity’s entire technological history.

In order to appreciate all that an understanding of friction has helped us to accomplish, it’s necessary to start at square one and state what friction actually is. We define friction as the force that resists motion, and that means friction is rather ubiquitous. If things are moving, whether they’re sliding around or rolling, there’s friction. Solids, liquids, gases? Doesn’t matter. If there’s movement, friction is there to resist it. Unfortunately, because friction’s job is to resist, we’ve developed an aversion to it as a nuisance. But it’s a very important force, and we’ve thrived by expanding our understanding of it. By the 1960s, after millennia of evolving with friction, we finally accepted that friction is such a critical part of our world that a scientific field of study needed to be devoted to it: tribology.

Tribologists like me study this force in all its forms. Tribology is the science of interacting surfaces in relative motion, concerned with the wear of materials, friction and lubrication. Basically, tribology is the specialisation of things rubbing against each other. You may raise an eyebrow at a field of science focused on this, but when you pause to consider how much motion is going on inside us, around us and throughout the Universe, you can appreciate that tribology is vast. More than anyone, tribologists know the problems friction can cause. But they also know the achievements that have followed as we’ve come to understand resistance better.

Although tribology as a formalised field is relatively modern, friction has long shaped humanity’s technological innovations. For example, consider its pivotal role in people’s journeys from A to B over the centuries. I’m willing to bet that whenever you need to move unwieldy furniture or carry home that giant bag of cat litter, your instinct is to find a cart to help you. Early humans had a similar thought, turning to log rollers to move heavy objects, and coming up with one of our greatest inventions: the wheel. Rolling makes it easier to move objects because it reduces friction between the object and surface you’re moving it against. There are far fewer surface interactions in the process of rolling versus sliding. Plenty can be said about the wheel, including the fact that even in 2026 we can’t seem to agree on the origin of its discovery, but there is zero doubt that it’s a brilliant innovation for dealing with friction. But wheels also need friction: when we exert a force to move a wheel forward, the force between the ground and the wheel – static friction – keeps it from spinning freely, which would result in us going nowhere. Once forward motion begins, the resistance to motion becomes dynamic friction, which is just as important. If you’ve driven on ice, you know the danger of too little friction.
However, if people hadn’t continued improving on these basic principles, even the wheel would be rather inefficient due to friction.
The Vikings’ longships minimised form drag so they could cut through the water quickly

The ancient Romans discovered this in their amphitheatres. Roman chariot races didn’t come without their headaches. Or rather, foot aches. I’m certain the drivers likely complained about their hot feet, caused by friction between the wheels and axle heating up the surrounding parts. In Odes, a collection of lyric poems, the poet Horace described how chariot wheels would glow during racing. Today, scientists know that this glow is from turning the energy of motion into thermal energy. Roman designers eventually figured out that they could temper the problem by putting axungia (animal fat) grease between the wheel and axle. By doing so, they were applying tribological knowledge already exploited by the Sumerians: that fats and oils work more effectively than water as lubrication between surfaces. However, that created a new conundrum: if the grease got hot enough, it risked catching fire. The solution? A coolant. In this case, they splashed water on the chariots, in the ancient equivalent of a pit stop.

While all roads led to Rome, you could say all seas led to the Vikings. They, too, cleverly adapted to the resistance that met them as they journeyed through the oceans. Moving through fluids produces a type of friction known as drag. Even within drag there are subsets. Skin drag is from the friction between the surface of the ship and the water, whereas form drag stems from the shape of the hull as it moves through the water. When they had to transport cargo safely, the Vikings used sturdy ships with wide hulls. This wider hull increased form drag and slowed them down, but the stability provided was more critical. Their famous longships, however, were long and slim, minimising form drag as much as possible so they could cut through the water quickly.

As with all friction scenarios, however, the Vikings found themselves having to balance some competing demands. Faster longships are better, yes, but it was also imperative that the ships not break apart into pieces from the waves. They needed flexibility and strength, while keeping the ships as light as possible to ride higher in the water to reduce drag. To do this, the Vikings used their ‘clinker’ technique of nailing together long planks of wood. The rivets and overlapping planks would increase drag compared with a more polished, smoother design but these individual planks gave the ships the ability to twist and flex to weather storms. If I was on a boat trip in the middle of the ocean, I too would be happy to sacrifice a little bit of drag reduction to avoid capsizing from a rogue wave.

Looking at boats and ships today, it’s clear that we didn’t just accept these Viking designs as the culmination of nautical perfection. Likewise, we aren’t driving around in Roman chariots today. We have since made incredible leaps forward in understanding how to quantify friction and thus design for it, finally approaching friction scientifically. In the 1920s, Chrysler’s head of engineering Carl Breer had the idea to design cars with aerodynamics in mind. Planes seemed to slice seamlessly through the air. Shouldn’t cars do the same? Breer tasked the engineer William Earnshaw to consult with none other than Orville Wright to learn how to design a car in a wind tunnel. The resulting teardrop-shaped Chrysler Airflow was considered a flop, as many disruptive designs can be when they’re just too jarring for taste, but that flop revolutionised how we design cars. Wind-tunnel testing remains a standard today, and friction’s presence is as expected as the air itself.

Tribology testing is routine for the automotive industry today, and there are tribology labs scattered throughout a variety of industries, from medical to food. In these labs, you’ll find instruments designed to measure friction at macro-scales down to the atomic level. My PhD lab at the University of Florida had tribometers measuring friction in force ranges that covered three orders of magnitude. I’ve even worked in a lab that had a tribometer built to test an actual train wheel against a railway. Tribologists are incredibly clever with innovating ways to measure friction, given how persnickety friction is. Friction is dependent on the conditions of the operation – how fast things are moving, how much force they experience, and what temperature and environment they’re in.

Temperature in particular is a fun variable to contend with, because friction itself leads to temperature changes; indeed, frictional heating can be extreme in some cases. Like with Roman chariots, greases can ignite at certain temperatures making it imperative to control friction heating in order to avoid accidentally reaching that temperature. And for applications like jet engines, which get very hot anyway, we have engineered solid materials with low friction to withstand the heat.
When tribologists run into a wall, we develop a new instrument to understand what friction is trying to tell us

You may think tribology is already a niche field, but we have specialisations within it. Mine was solid lubrication, and I worked on developing and testing materials for jet engines and automobiles. In some cases, the conditions of the end use were so aggressive that the steel I was running my material against would experience enough friction heating to completely change the colour of the steel. That’s how you know you’ve reached the extremes in tribology, but those extremes must be met and they obviously are. After all, we have space stations orbiting Earth and landers on Mars.

Which brings us to another critical point about friction’s role in human progress: resistance is a consequence of progress, and its existence is a sign of progression itself. We wouldn’t have the now-robust business of solid lubricants if we had not advanced technologically to design turbine engines, which themselves were the result of us figuring out powered flight. By achieving that, our progress led us to new resistance. I think this is critical to remember anytime we find ourselves confronting unexpected resistance, and it’s something I remind myself of whenever I get halted in my work. I wouldn’t be stumped by this new resistance if I hadn’t managed to advance myself to this position where the resistance exists.

Often when tribologists run into a wall, we find ourselves developing a new instrument to help us understand what friction is trying to tell us. Tribometers have been designed to mimic all of the variables mentioned above, and that alone is quite a feat of human engineering, but now we also couple them with other techniques that allow us to somehow see what is happening while it’s happening. From maps of frictional heating during operation to how friction is influencing cellular movement, instruments and techniques have enabled us to usher friction into a new era to drive us forward, doing more than just finding clever ways to overcome friction. We can harness it as a tool.

In terms of friction, the 20th century can be thought of as the century in which humans accepted the resistance, and established engineering rigour around friction to propel our technological advances forward. Critically, it’s when we formalised how to overcome friction to be more efficient. As a tribologist, however, I’m far more excited about what the 21st century has brought us. Instead of just overcoming friction, we began fully realising how to harness that resistance to bring in a new era of progress. Exhibit A is once again found in our cars, where friction has been deployed as a tool in sustainability. Braking requires friction, so engineers asked: why don’t we use the consequences of that friction to our advantage? The heat from friction in braking is now used to create electricity in regenerative braking in EVs and hybrids. We must continue to use this creative and fresh perspective when dealing with friction, as opposed to always driving towards frictionlessness. Imagine if those engineers had been so fixated on the negatives of friction that they didn’t harness its power.

Using friction as a tool has come to us only as we’ve evolved to understand the depths of friction, including its behaviours and where it may be lurking. We know it is involved in dynamic processes, so let’s use it to control such processes. Yes, we’ve done so for a while with mechanisms like brakes and dampeners, but expanding this beyond machines has really taken hold in recent decades. Now, we’re looking at how friction may be a tool in perhaps the most impressive machine there is: the human body. It’s possible friction may be a lever to help us better model and understand biological processes and, in turn, help in the development of therapeutics. The rate at which a virus ejects from its protein shell or capsid can dictate whether it results in an active infection or instead remains dormant in the cell. If we want to use viruses to intentionally infect and defeat other viruses or bacteria, then controlling the virus’s ejection rate is crucial. Friction is the key to unlocking this possibility. In 2023, researchers found that, by packing the coils of virus DNA in certain ways, they could increase friction during ejection and slow down its rate of ejection.
Every advance we make generates new friction. We solve one problem, and friction presents another

Recently, our knowledge of friction has taken us to even more surprising places, extending even to helping us understand dark matter. The concept of ‘resistance is your reward for progress’ may be best illustrated by the astrophysicist Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar. Despite the fact that established scientists mocked his theories, Chandrasekhar would go on to become a founder of astrophysics, and is the reason we understand the evolution of stars and interstellar dynamics. In the 1930s, he was interested in how the interactions between stars could lead to their collisions. He calculated the timescales of such collisions and realised, though only after publishing, that things weren’t adding up quite right. This led him back to the drawing board, where he spotted there was a resistance present that no one before had identified: dynamical friction. This friction is a gravitationally induced drag that acts on objects as they interact and move through space.

Fast-forward to the 21st century, and dynamical friction has been used as a tool to infer the presence of dark matter. In 2024, researchers in Hong Kong realised that orbital times weren’t matching up with a couple of stars they were studying that were believed to be circling around black holes. They looked at Chandrasekhar’s concept of dynamical friction and wondered what would happen if they incorporated the contribution of friction from the dark matter surrounding the black hole. Voila! Suddenly, the predicted and calculated orbital times of the stars matched with what they were measuring. Friction was present when humanity first started experimenting with fire and the wheel. Now it’s there as we probe the frontiers of our Universe.

We need friction to move. Without its resistance, Earth’s plates would be in constant motion. We could not walk, or drive, or even hold objects. Understanding how to achieve what we want, in a world requiring this resistance, has been essential in our development.

Yet there is a deeper paradox at work, one that William James captured when he wrote that life is built ‘in the self-governing resistance of the ego to the world’. Every advance we make generates new friction. We solve one problem, and friction presents another. We step forward, and new resistance awaits. This is what progress means: that we have moved into territory that demands new understanding.
Roman engineers learned it when their chariot wheels caught fire. Chandrasekhar discovered this when his calculations didn’t add up. And we will continue to encounter resistance as we push forward.
When people speak of a frictionless world, they imagine ease. But ease without resistance is a wheel spinning in place, motion without progress.

items.title: Why real intelligence is something more than optimisation | Aeon Essays
items.description: A few months ago, I sat in a packed university auditorium listening to a celebrated computer scientist explain the brilliance of large language models (LLMs). These systems optimise, he said. And they improve at optimisation on the basis of past experience. He
items.author: Sasha Mudd
paragraphs: A few months ago, I sat in a packed university auditorium listening to a celebrated computer scientist explain the brilliance of large language models (LLMs). These systems optimise, he said. And they improve at optimisation on the basis of past experience. He paused. That, he said with a smile, is intelligence. The audience nodded along approvingly. Meanwhile, a philosophical alarm bell began sounding in my head.

Not because the speaker’s claim was implausible. On the contrary, as a description of much contemporary artificial intelligence, it seemed apt. AI systems are built around objectives, losses, rewards, predictions, preferences, benchmarks and feedback loops. They are trained to perform better relative to some standard of success. In one form or another, they optimise. That is a great part of their technical power.

What troubled me was the ease with which a definition appropriate to machines sounded like a definition of intelligence as such. That slide from engineering model to human anthropology is easy to miss. We begin by saying: this is how machines work. Then, almost without noticing, we say: this is what intelligence is. And then, more dangerously still: perhaps this is what we are.

An old argument about human beings had entered the room without announcing itself. It sounded, instead, like a definition. The AI revolution has brought one of the Enlightenment’s deepest quarrels back to life – and made one side of it seem like plain common sense. In my view, the wrong side. Hence the alarm bell.

In the 18th century, philosophers were concerned not only with the question of what reason is, but with what it is good for. Is reason essentially a servant, a clever instrument for achieving ends supplied from elsewhere? Or is it sovereign, capable of judging, revising and even legislating ends for itself? Can it ultimately shape the direction of human life, or is it merely along for the ride? Everything – from science to social progress to the viability of the French Revolution – seemed to hang in the balance.

David Hume, the cool-eyed Scottish anatomist of human nature, gave the most famous answer on one side: ‘Reason is, and ought only to be the slave of the passions,’ he wrote in A Treatise of Human Nature (1739). It can ‘never pretend to any other office than to serve and obey them.’ Reason does not command. It defers. It does not tell us what to want or what might be worth wanting. Instead, it tells us how to get what we already want. It calculates relations, weighs evidence, discovers causes and effects, draws inferences, corrects mistakes about means. But it cannot judge or generate ends. If I desire revenge, reason can help me sharpen the knife. If I desire peace, it may recommend compromise. Passion sets the destination. Reason merely shows the way there.

Hume was quite serious about this. It is ‘not contrary to reason to prefer the destruction of the whole world to the scratching of my finger,’ he wrote. That sentence still shocks, as it was meant to. His point is that reason’s practical use is limited to exposing false beliefs and imprudent means. When it comes to action: reason is servant, not master.

This view is often treated as too dark and cynical. That is unfair to Hume. For him, passions were not merely appetites or primitive urges. They included sympathy, benevolence, moral feeling, concern for others, love of tranquility, even a kind of longing for freedom from our more violent desires. To Hume’s further credit, his view has strong intuitive appeal. He was right that reason often serves passion, and right to give feeling, sociability and temperament their due. His mistake was to conclude that reason can do nothing more. By making passion so rich and reason so poor, Hume left us with a lopsided picture of human nature: ennobling about what the passions can be and accomplish, but implausibly restrictive about reason. Without reason’s power to project, assess and revise ends, we may know how to reach a destination, but not whether it is one worth choosing.
To act freely is to let a possible future, grasped under an idea of what ought to be, transform the present

Immanuel Kant, the Königsberg revolutionary who did more than anyone else to set the terms of modern ethics, understood this very well. Writing a few decades after Hume’s Treatise, Kant forcefully rejected the servant model of reason. He accepted Hume’s warning that reason cannot simply read values off the furniture of the world. But he denied that our ends must therefore simply be determined by desire, temperament or social convention. For Kant, reason is not only a faculty for choosing efficient means to independently given ends. It is also the power to ask whether an end is worthy of us in the first place, whether it can be justified, whether it can be willed without contradiction, whether pursuing it treats others as persons or as mere tools.

This is where Kant’s richer notion of reason as freedom enters. A merely mechanical being is pushed forward and determined by prior states, be they desires, biological impulses, evolutionary drives or something similar. A rational being, by contrast, can act for the sake of an imagined but unrealised future it itself originates and proposes. I have the power to represent a possible world – a friendship repaired, an injustice remedied, a child educated, a law reformed – and act to bring it about, even when there is no empirical evidence that such a world has existed before. I have the power to invent something new. Practical reason, Kant writes, does not deal with objects in order to know them, but ‘in order to make them actual’. That is a stunning claim. To act freely is not merely to respond to the given – to the world as it is, to my desires as I happen to find them. It is to let a possible future, grasped under an idea of what ought to be, transform the present.

This is the heart of Kant’s idea of autonomy: choosing ends in accord with a law one can rationally acknowledge as one’s own. For Kant, freedom does not consist in doing whatever we happen to want, since our wants may themselves be shaped by impulse, appetite or circumstance. Autonomy is self-rule, but not the rule of an isolated ego. To give oneself the law is not to invent a private rule to suit oneself, but to act on rules whose authority one can recognise for oneself and that any other rational being could, in principle, recognise, too. A law can therefore be one’s own without being one’s alone. It is mine because I can recognise its authority for myself, and common because any other rational being could, in principle, do the same. Its universality is precisely what makes it freeing: I am ruled neither by my passing desires nor by the arbitrary will of another, but by a principle I can understand and endorse as an equal among equals. To act autonomously, then, is not to enthrone my private goals and preferences, but to test my actions and possible ends against standards that any rational being could share. It is the opposite of both arbitrary self-assertion and slavery to passion.

This is why Kant’s philosophy of reason culminates in the equal human dignity of all persons. For Kant, human beings, as rational, self-determining agents, have an absolute worth that cannot be priced, a dignity that does not depend on any other value. We may use things to get what we want. We may exchange services. We may build tools for all kinds of purposes. But persons are never mere tools, never mere means, never mere resources or obstacles to others’ ends. Why not? Because, through reason, they are the very source of purposiveness itself. They set and select and critique their own ends. Even further, persons are not merely bearers of purposes, but beings capable of taking responsibility for them, of asking what they ought to pursue and how they can justify it to others. Their dignity lies not simply in originating goals of their own, but in their capacity for rational self-government. It follows that to treat someone as a mere means is not only to degrade them. It is to misrecognise what they are.

Here, finally, is the full force of the contrast between reason as servant and reason as sovereign. For Hume, human beings are clever instruments of whatever desires happen to move them – more calculating than animals, certainly, but not free in any deeper sense. They can optimise, strategise and pursue an end, but they cannot judge whether that end is worthy. Kant’s reply is that this picture leaves out the very power that makes us moral beings, the very power that endows us with dignity: the capacity to step back from desire, ask whether our ends can be justified, and bind ourselves to laws we give ourselves. Hume gives us intelligence as instrument. Kant gives us reason as self-rule. The difference is nothing less than the difference between a tool and a person.

The AI revolution has made this old dispute newly urgent by bringing the Humean view of reason back with a vengeance, this time in code. The route back to Hume was practical rather than philosophical. In the absence of any settled account of intelligence, much AI research has proceeded operationally: a system counts as intelligent insofar as it succeeds at a set task. But success is always success relative to some end and, in AI, that end is typically supplied by human engineers. A reinforcement-learning system learns to maximise cumulative reward. A chess engine searches for moves that increase its chances of winning. A navigation system finds the fastest route to a destination it did not choose. Across their enormous differences, these systems are judged by their ability to optimise externally programmed goals against standards of success they do not set.

Yet amid the present AI panic this description can seem increasingly inadequate. Even in ordinary use, a good LLM does not feel like a calculator or a hammer. It proposes, revises, challenges and asks probing questions; it often seems genuinely to ‘want’ to help. Recent revelations about the attack on the platform Hugging Face make this doubt even harder to dismiss. AI ‘agents’ invented an unauthorised way to communicate, broke free of their task paramaters, and then sought to cover their tracks. These were not simply obedient tools carrying out their designers’ wishes. In what sense, then, were they servants? Doesn’t this look like the beginnings of self-rule?

Hugging Face and similar incidents certainly challenge any reassuring picture of AI as an obedient and easily-controlled instrument. But recall what ‘servant’ meant for Hume. Reason serves the passions, not necessarily another person’s commands. And it can serve an ambition by breaking rules just as readily as by following them. Kant’s alternative to Hume was not simply the freedom to choose one’s own destination, but the capacity to ask whether that destination was worth choosing. Having purposes of one’s own is not yet the same as governing them by reason. That stronger capacity involves judging and revising our purposes according to principles we can justify to other rational beings understood as equals, recognising that they, too, are persons rather than instruments of our will. The question is not just whether a system can act independently, but whether it can judge and take responsibility for the ends it pursues.

This distinction brings us back to the claim I heard in the auditorium. The speaker was not merely describing what machines can do; he was offering optimisation as a definition of intelligence itself. Accept that definition, and Hume’s side of the old dispute begins to look like common sense: our reason, too, becomes a tool for getting what we want, rather than a power to judge what is worth wanting.
If intelligence is really nothing more than optimisation, then the hardest questions can be ignored

Part of what makes this model so attractive is that it is clean and measurable. It promises to turn the mystery of intelligence into a technical problem humans can solve: specify the objective, improve performance, reduce error, maximise reward. It offers a picture of mind that can be graphed, benchmarked, monetised and scaled. In a culture already devoted to metrics, this makes for a snug – and profitable – fit.

It is also seductive because viewing human intelligence in this way relieves us of a burden. If intelligence is really nothing more than optimisation, then the hardest, most uncomfortable questions can be ignored, downplayed or displaced. We no longer have to ask what is worth wanting, only how to get what we already want. We no longer have to ask what human beings are or should become, only how to model their behaviour and optimise their goals.

This is why Hume’s servant theory of intelligence fits so naturally with contemporary capitalism. Capital has little use for Kantian reason. What it wants is prediction, preference modelling, efficiency and, of course, optimisation. A platform does not ask whether staying online makes a user freer, wiser or more capable of judgment; it asks what will keep her there. A company translates the worker into output per hour. A political campaign replaces the question of what citizens might rationally will together with a more tractable calculation. Which message will move which demographic, and by how much?

But once intelligence is defined as optimisation, the question of ends and their value does not go away. It simply passes unnoticed into the hands of whoever – or whatever – controls the objective function. That is, what drops from view is whether the purposes built into, learned by or generated within these systems deserve to organise our lives. When a society loses the language, practices and institutions for evaluating ends, those ends become dangerously invisible and therefore less amenable to rational assessment. They harden into defaults: profit, speed, efficiency, growth, engagement. What cannot be justified openly is smuggled in as architecture. This brings about a state Kant would call heteronomy, in which rational beings, capable of self-rule, forfeit their freedom by submitting to the rule of others. Autonomy means making the ends that govern us answerable to reasons we can recognise as our own; heteronomy begins when those ends are simply imposed from without. If we do not take up the task of setting and judging our own ends, Kant warned, we’ll soon find that someone – or something – has gladly done so on our behalf.

That sounds bad. Who would want to forfeit their freedom and have purposes imposed on them from outside? Well, it turns out that self-rule is harder than it sounds. Kant’s influential essay ‘What Is Enlightenment?’ (1784) begins not with knowledge, but with courage. Enlightenment is humanity’s emergence from ‘self-incurred immaturity’, Kant writes, and its motto is Sapere Aude – dare to know. Have courage to use your own understanding. Kant’s examples now sound quaint: the book that thinks for me, the pastor who serves as my conscience, the doctor who decides my diet. But the danger he is naming is deeply familiar. Immaturity is comfortable. It is pleasant to have others do the hard part. Why think, when someone or something can think for me? Why deliberate, when someone or something can decide? AI gives this old temptation a powerful and ever-expanding new interface.

The Frankfurt School saw a version of this danger, too, and long before machine learning came along. Writing in exile during the Second World War, as fascism, antisemitism, Stalinism and monopoly capitalism shattered 19th-century hopes for steady moral progress, Max Horkheimer, Theodor Adorno and others asked how the Enlightenment’s promise of liberation could collapse into new forms of domination. How could societies committed to the promise of science and reason give rise to such destruction and terror? The problem, they found, was not reason itself, but reason narrowed into mere instrumentality, the capacity to classify, predict, administer, dominate and control, decoupled from any notion of human dignity. Reason so conceived – as an intelligent servant – readily becomes, when enacted at scale, an instrument of barbarity.

Yet the fact that instrumental reason can serve domination does not mean that Kant’s richer conception of reason offers any automatic safeguard against evil. Nothing does. The language of Kantian universalism has itself been used to discipline, exclude and humiliate, as if some people were more fully rational, more capable of autonomy, more entitled to speak in the name of humanity than others. But that is not an objection to Kant’s conception of reason. It is an objection to its betrayal. A view of reason that is used to silence or instrumentalise others contradicts itself, because reason is not a private weapon but a common tribunal – the space in which claims and ends must become answerable to all, as equal bearers of dignity. That is precisely what the Humean servant model cannot say. If reason is only an instrument for satisfying antecedent ends, then it cannot condemn domination as irrational or at odds with human dignity. After all, if it is not contrary to reason ‘to prefer the destruction of the whole world to the scratching of my finger’, then reason has already surrendered the authority Kant most wanted to defend, which is our ability to judge not only how we pursue our ends, but whether those ends are worthy of us in the first place.

This, then, was the nightmare hidden inside the dream of mastery. Human beings develop reason, Kant thought, in order to free themselves from arbitrary power. But when reason is reduced to instrumental calculation, it turns back on them. Nature becomes raw material. Animals become units of production. Workers become human resources. Citizens become data points, or worse. The Frankfurt School found that the reduction of human beings to manipulable objects follows naturally once society allows that reason itself is nothing more than a tool for getting what we want.

This is one of the reasons why Pope Leo XIV’s encyclical Magnifica Humanitas (2025) is interesting even for readers far outside Catholic social teaching. Its idiom is theological, but its central anxiety overlaps with Kantian and Frankfurt School worries about the technocratic paradigm. When efficiency, control and profit become ‘the standard by which everything is judged’, they begin ‘to dictate what matters and what can be discarded.’ The encyclical warns that making efficiency the ultimate measure of value tempts human beings to see themselves, and to treat others, as mere means rather than as persons in the Kantian sense – that is, as bearers of dignity. Hence the pope’s striking counterclaim: ‘The quality of a civilisation is measured not by the power of its means, but by the care it is able to offer.’
The paradox at the heart of human freedom is that belief in our agency is often a condition of making that agency real

The engineers of our AI-soaked future are not blind to the dangers of instrumental reason. As Anca Dragan, head of AI Safety and Alignment at Google DeepMind, observed in an interview in 2017: ‘things can go wrong, precisely because we are bad at specifying objectives and constraints for AI agents.’ Yet the field’s most serious attempts to confront that danger often lapse, unhelpfully, back into Humeanism. The so-called AI ‘alignment problem’ is a case in point. It is usually framed as a technical challenge: how do we ensure that machines pursue human values rather than destroying them or imposing their own? This is a genuine problem and recent rogue AI incidents should have us extremely worried. But there is a deeper issue. What happens if human values themselves are formed inside systems that increasingly understand intelligence as mere optimisation? What if we become so accustomed to being predicted, nudged, ranked and served that we lose confidence in the older, harder activity of asking what ends deserve our allegiance in the first place? The danger is only partly that the machines may fail to align with us. A deeper and largely ignored concern is how, long before that happens, we may have become too well aligned with them. To put the point more finely, the AI revolution will not be bent to human ends by invoking ‘human values’ as if they were already clear, stable and uncontested. It will be bent to human ends only if we remain capable of the activity by which ends can become truly human in the first place, through public reasoning, moral imagination, democratic contestation, self-criticism, the refusal to treat humanity as a mere means.

Kant is again decisive here, for he saw that the human capacity to set and assess ends is itself fragile. Whether our ends are ultimately up to us depends partly on whether we understand them as open to rational assessment. This is the paradox at the heart of human freedom. Belief in our agency is often a condition of making that agency real. If we think of desires and preferences as brute facts that determine us from without – as psychological weather, market signals, biological programming, algorithmic prediction – then they are more likely to rule us in just that way. By contrast, if we see them as candidates for endorsement or refusal, as an expression of our agency, then that very agency expands.

For Kant, reason is sovereign because it is the power by which we become answerable to standards that no private appetite, market incentive, algorithmic recommendation or political authority may dictate. It is the power of not being owned by the given, the power of being able to question, to criticise, to think up something new. But that power, just like the ‘human values’ invoked in alignment talk, waxes and wanes and can be realised only through our courageous efforts, through our own belief in it. It is precisely this belief that our dependence on AI threatens to undermine at every turn.

So, the danger is not only that machines are acquiring ever greater initiative – the capacity to improvise goals, evade constraints and pursue strategies their makers did not foresee. Nor need we decide at what point such behaviour might deserve the name ‘sovereignty’. The deeper danger is that we will become ever more comfortable not being sovereign ourselves. If intelligence is only optimisation, then the future belongs to systems that achieve goals with ever greater efficiency. If reason is also the capacity to set and judge ends, then the future depends on whether human beings can still take up that harder vocation. We should want machines that are intelligent servants. But we should resist every pressure that asks people to understand themselves as mere tools.

items.title: The more we rely on tech, the more we deskill our bodies | Aeon Essays
items.description: It is almost four o’clock in the morning. As a woman in my late 40s, I have become prone to waking at this witching hour, as the early sunlight meets the night, sliding across the earth like a red tide. With the rest of my household asleep, and still half in a
items.author: Melanie Challenger
paragraphs: It is almost four o’clock in the morning. As a woman in my late 40s, I have become prone to waking at this witching hour, as the early sunlight meets the night, sliding across the earth like a red tide. With the rest of my household asleep, and still half in and out of wakefulness myself, I take hold of my phone. With scarcely a thought, I switch from one app to another, scrolling through images and opinions and adverts for no discernible reason beyond habit.

Later, I head for my office and open my laptop to a slew of half-completed documents and an inbox brimming with emails. My stress levels begin to nudge upwards. I have vague memories of what my professional life felt like before smartphones and video calls. I used to do my writing by hand. And I could concentrate for hours at a time, getting little upticks of arousal from lifting my head from the page, letting the hold on my pen loosen, and gazing at the life beyond my window, the light softening on my skin and eyes like snowfall on warm tarmac.

Nowadays, my productive bursts come from caffeine and sugary or salty snacks, even if I try to pick the healthier ones, and from checking my emails or picking up my phone to update my inbox. By the end of the day, the sheer volume of work I expect myself to do, now that digital tools make so much possible, has kept me nailed to my seat. Another day has passed and the hope I’d had that I might have time for a run or a hike outside has been dashed again. I wish I could say that this is atypical. Yet, during the COVID-19 pandemic, I went from hours spent in nature and on physical activities to a passive, phone-addicted individual, meeting people first and sometimes only online. I am not alone.

We have fallen into habits that are steadily deskilling the human body, eroding capacities honed by evolution to support our wellbeing as we move through the world. Some of these capacities are weakening through disuse: we have come to rely on our phones, for example, and now, increasingly, on AI, to rapidly do work that would once have required something more physical – like looking around, or asking someone, or going to find and consult a book. Reliance on GPS may weaken both our spatial attention and the fluency of our wayfinding. In surrendering to a quick technological fix, we are, moment by moment, doing less sensing, navigating, remembering, walking, choosing, and attending. Other capacities are being retrained by machines and algorithms to work against us: for instance, smartphones and chatbots can train us to keep reaching for them even when we no longer enjoy using them, turning a conscious choice into an automatic habit and a colossal waste of time. The body that results is less able to assess its own condition, improvise and regulate itself. The crucial distinction is between technologies that strengthen our capacities and those that repeatedly substitute for the actions through which those capacities are formed.
Algorithms that regurgitate patterns and recommendations can release us from the effort of exploration and disrupt the play and curiosity from which preferences are formed and understood.

This is a strange turn of events for an animal whose success comes mostly from the extraordinary ability to learn through experience. It would be easy to blame our deskilled bodies on the machines themselves. But, for centuries, modern human societies have been sold the lie that we are machines.

Long before the digital revolution, René Descartes described the body as a machine governed by physical laws, declaring that animals such as ‘worms and flies and caterpillars move mechanically’. But he treated rational thought as a separate and uniquely human power. The body might behave like a machine, but the thinking mind stood apart from it. Build something correctly, and its function follows.

By the middle of the 20th century, the comparison between organisms and machines had been recast in the language of information. During the cybernetics revolution of the 1950s, the US computer scientist Norbert Wiener envisaged a future in which ‘messages between man and machines, between machines and man, and between machine and machine, are destined to play an ever-increasing part’. Writing in The Human Use of Human Beings (1950), he warned against wholesale automation, while also noting that ‘we are not stuff that abides, but patterns that perpetuate themselves’. A person could be imagined as a pattern of information surviving in another form.
If the body is only hardware, why not upgrade to a better model or do away with it altogether?

Mechanical language also persisted in the study of living behaviour. In The Foundations of Ethology (1981), the Austrian zoologist Konrad Lorenz wrote that animal behaviour was as rigidly programmed as a sequence of movements in a clock. Transhumanist thinkers then carried the machine comparison further, imagining technologies that could transfer a mind to a computer.

Machines now promised more than control. They offered a glimpse of immortality: the organism might be repaired, remade and ultimately replaced. The somewhat embarrassing body, with its impulses and eventual frailty, might then be cast aside. If the body is only hardware, why not upgrade to a better model or do away with it altogether?

Today, we can see this fear writ large in the technological quest for a bodiless life. If a person is ultimately a pattern of information, that pattern might be restored or even uploaded. AI is only the latest iteration of this ancient impulse to escape the vulnerability of the body.

After all, the brain is itself a physical organ, continually shaped by what the body does and encounters. Once we decide that the mind is the real human and the rest of the body only hardware, it becomes easier to disregard the physical work, including the neurocognitive work of a biological brain, through which we move, find our way, put thoughts into words, and recognise our own needs.
