items.title: Prince William Declares His Love for Christopher Nolan Movies and ‘The Traitors’ in Surprise Appearance on ‘The Graham Norton Show’
items.description: Prince William has made a surprise appearance on Graham Norton’s sofa, where he admits he’s a “big fan” of director Christopher Nolan and gameshow “The Traitors.”
items.author: K J Yossman
paragraphs: Prince William has made a surprise appearance on Graham Norton’s sofa, where he admits he’s a “big fan” of director Christopher Nolan and gameshow “The Traitors.”

The episode, which was recorded on Thursday and will air in the U.K. on Friday, sees His Royal Highness the Prince of Wales (to give him his full title) grace the famous red sofa alongside Cate Blanchett, Hannah Waddingham and conservationist Robert Irwin.
All Norton’s guests this week are involved in the Earthshot Prize, which William spearheads.
Jorja Smith also appeared on the show, performing live before joining the other guests on the sofa.
During his appearance, the British royal told Norton he switches off with “music and film.”

“I love getting immersed in deep-thinking films,” William told the talk-show host. “I like action films too, but I like something a bit different. I’m a big fan of everything Christopher Nolan does. His films are fantastic – ‘The Dark Knight’ series is psychologically dark and deep and I absolutely love that. He takes concepts that are completely out there and makes them incredibly entertaining.”

William also revealed he watches “The Traitors” with his two youngest children, Princess Charlotte and Prince Louis. “I love it, the family love it. Charlotte and Louis are obsessed with it. It’s really good telly,” he said. “I saw [‘Celebrity Traitors’ contestant] Ross Kemp the day after the first episode and I couldn’t help but try – in the most appropriate way – to touch him to see what reaction I got from him. Turns out he was really jumpy!”

Asked if he ever fantasized about having any other job William said: “I did want to be a policeman when I was younger, I thought I could make a good one. And then I went through a phase of wanting to be a DJ – I wasn’t very good.”
As well as sharing some insight into the Earthshot Prize and his family life, William helped act as a judge for audience members who came up to the stage to tell their funniest stories.

items.title: James Bond Final Screen Tests Are Happening This Week
items.description: The crowning of the next James Bond is upon us.
items.author: Ellise Shafer
paragraphs: The crowning of the next James Bond is upon us.

Final screen tests for Amazon MGM Studios‘ new 007 are set to happen in the next week, sources tell Variety, beginning as early as Friday. Though who exactly will test is up in the air, Callum Turner and Jack Lowden appear to be in the mix.
Reps for Turner, Lowden and Amazon MGM did not immediately respond to Variety‘s request for comment.

Denis Villeneuve is set to direct the new Bond movie for Amazon MGM, with casting extraordinaire Nina Gold helming the audition process. A timeline has still not been given for when Amazon will officially name its next Bond, though the expectation is before the end of the year.

Turner and Lowden have each had their moment in the Bond rumor mill, with Lowden recently moving to the forefront. Speculation reached fever pitch when the Scottish actor’s “Slow Horses” co-star Gary Oldman appeared to suggest that Lowden had made the shortlist. Lowden’s wife, Saoirse Ronan, later weighed in on the buzz, saying that it’s “not really a subject that’s coming up in our house.”

British star Turner was a favorite for the spy earlier this year, with fans even fantasizing about the possibility of a Bond theme song by his wife Dua Lipa. While promoting arthouse film “Rosebush Pruning” at Berlin Film Festival in February, he was immediately asked about the rumors. “It’s very early for that question,” Turner said with a Bond-esque smirk. “I’m not going to comment on it.”

items.title: Quentin Tarantino Shows Off First 17 Minutes of ‘Cliff Booth’ and Explains Decision to Revive Character
items.description: Quentin Tarantino had quite a surprise in store on Friday night.
items.author: Kirsten Chuba
paragraphs: Quentin Tarantino had quite a surprise in store on Friday night.

The filmmaker made an appearance at AFI Fest in Los Angeles for a screening of Once Upon a Time in Hollywood, sitting down for a Q&A afterwards about his hit movie. But just as the night seemed to be wrapping up, Tarantino surprised the crowd at the TCL Chinese Theater with a first look at The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth, showing off the first 17 minutes of the follow-up film.

Tarantino wrote the script for Cliff Booth, with David Fincher stepping in to direct this time around. The new project sees Brad Pitt reprise his Oscar-winning role as stunt double Booth, and is set in 1977, eight years after the events of Once Upon a Time.

Before showing off the footage — which saw Booth working as a cinema projectionist while handling some more unsavory business on the side — Tarantino explained his decision to revisit the character in the first place.

“I tend to not remember good reviews of mine in quotes; I kind of remember the bad reviews in quotes, but I don’t really remember good reviews of mine in quotes. But one quote that I do remember somebody writing about Once Upon a Time in Hollywood, it was like, ‘This seems like the first world Quentin Tarantino has ever created that he would like to live in,’ and there is that aspect,” he told the crowd. “I loved the Cliff Booth character, I loved the way that Brad played him, and there was this aspect of him as sort of like a paperback hero. I could see like a series of paperbacks with Cliff Booth getting involved with this adventure or that adventure or something like that.”

Tarantino continued, “As time went on, I just thought about coming up with a different adventure, getting him in now a misadventure. I wanted to see what would happen with that.” He also noted how immersed he has become in the film’s world — having also written a Once Upon a Time novel — and explained, “I’ve got nothing to do but just invest in this mythology. I invested in it before I did the movie, and then I invested in it in the years since I’ve done the movie, just so I know the mythology. The audience doesn’t need to know everything, but it’s kind of nice that I know everything, and you can trust me that I know it.”

During the conversation Tarantino also revealed that “if I’m going to watch any of my movies, it would be this one,” and it’s a film that he can watch again and again. He added, “Don’t get me wrong, I love my stories. I really, really love my stories, and I invest in my stories. But I kind of like that this doesn’t really have a story. I like that you’re just hanging out with them.”

About to head into rehearsals for his upcoming play, Tarantino explained his current mindset is of being a writer first, as was put into action with opting not to direct Cliff Booth. “As I’m getting older, being a man of letters is more my thing,” he noted, “so screenplays and books and plays — everything except poetry.”
The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth is releasing in IMAX on Nov. 25 and streaming Dec. 23 on Netflix.

items.title: Jamie Lee Curtis Leaning on “Love and Service” in Honoring the Late Rob and Michele Reiner: “Every Day With Them Was Activism”
items.description: Suit up, show up and celebrate the lives, activism and legacy of Rob and Michele Reiner.
items.author: Chris Gardner
paragraphs: Suit up, show up and celebrate the lives, activism and legacy of Rob and Michele Reiner.

That’s how Jamie Lee Curtis is approaching the night of Nov. 8, a date that will find her become the inaugural recipient of the Michele and Rob Reiner Champion for Change Award during the Children’s Institute’s Cape & Gown Gala. It’s an honor created in partnership between the Children’s Institute, its president and CEO Martine Singer (Michele’s sister) and the couple’s children, Jake and Romy Reiner, to recognize the Reiners’ “lifelong commitment to improving the lives of children and families and strengthening communities across Los Angeles, throughout California and beyond.”

When news broke of the honor and that Curtis would be its first recipient, the Oscar winner said she was “deeply honored” to be selected as it’s a testament to the legacy of the late Reiners, a couple she had known for decades and with whom she shared a duty for activism. (She and her husband, Christopher Guest, were also married at Rob’s home in 1984, and he served as the best man.) “They didn’t just create together. They lived a life of service, building something greater than themselves and giving so much to the world around them. And that is something worth honoring again and again,” Curtis said in a statement when she was announced as the award recipient. “The world needs so much more of what they gave us: their love, their courage and their joy. I am forever grateful to carry a small part of their legacy forward.”

She’s hoping that joy surfaces at the upcoming gala. “Rob and Michele’s [lives are] celebratory. They would not want this [event] to be morbid and funerallike. It has to be a celebration,” Curtis told The Hollywood Reporter in a new interview about the award and the Reiners. “So, I’m going to suit up, show up, do my thing, stand there in community and say thank you to them.”

Below, she opens up on how she’s walking through this emotional time by placing a focus on “love and service,” how her appearance at the recent Emmy Awards came to be and the indefatigable nature of the Reiners’ work on a variety of causes: “Every day with them was activism.”
(Read an edited transcript of the conversation below, or listen to an audio version here.)
We’re sitting here at the Children’s Institute on Temple Street in Los Angeles for a special reason.

First of all, this institution has been around for 120 years. They’ve been raising money to help children in the City of Angels for 120 years. That alone is enough to kind of be like, “Whoa.” And, of course, we’re here because the Children’s Institute is run by Martine Singer, the sister of Michele Singer Reiner and sister-in-law of Rob Reiner. We are here at the Children’s Institute specifically because Martine runs the institute and was the sister of Michele Singer Reiner and the sister-in-law of Rob Reiner. Rob and Michele were big supporters of the Children’s Institute, and Martine has been a beautiful, beautiful aunt after that awful experience in December.

Rob and Michele supported the Children’s Institute for years. The institute is having its big event on Nov. 8 and is naming an advocacy award in Rob and Michele’s name. I am the inaugural recipient of that award, and I’m very moved to be so. Today, we came to the institute to be with the children, see more of the programs and have some public conversations about the institute, Rob and Michele and their advocacy for children. Jake Reiner was with me today and did a few press interviews. We’ve been talking about Rob and Michele all day long.

Very emotional. We haven’t had a big public group hug yet. There’s the very small circle of family, then their very closest friends and then the concentric circles that go out from there: friends, colleagues, advocates and, finally, the public: people who just loved his movies, loved his television shows and loved his father. The circle gets wider and wider, and none of us have come together yet to grieve this terrible loss. It’s been an emotional day because I’ve been talking about my relationship with them and talking about them in the past, and it’s only nine months later. It’s been difficult but important because we just want to carry on their work.

We’re also sitting here right after the beautiful moment at the Emmys when you offered some remarks about Rob, and the camera panned to the audience to show how touched people were. And we could see how emotional you were. Now feels like a good time to have this conversation.

I’m obviously a close friend of theirs; we got married at Rob’s house on Dec. 18, 1984. Rob was the best man. My late sister Kelly was my maid of honor. So we are close. Rob is our daughter Annie’s godfather. When Michele married Rob, she and Rob became my daughter’s godparents. We have a closeness, of course. What I’m trying to say is that I felt a responsibility to represent everyone — strangers, fans, colleagues, friends, close friends and family — in that moment at the Emmys. I was fine and happy to do it.

I went to the rehearsal, and they were playing “Bridge Over Troubled Water.” There’s an exercise in grief about desensitizing yourself, so I listened to that song for the next day, trying to get used to it. It’s so moving to me naturally, and then it was sung live. It was very challenging because it was challenging enough to represent everyone and try to honor, in this case, particularly Rob’s passing, but I also have feelings of my own.

I was happy to do it, but it was a little tougher than I anticipated. The way media works, words like “breaking silence” and “first comments after” start being a little strange. I’m here for the Children’s Institute. I’m here to support their work. I’m going to be at the event to support the work that Rob and Michele did, and it shouldn’t be about me. And yet I’ve been the one talking a lot about them. So it’s been a little strange because it’s a very private grief, and yet I’m a public-facing person. I’m trying to walk that line a little bit.

The work of the Children’s Institute is focused on so many pillars of lifting up children and families, with education and literacy chief among them, issues that are also very important to you and your work as a children’s author. How do you wrap your head around the way all of these threads are connected?

Love and service aren’t compartmentalized. They’re expansive. It’s not about me at all. I just read a beautiful book by Ann Patchett called Whistler — the new novel. It’s about impermanence at its core. I’m not a particularly religious person, but I’m sober and it can’t be about me. It has to be about love and service. If we’re just expanding love and service in whatever way we can, that’s what they did, that’s what I try to do, that’s what you try to do. It’s just what we do. It’s what these people do. It’s what Martine does here in this office.
And that’s what you’re doing. I’ll point out that you’re wearing a “Love and Service” pin right now.

I wear it often, particularly when we need to be reminded: What are we doing? What are we doing? I don’t need more attention. I’m pretty comfortable with who I am, and I know who I am pretty honestly. I’ve reached a ripe old age, I’ve had a good amount of psychoanalysis, I’m sober and I’m a grandma. I’m pretty clear that if love and service is at the center of what I do, then I’m good. I can take a little of the energy and appreciate it, and really want to reflect it back onto Rob and Michele and what they dedicated their lives to — the betterment of the world because they were in it.
Do you remember any conversations you had with them about service or activism?

Every day with them was activism. They were enraged at the way the current administration had decimated progressive policies toward children, women, people of color, gay people and transgender people. I mean, don’t even get me started. Rob was a firebrand. I can talk a good game, and I’m a passionate advocate, but Rob had the acumen and the political savvy. I don’t have political savvy. He was able to find common ground with people he disagreed with and was a powerful leader.

Many of the times Rob stepped into that position of power were because Michele Reiner said, “Rob, come on. You can do this. You need to do this.” Much of that advocacy was fueled by Michele saying, “You need to do this.” She was the lighter of that firebrand. She got it hot, and then Robbie took it. That was his great skill, but it was a partnership and that’s just impressive.

Some of the work you do with Children’s Hospital Los Angeles overlaps with the institute. How did you decide that CHLA would be one of the focuses of your activism and advocacy? You’ve raised millions for CHLA through My Hand in Yours, and it’s a hospital you’ve supported for many years.

I was working on a forgettable movie called Grandview, USA, about demolition derby in Pontiac, Illinois. We shot there, and I was in town for 12 weeks, which is a long time. In Pontiac, there was a family whose daughter, Lori Tull, [had one of the first successful heart transplants]. The town was putting on a fundraiser for Lori and her family because, at the time, the insurance company said it was experimental surgery and wouldn’t pay for it. It was an enormous amount of money.

The movie company joined forces with the town because we were there for 12 weeks. We sold kisses at booths; it was like a fair. Lori and I became friends. She ultimately had a second heart transplant at Children’s Hospital of Pittsburgh and died at 19, but we stayed close. I made a connection to that hospital in Pittsburgh and, for many years, went back to work with them. I became friends with another patient named Katie Westbrook, who had bone cancer.

If you’ve ever seen a picture of me in a pink wig, I wear a pink wig when I do children’s hospital work. That was Katie’s wig. She wore it when she lost her hair because of chemotherapy. When she died, her mother gave me the wig. I wear it to remind people: This is what this young girl wore while she was fighting for her life. She was saying to everybody, “Look at me,” because if you’re looking at me in this, you understand that I’m fighting for my life here.

I helped them raise a lot of money at the hospital. When I came back from one of my trips to Pittsburgh, I realized, “Wait, I live in Los Angeles.” I cold-called Children’s Hospital Los Angeles and said, “My name’s Jamie Curtis. I’ve been going back and forth to Pittsburgh and working with them for many years, and I live here. I was born and raised here in the City of Angels. What can I do to help you?”

It was right when one of the propositions was going to be on the ballot — one of the children’s hospital bond acts — and I became the face of it. I said, “Yes, I’ll do whatever you want. Commercials? Sure, let’s do commercials for the children’s hospital bond.” It passed, and it raised hundreds of millions of dollars for various children’s hospitals, including CHLA. That began my advocacy with them.
Can you take me back to getting the call for this award?

Martine, Jake and Romy called me this summer when I was away with my family. Martine had texted, “Can you talk? The kids and I want to talk to you about something.” I didn’t know what it was, obviously, but I said, “Yes, of course.” When I called them, the three of them said, “We want to support Martine and the Children’s Institute in the name of our parents and we would like you to receive the inaugural award in their name.”

Obviously, I said yes. When I got back home, it was about trying to connect more dots here at the institute in a way I hadn’t been able to. I’ve been working a lot, so it’s taken me a minute. But, again, we haven’t had a public gathering. This will feel a little bit like that. By the way, this award conversation predated the Emmys. The Emmys happened about a week after the award was discussed.
How did the Emmys appearance come about?

I don’t think they had really thought it through. The weekend before, Rob won an Emmy, and the entire room stood up. So I think they must have been thinking, “Oh, we haven’t really addressed this yet. It’s tricky.” There were so many people lost this year, particularly in television, who had big careers. It was unexpected. I hadn’t planned on that.
The fact that he got it for The Bear, on which you were ferocious, award-winning and incredible — what a moment.

It was. Rob called me and said, “I’ve been offered a part on The Bear. Should I do it?” And I said, “Yes, Robbie, you should absolutely do it.” I didn’t know how that character was going to fit in or who he would be, because obviously I didn’t know any of that. But my experience on the show was transformational. It was a fantastic writing opportunity and something I had never had the opportunity to do before. So I said, “Yes, you should do it.”
You’ll accept the inaugural Michele and Rob Reiner Champion for Change Award in November. How do you approach a speech?

I’m not that girl. I have a poem I may read. It was given to me as a gift by Moye Thompson, a ceramicist whose work I collect. The poem is called “To Be of Use,” by Marge Piercy. Moye imprinted the words of the poem on a bowl, all the way around it — individual letters, the whole poem. Then she took the poem and broke it into individual words and printed those on little pieces of porcelain. It’s a beautiful art piece: the collective poem, with each individual word inside the bowl.

It’s a beautiful poem about activism, about being of use as a person and about the kind of people I like to know. I looked at that beautiful piece of art the other day and thought, “That’s Rob and Michele right there: to be of use.” Stay out of the way. Be of use. Link up and get dirty. Do your work. Get sweaty.
Is that what you think of when you think of them?

Yes. Just to be of use. It brings back to me the song “That’s Why I’m Here” by James Taylor, where he basically says, “That’s why I’m here.” I think, “Why am I here?” I’m here to be of use, to connect people, whatever it is. It’s just service. Love and service. It goes back to love and service. It always will. At the end of the day, it really does.
Congratulations again on the honor.
Thank you. I’m honored — truly honored. I also have to crack jokes. I want to crack some jokes. I don’t want to …

But it doesn’t have to be. It’s not a memorial. This is a celebration of 120 years of an institution showing up for people from ZIP codes that you and I may never visit in the City of Angels. There are probably areas of this city I’ve never been in, you’ve never been in and may never be in, whose residents can come here and get the services and support the Children’s Institute offers. That alone makes it very important that this is a celebration: a celebration of all the years of people like Martine, all the staff and all the teachers I worked with today in the classroom — everyone coming together to help these people.

Rob and Michele’s [lives are] celebratory. I want to make sure that’s included, too. They would not want this to be morbid and funeral-like. It has to be a celebration. So I’m going to suit up, show up, do my thing, stand there in community and say thank you to them.
Beautiful. And John Mayer is going to perform.
John Mayer’s going to perform, and he’s a great communicator, a great singer and a great lyricist.

Knowing he was going to be there made me wonder what Jamie Lee Curtis listens to when she wants to roll up her sleeves. You mentioned James Taylor, but when you’re either doing the work or want to shut off, what music do you turn on?

I’m eclectic as hell. I listen to everything from John Coltrane to yacht rock. You have to remember, I came of age in 1976, ’77 and ’78. ’70s music — the Eagles. Are you kidding? I’ve seen the Eagles documentary 25 times. It’s three hours, by the way. But I’m eclectic: yacht rock, Coltrane, the Eagles and Wyclef Jean. That was two weeks ago. I randomly listened to Sam Sanders and Wyclef Jean was interviewed by him. I want you to download the Sam Sanders podcast — or whatever radio show it is — and listen to his interview with Wyclef Jean.

Drive back to Santa Monica and listen to it. Then download all of the albums Wyclef Jean has just released. You’re going to hear someone with wildly deep, immersive talent. It knocked me sideways. I’ve been obsessed with Wyclef Jean ever since.

items.title: The Past and Future of Giorgio Armani
items.description: This article was featured in New York’s One Great Story newsletter. Sign up here.
items.author: Chantal Fernandez
paragraphs: This article was featured in New York’s One Great Story newsletter. Sign up here.

Pantaleo Dell’Orco is a shy 73-year-old with a scruffy mustache and round glasses that give him the look of a modish classics professor, one who is rarely out of black or navy clothes. In Milan, where he lives, he is known as Leo, the man who for five decades was Giorgio Armani’s shadow. The two of them shared a palazzo in the stylish Brera neighborhood and worked together at the vast fashion company Armani founded in 1975 and ruled independently as designer and chief executive until his death a year ago at the age of 91. Dell’Orco is now the creative director of menswear and the largest single shareholder in Giorgio Armani S.p.A., which is said to be worth between $6 billion and $8 billion. He is also the chairman of the board, the directors of which include Armani’s nephew Andrea Camerana and niece Silvana Armani, who is in charge of women’s ready-to-wear and haute couture.

In his will, Armani, a famously exacting boss who divvied up his fortune down to every last Andy Warhol and Man Ray, instructed his heirs to either pursue a public offering or sell the company to LVMH Moët Hennessy Louis Vuitton, EssilorLuxottica, or L’Oréal. He gave them a deadline of March 2027 to start the process by selling an initial 15 percent stake.

The question of what happens next to one of fashion’s largest self-made brands has consumed an industry stuck in a multiyear sales slump and beset by change, especially in Italy, where Versace, Gucci, Valentino, and Bottega Veneta have all appointed new creative directors in the last few years with varying degrees of critical and commercial success.

Dell’Orco, who has shunned the limelight for most of his life, is unbothered by the speculation about the future. He has a friendly demeanor and carries himself like someone who knows he doesn’t have to speak too loudly to be heard. In fact, he seems amused by the gossip. “It’s good for the company, the chitchat,” he tells me in August. The following month, the company made its first big move since Armani’s death, hiring Dario Vitale, a 42-year-old Neapolitan who is the most exciting new name in fashion despite having lasted only one season at Versace. He will design the diffusion line Emporio Armani, as well as accessories for the Giorgio Armani label, reporting to Silvana and Dell’Orco. The appointment positions Vitale to one day take over all of Armani and shows that Dell’Orco, like his longtime partner, makes decisions on his own terms.

Dell’Orco and I first meet in May, less than a year after a public wake drew thousands of mourners over the course of two days to Armani’s austere Tadao Ando-designed Teatro. “The whole city was there,” says Carla Sozzani, the magazine editor and founder of the influential boutique 10 Corso Como. “It’s like the king of Milano passed away. He was one of those people that you think are immortal.” Dell’Orco didn’t have much time to grieve. It was weeks away from a 50th-anniversary spectacle, and there was work to be done. “I told myself, ‘I have to be strong,’” he says.

We are at the company headquarters, a 17th-century palazzo on Via Borgonuovo not far from his own. Dell’Orco is leading a design meeting ahead of the spring 2027 collection of the flagship label, which he and Armani designed together. Now he is in charge and his nephew Gianluca Dell’Orco is his deputy. Mood boards line the wall with reference images: loose linen looks from past shoots and runway presentations, Al Pacino in a billowing khaki jacket from the mid-1990s, a sweaty Richard Gere in a nearly sheer white top. At the bottom of one board, a pinned notecard reads DANDY LATINO and LA DOLCE ELEGANZA.

The collection does not appear to stray far from the signature soft-tailored look Dell’Orco helped define, though there are subtle differences: The pants are slimmer, the jackets longer. He is not inclined to stage some kind of flashy runway stunt or drop a surprise collaboration. “Doing something just so people talk, that’s not me,” he says. “I’m not interested in being Prada.”

A refusal to bend to trends served the company’s namesake well. Armani was fully in command of his empire — three stand-alone subbrands making at least six runway collections a year; lines of accessories, beauty, fragrances, furniture; clubs, restaurants, megayachts, and even residential buildings, such as a 12-story condo in Lenox Hill — and felt little obligation to cater to commercial whims besides his own. When he decided to crash the stuffy world of French haute couture with his own version, many were skeptical, but Privé just turned 20 and is said to be one of the most successful lines within the Armani Group.

Those who know Dell’Orco well say he is as single-minded as Armani, who appreciated his candor. “Italian fashion companies are like Renaissance courts,” says one former Armani executive. “They have their prince and the courtiers. Leo would say things to Giorgio other people wouldn’t dare say.”

For many years, Stefano Pilati, who worked with Dell’Orco in the ’90s before he went on to run Yves Saint Laurent and Zegna, was rumored to be the designer to one day take over Giorgio Armani. “I found it almost offensive because it was like a way of saying to Mr. Armani, ‘You should move on,’” he tells me. “Leo is the Armani man, period. Everybody’s waiting for Armani to change somehow, but Armani has never been like this. Modernizing the brand without losing its essence requires great skill. Who else could do it? The minute it’s not Armani, it’s not Armani.”

Sozzani, who met both men in the 1970s, sees Dell’Orco as the last thread connected to the label’s origin story, someone who can’t be easily replaced. “He grew up from a child, almost, with Armani. He was born of Armani. Who else has that knowledge, that experience, that taste?” she says. “Why look for somebody else? To do what, exactly? Stay there for three seasons and then go? The accent changes, the logo changes, the packaging changes.”

An employee since long before American Gigolo and Miami Vice made Armani a global sensation, Dell’Orco has watched the brand move from upstart to powerhouse to something taken for granted by snooty magazine editors and blatantly cribbed by younger designers. He is skilled at tuning out industry talk. “Sometimes I do listen to other people’s opinions. Ninety percent of the time, I decide to do exactly what I would have done anyway,” he tells me. Plus he is not a worrier.

“I am rarely stressed,” he says. Armani himself was the opposite. To the outside world, he was the imperial control freak called “King Giorgio” by the press. But Dell’Orco remembers the private Armani who would often have nightmares before runway shows, tortured by a nagging sense he had something to prove. “He was simple, he was instinctive, he would say exactly the words you wanted to hear. He was perfect at that,” he says.

It is after 3 p.m., and we are at Dell’Orco’s home, where he now lives alone with two cats and an Indian blackbird named Merlino who chirps “buongiorno” and “Giorgio.” He receives me in an immaculate living room with slick black floors and elegant 1930s-style furniture that he is keeping just as Armani intended. Armani’s presence is everywhere. From the corner of my eye, I see his blue eyes gazing out from a Warhol portrait. “The hardest part of all was when he was holding my hand and then suddenly, I could no longer feel his touch. It was absolutely devastating,” Dell’Orco says, his voice catching. He pauses. “Sometimes I still dream about him.” In his imagination, they’re getting ready for another runway show, as they did so many times: “There are clothes everywhere.”

Leo Dell’Orco and Giorgio Armani met in the summer of 1976. Dell’Orco was a tall, handsome, athletic 23-year-old hanging with two friends at a dog park off Via Gerolamo Tiraboschi. The group was debating whether to see a movie or hit a nightclub when a friendly dog, a boxer named Jago, wandered over. He belonged to a 41-year-old man with an intense stare and graying hair. “It was fate,” Armani wrote years later. “It was a particular meeting that could only have happened in that moment,” Dell’Orco says.

Dell’Orco had never heard of the designer, who had founded his business a year earlier with money from the sale of his Volkswagen Beetle. Dell’Orco was a technical draftsman from Puglia working at a large gas company, and soccer was his only interest outside the office.

Armani, meanwhile, had been a stilista since the 1960s, working for Nino Cerruti and designing lines for manufacturers such as Ungaro and Zegna. He ran his burgeoning namesake label with his partner, Sergio Galeotti, who focused on the business side of the operation and had encouraged Armani to strike out on his own shortly after they met at the beachside nightclub Capannina di Franceschi in Forte dei Marmi in the summer of 1966. The relationship was romantic for a time, but as Armani once put it, “the term love is too narrow. We were allies in the face of life and the rest of the world.”

At the dog park, Dell’Orco’s friend struck up a conversation with the designer, who invited them over to his house for an aperitivo. There, he asked if they might be interested in modeling in his upcoming runway show. “I said, ‘Hmmm, why not?’” Dell’Orco says. A few days later, he and a couple of friends showed up at a small studio on Corso Venezia, where a secretary handed them some clothes to try on. One friend was declared too short. Dell’Orco made the cut.

“The whole atmosphere of doing a runway show, the rehearsal, it was all very exciting,” he says. In a photograph in the trade newspaper Footwear News the following spring, Dell’Orco saunters down a runway with a jacket thrown over his broad shoulders, one hand in his pocket. He became a part-time fixture at Armani’s studio, doing odd jobs and helping to develop fabrics.

At the time, French fashion was more popular and prestigious than Italian labels. When Miuccia Prada handed out leaflets for the Italian Communist Party as a college student, she wore Yves Saint Laurent and Courrèges; the business her grandfather started in 1913 made only leather goods then. Armani was part of a competitive cohort of Italian designers, including Gianni Versace and Walter Albini, who challenged French superiority with wearable clothes for Italian yuppies, the paninari. “Milano became the capital of fashion in quite a short time,” says Sozzani, who until the late 1970s was almost always wearing Saint Laurent. “There was this square in Milan, Piazza San Babila, where everyone wore a down jacket, Armani jeans, Timberlands, and an El Charro belt,” Dell’Orco says. “It was a democratic fashion. That is to say, if you were good-looking, it showed.”

From his first collection, Armani’s sales pitch for men was a relaxed, unpretentious style, one he would obsessively refine again and again: unstructured suits made from soft, sensual fabrics such as silky gabardines traditionally used for women. “He invented the sexy suit,” says Gene Pressman, the former co-CEO of Barneys, which introduced the brand to the U.S. “Before that, men didn’t wear greens and browns. They were strictly navy and gray. Armani introduced a whole palette. He used all the wonderful colors of Tuscany. It was very revolutionary.”

At first, Armani’s suits were too avant-garde for most Americans looking for standard-issue office suits. Then, in February 1980, American Gigolo premiered, and Richard Gere turned Armani’s soft jackets and front-pleat trousers into the most seductive thing a successful man could wear. “Wall Street went nuts, and all of a sudden, these young kids were buying ten suits at a time,” says Pressman. “They’d lay out like 30 shirts, 20 ties, all kinds of accessories, and we couldn’t get them on the racks fast enough to go over to the alterations department.”

Months later, Armani staged an elaborate runway show underneath the Prometheus statue outside Rockefeller Center for 1,000 people, including Carrie Fisher and Lauren Hutton. Dell’Orco, on his first visit to Manhattan, modeled. “It was the most over-the-top place, a surreal place. You didn’t understand where you were,” he recalls. “It was exciting, doing the runway show next to Iman.” Emporio Armani launched in 1981, followed by jeans, fragrances, and a children’s line. Revenue tripled to 26 billion lire, the equivalent of $63 million today. “Armani, at that time, was really a god in Milan,” says Pilati. The next year, “Giorgio’s Gorgeous Style” landed on the cover of Time.

Around then, Armani and Galeotti hired some relatives to join a team that had grown to about 100 employees: Silvana, the daughter of Armani’s older brother, Sergio, and two of Galeotti’s nieces. “That marked the turning point. From that moment on, the company became more of a family affair,” says Dell’Orco, who had joined the men’s-design team full time. His relationship with Armani had also evolved. “There are some things that are hard to explain. It happened naturally,” he says. “A 20-year age difference was a lot, but I must be sincere: It’s something that came on its own.” Though it was not publicly discussed, everybody understood Dell’Orco to be especially close to the boss. “Leo was a humble assistant in a superior position because there was a relationship,” says another colleague from the early years of the business. “He learned everything from Armani. He was next to him all the time.”

In 1984, as sales soared, Galeotti was diagnosed with AIDS and sought treatment in New York. Armani visited every month. “A couple of times, I went along as well, and those were not easy visits,” says Dell’Orco. The disease was ravaging the fashion industry, and everyone knew someone affected. The designers Chester Weinberg, Willi Smith, and Roy Halston Frowick would die from AIDS-related illnesses by the end of the decade. Armani threw himself into the business. “During that dreadful year, I lived as if I was holding my breath, without thinking about the inevitable, working day in and day out,” he wrote in his memoir.

Galeotti died in August 1985 at his home outside Paris with members of his family by his side as well as Armani and Dell’Orco. He was 40. The New York Times attributed the cause to a heart attack brought on by leukemia. Armani was bereft. He described Dell’Orco as a great source of comfort: “I will never forget how much he helped me through the sad events surrounding Sergio’s illness, in that undisturbed countryside not far from Paris.”

Resilience was written into the Armani story from the beginning. In his memoir, he described growing up under Mussolini in Piacenza, which was a frequent target of Allied bombing during World War II. The oft-repeated story goes that he was 10, playing with friends on the street, when someone stepped on an undetonated packet of gunpowder, killing one boy and landing Armani in the hospital with severe burns. He never tired of telling people that doctors were convinced he wouldn’t see again. After Galeotti’s death, he felt underestimated once more. He was now the sole owner of a complex and growing company, and he didn’t have a partner to handle business affairs while he designed. A string of key deputies left, and the business seemed troubled. “Many believed I would collapse psychologically,” he wrote.

Instead, Armani took on Galeotti’s job as the head of the finances, assuming a dual business and creative role that he would hold for the rest of his life. The label flourished. “Giorgio never listened to anybody. He knew exactly what he wanted,” says Sozzani. “Until the end of the ’80s, early ’90s, there were five big players in Italy: Valentino, who was in Rome, and in Milano there was Gianfranco Ferré, Krizia, Versace, and Armani.” Today, none except Armani is independent — Versace, a once-formidable competitor, is owned by Prada, and a Qatari investment fund controls 70 percent of Valentino, the famous founder of which died earlier this year; Krizia and Ferré are glorified licenses owned by foreigners. Armani had the foresight to set up highly profitable licensing agreements for makeup and fragrances with L’Oréal and for sunglasses with the eyewear giant Luxottica. Throughout the 1990s, sales grew by double digits every year. And later, he brought manufacturing in-house so as to control a larger share of the profits. Through it all, Dell’Orco was by his side.

“The sense of calm I projected was something he appreciated,” Dell’Orco says. “I was happy there, and the years passed without me realizing it.” He doesn’t even remember when exactly he moved into the palazzo on Via Borgonuovo.

Though they had been together for decades, Dell’Orco remained in the margins of Armani’s public life. He was sometimes mentioned as a close friend in articles, but the news media, especially in Italy, afforded King Giorgio an unusual degree of privacy. Discretion suited Dell’Orco, too. Gay marriage isn’t legal in Italy, but when I ask if he and Armani ever talked about getting married, he shakes his head, as if I were breaking some unspoken rule. Did he feel married? “It is something I never thought, never said.” They were known to bicker over decisions small — hats in a collection, which Armani loved and Dell’Orco less so, or heels, which Dell’Orco preferred over Armani’s usual choice of flats — and big, like the 2004 launch of the activewear line EA7, which Armani initially fought but Dell’Orco knew would sell well.

“Leo is from another generation, so obviously he pushed for younger trends,” says Pilati. “Mr. Armani either took his ideas or said ‘Leo, piss off.’ But even if they were fighting, Leo never bitched about Mr. Armani. That was one of his best qualities. I’ve never seen someone so serene.” Federico Marchetti, the founder of the e-commerce giant Yoox, joined Armani’s board in 2020 and observed their dynamic. “Leo was the person Mr. Armani listened to the most,” he says. “In the middle of all these people saying ‘yes, yes, yes,’ he is someone who sometimes said ‘no.’ He’s that kind of a partner.”

Dell’Orco laughs when I ask about the quarrels with Armani. It took years for him to feel comfortable speaking his mind in the atelier. “Giorgio was, let’s say, more conservative. I wanted to inject a bit of youthfulness into things. Little by little, he came to trust me,” he says. “If we fought at 1 p.m., we would go have lunch after, and for me it had already passed. That’s the thing that made it work. If not, it would have been a whole drama.”

The duo finally took a bow together at the end of a men’s-fashion show in 2021. In matching navy T-shirts, slacks, and white sneakers, they raised clasped hands to a standing ovation from the crowd. Quietly, Armani, long resistant to public discussions about retirement or succession, had made moves to set up the company for the future. In the early aughts, when the luxury industry began to rapidly consolidate, he shared a much-scrutinized cup of tea with Bernard Arnault, the chairman of LVMH, and he came close to selling to what was then known as the Gucci Group, a precursor to Kering, before pulling out at the last minute. “He was very concerned about keeping absolute control over the company, which I respected,” says Domenico De Sole, who was CEO of the Gucci Group at the time.

The fear of losing control never left Armani, and in 2016, he created a foundation to oversee the management of the company, led only by himself, his financial adviser, and Dell’Orco. His will stipulated that the foundation would always retain at least a 30 percent stake in the company to ensure it is run with a series of founding principles, including a creative mandate to maintain “an essential, modern, elegant, and unostentatious style with attention to detail and wearability.” Dell’Orco, who now chairs the foundation, supported the approach, which would guarantee a continuation of what they had built: “He’d say things like, ‘Let’s sell everything!’ and I’d reply, ‘Sell it to whom?’ He never actually meant it.”

The two sometimes fantasized about retirement, but the idea was just as quickly shrugged off. “As long as he was working, he felt good,” Dell’Orco says. “Work was his life. He had no hobbies.” Once, a couple of years ago, Armani asked how much longer he intended to keep going. A decade, Dell’Orco told him. “Look, it’s tough,” Armani warned him. “You worked until you were 90. Why can’t I?” Dell’Orco responded.

Still, they never explicitly discussed Dell’Orco one day becoming chairman of the board and having voting power in the company’s most important decisions. “In a way, deep down, I understood that eventually I would be the one,” he says. “But it’s something I never voiced aloud, nor did I ever put myself forward for it. He figured it out on his own.”

At the end of the summer, Dell’Orco WhatsApps me while on vacation near Mykonos from the family’s 65-meter superyacht Maìn (the nickname of Armani’s mother). Armani preferred Pantelleria: He found Greece too windy, but Dell’Orco appreciates the water here, the local taverns. For once, he is out of his dark uniform, wearing a white T-shirt that highlights his gray hair. Armani would sometimes scold him for wearing other designers, but lately Dell’Orco has been adding to the mix — Rick Owens, Sacai, Comme des Garçons. By his sunburned face, I can tell he has been enjoying his time off. He even went out in Ibiza, though he was taken aback by the looks he saw. “Men are more dressed, and women are much less dressed,” he says. “I want a woman who’s more chic.”

The collection he had first shown me in May was well received during Milan Men’s Fashion Week, where it was presented alongside Silvana’s cruise lineup. Gone were the hats that were the subject of so many arguments with Armani. Shirts and pants looked lived-in, the bags almost beaten up. Fabrics leaned heavily on linen, washed silk, and ultrasoft denim. The styling was more casual, and the models seemed at ease, not like the stiff Italian Ken dolls of the past. It was the most relaxed Armani has looked in years, and still some critics complained that it lacked the cool of labels such as Prada, where punk skinny jeans and leather jackets portended a change in men’s silhouette, or Ralph Lauren’s surprisingly trendy prep maximalism.

From his floating mansion in the Aegean, Dell’Orco isn’t too broken up by the critics, nor is he overly impressed with the season. “I saw that quite a few designers tried to do things that were a bit out there,” he says diplomatically. “I like to stay the course. I don’t push just to push.” For now, that means embracing what the brand does best, like tailoring and suiting, a sound strategy given how popular vintage Armani is on the resale market. Last year, to capitalize on the hype, the label reissued several classic Armani styles, such as single-pleat trousers from 1990 and a double-breasted leather jacket from 1979, for a capsule collection called Archivio. “Giorgio always wanted to create something new so that people talked about him more,” Dell’Orco says. “For him, the suit was too banal. At this moment, I feel we need to get back to it.”

Perhaps more urgent than whether the pants are skinny enough is the looming question of Armani’s ownership. Since we last spoke, a report in La Repubblica suggests the initial 15 percent stake sale could be split among the three preferred suitors, a move that is widely seen as a way to leave open the possibility for a potential majority sale later on. The stake sale might also be delayed beyond Armani’s self-imposed 2027 deadline, sources told the newspaper, because of headwinds in the luxury market. Like many of its competitors, Armani is experiencing a dip — revenue, not counting licensing royalties, declined 5 percent in 2024, to $2.7 billion, and 2.8 percent in 2025, to $2.6 billion. It’s not a crisis, not yet, but it’s far from an ideal track record for going public or selling at a high valuation. A listing comes with its own complications, too. For one, the company has to demonstrate it can grow profitably at a vigorous pace and keep up quarter after quarter. “People are not buying the past in the stock market. They want to buy the future,” De Sole says.

Armani, though, is a unique asset: It is globally recognized and has substantial cash reserves and no debt. Its licensed lines with L’Oreal and EssilorLuxottica generated an estimated $2.3 billion in 2025. The brand is diversified while avoiding the kind of overexpansion that can turn blue-chip labels into discount slop. “The foundations are beyond rock-solid,” says Graziano de Boni, a former CEO of Armani’s North American subsidiary. “It is the only fashion brand that goes from fast fashion to couture and nobody complains.” The stability of the business, and its snoozy reputation, may actually work in its favor. “They didn’t have all these swings that many other fashion houses had in the past,” says Marchetti, who navigated the Yoox IPO almost 20 years ago. “That’s what the family and the board are trying to continue.”

Dell’Orco cannot make any major decisions about an outright sale or a public offering without the support of either Silvana Armani or Andrea Camerana. The family has so far avoided painful disagreements, the kind of succession drama that plunged Luxottica into a messy squabble after the founder, Leonardo Del Vecchio, who died in 2022, left the $46 billion fortune in the hands of eight heirs from three different marriages. That is not the Armani way. When Dell’Orco and Silvana meet with employees to discuss pending items, or sospesi, they still leave the head of the table, Armani’s seat, empty. “Managing to keep everyone together — the whole group — is the most important thing Giorgio did,” Dell’Orco says. “Before long, we’ll be bringing in some partners.”

Although he anticipates the initial stake sale will go forward as planned by next spring, Dell’Orco does not seem to feel much urgency. “We cannot simply remain as we are,” he says. “I want to grow gradually, to reach a revenue level that is a bit higher — let’s say $4 million or $5 million — compared with where we stand right now.” Instead of selling a majority stake, Dell’Orco tells me he hopes Armani will go public at some point: “Because I would feel more free.”

The first time we speak, his own future does not seem in doubt. Like Armani, he loves the work. Still, he allows that change is inevitable. “But change to what extent?” A month before Vitale is formally hired, he seems closer to answering his own question. An outsider, someone who is not beholden to the past, is good for the company, he says. “They need to be someone who has a clear vision. They need to be able to see things for themselves, to make a judgment and then step in.”

items.title: Чем заняться дома: проделки мозга, «Полураспад», «Квест Вижна» и Sade
items.description: Чем заняться дома: проделки мозга, «Полураспад», «Квест Вижна» и Sade
items.author: © Disney
paragraphs: Чем заняться дома: проделки мозга, «Полураспад», «Квест Вижна» и Sade
Кадр из сериала «Квест Вижна»

Белый Вижн (Пол Беттани), созданный после гибели супергероя в фильме «Мстители. Финал», скрывается в Эдинбурге, работает в пабе и пытается себя осознать. В его цифровой голове живут несколько искусственных интеллектов, включая Альтрона (Джеймс Спэйдер), однажды едва не уничтожившего человечество. Когда за Вижном начинает охоту наемник, андроид отправляется в бега с подростком Томасом Шепардом, который может оказаться реинкарнацией его сына. Шоураннер Терри Маталас («Звездный путь: Пикар») завершает трилогию Marvel, начатую «Вандой/Вижном» и продолженную сериалом «Это все Агата», фантастической историей о памяти, отцовстве и попытках искусственного разума стать человеком.
Кадр из сериала «Квест Вижна»

14 сентября 1954 года на Тоцком полигоне под Оренбургом провели масштабные военные учения с применением ядерного оружия. В операции участвовали 45 тыс. военнослужащих, а сведения о ее последствиях десятилетиями оставались засекреченными. Сценарист «Трассы» и «Аутсорса» Олег Маловичко положил эту историю в основу масштабной драмы о журналистке Надежде Келлер (Анна Михалкова), которая в годы перестройки расследует обстоятельства учений и пытается разобраться в судьбе собственного отца. Сериал поставил Максим Свешников («Плейлист волонтера»), в актерском составе — Филипп Янковский, Сергей Шакуров, Евгений Стычкин. На постерах «Полураспад» уже претендует на звание «главного сериала года». Заявка серьезная, учитывая исторический материал, его болезненную актуальность и репутацию сценариста.
Кадр из сериала «Полураспад»

Легендарный слэшер «Пятница, 13-е» получил восьмисерийный приквел от студии A24, в котором главной героиней стала мать Джейсона Вурхиза. Памела (Линда Карделлини) переживает гибель сына, утонувшего в летнем лагере «Хрустальное озеро», и постепенно превращается в одержимую местью женщину. За новую версию истории отвечает Брэд Кэйн, работавший над сериалом «Оно: Добро пожаловать в Дерри». Он разворачивает знакомую хоррор-вселенную в сторону психологической драмы с кровавыми убийствами, черным юмором и отсылками к оригинальному фильму 1980 года.
Кадр из сериала «Хрустальное озеро»

Маргарет Куолли из «Субстанции» в романтической драме Рэйчел Моррисон («Огонь внутри») играет медсестру Майю, чья счастливая семейная жизнь обрывается со смертью мужа в начале пандемии коронавируса. Пытаясь справиться с горем, героиня отправляется в путешествие по разным городам и странам, заводит новые знакомства и постепенно учится жить самостоятельно. Компанию Куолли на экране составили Гэбриел Бассо, Аарон Пьер, Патрик Шварценеггер и Кэтрин Кинер. Продюсером фильма выступил Райан Гослинг, а сама история о любви, потере и поисках себя разворачивается на фоне живописных пейзажей Португалии, Лондона и Нового Орлеана.
Кадр из фильма «Любовь твоей жизни»
- Диско Юрия Чернавского — эссе канала «Спасибо, послушаю» о мелодисте, который написал, например, магическое «Кафе танцующих огней» для Аллы Пугачевой.
- Как устроен «Человек-паук. Новый день» — эссе «Кинопоиска» о неожиданно самой скандальной российской теневой премьере лета 2026 года.
- «Маленькая фея» — ностальгическая и поучительная история главного бьюти-бренда 2000-х и феномена детского маркетинга.
- Секрет группы Sade — видео, под которое танцует здоровый человек: проект «Тихое место» объясняет, почему это музыка для интеллектуалов и неформалов одновременно.

- «Почему любовь сломалась» — что такое лимеренция и какие последствия в связи с ней ждет современное общество, рассказывает исследователь философской антропологии Макс Неаполитанский в лекции о кризисе романтических отношений.

- «Очень странные дела в космосе» — астроном Кирилл Масленников рассказывает, как устроены на первый взгляд необъяснимые явления во Вселенной: черные дыры в галактиках не поглощают звезды; темная материя не дает себя обнаружить; следы инопланетных цивилизаций оказываются не такими, какими мы ожидаем.

Нейробиолог Магомед-Амин Идилов в программе Евгения Тихоновича «Качество жизни» рассказал, почему человеческий мозг так любит различную оптимизацию и гонится за дешевым дофамином. Один из способов противостоять этому — осознанно ограничивать быстрые источники удовольствия: бесконечный скроллинг, залипание в короткие видео или привычку заедать скуку. Но ударяться в жесткий аскетизм не обязательно. Достаточно научиться замечать сиюминутные импульсы и вовремя останавливаться.

Российский fashion-бизнес переживает процесс, который может очистить рынок от компаний без устойчивой экономики, — таким мнением в эфире программы «На показ» поделилась кандидат экономических наук и основатель JKey Buro Юлия Кудрявцева. Как только рынок избавится от «количественных» брендов, останутся качественные.

Новая песня башкирских фолк-рокеров, претендующих на «Грэмми». В ее основе — стихотворение Александра Пушкина «Адели» («Играй, Адель,/ Не знай печали...»). Песня родилась из личной истории музыкантов. Вокалистку коллектива зовут Адель, а ее родителей — Руслан и Людмила, как героев пушкинской поэмы. Они в свою очередь назвали дочь в честь стихотворения, которое теперь стало песней. В аранжировке, разумеется, звучат башкирские традиционные инструменты курай и кубыз.

Сингл передовых электронщиков страны о животных инстинктах и потребительском отношении людей друг к другу. Как в любви, так и в дружбе. Социально-философский эксперимент на грани антропологического исследования. Звучание выдержано в рамках альбома «Истерика», который склоняется к электро-хаусу нулевых и электроклэшу с фольклорной мелодикой. В обложке к треку зашита спектрограмма его концовки, куда музыкант Илья Гадав поместил изображение анимешного лица Алисы Стяжковой с помощью плагина beepmap. Так что шум в конце песни — это звучание картинки.
Трой Сиван — She’s the Best

После шумного тура Sweat с Charli XCX австралийский поп-певец Трой Сиван записал четвертый альбом о жизни за пределами танцпола. Хаус, шугейз, трип-хоп и оркестровый поп сопровождают его музыкальные признания об одиночестве, мимолетных романах и мечтах о большой любви. Заглавная композиция посвящена подругам и женщинам, которые помогали Сивану принимать себя и справляться с трудностями. Над пластинкой работали Джек Антонофф, Финнеас О’Коннелл и Джордж Дэниел, голоса Charli XCX и Лили-Роуз Депп добавили ей интимности. Получился чувственный музыкальный дневник о поисках близости.

items.title: Iowa’s GOP Candidate for Governor Might Not Live in Iowa
items.description: The term carpetbagger was originally applied to Northerners who moved South after the Civil War to launch political careers under the protection of military Reconstruction; it referred to the hastily procured bags manufactured from carpet scraps the transplant
items.author: Ed Kilgore
paragraphs: The term carpetbagger was originally applied to Northerners who moved South after the Civil War to launch political careers under the protection of military Reconstruction; it referred to the hastily procured bags manufactured from carpet scraps the transplants allegedly used. More recently, the term has been applied to politicians who conveniently relocate themselves into the vicinity of political opportunities. New York has often been a magnet for alleged carpetbaggers. In the 1960s alone, two former U.S. attorneys general, Robert F. Kennedy and Ramsey Clark, moved to the Empire State and ran for the Senate (the former successfully, the latter not so much), and a generation later, so did former Arkansas First Lady Hillary Clinton (like RFK, she won).

So in itself, the decision by conservative ex-lobbyist and businessman Zach Lahn to move from Kansas to Iowa in 2024 and then run for governor — winning the 2026 GOP primary in a big upset — isn’t so remarkable. Indeed, Lahn was born and grew up in Iowa, where his family had lived for generations, and owned property there.

What has made his case interesting — and for supporters of his Democratic opponent, Rob Sand, hilarious — is his difficulty making a clean break with it. He seems very involved in Kansas matters. He remains president of the board of an unaccredited Wichita private school he co-founded with his wife, albeit when they were both married to other people (in her case to a scion of the Kansas Koch family empire, with whom she financed the Wonder School, as they called it). And the children from the blended families he and his wife left in Kansas have given Lahn a reason to fly his private plane back to Wichita a lot — at least 37 times since he began running for governor, according to the Des Moines Register. But that isn’t the only evidence that Lahn has Kansas on his mind. Last month, the Daily Beast reported that a Strava fitness-app user with the name “Zach Lahn” recorded four long bike rides starting at Lahn’s Wichita estate over three months in early 2025, long after his supposed relocation to Iowa.

Perhaps more eyebrow-raising have been his public musings over the amount of time he’ll need to spend away from Iowa’s capital if he does become the governor of the Hawkeye State. “We’ve already had discussions about this and how that would work,” he told the Register in May. “But if I’m elected governor, it would be a different arrangement, and we’d work it out. Because, you know, we’d be in Iowa as much as humanly possible.”

That has to be comforting, but it certainly hasn’t quelled questions about Lahn’s state loyalties, considering his campaign’s Trump-modeled message is “Iowa First.” Or at least since October 17, 2024, which was when he transferred his voter registration to the state. You’re required to have Iowa residency for at least two years to run for governor there, so he got in just under the wire.
Unsurprisingly, Lahn’s shaky status as an Iowan has been bread and meat for Sand’s campaign, which has offered him Iowa travel tips:
And even more cleverly, Sand’s backers got Kansas’s Democratic governor Laura Kelly in on the action:

When Lahn first decided to run, his “outsider” status might have seemed like a positive credential. The current two-term Republican governor of Iowa, Kim Reynolds, is deeply unpopular (for many months, she’s reigned as “America’s most unpopular governor” according to polling from Morning Consult). So while he was campaigning in the primary against Iowa GOP Establishment candidate Randy Feenstra, Lahn made a logical choice by separating himself from the usual suspects in Des Moines and Washington. But Wichita is a little too “outside” Iowa for comfort. And in explaining the details of his family situation, Lahn has also drawn attention to his not entirely orthodox relationship with the insanely rich and controversial Koch family (for whom he worked as an Americans for Prosperity operative before marrying Chase Koch’s ex-wife). He’s not just any old dad with custody issues.

Other than the poor management of his residential status, Lahn was unlucky to have made his move back to Iowa for what is turning out to be a strong Democratic year in a state that turned deep red in 2014 and has remained so ever since. Democrats have even odds of winning the Senate seat being vacated by Joni Ernst and could flip three of Iowa’s four U.S. House seats as well. In Sand, the sole member of his party in statewide office, Democrats have a solidly established centrist candidate who is difficult for the GOP to label as a “radical” or “socialist” (though it has tried). Lahn has sought to adopt a populist stance by criticizing both major party establishments and has a MAHA strain in his ideology that has enabled him to attack polluters with whom Republicans often snuggle. The two candidates are more or less evenly matched financially.

In part because of a vast advantage in name ID, Sand has led Lahn in public polling from the get-go. In the Silver Bulletin polling averages, Sand leads by a robust 7.3 percent, though the most recent polls show the race tightening a bit. As in other midwestern states, Democrats are nervous about possible polling errors (Iowa is, after all, where the legendary pollster Ann Selzer infamously showed Kamala Harris leading Trump in 2024). The Trump administration, meanwhile, is working overtime to deliver tasty treats (e.g., fuel assistance to hard-pressed farmers and a new federally assisted steel mill) to Iowa voters.

If Sand nonetheless prevails, Republicans will naturally wonder if a more Iowa-centric candidate like Feenstra might have won. And Lahn may wonder whether he picked the wrong “home state” for his gubernatorial dreams.

items.title: 7 Ways Trump Lost His 2024 Coalition
items.description: Though the results could yet surprise us, it’s very likely the key story of the 2026 midterm elections will be the Republican Party’s loss of support from non-MAGA elements of the electorate who temporarily backed Donald Trump in 2024. To that extent it’s not
items.author: Ed Kilgore
paragraphs: Though the results could yet surprise us, it’s very likely the key story of the 2026 midterm elections will be the Republican Party’s loss of support from non-MAGA elements of the electorate who temporarily backed Donald Trump in 2024. To that extent it’s not just a matter of the White House party predictably losing ground in a midterm, which happens far more often than not. It’s a tale of trends reversing themselves that robbed Trump and his cohort of what many thought might be a political realignment making the GOP the majority party for years. So it’s worth a closer look: How, exactly, did Trump alienate these onetime supporters? Here are some tentative answers.
Trump’s 2024 coalition was never as big as he claimed

The president has incessantly exaggerated his winning share of the electorate in 2024. On Election Night, he claimed an “unprecedented and powerful mandate.” Shortly after taking office, he told supporters he had “achieved the most epic political victory our country has ever seen” and “the biggest mandate in 129 years,” and one of his spokespeople boasted he had “decisively won every battleground state and became the first Republican to win the popular vote in 20 years,” lines he would repeat often on Truth Social. In fact, he narrowly won the popular vote by 1.5 percent, far short of the usual 10 percent threshold for a “landslide,” which was smaller than the margins of victory for Joe Biden in 2020, Barack Obama in 2012 and 2008, and George W. Bush in 2004 (and smaller, for that matter, than Hillary Clinton’s popular-vote margin over Trump in 2016). Winning all seven battlegrounds is no big accomplishment, either; these were very close states, which is why they were called battlegrounds. Suffice it to say that Trump’s victory was legitimate but no great shakes by any historical standard.
Some of Trump’s gains were circumstantial, not a realignment

What had some Republicans buzzing about a “realignment” were the gains Trump posted among Hispanic, Black, and under-30 voters. The size of these gains varied by sources, but probably the most reliable, Pew’s “verified voters” analysis, showed Trump gaining 12 percent among Hispanics compared to 2020 (and 20 percent compared to 2016); 7 percent among Black voters (and 9 percent since 2016); and 4 percent among under-30 voters (and 11 percent since 2016). Considering how aggressively reactionary Trump had been in the intervening years, these were indeed impressive numbers in those demographic groups and cause for concern among Democrats, who had arguably taken them for granted. But Trump has now squandered these gains by every measurement we have.
The high price of breaking cost-of-living promises

Hispanic, Black, and under-30 voters are on average more economically vulnerable than other Americans, and there’s not much question a big part of their pro-Trump trend in 2024 involved unhappiness with Joe Biden’s record on inflation and Trump’s promises to lower the cost of groceries, fuel, and housing. He was not able at all to keep those promises, which were not realistic to begin with. While this isn’t the only reason he’s lost ground with these voters, it is clearly important, and it’s hard to overstate the depth of his failure. According to the latest high-quality New York Times–Siena survey of likely voters, Trump’s job-approval numbers on “the cost of living” are 20 percent approval and 79 disapproval (with 65 percent strongly disapproving) among Hispanics, 3 percent approval and 91 percent disapproval (with 88 percent strongly disapproving) among Black voters, and 13 percent approval and 86 percent disapproval (with 73 percent strongly disapproving) among under-30 voters. There is no way to sugarcoat these numbers on the most important issue of the midterms.
Latinos are unhappy with mass deportation

It was reasonably clear that the Latino/Hispanic voters who trended Republican in 2024 supported Trump’s border-control policies (most still do) and believed his claims that he would deport only violent criminals. But again, Trump broke his promises. A March 2026 Equus survey of Latinos found that by “a wide 65-30 margin, Latinos believe Trump’s actions on immigration ‘are going too far, and instead of deporting criminals, he is targeting the types of hardworking immigrants who strengthen our nation.’” The same survey showed 72 percent of Latinos weren’t happy with ICE, “whether that means they support reforming ICE to prevent violence and ensure accountability (37%) or abolishing ICE because it is out of control and no training or accountability could reform it (35%).” The Times-Siena poll showed 60 percent of Hispanics “strongly disapproving” of Trump’s immigration policies overall.
Trump has offended Black voters as much as possible

If you are a Republican who wants to increase your party’s fragile beachhead with Black voters, here are some things you should probably avoid doing: (1) devoting all the civil-rights organs of the federal government to a fight against alleged discrimination against white people; (2) virtually criminalizing diversity efforts in federal or federally supported hiring; (3) successfully encouraging the U.S. Supreme Court to atomize the Voting Rights Act of 1965; (4) successfully encouraging southern state legislatures to dismantle congressional and state legislative districts that elected Black people to office; and (5) making white Afrikaners from the former apartheid state of South Africa the one remaining recognized beneficiary of refugee status. That the Trump administration has done all these things helps explain why in the Times-Siena survey only 7 percent of Black voters gave the president a positive job-approval rating while 78 percent strongly disapprove.

Aside from being very sensitive to living costs, young voters are famously disinclined to support wars of choice (i.e., those that aren’t a matter of national self-defense), perhaps because they are often of the same generation as those who are dying or risking their lives in such wars. Trump’s war of choice against Iran is generally unpopular; according to the Times-Siena survey, 33 percent of likely voters support the war while 66 percent disapprove (57 percent disapprove strongly). Young voters really hate it, with only 9 percent supporting it (and just one percent supporting it strongly) and 86 percent disapproving of it (75 percent strongly). No wonder 79 percent of under-30 voters disapprove of Trump’s overall job performance (71 percent strongly).
Trump is now only focused on his base, because it’s all he has left

No wonder the president is traveling from red state to red state to rally his most loyal MAGA supporters to show up at the polls and mitigate his party’s losses. He has deliberately chosen to alienate everyone else, including voting groups that were open to changing sides. At this rate, Trump will leave the GOP in worse shape than he found it.
