One of Sennett’s stars was Harry Langdon, the definition of what Macbeth calls a “cream-faced loon.” To our eyes, his eminence is baffling, but Capra got the point. “Chaplin thought his way out of tight situations; Keaton suffered through them stoically; Lloyd overcame them with speed. But Langdon trusted his way through adversities,” Capra wrote in his memoir. Armed with that acuity, he directed Langdon in “The Strong Man” (1926) and “Long Pants” (1927). Then, with the insouciance of Daniel strolling into the lions’ den, he went to work for Harry Cohn.

So much has been written about Cohn, the roaring beast who ran Columbia Pictures, that it’s easy to overlook his genius for finding and fostering talent. The studio was on Gower Street, off Sunset Boulevard, which meant that it was on Poverty Row, which in turn meant that—unlike M-G-M, say, or Paramount—its facilities were crummy and its budgets were laced up tight. But, as Capra conceded to Cohn, the personnel were great. “You can bet your Aunt Tilly’s tits they’re great,” Cohn replied, adding, “Get to work, you damn Dago.” Cohn was a comprehensive bastard with a mouth like a soil pipe, and the way to deal with him, as Capra rapidly twigged, was to stand up straight, take your lumps, and lump him right back again. What got you fired (as opposed to being merely in bad odor, which would wash off after a while) was indecision, and one thing that rises from Wasson’s pages is Capra’s knack for seizing the initiative, marshalling his troops, and marching on.

One example: on Monday, July 9, 1928, Capra surprised the cast and crew of “Submarine,” a new Columbia production, by showing up on set and assuming control. The previous director had been sacked over the weekend, and Capra had read the script on Saturday. In short, if your movie needed saving, he was your guy; if someone else had chickened out or lost the plot, he would chicken in. He had already done so for “The Strong Man,” and he would do it again for “American Madness” (1932), one of his finest early pictures, for which he insisted on reshooting everything that had been filmed by other hands and even on having the set rebuilt. Henceforth, the movie would be molded by his hands. Among those observing the process was the film’s sound man, Edward Bernds, who later said, “I fully realized, for the first time, what directing really was.”

Given such authority, it’s no wonder that Capra could command enduring loyalty. Bernds, who collaborated with him through to “Mr. Smith Goes to Washington,” was one of the gang. Others included the editor William Hornbeck; the assistant director Art Black, an ex-plumber who was famous for the candor of his instructions on set (“Don’t just stand there like somebody’s milking you”); and the screenwriters Riskin and Jo Swerling—“a squat, heavy-set, seething young man, furiously chain-smoking strong White Owl Cigars,” as he is described in “The Name Above the Title.” With a lovely Dickensian flourish, Capra adds, “One got the odd impression the cigar was smoking the man.” McBride is indignant on behalf of these and other invaluable folk, accusing Capra of sidelining their contributions to the films he directed. Ingratitude is indeed sharper than a serpent’s tooth, and McBride isn’t wrong, but since when has Hollywood not been a pit of snakes? Every year, as we see Oscar winners churning out thanks to their agents, their deities, and everyone in between, we can’t help hearing the chant inside their heads: “This is all mine and not yours.”

In his autobiography, Capra is, without a doubt, a hundred times less reliable than Wasson and McBride. The darnedest thing is that he’s also ten times zippier. (“As with heroin, the antidote for film is more film,” he tells us. “It bosses the enzymes.”) What matters to Capra diehards is that, when you treat yourself to almost any of his features from 1930 to the outbreak of war, you feel swept along by the efforts of a well-drilled outfit. Was it a happy ship? Not in the case of “Lost Horizon” (1936), for sure, which was about a quest for Shangri-La, and which, thanks to reshoots and overruns, cost twice its original budget. On the other hand, don’t forget a handsome tribute that was paid by Clark Gable, who was loaned out by M-G-M for “It Happened One Night.” He showed up at Capra’s office drunk, but soon realized that the change of air might just do him, and his image, good. According to Bernds, “I think what Gable felt when he came to Columbia was, ‘Jesus Christ, picture making can be fun!’ ” Two weeks into the shoot, Gable said to his co-star, “You know, I think this wop’s got something.”

If that movie doesn’t give you a healthy jolt, ninety-two years on, you should probably try another art form. What hits you, aside from its momentum and the lightness of its wit, is how absurdly beautiful it is, and with what ease the beauty kindles a sensuality so unexpected that it’s virtually a twist. The celebrated haystack sequence, in which a roguish reporter (Gable) fashions a couple of scratchy beds, by moonlight, for himself and a wealthy heiress (Colbert), who lies there and looks over her shoulder at him in a trance of desire, belongs to the world of “A Midsummer Night’s Dream.” The resident Titania is Joseph Walker, Capra’s favored cinematographer and, for what it’s worth, a hero of mine.

Born in Denver in 1892, Walker had a feline taste for the dark, especially if the silk of it was shot through with light. To double the magic, running water could be added to the mix. Check out Jean Harlow and Robert Williams, in Capra’s “Platinum Blonde” (1931), leaving a bright soirée for a shadowy garden, the better to make out behind a fountain that transforms their kisses into a rippling blur. (Williams, who used his dialogue to muse aloud and fast, as if life were on the verge of comic verse, died of complications from a burst appendix days after the movie opened. His loss was, and remains, a calamity.) Walker was also a dab hand at hats, the gradual disappearance of which from American heads has been indisputably bad news for motion pictures; what could be nobler than Gary Cooper, in Capra’s “Mr. Deeds Goes to Town” (1936), gazing down at Jean Arthur with raindrops gleaming on his trilby’s brim?

Hang on, though. Given that a similar rain drips from Cary Grant’s hat in Howard Hawks’s “Only Angels Have Wings” (1939), during an unforgettable deathbed scene, and that Walker was the director of photography on both films, what’s so special about Capra? Aren’t both masters being served by the same supreme technician, and doesn’t he deserve the credit? True, yet each movie has a distinct social mood—tenser for Capra, looser for Hawks—and it is Capra who seems more discernible, so to speak, at the forefront of the action, whereas Hawks is content to hang out behind the arras.

For further proof, I refer you to a couple of trailers from 1941. First, Hawks’s “Ball of Fire,” which begins with the phrase “What a Pair of Gams!” blazoned across the screen before glancing at the plot and announcing the leading players, Cooper and Barbara Stanwyck. Only in the last ten seconds does Hawks rate a mention. Compare this to Capra’s “Meet John Doe,” released a few months before. It, too, stars Cooper and Stanwyck, but they get second billing in the trailer. Instead, in gigantic letters, up come the words “Frank Capra,” followed by a slow crawl of the kind that we associate with “Star Wars,” listing the director’s earlier triumphs in chronological order. Then, at the end, a homely touch—“It’s your story, and it’s great!”—and a final plug for Capra. You get the feeling that, as far as he was concerned, his name belonged not just above the title but before, after, and practically instead of it.

It is the puff of that self-belief, in part, that provokes the ire of Capra’s detractors. “One man, one film,” he said, and in that preëmptive claim to the status of an auteur he left himself open to censure. Yet Capra’s movies from his golden years do look and sound like his and nobody else’s, with their signature blend of blends: the loner and the bunch of pals, the cracker-barrel and the wisecrack, and the accelerating narrative that finds time to stop and stare. For Capra, as for Dickens, a mob could be either a chorus, pleading for justice, or a milling source of dread. Death itself could be used as a tool. Near the start of “Meet John Doe,” a journalist played by Stanwyck (the archetypal Capra actress) chatters like a ticker tape about her fancy plan—find a hobo to play a hobo who might jump from the top of City Hall. It’s really no joke, but the glee of her riff somehow turns it into a lark.

Nothing about Capra is weirder, to be honest, than the way in which, from one film of his to the next, suicide tugs at our sleeve. In “The Bitter Tea of General Yen” (1933), the tea is lethal, and the General knowingly drinks it; in “Mr. Smith Goes to Washington,” a disgraced senator pulls a gun on himself and cries, “I’m not fit to live!”; and, in “It’s a Wonderful Life,” James Stewart, as George Bailey, leans over the parapet of a bridge with maddened eyes, while the river roils below. How did such a nightmare end up as America’s most beloved Christmas movie? Because George is saved by an angel, I guess, and by generous mounds of cash.

As for Capra’s politics, search me. Readers of McBride’s 1992 book were alarmed by the revelation that Capra was a flinty Republican who voted against Roosevelt “because I thought he was getting too big for the country’s good.” However, as Wasson informs us, when the first of the “Why We Fight” documentaries, “Prelude to War,” was shown at the White House, in 1942, all of Capra’s reservations dissolved with one shake of the President’s hand. (“Every man, woman, and child in the world must see this film,” F.D.R. said to the assembled gathering.) Bernds reckoned that Capra was “muddled and reactionary.” To the screenwriter Julius Epstein, he was “a right-wing populist.” At the same time, Epstein said, “I was not sure how he felt outside his pictures.”

There’s the rub. It’s the pictures that do the talking, and the raging, and—if Cooper is around—the keeping mysteriously quiet. The fact that Capra’s political persuasions, such as they are, fail to square with the deeds of his protagonists is more of a relief, I’d say, than a reason to charge him with hypocrisy. Who wants to watch a film that unwaveringly demonstrates the voting intentions of its maker? The crazed filibuster that concludes “Mr. Smith Goes to Washington” (Stewart, as Jefferson Smith, had his throat dabbed with dichloride of mercury to make him hoarse) sounds more ominous than uplifting in the age of Donald Trump, and the reactions to the film were equally nuts. James F. Byrnes, a Democratic senator from South Carolina, protested that “the thing was outrageous, exactly the kind of thing that dictators of totalitarian governments would like to have their subjects believe exists in a democracy.” Wrap your head around that.

“Mr. Smith” was written by Sidney Buchman, a card-carrying Communist. Riskin, who wrote for Capra to miraculous effect for a decade, starting in 1931, was snappier, subtler, and less ideologically heated, but he, too, was nonetheless a man of the left. (He was also a swell; he dated Carole Lombard and married Fay Wray, which must have been a scream.) The point is that Capra surrounded himself with the best and the smartest, whatever flavor they came in; Stanwyck, Colbert, Gable, Cooper, and Stewart were all solid Republicans, and it’s unlikely that Capra gave more of a damn about their politics than their adoring public did. A movie screen is a dream, not a pamphlet. “What did Capra want to say in his films?” McBride asks, but we don’t watch them for the sake of the saying. What they bequeath to us is not a set of ideas but the fluent, rhythmical beat of a story and a treasury of looks.

The decline of Capra, in the wake of the Second World War, was a sorry spectacle. He made many films after “It’s a Wonderful Life,” but the wonders pretty much ceased. In 1951, he was invited by the president of Caltech, his alma mater, to join a secret Cold War think tank, but was denied security clearance; in a bid to prove his worthiness, he named the names of left-wing sympathizers, including Buchman. (Among the sins of which McBride accuses Capra, this midlife ratting may be the gravest.) Ornery, unwanted, and adrift, Capra found his schemes for movies running out of gas. A bio-pic of St. Paul, starring Frank Sinatra, was never going to fly, though I can’t help imagining the result (“How ya doin’, Colossians?”).

Yet all was not lost. With his second wife, Lucille, whom he had married in 1932, after his first marriage foundered, Capra went to live on a ranch that he had bought in Fallbrook, a hundred miles from Hollywood. He planted fruit trees and produced his own olive oil. Later, the Capras moved to Palm Springs, where he played golf with Gerald Ford and Barry Goldwater. That may not be everybody’s notion of delight, but each to his own. There is a heartening swing, too, in the final chapters of Wasson’s book, as we learn that the maker of “American Madness” got to watch “Mean Streets”—“a helluva beautiful picture,” he called it—and, after the publication of “The Name Above the Title,” began to revel in the company of students, who lapped up his tales of times past (or, for McBride, “his self-aggrandizing pseudopersonality”). For their benefit, he would take apart the mechanism of an old movie, like a clockmaker, and explain how it had been put together.

What kept Capra all wound up and ticking? Wasson detects a lingering resentment in the poor Sicilian kid gazing up at the idle rich. “He would get them. If it would take his whole life, he would get them,” Wasson writes. But where, exactly, is that hatred to be found in the films? They seem tolerant rather than vengeful, and a movie like “Platinum Blonde” is far more amused than appalled by the antics of the well-to-do. Where Capra did strike back was in the sheer vigor of his anti-idleness; he did so much so well, and, if he was amazed by the country he lived in, and confused by what sort of place—horrific or tranquil—it might yet become, well, he is hardly alone in his bewilderment. It was John Cassavetes, a director about as distant from Capra as one can be, who delivered the most haunting homage of all. “Maybe there really wasn’t an America,” he said. “Maybe it was only Frank Capra.” ♦

items.title: Louise Glück’s Life in Restaurants
items.description: If Maria Rondeau and JuanMa Calderón were literalists, they might have put nasturtiums on the menu at Rosa y Marigold, the Peruvian restaurant they opened in April, in Boston. They took the name from the novella “Marigold and Rose,” the final book published by
items.author: Hannah Goldfield
paragraphs: If Maria Rondeau and JuanMa Calderón were literalists, they might have put nasturtiums on the menu at Rosa y Marigold, the Peruvian restaurant they opened in April, in Boston. They took the name from the novella “Marigold and Rose,” the final book published by their friend Louise Glück, the Nobel Prize-winning poet, before she died, in 2023. The story is told from the perspective of infant twins with divergent personalities—Rose is unguardedly buoyant, whereas Marigold is watchful and introspective. “The garden relied on nasturtiums, which Mother and Father ate,” the narrator observes. “It was strange to see the grilled fish with nasturtium butter melting over it. . . . But once you try it, Mother said, the taste is magic. The twins knew what magic was. It made the sun rise. Now they knew it had a taste.”

Rondeau, who grew up in Guatemala, is an architect; Calderón, her partner in life and in restaurants, is a filmmaker and chef from Peru. In September, I sat at Rosa y Marigold’s sleek U-shaped bar with Rondeau and the poet Dan Chiasson, a regular contributor to this magazine and another close friend of Glück’s, sharing thin strips of charred beef heart, tendrils of squid blanketed in a silky, lavender-hued olive mayonnaise, and a formidable mound of chaufa de mariscos—Chinese Peruvian seafood fried rice. To drink, Chiasson ordered his usual, a gin Martini, recalling fondly how Glück would fish the olives out of his glass. As an epileptic, she abstained from hard liquor, but she loved the flavor.

“The whole book is about this idea of duality,” Rondeau said. “It’s an allusion to her two grandchildren”—Glück’s only child, Noah Dranow, is the father of twins—“but it’s also Louise. I think many people are two sides.” Rondeau designed Rosa y Marigold’s dining room to have two sections, each with a mirrored-steel slab hanging overhead, slightly angled to offer a glimpse of the other side.

That afternoon, we’d visited Celeste, the couple’s first restaurant, which they opened in the spring of 2018 in a tiny triangular storefront in Somerville. Glück, whose apartment was nearby, soon became a regular, with a regular order: a cold beer, the arugula salad with lime and Parmesan, and the ceviche, sometimes followed by the sudado de pescado, a Chinese Peruvian dish of steamed fish and vegetables. She always came with a friend, occasionally two, and often requested that the music be turned down.

The couple knew little about her until, one day, Glück left behind an envelope return-addressed to Yale, and Rondeau looked her up, to get it back to her. After that, Glück made her reservations with Rondeau directly. “If anything was off—the salt, the lime, the fish—I would get a text,” Rondeau said affectionately. “She had a perfect palate!” Chiasson added. “She was our in-house critic,” Rondeau continued. “And I would always be extremely grateful, because she kept it real.”

One evening, Rondeau and Calderón mentioned that they’d been approached about writing a cookbook. The next time they saw her, she handed them a typewritten foreword, detailing how she’d first encountered Celeste in Boston magazine, which had published a photo of the ceviche. “It was a summer day and I wanted that ceviche immediately,” she wrote, admiring how it was “not drowned by the chef’s noisy creativity in shards of coconut or a confetti of pomegranate seeds / A very pure looking dish of glistening blue cod.” At the restaurant, Glück became “more like a citizen” than a regular, she wrote. “And Celeste is a world. But a world so much more wonderful and reliable than our real world.” Glück ate dinner at Celeste on the day she won the Nobel, surrounded by friends of Rondeau’s and Calderón’s, whom they’d invited to insure her privacy.

I first learned about Glück’s passion for restaurants in the spring of 2020. At the time, I was this magazine’s weekly restaurant critic, and I had shifted, suddenly, from dining out all over New York City to chronicling the industry’s attempts to stay afloat during lockdown. Glück e-mailed me to commiserate, and to ask if I had ideas for how to help. “Among so many horrors, the collapse of these enchanted worlds seems somehow desperately poignant,” she wrote.

I was lightly shocked to hear from her. I knew and revered her as one of the great living poets, and imagined her as particularly godlike, too high-minded to care about something as earthly as food. There was also the fact that she had struggled with anorexia as a young woman, which she wrote about in her 1989 lecture “Education of the Poet.” We struck up a sporadic correspondence. “I love to cook and have been a terrific and fastidious home cook,” she wrote with refreshing candor, but she yearned for the ritual of dining out. (Later, I learned that she’d bought a heat lamp for Celeste so that she could eat there outdoors.)

In “Education of the Poet,” Glück, who was born to a wealthy family in New York, in 1943 (her father, a Hungarian Jewish immigrant, helped invent the X-Acto knife), described her anorexia as an attempt to “establish a self with clear boundaries.” “The conflict played itself out most fiercely with my mother,” she wrote, who “only wavered when I began to refuse food, when I claimed, through implicit threat, ownership of my body, which was her great accomplishment.” By all accounts, Glück’s mother, Beatrice, was a wonderful cook; Glück’s papers, archived at Yale’s Beinecke Library, make clear that she grew up among people who loved to eat. In one letter from summer camp, addressed to her younger sister, Tereze, Glück wrote, “I miss—sundaes, shrimp cocktails,” next to tiny sketches of each.

Glück recovered from anorexia through years of psychoanalysis—years during which she also studied poetry with Léonie Adams and Stanley Kunitz. She published “Firstborn,” her début collection, in 1968, when she was twenty-five. Later letters detailed lavish hotel meals in Europe with her first husband and dinner parties in Plainfield, Vermont, where she taught writing at Goddard College and worked part time at a café, baking pastries in exchange for child care. (Noah, her son, grew up to be a sommelier.)

In 1980, John Dranow, Glück’s second husband and the director of the writing program at Goddard, co-founded the New England Culinary Institute, a small cooking school that operated restaurants in Montpelier. Glück sat on the board of directors until the nineties, when they divorced and she moved to Cambridge. In one poem from “Meadowlands,” an unsparing, darkly funny collection from that time, an unidentified husband and wife argue over food. “I stopped liking artichokes when I stopped eating / butter. Fennel / I never liked,” he says. “Living with you is like living / at boarding school: / chicken Monday, fish Tuesday.”

“Why do you call it rigidity?” she retorts. “Can’t you call it a taste for ceremony? Or is your hunger for beauty / completely satisfied by your own person?” The husband has the last word, accusing her of joyless pleasure-seeking: “When you make artichokes, / make them for yourself.”

The word “poet,” Glück wrote, “must be used cautiously; it names an aspiration, not an occupation. In other words: not a noun for a passport.” She could go years without writing, though she rejected the notion of writer’s block, perceiving instead a liminal state of waiting for poems to arrive. During fallow periods, Glück occupied herself with teaching, which she loved, gardening (she claimed to have read nothing but catalogues for two years), and eating at restaurants. “Dinner takes a certain shape,” the poet Katie Peterson, who ate with her frequently at Chez Panisse when Glück taught at Stanford, observed. “A familiar menu is like a rosary.”

In Cambridge, Chiasson pointed out Koreana, the restaurant where he, as a worshipful Harvard grad student, had first spotted Glück, in 1997, having dinner with the poets Robert Pinsky and Frank Bidart. (Bidart, Chiasson’s mentor, eventually introduced them.) Chiasson showed me an unpublished poem that he’d written for Glück after she died: “back before anything happened / yet it was still the bitter end / three poets sat around a lazy susan / kimchi, Tsing Tao, bibimbap, gossip.”

Earlier that day, we’d dropped in on the poet Henri Cole, in Boston’s South End. The two men, who had each shared countless meals with Glück, but never together, delighted in comparing notes, remembering her habit of sampling several wines before inevitably choosing something crisp and dry; her insistence that no meal was complete without greens; and the decisiveness with which she could turn on a place she’d loved. She almost always ordered the fish. She almost never ordered dessert, but would happily pluck the raspberry off of someone else’s crème brûlée. She preferred to eat early, and would wait outside her home, ready to be picked up.

Chiasson and Cole had last seen each at La Royal, another of Rondeau and Calderón’s restaurants, at a memorial for Glück, packed with her dinner companions. When Rondeau first told Glück, in 2021, that she and Calderón were considering opening a new place, Glück advised against it, then immediately changed her mind on a visit to the empty storefront, in a beautiful brick building from 1910, facing Royal Avenue in Cambridge. Not long before she died, Glück weighed in on the menu—both the dishes served and the printed layout—and chose the restaurant’s name.

Chiasson theorized that his friend’s love for both restaurants and poetry stemmed from her interest in “primal urges.” “We build these institutions to contain them and express them,” he said. “Marriage, restaurants, homes—they’re frames for containing all this passion.” In 1999, Glück imagined a creation story of sorts, describing small worlds that appeared in the fissures of a larger, shattered one. “On Huron Avenue they became / a block of stores,” she wrote, “whatever / they were or sold, they were / alike in their function: they were / visions of safety. Like / a resting place.” She called the poem “Formaggio,” after her favorite cheese shop, in Cambridge. ♦

items.title: New York’s EMS Crisis Could Kill You
items.description: Sooner or later, the slow-motion collapse of New York’s response system for medical emergencies will force city leaders to get off their asses and address problems that should have been fixed long ago. Innocent people are already paying the price of City Hall
items.author: Errol Louis
paragraphs: Sooner or later, the slow-motion collapse of New York’s response system for medical emergencies will force city leaders to get off their asses and address problems that should have been fixed long ago. Innocent people are already paying the price of City Hall perennially starving ambulance first responders of the salaries, benefits, and work conditions they deserve.

Over the last decade, response time on life-threatening medical emergencies has jumped by nearly four minutes, an increase of more than 41 percent, according to a recent report by City Comptroller Mark Levine. Non-life-threatening response time has more than doubled, by almost 15 minutes. That extra time can be the difference between life and death.

“Most critical, which would be cardiac arrest, was somewhere around 14 minutes. That’s serious,” Vincent Variale, president of the Uniformed EMS Officers Union, told me. “We know brain death begins at four to six minutes. So if I’m arriving at 14 minutes, I still need time to get into your house or your building and find you, that’s probably another three to four minutes. So it’s almost 20 minutes before we actually get down and work on the patient. Brain death has already started. The survivability of that patient has plummeted.”

Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s administration is aware of the problem. “We know this is unacceptable, and we are working tirelessly to reverse this trend,” said FDNY’s chief of department, John Esposito. (Emergency Medical Services is a division of the Fire Department).

The root of the problem, as union leaders warned in March, is the absurdly low pay that New York’s frontline “street doctors” get. First-year emergency medical technicians (EMTs) make only $43,932, far lower than the entry-level salaries of firefighters ($54,122) and cops ($55,942), and less than what we pay first-year sanitation workers ($47,752). And while other uniformed personnel hit $100,000 within five and a half years, EMTs have smaller increases and top out at $68,700, with paramedics capped at $86,348.
“You have EMTs starting out at minimum wage, a little over $18 an hour,” says Variale. “To live in New York City at that kind of salary, it’s very hard to do it. And that’s why people are leaving.”

The low wages have led workers to look for part-time work; take the exam to snag a better-paying job as a firefighter; sleep in their cars a few nights a week; or simply quit. Some even end up in homeless shelters, according to union leaders, and 14 have committed suicide since 2020.

“More and more EMTs and paramedics are leaving the job. We estimate by the time this is over, 1,500 will be gone,” says Variale, noting that 500 EMS workers have left so far this year. “It’s terrible. The main cause of response times going up is people leaving the job.”

A shrinking workforce prevents the city from having a sufficient number of ambulances ready for action. The average number of ambulances in service over the last five years was only 332, a number that recently rose to 416, but remains far below the department’s official target number of 488, according to Levine, even as volume has hit a record high of more than 1.1 million calls per year.

Reports of long waits for help during medical emergencies are starting to multiply. Last year, 14-year-old Kevin Daly had a stroke while at school; after an hour of waiting that included three calls from the school nurse, Daly’s mother came to the school and drove him to the hospital herself. In another case, the closest responder to a call on Staten Island was an ambulance in Manhattan that took 64 minutes to arrive, says Variale, who estimates that the slowing response times means 4,000 excess deaths a year.

Fixing the problem won’t be cheap. Prior to getting elected, Mayor Eric Adams promised EMS workers parity with other uniformed workers, winning the union’s endorsement, but he reneged after his inauguration; the workers have been without a contract since 2022. Levine estimates that bringing EMS workers into full parity with firefighters would cost about $1.23 billion if applied to the current contract period (2022 to 2027) and then cost an additional $289 million a year. A less expensive alternative, pegging EMS salaries to what private ambulance companies pay, would cost $352 million for the current contract and then an additional $98 million a year.

The missing ingredient here is leadership. A recent City Council hearing raised important workplace issues like the fact ambulances tend to be stationed at key intersections to speed response time, leaving EMS workers unable to take meal and bathroom breaks. The hearing also touched on the idea of increasing the number of FDNY personnel trained as paramedics ready to handle complex medical emergencies, a “fire-medic” model used in the other cities. But operational changes don’t address the core problem of low pay.

I recently asked Mayor Mamdani why New York doesn’t follow the lead of cities like Philadelphia, Portland, and Denver, which have established a minimum wage for municipal workers. “We’ve been having productive conversations with our partners in organized labor, especially when it comes to EMS workers. And we’re talking about people who it’s truly not hyperbolic to describe their work as having the consequences of life or death for New Yorkers,” Mamdani told me. “And yet, we’ve seen that they haven’t been recognized as such. I’m hopeful that those conversations not only continue but they continue to be productive.”

But hope, as they say, is not a strategy. City Hall should not wait for a tragedy to occur to make EMS first responders a job that pays a living wage and enables these public servants to build fulfilling careers saving lives.

“This mayor and this administration did not cause this problem. This problem started before they got here. And I’m happy to hear when they talk about affordability and pay equity and stuff like that. This should be right in the mayor’s wheelhouse,” says Variale. “I just think it needs to be moving a little quicker to get there. Because every day that goes by, more people are dying. Literally.”

items.title: ‘Clayface’ Soaks Up $3.5M in Box Office Previews as ‘You Can See Everything’ Expands
items.description: Clayface is rolling into theaters this weekend with an array of other new pre-Halloween titles as You Can See Everything expands after a much-discussed box office debut.
items.author: Ryan Gajewski
paragraphs: Clayface is rolling into theaters this weekend with an array of other new pre-Halloween titles as You Can See Everything expands after a much-discussed box office debut.

Warner Bros. releases Clayface in more than 3,400 North American theaters on Friday, with the DC Studios body-horror movie earning $3.5 million in Thursday previews. The studio has projected an opening between $25 million and $30 million domestically, along with an additional $20 million to $25 million internationally, for the $44 million-budgeted Clayface. It is the first DC Studios title to launch since Supergirl faced box office headwinds over the summer.

Tom Rhys Harries and Naomi Ackie star in the story of Matt Hagen (Harries), an actor who turns to a scientist (Ackie) for assistance when his face becomes disfigured. In his review for The Hollywood Reporter, critic Frank Scheck called Clayface “a big swing that definitely pays off.”

You Can See Everything added $2.2 million on Thursday from 855 North American locations to bring its domestic cume to $25.6 million. Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim‘s documentary about disgraced Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes widens to 2,600 theaters domestically on Friday for its sophomore frame. Its $15 million opening marked the highest-grossing launch for a release under 1,000 theaters since 2006’s Borat.

Wicker lands in 1,471 North American theaters from Black Bear, grossing $620,000 in Thursday previews for directors Eleanor Wilson and Alex Huston Fischer’s romantic fantasy that premiered at Sundance. Olivia Colman and Alexander Skarsgård star in the movie about a woman in a quiet village who gets a wicker husband. In his review for THR, critic Richard Lawson praised Wicker’s “winning mix of irreverence and compassion.”

Klara and the Sun collected $85,000 from Thursday previews for the Sony Pictures release that stars Jenna Ortega and Amy Adams. Hailing from 3000 Pictures and Spyglass Media Group, director Taika Waititi’s feature adaptation of Kazuo Ishiguro’s novel hits 850 theaters Friday and follows a robot companion connecting with a sick girl. THR chief film critic David Rooney deemed it a “wretched mess.”

Also opening this weekend are Laika’s stop-motion animated feature Wildwood, with director Travis Knight’s film screening in 2,926 North American theaters, and Amazon MGM Studios’ Sacha Baron Cohen-led comedy Ali G: Who Iz I?, which hits just 125 locations for one week only.

items.title: Size Really Does Matter: How Alexander Skarsgard’s ‘Wicker’ Man and Member Came to Life
items.description: [Warning: this story contains spoilers for Black Bear’s Wicker.]
items.author: Carly Thomas
paragraphs: [Warning: this story contains spoilers for Black Bear’s Wicker.]
The internet went feral over Alexander Skarsgård’s wicker penis in the highly anticipated romantic fantasy Wicker that hit theaters on Friday. However, it almost didn’t make the cut.

“The wicker man was already designed, the prosthetic face and the upper body,” costume designer Tóth András Dániel recalls. “And just one week before the shoot started, the directors [Eleanor Wilson and Alex Huston Fischer] came up with this idea: ‘He’s so sexy. We should see him naked.'”

Fans clearly agreed. After a Wicker teaser dropped in August, the internet instantly got hot and bothered over this attractive man made from wicker. The film, based on author Ursula Wills-Jones’s short story, The Wicker Husband, follows a fisherwoman (Olivia Colman) who commissions the local basketmaker (Peter Dinklage) to weave her a husband (Skarsgård), sparking jealousy and chaos in the quiet village.

The character’s masculine build initially caught the horny BookTok girlies’ attention, but it was the thought of what’s underneath Skarsgård’s tailored suit that had them really drooling. “Hell yeah! 50 shades of Pinocchio!” and “The bar is so low for men we’re romanticizing baskets” were among thousands of similar comments shared on social media at the time.

Wētā Workshop, which designs specialty costumes for film and television, worked with 50 people for a year to build the upper half of Skarsgård’s wicker suit. The attention to detail was evident from the way the suit moved to how it blended in with the prosthetic face.
However, Dániel and fellow costume designer Attila Godena-Juhász had a much harder task when it came to creating the lower half, as time wasn’t on their side.

“There was no time for Wētā to prepare the whole bottom part of [Alexander’s suit], including the wicker penis, which was such a big subject about the size and everything,” Dániel says, adding, “We had one week with four people in the workshop to seamlessly continue the wicker bottom part.”
Given that the costume designers had different materials to work with than Wētā, Dániel says they “had to experiment and invent a kind of new technology” to mimic what was already created.

“Attila came up with this idea that we should use this special paint that you can see printed on textile, and if you treat it with heat, it gets three-dimensional,” he explains. “So it’s really giving you this woven textile feeling, but that was still [the color] white. So every little detail we had to hand-paint with tiny brushes and shade it and match it with the color that was used for the whole upper prosthetics.”

Unfortunately for fans who had been eagerly hoping to see Skarsgård’s wicker member up close and personal in the film, they might be slightly disappointed. The only full frontal is when the fisherwoman (Colman) is looking at the nude wicker man off in the distance in the water.
That was intentional. “That was a decision from the directors,” Dániel says. “They just wanted to give the audience a peek of him being naked, but they don’t want it to show everything.”

However, for audiences still pondering, this writer — who got a close-up look at the lower half of Skarsgård’s costume before it was painted, via a photo from the costumers — can confirm Colman’s fisherwoman definitely wasn’t complaining about size.
Skarsgård’s wicker willy wasn’t the only thing that was impressive, but rather his whole physique. And Dániel and Godena-Juhász took that into account when dressing him.

“Because Alex is such a huge guy, with the prosthetic on, it made him even bigger and more muscular. So the idea was that his costumes shouldn’t fit perfectly because nobody was prepared that one day a wicker man would knock on their door and ask for a suit,” Dániel explains to THR. “The lengths are shorter on purpose because it really gives you the feeling that at first he’s such a huge man.”
Going into the film, it was important for the filmmakers to create “this sexy beast as realistic as it can be,” Dániel says.
Ahead of release, multiple people on social media posed a question about the logistics of having sex with a man with a wicker penis. One wrote: “Can you imagine the splinters?”

These are obviously fictional problems, but Dániel reassures that “the bottom part was 3D printed in a special rubber-like material,” with Godena-Juhász adding that it’s “obviously softer than the real wicker.”
The costume designers also got a kick out of the film and their creation transcending into the mainstream. Even IKEA got into the game, marketing its rattan furniture as “husband material.”
Dániel says, “That was our goal: to do something that can inspire mainstream fashion. But it was still a surprise that the hype is so big around the movie.”
Wicker, also starring Elizabeth Debicki and Richard E. Grant, is currently playing in theaters.

items.title: Sandra Hüller Set for Cameo Role in ‘Avengers: Doomsday’
items.description: Sandra Hüller, the German actress who earned an Oscar nomination for Anatomy of a Fall and appeared in this year’s Project Hail Mary, is part of the all-star cast of Avengers: Doomsday.
items.author: Borys Kit
paragraphs: Sandra Hüller, the German actress who earned an Oscar nomination for Anatomy of a Fall and appeared in this year’s Project Hail Mary, is part of the all-star cast of Avengers: Doomsday.

Rumors have swirled around the actress regarding the Marvel movie since her name popped up on the British Stunt Register a couple of weeks ago. The Hollywood Reporter has confirmed the actress’ involvement. Marvel had no comment.

While much of the plot still remains hidden in the eastern European nation of Latveria, it is known to feature heroes from different timelines that team-up to fight the universe-shattering peril of a sorcerer scientist named Doctor Doom.

The feature, which is deep in post-production as it heads towards a Dec. 18 opening, stars Robert Downey Jr. as Doom and featured the casts of several recent Marvel movies, including Thunderbolts*, Fantastic Four: First Steps, Black Panther: Wakanda Forever, the Thor movies and the classic X-Men movies. In addition to Downey making a return to the Marvel movies is Chris Evans’ Steve Rogers. (Evans appeared in Deadpool & Wolverine as Johnny Storm.)

Hüller’s role is, naturally, being kept secret although it is being described as a cameo. The rumour mill has her potentially playing Doom’s mother, a witch, or part of select group of hooded enchantresses known as Latverian Witches. Marvel displayed color-coded Latverian robes at this year’s San Diego Comic-Con.
Anthony and Joe Russo are directing Doomsday.

The UTA-repped Hüller gained Hollywood’s attention with starring turns in both Anatomy of a Fall and Zone of Interest. She had a key role in as the person who recruits Ryan Gosling to save the planet in Project Hail Mary (and memorably sings Harry Styles’ “Sign of the Times,” a song she pushed for during karaoke sequence.) She was most recently seen as Tom Cruise’s sister in Digger.

items.title: The Physics Behind Tesla’s Flying Roadster
items.description: We’ve been promised flying cars for decades. We finally have one. Well, sort of.
items.author: Rhett Allain
paragraphs: We’ve been promised flying cars for decades. We finally have one. Well, sort of.

Last week, Elon Musk revealed Tesla’s long-delayed Roadster 2 with a few bells and whistles. The car flies—but not for very long—and the prototype also did a few other things normal cars can’t, like driving up a vertical wall and jumping over Tesla’s entire lineup of vehicles.

This raises two questions: Should we let humans drive up walls and into the air? Given their trouble navigating two-dimensional roads, this seems like an obvious no. But that’s one for lawyers and the Federal Aviation Administration to figure out. The other question is, how did the Roadster 2 prototype do this stuff? We can answer that ourselves, with physics.

Let’s start with how the car drove up a circular ramp and then stayed glued to it Spider-Man–style, completely upside down. I don't think you should ever do this, but this feature of the Roadster 2 can actually improve performance on normal roads. It has to do with friction.

When two surfaces interact—like rubber tires and a road—there can be a force that prevents the surfaces from sliding relative to one another. This interaction is called static friction. We have a simple model for this static friction force where the magnitude (Ff) depends on how hard the two surfaces are pushed together (FN) and the two types of surfaces (μ).

The force pushing the surfaces together is often called the “normal” force, since it's perpendicular to both surfaces. The coefficient of static friction (μ) describes the types of materials interacting. The practical maximum coefficient of friction is 1, and for rubber on asphalt, the value is somewhere around 0.6. What about that ≤ sign? This is because static friction is a “force of constraint.” It applies the force needed to prevent sliding—up to some maximum value.

Suppose a mere mortal car tries to drive up an incline. Here's a force diagram showing the three important forces: friction, normal force, and gravity (the product of mass and the gravitational field).

As the angle (θ) of the incline increases, the gravitational force (mg) has less of a component in the direction perpendicular to the surface. This means the normal force (FN) also decreases, as does the maximum frictional force. If this frictional force is less than the component of the gravitational force pulling down the incline, the car will slip. With a coefficient of 0.6, this maximum angle is about 31 degrees. That's not vertical. It's not even close to vertical. Even with a coefficient of friction at 0.9, you still only get to an incline of 42 degrees.

So how can a car drive up a vertical wall? The answer is to increase the normal force—and, by extension, the frictional force. For a vertical wall, this friction force must be equal to the gravitational force to prevent the car from slipping.

Here's where the Roadster 2 does its first trick. It uses fans to blow air out from under the car. With some side flaps, this lowers the air pressure under the car, akin to how a vacuum cleaner works.

Just for fun, let's estimate the pressure under the Roadster 2 that you would need for it to stick to a wall. The company says the car has a target weight of 1,700 kilograms. We also need to know the contact area. Let’s ballpark it at around 2 square meters. Remember that F = P × A, where P is the pressure and A is the area. But this is really a pressure difference with the external atmospheric pressure at about 105 newtons per square meter. Cranking the numbers gives a bottom pressure of 86 percent of atmospheric pressure. That seems very plausible. Of course, since the seal around the bottom isn't perfect, the fans will need to continue pulling out.

The upside-down Roadster 2 makes for a compelling sales pitch, but the suction actually has a strong use case when it’s driving right side up. Frictional force is the thing that makes a car accelerate. More frictional force, better performance. Pushing the car down means you can accelerate faster and brake faster and make sharper turns. (Performance automakers have harnessed this principle for decades, though not to the degree of Tesla’s new prototype.)

The Roadster 2 also boasts an acceleration of 0 to 60 mph in less than a second. For a traditional car, this is impossible. Since a normal car uses the frictional force between the tires and road to accelerate, it's limited by the coefficient of friction. Using a coefficient of friction at 0.6 (reasonable), the best you can do is 0 to 60 mph in 4.56 seconds. Yes, you can get better tires and you can also increase the frictional force once the car moves faster and interacts with the air (pushing it down)—but those improvements still won’t get you to 60 mph in a second.

The Roadster 2 relies on another form of force: compressed air shooting out the back. This is how rockets work. Since most of us don’t have rockets handy, consider the simple experiment of a toy car propelled by an inflated balloon.

Once the balloon is released, the stretched rubber acts as a force that pushes the air out of the balloon and through an attached tube. But since this air has mass, it will take a force to accelerate it from rest to its exhaust velocity. Here's the cool thing about forces—they are an interaction between two things (like the balloon and the air). That means that when the balloon’s walls push on the air, the air pushes back with an equal force in the opposite direction—an example of Newton’s third law. This push-back force on the balloon is what makes the toy car accelerate. Instead of a wheezing balloon, the Roadster 2 relies on a tank of compressed air.

Now, we get to the flying car part. The Roadster 2 uses the same compressed-air method to push up on the car and get it off the ground. That’s stretching the limits of the term “flying,” especially because there's only a few seconds of thrust that it can get from the tank before the pressure drops. With a lower tank pressure, the air comes out with a lower velocity and less thrust. If I was going to have a flying car, I would hope it could at least fly for 10 minutes of air time.

There's a second issue—acceleration. Since the rockets only last for a short time, they need to apply a large force to get a change in velocity and get the car to leapfrog over a truck or some other obstacle. But with a large force, you also get a large acceleration, and large accelerations are generally bad for humans. We can estimate this acceleration using video analysis. I'm going to use Tracker Video Analysis to mark the location of the car in each frame as it jumps over a Tesla Semi truck. Because we know the truck is about 4 meters tall, we can get the position of the car as a function of time. Here is the vertical position of the Roadster 2 during this jump.

Right there at the beginning of the motion, the vertical velocity of the car is zero, and then it accelerates upward. If we assume constant acceleration during this jump, then the position-time data should be in the shape of a parabola. Fitting a quadratic function to this data gives the acceleration. For this particular motion, I get a rough estimate of about 98 meters per second squared of vertical acceleration. That's right around 10 g’s for humans. That’s just an estimate, of course. Humans can survive that level of force for a short period, but it wouldn’t be pleasant, and it still comes with risks. Maybe that's the reason this particular demo had a robot behind the wheel.

items.title: Mercury Retrograde In Scorpio Is Here — & More Drama Is Incoming
items.description: Mercury retrograde’s last dance in 2026 occurs from October 24th to November 13th in Scorpio. With the backspin, we will face miscommunications, travel delays, and other frustrating hiccups. The celestial cauldron is being stirred as we approach Halloween — ee
items.author: Lisa Stardust
paragraphs: Mercury retrograde’s last dance in 2026 occurs from October 24th to November 13th in Scorpio. With the backspin, we will face miscommunications, travel delays, and other frustrating hiccups. The celestial cauldron is being stirred as we approach Halloween — eek! The spirits and ghosts are definitely going to spice up spooky season this year.

The final and most dramatic Mercury retrograde of the year makes a big splash into the enigmatic waters of the zodiac sign Scorpio. As we backpaddle through the trepid tides, we look past the surface and into our subconscious, ruminating on and resolving matters that have held us back for years. Mercury in Scorpio pushes us to look within, so focus on nurturing and caring for the edgier elements of our personality that could use a hug. These traits are our secrets and skeletons that are yearning to come out. The taboo is going to have its day in the sun, as it’ll be socially acceptable to release ourselves from the shadows during the planetary moonwalk.

Taking stock of who and what we value is vital, too. At the same time, Venus retrograde is making us reassess our relationships, dynamics, and feelings. Combined with Mercury retrograde, the two are forcing us to dig deep and assess whether we want to continue certain partnerships. Our exes may come back, or we might be the former love they post on social media; however, that doesn't mean we have to take them back. Perhaps we need closure instead of reigniting an old flame — even though the temptation is high. Their promises and words might prove to be faulty after the retrograde ends. The same applies to us, which is why we should be careful who we sweet-talk.

Believe it or not, retrogrades do have a silver lining: they let us imagine and reconfigure projects left on the sidelines. Now we can take a second or third look at what we want to complete and comprehend the best tools to help it move forward. For all we know, a forgotten opportunity from months or years ago could come back and land in our laps. Keep an open mind to ensure we are ready for these surprises when they happen. If you never heard back about a job interview, an email from the company might mysteriously emerge in your inbox or you may find their responses in your spam folder.

There usually is one day that offers resolution from the cosmic madness — this year November 4th is an instrumental date due to the Cazimi aspect that occurs when the sun and Mercury retrograde connect in the sky. Cazimi, which translates from Latin to English as in the heart of the sun, is a glorious moment when we can see past the confusion that has been playing on our minds and envision our future. So if you need to schedule appointments, settle bills, or meet up, plan for November 4th, because it will help you achieve what you're aiming for.

Remember, pre- and post-retrograde cycles start and end the journey. The pre-shadow phase began on October 4th, when Mercury slows down, the day after retrograde in Scorpio, and ends in the post-shadow on November 30th. The first week of the pre-retrograde, from October 4th to 11th, proved to be pivotal in the tale that comes to life during the retrograde. Particularly October 5th, when Mercury and Venus retrograde sync up in Scorpio, giving us the strength to express ourselves and stand up for our desires.

The advice for dealing with Mercury retrograde in Scorpio is to practice self-care and to be kind to ourselves. Don't be too hard or overly critical of mistakes that are made — we are only human. Remember, this is a moment and won’t last forever.

items.title: Sorry, Jeans! Fashion Girlies Are Wearing Their Sweaters With These Cool Pants Instead
items.description: All linked products are independently selected by our editors. If you purchase any of these products, we may earn a commission.
items.author: Alexis Bennett Parker
paragraphs: All linked products are independently selected by our editors. If you purchase any of these products, we may earn a commission.

No need to worry about the skinny or baggy jean debate because those baby blue denim pieces are being eclipsed by ultra-soft pull-on pants this fall. I know silk or satin aren't exactly the first fabric that comes to mind when you think of cold-weather essentials, but trust me. The juxtaposition when paired with a chunky knit sweater just makes so much sense. If you're looking for a way to make your cardigans and crewneck knits feel brand new again, a flowy pair of satin trousers is your chic solution.

I have a splurge-worthy pair from Kallmeyer that makes days at the airport look a bit more polished without sacrificing any comfort. In fact, I'd argue that the cool silk fabric feels even more heavenly on my legs than cotton. In addition to wearing them with my knits, I often wear mine with a button-down shirt for a sophisticated touch. It's truly a versatile wardrobe hero I turn to over and over again.

With the holidays on the horizon, the fancy-looking fabric could do double duty in your closet too, taking you from everyday fabulousness to any party on the calendar. Just swap out your go-to sneakers for a pair of heels and your cozy knits for a frilly blouse, and voilà. You've got a pair of pants that works for day and night. That matters because nobody wants to add more stuff to their closets, especially if it's not something you can wear over and over again.
Start your search for the perfect pair of silk or satin pants below. You'll find everything you need to master the look, from Reformation's viral takes to Donni's investment-worthy creations.

items.title: Prune Nourry goes large on female sculptors in Paris
items.description: Gathered in the light-filled spaces of the Petit Palais in Paris, blending into the museum’s permanent collection of work, from antiquity to present day, are 18 figures, visionary women cast in plaster. They are a new addition, courtesy of Paris-born artist Pr
items.author: Hannah Silver
paragraphs: Gathered in the light-filled spaces of the Petit Palais in Paris, blending into the museum’s permanent collection of work, from antiquity to present day, are 18 figures, visionary women cast in plaster. They are a new addition, courtesy of Paris-born artist Prune Nourry, who is looking to redress a balance that currently sees only 4 per cent of the Petit Palais’ collection created by female artists.

Working in plaster was a conscious choice for Nourry, who was invited by the Petit Palais to include her works as part of her ‘Visionaries’ exhibition. Surprisingly, almost 70 per cent of the works in the museum are ‘studio plasters’, works that were never intended to be displayed, but have survived the decades, unlike their bronze counterparts, which were originally destined for posterity.

It is a fitting analogy for the works themselves. Nourry has populated the Petit Palais with the figures of lesser-known female sculptors, a generous addition to the four female sculptors who are already included in the museum’s collections. As a subject, however, women are prolific.

Upon discovering this, Nourry began to work with three art historians, researching female sculptors in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, collecting their writings and portraits in order to gain a sense of who they were. Featured sculptors, including Käthe Kollwitz, Nancy Elizabeth Prophet, Hélène Bertaux, Jane Poupelet, Consuelo de Saint-Exupéry, Selma Hortense Burke, Daria Gamsaragan, and Sarah Bernhardt, share a strong aesthetic identity to which Nourry was drawn.

Nourry enjoyed the process of creating their representation in plaster – but it was stressful, she adds. ‘Very stressful. Obviously it's an interpretation of them and their portraits, because sometimes on the archive images I have of them, you only have the front, or the profile. If you have different images, they don't look like the same woman – they are from different parts of their life. I had to accept that interpretation was a huge part of this, and I hope that they forgive me.’

Sculpture is an instinctive process for Nourry, the sensuality of which she began to appreciate after being diagnosed with cancer in 2016, at the age of 31. ‘Sculpture is where I discovered the connection between my eyes and my hands – when I went through chemo, I lost the touch within my fingers,’ she says. ‘After that, I started a project where I would be blindfolded and sculpted only with my hands to make them work even more. Because I had the fear of losing them, I focused only on them. Sculpting is what moves me.’

The works here are led by the character of the women themselves, or what Nourry learnt about their character through scrupulous research. While they share arresting marble eyes, in line with the Petit Palais’ sculptures, the busts on show play with scale, a thoughtful consideration of the space a woman can require.
Receive our daily digest of inspiration, escapism and design stories from around the world direct to your inbox.

‘I could have done very different styles according to each of their work, but I chose not to,’ says Nourry. ‘The portraits I have are from that time in the 19th century, when you went to the photographer who would arrange you in a certain posture. You wouldn't smile, and you would be quite front-on to the camera. That posture is what you feel in the portraits.’

She wanted the busts to go beyond the concept of the body itself, Nourry adds. ‘I wanted it to be about them as human beings. I did very different sizes, also to show that sculpture can be in very different sizes, and it is not a hierarchy here. It was just based on whose pictures I got first, and I would then start to sculpt first – they would be big because, in terms of the process, this is the timing you have to respect.’
Ultimately, it has been a labour of love for Nourry, and an essential expression of her role as an artist. ‘Sculpture is like my spine,’ she says. ‘It's what keeps me straight.’
‘Prune Nourry: Visionaries’, from 20 October 2026 – 24 January 2027 at Petit Palais; prunenourry.com

Hannah Silver is Head of Art & Culture at Wallpaper*. A writer, editor and author with over 20 years of experience in journalism, spanning national newspapers and independent magazines, she has overseen offbeat art trends and conducted in-depth profiles for print and digital, as well as writing and commissioning extensively across the worlds of culture and luxury since joining in 2019.

items.title: Apple’s smart-home offering just got an upgrade – meet HomeView
items.description: How do you interact with technology in the quiet comfort of your own home? Anecdotal evidence suggests that too many of us simply take our scrolling habits home with us, distractedly swiping away through family meals or double-screening during boxsets. If we c
items.author: Jonathan Bell
paragraphs: How do you interact with technology in the quiet comfort of your own home? Anecdotal evidence suggests that too many of us simply take our scrolling habits home with us, distractedly swiping away through family meals or double-screening during boxsets. If we can’t give up our hard-won instant access to information, trivia and diversion, we can at least find ways of managing it.

Enter the home hub or home display. A category that barely existed a decade ago, these fixed-position second screens serve as portals to digital assistants as well as streaming devices, alarm clocks, kitchen timers and any number of hands-free, voice-controlled functions, as well as meshing and controlling smart home ecosystems. Amazon launched its Echo Show back in 2017 with Google following on the following year with its Home Hub.

Now it’s Apple’s turn to enter the fray. HomeView is Apple’s first-ever home assistant display, a characteristically polished device that foregrounds the physical design, the user interface and the close integration of Siri AI and Apple Intelligence.

If the design doesn’t wow you – and it should, especially when compared to the often rather plasticky offerings from its rivals – then Apple hopes the onboard intelligence and stringent privacy functions will encourage you to switch over to HomeView.

Featuring a seven-inch Liquid Retina display with adaptive brightness that goes all the way down to a soft glow for nightstand use, HomeView is finished in Apple’s signature aluminium. In addition to a wall-mounted version, the principal device sits on a domed speaker base, joined by a well-engineered stainless-steel hinge to adapt the viewing height. Right now, it’s available in silver, starlight, rose pink and space grey (Apple helpfully and predictably matches its USB cable colours to the case colour).

A lot of thought has gone into making HomeView intuitive. In addition to smart home management, streaming audio and making calls, the device has been tailored for use in multi-person households. If you have several Apple accounts on the go, HomeView has facial recognition, so it’ll bring up personalised content when you approach the device. Likewise, the proximity sensor keeps information bold and legible from across the room and switches automatically to a more detailed display as you approach.

What you have on your HomeView is very much up to you. As well as making Facetime calls and sorting through calendars, it can serve up photos from your camera roll and serve as the primary dashboard for smart home devices, from the thermostat and lighting controls through to doorbell cameras and more.
Receive our daily digest of inspiration, escapism and design stories from around the world direct to your inbox.

You’ll need a supported iCloud+ subscription to delve into the expansive options, which include new devices in the Apple Home Collection, but in principle it frees up the mind and hands from reverting to familiar scrolling patterns.

Access to the latest Siri AI model is the icing on the cake for those of us who have become used to simply asking random questions out loud, hoping that a suitable device is in earshot. Apple Intelligence is also used to add a layer of sophistication to HomeView’s syncing abilities, whether it’s continuing conversations across devices, recalling personal playlists, messages and calendar items, or simply being contextually aware of who is engaging with the device.
Another neat feature is the ability to dissemble online recipes into a series of bullet points, complete with handily placed timers, to save endless pinching and zooming around a web page.

The interface is clean and beautifully animated with extensive personalisation offerings. Clocks, weather panels, photos and more can be swapped in and out, with the friendly Snoopy IP also making a comeback.

The display contains two speakers with a bass woofer in the stand, making it a pretty decent option for listening to music and podcasts; Apple’s Handoff function seamlessly transfers the current song or episode from car or phone to the device. It can also sync with AirPlay-compatible speakers.

Apple’s inevitable arrival in this space has been achieved with typical panache, allowing those already immersed in the company’s ecosystem to carry on playing within its fragrant walled garden. For everyone else, the quality bar has just been raised.
Apple HomeView is available in silver, starlight, rose pink, and space grey for £299. HomeView Wall Mounted comes in space grey and silver for £299, Apple.com

Jonathan Bell has written for Wallpaper* magazine since 1999, covering everything from architecture and transport design to books, tech and graphic design. He is now the magazine’s Transport and Technology Editor. Jonathan has written and edited 15 books, including Concept Car Design, 21st Century House, and The New Modern House, and co-edits the long-running things magazine weblog.

items.title: A Breakup Only Made Boy Harsher Stronger
items.description: There was a moment when Jae Matthews decided that she wanted to keep Boy Harsher going. It was in Marfa, Texas, where she’d rented out a barn to escape the East Coast winter. (Although, she says, “it was still fucking cold.”) She remembers sitting in said barn
items.author: Claire Landsbaum
paragraphs: There was a moment when Jae Matthews decided that she wanted to keep Boy Harsher going. It was in Marfa, Texas, where she’d rented out a barn to escape the East Coast winter. (Although, she says, “it was still fucking cold.”) She remembers sitting in said barn and contemplating the future of the band she’d started in 2013 with Augustus Muller, her musical and romantic partner. They’d broken up in 2024, and the project was in limbo.

“I was so back and forth, and the process was so painful; there were many days that I was telling myself, ‘I can’t do this,’” Matthews says. But “my mantra is, ‘We build our own prisons.’ And I realized that I couldn’t do the wishy-washy thing. I was like, ‘Alright, I am committing to moving forward.’”

A lot had happened to upend her life: there was the breakup, her mother had died, she’d started ketamine therapy. So much had changed, and she didn’t want her musical partnership to change, too. “As chaotic as it was, Boy Harsher felt like the only anchor,” Matthews says. “I felt like I had lost everything in my life and couldn’t afford to lose anything else.”
“It’s often fraught, but we can't deny the fact that there is an alchemy between us when it comes to generating music,” she adds. “And that is, I think, incredibly rare.”

So, they pulled through. And it’s a good thing they did. Matthews is speaking to me from a wood-paneled office in Beckett, Massachusetts, an isolated area in the southern Berkshires. Her two dogs are running around at her ankles, one fawning after the other; her sharp features are framed by dark bangs. Muller dials in from a concrete box in Boston with bad wifi. The sun gradually sets as we talk, leaving him in partial shadow. It’s release day for Boy Harsher; Get Mean, their first studio album in seven years — and their first on major label Atlantic Records — is finally out in the world. And people seem to like it. At an album-release party at Oberon in New York, enthusiastic 30-somethings in dark clothing mixed with the likes of The Frost Children and others from Muller’s and Matthews’ creative universe. The album received a 7.0 rating on Pitchfork, and the band’s corresponding tour has sold out in a dozen cities.

The darkwave duo offers something new on songs like “Ronny,” which opens on a sunny layer of ’80s-style synth, and “Jeans” and “Faulty,” bouncier dance tracks that feel optimistic even as they’re shot through with melancholy. Rich chords of live guitar also make their way into the album — the first time in a long time that the band has recorded with the instrument itself, rather than its synthetic counterpart.

Matthews and Muller are still watching the reception to the album play out and trying to absorb the fact that they’ve made something good together — again. “We were wrapping up [the album], and I would drive around the middle of nowhere Massachusetts blasting ‘Faulty.’ I was like, ‘This song fucking rips. It’s such a good song,’” Matthews says. “I have this paranoia that because I love this album, no one else will. We were talking about this a little bit last night and this morning: It’s just really difficult to sit in success and joy. I think that it comes from maybe also believing you don’t deserve it.”

If “deserving” something means going through the ringer and coming out on the other side, Matthews and Muller are more than eligible. They went through periods of not speaking to each other. They were both angry. But “out of all of the stuff going on in our lives — as chaotic as it was — Boy Harsher felt like the only anchor,” Muller reiterates. “It was something that we fully understood and had confidence in. It was like, you wake up, and it’s the thing that makes sense. And we’re going to work on it.”

For both of them, moving forward looked like diving into the process of record-making. The way Muller and Matthews work is as follows: Muller creates a loose instrumental track and sends it over. It’s usually a bass synth, some type of pad, maybe some percussion. Then Matthews tries singing on it, exploring whether her voice gels with that specific combination of sounds. Sometimes the answer is “no, which is tragic; there have been so many pre-demos that I love, and I want so badly to make them work,” she says. But ultimately, there’s no forcing it. “I’m not a trained vocalist,” Matthews explains. “If I was really singing on top [of a track] in a classical way, it would not be a Boy Harsher song.”

As they started to make Get Mean, Matthews and Muller were exchanging tracks and notes at a furious pace. “I was sending her probably three sketches a day,” Muller says. “We were so eager to do this.”

When they agree that something is working, Matthews starts to flesh it out. “I plug the track into Ableton and kind of sing gibberish over it,” she says. “These will be really short clips — maybe 15 seconds. The objective is to figure out, do I even fucking sound good? I’ll send those 15 seconds to Gus and he’ll be like, ‘Alright, it sounds good. Can you try to write a melody?’”
“You rarely sing gibberish though,” Muller interjects. “You always have lyrics.”
“Well, it’s gibberish in the sense that it’s non-directed,” Matthews says.
There is a bit of back-and-forth about the gibberish question during which Matthews says, at one point, “Well, as the one doing it…” But ultimately there is consensus that her process is “intuitive.”

Then come the lyrics. Matthews “digs into the vaults” where she keeps notes on experiences, feelings, and moments she can mine to power a song. For this particular album, she dove into the journal she kept in 2024 — that banner of a shitty year. “It’s so fucking dark, and I’m really bad at diaries, so it’s all over the place,” Matthews says. She thinks a lot about the ways in which she desires people, and the ways in which she has felt rejected. She tries not to get too morbid. “My mom had died, and I was like, ‘It would be really hard for me to write a song about her right now.’” For one thing, it was too soon; she hadn’t had enough time to process. For another, “We’re trying to figure out what Boy Harsher is, and I’m like, ‘I don't know if anyone wants to be throwing ass in the club to a song about my mom having dementia and dying. It doesn’t feel right.’”

In fact, Matthews struggled to get words onto paper. She traveled to Mexico, hoping it would cure her writer’s block. She credits Muller with midwifing several songs on the album, including “Tough Luck (When You Don’t Call)” and “Jeans.” The latter song is told from the point of view of “me as a New York City girl moving to Dimes Square and figuring it out,” Muller says. “I always assign each song a character. There’s a lot of role playing.”

After firming up the songs, Muller and Matthews started thinking about production. They were invited to New Braunfels, Texas, to a store called Syntaur, which houses a massive collection of vintage and analog synths. “I touched basically everything,” Muller says. “It was awesome. Our music has always been defined by the limitations of bedroom recording, but now you have unlimited options. It was like, ‘Wow, we can explore all these sounds.’” It was classic kid in a candy store. “Needless to say, we overproduced those demos.”

Listening back at their engineer’s studio in Italy, Muller heard “maximalism in a way that was making me dizzy.” They started stripping things down. That’s when he noticed a guitar sitting in the studio. So many of their songs used guitar samples or sounds, and he set about replacing them with the real thing. “It was refreshing for me to hear an analog instrument,” he says. “The guitar is so rich that it can replace five [other] sounds. And then you can hear everything again.”

Around the same time all this was going on — as if it wasn’t enough to try to heal a relationship and make a record — Matthews and Muller were also working on their first-ever feature film. The Lonely Woman, which is set to release next year, stars Chloë Sevigny and FKA Twigs and was written, directed, and scored by the band. Muller and Matthews have had some scattered experiences with Hollywood, including creating a song for the 2022 film Halloween Ends that came about because director David Gordon Green would, in Matthews’ words, “go cycling every morning and listen to Boy Harsher.” Their indie horror short, The Runner, came out the same year, a COVID-era project that found legs.

After that, they had some momentum; they also started work on The Lonely Woman in 2022. They quickly learned that making a feature-length movie is “the longest, hardest process,” Muller says. “If an album takes two years,” as Get Mean did, “a movie is that 20-fold. We started and stopped one hundred times.”

The experience taught them a lot, Matthews says. “You meet a lot of Hollywood characters who are like, ‘Kid, we’re gonna make a movie.’ When you’re naive like us, you believe them. That did happen several times,” she says. “So then, when it really does get greenlit, you don't believe it. But you should believe it because often that green light is for half the budget you need.”

She starts to describe the premise of The Lonely Woman: how she and Muller were so committed to the characters from The Runner that it is, essentially, a spinoff for one of them. But Muller interrupts her, not wanting to talk about the project — which is currently in post-production — until it’s finished. “I’m superstitious. I can’t. This is completely hypothetical,” he says. “We’re still editing. It might become a comedy, and we might re-shoot and put Paul Giamatti in it.” (Muller has always been like this, including with early Boy Harsher demos. He prefers to let “the work do the talking” — a holdover from when he moved to Austin, Texas, at 18, in 2007, and heard everyone talking big about “starting a screen-printing company” or what have you. Then, the housing market crashed, and everyone’s plans fell apart. Empty bluster.)

Still, there’s a lot of chatter about the film, which has been described, per Deadline, as a “bleak, sensual and atmospheric horror-thriller.” One can imagine an eerie element — a sensibility that’s similar to what has always defined Matthews’ and Muller’s dark electronica. “We love genre films,” Muller says. “We like taking a vessel and putting something in it. It’s like watching an M. Night Shyamalan movie about growing up in a bad household, but he tells it through genre, and it helps you understand.”

The movie doesn’t yet have a release date; Muller and Matthews will be editing and submitting it through the fall. They’re also touring — first the U.S., then internationally — through December. And somehow, they’d also like to find time to get back in the studio. “We know what we want to do. There’s just not enough time in the day to do it all,” Muller says. “But we’re going to try.”

items.title: State of the Art: This Hollywood “Badass” Added PALY to His 700-Film Repertoire
items.description: In State of the Art, a column for Highsnobiety, Chris Erik Thomas untangles the crossover between fashion and art.
items.author: Chris Erik Thomas
paragraphs: In State of the Art, a column for Highsnobiety, Chris Erik Thomas untangles the crossover between fashion and art.

When you create a clothing brand steeped in Hollywood myths and monsters, booking its biggest stars for ad campaigns feels like the logical move. Doubly so if your brand name is literally Paly Hollywood, you count a movie star as a co-founder, and happen to be based in Los Angeles. But PALY, as the brand prefers to be known these days, isn’t much interested in logic or standard-fare stars.

Instead, it's built itself up over the past six years as a dreamlike specter, tapping nepo-baby talent from deeply rooted Hollywood families for its lookbooks: people like Landon Barker, Skyla Sanders, and Max Madsen.

The casting decision fits PALY’s vibe as a ghost of smoky Viper Room seshes past: a grunge-luxe purveyor of $1,550 ripped jeans and $495 long-sleeve tees with faded, distressed graphics ripped straight from Tinseltown. It’s a winning formula that's attracted an appropriately cult-like following; its releases often sell out in what feels like milliseconds, solidifying the young label as a cultural force on par with Enfants Riches Déprimés.

PALY now feels like the sartorial king of LA, a reputation that sticks even when the brand decamps to, say, a spooky animal sanctuary in rural France. In its new Fall/Winter 2026 campaign film, premiering exclusively today on Highsnobiety, PALY has flown the Hollywood coop for a twisty visual tale directed by Pietro Coppolecchia and narrated by Hollywood’s most-credited living actor (and SS26 campaign star), Eric Roberts.

It's a moody fever dream and a stark vibe shift compared to the brand’s sunny, LA-set ads from just a season ago. “At first watch, the film doesn’t necessarily scream Hollywood,” PALY co-founder Kyle Lindgren tells Highsnobiety. “But [its] influences have shaped the entire process, from production to the film's themes.” With a crew tied to everyone from Luca Guadagnino and Steven Spielberg to Ridley Scott and Luc Besson, the film follows a doomed French couple who find themselves in a surrealist house where humans may or may not be turning into animals. Very “Circe in The Odyssey” coded, sure, but also a perfect metaphor for the transformative power of acting.

Compared to the usual crop of fashion campaigns, which tend to involve very famous people wearing clothes from a brand they’d otherwise never be caught dead in, this one actually hits. It’s weird and textured, and it feels more focused on spinning this strange narrative of transformation than on selling clothes (which, ironically, made me want to wear everything this doomed French couple is wearing).
Ahead of the film’s release, we emailed Lindgren and called Roberts (and his wife and manager, Eliza) to chat about the making of PALY’s swirling surrealist film.
Kyle, how do you choose who wears PALY, and what does Hollywood lineage bring to a brand built on Hollywood's stories?
