items.title: En la era del algoritmo: El Mundial todavía hace lo que el internet no puede
items.description: El consumo de entretenimiento colectivo está en extinción. Habitamos la era de la individualidad en donde cada vez más, divertirnos con series, películas, música y arte se vive de manera hiper personalizada. ¿Y cuál es el problema? que ya no convivimos, que ya
items.author: Ricardo Diaz
paragraphs: El consumo de entretenimiento colectivo está en extinción. Habitamos la era de la individualidad en donde cada vez más, divertirnos con series, películas, música y arte se vive de manera hiper personalizada. ¿Y cuál es el problema? que ya no convivimos, que ya no se construyen recuerdos.

El tiempo y la vida nos han llevado a acomodar el entretenimiento en los momentos que nos alcanzan: en el bus, a la hora de comer, antes de dormir. ¿Cuándo fue la última vez que te reuniste con más de dos personas a ver una película? Es claro que la colectividad del entretenimiento no ha parado de mutar desde la llegada del internet y todos los días siguen cambiando las reglas del juego.
Pero ¿será que el Mundial es uno de los últimos eventos globales que aún logran despertar el sentimiento de colectividad?
Christian Nodal, El Mundial es Nuestro

“El Mundial Es Nuestro” de Telemundo, alineó una noche inaugural para encender el ánimo futbolístico que regresa cada 4 años. Tuvimos la oportunidad de estar en el backstage del concierto y conversar con cantantes, futbolistas y presentadores deportivos.

Mauricio Ochmann y Jacky Bracamontes, fueron los conductores de la noche y también de los primeros en pasar por la alfombra roja. La mexicana confesó que el amor por el fútbol lo heredó de su padre “El Profe” y que aún conserva una de sus primeras fotografías de niña con vestido rosa y un balón en brazo. Mientras que Mauricio recordó cuando en el mundial del 86’ estaba en su natal Querétaro y conoció al equipo de Dinamarca.

Siempre hay recuerdos, siempre hay algo memorable. Y es que hablar del Mundial no necesariamente tiene que ver con canchas, goles o trofeos, sino con una experiencia que se construye. Emilia, Xavi, Wisin y Carlos Vives lo entendieron e hilaron “Somos más” entre luces, bailarines y mucho color al detonar el ánimo de la noche.
Wisin, Emilia, Carlos Vives, Xavi, El Mundial es Nuestro

“Esta canción busca unir a la comunidad. Históricamente el Mundial se ha disfrutado en familia, en vacaciones, con amigos. Creo que es una oportunidad de encontrarse. El fútbol es amistad y escribimos esta canción buscando este sentimiento” - nos contó Carlos Vives.

La noche avanzó y con ella Lupillo Rivera imprimió el romanticismo, mientras que Elena Rose se diluyó entre luces azules y amarillas para interpretar “Tututu” en el escenario. “Recuerdo que de chica en Venezuela siempre que había un BBQ, era inevitable la televisión transmitiendo un partido de fútbol. Con el tiempo he logrado entender la pasión de mis amigos y familia por este deporte” - confesó Elena.

Otra de las sorpresas del show fue la nueva canción en colaboración de Yahritizia y su Esencia con Low Clika, quienes nos contaron que “So Bella” representa muy bien el espíritu de competencia, pasión y latinidad. Por su lado, Grupo Frontera estrenó “Un solo corazón”, el himno de la selección mexicana. Y es que tras 40 años, la sede del mundial regresa a México y tras 32 a Estados Unidos y esto no es poca cosa. Históricamente vivir el fútbol como latinos habla de una identidad arraigada que se respira, que se hereda.
Elena Rose, El Mundial es Nuestro

“En mi casa todo era fútbol. Mi papá siempre nos lo fomentó y de hecho, recuerdo que mi hermano, quien es 9 años mayor que yo, me contagió esa pasión por los juegos. Durante el Mundial del 2002 Corea / Japón, nos despertábamos a las 3 o 4 de la mañana por el cambio de horario a ver los partidos. Fui muy feliz en esa época” - nos contó Andrés Guardado.

Luis Fonsi, Natalia Jiménez, David Bisbal y Christian Nodal se sumaron al concierto, recordándonos que la música y el fútbol comparten una fuerza masiva capaz de hacer lo que el internet aún no puede: construir recuerdos en la vida real.

Vivir un Mundial es una experiencia colectiva, una de esas raras ocasiones capaces de juntar a varias generaciones frente a una misma pantalla. Quizá dentro de diez años no recordemos quién levantó la copa o quién terminó como máximo goleador, pero sí dónde estábamos, con quién celebramos y quién nos enseñó a sentir que esos noventa minutos significaban algo más que un partido.

Tal vez por eso, después de más de cuatro décadas narrando fútbol, Luis Omar Tapia "El Panda" cuando habla de recuerdos, no menciona campeonatos ni estadísticas. Lo hace recordando a su abuelo en Chile, quien le repetía una frase que todavía conserva intacta antes de cada partido: "Ahora comienza el deporte más hermoso del mundo."
Carlos Vives, El Mundial es Nuestro

items.title: I Can’t See Anything: A Tale About Elizabeth Holmes, Billy Evans, A24, and Me
items.description: Sometime in August, I sent a LinkedIn message to Billy Evans. At the time, rumors of a forthcoming documentary about him and his partner, Elizabeth Holmes, were just that. But it’s never a bad time for a profile, as long as the father of the Theranos founder’s
items.author: Dan Adler
paragraphs: Sometime in August, I sent a LinkedIn message to Billy Evans. At the time, rumors of a forthcoming documentary about him and his partner, Elizabeth Holmes, were just that. But it’s never a bad time for a profile, as long as the father of the Theranos founder’s children is single-parenting and making trips to the Texas federal prison where Ghislaine Maxwell and, until recently, former Real Housewives of Salt Lake City star Jen Shah are doing time with the woman he has described as his “soulmate.”

Evans replied almost instantly. The content tracked with some of the expectations you might have of a person who is one half of this particular relationship. Holmes was convicted of defrauding investors in 2022; she and Evans met in 2017, when she was under federal investigation but not yet indicted. Their first child was born just before her trial, and their second just before she reported to prison.

“Probably not,” was Evans’s response. “But send me an email from your VF email to prove identity along with a picture of your business card with my name written in it in green pen … We can take it from there.”

While I was able to quickly comply with this oddly specific request because I am in fact a staff writer here with proximity to VF’s art department—and while I got to know him off-record in the months to come—Evans has not (yet) granted an interview. But You Can See Everything, Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s A24 documentary about Holmes and Evans, has now arrived with a level of stealth and intrigue befitting its absurdist material. And one result of the rollout, to say nothing of the film itself, is that Billy Evans has emerged as the primary villain.

The secrecy surrounding the project is more or less unprecedented in the documentary world. As A24 said in press notes circulated after Wednesday night’s New York premiere of the film, Fielder and Oppenheim assembled a tight crew of seven collaborators to keep their pre-incarceration trips to Holmes and Evans’s Del Mar beachfront home under wraps, even as paparazzi swirled the premises with Holmes’s prison reporting date looming.

The film was not known to the public until the moments leading up to its surprise screening at the Telluride Film Festival in September. In the past few weeks, the studio has taken pointed measures to prevent the documentary’s plot points from circulating, particularly its central dramatic turn about halfway through. Before a Q&A with Fielder and Oppenheim at this week’s premiere, New York Film Festival programmer Dennis Lim told the audience, “I think part of the effect of the film you just saw is the sense of surprise and disbelief at what you’re seeing. So I think just in the interest of trying to preserve a relatively spoiler-free experience for later audiences, we ask that you not film and post this conversation.” Attendees clapped, and Fielder underscored the point, asking if attendees “should … be shaming others” spotted filming. Most—but not all—put their phones away.

This pursuit itself presented a sort of high-wire act, with the standby line to get into the theater beginning at 8 a.m., as my colleague Hillary Busis reported. There was no embargo on the New York premiere, the term of art for a reporter’s agreement to hold off on publishing certain information until a certain time. One minor revelation in the film is that Evans posts on X on Holmes’s behalf.

After learning that I was interested in a story on Evans—and after Holmes’s account posted a tweet that seemed to suggest that Evans was aware of this detail’s inclusion in the film, which he had not yet seen—A24’s publicists vetted my attendance at the premiere by asking whether I could hold off on publishing key plot points about Evans’s involvement. We couldn’t come to terms, as it were, and they said they had no more tickets but would be happy for me to see it another time.

Among the central twists in You Can See Everything, as I understand it secondhand, is that Evans comes out the worst. The news last year that he and Holmes are in the process of launching another medical testing enterprise already raised eyebrows, but as Busis wrote, Evans is portrayed as “a smarmy, self-satisfied Svengali figure who sniffs conspicuously and blithely brags about his own prowess in a variety of arenas.” (“I’m pretty strategic and well-resourced,” he tells Fielder at one point. “I know people who can do just about anything.”)

The filmmakers and Evans have since grown estranged, according to Fielder. “Near the end of filming, Billy was trying to exert a level of control over the project that made us uncomfortable, and communication with him sort of broke down because of that,” he told the audience at Telluride. As of Wednesday’s premiere, Evans hadn’t seen the film, but according to a source familiar with his thinking, he doesn’t feel that his relationship with Fielder and Oppenheim is broken. (A24 didn’t immediately return a request for comment.)

In my own efforts to understand Evans, I spoke to people who knew him before he got together with Holmes. He sounded relatively normal, if intense and offbeat—or as normal as one could be while committed to this particular cultural figure. “I’ll put it in the context of, he fit into Silicon Valley,” another employee at Luminar, the self-driving car company where Evans was working when he met Holmes, told me. “It’s a very unique crowd, just really smart people, but also niche smart. ... These are people where you wonder, Where does your brain come from? This is so bizarre. Billy fit right in, and it’s an element of level of intelligence.”
“I felt a little bit silly when Billy started talking about dating Elizabeth Holmes, and my thought was, Wait, I know that name,” the employee recalled. “And he’s like, Right, founder of Theranos.”

“That was the most I understood of his personal life outside of just getting shit done at Luminar,” they went on. “So for him to be talking about her and meeting her, I thought, Whoa, he’s crazy about her right off the bat.”
“Weren’t you worried she was sort of scamming you?” Fielder asks Evans in the film.
“A hundred percent,” Evans concedes. “But what did she have to gain from me?
“Well, isn’t your family rich?” Fielder says.
“Yeah,” Evans says. “I think that there’s, like, a lot of different levels of wealth.”

The line plays for a laugh, but one acquaintance of the Evans family in San Diego, where they operate a trio of luxury hotels, said there was an element of truth to it. “It’s not like New York wealth or tech wealth,” they said. “I don’t think [Holmes] would have seen Billy as a way to wealth. There are billionaires floating around, they were not one of them.”

Growing up, Evans had a reputation for dating “older girls, prettier ones,” and his family was known in part for their idiosyncrasies—a milder version of the Kennedys, as the acquaintance put it. (Evans’s father, Bill, was an incognito presence at Holmes’s trial, telling reporters that he was a media watchdog named Hanson and that he fixed up old cars for a living. And Evans did agree, at least, that I could print a list of his animals: a blue Argentine tegu, a corn snake, a curly-haired tarantula, blue death-feigning beetles, and two Burmese forest tortoises.)

Hearing that, I had a somewhat clearer picture of the world assembled around the documentary of the year that I hadn’t seen: Here in the Fielder-Holmes-Evans orbit was a collection of oddballs all the way down. No wonder everything in their blast radius had a funhouse quality to it, including the mere act of seeing the film.
This story has been updated.

items.title: DM My Rep! The Top Lawyers, Managers and Agents Driving the Creator Economy
items.description: This is their world and, for better or worse, we’re just living in it. Those populating the creator economy are swaying elections (Hasan Piker), reimagining independent film (Mark Fischbach, aka Markiplier) and selling out capsule collections at the Gap (serio
items.author: Taylor Lorenz; Claudia Rosenbaum
paragraphs: This is their world and, for better or worse, we’re just living in it. Those populating the creator economy are swaying elections (Hasan Piker), reimagining independent film (Mark Fischbach, aka Markiplier) and selling out capsule collections at the Gap (seriously, Hailey Bieber, are there any of those jeans left?). But even the best business and marketing minds on the internet can’t build an empire without a team.

Without their reps, the world these creators built would be a fraction of what it is today … and, worst of all, we’d have no idea who to call daddy. So let’s take a look at the most powerful reps in the creator space, all they made happen and all the money they moved in 2026.
Ali Berman, Raina Penchansky, Oren Rosenbaum and Hilary Williams

UTA Creators and its Digital Brand Architects are home to a daunting roster that includes Markiplier, Kareem Rahma, Colin and Samir and Olandria Carthen. Among the year’s marquee moves were populating Netflix’s new video podcast slate (The Rotten Files With Stephanie Soo), brokering that infamous MrBeast-James Patterson novel collab, expanding Emma Chamberlain’s Chamberlain Coffee (hello, Abbot Kinney!) and putting Alix Earle with the Netflix series Earle Meets World.
Keith Bielory, Melissa DeMarco and Jade Sherman

Gersh’s digital division sees Sherman, Bielory and DeMarco continuing to push clients further into mainstream entertainment and culture, facilitating record-breaking runs for Broadway’s Chicago thanks to reality star clients Ariana Madix, Whitney Leavitt and Mark Ballas. The team also helped online health expert Doctor Mike surpass 30 million followers and snagged Eli Rallo a deal for a book that became a New York Times best-seller.
Payton Booker, Skye Petrie and Alexis Ramos

Ramos has grown Sixteenth’s sports division from the ground up, now representing top sports names in the NFL, WNBA and track and field. Petrie brought a massive U.K. roster to the company, helping British internet stars like Maddie Borge go global. Booker has secured major partnerships, including a $90,000 brand campaign for Charles Brockman III.
Christopher Chatham and Ellie Heisler

As Alan Chikin Chow delivers more of Alan’s Universe to his 100 million-plus YouTube subscribers, Chatham and Heisler widened Chow’s audience with distribution deals at the Roku Channel and Tubi. Chatham also reps multiplatform lightning rod Logan Paul and brokered deals for his Impaulsive podcast as well as for streamer IShowSpeed (61 million YouTube subscribers). Heisler works intimately with Jordan and Salish Matter and structured Salish’s collaboration with Chipotle — making her the youngest person to launch a digital menu item with the brand.
Daniel Daks and Josh DeAngelis

Founding Palette during the 2020 TikTok boom, Daks and DeAngelis have since built out a roster of talent spanning comedy, lifestyle and infotainment including Spanish news creator Carlos Eduardo Espina (he launched his Creator Cup, which twice sold out MLS’ Houston Dynamo stadium) and Roblox star Lana Rae. The latter’s consumer product line has done more than $20 million at retail in the past five months.

Managing partners Brian Sokolik and Nate Ruff recruited Das to the management company where he’s since made a name for himself for representing social impact creators. For client Hunter Prosper, a storyteller and interviewer, he closed a book deal and helped him launch a series with Barack Obama’s production company Higher Ground. Das also helped video creator Jesus Morales, who tells Latinx stories around Los Angeles, launch a nonprofit that has already earned six figures in donations.

Davis closed a reported $100 million first-of-its-kind pact for Jay Shetty and his On Purpose podcast to have joint exclusive rights at Netflix and Spotify. Dayeh and Davis, who co-head the digital department, also helped reality stars Paige DeSorbo and Hannah Berner secure major brand partnerships, including Hannah’s multiyear ambassadorship with Lululemon.

As Entertainment 360 seeks a bigger piece of the digital pie, Devlin joined this year to further expand its creator business. While at WME, she brokered Paige DeSorbo’s Super Bowl commercial with Kinder Bueno and negotiated finance guru Vivian Tu’s SoFi Bank ambassadorship.
Matt Dysart and Eric Perlmutter-Gumbiner

Serving as corporate and strategic adviser to digital marketing and talent firms, Perlmutter-Gumbiner works with creator-led Palette Media Talent Management and Marketing, Jake Rosen Entertainment, Get Engaged Media, Underscore Talent Agency, Made by All and Dhar Mann Studios. Dysart is heavily invested in the digital space, representing Slow Ventures, Kynetic Content, UnderCurrent, Palette Media and Creator Society, among others.
Stephanie Field and Lindsay Nead

Parker Management kicked off the year by acquiring Estate Five, expanding their portfolio of creators across the fashion and beauty spaces. Recent signings include Alex Bennett, Abigail Erb and Dan and Samantha Matthews, joining a deep bench of top lifestyle, family and home creators, as well as Bachelor Nation talent. The firm secured campaigns with Google Pixel, Abercrombie & Fitch, Tuckernuck and Lincoln, to name a few.
Lisa Filipelli, Brittany Maxwell and Caroline Nardilla

Select keeps leaning into the intersection of the creator economy and Hollywood, delivering new seasons of The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives (not messy work at all!) and franchise expansion TSLOMW: Orange County, both populated with Select clients. They also launched Select Sports, which reimagines athlete representation for the social media era, landing Super Bowl campaigns with Meta x Oakley glasses and Toyota for Sky Brown and Oksana Masters.
Dylan Flinn, Mallory Llewellyn and Kyle Stevens

Llewellyn landed four of her clients on Netflix’s Calabasas Confidential, for which she serves as consulting producer. Stevens helped Kareem Rahma turn SubwayTakes into an Emmy-nominated series, while launching Rahma’s second show, Keep the Meter Running. Flinn has become the go-to manager for top AI creators, landing one of the first celebrity likeness deals with HiggsfieldAI and securing a studio development deal for AI content creator Chloe vs History. Team History!
Arleta Fowler, Andrew Graham, Brent Weinstein and Sophie Wiener

Over the past year, the agency has signed some of the biggest creators in the world, including Rhett + Link, Valkyrae, Stokes Twins, Deestroying, Rebecca Zamolo, Nara Smith, Jack Goldburg (aka Jack’s Dining Room), Reckless Ben, Max “Career Ladder” Klymenko and Reece Feldman. In June, CAA and Integrated Media Co. launched a $250 million venture called Compound Creative Holdings, aimed at acquiring, operating and growing companies in the creator economy.
Brandon Freytag and Yoni Ginsberg

Freytag and Ginsberg have spent nearly a decade building careers and brokering livestreaming’s biggest deals. Loaded represents the largest share of Twitch livestreamers by watch time, including TheBurntPeanut, Cinna, Maya Higa and Shroud. They’ve landed recent deals with Google, EA, Epic Games and Tencent and recently negotiated a “Protect the Peanut” campaign with Battlefield, one of EA’s most successful creator campaigns.
Andy Galker and Eric Weissler

Representing Mark Rober, the former NASA engineer, ex-Apple product designer and inventor with nearly 82 million YouTube subscribers, as well as late night host Jimmy Kimmel, Galker and Weissler keep busy. They closed the deal that put Rober’s CrunchLabs and Kimmel’s Kimmelot into business together on Netflix’s upcoming competition series Schooled. Rober will host and executive produce the show that will pit teams of students against each other in a gantlet of creative science challenges.
Joe Gilliland, Josh Morgan and Marcela Woessner

Woessner inked gymnast and Instagram star Livvy Dunne’s partnership with Miller Lite and turned an embarrassing viral moment (sweat stains are unavoidable!) into a partnership with deodorant brand Secret. The Team acquired Provisions, a leading golf creator agency founded by Gilliland and Morgan. The two developed the Creator Classic, a tournament where 12 of YouTube’s top golf creators compete, and built Your Golf Tour, a YouTube series featuring the sport’s biggest creators and pros.
Ryan Goodell, Todd Rubenstein and Kevin Yorn

Alix Earle has evolved from creator to entrepreneur under Yorn and Rubenstein, who helped launch her skin care brand, Reale Actives, and negotiated the Netflix series Earle Meets World. Yorn advised Hailey Bieber on her 2026 Gap collection (long live the baggy jeans renaissance), among many major brand deals, while Rubenstein represented the multitalented Charli D’Amelio (see page 48). As for Goodell, he has chef Nick DiGiovanni (75 million-plus followers), who served as Fox Sports’ official chef for the FIFA World Cup this year.
Michael Gordon, David Huntzinger and John Nelson

Night has had another blockbuster year, acquiring IRL marketing firm Experiential Supply Co. Nelson brokered deals for Twitch star Kai Cenat’s record-breaking Streamer University with partners including Red Bull, Dell and Fortnite. Huntzinger expanded progressive influencer Hasan Piker’s merch line amid skyrocketing fame and national attention, and brokered YouTubers Sam & Colby’s Netflix partnership. Gordon oversaw the eight-figure sale of true-crime YouTube channel Dr. Insanity to an investment company.
Shaun Gordon and Jessica Marlow

With Gordon’s legal guidance, client Alex Cooper has grown Call Her Daddy from a buzzy podcast into an aspiring media empire that now includes the podcast, the Unwell Network, Unwell’s expanding film slate, live events, touring and major brand partnerships, including its distribution relationship with SiriusXM. In the past year, Unwell raised its first outside capital at a reported $500 million pre-money valuation. Marlow’s clients include Claudia and Jackie Oshry of The Toast; Remi Parsons, co-host of the Webby Award-winning Pretty Basic podcast and Basically Unfiltered podcast, which debuted at No. 1 on both Spotify and Apple; and Chris Olsen, one of the most recognized comedic voices on TikTok and author of the memoir I Think My Therapist Hates Me.

Howard works with Kansas City Chiefs quarterback Patrick Mahomes and wife Brittany, advising them on endorsement and promotional partnerships, along with other business issues related to the growth of their personal brands. Howard also counsels gamer Andre Rebelo (aka Typical Gamer, which has 16 million YouTube followers), Karl Jacobs, Chicago Bears quarterback Caleb Williams and, on the other side of the table, she represented Gap in the Hailey Bieber collab. Loose denim forever!

Acquiring Studio71 gave Fixated a combined global network of more than 1,000 creators. It operates a 25,000-person clipper network and has racked up 3 billion monthly impressions on its owned social pages. Howe brokered deals for children’s gaming expert Mackenzie Turner with Disney and Nickelodeon and led the creation and launch of her Roblox experience (100 million visits in its first 30 days).
Seth Jacobs and Brittny Turner
Brillstein Entertainment Partners

Jacobs helped the true-crime show Morbid sell out Radio City Music Hall on a live tour. He also launched Unbiased Politics, a daily video show with lawyer influencer Jordan Berman. Turner helped YouTube star Tana Mongeau launch her podcast Brand Safe and secured partnerships with SeatGeek, DraftKings, Skims and Celsius.
Will Jacobson and Matt Rosen

Jacobson closed deals for beauty vlogger Bretman Rock (19 million on Instagram) to front a global campaign for Kate Spade New York and a partnership to make him the face of K-beauty brand Dr. Groot in the U.S. Rosen’s client Noah Beck has been showcasing his acting talent in the popular Tubi rom-com franchise Sideline: The QB and Me, with Rosen ironing out deals for the second and upcoming third and final film, along with helping get him cast on Fox’s Baywatch reboot.

Outshine Talent has built out its sports business significantly, representing internet-famous baseball stars like the Savannah Bananas’ Kyle “KJ” Jackson and RobertAnthony Cruz (aka Coach RAC), who just launched a custom product line with Under Armour. Jones also helped comedian and actor Tyler Gaca develop a horror film and comedy creator Lala Sadii secure a Disney Channel scripted project.
Adam Kaller, Ryan Pastorek and Lauren Partipilo Schwartz

In a landmark creator economy story, Mark Fischbach (aka Markiplier) pushed fans to call theaters to screen his self-funded $3 million Iron Lung. It’s since netted $50 million worldwide, with Kaller and Pastorek by his side as his options have blown wide open for a second act. That pair also represent SmartLess, Crooked Media, The Bulwark, Smosh, Mythical Entertainment, Emma Chamberlain, Liza Koshy, Lilly Singh and Valkyrae, among many others. In addition, Pastorek and Partipilo sealed Hannah Berner and Paige DeSorbo’s Giggly Squad signing of a multiyear deal with SiriusXM. Partipilo also negotiated for RHOSLC‘s Bronwyn Newport to appear on this upcoming season of The Traitors.
Josh Kaplan and Jenny Rothenberg

Founded by former Morning Brew executives, Smooth Media has built one of the fastest-growing management firms representing knowledge creators. The company has helped execute major campaigns for brands including Anthropic, Notion, Microsoft, Ramp, Canva and Google. It partnered with Colin and Samir to build creator industry publication The Publish Press, and, just this month, creator Cat Goetze (known online as CatGPT) took an equity stake in the company and joined as a strategic adviser.

Snow and Lee have the uplifting (and lucrative) job of representing kids creator Ms. Rachel, who gained 10 billion views worldwide. They negotiated her Netflix series Ms. Rachel, one of the most watched seasons of any children’s show on the service with 53.4 million views, and her debut album, I’m So Happy. They also rep former Mormon Wives star Whitney Leavitt, whose run as Roxie Hart in Chicago grossed more than $8 million in its first six weeks.

With more than 55 million followers tuning in for 23-year-old Brooke Monk’s beauty tips, Marder helped her launch her Doting Beauty brand this year as he handled all of her legal and endorsement work. Marder also represents social media star and U.S. Navy veteran Bella Poarch (91.6 million followers on TikTok alone).

McNeily recently closed a podcast deal for top horror creator Heidi Wong and put scripted adaptations of lifestyle influencer Tinx’s best-selling books The Shift and Hotter in the Hamptons into development at Amazon and Hulu. She also secured a major partnership with Kérastase promoting its luxury hair care products with tastemaker Stassi Schroeder.
Worthy Patterson, Mariam Rastegar Ross and Eman Redwan

As co-head of digital, Redwan oversees 25 executives who have closed more than $100 million in deals over the past year and a client roster that includes Nara Smith (ASMR alert). Rastegar Ross recently brokered Chris Appleton’s seven-figure deal with hair care brand Schwarzkopf, while Patterson developed influencer Beca Michie into a top fashion creator, placing her at major fashion shows and closing seven figures worth of deals.

Launching a studio this year, Made by All aims to turn creators into Hollywood talent and owners of original IP. Perice works with comedy heavyweights (Adam W, Hannah Stocking, Josh Peck) along with internet-native artists like Devon Rodriguez. She has helped foster partnerships with mainstream Hollywood talent including Kevin Hart, Tom Holland and Jennifer Lopez.
Douglas Pinsky and Jake Williams

As AI creators have attracted more interest from big brands, RKM surpassed $50 million in gross partnership revenue in 2026 with their clients gadget guru Carterpcs; tech and robotics creator Rowan Cheung; Natalie Fratto, who draws deep tech explainers; and Austin Nasso, a comedian who hosts the Tech Roast Show. Williams and Pinsky sold Roberto Nickson’s Life With Claude series to Anthropic and have negotiated several million dollars’ worth of partnerships with OpenAI, Google, Meta, Nvidia, AMD and SpaceXAI.

Client Lala Sadii’s viral TikTok comedy skits have propelled her to more than 37.5 million Instagram followers, and Randolph advised Sadii through the development of Lala IRL, a live-action scripted Disney Channel and Disney+ series inspired by her rise as a social media star. Randolph’s other clients include Olympic track and field power couple Tara and Hunter Woodhall (7 million-plus followers), best-selling author Erin McGoff (6.2 million followers) and The Lipstick Lesbians (1.9 million followers), the latter puckering up with Clinique, Marc Jacobs Beauty, Tatcha, NYX, Morphe, Estée Lauder, Fenty, Milk and Goop partnerships.

Sauer’s clients Colin & Samir have interviewed everyone from Mark Zuckerberg to MrBeast, while Sauer has negotiated the duo’s partnerships with Google Gemini, Adobe and LinkedIn. He also represents Ryan Trahan, who is known for his charity fundraisers and viral video challenges, including the Penny Series, in which he tries to travel across the U.S. starting with only one penny.
Tara Senior and Todd Weinstein

For MrBeast, the first individual creator to hit 500 million YouTube subscribers in June, the duo serve as lead counsel, structuring the deals behind Amazon Prime Video’s Beast Games seasons two and three — each budgeted at more than $100 million. They’re also lead counsel to Dhar Mann Studios, the largest scripted creator-led studio in the business pulling nearly 300 million views a week across platforms, with Mann retaining full creative ownership and independence. (No script notes on those videos …)
Pasha Tasvibi and Matt Waldstein

UTA’s industry-leading creator group has Waldstein and Tasvibi — both partners and business affairs senior vps — to thank for structuring multimillion-dollar deals for the agency’s top creator clients. Specialists in audio and video podcasting, the duo, who work alongside UTA creators co-head Oren Rosenbaum, helped navigate Netflix’s entry into podcasting and are known for crafting deals that turn creator franchises into premium media businesses. Waldstein has brokered landmark deals across sports, comedy and culture, including Barstool Sports’ Pardon My Take (hosted by Dan “Big Cat” Katz and Eric “PFT Commenter” Sollenberger) and Spittin’ Chiclets (hosted by Ryan Whitney, Paul “Biz Nasty” Bissonnette and Brian “Rear Admiral” McGonagle), as well as The Ryen Russillo Show for both Netflix and Barstool. Together, he and Tasvibi also closed the deal for Small Town Murder, hosted by James Pietragallo and Jimmie Whisman. Tasvibi has led first-of-their-kind deals connecting true crime and IP-driven programming with major podcast networks. These include Stephanie Soo’s The Rotten Files, which expanded Netflix’s original true crime slate; John Allen’s MrBallen Podcast: Strange, Dark & Mysterious Stories with SiriusXM; and Ashley Flowers’ award-winning media company Audiochuck including the No. 1 global true crime podcast Crime Junkie (in partnership with Red Seat Ventures).

Thompson represents Alex Cooper and focuses on the transactional side including investments, joint ventures and partnerships, notably that aforementioned influx of cash. Thompson’s work for Unwell included a multiyear partnership with Google, a brand co-ownership deal with Nestlé to launch Unwell hydration and the Call Her Daddy podcast deal with SiriusXM that made Cooper the highest-paid female podcaster in the world.

Zielinski has become a go-to manager for creators on X and LinkedIn, brokering major deals for cross-platform educational creators Colin Rocker and Aishwarya Srinivasan. Elsewhere, the Drive Agency has landed deals with Adobe, Lovable, ElevenLabs, Dell, Google Gemini, Replit, Spotify and Meta.

items.title: ‘Nobody Wants This’ Creator Erin Foster Reacts to Adam Brody Saying He Supports “A Free Palestine”: “It’s Complicated”
items.description: Nobody Wants This creator Erin Foster is sharing her opinion on Adam Brody recently telling GQ he is in support of “a free Palestine.”
items.author: McKinley Franklin
paragraphs: Nobody Wants This creator Erin Foster is sharing her opinion on Adam Brody recently telling GQ he is in support of “a free Palestine.”

During an upcoming appearance on the Not Skinny But Not Fat podcast, per Entertainment Weekly, Foster was asked by host Amanda Hirsch how she felt about the actor’s previous comments about the Israel-Gaza war.

“You know, it’s complicated. I think our work environment, our set is very similar to dinner tables around the world where people are having debate and discussion and disagreeing,” the series creator said. “While I love Adam, I also disagree with him, and that’s okay.”

“I think that as the creator of the show, all I can say is that I want our Jewish fans to know that I see you and I hear you and I understand how you feel,” Foster continued. “And the show has always been and always will be a love letter to Judaism. That is why I made this show. It’s because of how beautiful of an experience I’ve had becoming Jewish and being a Jewish person, and sitting here right now at this time in the world where there is almost zero positive representation of Jewish people, I think it’s so important to have that.”
“That being said, everyone is entitled to a different opinion than me. I can just tell you what I created this show for, what the intention of the show is,” Foster concluded.

During a September profile with GQ, Brody, who appears on the Netflix series as a rabbi, discussed his political activism, and was asked if he thinks Hollywood has gotten more conservative. “I guess outspokenly so, yes. … Between COVID, a second Trump term, Israel-Gaza, it’s really brought out some different beliefs that I was ignorant to, and then disheartened by.”

The O.C. actor was asked how Israel-Gaza has come up in his messaging, to which he responded, “Truthfully, it hasn’t. I have spoken a lot about it privately. I haven’t spoken much about it publicly.” When asked if he’d like to speak about the topic, The O.C. actor said, “Put me down as thinking it’s a genocide. Put me down as wanting a free Palestine.”

“It’s awful that it’s taken so much death and misery, but it does feel like it’s reaching a breaking point that it should have a while ago,” he added. “I’m hopeful that another administration can really do some good and correct some of these policies that are helping that situation be as awful as it is.”

In an August 2025 interview with The Hollywood Reporter, Foster said of the show, “It was really important to me and continues to be really important to tell positive Jewish stories. I know that it can be polarizing, but it shouldn’t be. This is not the show to tackle conflict in Israel and Palestine.”

“I’m not the person to tell that story,” Foster added. “And after [the attacks on] Oct. 7 happened, there were conversations around if we were going to dive into it, and the truth is, the way that I can get my message across best is by shedding a positive light on Jewish characters and Jewish traditions. I don’t think somebody watching wants to see another voice give you their opinion on what’s happening.”
Nobody Wants This released its third season on Netflix Thursday. Brody was nominated for a 2025 Emmy for his role in the series, and won the Critics Choice Award for best comedy actor that same year.

items.title: Can ‘Sleep Banking’ Boost Your Productivity and Performance?
items.description: Using the weekend to lie in and catch up on sleep is a way of life for anyone with demanding work or social lives. But could consciously ‘banking’ extra hours of slumber over multiple nights help to counteract the effects of an upcoming period where you predic
items.author: Katie Wright
paragraphs: Using the weekend to lie in and catch up on sleep is a way of life for anyone with demanding work or social lives. But could consciously ‘banking’ extra hours of slumber over multiple nights help to counteract the effects of an upcoming period where you predict you might get less-than-stellar shuteye? The concept of ‘sleep banking’—which was first studied in 2009 as a method to help US soldiers improve alertness before missions—has been recommended by wellness leaders like neuroscientist Dr. Matthew Walker, who describes sleep banking as a ‘safety net’ when you know you’re going to be burning the candle at both ends. Longevity specialist Dr. Vassily Eliopoulos says it can aid resilience and recovery, and physical therapist Jason Silvernail recommends it for preserving mental performance when you’re jetlagged. But some researchers argue that sleep functions more like a credit card than a piggy bank—it can’t be saved up for later. We asked health experts to settle the debate once and for all.

Everyone has experienced the misery of slogging through a day at work after a bad night’s sleep (or several in a row), trying desperately to stop your eyelids dropping during a particularly boring meeting or keep your head from lolling onto your laptop. Not only can a sleep deficit leave you feeling exhausted and irritable, it’s also detrimental to your health.

“In addition to performance and alertness, sleep impacts your metabolic functions and cardiovascular health,” says Elizabeth Klerman, professor of neurology at Massachusetts General Hospital and Harvard Medical School. “It may be that you only need, for example, six hours of sleep to feel rested, but you might need seven and a half hours of sleep for metabolism.” Sleep deprivation is associated with a range of cognitive disorders, says Dr. Valentin Dragoi, neuroscientist at Houston Methodist and Rice University. “In the long run, it could cause Alzheimer’s and dementia, because metabolic waste that accumulates in the brain is eliminated during sleep.”

Unfortunately, the average person doesn’t always register when they’ve racked up a lot of sleep debt, says psychologist and neuroscientist Dr. Lindsay Browning, founder of Trouble Sleeping. “There was a study in 2003 where participants were given two weeks of restricted sleep, but that didn't increase how sleepy they felt, even though they were continually sleep-deprived.”

The term sleep banking was coined in 2009 with a two-week study carried out at the Walter Reed Army Institute of Research. The experiment split 24 adults into two groups. During week one, the first group slept for their usual seven hours a night, while the second extended their time in bed to 10 hours, allowing them to bank extra sleep. During week two, both groups were only allowed to sleep for three hours a night. The results showed that the sleep banking group had better concentration and reaction times on performance tests during the sleep deprivation week, even though they didn’t feel less tired, according to self-report measures.

The theory has since been tested in a variety of other settings. A 2023 experiment found sleep banking for 30 to 60 minutes per night for a week improved performance effectiveness among doctors working night shifts at a Miami hospital, and a 2026 review of 12 studies found that ‘preemptive sleep extension’ improved alertness, reaction times, and mood.

While studies may indicate improvements in physical and cognitive performance following sleep banking, debate exists around whether participants are actually banking sleep, or simply ‘paying off’ existing debt.

“There's no such thing as sleep banking,” says Klerman, who coauthored a paper refuting the claims of the initial 2009 study. “There's no evidence that you can bank sleep when you don't need it. All the studies that claim sleep banking is happening are actually restoring a sleep deficit, like paying off a credit card, not putting money into a savings bank.”

Browning believes there are benefits to intentionally increasing the amount of sleep you get ahead of a time when you need to be at peak performance. “A study of basketball players found that deliberately extending their sleep over a long period—five to seven weeks—was associated with better sprint times and accuracy in their shooting, and improved mood as well.” However, this study didn’t include a period of sleep deprivation, so it can’t technically be placed in the category of sleep banking. Besides, Klerman points out, going to bed earlier doesn’t automatically lead to better sleep. “Going to sleep an hour or so earlier than you usually do is difficult to do because your circadian system decides when you're able to sleep and when you're awake and your circadian system paradoxically promotes wakefulness until a few hours before your usual bedtime to enable you to remain awake for 16 hours.”

Sleep banking is more worthwhile for people who work nights, says sleep medicine and pulmonary physician Dr. Saema Tahir. “I look at sleep banking as a refresher for people who need a boost in alertness and functioning while they’re off of their normal circadian rhythm.” She believes that neither the credit card nor piggy bank analogy is accurate. “You can never really pay back that debt. Can you reset your sleep by starting from scratch and adhering to a schedule and prioritizing it? Yes. But once it's gone, it's gone.”

While experts may disagree about whether sleep functions as a credit or debit system, they’re on the same page about one thing: consistently getting enough sleep is far better for your performance, productivity and mood than hatching any kind of catch-up scheme.

“People should not build up a sleep deficit in the hopes of later paying it back. They should instead obtain sufficient sleep now,” says Klerman, adding that if you have to use an alarm clock instead of waking up naturally, you’re already sleep-deprived.

According to National Sleep Foundation guidelines, adults aged 18 to 64 need seven to nine hours of sleep a night, but requirements can vary greatly between individuals. “If you're sleeping more than nine or 10 hours regularly, your bed partner says you snore or stop breathing or do a lot of kicking in bed, or you still feel tired after nine or 10 hours, you should probably see a sleep specialist,” Klerman says.

Who on earth, you might be wondering, has time to catch nine hours of Z’s? With the pressures of work, social and family commitments, not to mention sleep disruptors like pets, kids, and smartphones, getting to bed and staying asleep is a challenge at the best of times. If you work from home, or are lucky enough to have a place to snooze at work, napping could be a better way to add to your daily sleep total, experts say—with some caveats.

“I often recommend to athletes, or even people who are competing not on a professional level, that short naps earlier in the day are very good for alertness and improving functioning,” says Dr. Tahir. “Never past 3 p.m., and always less than 30 minutes, because the longer they are, the more you risk getting into a deep stage of sleep that's harder to wake up from.” The only exception is if you struggle to fall asleep at night, as napping during the day can reduce the ‘sleep pressure’ needed to drift off later.

“Even a six-minute nap will improve your performance immediately after, and there's evidence that if you close your eyes and try to relax and empty your thoughts, that is also beneficial,” says Dr. Dragoi. So in lieu of sleep, adding a nap into your schedule could be the energy boost you need to feel rested and refreshed.

items.title: How Many Billions Would It Take to Hold Meta Accountable?
items.description: Earlier this week, a New Mexico judge ordered Meta to pay a $25 billion fine for violating consumer protection laws dating back to the Cambridge Analytica scandal. $25 billion is a massive fine, the largest Meta has ever faced, but it still had us folks at WIR
items.author: Lauren Goode
paragraphs: Earlier this week, a New Mexico judge ordered Meta to pay a $25 billion fine for violating consumer protection laws dating back to the Cambridge Analytica scandal. $25 billion is a massive fine, the largest Meta has ever faced, but it still had us folks at WIRED wondering: Would Meta even feel the pain?

A quick recap of the case: Filed in 2021, the suit alleged that the company violated the state’s Unfair Practices Act by lying to Meta users about the way it handled their data. (Later, New Mexico’s attorney general also made claims against Meta’s content moderation policies.) In September, a jury ruled in favor of the state. Then came the multibillion-dollar penalty.

“This ruling, and the Attorney General's approach to enforcement, makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico,” C.J. Mahoney, Meta’s chief legal officer, said in a statement. “At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online. We are confident we will prevail on appeal.”

Meta’s legal troubles have proliferated so much this year that it’s hard to keep track of them. Earlier this year in New Mexico, a jury ruled that the social media company should pay $375 million for violating the state’s Unfair Practices Act. That trial was related to child safety. A second phase of the case resulted in Meta being ordered to pay $567 million.

Meanwhile, a Los Angeles County superior court found Meta—and Google-owned YouTube—liable for harming a user’s mental health with the addictive design features of their apps. The plaintiff, a young woman, was awarded $6 million; Meta is on the hook for the bulk of that payment. Then in August, Meta settled a landmark federal case brought against the company by the majority of US states. This suit, once again, centered on addictive features in its apps that were alleged to be harmful to kids. As part of that settlement, Meta will pay the states between $17 and $18 billion over 10 years.

Added up, that’s a lot of billions. And yet: It’s still just the cost of doing business for Meta. Reuters reports that in the most recent New Mexico trial, the state’s attorneys originally asked Judge Francis Mathew to award the state between $35 and $45 billion. That would’ve been significant for the state, but would that extra $20 billion have kneecapped Meta? Nope.

Even if Meta was forced to pay the total maximum fine of the New Mexico ruling—a whopping $219 billion, or $5,000 across 43 million violations, reduced by the judge to $25 billion—the company would have felt only a mild sting. As of writing, Meta is worth around $1.7 trillion. Its stock took a hit on Thursday, but that was due to a confluence of factors, like Meta’s earnings report on Wednesday, the company’s massive capital expenditures on AI, and AI stocks dragging overall.

At this point, with no immediate monetary damage to Meta, it would take an accumulation of events to force some kind of change, legal experts tell me. For one, Meta has a clear perception problem: Juries are ruling against it, protesters have railed against it, even its own employees have been more vocal about the company’s internal policies.

Every time Meta doesn’t settle a case, the evidence presented during trial can be scrutinized by the public and used in future cases against Meta, says Corban Rhodes, partner at DiCello Levitt, the outside law firm representing New Mexico in this case. “This trial included more than 100 exhibits that we were able to put into public record, things that had been kept secret for more than a decade since Cambridge Analytica,” Rhodes told WIRED.

One such item is a 2018 email that then COO Sheryl Sandberg sent to a few colleagues days after the Cambridge Analytica scandal broke. Sandberg wrote, “The single biggest issue we face—and I really need everyone to know this—is that there were a MILLION developers with access to the data. We are going to have many, many, many more moments like this in the next month and year.”

There are early signals that private insurers may start balking at having to cover the cost of a tech company’s legal defenses. Some experts are suggesting that insurance companies could even end up being de facto governance for AI, as they “inject responsibility into how AI is designed, developed, and deployed as a condition for obtaining insurance.” Meta learned this firsthand in March, when a Delaware judge ruled that insurers do not have a duty to defend Meta against the literal thousands of lawsuits being brought against it.

There’s no well-defined number at which Meta suddenly becomes vulnerable—the company is unlikely to ever fold from legal penalties alone. But problems could crop up if shareholders or board members stop seeing the company as some inanimate entity and start to focus on the individual directors or officers who have been making bad decisions, says Brian Quinn, a law professor at Boston College Law School who studies corporate law, M&A, and transaction law. Like, say, the people who keep appearing in lawsuits.

“The way that indemnification law is written right now, the fact that a person in a company was found to have violated a law doesn’t necessarily make them liable. It can be believed that they were acting in good faith, or in the best interest of their company,” Quinn says. “But problems start to arise if shareholders say, wait a minute, there’s not only evidence that this director or operator is violating the law, but it has appeared in the same set of facts seven times now.”

After a huge accumulation of these kinds of results, Quinn says, some angry shareholders might stand up and say the corporation should no longer be able to indemnify those directors. That’s when you might see change, because Meta’s executives would no longer be as protected.

Finally, since litigation is often behind the curve on society-disrupting technology, Meta’s legal woes are likely far from over—especially as it wades deeper into AI. “Regulators and courts have for a long time been focused on the impact of social media 1.0 and 2.0, and I think we’re moving on from that era,” says Rhodes. “I expect the next wave of litigation will be focused on AI.”
This is an edition of Steven Levy’s and Lauren Goode's Backchannel newsletter. Read previous newsletters here.

items.title: The Spookiest New Shows to Watch This Halloween Season
items.description: Scrolling through 12 streaming platforms but still can’t find something to watch? You’re not alone. Our television columnist Michel Ghanem, a.k.a. @tvscholar, watches over 160 seasons of television each year, and he is here for you. Perhaps you’re in the mood
items.author: Michel Ghanem
paragraphs: Scrolling through 12 streaming platforms but still can’t find something to watch? You’re not alone. Our television columnist Michel Ghanem, a.k.a. @tvscholar, watches over 160 seasons of television each year, and he is here for you. Perhaps you’re in the mood for a hidden gem that’s sitting undiscovered on a streamer or a series with mysteries so tantalizing you can’t stop thinking about them long after the credits roll. It’s all about carving out time for the shows that are actually worth it — your appointment viewing. Fire up that group chat because we’ve got some unpacking to do.

Witches, sea hags, and telekinetic teens — we couldn’t settle for one spooky show this month, so we’ve selected four promising offerings. We’ve previously covered scare-inducing hits like Widow’s Bay and Alien: Earth, but this October there is an unusually large selection of spine-tingling shows — from more witchy horror on AMC+’s Yaga and foreboding mysteries with Hulu’s Phony. If sea monsters are more your thing, we have a recommendation for that too. Happy Halloween!
Yaga (AMC+, premiering October 23)

The Slavic folklore character of Baba Yaga has long been a fascination of popular culture, and she takes on many forms depending on who’s telling the story. She may be a witch living in a hut in the woods, sometimes she’s an old woman who eats children, or perhaps it’s more nuanced than those common tales. Yaga, created by Canadian playwright Kat Sandler and based on her 2019 play, is telling a new story of the ol’ witch. The first two episodes screened at the Toronto International Film Festival in September and will feel initially familiar to fans of True Detective — before things start getting supernatural.

In the small coastal town of Whittock we follow Carson (Clark Backo), a local police detective who reluctantly partners up with Rapp (Noah Reid), a private investigator who’s been hired by the wealthy parents of Henry (Hudson Williams), a missing college student. They venture around town interviewing folks and figure out something is definitely amiss with Henry’s osteology professor Katherine (Carrie-Anne Moss), who studies bones and has a reputation for perhaps boning her students.

We don’t quite yet know the role of Baba Yaga in the show, but brace yourselves for huge twists ahead in the eight-episode season. The spooky vibes and mysterious witchy phenomena make it a satisfying Halloween watch. And yes, there’s the Williams of it all. This is another Crave production, the streamer that brought you Heated Rivalry, and it’s a little horny too. Williams pulls double duty as Henry’s roommate Logan, and there’s a long scene in which all he wears is overalls. So make of that what you will!

Phony is having some awkward timing with the recent release of the horror movie Other Mommy — but trust me when I say this story is much, much better. Sonny (Sam Nivola) is a jolly high-schooler with a tender relationship with his mother, Ellen (Connie Britton), who raised him as a single parent and also happens to be the principal at his high school. A sudden car crash sends Sonny into a weeklong coma, only to wake up and find his mother by his hospital bedside. But she looks … different? Through the four of eight episodes provided to critics, I couldn’t quite put my finger on what Britton and the Phony team did to make her face look so subtly different: a makeup trick, face tape, an intentional change in facial expressions? Some combination of all of the above? Unfortunately, no one else in Sonny’s life sees the difference, and he ends up resorting to seeking out a private investigator to help him get to the bottom of it. Phony is classified as a comedy but the mystery here is pretty spooky, especially as the show keeps dangling short snippets of a dead body at the end of each episode.

I have a bunch of theories for Phony and I can tell it’s the kind of show that will send Reddit into a frenzy. Midway through the season, it still holds its cards very close to the chest — my money is on either a twin sister or Invasion of the Body Snatchers–style aliens. The show zips by in half-hour episodes and has a certain quirky charm to it; creator Nick Paley co-wrote Marcel the Shell With Shoes On and edited episodes of Broad City, which gives you a pretty good idea of the tone here. There’s a certain clumsy teen realism to Phony that even feels reminiscent of Sterling Point. Long live mumblecore!

We all know this one. And while there have been many adaptations of Stephen King’s famous Carrie novel, this is the first television adaptation of the story. The episodic format lets a lot breathe, here: Summer H. Howell plays the titular telekinetic character and you can see her bright-eyed optimism fade as the formerly homeschooled teen gets increasingly bullied by her peers. The drama really kicks off when Carrie — who was not taught about the menstrual cycle growing up — freaks out at the sight of her first period after gym class. In both Brian De Palma’s 1976 film and in this adaptation, the group of teens pelt tampons at poor Carrie who’s been pushed into a shower stall while they all chant “plug it up” (so mean). The difference here is really what sets the modern adaptation apart — everyone pulls their phones out to film her. Ringleader Chris Hargensen (Alison Thornton) ends up posting the clip on “Carrie Red,” an Instagram account she creates to make fun of Carrie, other students, and faculty. She basically becomes the Gossip Girl of the school, a clever modernization of an old bullying story.

A lot more is expanded on, too: Margaret White (Samantha Sloyan) is much more fleshed out, becoming very involved in the Carrie Red of it all, and launching her own influencer account to meet the bullies where they are. There have been some fan complaints about the season’s ending, which opens up the show to branch off to something completely different from the original — and there is speculation that Mike Flanagan might be interested in connecting his Carrie to The Dark Tower, another King series, since the show features other individuals with superhuman abilities. Flanagan did mention he has a three-season plan in mind going forward, and it’s been renewed for a second, so we’ll have to wait and see. As a Flanaganhead who has loved everything he’s made from Ouija: Origin of Evil (a genuinely terrifying and underrated film) to The Haunting of Hill House (should have won Emmys), I will be tuning in.

Remember the sea hag from Widow’s Bay? She’s back! Well, sort of. The hag does make an appearance in Below, a seaside supernatural series created by Jesse McKeown, but Below has got a lot more going on: a Kraken haunting the Newfoundland coastline, the townspeople going mad from drinking contaminated ice, and Josh Hartnett in cozy cable-knit sweaters (this last bit is very important, at least to me). Hartnett plays Calvin Penney, a single father of three kids and fisherman in the remote town of Snook’s Arm, Newfoundland. The small community is facing resettlement (which did actually happen to the real-life Snook’s Arm, population: ten) and all of Calvin’s kids are in town to visit. Meanwhile, marine biologist Fonda Howander (Mackenzie Davis) is picking up on some unusual activity in the sea.

Below is a quick binge as a six-episode limited series and the frights are just as entertaining as the very thick accents. The special effects aren’t amazing and it’s not as polished or comedic as Widow’s Bay, so comparing them feels unreasonable, but I still had fun watching Hartnett and Davis save this little town from a sea monster. It also pales in comparison to something like Davis’s last television project, Station Eleven, which ranked at 93 on the New York Times’ list of best shows of the 21st century (and actually is a bit spooky too now that I think of it). Luckily, anything ocean horror is an easy grab — the real deep-sea creatures in Planet Earth are enough to give me nightmares.

items.title: Billie Eilish Is the Proud New Owner of a Bob
items.description: Billie Eilish has enlisted in the Bob Army. On Thursday, she posted a video of herself with a new hair look — a ginger bob with piece-y, flippy ends. Unlike those of us who’ve waded too impulsively into the waters of Bobland, Eilish looks incredible.
items.author: Sam Reed
paragraphs: Billie Eilish has enlisted in the Bob Army. On Thursday, she posted a video of herself with a new hair look — a ginger bob with piece-y, flippy ends. Unlike those of us who’ve waded too impulsively into the waters of Bobland, Eilish looks incredible.

Though some people read a bob as a cry for help, I’m choosing to believe that Eilish was just ready for a change. She was already moving in this direction — the cut is just a couple of inches shorter than the style she was wearing in photos from earlier this month and in the ads for her and her brother Finneas’s new John Hardy jewelry collection.

Eilish set the big reveal to Pavement’s “Cut Your Hair,” which is an ironic choice given the song opens with the lyrics, “Darling don’t go and cut your hair,” but hey, it works. Sometimes you get a really good haircut and you’re so excited that you post about it from the car on the way home from the salon. Happy for you, Billie Bob!

items.title: I'm 36, I Make $145K & I Really Love Glitter Gel!
items.description: A Week In San Francisco, CA On A $145,000 Salary
items.author: R
paragraphs: A Week In San Francisco, CA On A $145,000 Salary
This week: A scientist working in biotech who makes $145,000 per year and spends some of it on body glitter gel.

If you'd like to submit your own Money Diary, you can do so via our online form. We pay $150 for each published diary. Apologies but we're not able to reply to every email. We are legally unable to publish any diaries that have been written with the use of AI.
Interested in taking our latest Money Diaries survey? We'd love to hear your thoughts here.
Location: San Francisco, CA
Joint Income/Financial Setup:
HSA: $7,243 (plus somehow $950 in an app intended to teach teens about the stock market and investing that I've put maybe $200 total into).
Paycheck Amount (2x a month): $3,600
Housing Costs: $3,150 (one-bedroom apartment with parking and pet rent).
Loan Payments: $521 (for my car)
Phone: $30 (US line); $11 (JP line)
Was there an expectation for you to attend higher education? Did you participate in any form of higher education? If yes, how did you pay for it?

Yes. Both my parents valued education highly, and it wasn't a question whether or not I would get an undergraduate degree. Thankfully, there wasn't a lot of pressure as to what sort of degree. I was able to graduate without debt because my grandparents set up a college fund for me, and I was an overachieving student: I got scholarships that covered about half of my tuition and graduated with two degrees in four years to maximize my time and interests. That said, I was scrambling to pay for the last semester. My master's degree was more like a paid internship, but it meant the company I worked for paid my tuition and a small stipend in exchange for my labor. I racked up a lot of credit card debt trying to balance everything during those years.
Growing up, what kind of conversations did you have about money? Did your parent(s) educate you about finances?

It was a weird mix. On the one hand, my dad didn't have much money growing up and once he did have money to spend, he became the sort to buy things without caring how much they cost. He's almost an example of what not to do with money. My mother, on the other hand, is very careful with money but came from a family and culture where it was considered rude and unnecessary to talk about finances in public, especially with children. So I was taught to save if there were things I wanted, how to write a check and the importance of having a savings account, but not much beyond that. My first overdraft fee in college was certainly a shock, and there's also an infamous story about one of my first summer jobs: I ended up owing far more money for taxes than I actually had, because no one told me about the difference between being an employee and an independent contractor when it came to tax deductions. When I told my dad that I thought my paycheck was mine and taxes had been deducted already (they hadn't been), he got mad that I would suggest I had been wronged because no one explained the difference at hiring. So I learned pretty quickly to educate myself on everything financial.
What was your first job and why did you get it?
When I was 16, I became a summer lifeguard and swim instructor at our city pool. I was driving the carpool to school and needed money for gas.
Did you worry about money growing up?

No. Both of my parents worked and had fairly lucrative jobs, although when I was about 12, my mother quit the corporate world and went back to teaching, which is not so lucrative. We were firmly middle class. When they divorced, there were a lot of questions as to how things would be split and what that would mean for the household and for me, but there was never concern about not having enough.
Do you worry about money now?

Sort of? It's hard not to, living in SF with its high cost of living and constant layoffs, but I'm very lucky to have a good, stable job and a breadth of skills that would hopefully mean that if something did happen, I wouldn't be on my savings for too long. The addition of an increase in rent and my car payments essentially taking an entire paycheck sometimes wakes me up at night. I worry about money more in the abstract than the particular. In my head, my non-liquid savings basically don't exist as something that can be spent and I think I've calculated how much my severance would be about six times by now.
At what age did you become financially responsible for yourself and do you have a financial safety net?

At around age 23, when I graduated from my master's program. I lived with my dad at the time, which became unsustainable for several reasons, including the four-hour commute to my job. While I don't get any financial support from either of my parents, I know that if anything drastic happened, I could live with one of them until I got back on my feet. I also have several friends in the area and while their support would likely not be financial, it would be in big ways that would help me save money.
Do you or have you ever received passive or inherited income? If yes, please explain.
Both of my parents (my dad in particular) have been vocal about spending what they have in their later years, so I have no expectation that money or property will come to me.

I feel like I did pretty well this week — it definitely helped that I had a lot of food on-hand and leftovers, but also that I was busy enough to not take side trips that lead to impulse purchases. It's hard to break the habit of getting myself little treats, but I should try and be better about those.
