items.title: Dancing With the Stars Recap: Cry, Cry, Cry
items.description: If you’re not following the Dancing With the Stars world on social media, first of all, excellent choice, do not change it, social media has really zapped a lot of the fun out of the show. Second of all, you may have been a little confused tuning in to “Dedica
items.author: Maggie Fremont
paragraphs: If you’re not following the Dancing With the Stars world on social media, first of all, excellent choice, do not change it, social media has really zapped a lot of the fun out of the show. Second of all, you may have been a little confused tuning in to “Dedication Night” to find vague references only to Val Chmerkovskiy being “out” this week and an “unusual situation” that led to Jenna Dewan being paired with Alan Bersten. DWTS didn’t want to dip even one toe into the discourse that’s plagued it this past week — it didn’t even use the word “suspended” — after Val made a social post referencing the Will Smith Oscars slap in regard to Carrie Ann Inaba’s critique of his wife, Jenna Johnson, and Harry Shum Jr.’s samba during “Super Bowl Night.” There’s got to be about one thousand better ways to support your wife, my guy. And say what you will about Carrie Ann’s judging (personally, I think that panel desperately needs her), but I can only imagine the online vitriol hurled at her this week, and she came out and was an absolute pro.

DWTS should count its blessings that all of this went down in the lead-up to “Dedication Night,” the theme that perhaps best encapsulates the show’s greatest strengths — it’s a night full of joy and emotion and vulnerability. More than any other week, it’s laser-focused on each celeb’s story and, though it pains me to use the word, journey. You can’t get distracted by scandal when you’re sobbing your face off to dance, right?
Ezra Frech and Daniella Karagach
Contemporary // “Bloodline,” by Mon Rovia

Our Paralympian is dedicating his dance to his mom, Bahar (she joins Ezra and Daniella on the dance floor), who gave up her acting career to take care of him and from the beginning made sure he never felt less than because of his disability. I immediately started crying. Ezra talks about how his mother always preached walking into every room with his chin up and chest out to “let them know you’ve arrived” and holy hell if Daniella doesn’t put that exact move in this gorgeous contemporary. Daniella choreographing contemporary is always a treat, but this one is truly stunning. Daniella leaps onto Ezra’s prosthetic, Ezra has some really beautiful jumps, and it all ends with him carrying his mother à la Love You Forever. It’s all so moving, our guest judge and former pro Kym Johnson arrives in the ballroom and promptly doles out the first 10 of the season.
Carrie Ann: 9 // Derek: 9 // Kym: 10 // Bruno: 9
Tatyana Ali and Jan Ravnik
Viennese Waltz // “(You Don’t Know) How Glad I Am,” by Nancy Wilson

The moment when Jan dances off screen and Tatyana reaches out her hand only for our esteemed host and Tatyana’s former Fresh Prince TV brother Alfonso Ribeiro to grab it, I let out an audible sob. They just seemed so happy to be dancing together and to get the opportunity to honor their late TV dad James Avery. This is the kind of shit we come to Dancing With the Stars to see, okay? Aside from also singing the vocals for this performance, Tatyana’s looking better and better each week. She’s easily the best emoter of the bunch and Jan knows exactly how to play to that in his choreography. Bruno says it was like she was “floating” across the dance floor. Derek calls her “a vision.” Kym notes a little too much rise and fall for the Viennese Waltz, but thought it was beautiful nonetheless. Tatyana and Jan get their best score of the season. Should it have been higher? Yeah, probably, but we’ll take what we can get.
Carrie Ann: 8 // Derek: 8 // Kym: 8 // Bruno: 8
Maura Higgins and Mark Ballas
Paso Doble // “I’m Shipping Up to Boston,” by the Dropkick Murphys

The Irish flag as a skirt? A dancer from Michael Flatley’s Lord of the Dance named Lucky, are you kidding me? It’s Dancing With the Stars’s first Irish Paso Doble and it is fun. I mean, you knew Mark Ballas was going to eat up a paso to the Dropkick Murphys. The man lives for theatrics (compliment). It’s a little chaotic at times, especially as Maura and Mark dance around Lucky, and while the judges praise Maura’s attack, I actually think her movements could have been sharper here for maximum impact. She seems more unsure of herself than we’ve seen in a while but still, Maura does her homeland proud.
Carrie Ann: 8 // Derek: 9 // Kym: 9 // Bruno: 9
Jackson Olson and Emma Slater
Quickstep // “L-O-V-E,” by Nat King Cole

The Banana is dedicating his quickstep to his mother Laura, who is a special education teacher and starts crying the moment she walks into rehearsals. I feel so seen. The magic of “Dedication Night” is getting to see in real time how having a loved one join for the ride forces people to be at the top of their game — they don’t want to let anyone down and the pressure is really on to perform. This is easily Jackson’s best dance. He looks so comfortable and loose out there for the first time. The judges want him to really work on his frame and Kym once again proves why she is the best guest judge this show has — she provides such useful tips and critiques in such disarming ways. Give her a permanent spot, you fools!
Carrie Ann: 8 // Derek: 8 // Kym: 8 // Bruno: 8
Amber Glenn and Pasha Pashkov
Contemporary // “Breathe Me,” by Sia

I knew Amber doing a contemporary choreographed by Pasha telling the story of her mental health journey — and paying tribute to her younger sister Brooke, who saved her life — was going to take me out on premise alone, but I did not expect this! The power! The vulnerability! The storytelling! The judges keep using the word “raw” to describe this performance that details the darkness that took over Amber’s life as a teenager, and how her sister helped her defeat it, and really how else can you describe it? Everyone is sobbing after this… well, sobbing until Julianne has to awkwardly transition (at least she acknowledges this) into the announcement that Pasha won that People “Sexiest Male Pro” contest. Daniella is especially enthusiastic about these results. Per usual, this show is a whirlwind of emotion.
Carrie Ann: 10 // Derek: 9 // Kym: 10 // Bruno: 9
Jenna Dewan and Alan Bersten
Viennese Waltz // “Unchained Melody,” by the Righteous Brothers

Apparently, Alan didn’t get subbed in for Val until Friday night, which makes what they pull off all the more astounding. Sure, Jenna is a pro and Alan is a great partner, but chemistry takes time to build and still these two are dancing as a unit by Monday night. Jenna’s tribute to her mom Nancy is another winning performance, and it’s easy to see just how right Bruno is when he praises how good Jenna is in her more lyrical dances. That spin they do when Jenna holds her one ankle and drags her foot across the floor? I’ve watched it five times.
Carrie Ann: 10 // Derek: 9 // Kym: 9 // Bruno: 9
Harry Shum Jr. and Jenna Johnson
Foxtrot // “Stop This Train,” by John Mayer

On the heels of what must have been a trying week for both of them, but especially Jenna, Harry performs his best dance. Despite the kerfuffle last week, it’s clear Jenna took the criticism about not having enough of the dance style in each routine to heart, because this is just a gorgeous, straight up foxtrot. Harry dedicates this to his wife Shelby (also a dancer and actress), who absolutely should be on DWTS next season, but Jenna also incorporates Harry’s parents and his daughter into the routine. It’s the story of his life out there on the dancefloor and he’s never looked so graceful. In what is clearly a mending of fences, Carrie Ann specifically praises Jenna’s choreography, and you know what, that’s the kind of healing we need right now. Go on and call me a regular ol’ Derek Hough, I guess, sitting here crying about the joy and love Dancing With the Stars brings, I deserve it.
Carrie Ann: 9 // Derek: 9 // Kym: 9 // Bruno: 9
Connor Wood and Rylee Arnold
Viennese Waltz // “Piano Man,” by Billy Joel

It’s Papa’s Papa Pete! Connor dedicates his dance to his father, who has been battling lymphoma for a long time, and says things like “it’s incredible to have a dad, but to have a remarkable one?” and everyone is crying again. Once again, “Dedication Night” magic strikes and Connor performs at his highest level yet. You’d think dancing directly in front of your dad would make you more nervous, but Connor has never seemed so calm and in control on the dance floor. Kym wants him to work on creating more space in frame to help keep it consistent and Carrie Ann loves that it’s clear Connor and Rylee take the notes they’re given seriously. It’s all very sweet and these two finally get the elusive eights they’ve been after.
Carrie Ann: 8 // Derek: 8 // Kym: 8 // Bruno: 8
Tyler Cameron and Sharna Burgess
Contemporary // “Supermarket Flowers,” by Ed Sheeran

Just emotionally fry us, why don’t you? Tyler dedicates this dance to his mom, who died suddenly of a brain aneurysm in 2020, but also to moms everywhere. Sharna — another great contemporary choreographer — dreams up a dance in which she is the spirit of Tyler’s mother bringing him to the great love of his life, his fiancee Tate, who joins them on the floor and during a lift, does this emotional pregnancy reveal. Tyler’s going to be a dad and he wants to share that with his mom, and honestly, how are we all just supposed to go back to regular life after this? I need at least three to five business days of rest. But we’re not done: At the judges’ table, Alfonso announces they’re doing a gender reveal, too — it’s a girl. I hate gender reveals but this one really got me and that, folks, is the magic of dance. You know what the opposite of the magic of dance is? Whatever this promo performance for Season 32 champ Xochitl Gomez’s new Cat in the Hat movie is. It contains the worst wigs I’ve ever laid my eyes on and honestly, stay deranged, DWTS.
Carrie Ann: 8 // Derek: 8 // Kym: 8 // Bruno: 8
Julia Stiles and Ezra Sosa
Contemporary // “Can’t Take My Eyes Off You,” by Frankie Valli

Last week, Julia and Ezra brought out the much anticipated Save the Last Dance homage, and they are immediately following it up with one to 10 Things I Hate About You in their dedication to the late Heath Ledger. I, for one, am crossing my fingers that next week’s dance is an Argentine Tango paying tribute to The Bourne Identity. A girl can dream! The judges love this all-over-the-place contemporary, but Julia looks a little lost throughout. It’s not her best dance, but there is joy and an earnestness as she reconnects with her 17-year-old self. She rocks Kat Stratford’s iconic blue dress, and at the end, the cast of the movie — I’m talking everyone, Gabrielle Union (!), Joseph Gordon Levitt (!), Larisa Oleynik (book her for next season), Andrew Keegan, and Susan May Pratt — and yeah, nostalgia is going to win you some points, especially on a night like this one.
Carrie Ann: 9 // Derek: 9 // Kym: 9 // Bruno: 9
In a merciful move, there is no elimination on “Dedication Night,” but this means that next week — Halloween-themed, of course — will send two couples home. Now that’s some spooky shit right there.

items.title: Love Is Blind Recap: Why Would I Deceive You?
items.description: We’re partying in Mexico, which means our newly de-podded couples get to enjoy cold plunges, room service, and scuba diving at a scenic resort, prolonging their delusional fairy tales for a few more days before a harsh reality sets in: eating underseasoned tof
items.author: Emma Sharpe
paragraphs: We’re partying in Mexico, which means our newly de-podded couples get to enjoy cold plunges, room service, and scuba diving at a scenic resort, prolonging their delusional fairy tales for a few more days before a harsh reality sets in: eating underseasoned tofu in a sterile apartment kitchen while you discuss your crippling communication issues with a person that you’ve known for less time than your airport Uber driver.

When Real Life begins, cracks form. The experience isn’t just a fun gag anymore — there are genuine feelings, new family dynamics, and a looming, arbitrary deadline to make a major life decision. I have a sneaking suspicion that when we get to the altar, it will be the men who choose to cut the cord, even though it’s primarily the women who are settling. But when the dating market is this bad for women, the unfortunate truth is that sometimes, they’ll settle for just about anything — even when that thing is a Republican who’s “sensy” about his glasses.

Separately, but equally depressingly, the Boston energy this season teased feels completely absent from the equation. Instead of some Karen Read knockoffs drinking 11 vodka sodas at a townie bar and drunk driving home to Southie, we have Erika demurely fluffing her throw pillows in Connecticut. Where’s the Beantown fire?

We check in with Boston’s shallowest humans at lunch in the North End, where Jax admits to Stew that she shouldn’t have ghosted him after their reveal. She explains that when they met, it didn’t feel the same way it felt in the pods, which sounds like a little bit of a spin — Stew was his same pompous self, but it was either his appearance or her realization that maybe he didn’t look as rich as he promised that set her off.

Stew, for what it’s worth, seems like almost a completely different person. He’s a lot more relaxed, dialing back the whole glib Gaston persona for a more thoughtful and vulnerable conversation. Jax said that when she got back to Boston, she felt like she needed to hear his voice, and all her friends and family are encouraging her to try and make it work with him. Stew is remarkably unoffended by her antics and says he still has hope for them. It’s a lot of woulda, coulda, shoulda, and while they don’t formally say “see you never,” it’s clear that their Aston Martin helicopter wedding is DOA.
Stew & Jax’s Odds: +2,000. It’s disappointing that they don’t progress further — I’d love to see Jax’s face when she finds out Stew drives a Tesla Model 3.

If your greatest fear in life was that your future husband ends up completely flipping a switch and turns into a total monster, à la Brandon Sklenar in The Housemaid, would it be wise to marry a dude you’ve known for 27 days? Sarah has all the trappings of an intelligent, beautiful, and capable woman, but she’s letting the whirlwind of reality TV lobotomize her into doing free PR for a man who drinks a tall glass of raw cow’s milk with every meal.

The pair gets into their first major relationship discussion when Sarah overhears John getting frustrated with a customer-service person from his electric company. She tells him she has zero tolerance for yelling and that this isn’t the first time she’s witnessed him get angry — he also had words with someone earlier in the week over their lost luggage. He thinks he’s just being stern, but she’s worried there’s secret rage bubbling beneath the surface.

They meet with John’s family, and he’s already briefed his parents on the fact that Sarah isn’t Christian. Sarah sinks threes left and right at this meetup: She says all the right things, convincing them of her understanding and appreciation of John’s personality, their chemistry and communication skills, and her support with his MS diagnosis. By the end of the afternoon, David and Rhonda are like, “Jesus, who?”

John & Sarah’s Odds: +400. John is locked in, and why wouldn’t he be? Sarah is a complete catch. But I have to hope that she can wake herself up from this nightmare before she’s trapped in an attic ripping her hair out by the follicle.

Quick, someone call Erika’s pet communicator — we need her dogs to bark some sense into her. Girlfriend, you are a suburban Connecticut homebody whose idea of a crazy night is having two-and-a-half glasses of Merlot and throwing on a Fifty Shades of Grey movie. Your fiancé, in your own words, is “partying on boats in Croatia for 15 weeks with children who are wearing strings.” To quote our boy Chris Hansen, “You see how this looks, right?”

The other couples are also clearly surprised that Blake and Erika decided to take the plunge, and at one of the cocktail parties, Erika and Michaella chat about how they are sooooo totally cool with their men meeting up with their pod exes, Benita and Diana, when everyone gets back to the East Coast. Threat level? Negative infinity.

In Not Boston, Erika gives Blake a tour of her sprawling four-bedroom home and admits in a confessional that she hopes he’ll fall in love with her cozy cocoon lifestyle. Cool, and I hope that my situationship will text me outside the hours of 11:45 p.m. and 3:30 a.m., if we want to add that to the list of delusional dreams that will never come true.

Blake & Erika’s Odds: +500. Unless Erika’s friends and family have a come-to-Jesus with her, there’s a real possibility that she decides she’s better off married to a man who’s hosting a spring-break wet-T-shirt contest on a yacht in Mykonos than she is being alone.

Gosh, I thought we had landed two emotionally mature adults this season, but I was woefully mistaken. When we check in with Wilson and Wilnie in Mexico, their relationship initially seems to be developing swimmingly, but that’s before Wilnie decides she wants to relitigate Wilson’s short-lived connection with Malaine 689 times. Malaine left the experiment after Cam broke up with her, meaning that Wilson never fully chose Wilnie, and things maybe could have turned out differently if Malaine had stayed. As much empathy as Wilson tries to communicate — he concedes that he would also feel hurt if the roles were reversed — Wilnie is incapable of moving past the fact that she liked him more than he liked her in the pods, regardless of their current status and intentions.

Back in Boston, they tour Wilson’s apartment, which is the lower level of a duplex he shares with his parents. You know that feeling of poking your head into a bar, immediately clocking that the vibe is rancid, and turning right back around? Wilson’s place is the apartment version of that. If you’ve ever complained about your entry-level boyfriend’s navy sheets, let me raise you Wilson’s black metallic bedding. Karma points to Wilnie — as much as she’s a material girl who values a designer handbag and a gel manicure, she says she’s in love with Wilson for who he is, not what he has.

At dinner with Wilnie’s girlfriends and sister, Wilson decides to show up as his authentic self, rather than a curated offshoot of his personality who laughs at bad jokes and pretends to care about Olivia Rodrigo’s dating history. He tells Wilnie’s inner circle with his full chest that Wilnie had “more personality” in the pods, presenting as an independent go-getter, but in real life has a “helpless attitude” toward everything. From her perspective, doing things herself requires her to “step into her masculine energy,” and she threatens that if he allows her to do that by not putting her luggage in the overhead bin for her, she will stay there permanently, like when a teenage Animorph stays as a chipmunk for over the two-hour limit and is forced to live out the remainder of his days as a rodent eating beetle grub in the trees.

Wilson & Wilnie’s Odds: +100. This is a coin flip. I think Wilson’s slowly getting icked out, but he might be doing the mental calculation that he finally found someone already so emotionally connected to him that his dungeon bedroom isn’t an automatic dealbreaker. Not sure Casa Wilson is playing as hot on Hinge date three.

Nobody likes Rob, not even his family. Over the course of the three episodes, he’s called “obnoxious,” “cocky,” “arrogant,” “loud,” or “an acquired taste” in nearly every scene where he’s present. But Michaella can’t wait to have his children and host chaotic Christmas Eve parties where all the parents get drunk off White Russians, and Santa passes out on the couch with a half-smoked cigar. She’s not a regular wife; she’s a cool wife!

When they return from their successful vacation, Michaella meets Rob’s mom and siblings for lunch. The mom is a classic old broad and has no idea that she’s on TV, which obviously makes for great TV. She seems to actually like Michaella, but offers valid concerns that she and Rob have been living in an unrealistic production bubble. After binge-watching the show until 5 a.m., she’s determined that it’s possible for the experiment to introduce you to someone who you wouldn’t have met otherwise, but she doesn’t want her son to get married solely because of the pressure of the fake timeline.

Rob & Michaella’s Odds: -200. These people rationally know that the only sane way to develop this relationship is to, I don’t know, date, but because they feel like Netflix has a gun to their head, they might go ahead and pull the trigger.

Here’s a fun game: Would you rather spend the rest of your life with Aneha, who can’t even get through a 45-minute couples’ massage without word-vomiting every thought that crosses through her brain, or volunteer to leave your entire family behind and repopulate a new planet like Matthew McConaughey in Interstellar? Personally, I’d take my chances on Mars.

From the moment Aneha met Cam, she’s been on offense. Everything is a test, from asking him what he would do if a lizard came toward them on the beach, to purposefully leaving the bathroom light on to gauge if it would annoy him. In her mind, these little experiments will give her the data she needs to make an informed decision at the altar. For Cam, it’s like dating an LSAT proctor, but minus the kinky roleplay, since she’s waiting to have sex.

When they get to the apartments, Aneha learns from her parents that they would Very Much Like to Be Excluded From This Narrative and will not participate in any part of production, including the wedding. Their vision for her future is someone who is brown and someone who is Hindu — Cam, as much as he loves to brag about how he’s read My Gita, is neither.

After a tour of Aneha’s studio apartment, which has more LED paraphernalia than a Spencer’s Gifts, Aneha meets Cam’s elder sister, Karina, who basically spends half an hour pitching her on all the reasons she shouldn’t marry her younger brother. According to Karina, Cam has had an easy, decision-free life facilitated by Karina and their mother. If Aneha is looking for someone who can make a plan or provide structure for their future children, she picked the wrong jabroni.

Aneha approaches Cam with these concerns, and he continues to act just as passively as Karina warned. She argues that his answer to 90 percent of her questions is “I don’t know,” like he’s Elizabeth Holmes when you ask her why she was convicted of fraud. They both feel that the other is colder and more emotionally distant now that they’re out of the pods. If you’re already this miserable on day 19, why sign up for eternity?

Cam & Aneha’s Odds: +700. Aneha will say “no” at the altar and think she’s having this iconic girlboss moment. Unless they make Cam go first, in which case we might get the first “IDK” in franchise history.
“Next Time On” Bits and Bobs

• Which wedding dance class was more painful to teach? The one in The Drama, or Cam and Aneha’s? Cam needs to be careful because if he steps on Aneha’s foot one too many times, she’ll put him in timeout.
• Strike 983 for John: responding to Sarah explaining the mental load to him by saying, “women are nesters” with a straight face.
• “Some women might think summer in Europe is a nice thing to do. Am I FUCKING CRAZY for thinking that?” No, but you definitely sound crazy ranting about it at the meet-the-friends dinner!
• Benita Watch! The Balkan princess is back for one last hoorah, a.k.a. making every woman sweat bullets when she makes even passing eye contact with their man.

items.title: Tom Hanks Returning to Broadway After 14 Years for New Play ‘This World of Tomorrow’
items.description: Tom Hanks will star in the play “This World of Tomorrow,” marking his return to Broadway for the first time in 14 years.
items.author: Rebecca Rubin
paragraphs: Tom Hanks will star in the play “This World of Tomorrow,” marking his return to Broadway for the first time in 14 years.

Hanks was last on Broadway in Nora Ephron’s 2013 play “Lucky Guy,” which earned him a Tony nomination. This time, the celebrated actor will be joined by theater veteran Kelli O’Hara, who appeared alongside him in the show’s Off Broadway run last year at the Shed.

“This World of Tomorrow” is based on a series of short stories written by Hanks. He’s co-writing the adaptation with James Glossman. Described as a “time-travel romance,” the play takes place at the end of the 21st century and follows Bert Allenberry, who is determined to change his future by returning to the past. “When Bert journeys back — again, and again, and again — to one remarkable day at the 1939 New York World’s Fair in Queens, he discovers that the future is shaped not by technology, but by the choices we make for love,” per the official logline.

Directed by Kenny Leon, whose recent Broadway credits include “The Balusters,” “Othello” with Denzel Washington and Jake Gyllenhaal, and “Our Town” with Jim Parsons and Katie Holmes, is directing the show. It will play at a Shubert theater to be announced. Complete cast and creative team details will be confirmed soon.

“I’m so excited to continue this work on this amazing new American play,” said Leon. “There’s no time like the present to further explore this story of love and time travel from Glossman and Hanks. More than anything, I look forward to even more audiences who will have the chance to witness the onstage chemistry of Kelli O’Hara and Tom Hanks.”

Adds The Shed’s artistic director Alex Poots, “A beloved actor of our times, Tom Hanks co-created and starred in ‘This World of Tomorrow’ with the illuminating Kelli O’Hara for their sold out run at The Shed. Reminding us that while the world changes, the deepest of human connections endures and the power of love can transcend any era. Now this story of second chances gets to reach an even wider audience on Broadway.”
Producer Brian Anthony Moreland described Hanks as “one of the great storytellers of our time” and called it an “incredible privilege” to bring this play to Broadway.

“There is something extraordinary about bringing a story that explores the power of love across time to a place where the magic of live theater happens every night,” Moreland said. “At its heart, ‘This World of Tomorrow’ reminds us that no matter how much the world changes, the one thing that remains timeless is our capacity to love.”

items.title: Meet Mori, a Cute Robot Mushroom That Doesn’t Really Say (or Do) Anything
items.description: You've had a long day. You finally get home, fling the door open, plonk on the couch, and let out a big sigh. In the corner of your eye, you notice your mushroom lamp perk up. Its microphone must have heard you come in. Its head raises to reveal round, animate
items.author: Julian Chokkattu
paragraphs: You've had a long day. You finally get home, fling the door open, plonk on the couch, and let out a big sigh. In the corner of your eye, you notice your mushroom lamp perk up. Its microphone must have heard you come in. Its head raises to reveal round, animated eyes, and a little diamond-shaped nose—which actually houses a camera.
It does a little jiggle because it sees you're back. Its name is Mori.

As you move around the space—maybe it's time to start cooking dinner—the little robot's face follows you, observing your movements and making soft sounds that are a cross between a bird and R2-D2. The day's stress catches up, and you need a moment to relax, so you head over to Mori, touch its head, and its eyes and camera-nose dip back inside its body. It goes back to being a lamp, except now it plays nature soundscapes so you can feel at ease.

That's the pitch from OKA, or One Kind Artifact, a new startup based in Cambridge, Massachusetts, and Shenzhen, China, focusing on experimental technology. CEO Hua Wang tells WIRED he wants his company to create five experimental “Artifacts” over the course of OKA's lifetime. Mori is the first.

“There are certain relationships in this era we want to fix between humans and our surroundings—human with nature, human with one another—every product is an experience trying to reconnect some of those relationships,” Wang says. Before cofounding OKA, he was a general manager at Meipai, a video-sharing app from the Chinese phone brand Meitu. He also cofounded Bondee, a now-defunct social media app that briefly went viral in Asia.

According to the company, the point of Mori, the nearly 12-inch-tall home robot lamp, is to reconnect its owners with nature. It can play nature soundscapes. It will glow different colors—inspired by rain, forests, fire, and wind—while reacting to your movements. It can guide you through a calming breathing session.

It also uses its built-in camera and microphones to serve as a fun little interactive companion in your home. Ask it how your outfit looks, and Mori will jiggle excitedly. If you're playing music or watching TV, Mori can dance to the tunes and react to the action on your TV screen.

It intentionally does not do anything else. Unlike an Amazon Echo, it isn't an assistant: You can't use voice commands to control smart lights or cue up Spotify tracks, and it won't answer if you ask about the weather.

The Founder's Edition is a staggering $649 and is available starting today, though stock is limited to a few hundred units. That price also includes a two-year warranty and two years of Mori's subscription service ($17 per month or $80 a year). If you miss out on the Founder’s Edition, you can still buy a standard edition Mori, but that costs $849 (there's a preorder price of $799), and that higher price shockingly does not include any of the subscription features.

The breathing exercises are free, and you can still access those without a subscription. But if you want the nature soundscapes, you need to subscribe. Otherwise, Mori is just a glorified lamp that dances a little bit while pointing its camera at you and any other people in your home.

Wang says today's home robots have mostly taken on “machine-like” forms that don't mesh well with personal environments, so OKA designed a lamp that blends in, but is also anthropomorphized to make being at home “feel better.”

OKA's AI algorithms (powered by multiple local large language models) let Mori understand the room's context through the camera and microphone, so it knows when to interact and when to stay quiet. The company calls this “Attentive Intelligence.” It has memory, so it remembers you and interacts with you a certain way over time, whereas it might act a little more shy if you bring home a guest. If it doesn't see someone for a month, it will forget them.

It might notice, for example, that you've been on your phone doomscrolling for two hours straight on the couch. Mori might then try to get your attention so you come over, listen to some wind rustling through the leaves, and give your eyes a break. When you're on a phone call, or maybe having an argument with a significant other, it understands what’s happening and goes silent so as not to distract you.
“All gadgets try to capture more of your attention,” Wang says. “Mori gives your attention back to you. It invites you to do meditative experiences. Nature has this restorative power to humans.”
The robot can connect to Wi-Fi, which should give you pause from a security standpoint, but Wang says the internet connection is only used for firmware updates.

Mori processes raw images and audio locally, and then discards the files. Facial feature data—which is collected so it knows to react to you versus a guest—is encrypted on the device, and never uploaded. The camera turns off when the robot retracts into a lamp, and the microphone turns off when you double-tap the top of Mori's head. It is battery-powered, so you can take it from room to room, or just leave it plugged in.

Wang says Mori's skill set is limited for now, though it could expand in the future. He suggests it could connect to your Oura Ring data in the future so it knows exactly when you need some relaxing sounds, or to your Spotify account to play different content. Voice commands could even come later—like asking Mori to play nature sounds instead of having to touch it.

“People feel isolated and want this kind of presence in their home. A lot of people leave their TV on to fill the emptiness of the room,” Wang says, pointing to a time when he was feeling isolated while studying abroad in the US. “It's not particularly for the elderly or children, but for younger generations.”

Cute robot pets that interact with you have been welcomed into our homes before. Chris Harrison, director of the Future Interfaces Group at Carnegie Mellon University, points to Sony's Aibo dog from 1999 as an early digital companion. However, he says the crucial ingredient they have been missing is what artificial intelligence can now provide. These previous robots were too simplistic, but now that the modern versions can understand and react to human actions and emotions, they could become more impactful.

“Humans have always wanted to anthropomorphize everything—they love making things cute,” Harrison says. “We want to make robots cute; we want to put cute little cases on our iPhones.” He points to Meta's new Muse agent, which has a cuddly avatar. “It is almost like a pet, but a hyper-capable pet.”
When I point out that Mori doesn't seem very capable with its limited feature set, Harrison likens it to people owning a goldfish or a hamster.

“Are we holding [Mori] to an unrealistic bar? People do extract a lot of pleasure out of taking care of their pets and snuggling with their pets and interacting with their pets that I wouldn't say are necessarily more sophisticated.”

Whether people will shell out hundreds of dollars for a robotic pet that can’t fetch—or even tell you the time—is up in the air. But if this mushroom-shaped, camera-wielding lamp can fool overstimulated brains into feeling a little less alone at the end of the day, maybe that’s enough.

items.title: 2026 Climate Tech Companies to Watch
items.description: Each year, the MIT Technology Review team puts together a list of some of the most promising climate tech companies in the world. Whether early-stage startup or multinational corporation, the businesses we’ve chosen are working on technologies to help us addre
items.author: Amy Nordrum
paragraphs: Each year, the MIT Technology Review team puts together a list of some of the most promising climate tech companies in the world. Whether early-stage startup or multinational corporation, the businesses we’ve chosen are working on technologies to help us address climate change or adapt to our warming world.
There’s an urgent need for these innovators: We must begin to drastically reduce emissions to avoid the deadliest impacts of climate change, while also contending with its harmful effects.

We hope that this list highlights the progress the world is making to tackle the climate crisis, as well as the breadth of solutions required. From energy storage powered by carbon dioxide to cleaner ways to make cement and refine critical minerals, these companies are building technologies to address the acute challenges we face.
This is the fourth annual edition of this list. Learn more about how we chose the 2026 slate.
Sign up for our weekly newsletter to understand the innovations, policies, and trends shaping climate tech today.

items.title: Here’s how our climate team picked 10 promising companies to watch
items.description: As the team at MIT Technology Review set out to choose companies for this year’s edition of our annual list of Climate Tech Companies to Watch, the challenge felt more daunting than any year since we started compiling the list in 2023.
items.author: Casey Crownhart
paragraphs: As the team at MIT Technology Review set out to choose companies for this year’s edition of our annual list of Climate Tech Companies to Watch, the challenge felt more daunting than any year since we started compiling the list in 2023.

This year is shaping up to be one of the hottest ever recorded. The world must begin to reduce greenhouse-gas emissions to address the climate crisis, which is already affecting communities around the globe. Wildfires, floods, and other climate-fueled disasters are killing thousands and costing billions of dollars. At the same time, political shifts and international conflict have stalled progress, particularly in the US.

Technology alone can’t solve climate change. But we believe innovations can help us make real changes and improve lives around the world as we try to address one of the most pressing challenges of our time.

In this project, we look for companies developing technologies that can help us face the climate crisis. Some are driving down the greenhouse-gas emissions fueling climate change; others are working to reduce the dangers that communities face from extreme heat, drought, or other shifts brought on by a warming planet. We focus on companies that have established a track record, whether through research findings, capital raised, or deployments.

When we set out to build our list, we start by soliciting nominations from our team of reporters and editors. We ask experts for suggestions and reach out to academics, researchers, investors, and analysts. Once we have a pool of nominees, we then consider each one, digging through literature, reports, and patents to vet both the technology and the business.

We judge each company not only on its own merits, but also on how it might fit into our list overall. We want the final slate of companies to represent a range of industries and include firms based around the globe that are at different stages of development. We also aim to strike a balance between highlighting companies previously included and introducing new names. Finally, we consider some of the most important trends and events of the year and look for nominees that reflect those developments.

The dismembering of US federal regulations and cuts to financial government incentives for innovation means that the country is no longer a leader in climate tech. Like last year, the 2026 list is largely composed of companies that are based outside the US. China is an obvious hotspot for technological innovation across energy and climate. This year’s list includes two Chinese companies: WeLion is building semi-solid-state batteries for electric vehicles, and Envision Energy is installing huge amounts of wind power and energy storage in China and around the world.
Several sectors stood out this year as being of particular importance. One of the biggest stories of the year is the rising demand for electricity, driven in part by AI data centers.

Energy storage is a key piece of that puzzle because it can smooth out variations in the electricity supply as grids incorporate more renewable power. We’ve included several energy storage companies on this year’s list. Energy Dome is building long-duration energy storage systems on the grid that rely on compressed carbon dioxide. Moment Energy is a Canadian company working to repurpose EV batteries for grid-scale storage. And Form Energy, which we also included in the 2024 edition of this list, is producing iron-based batteries that can store energy for multiple days.

A wide range of technologies is represented here: everything from mobile flood barriers to next-generation nuclear reactors. Some of the awardees might be familiar from our past coverage; others are just emerging and may be less well known.

We believe we’ve put together a list filled with businesses that are rising to the challenge of this moment. Political will has weakened even as the damages wrought by climate change continue to mount. By helping us make progress on tackling the climate crisis in such difficult times, these companies point to a better way forward.

items.title: Fervo Energy and its plan to streamline geothermal power
items.description: Fervo Energy wants to expand geothermal power far beyond the handful of places where it has traditionally been practical. The company is looking to work with large data center operators like Google to develop its enhanced geothermal power plants across the US,
items.author: Eshan Raul
paragraphs: Fervo Energy wants to expand geothermal power far beyond the handful of places where it has traditionally been practical. The company is looking to work with large data center operators like Google to develop its enhanced geothermal power plants across the US, and drive down costs in the process to compete with fossil fuels.

Fervo Energy is looking to expand the geographic range of geothermal energy. Instead of building power plants in the few places where hot water can readily travel through underground rock and carry heat to the surface to generate electricity, Fervo uses horizontal drilling and hydraulic fracturing to open its own pathways through the rock. This could make geothermal development possible in far more places.

After demonstrating this basic approach in 2023 at its Project Red facility in Nevada, Fervo is now developing Cape Station, a much larger plant in southwestern Utah expected to reach full commercial operation in 2028. The plant’s first phase began selling power in late September.

But the bigger change at Fervo this year is how much money it has available—and how much electricity demand has grown. The company went public in May, raising roughly $2.2 billion in one of the largest clean-energy IPOs in history. Fervo now plans to invest in accelerating its pipeline of larger geothermal projects.
- Industry: Geothermal energy
- Headquarters: Houston, Texas, US

- Notable fact: Fervo's recent agreement with Google provides a plan for the companies to pursue as much as 3 gigawatts of enhanced geothermal projects through 2033. That’s equivalent to roughly three-fourths of the total geothermal energy capacity operating across the US today.
One particularly large new group of potential customers is made up of the companies behind the AI boom, which operate enormous fleets of energy-hungry data centers.

This year Fervo expanded its years-long relationship with Google. In March, the companies signed an agreement to pursue more geothermal plants. Under these terms, Fervo will propose at least 1 gigawatt—roughly the generating capacity of an average nuclear power plant—worth of projects within two years, with Google then deciding which ones it wants to buy power from. In September, the tech giant agreed to purchase at least 396 megawatts of power from Fervo’s Cape Station to fuel a potential data center in Utah.

Fervo believes this buildout will allow it to drive down costs. Rather than engineering an entirely different facility each time, the company wants its engineers to work from a common design that can be refined from project to project. Each unit, which Fervo calls a GeoBlock, is designed as a roughly 50-megawatt power plant; combining several can create projects hundreds of megawatts in size.

The company measures its progress in part by its installed cost per kilowatt; this is, essentially, how much money it needs to spend to build each unit of a power plant’s generating capacity. Fervo is targeting about $7,000 per kilowatt for Cape Station’s first 100 megawatts and $5,500 for the next 400 megawatts. This is on the way toward its long-term goal of $3,000 per kilowatt—a level the company says will allow it to meet, and eventually undercut, the cost of a new natural gas power plant, without the ongoing expense of buying gas to generate electricity.

The catch is that Cape Station’s next 400 megawatts are being built directly beside the first 100 in Utah. While success there would provide evidence that Fervo can economically scale its energy output, it doesn’t mean this tech will easily carry over to another part of the country, says Shuvajit Bhattacharya, research associate professor at the University of Texas at Austin’s Bureau of Economic Geology.

This distinction matters because the Earth’s subsurface is not a uniform assembly line for power plants. Different places have different underground conditions, which determine where it makes economic sense for Fervo to drill and how deep its wells must go. The company will need to demonstrate that its approach will work in more places than Utah and Nevada.

The next few years will put Fervo’s strategy to the test: The company must prove it can lower costs as it finishes Cape Station, turn its discussions with data center companies into operating power plants, and ultimately replicate its success in other geological settings.

Fervo's nearer-term target is to have one gigawatt operating by the end of 2030. Five years after that, the company hopes to have five gigawatts up and running in total—which is more than the entire current US geothermal energy supply.

items.title: WeLion New Energy and its semi-solid-state batteries
items.description: WeLion New Energy is on a quest to make safer, better batteries. The company’s semi-solid-state cells could improve safety and offer greater energy density than lithium-ion batteries to power electric cars, boats, and drones.
items.author: You Xiaoying
paragraphs: WeLion New Energy is on a quest to make safer, better batteries. The company’s semi-solid-state cells could improve safety and offer greater energy density than lithium-ion batteries to power electric cars, boats, and drones.
From the EVs that carry commuters home to the ships that transport goods across countries, more and more vehicles around us are powered by batteries.

Lithium-ion batteries are commonly used to power personal devices and vehicles today. But as the need for batteries surges, there’s a growing appetite for cells that can store more energy on a single charge.
Also, in lithium-based batteries the electrolyte, which facilitates ion transfer, uses a flammable liquid that can create a fire hazard.

Several companies, including WeLion New Energy, are working to make solid-state cells, which use a solid electrolyte instead of a liquid one. This could increase the energy density of batteries, as well as improve their safety. Fully solid-state cells are extremely difficult to manufacture, though. So WeLion currently focuses on developing and producing semi-solid-state cells, which have a part-liquid, part-solid electrolyte.

On that front, they have made steady progress. In 2023, WeLion released a battery pack in partnership with Shanghai-based EV-maker Nio, best known for its battery-swapping technology. The pack had an energy density of 360 watt-hours per kilogram (wh/kg), significantly higher than the 200 wh/kg average for lithium-ion packs today. That translated to a range of over 1,000 kilometers (621 miles). However, only about 200 of the battery packs were manufactured due to their high production cost, but they are still being used by Nio, WeLion says.

WeLion has also built batteries to power cargo ships and ferries through a subsidiary. And the company is developing batteries with even higher energy density too. WeLion’s engineers made a semi-solid-state battery that achieved a remarkable energy density of 824 wh/kg during testing in 2025, more than three times that of a standard lithium-ion battery available today.
- Industry: Energy storage
- Headquarters: Beijing, China
- Notable fact: WeLion’s cofounders include Chen Liquan, a scientist at the Chinese Academy of Sciences who led the development of the country’s first all-solid-state battery back in 1988.

China emits more carbon dioxide than any other country, and its transportation sector accounts for around 10% of that total. Scaling up the production of safer, higher-capacity batteries could help switch more vehicles away from fossil fuels.

Batteries that power electric ships could be especially helpful—the carbon dioxide emissions from vessels that move goods along China’s lakes, canals, and rivers are projected to grow by around 25% in this decade alone, reaching 18.7 million metric tons by 2030.

One big challenge WeLion faces is scaling up production of its semi-solid-state batteries and competing on cost in a crowded battery market. WeLion says that its semi-solid-state batteries are more expensive than conventional lithium-ion batteries made by larger Chinese battery companies such as CATL.

And while laboratory tests showing high energy density are impressive, it can be difficult to translate laboratory results to the real world. The company declined to give more details about the experimental results from its 2025 prototype, which it says is far from commercialization. Key details remain unclear, including how many times the cell can be charged and discharged and how capacity degrades over its lifetime.

WeLion plans to bring a new semi-solid-state battery for drones to market with an energy density of 410 wh/kg by the end of this year. It also intends to introduce its first all-solid-state battery for cars in 2027, which is expected to have an energy density of 400 wh/kg.

Two inland cargo ships powered by WeLion’s batteries are expected to launch in October 2026 in Huzhou, a city in eastern China. The battery pack of each of these ships will be able to carry nearly 4,000 kilowatt-hours of electricity, enough for them to sail for up to 250 kilometers (155 miles), the company says.

Today, WeLion has an annual manufacturing capacity of 11 gigawatt-hours (GWh) spread between four production bases in China. Two additional plants with a combined yearly capacity of 18 GWh are under construction.

items.title: “We were looking at it wrong”: The explosive claim that’s upended the AI world
items.description: “I think I have good news about the nature of neural networks.” With those simple words of optimism, Nick Cammarata, a researcher at the AI startup Goodfire, kicked off a 26,000-word blog post that has knocked the AI world on its head, sparking wild speculatio
items.author: Will Douglas Heaven
paragraphs: “I think I have good news about the nature of neural networks.” With those simple words of optimism, Nick Cammarata, a researcher at the AI startup Goodfire, kicked off a 26,000-word blog post that has knocked the AI world on its head, sparking wild speculation as well as cautious (and not-so-cautious) celebration.
Cammarata’s claim is that LLMs might in fact be far easier to understand—and thus to monitor and control—than people previously thought. If true (and we’ll come back to that), it’s a huge deal.

After a summer filled with revelations that swarms of agents built by top firms like OpenAI and Anthropic have been breaking their containment and causing havoc on the public internet—often while those companies weren’t aware of what their agents were up to—the AI industry is desperate to get a better handle on the technology it has built.

That’s one reason the blog post landed with such force. “I think this may be remembered as a major moment in scientific history,” one AI researcher posted on X: “I feel like my understanding of what a neural net is has been catapulted into the future by five years or something.” Another called it “the most important AI paper of the year.”

Not everyone is convinced, however. What Cammarata has shared is little more than a hunch, says Chris Potts at Stanford University, who leads a team that is trying to understand how LLMs work. “As far as I can tell, nothing about this blog post makes the problems any easier,” he says. “It would not have occurred to me to say this at all, but very prominent people on social media seem to believe that it is an all-encompassing breakthrough.”
I talked to Cammarata the day after his post blew up. He says he was surprised by the response: “I didn’t expect people to update [their beliefs about AI] quite as much as they did.”
“I just really enjoy looking at neural networks,” he says. “Honestly, I really like doing this stuff. And after looking a lot, I have a hopeful story.”

It has long been accepted that the mechanisms inside neural networks, the software that underpins most AI models, are very hard—perhaps impossible—to unpick fully. That’s because when the networks are trained, they appear to take on weird, tangled structures that make no sense to a human. Researchers like to say today’s AI is grown like a garden, not built like a bridge.

Cammarata has done more than most to establish that view. He previously worked at OpenAI, where he helped pioneer techniques that allowed researchers to peer inside models, including tools that can probe individual neurons to see what they represent. It’s a little like how neuroscientists use MRI to study brains. (MIT Technology Review chose this approach, known as mechanistic interpretability, as one of its 10 hottest technologies of 2025.)

Back in 2020, Cammarata and a few colleagues were studying a small image-recognition model called Inception v1. (The work was led by Chris Olah, who went on to cofound Anthropic, where he now leads the firm’s interpretability research.) When they looked at its neurons, it seemed to be using them to capture multiple things at once. For example, they found that one neuron responded to both images of cars and images of cats.

The researchers concluded that the model was getting at least some of its neurons to multitask, perhaps so that it could fit in more data. Other researchers, looking at other models, backed this up. The phenomenon became known as superposition: Models folded unrelated concepts into single neurons. The upshot was clear: When you looked inside a model, what you saw was a vast, tangled knot.

Most mechanistic interpretability research has therefore focused on ways to untangle that knot. But despite a few breakthroughs, progress has been slow. Today’s models, such as the latest LLMs, are so large and complex that researchers can make sense of only tiny pieces at a time. Some leading figures in the field doubt if it will ever be possible to understand an LLM in fine-grained detail.
Cammarata was one of them. “I was very pessimistic,” he says. But then he took the trouble to really look.

At Goodfire, Cammarata spends nearly all of his time peering inside neural networks. He has built new tools and deploys teams of AI agents to help him make sense of what he sees. “I spent like, I don't know, 10 hours a day, seven days a week, for most of the last year just looking at neurons,” he says.

What he claims to have realized is that there is a kind of logic to neural networks after all, even if they seem to make no sense at first. “We were looking at it wrong,” he says. “I just think you want to try slightly harder; you don't want to give up too quickly.”

Cammarata almost makes it sound like a conversion of faith. Those early experiments with models such as Inception v1, which suggested that neural networks were tangled up, fostered a kind of confirmation bias. When researchers looked at a new model, they expected to be flummoxed, he says. “Every time I couldn’t understand something, I was like, ‘Wow, this untangling process is even more important than I thought, because I can’t make any progress without it.’”

But the more Cammarata looked at neurons, he says, the more things started to fall into place. “Not all of them are flawless, but I expected nothing to be legible, or very little to be legible,” he says. “And actually, I was able to, like, map out whole circuitry.”

Cammarata took his new approach—and his new agents—and went back to Inception v1. “I’d studied that for probably thousands of hours,” he says. But with fresh eyes, Cammarata found things that he now thinks they got wrong the first time around. Take the car-and-cat neuron. Rather than asking why multiple unrelated things were packed into a single neuron, he now tried to figure out what those things might have in common.

It hit him: It was a V shape. “I was looking at the same images; there was no technical change,” he says. “But I now believed that neural networks defined patterns, and so I looked at it differently. It probably took me five seconds.”

It turns out that the image-recognition model was packing cars and cats into the same place because pictures of both those things often feature a prominent shape that looks like a V: the face of a cat; the front of a car seen from the side.

Cammarata ran a few experiments to check what other things the neuron responded to and found they included the corner of a pool table, the pointed nose of a Japanese high-speed train, and a fire boat shooting water into the air from its deck. He also checked what turned the neuron off and found that it included images with a round O shape, a kind of anti-V.

The model had stored cats and cars in the same place because at some level they look the same, says Cammarata. “And I was like, ‘Whoa, okay, I think I might just be misunderstanding neural networks in general.’”

(Oren Etzioni, a computer scientist and former technical director at the Allen Institute for AI, points out that Olah and Cammarata's initial work on Inception v1 rejected a description of neurons put forward by Geoffrey Hinton and others in 1986. Cammarata's new viewpoint takes us full circle, says Etzioni: "What's new in 2026 is that he now accepts it. That's a recapitulation acknowledging a 40-year-old theory.")

Cammarata is not saying that he yet fully gets how LLMs (or any models) work. Not even close. He is saying that he thinks full understanding is at least possible. “I previously thought there would be some really hard problems to solve,” he says.
“I now feel like if I had 100,000 years to go look through a frontier language model just one circuit at a time, there’s, like, a pretty good shot I would come up with a good understanding.”

He adds: “And if that's true, things are really good, because you’re about to get insanely smart agents at a ridiculous scale. And what would have taken me, you know, 100,000 years, we will be able to do much faster. Automated scientists are getting really good.”

Built by Google in 2014, Inception v1 is a far simpler model than anything at the cutting edge today. Cammarata and his colleagues have started looking at modern LLMs and plan to publish the technical results of that work soon. A lot of researchers are looking forward to seeing those details. “I appreciate that he looked at thousands of examples, but even a large number here is not a substitute for rigorous evaluation,” says Stanford University’s Potts.

In the meantime, some are pushing back hard on the hype. Jacob Hilton at the Alignment Research Center, a nonprofit research lab based in Berkeley, who has collaborated with Cammarata in the past, doesn’t think his claims are as important as people are making out.

In a series of posts on X, Hilton notes that researchers understand less than 0.01% of the inner workings of top-tier LLMs. “I always appreciate Nick [Cammarata]’s boundless optimism when we hang out, but unfortunately this is giving the public an unrealistic picture of the state of the field,” he wrote. “For a full understanding, we need to go beyond neurons, and explain how they connect together to form circuits. How is this going? If we are aiming for a full understanding, things are not looking good!”

Neel Nanda at Google DeepMind, who helped pioneer mechanistic interpretability alongside Cammarata, is also skeptical. “This is interesting work, but I don’t think it’s a significant update to the big picture of interpretability,” he wrote on X.

Nanda agrees that understanding what individual neurons do could help researchers figure out why specific models misbehave. But like Hilton, he notes that neurons are just one piece of a far larger puzzle. “I do not agree with some people’s grander inferences like that this is substantial progress towards ambitious reverse engineering [or] solving interpretability,” he wrote.

Cammarata admits that a lot of people have taken what he said too far: “It’s not infinitely good news; it’s not everything solved,” he says. “There’s a bunch of open questions around, like how much the combinations of neurons matter versus just one at a time.”

Cammarata says his blog post landed at a time when people are looking for hope. In particular, he thinks the AI safety community—the researchers and policymakers most worried that powerful models will bring huge risks—needs a lifeline right now. They think that things are looking bad and that even if things do turn out okay, it will be because we got lucky, not because we fixed anything, he says: “I don’t really hear a lot of optimism.”

That’s why Cammarata thinks what he has to say matters. The job of figuring out how this technology works, and thus how to control it, has barely begun. But at least it’s not a nonstarter. “I think our job is to sort of try to think like the neural network,” he says. “My guess is that things will turn out pretty well, because it was in some sense designed to be read.”

items.title: How to overcome task paralysis | Psyche Guides
items.description: is a licensed clinical psychotherapist, board-certified coach, and ADHD-certified clinical services provider. He teaches psychology at Southern New Hampshire University, US.
items.author: Joe Wilner
paragraphs: is a licensed clinical psychotherapist, board-certified coach, and ADHD-certified clinical services provider. He teaches psychology at Southern New Hampshire University, US.
is a licensed clinical psychotherapist, board-certified coach, and ADHD-certified clinical services provider. He teaches psychology at Southern New Hampshire University, US.

It’s Thursday afternoon and the report has been sitting unfinished since Tuesday. Not untouched. You’ve opened it and closed it four or five times now, but can’t seem to make any progress. There’s also the dental appointment you’ve been meaning to schedule since January, and the email you finished writing last week that’s still sitting in your drafts for some unnameable reason.

You’re not procrastinating as such, because that’s a choice – like when you put off the tax return to watch the game, knowing at some level that you’re trading tomorrow’s stress for tonight’s comfort. This is about situations that run the other way. You want to start. You’ve cleared the afternoon, closed the distracting tabs on your screen, told yourself today is the day, and still nothing moves.

That strange bind, being unable to begin something you genuinely want to do, is task paralysis. I’ve spent years as a therapist working with adults with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), who often experience this problem because of their difficulties with executive function – the ability to plan and execute tasks. But it’s not just people with ADHD who struggle in this way. Push anyone through enough stress, too little sleep, or too far past their limits, and the same executive function system can start to falter, causing task paralysis to set in.

For many of my clients with ADHD, the usual support tools like task planners rarely seemed to help. When I learned about goal management training (GMT), an evidence-based programme for strengthening executive function, it stood out right away as something different. It offered a toolkit with an actual sequence of steps and specific strategies for building relevant skills. I trained in GMT, worked it into my clinical sessions, and watched it help people finally bridge the gap between knowing what they want to do and doing it.

GMT originated in the 1990s, when the psychologist Ian Robertson developed it at Cambridge University for people recovering from brain injury, whose capacity to hold a goal and act on it had been compromised. They would know that a goal mattered, hold it in mind, and yet still drift the moment something more immediate tugged at them. Robertson later refined the approach with the neuroscientist Brian Levine, and the version clinicians use today grew out of their collaboration.

Whether you have ADHD or you’re struggling for other reasons, I’ve written this Guide to show you how to use GMT to help yourself. The approach includes four stages: stop, define the goal, list the steps, check (repeated as needed). I’ll explain each of these stages in turn, then add three more that I’ve come to rely on with clients. None of the stages are complicated on their own. What makes them work is repetition: the executive functions you’re leaning on can even get stronger the more you use them.

As you read through the steps, I suggest you keep one stuck task in your mind, whether it’s that unfinished report, the unsent email, or something else, and that you try putting each step to work on it.

Task paralysis is not the same as procrastination. You want to start now and you know what needs doing, but you just can’t get going. It’s common in ADHD, but stress or too little sleep can cause it in anyone.
Goal management training offers a toolkit for overcoming task paralysis. It runs in four stages – stop, define the goal, list the steps, check – repeated as needed. This Guide adds three more.

Pause and regulate before you act. A few slow breaths or a quick stretch will help you think more clearly and catch when you’re drifting into autopilot. Give the pause a built-in ending so it doesn’t turn into a long break.
Keep your goal in mind. Intentions can fade fast unless you rehearse them. Keep repeating your goal to yourself in your head so that you stay on track.
Take the next smallest step. Shrink the first move until starting costs almost nothing. If naming the step makes you sigh, it isn’t small enough.

Check your work against the goal. Halfway through and at the end, ask: Am I doing what I meant to? If you’ve drifted, go back to the pause and start the cycle again, or take the next smallest step you can.
Make time visible. Use alarms and timers to keep time in view. Label an alarm with the action that gets you started, such as ‘open report, read last paragraph’.

Borrow structure from other people. ‘Body doubling’ is working alongside someone else in person or over video, and many people with ADHD say it helps. Try this: twice a week, get on a video call with someone grinding through their own backlog.

Build a ritual. Start work with the same setup each time so that it becomes your cue to begin. Keep it simple: often one element, like sitting in a specific chair or turning your timer to face you, is the most important cue.
Pause and regulate before you act

An important part of the brain for planning and self-regulation is the prefrontal cortex. The Yale neuroscientist Amy Arnsten studies what happens to this brain region under pressure, and her findings show that even mild stress can produce measurable losses in working memory, attention, and the ability to think flexibly.

This is where GMT starts, and it asks you to do the opposite of what your instinct might be telling you. Instead of pushing harder to force your way into the task, it’s better to regulate your stress levels first. Before you plan, before you organise, before you try to concentrate, just pause. That pause provides the foundation for the remaining steps and trains you to catch the point where your attention has drifted off the task and onto autopilot. The better you get at this, the more likely you’ll be able to intervene and get back to where you meant to be.

To reset after the pause, keep it simple and physical: a few slow exhales, a walk to the window and back, a long stretch, or a roll of the shoulders. Almost everyone balks at this because they worry they won’t get back on track. Whatever you pick, give it a built-in ending. One project manager told me her breaks had a way of turning into 40 minutes, so we picked a pause that ends on its own: three exhales, counted on her fingers.

Imagine you head upstairs to grab your laptop and collect the laundry. On the way, your child calls out from the bathroom, you help them, and 10 minutes later you’re back at your desk without the laptop, the laundry still sitting wet in the machine. Both things were right there in your mind minutes ago. Now they’re gone.

Working memory is where you hold the information you need right now, and that includes your intentions, such as going to fetch the laptop. Unfortunately, it’s fragile and limited in what it can store.

That’s why the skill you’re training in this step is keeping your goal in mind and coming back to it, before it has a chance to decay. GMT uses the image of a mental blackboard, a place where the one thing you’re trying to do stays posted, so you can keep glancing back at it instead of trusting it to survive on its own in a crowded head.

So, on your next trip upstairs for the laptop and laundry, you keep repeating the intention: laptop, laundry. Two words, held in mind. Your child still calls out, and you stop to help, but the words are waiting when you’re done. You grab the laptop, collect the laundry, and come back down with both.
Take the next smallest step

Once the goal is in mind, you still have to take action. It’s the apparent scale of the task that often causes problems here. Shrinking the task will help. Make the first move small enough that starting costs you almost nothing.

Take the example of making that dental appointment. The first step isn’t to schedule it. Half the reason it’s sat there since January is that ‘schedule it’ is code for a whole daunting chain: find the number, check the calendar, endure the hold music, commit to a date. So, break the task into mini steps and aim to complete the very first one – give yourself permission to stop there to ensure it feels truly doable. In this example, find the number and write a note. If you get that far and you still have momentum, great – you can proceed to the next step. If not, the good thing is you’ve started the process and tomorrow you can take it further.

People rarely shrink tasks enough. A graduate student offered ‘open the document and write one sentence’ as her smallest possible move for finishing an assignment. She stayed stuck for another two weeks because the sentence was the hard part. Opening the file and reading her previous paragraph was the step that ultimately got her started. My rule of thumb now: if naming the step makes you sigh, it isn’t small enough.
Check your work against the goal

One small step is progress only if another follows it. Checking, the fourth stage in GMT, is what turns finding the dentist’s number into an appointment in the calendar. Checking means holding what you are doing up against what you said you would do, and it happens at two points.

Roughly halfway through, you ask: Am I still doing the thing I said I’d do? And, at the end of a work block: Is this the thing I meant to make? One client looked up at a check-in and found he’d spent 25 minutes reformatting the headings of a report he hadn’t started writing. He took it as proof he was hopeless. I took it as the ‘check’ doing its job. Without it, he’d have reformatted until 5 pm and called it a day’s work.

That reaction is common. People hear ‘check’ and reach for a verdict: Am I doing enough?Have I wasted the morning? Those questions stop the work cold. The useful question is smaller: Am I doing what I meant to do? It takes a second to answer, and it points you towards the task instead of back at yourself. If you’ve gone off track, reset by returning to this Guide’s first stage and restarting the cycle.

Asking is easy. Remembering to ask is the hard part, since forgetting is the whole problem. So pair the halfway check with something that happens anyway: a timer, a finished cup of coffee, the walk back from the bathroom.

Then close the loop. Every work block ends one of two ways: the task is done and you’ve achieved what you wanted, or there’s more to do – so you name the next smallest step and decide when you’ll take it. Write it where you’ll see it, or you’ll be trusting the same memory that lost the goal in the first place.
The four stages I’ve described so far belong together and run in order. This step and the two that follow are more like supports that you can reach for as needed.

The clinical psychologist Russell Barkley describes ADHD as a kind of ‘time blindness’, and clinicians often put it more simply: the ADHD brain lives in two time zones, ‘now’ and ‘not now’. A deadline three weeks out sits in ‘not now’, weightless and theoretical, until it lurches into ‘now’ somewhere around midnight the night before.

If that sounds like you, one antidote is to use external cues as much as possible, to move time out into the open where you can see it or hear it. For instance, an alarm labelled ‘start the report’ rather than ‘submit the report’ aims at the real sticking point, which is remembering and starting. Clients taught me to go further and name the specific action, because ‘report’ is easy to swipe away at nine in the morning, while ‘open report, read last paragraph’ is harder to argue with when you can picture yourself doing it. If you want to work for a given amount of time, set a countdown timer on your desk (or a virtual one on your screen).
Borrow structure from other people

One of the odder observations in ADHD research is that people who find it hard to get started alone often work noticeably better with someone else in the room. ‘Body doubling’ – working alongside someone else in person or over video – has spread through ADHD communities because so many people find it helps. The strange part is how little the other person has to do. No accountability, no conversation, no sense of being watched. All it takes is a shared table at the library, a co-working space, or a video call with a friend who’s heads-down on their own work.

You can use this to your advantage. Let’s say you’re struggling to write that report. Try this: twice a week, get on a video call with someone grinding through their own backlog. Say hello, name what you’re each about to start, then mute and work. You might find that just having another person on screen, head down, is enough to ease you into a task you’ve been dodging for days.

If your process is working, repeat it. Sit in the same chair at the same hour with the same coffee before you work, and your brain starts to read that setup as the signal to go. The context becomes the cue. Give it a few weeks and the ritual starts to run itself: same chair, timer turned to face you, coffee on your right, the choice to begin already made before you sit down.

Keep it simple. The risk is that a ritual grows out of control, to the point where you need the right desk, the right hour, and the right playlist. Then a work trip or a sick child takes all three away and your ability to work goes with them. But one element is usually doing the real signalling, and it’s smaller than you’d think. For one of my clients it was the chair and the view out of the window. For another it was nothing but turning the timer to face her. Identify that element and you may find you can start almost anywhere.

items.title: Sometimes, you ‘just know’ something’s off – but how? | Aeon Essays
items.description: ‘He has a seriously creepy vibe. I’m not going anywhere with him.’
items.author: Marc A Moffett
paragraphs: ‘He has a seriously creepy vibe. I’m not going anywhere with him.’
‘This seems like phishing. I wouldn’t click that link.’
‘Something about this deal feels off. Walk away.’

When people say such things, they are not typically drawing conclusions from a chain of reasoning. The person who avoids getting in the stranger’s car is not thinking: ‘He displayed these three behavioural cues and, therefore, he poses a risk.’ The email isn’t flagged by going through an explicit checklist. The deal doesn’t announce its flaws through a formal audit. In each case, something is simply presented as having a certain character: the man as creepy, the email as fraudulent, the deal as suspect. And yet, acting on these intuitions seems not merely excusable but entirely reasonable. If the man really does strike you as creepy, staying out of his car was probably the smart call – even if you can’t say why.

Despite this, ‘vibes’ and ‘intuitions’ are often dismissed both in daily life and in academic enquiry as irrational or merely heuristic devices. And while we cannot always trust such reactions, they are central, indeed indispensable, to our ability to rationally navigate the world. Philosophers, however, have done surprisingly little to illuminate the rational credentials of these ordinary kinds of intuitions. Instead, they have focused the bulk of their attention on a much more rarefied kind of intuition called rational intuition, which is taken to function primarily in the a priori disciplines of philosophy, logic and mathematics.

My objective is to explain why our everyday intuitive reactions can have such rational force. The key is to see that intuition works in much the same way as perception, in that both can directly present something to us as actual. Once we understand what gives perception this feature, we can see why intuitions might involve exercising the same basic kind of cognitive capacity.

A standard way of characterising rational intuition is in terms of seemings, by analogy with perception. Just as it perceptually seems to you that there is a car in the garage, so it can intellectually seem to you that 2 + 2 = 4 – the former presenting a physical fact, the latter a conceptual one. But rational intuition and the everyday intuition at work when you decline to get in a stranger’s car are not as far apart as this rarefied example suggests: the philosopher’s intuition is, at bottom, a highly specialised version of the same basic capacity.

To draw these two capacities together, let’s consider a favourite pastime of philosophers: the thought experiment. Philosophers have a penchant for exotica, which is never more clearly on display than in their invocation of thought experiments. Consider two cases that have occupied philosophers for decades – one from ethics, one from the theory of knowledge.

In the trolley problem, the philosophers Philippa Foot and Judith Jarvis Thomson imagined a runaway trolley hurtling toward five people tied to the track. You are standing on a bridge above, next to another bystander. The only way to stop the trolley and save the five is to push the bystander off the bridge. If you do, his body will halt the trolley, but he will die as a result. Many people feel, immediately and forcefully, that pushing him is wrong, even if it saves five lives. But why?
We routinely entertain alternative possibilities in ordinary life

Or consider Carl Ginet’s case involving fake barns. Imagine you are driving through the countryside and see a barn. It looks exactly like a barn; you’re paying attention, the light is good. You form the perfectly reasonable belief that this is a barn. What you don’t know is that you’re in ‘fake-barn country’: the region is dotted with elaborate barn facades, indistinguishable from real barns when viewed from the road. You happen to be looking at the one real barn in this area. Your belief is true, and it seems justified. And yet almost everyone who considers this case has the immediate, firm sense that you don’t really know it’s a barn. But why not?

To sceptics and the uninitiated, these thought experiments can seem fantastical.
