Once all the smoke clears, there are signs of things returning to normal with Lamb toasting his fallen joes (and a hobbled Louisa, who may or may not be back) and Taverner successfully scapegoating both Cantor and Peter Judd, whose ambitions to get back in the game make him a natural fall guy to lay before the Home Secretary. But Taverner’s issues with her Russian counterpart, Vassily, are not over, and nothing is settled in the closing sequence where River’s romantic moment with Sid is drastically short-circuited. In the second episode, he brought a crowbar into his grandfather’s house to confront the person he’d assumed to be Harkness. Now, a poisonous residue on the same crowbar has left him incapacitated.

What does the ending imply about River and Sid’s relationship? That’s a question for next season, but their flirtation has been built around Sid’s ambiguous motives from the beginning. Just before she was shot, in the second episode, Sid confessed to River that she had been asked to spy on him for Taverner, and not every question about what she’d been doing in the years since has been answered this season. As much as it feels as though there’s something real between them, it feels just as much as if she’s hiding a card or two from him.

• There’s no time for anyone in this episode to process Coe’s death — and probably not a huge amount of sentimentality around him given his relatively brief tenure under Lamb — but the sigh Oldman lets out when he realizes Coe is gone carries a surprising amount of weight. Lamb cares about his charges, part the billionth.

• Clever idea for Lamb’s confrontation with Natasha to take place with her child’s birthday party as the backdrop. Her daughter confuses this disheveled man for a clown, then he helps himself to finger sandwiches in front of Natasha’s armed henchmen.
• Sad words from Shirley to Reece about processing traumatic memories like seeing his father murdered: “Bury them. Just push them down really deep and pretend they’re not there.”
• In the end, Cantor discovers being a billionaire doesn’t shield you from accountability. Slow Horses is a very good fictional show.
• Harkness’s line “I’m the same as I always was. It’s the jobs that got small” nods to Norma Desmond in Billy Wilder’s classic Sunset Boulevard: “I am big. It’s the pictures that got small.”

• Slow Horses recap recommendation corner: (1) The folk song underscoring River’s fateful trip to his grandfather’s house in the closing scene is Nick Drake’s “One of These Things First,” a great song off his 1971 album, Bryter Layter. Those new to Drake’s music are often directed to his much sparser 1972 LP, Pink Moon, but I prefer the lusher orchestrations on the earlier record. (2) Coe is not dead, at least if you happen to see the latest (and quite solid) adaptation of Sense and Sensibility. The man who plays Coe, Tom Brooke, stands out unmistakably as John Dashwood, the mostly amiable gentleman who inherits the estate where his half-sisters, Elinor, Marianne, and Margaret, live with their mother.

items.title: VisionQuest Recap: Movie Marathon
items.description: Time for some backstory and some answers! Episode four of VisionQuest digs into Butcherbird’s origins and identity while raising fresh questions about her. It also addresses a mystery from episode two about a painting of a blazing figure Vision called “the fir
items.author: Tasha Robinson
paragraphs: Time for some backstory and some answers! Episode four of VisionQuest digs into Butcherbird’s origins and identity while raising fresh questions about her. It also addresses a mystery from episode two about a painting of a blazing figure Vision called “the first of us” and “a cautionary tale.” There’s a lot of exposition to swallow this time around, so to keep things spicy, we start the episode in a horror movie, segue to a true-crime feature, jump to a heist film, and wrap up with an action movie. It’s an entire movie marathon in just 48 minutes!

The horror movie takes place in Vision’s mind-mansion, which Butcherbird has filled with red light, dark shadows, and ominous imagery. She says she wants to change the world and demands he stay out of her way, or she’ll hurt Thomas. Vision assumes she’s a new S.W.O.R.D. synthezoid, and she doesn’t correct him. She just implies humanity will always keep making new AIs. “These are not people who understand the word enough,” she snarls.

Edith treats Butcherbird like a horror-movie demon, dressing up as a priest to exorcise her by reading from Programmer’s Bible: Vision Testament: “I break thee from thy loop with batch command, end function! I sever thine process with backslash body in all targeted nodes!” Ultron clearly finds this hilarious: “The power of code compels you!” he shouts, and they boot Butcherbird out of Vision’s head.

They also boot themselves straight into the kind of crime procedural where the villain’s threats helpfully direct the protagonists toward a conspiracy instead of away from it. Ultron smugly briefs the AI crew on Butcherbird’s murders, since they haven’t been following human news. Ultron and Vision sneak into Interpol’s servers for more information about Butcherbird’s victims, in a light, jokey sequence that spoofs security programs, AI bots, CAPTCHAs, and social media. These two supposed enemies make a surprisingly natural mismatched buddy-cop duo.

The Interpol files reveal that Butcherbird is probably collecting biometric keys from her victims: She’s taken blood, fingerprints, and an eye. The AI crew connects the victims via string boards, amusingly labeled “map with pins” and “human murder board.” The victims were all on a five-person team that created the original architecture for stable AI consciousness at a company called Markridge Biotech. Stark Industries later bought that architecture, using it to develop our AI cast members.

The team co-lead, Dr. Josephine Carrington, died of natural causes in 2008 — an immediate red flag in a crime drama that’s missing an obvious mastermind. The team’s final member, Katerina Wells, is now Markridge’s CEO and Butcherbird’s probable final target. And surprise, Katerina is throwing a big transhumanist charity gala that very night! And who has the skills to infiltrate it? Grifter supreme Thomas Shepherd!

Meanwhile, in the real world, we learn that Vision’s superpowers are all offline until he has time for significant repairs, so he can’t just phase or zap his way through whatever comes next. It’s also clear a confrontation is looming, since Thomas keeps asking pointed, suspicious questions about the “imaginary friends” Vision talks to. He doesn’t know Ultron is one of them, but he’s clearly going to figure that out.

But first, cue the heist movie! Thomas brings in his partner Lisa, who steals fancy clothes and gala passes for herself, Thomas, and Vision. Just as the previous segments lampooned horror and crime movies, the heist veers into meta humor, as Vision and Thomas divert attention from Lisa’s pickpocketing by having a screaming fight in Italian. Briefly, they roleplay as a boss and his hapless assistant. Soon, though, they’re just yelling whatever comes to mind: “Angrier! We gotta give Lisa time!” “Too loud! Now it’s weird!”

Their heist-craft is terrible, between Vision and Thomas immediately breaking character and Lisa gleefully waving her stolen passes at them while she’s still two feet away from the original owners. But that doesn’t matter: This episode is mostly a breezy, fluffy, connect-the-dots puzzle. Whenever the lines between dots are scribbled in hastily, it’s intentional, for comedy value. Less funny: When Lisa gets Thomas alone, she points out how completely and uncharacteristically he came to trust his new synthezoid father figure. Thomas gets defensive — and brutal. “Why are you trying to ruin this for me?” he snaps. “Maybe it’s because only one of us is an orphan now?” Ugly! Sure, Thomas is juggling abandonment issues, a ton of recent trauma, and a ghost in his head only Vision believes in. But he still doesn’t get a free pass to weaponize everything he knows about Lisa in order to hurt her more effectively.

Back in the mind-mansion, Edith doles out more exposition about the Howard Stark employees Tony Stark used as his AI templates and wonders whether her code includes the pain her template, test pilot Edith Marks, suffered upon losing her husband, Edward. (Apparently it’s Edith’s turn to shoulder VisionQuest’s identity themes, though the episode itself does plenty of identity-switching.) Ultron is uncharacteristically kind to Edith, even when she diffidently asks why he chose, uh, that human avatar. He says he doesn’t know; it just suits him. Paired with Friday and Edith’s musings in the last episode, it does seem clear we’re headed for a reveal about the human origin of Ultron’s appearance and personality. Anyone have a picture of Edward Marks handy?

At the gala, an audiovisual presentation compares Vision and Ultron as the apex and nadir of AI possibility. Neither enjoys the comparison, though it’s a cool bit of production design to have their real faces hovering meaningfully in the background as they play at being human. Katerina, surrounded by security, fills in some guests on the history of J.I.M., a.k.a. Synthetic Man, first glimpsed in Captain America: The First Avenger, and mentioned as the mysterious “first of us” in episode two. He was the first automaton AI, and his source code inspired Markridge Biotech’s work. Katerina says J.I.M. was deactivated “due to a series of incendiary mishaps,” but Vision tells Thomas that J.I.M.’s clockwork body caught fire while trying to run fast enough to process his emotions. He “felt to death,” as Thomas puts it. Apparently, the first Vision escaped that fate because the Mind Stone helped him “navigate the complexities of the mind and the heart.” The Mind Stone is long gone, but current Vision says he has “enough of that power” to keep himself regulated. That sounds deeply improbable, and seems like a potential issue for Butcherbird, Ultron, and any other synthetic life that never touched the stone.

Three threads come to a head at once as we enter action-movie mode. Vision slips up verbally, and Thomas realizes he preserved an internal copy of Ultron. Butcherbird arrives. And Katerina, onstage, publicly admits her guilt over helping develop the AI that led to Ultron and the Sokovia attack. We’ve been hearing her deny any guilt over Sokovia in a TV interview all episode: Butcherbird sends Vision an audio clip, and the interview plays on TVs at the hotel and in Vision’s mansion. Hearing Katerina admit her sense of responsibility for Ultron feels significant, though most of the story is still missing. But Butcherbird interrupts her speech. The episode’s action-movie finale drops the rest of the episode’s spoofy meta humor and aims at straight drama, as Butcherbird smashes through Katerina’s security detail and drops her disguise. She isn’t a Vision-like synth; she’s an Ultron-like metal bot with Dr. Josephine Carrington’s face.

Katerina pleads that she’s changed, and she’s “finally trying to create the world that you wanted.” “Peace in our time,” Butcherbird responds — Ultron’s manifesto when he was trying to end war by exterminating humankind. But Butcherbird still vows to “take back what you took from me, starting with your face.” Thomas superspeeds Katerina to safety and Vision fights Butcherbird, but Butcherbird is faster and stronger. Vision calls out to Jo Carrington, who he presumes was Butcherbird’s personality template. “I am not based on her. I am her,” she snarls, beating Vision down again.

Vision admits to Ultron that he can’t win this fight, and Ultron offers to take over their body and ensure both they and Butcherbird survive. (His argument is terrible — essentially “You’re too worried about Thomas’s safety to win. I’ll be better at this because I don’t care whether he dies.”) But Vision still gives in. Ultron takes over his body then tricks Butcherbird into disintegrating Katerina, intuiting that she wanted Katerina’s face as a fourth biometric key. With Katerina gone, he says they don’t need to fight anymore.

“This isn’t over,” Butcherbird snarls, and she flies away. Ultron seals Vision and the AI crew into Vision’s mind-mansion, then wraps a controlling arm around Thomas to guide him into the wings for “a little chat.” With him taking over Vision’s body (though keeping his own voice!), we veer all the way back into possession horror again — a nifty little closed loop for an episode that otherwise often feels like the writers have been rushing past anything that got in the way of reaching exactly this point in the story.
• This isn’t officially part of the story yet, but the credits and subtitles now identify Butcherbird as Jocasta, a known Marvel Comics superhero created by Ultron.

• What’s up with Vision saying Thomas will be safer if he stays close to Vision, when just two episodes ago, he said the exact opposite? Is this just wishful thinking because he wants to be near his son?
• “Incendiary mishaps” feels like a bit of a gag reference, given how the comic version of Synthetic Man connects to the Human Torch.

• Sure enough, when Ultron “takes the wheel” in Vision’s head — an old-timey ship’s wheel, with a surging ocean in the windows behind him, for one more movie-esque visual — he starts singing “I’ve Got No Strings” again. Called it!

items.title: VisionQuest Recap: Puzzle Pieces
items.description: At this point, we really should talk about Ultron, the snarky spark VisionQuest is built around. He’s having most of the fun in this show and providing most of the fun for viewers. But he’s also doing most of the narrative work, stabilizing everyone else and c
items.author: Tasha Robinson
paragraphs: At this point, we really should talk about Ultron, the snarky spark VisionQuest is built around. He’s having most of the fun in this show and providing most of the fun for viewers. But he’s also doing most of the narrative work, stabilizing everyone else and counterbalancing their flaws. He’s confident and self-assured where Vision is vacillating and confused. He’s snarky and sly where the other AIs are achingly perky and sincere. He’s wise and knowledgeable when the others are scrambling for information or direction. He keeps pushing the story forward, creating dynamic situations where Vision wants stability and isolation.

Does Vision recognize how much he needs Ultron as a foil? Even though Ultron purposefully destabilized Vision’s quiet, well-ordered life, causing Fiona’s and Jarvis’s deaths and Vision’s near-destruction, Vision still treats him more like a bristly colleague than a dangerous enemy. And while Vision spends a lot of “Reboot” too incapacitated to resist, reject, or re-incarcerate Ultron, he doesn’t even mention Ultron’s escape from mind-prison. Maybe he doesn’t think Ultron’s mildly enhanced freedom as a persistent hallucination matters that much. But given how much of “Reboot” Vision spends trying to survive the aftermath of Ultron’s schemes, it’s alarming that Vision isn’t more alarmed.

“Reboot” starts with Ultron watching another news report about the Butcherbird Killer, with clearer information: Someone’s murdering tech moguls and carving stylized wings around their bodies. Elsewhere, a man in a high-rise apartment panics over that news report, pulling out a 12-gauge shotgun. But someone shuts down his security system, and a robed, hooded figure with glowing red eyes similar to Vision’s emerges and stalks in, unfazed by his shotgun blasts.

On the road away from Saint Mabyn’s, Thomas tries to help Vision, who addresses a particularly bad wound, passes out, wakes up, malfunctions, then mostly seems fine. The two check in at a hotel together, hiding from Paladin’s pursuit, but Vision breaks down again and needs Thomas to restart him.

This all plays out with a lot of frequent jarring tonal mismatches, and some bafflingly overwrought dramatic beats, especially around Vision’s makeshift self-repair. It’s not enough for him to be badly damaged: His AI crew says he’ll die if he doesn’t seal the wound within 183 seconds, and he cauterizes it with battery acid with just 20 seconds to spare. Then the Greatest American Hero theme kicks in, turning his last-second survival into a gag. Similarly, at the hotel, Vision and Thomas are joking about humans and poop when Vision glitches, then abruptly says, “I only have minutes of life remaining.” That’s ridiculously melodramatic already, but to compound the drama, he says if he dies, he’ll explode, vaporizing Thomas and a lot of London. These rushed, outsize threats are so over-the-top, they feel like jokes, especially as they’re sprinkled between actual jokes.

The sidebars with the rest of Vision’s AI peanut gallery are similarly all over the place tonally. Friday, Edith, and the maintenance bots are sometimes goofy comic-relief clowns. But “Reboot” also gives them each a central, personal moment, which feels like loose puzzle pieces randomly crammed into the big picture. Edith’s musing on death and Friday’s monologue about failing Tony Stark have obvious resonances with Vision’s struggles for survival and hint at how they’ll react as the stakes continue to rise. But they feel like clunky foreshadowing — especially when Friday reveals, as a complete non sequitur, that she, Edith, and Jarvis were all based on real people Tony Stark knew. Friday seems to think it proves Edith meaningfully understands death, but it really doesn’t. What it does do is raise the question of whose human DNA Ultron is carrying.

The bots hold a funeral for Jarvis, where DUM-E speaks for the first time, quoting Keats’s poem “On Death,” and U sings “Danny Boy.” Vision and Ultron argue about love, death, and grief. This is sweet, but it interrupts the episode’s flow significantly: All this mindscape stuff takes up no real-world time for Vision, who can instantly run a quintillion theoreticals right before a conversation. But it takes up our time.

“Reboot” can’t find a consistent tone for Thomas and Vision’s evolving relationship, either. Thomas keeps trying to discuss their shared illusory history, but Vision is distracted by everything from Paladin’s pursuit to Thomas not using turn signals. Vision is dodging any discussion of Westview and Tommy Maximoff, though, because he doesn’t know how to comfort Thomas. When he does finally try, the emotional stakes seem high, until it turns out he’s just running one of many simulations of how that talk might fail. In his sims, Thomas is fragile and high-strung — but that’s because we’re watching Vision play out his anxieties about being awkward with people and bad at emotions. Ultimately, Vision punts and suggests recuperating before any conversation.

This episode creates some intriguing parallels. While Vision patches himself up from the Paladin fight and suffers through Ultron’s barbs, Paladin patches his own wounds and takes similar guff from his handler. Paladin even has his own AI crew: the drones Bing, Bang, and Boom, which he sends to track Vision’s coolant leak. Paladin thematically syncs up with Thomas as well: Both men have trauma flashbacks back-to-back, with Thomas reliving his drowning, and Paladin reliving a bloody moment from childhood. The creators seem to be telling us Paladin has more in common with the protagonists than with his mysterious client, who calls him yet again for some completely redundant threats.

Vision’s simulated conversations may not give Thomas enough credit, but the kid is frustrated enough to freak out over a malfunctioning vending machine, which, like Vision, is broken and isn’t helpfully dispensing what Thomas wants. The freakout is a reminder that he doesn’t have conscious control of his powers: He winds up with one hand phased into the machine. That brief crisis leads Thomas to tell Vision (and us) how he ended up in jail: In the pool accident where he drowned, his speed powers activated and the pool water boiled around him. He was blamed for the other poolgoers’ injuries.

Meanwhile, Paladin accidentally tracks down the Butcherbird Killer, a female synthezoid who’s leaking coolant just like Vision. Paladin reaches the high-rise apartment from the episode’s opening and finds the shotgun-wielding man dead, with wings carved into the floor below him and one of his eyes ripped out. Butcherbird, who’s still there, attacks Paladin with Vision-like powers, entering his mind and revealing the traumatic past we saw flashes of earlier. A previous Paladin killed this Paladin’s abusive father, then raised our Paladin as his successor. With the job came a code: “My contract is my oath, my blood, my life.”

Butcherbird says that means our guy isn’t a true Paladin, because he isn’t part of the bloodline. “All you’ve ever wanted is to feel real,” she says, further connecting Paladin and Vision. (And Pinocchio, whom Ultron keeps evoking with his “strings” references.) Paladin escapes by setting his drones on Butcherbird. Before long, though, his client calls to fire him for failing to capture Vision. That’s a big problem, since we’ve just learned Paladin considers a contract an unbreakable vow, and keeping that vow makes him feel “real.”

Back at the hotel, Vision boots up his head-laser when Paladin’s drone approaches. Before the drone notices him, Paladin recalls it to help fight Butcherbird, but the damage is done. Vision has overclocked his failing systems and needs to shut down. Then he needs Thomas to overcome his trauma, master his powers, and reboot Vision with a power surge. Thomas is anxious, but with death looming, Vision finally nails the conversation he’s been practicing by investing it with real emotion, conviction, and support. He confirms that Tommy Maximoff and Thomas are both real and puts himself in their hands. Vision’s life flashes before his eyes within his mind-mansion’s screening room, but Ultron redirects him toward WandaVision footage of Billy and Tommy to make Vision want to survive. Ultron may be a genocidal villain, but he does have a heart! Or maybe, in spite of urging Vision to delete him in episode one, Ultron is having second thoughts after this episode’s many death discussions.

Thomas shocks Vision back to life, but this somehow alerts Butcherbird; Vision’s mindscape fills with oppressive red lighting, ominously circling birds, and TVs crackling with static. Vision, eyes glowing red, floats in midair in the classic “demonic possession victim” pose as Butcherbird psychically invades him. Clearly, if neither Ultron nor Paladin are going to be this series’ Big Bad — if they’re both headed toward reconciliation with the heroes — someone else has to be the real threat, and it seems like she’s finally arrived.

• This episode has more MCU fan-bait allusions than past installments: Paladin got his adamantium armor from the Ten Rings Syndicate, once confronted a thing “halfway between a man and a wolf” who was a “perfectly reasonable fellow by day” (a Werewolf by Night gag), and got a concussion from a billy club to the noggin in Hell’s Kitchen (Daredevil’s turf and chosen weapon).

• I know Vision’s summary of WandaVision’s finale is meant to be a little off because all his simulations are, but “she realized what she was doing was morally abhorrent, so she collapsed the hex” is a phenomenally generous read on how that show ended.

• Where are we on theorizing about Paladin’s mysterious, impatient, all-knowing client, who clearly isn’t Butcherbird? Tyler Hayward still seems possible, but surely there’s a more interesting option.
• Fun little note on DUM-E’s Keats poem: The line right after the couplet he recites is “the transient pleasures as a vision seem.” Maybe quoting that would have felt a little too on the nose?

items.title: The Real Housewives of New York City Recap: Roach Motel
items.description: It’s another morning on Moskito Island, and Daisy Toye wakes up to find Sabrina, the dutiful housekeeper, awake to make her coffee so that she doesn’t have the mental strain of trying to figure out where to put a K-Cup first thing in the morning on a private i
items.author: Brian Moylan
paragraphs: It’s another morning on Moskito Island, and Daisy Toye wakes up to find Sabrina, the dutiful housekeeper, awake to make her coffee so that she doesn’t have the mental strain of trying to figure out where to put a K-Cup first thing in the morning on a private island. She’s going to need all of the caffeine she can get, though, because she’s in her room playing “La Cucaracha” so loud that the Mexican Embassy calls and convicts her of a hate crime. Yes, there was a roach in Daisy’s room, to which I say, so the fuck what? You are on a remote island in the Caribbean. You think there aren’t going to be bugs? This is basically the jungle. She’s lucky that some spider didn’t crawl down from the ceiling and lay eggs in her eyebrows while she was sleeping. Don’t ever let Daisy go to Australia, where there are bats in the middle of the city. I mean, what is one bug? Didn’t she grow up in the city? She probably had a teenage rat as a classmate at P.S. 20, and she’s worried about one little roach?

When the ladies gather in the morning after a night of arguing and dancing wearing knock-off Elton John sunglasses, they all have concerns. Erika is concerned that Daisy won’t stop complaining about her free vacation. Carole is concerned that Sai brought up the Epstein files. Erin is concerned about the spectacle that happened at dinner the night before. No, not Erika getting her rented J.Lo knockoff dress caught on a cactus and nearly dying of outdated fashion references. She’s mad about the fight between her, Sai, and Jessel.

When Erin arrives at dinner with a hot-pink bandana wrapped around her trunk like a go-go boy would tie it around one leg to cover his junk (if you ever went to the Urge in the aughts, you know what I mean), she is upset that Sai may have told Jessel about a rumor she repeated about Pavit three years ago. Erin asks Sai what the rumor is, but Sai says she won’t repeat it because it’s so “despicable.” Um, didn’t she already tell Jessel and, by extension, us, so she might as well just say it? The two call each other despicable a few times like they’re in a Daffy Duck lisp-alike contest, and then Erin says she doesn’t want to talk about it with them, even though she is the one who started this conversation in the first place.

The best part about this fight, however, is that we learn that everyone has already heard the rumor about Pavit being gay, including Carole, who just joined the reboot this year. She says she heard it from Mason, her shopper at the RealReal store. Yes, that same Mason from the premiere who Ge-Z stared Daisy into giving up a leather trench coat. Wait. Why is Mason not a friend of? Wait. Why is there not a show about the staff of the RealReal store in Manhattan? Should Ava Dash get a job there next season of Next Gen NYC now that her father is bankrupt?

Erin is upset that Sai brought up this rumor because she says she told Sai in confidence. I’m sorry, but that is not how rumors or being told something in confidence works. Now, if Erin were to tell Sai something about her own life that she did not want shared, say, a cancer diagnosis, and then Sai went and shared that with other people, then Erin could rightfully be pissed. (We had this exact thing play out between Guerdy Abraira and Larsa Pippen on The Real Housewives of Miami.) However, a rumor isn’t something you can tell in confidence because it has nothing to do with Erin’s life and, by the very nature of a rumor, is already out there. A rumor is the mortal enemy of confidence. A rumor would tiptoe into confidence’s room at night and murder its teddy bear. That is just how rumors work, and Erin can’t have the protection of confidence when this story already has less confidence than a five-foot-three man on a first date.

But it’s the morning, and we’re not talking about this fight except that we totally are. Well, not Hailey. She’s worried that someone is drinking out of the cup she peed in while trying not to disturb Sai in the middle of the night by using the bathroom in her room. Sai was more disturbed by her conversation with Carole about the Epstein files, and while the two sit on the beach together, they rehash that conversation. Carole says that she thought that Sai’s questions were kind of “shitty” and that she felt like she was being accused of something she didn’t do. Sai relents and admits that she judged Carole for her relationship with Ghislaine Maxwell before she knew any of the particulars from Carole.

What’s funny is that Carole asks Sai about her relationship to this guy, Daddy Warbucks, that she wrote about on her Substack. They were close enough that he paid her $10,000 to hang out with her and offered to buy her a house. When Carole asks what happened to the guy, Sai says that he was wrapped up in a Ponzi scheme and she had no idea, which just proves that you never know what people are up to. Exactly! That was exactly Carole’s point! No matter how well you know someone, they’re not going to put their worst behavior front and center. Well. I would. Just buy one cup of coffee (I don’t drink coffee) and I’ll tell you about every VIP section I’ve broken into, every person I’ve talked shit about, and how much I hate almost all of Erika’s wardrobe, including the giant seashell earrings that look like she got them for 80 percent off at the worst store in Palm Beach.

For lunch, Erika takes them to a beach that Daisy finally likes. Everyone is so shocked they pass out in the sand and wait for the tides to drag their lifeless bodies over to Dickie Branson’s island to ruin his shores for a change. Carole tells a crazy story about a watch she owned that ended up cursing Kim Kardashian. She told a much better version of this tale on The Moth and wrote about it on her Substack. The real victim at lunch, however, is Hailey Glassman, the vaping queen of Hell’s Kitchen. Everyone wants to know where her money comes from and, honestly, same. I like Hailey. She seems like a blast and, like Sting once said, every little thing she does is magic. Other than her association with Jon Gosselin and her narcissistic mother, we know nothing about her. This seems like a very good place to start.

Hailey says she thinks it’s gross to talk about money and she’s kind of right, but I will talk about money as quickly and as often as gay fitness influencers talk about Bulgarian split squats. No one is asking how much she has in her bank account. (Well, maybe Erin is because she might need help buying all new furniture for the Hamptons house.) They just want to know something about her. They ask if she has a trust fund; they ask how rich her parents are; they ask if they’re helping out; Hailey doesn’t really answer anything. They ask about her husband’s business, and she says he owns Vineyard Time, a fancy watch store in Martha’s Vineyard. Okay, that sounds nice, but not two houses in Manhattan, owning an Audi, and not thinking Gucci is expensive nice. They ask what she does for a living. She says she’s a publicist, but she can’t even say how many clients she has? And if she were even a medium-size publicist, wouldn’t Jessel, who is a legit fashion publicist, know some of the same people and could vouch for her? I know Hailey has been burned in the public eye before, but she has to give the audience something, and she really needs to give these women something if she wants to maintain relationships with them.

At dinner, everyone is in a gown except for Carole, who is wearing a vintage T-shirt and a pair of jeans. Carole is right that this is what you should wear for a low-key dinner at a friend’s house on a private island. You want to be comfortable, and who is going to see you, right? Well, except for the cameras and all of us at home and Dickie B across the bay staring into their windows with his high-powered telescope. (Just kidding. Kate Winslet destroyed his last high-powered telescope on her last visit.) It’s funny that Carole doesn’t know this. I don’t remember her dressing like someone’s hippie grandmother the last time she was on the show. Didn’t she turn looks when chilling at Blue Stone Manor? How is this so much different?

Finally, Daisy gives a toast to this beautiful island, this beautiful trip, and how nice the accommodations are, except for their Pier One furniture. This woman can’t help herself, can she? I think she’s just a complainer. I think that Daisy is just never happy with what is in front of her, whether that is a private island, her husband, or all the nude lipsticks in the world, so she needs to blend 16 of them together to get the perfect shade for Martha. Oh, Martha Stewart. Have you heard of her? She’s Daisy’s client, and she would think this place is a dump. Erika responds by showing us her hidden talent, which is being able to burp whole words and phrases, and that made me love Erika so much more. She’s a little staid, but she’s a good time and seems to stay true to her roots, whether that is body-based humor or thinking that Gucci is expensive when she could have the whole collection each year delivered to her doorstep. (I love Erika’s excess frugality and I wouldn’t change it, but her complete lack of style is a problem she can easily buy her way out of. She should just hire a stylist and let them rent the clothes for her.)

Erin takes Sai out by the firepit for a dramatically lit discussion that would make Ariana Madix proud but also a little sad that no one got dumped from the island this evening. As much as I hate to agree with Sai, in this conversation she has Erin “Mew Mew” Lichy pegged like Pavit in the Equinox stream room. Sai says that Erin talks shit about everyone. We know this is true because we have eyes, and we also saw her tell everyone on Ultimate Girls Trip about how much she hates Jessel. Erin says that they all talk about each other, and she’s right. Erin’s problem is that when it happens, she denies it, pretends she’s better than doing that, and turns herself into the victim. If she just took a dose of Lisa Rinna’s brand of Own It! chewable vitamins, I don’t think Erin would have a problem. Sai says that it was one thing for Erin to repeat the rumor about Pavit, but when she did it in front of Sai’s makeup dude, she knew that Erin wasn’t discreet and would do it to her one day. And she’s right. The only reason I can handle Sai being right is that it means Erin is wrong.

Trying to exonerate herself, Erin lays out this confusing defense about how her makeup guy heard about Sai’s divorce at a beauty event. Is he the one who supposedly told Jenna about Sai’s divorce? Erin seems to think she’s innocent, but she’s not addressing the real crime, which isn’t telling Jenna, since Jenna said she found out indirectly through Erin. Even if Erin is innocent of this crime specifically, she is definitely guilty of the larger pattern in a way that Sai would, of course, believe that Erin was talking about her because she does it about everyone else. But as the shadows flicker over her face, as the breeze blows the embers into the wind like tiny critters about to be extinguished by the heel of Daisy’s boot, Erin still can’t see through the darkness, and she wants to howl at a moon that may not exist, but she knows, for sure, is out there somewhere.

items.title: James Bond Screen Tests to Happen This Weekend: Finalists Emerge for Next 007 Movie
items.description: Tomorrow never dies. But for all actors except one, the dream of being the next James Bond will likely die this week.
items.author: Borys Kit
paragraphs: Tomorrow never dies. But for all actors except one, the dream of being the next James Bond will likely die this week.
And that is due to — finally! — a very select group of actors getting in front of cameras to screen test for the role of British agent 007.

According to several sources, Callum Turner, who recently starred in the rom-com One Night Only, and Slow Horses actor Jack Lowden are said to be in the mix for the screen tests, which are taking place in London this weekend. They could begin as early as Friday, according to two sources.

It is unclear who else may be testing. Sources said at least three actors are part of the action but another source says up to five may be putting on the tux to see how it fits. Jack O’Connell (Sinners) was rumored to initially be in the mix, but that is apparently not the case, according to sources. And despite some reports, Euphoria and Frankenstein star Jacob Elordi is not testing.

Amazon had no comment and pointed to its previous statement, which said, “The search for the next James Bond is underway. While we don’t plan to comment on specific details during the casting process, we’re excited to share more news with 007 fans as soon as the time is right.”
The time looks to be nigh.
It is also unclear how involved these tests are, but they are understood to be comprehensive. Sources say there will be three components — stunts, camera presence and dialogue.

Twenty years ago, the tests for Bond included full hair and makeup and a full camera and sound crew on a set. Henry Cavill was among those vying for the role, but Daniel Craig emerged victorious, playing the role from from 2006’s Casino Royale until 2021’s No Time to Die.

Dune filmmaker Denis Villeneuve is directing the new Bond outing, with Amy Pascal and David Heyman producing and overseeing the franchise for Amazon MGM Studios, which bought out the creative rights from the Broccoli family in February 2025.

items.title: Elon Musk’s Stake in Skydance Could Transform Media As We Know It
items.description: In case the current media year couldn’t get any weirder, along comes Elon Musk to ask us to hold his Diet Coke.
items.author: Steven Zeitchik
paragraphs: In case the current media year couldn’t get any weirder, along comes Elon Musk to ask us to hold his Diet Coke.

With the biggest investigative takedown of him ever produced already playing in theaters, we now have the news that Musk is writing big checks to Skydance coming down and landing with a thud. Or is it a Mars-level explosion?

On Thursday came word that Elon would make a (start with?) $1 billion investment in the David Ellison company, according to a Semafor report. This comes after comments Wednesday from John Malone, who suggested (tipped?) that Musk was about to put even more money in via a SpaceX-centric deal with the Ellisons. “I think there’s a deal coming there,” the Liberty Media kingpin told a Paley Center summit earlier this week. “I would not doubt for a minute that before very long you’re going to see an announcement.” Malone was short on specifics but long on dollar amounts: Musk’s buy-in would run between $8-$10 billion. The $1 billion could be just a start.

A lot of the focus here has been on the Ellisons’ need for the money. David and his father Larry, who bankrolled much of the Warner Bros. acquisition, are in the hole for $79 billion, and you can only cut that much staff to make up the difference. A cool $10 bil from Elon, even if not all of it is in cash, takes the bankers’ pressure off you. A chill $1b already helps.

But the Ellisons’ financial breathing room (we should all feel such asphyxia) comes in a distant second, consequence-wise, to what such an investment would create: a backdoor for Musk to enter the media-entertainment world.

Owning a piece of Paramount-Warner Bros. (depending on the valuation the $10b could net as much as 15%) would give him a place at the table on the company’s biggest decisions. Even if it doesn’t come with a board seat (that depends on how many voting shares he’d get) it would certainly buy a channel into David Ellison. Musk already has this via Larry, a close business associate who bankrolled the Twitter buy, but writing an eleven-figure check has a funny way of prying open the canal further. And it would give Musk a content pipeline at X, a badly coveted resource. The mogul has tried to make such a push before, with original shows from Don Lemon, Tulsi Gabbard and Jim Rome as part of a Range Media Partners deal, and a plan for WWE mini-episodes.
But this changes the game for X and Musk much more dramatically. Access to Skydance content makes him more than just a dilettante in the content world — it makes him a streamer.

Episodes of Yellowstone, The Last of Us, NCIS, Game of Thrones — never mind plenty of live sports on Turner and CBS — would now all potentially live on X, on a paid or other kind of tier. And X would be strengthened by Skydance’s ad-sales team, providing an even further boost.

Don’t sleep on a key person who could make this all happen, by the way — Ari Emanuel. He’s close with Musk, close with the Ellisons and the kind of kingmaker who revels in bringing these worlds together (not least because it pushes his wallet folds further apart.)

The investment would officially come via SpaceX, but of course many of the biggest Musk properties are already under the company, including X, xAI and Starlink. And he’s re-started talk recently of his long-held fantasy to merge Tesla with it too. So make no mistake: a SpaceX entry into Skydance is a Musk entry into Hollywood.

So, yeah, if you were worried what it meant that Ellison was combining two legacy studios into one, imagine when 15 percent of the resultant company is owned by the world’s richest man. Who also is the biggest donor to Republican and Trump candidates (by a wide margin). Who The Wall Street Journal reports ordered Starshield slowed down, marooning Ukraine. As the Jon Spencer Blues Explosion once said, now I got worry.

And there’s another domino to fall: Starlink. The company that already provides Internet service to about five million Americans and many more people overseas could get a lot bigger and more central to our communication. SpaceX has been buying up spectrum in the past week in a bid for Starlink to compete directly with the major mobile carriers AT&T, Verizon and T-Mobile. This has been a huge priority for the company. Last year it inked $19 billion worth of deals with Dish TV owner Charlie Ergen that also included spectrum licenses. Snapping up one of those Big Three telcom companies wouldn’t be out of the question either.

If Musk both had a minority stake in two of the biggest studios and was also one of the biggest Internet providers around, he would achieve the kind of pipes-content verticality that no company has ever held in American media and communication, let alone a single person at the head of that company. (Musk holds about 85 percent of the voting shares in SpaceX.) Controlling a stake in HBO and CNN along with the ways we watch it — what could go wrong?

Plenty, of course, starting with the fact that some of the most well-platformed Musk critics, from John Oliver to Jake Tapper, would now be under the thumb of Musk. And he seems like a guy who takes criticism well. Those personalities and others at the old WBD are also among the biggest critics of MAGA and the Republicans — ie, the people Musk is currently shelling out nearly $300 million to keep in power.
Oh, and did I mention that HBO next year is slated to air Alex Gibney’s Musk takedown? I’m sure that’s something he’s eager to put on the air.

Gibney’s film etches a picture of an Elon intent on taking over the world. With the final credits barely up, Musk is acting out exactly that blueprint. For a guy who thinks he’s been the victim of a hit piece, he’s sure doing a lot to make Gibney look like a prophet.
There are only two things that could reasonably stop this rolling snowball of influence. The first is regulators. Except, well…
And, Trump aside, the FCC is chaired by Brendan Carr, one of the biggest Musk fanboys around. Asking him to stop Musk is like asking Kevin Feige to promote Superman.

Hope would lie with a change at the White House in 2028 — there was already plenty of regulatory heat on Musk under Joe Biden, one reason Musk went all in on Trump in the first place. Of course two years is an eternity in mogul-time, and even if the Democrats retake the White House in 2028, Musk may simply be too strong to regulate.

The second hope lies with Wall Street. Musk’s money and influence are pretty much all conferred on him by investors; if the Tesla and SpaceX stock prices drop far enough, his buying (and borrowing) power suddenly shrink. But I wouldn’t hold my breath. Investors love when Musk expands and wheels and deals — see how the SpaceX stock jumped by double digits Wednesday in part due to the Tesla merger buzz. The Skydance and Starlink investments will only send valuations further into outerspace. Of course the entire tech-stock and AI bubble could collapse, bringing Elon’s wealth and power down with it. But given the recession and portfolio-ruination that would cause, I don’t think we want to root for that either.
In Gibney’s film, Musk’s father Errol says with a knowing chuckle that anyone underestimating his son soon learns their lesson — he always, always wins.

The media was fooled once on Twitter — no way he would buy it, we all said back in 2022 — then quickly found ourselves without a place to park such trenchant commentary. Getting fooled twice would just be shameful.

items.title: ‘Newlyweds’ Review: Téa Leoni and Tim Daly in an Innocuously Bland NBC Sitcom That’s Straight Out of the Late ’90s
items.description: Although it’s premiering as part of NBC’s fall lineup for the 2026-27 season, the network’s new sitcom Newlyweds would have been a perfect midseason replacement to occupy the 9:30 Must See TV slot in the late ’90s, an innocuous fill-in instead of reruns of Win
items.author: Daniel Fienberg
paragraphs: Although it’s premiering as part of NBC’s fall lineup for the 2026-27 season, the network’s new sitcom Newlyweds would have been a perfect midseason replacement to occupy the 9:30 Must See TV slot in the late ’90s, an innocuous fill-in instead of reruns of Wings or The Naked Truth.

Note: If some parts of that sentence — “midseason,” “Wings,” “The Naked Truth,” “NBC” — were foreign to you, you probably are not the target audience for Newlyweds, a resolutely old-fashioned comedy that harkens back to the days when comedies were comedies and you knew they were comedies because the studio audience told you when to roar with laughter.
Cast: Téa Leoni, Tim Daly, Jamie Lee Curtis, Emma Meisel, Ignacio Diaz-Silverio, Bill O’Neill and Al Madrigal
Creators: Jamie Lee Curtis and Gail Lerner

Those were the days! Yes, that’s another gatekeeping reference aimed to differentiate between the target audience for Newlyweds and a hip, modern audience that thinks a “comedy” is a show that makes you squirm with discomfort or invest deeply in whether or not a fine dining restaurant secures a Michelin star.

At its absolute best, Newlyweds is low-impact comfort food, a wholly forgettable but generally inoffensive opportunity to watch real-life spouses Tea Leoni and Tim Daly being sweet and horny together, and an agreeable enough show for viewers who think better NBC comedies like St. Denis Medical and The Fall and Rise of Reggie Dinkins are too edgy. Those people deserve sitcoms, too.

Co-created by Gail Lerner, who recently was fired from the series due to “creative differences” — “creative” not being a word that will be used again in this review — Newlyweds focuses on Jeanie (Leoni) and James (Daly), who go out on a blind date and decide that life is too short for an elaborate courtship. So they get married almost immediately and build a relationship from there.
She’s a middle school teacher and widow with a daughter (Emma Meisel’s Poppy) and adopted son (Ignacio Diaz-Silverio’s Lolo).
He’s a philosophy professor with a ubiquitous ex-wife (co-creator Jamie Lee Curtis‘ Claudia) and a book he’ll never finish.

She’s a little bit free-spirited, though that’s not exactly how she’s been written, nor is it how Leoni is playing the part. He’s a little bit anxious and buttoned-up, though that’s not exactly how he’s been written, nor is it how Daly is playing the part. Let’s just say they’re slightly different kinds of people.
Will they be able to make this conventionally unconventional relationship work?
It’s a question the show doesn’t really want viewers investing in. It’s possible that Newlyweds has the lowest stakes of any TV show I’ve ever watched, which is absolutely a feature and not a bug.

These are two characters who are nearing retirement age with approximately zero anxiety. Once they decide to get together, their biggest source of adversity, through the three episodes sent to critics, is whether they’ll live in his extremely nice home or hers, which isn’t as nice because it doesn’t have a pool house. Oh, and there’s also some dispute over whether they’ll be able to have their dream honeymoon in Paris, Budapest and Tokyo, not because of financial difficulties but because they get married in the middle of the school year and she doesn’t want to wait.

I’m assuming future episodes will explain how a philosophy professor with an ex-wife whose job either isn’t mentioned or isn’t relevant is able to afford both a relative mansion and the beach house where Claudia lives.
I’m assuming future episodes will let her briefly express sadness about the death of her husband and will let him explain why he describes Claudia as “terrifying” when she seems, at worst, nosy.

The most emotion that anybody in the series expresses is Poppy, whose tear-filled reaction to a break-up with a boyfriend who wasn’t mentioned a single time before or after the split is played for laughs and — all credit to Meisel — actually gets a chuckle or two.

The point, though, is that Newlyweds is a wholly friction-free show by design — so frictionless that in order to add a jolt of comic irritation, Claudia is constantly around and, because that isn’t enough, the show has to introduce an Arvid (Bill O’Neill). What’s an Arvid? He’s a Norwegian teaching assistant assigned to James during the latter’s one-month teaching position in Oslo in the pilot. Then he decides to move to Los Angeles to work with James in the States. Work on what? Who cares? The only things that matter are that Arvid falls down a lot, speaks with a funny accent and comes equipped with the largest repertoire of Scandinavian quirks since Rose Nylund regaled her best friends with stories of life in St. Olaf.

The studio audience for Newlyweds loves Arvid and laughs at his pratfalls, his herring and the fact that his nickname is “Milky” because he’s pale — which, to me, read as more observationally accurate than amusing, but the studio audience disagreed.
The studio audience loves Arvid. They love Newlyweds and respond to every beat.

How, for example, would anybody know that Curtis was an Emmy- and Oscar-winning national treasure if the audience didn’t applaud her first appearance in every episode? (Pity poor Daly and Leoni, stars of hundreds of episodes of well-regarded television, but not worthy of scene-entering applause.)
And how, for example, would anybody know that it’s sweet that Jeanie and James are affectionate if the audience didn’t hoot whenever they kiss?
Newlyweds doesn’t need to be self-congratulatory about how retro its charms are. The audience offers that approval regularly.

It’s worth acknowledging that Newlyweds plays everything conspicuously down-the-middle, but it could be far, far worse. Yes, the show steers into a large number of sitcom tropes, from the wicked ex-wife to the wacky friends (Arvid is joined by Al Madrigal as Dan, who set Jeanie and James up on their date but seems to have no part of his own) to the predictability of ever-short-lived spousal disconnect. But there are countless hacky avenues that haven’t been tapped. Yet. The kids are Gen Z, but nobody has mentioned their pronouns or, really, any of the things lazy sitcom writers tend to ascribe to young people. The main couple is old, but somehow nobody has made a Viagra joke yet.

This is, for now, a show that coasts and, from the beginning, coasts with an easy confidence. Multicam directing icon Pamela Fryman (How I Met Your Mother) sets that tone early in a pilot that races through a lot of exposition without feeling as cumbersome and stultifying as an all-exposition comedy pilot like that of CBS’ vampire comedy, Eternally Yours.

Leoni and Daly have solid comic chemistry, but none of the occasional heat they brought to Madam Secretary. The writing is probably the biggest problem there; so far much effort has been put into having James and Jeanie frequently repeat the ways their characters are different — she’s a butterfly, he’s a gopher and you’ll learn what that means in the first 10 minutes of the pilot or you probably won’t care — and then talking about the sex they’re having, which is all you can do in primetime on NBC. Parents should have no concerns about watching Newlyweds with their children, who won’t stick around long enough for the first coupling anyway.

While Leoni and Daly are the stars here, most of my scattered laughs came from the young actors, all really good. Diaz-Silverio, who generally had to be the straight man in Freevee’s short-lived and vastly superior Primo, is able to land several likable punchlines despite playing a character who has been described — he was Jeanie’s student and he was in the foster care system and she adopted him — but not developed. Meisel, whom I actually remember fondly from a supporting role on Disney’s Doogie Kameāloha, M.D., gets chuckles despite, again, playing a character with no demonstrable written personality. And if Diaz-Silverio and Meisel are given little to do, it’s only because O’Neill’s Arvid has been given all of the show’s comedic business, which he plays with creepy enthusiasm.

Curtis gives the impression that she’s just happy to be as adored as she is by the crowd and she plays to them exclusively — whether Claudia is boasting about her breasts, tormenting Jeanie, whom she confuses with James’ maid, or even speaking Norwegian just for kicks.

Television doesn’t lack for comedies that deliver biting satire and cogent commentary — that are, in fact, so committed to commentary that nobody bothers to even include jokes. Newlyweds has no bite and its fingers are nowhere near a cultural pulse, but it’s bright and broad and lets you pretend that it’s 1998 again.

items.title: How to See the Orionid Meteor Shower and Other Upcoming Astronomical Events
items.description: Halley’s COmet won’t be visible from Earth for another few decades but you can see fragments of it streak across the sky this month in the Orionid meteor shower. The event began earlier this month but will reach its peak on October 21 and 22. Here’s how to vie
items.author: Ritsuko Kawai
paragraphs: Halley’s COmet won’t be visible from Earth for another few decades but you can see fragments of it streak across the sky this month in the Orionid meteor shower. The event began earlier this month but will reach its peak on October 21 and 22. Here’s how to view these shooting stars and other upcoming astronomical phenomena.

The Orionid meteor shower will be ongoing until November 7, but in the US, the best time for viewing is between dusk on October 21 and dawn on October 22. During this time, you may see up to 20 meteors per hour. That’s in dark skies. The moon will be approximately three-quarters full at this time, which may obscure some of the shooting stars. The best time for viewing is therefore in the early morning between when the moon sets and the sun rises for peak darkness.

However, these particular meteors are known for their brightness as well as their speed, and in some cases especially fast meteors can turn into “fireballs,” becoming as bright as the planet Venus. Dark conditions, however, will be best for viewing some other phenomena associated with this event, such as glowing trains of debris Orionid meteors have been known to sometimes leave in their wake.

The shower gets its name from the constellation Orion, as this is the shower’s “radiant,” the source a large portion of the meteors appear to come from. However, you don’t need to find Orion to enjoy the show. The best viewing is, in fact, often away from the constellation, and meteors should be visible from any part of the night sky.
Other Astronomical Highlights in October

Earlier this month, Saturn reached opposition, meaning the Earth passed between the sun and Saturn. Since the gas giant rises in the eastern sky around sunset and reaches its meridian around midnight, it can be observed almost all night long. On October 24, the moon will also come close to Saturn.

Not only does this present prime viewing for amateur astronomers, but it will provide researchers further opportunity to observe a bizarre geometric structure recorded in Saturn’s atmosphere—a decagon centered on the planet’s south pole. This recent discovery came nearly half a century after a similar 18,600-mile-wide hexagon had been discovered encircling Saturn’s north pole.

Scientists believe these phenomena have been caused by currents confining powerful atmospheric waves, and the wave in the southern hemisphere appears to be gaining momentum. Being at its closest point to Earth, opposition provides researchers with a valuable opportunity to observe the gas giant’s peculiar atmosphere.

At the end of the month, the moon will pass close by the Pleiades star cluster. The Pleiades have been the subject of stories in many ancient cultures, perhaps because these bright stars can be observed from almost anywhere in the world.

The best time for viewing the Pleiades in proximity to the moon is the evening of October 27 into the morning of October 28. Look toward the east and wait for the moment when the moon and the cluster rise high in the sky. With the naked eye, you may see what appears to be a faint cluster of six to seven stars. Since this occurs just after the full moon, the cluster may at first be difficult to see, but you’ll be able to observe it more clearly with binoculars or a telescope.

items.title: We can do impossible things
items.description: I’d wager everyone has a rehearsed response to what’s absolutely one of the world’s worst interview questions: “What’s your biggest weakness?” Whenever I’ve gotten it, I take a slow—even pensive—breath and rattle off my line: “I say no to myself too much.”
items.author: Corinne Iozzio
paragraphs: I’d wager everyone has a rehearsed response to what’s absolutely one of the world’s worst interview questions: “What’s your biggest weakness?” Whenever I’ve gotten it, I take a slow—even pensive—breath and rattle off my line: “I say no to myself too much.”

I won’t lie. It’s a bit shameless—a definite humblebrag. I’m a systems thinker: When an idea pops up, I immediately spin up a feasibility assessment in my head. I run lists, plot timelines, and tally budget line items. Sometimes a rough Gantt chart starts to take shape. (I’m a gas at parties, as you can surely tell.)

My brain, throughout my 20-plus-year career as a science and tech journalist, has played host to a near constant tug-of-war between ambition and reality. Learning to find that balance is a big part of what’s helped me survive in this industry and, ultimately, led me here. This past spring, I had the great privilege of joining the incredible team of journalists behind MIT Technology Review to take the reins of the print magazine.

If you’ve been reading along with us for the last handful of issues, you may have noticed a few changes starting to materialize. We’ve brought back a regular roster of lists and infographics (both things that magazines do particularly well). But the biggest change is only just beginning to take shape, which is why Mat Honan, our editor in chief, asked me to hop in to introduce myself—and the issue you’re holding in your hands right now.
We’re giving ourselves permission to play around and experiment. To be a little … audacious.

Because, practical though I may be, I do still have plenty of ideas. It’s just that I sometimes need a reminder to stop blocking myself and do the thing. That’s the spirit driving this issue in particular.

We wanted to end 2026 with a slate of stories that check in on impossible ideas. Why? Because it’s frankly a lot of fun to dream about living on the moon or uploading our brains. Because losing sight of ambition is all too easy when it feels as if we’re playing whack-a-mole with the world’s problems. But also because the scientists and engineers who absolutely refuse to give up on even the most daring endeavors—like making synthetic blood or decoding animals’ speech—remind us what this whole technology thing is supposed to do to begin with.

It’s supposed to take cutting-edge research and development and apply it to make life better, safer, healthier, even more joyful. And when we eff up and make things worse (see: forever chemicals, traffic deaths, and AI that encourages potentially dangerous user behavior), we’re supposed to dig back in, assess the damage, and find ways to fix what we’ve broken. Even when unraveling the mess might itself seem impossible.

Right before I came to MIT Technology Review, I edited a newsletter about individual actions that can help address the climate crisis, which some would call—and have called—a fool’s errand, given the sheer scale of the problem. They might say it’s as implausible as an AI kill switch, practical nuclear fusion, or a superconductor that works at room temperature. But if I learned nothing else from three years spent finding ways for li’l old me (or li’l old you!) to chip away at one of humanity’s biggest existential threats, it’s that focusing on what we can’t do only makes the darkness darker.
So yeah, this one’s for the folks who have the audacity to try, and who refuse to let anyone—themselves included—tell them no.
I hope you enjoy the ride.

items.description: Just before the Artemis II crew began its historic slingshot around the moon this past April, NASA announced plans to build Space Reactor-1 Freedom. SR-1, the first-ever nuclear-reactor-powered interplanetary spacecraft, is meant to fly an uncrewed mission to
items.author: Robin George Andrews
paragraphs: Just before the Artemis II crew began its historic slingshot around the moon this past April, NASA announced plans to build Space Reactor-1 Freedom. SR-1, the first-ever nuclear-reactor-powered interplanetary spacecraft, is meant to fly an uncrewed mission to Mars by the end of 2028, arriving in 2029. A successful mission would herald a new era of more efficient, potentially faster spaceflight—saving astronauts time and cutting their exposure to harmful cosmic radiation as they travel to Mars and beyond. “You wake up to that announcement, and it puts a big smile on your face,” says Simon Middleburgh, co-director of the Nuclear Futures Institute at Bangor University in Wales.

Running a nuclear reactor in space may sound like lunacy, but it’s not. The Soviet Union sent dozens of reactors into orbit, often to power spy satellites. And experts say there aren’t any major technical obstacles to making nuclear space propulsion happen. “I think it’s a very doable technology,” says Philip Metzger, a spaceflight engineering researcher at the Florida Space Institute.“I’m happy to see them finally doing this.”

Still, developing space propulsion using reactors has been slow going. The US has started—and terminated—several programs looking into it over the past 75 years. The latest casualty was DRACO, a collaboration between NASA and the Department of Defense, which ended in 2025. The project was canceled because of high experimentation costs, an inability to compete with conventional rocket propulsion on price, and difficulty ensuring that ground tests could be performed safely and effectively. (You are creating an incredibly powerful nuclear reaction, after all.)

After much wavering, it now appears that nuclear-powered interplanetary travel is a $2 billion bet NASA is willing to make. The agency is pursuing an approach called nuclear electric propulsion, which uses the neutrons produced in a self-sustaining, uranium-atom-splitting reaction to create heat and ultimately electricity. The electricity is used to ionize a gas, which is blasted out of the spacecraft with the help of magnetic fields, generating thrust. The approach “is very low thrust, but very efficient,” says Sebastian Corbisiero, the US Department of Energy’s national technical director of space reactor programs. “So you can use it for a long period of time.”

What might such a rocket look like? A presentation by Steve Sinacore, program director of NASA’s SR-1 program, offers some clues. So far, the concept art makes the craft look like a colossal fletched arrow. The back will house the power-and-propulsion system, while the tip will hold a uranium-filled nuclear reactor with a capacity of at least 20 kilowatts. (For context, a typical nuclear plant on Earth is about 50,000 times more powerful.) The “fletches” on SR-1 are large fins that help cool the reactor by radiating heat into space.

Like many other pieces of space hardware, the reactor will need to be put through its paces on the ground before it’s cleared for the rough rocket trip to space. “Going through the launch safely is going to be a challenge,” says Middleburgh. “You are being shaken, rattled, and rolled.” For safety reasons, the reactor will be switched on around two days post-launch, when it’s comfortably far from Earth. Uranium isn’t tremendously dangerous by itself, but that can’t be said of the waste products that emerge when the reactor is running. If SR-1 works as planned, its journey to Mars will take about a year.

Will this novel form of space propulsion actually reach the Red Planet by 2029? It’s possible. NASA says the Idaho National Laboratory, which is building SR-1’s reactor, is making progress and is on target for a late-2028 launch. “Procurement of major components is underway, and integration work on the power and propulsion element is advancing steadily,” Sinacore told MIT Technology Review. The outlook will get even sunnier if the Artemis program, which aims to start laying the foundations for a base on the lunar south pole by the decade’s end, keeps to its own bold deadline.

“It’s an aggressive timeline,” says Lindsey Holmes, who is vice president of advanced projects at Analytical Mechanics Associates, an aerospace company in Virginia. She suspects the push is being driven partly by China’s and Russia’s own deep-space nuclear ambitions. The two countries have spoken about plans to place a reactor on the moon’s surface in the mid-2030s to power a jointly operated lunar base. Whether it flies or fails in space, SR-1’s development should help NASA put its own reactor on the moon; the technology involved in the two projects is broadly similar, given that the lunar surface, like space itself, is a vacuum. If an interplanetary nuclear-powered spacecraft works, a nuclear reactor on the moon should too.
Progress meter . . . . . . . . . . . . 6
Most of the technology for SR-1 already exists; it’s going to come down to piecing it all together and then seeing how it performs in space.

items.title: Exercise in a pill
items.description: We all know exercise is good for us. It builds muscle, strengthens bones, lowers blood pressure, and boosts mood. By deciphering how movement benefits the body, researchers hope to develop medicines that can offer some of the same perks—without the workout. Th
items.author: Cassandra Willyard
paragraphs: We all know exercise is good for us. It builds muscle, strengthens bones, lowers blood pressure, and boosts mood. By deciphering how movement benefits the body, researchers hope to develop medicines that can offer some of the same perks—without the workout. The idea isn’t to replace exercise but to bring its upsides to people who struggle with frailty, disability, or chronic illness.

It will take a lot of experimentation to untangle the myriad pathways by which exercise promotes health. But IDing the cascade of hormones, enzymes, and other molecules related to physical activity is just the first step. Scientists need to figure out how to turn that knowledge into safe and effective drugs. That’s a tall order: More than 90% of treatments that enter human studies fail.

There are regulatory hurdles too. The FDA approves medications to treat diseases, not to enhance wellness, says Thomas Burris, a pharmacologist at the University of Florida whose work focuses on diseases that respond to exercise, like obesity, type 2 diabetes, and dementia.

There may never be a pill that delivers all the benefits of exercise, but research could lead to new medicines that mimic some aspects of working out. Scientists have already identified many important exercise-related signals and have even developed compounds to regulate them. (Some preliminary results have been so promising that doping authorities have proactively banned the compounds.)

Burris and his colleagues are focused on a receptor that’s always switched on, even without exercise. Working out appears to boost that receptor in muscle cells, which in turn helps bolster endurance over time. Burris’s lab has spent years designing a drug that cranks up the receptor’s activity directly, and mice treated with the drug ran longer and farther than mice that weren’t. They “become marathon mice without having to do any type of exercise,” Burris says. There are even indications—also in mice—that the compound mimics some of the cognitive benefits of exercise and could help treat heart failure. Burris founded a company called Pelagos to carry the work forward into a clinical trial.

Other workout-mimicking drugs have already entered human studies. In June, the biotech firm Cambrian Bio reported that its experimental drug ATX-304 boosted metabolism and reduced liver and belly fat in people with obesity and prediabetes. It activates a metabolic switch that helps cells sense when energy supplies dip and coordinates the production of more fuel—the same switch that helps us sustain long sessions jumping rope or swimming laps. Cambrian hopes it will help people lose weight without losing muscle, a common concern with GLP-1 medicines.
Progress meter ............ 5
Our understanding of how exercise benefits the body is still coming into focus, and drug development is prone to failure.

items.title: Cleaning up PFAS
items.description: Scrubbing Earth of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances—a.k.a. PFAS or forever chemicals—could eliminate a list of woes for people and planet. Used for decades in everything from nonstick pans to firefighting foams, PFAS have been linked to increased risks of f
items.author: Sara Kiley Watson
paragraphs: Scrubbing Earth of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances—a.k.a. PFAS or forever chemicals—could eliminate a list of woes for people and planet. Used for decades in everything from nonstick pans to firefighting foams, PFAS have been linked to increased risks of fertility challenges, developmental delays, cancer, and reduced immune response. They are known for a strong bond between carbon and fluorine, which the environment struggles to break down.

PFAS are everywhere: They spew from factories and slough off products and into water with normal use. Scientists have found them in everything from human blood to Antarctic snow. One 2022 report found that 89% of the US population had PFAS in excess of two nanograms per milliliter of blood plasma, a common threshold for potential adverse health effects, and 9% of the population had passed the riskier level of 20 nanograms per milliliter.
The PFAS monster is also a moving target. New compounds are still being created and used. There are more than 12,000 of them, and much of the cleanup research focuses on only a small handful.

Cleansing PFAS-contaminated soil is a project in its infancy, but it is possible to prevent more buildup by pulling the chemicals out of water systems. There are two ways to handle this: trap or destroy. Some scientists have found reverse osmosis—a process that pushes water through supertight filters—useful in point-of-use cases, like water filters at kitchen sinks.

Other techniques in the pipeline might be more suitable for large-scale removal—for example, at water treatment facilities. One, called foam fractionation, generates bubbles that capture PFAS. More approaches, like ensnaring the chemicals in nanothin layers of charged metal, are also under investigation.
Trapping, though, is imperfect. You’re left with PFAS-filled brine, which if not properly destroyed (an expensive and energy-sucking endeavor) can still end up in the environment.

Jack Huang, a professor of crop and soil sciences at the University of Georgia, is working on destruction. He’s testing a method called electrochemical degradation, which uses electrodes to break down the bonds that hold PFAS together. The product destroyed more than 90% of PFAS mass in tests and has already been licensed by the engineering consulting firm AECOM.

Ridding life of PFAS is also a policy challenge. There are alternatives; we just need the push to use them. And we’ve had success before: The EPA’s 2010/2015 PFOA Stewardship Program has helped slash the release of water-repellent perfluorooctanoic acid by 95%. More recently, Minnesota, Maine, and New Mexico have passed bans on PFAS in products like cookware and dental floss.
Progress meter ............ 6
Scientists are making strides toward removing and destroying PFAS—but it’ll be all for naught if we don’t turn off the tap.

items.title: Solid-state batteries
items.description: The rise of the lithium-ion battery, which powers everything from the smallest personal electronics to gargantuan energy storage systems, has been nothing short of revolutionary. But as anyone who’s boarded a plane in the last decade could tell you, storing an
items.author: Alexander C Kaufman
paragraphs: The rise of the lithium-ion battery, which powers everything from the smallest personal electronics to gargantuan energy storage systems, has been nothing short of revolutionary. But as anyone who’s boarded a plane in the last decade could tell you, storing and pumping out energy by moving charged lithium ions through a liquid electrolyte soup has its drawbacks, not least that the batteries have a troubling tendency to catch fire. Enter the solid-state battery, which swaps liquid for a solid ceramic or polymer, creating power packs that charge faster, last longer, cram more energy into smaller spaces, and (crucially) run cooler. A new generation of companies aim to bring such batteries to market, and if their bets pan out, the tech could substantially ease the shift away from fossil fuels.

Solid-state batteries have been “just a few years away” for more than a decade now. In laboratories, the technology works. But there have been challenges. In designs that pair the solid electrolyte with a lithium-metal anode (the side of the battery that releases electrons into an electrical circuit), needlelike filaments called dendrites tend to grow during charging, and they eventually push through the electrolyte and short the cell. Solid electrolytes are supposed to physically block the formation of dendrites, but many of them crack as the treelike projections break through like roots in a concrete foundation.

Then there’s the problem of manufacturing at scale. Mass production requires large quantities of defect-free sheets of ceramic-like material to make the electrolytes as well as dry rooms for assembly, since those electrolytes have a tendency to react with water. Would-be manufacturers quote a range of potential prices for solid-state batteries, but most expect them to fall in line with lithium-ion packs sometime in the mid-2030s.

Nascent as the technology is, solid-state batteries have already seen high-profile missteps. But one of America’s most advanced solid-state-battery companies says it’s closing in on being able to bring its product to market. The Bill Gates–backed QuantumScape launched in Silicon Valley in 2010 and built its battery around a class of ceramic materials that it says is compatible with lithium—meaning no dendrite formation. “We spent, then, like 10 years learning how to process it to satisfy all of the other requirements,” says Tim Holme, QuantumScape’s cofounder and chief technology officer. In 2025, the startup announced a proprietary, large-scale manufacturing method for quickly producing and heat-treating the ceramic electrolytes used in its batteries. “Nobody has ever done this in the field of ceramics before,” Holme claims. For 10,000 years, producing ceramics has involved slowly cooking the starting materials in an oven over the course of days. “We figured out a way to shorten that down to several minutes,” he says.

Plenty of other companies are pushing the tech forward as well. Toyota, the world’s biggest automaker, launched a research program on solid-state batteries way back in 2010. It’s now partnering with the global energy and petroleum company Idemitsu Kosan on a pilot plant, promising cars that can travel up to 745 miles after charging 10 minutes or less—a huge leap, if it works out. In China, CATL, the giant behind roughly 40% of the global battery market, is aggressively pursuing solid-state batteries too, pumping nearly $2.6 billion into a research program in 2024 alone. Mercedes, meanwhile, equipped one of its EQS sedans with solid-state batteries last fall; after driving nonstop for 750 miles, the car still had some range to spare.

Will the tech gain traction? Investing in vehicle batteries makes sense given the size of the potential market. But any little uptick in cost typically gets passed on to buyers, so the first solid-state EV batteries will inevitably be more expensive.

Grid storage buyers, who are working to meet the increasing demands posed by data centers, may also hesitate to purchase new technologies that still haven’t come down the cost curve. Then again, the promise of energy storage that lasts longer than lithium-ion’s typical eight hours could make them easier to persuade.

Some companies are taking a page from a playbook employed by outfits pursuing fusion: Focus on near-term markets with better margins to help fund development and bring down costs. Solid-state firms including California-based Solid Energies and Arizona-headquartered Sion Power are looking at selling batteries to the aviation industry or the military. “Those are sectors that are less sensitive to cost, and they typically require lower volumes as well,” says Evelina Stoikou, head analyst for battery technologies and supply chains at the consultancy BloombergNEF. “It’s a good way to prove your concept, then go through and fund the pilot plant where you can make that and eventually scale up.”
Progress meter ............ 7
The technology works, the capital is there, and demand is not far behind. But as with anything in manufacturing, unknown unknowns remain.
