THE THING I WOULD MISS ABOUT CREATOR LIFE IF I WENT FULL-TIME HOLLYWOOD “I like the independence. Turns out, it takes a long time to make a movie. So when I have an idea that feels timely, it’s cool to be able to self-publish.”

Once a member of Sway House, the frat-like content studio that dominated during the pandemic, Beck is now leveraging his roots (dancing shirtless on TikTok) for something ever-so-slightly less bro-y. In January, he’ll star in McG’s Baywatch reboot, in which he plays a lifeguard alongside Stephen Amell, Brooks Nader and Shay Mitchell. Beck also just wrapped production on Danny Ramirez’s directorial debut, Baton, opposite Lewis Pullman and Camila Mendes.
THE BIGGEST ROOKIE MISTAKE I MADE ONLINE “Responding to a comment that was addressing a completely different Noah …”

Blackwell got her start on the shuttered app Vine (she posted mostly physical comedy like clips of her falling during a cheerleading stunt) before eventually amassing more than 16 million followers across TikTok and Instagram. In her new, more Hollywood-focused era, she’s honing in on YouTube with her Feeding Starving Celebrities series, which sees her chatting and cooking with Meg Stalter, Tyriq Withers and Charli XCX. She ventured into traditional entertainment when she appeared as a heightened, dramatized version of herself on the first season of I Love LA but says she doesn’t want to choose between the two: “The plan was never creator or Hollywood, it’s both, and I own the show.”
THE THING I WOULD MISS ABOUT CREATOR LIFE IF I WENT FULL-TIME HOLLYWOOD “If I had to name it: being the one who decides when something is done.”
THE PERSON WHOSE SOCIAL MEDIA ACCOUNT I’D LIKE TO RUN FOR A DAY Oprah Winfrey. “I’d post one thing and then sit with the comments like it’s a book club.”

Feldman started as a PA capturing behind-the-scenes content on The Marvelous Mrs. Maisel and has grown to become Hollywood’s chosen creator thanks to his authoritative yet relatable POV. Under his guise of Guy With a Movie Camera, he’s been hired by studios and streamers to help promote their projects with his particular brand of BTS content. Christopher Nolan personally invited him to the set of The Odyssey to show fans what the massive production was like, and Feldman was just announced as this season’s Oscars ambassador for the Academy, a role that will see him hosting the official red carpet.
THE BIGGEST ROOKIE MISTAKE I MADE ONLINE “Reading every comment.”

With the pending end of Chicken Shop Date, Evans will officially have the last poultry-themed interview show standing. And in fact, he’s expanding — after dominating with Hot Ones (A-listers eating increasingly spicy wings while he delivers a very specific line of questioning about their bodies of work) and Hot Ones Versus (A-listers competing to see who can answer the most hard-hitting questions and thus be fed the least spicy wings), he’s now added Hot Ones Wing Pong (casts of shows like Adults and Outer Banks playing a version of beer pong) to the mix. The franchise is now so famous that Evans is called on to stage the series in movies like Happy Gilmore 2 and Verity.

CELEBRITY GUEST WHO MOST SURPRISED ME “It always surprises me when a guest runs the [wing] gantlet without even flinching. Shout-out to Demi Moore. Shout out to Karl-Anthony Towns. Shout out to Ariana Grande.”
MY DAILY MEDIA DIET CONSISTS OF … “MLB highlights on YouTube, movie screeners for upcoming Hot Ones guests and podcasts at 2.5x speed.”

As the self-coined Cupid of New York, Baira has been making videos about dating in the Big Apple since the days of the pandemic. She started by sharing her own (occasionally horror) stories and now hosts several viral dating-centric series — Take Me Out and StreetHearts — that lure in guests like Belmont Cameli, Snoop Dogg and Jennifer Lopez to talk about their careers and love lives. (She was also selected to appear as herself on the most recent season of Adults.)
CELEBRITY GUEST WHO MOST SURPRISED ME “Snoop Dogg once told me I was ‘pretty in pink’ during an interview, and I’ve truly never gotten over it.”

Entering her sophomore season of Saturday Night Live, Slowikowska is carving out a niche in what we’ll call lovable cringe comedy. She was cast thanks to the popular sketch comedy she posted on her TikTok page, and even though her schedule is increasingly full with Hollywood projects — she had a small part in One Night Only and next will appear in Craig Zobel’s Turpentine alongside Melissa McCarthy and Connor Storrie — she continues to create alongside her boyfriend and collaborator Kyle Chase. “There’s no green lights or auditions or Hollywood producers running my page,” she says. “It’s just me, and it feels liberating.”
THE BIGGEST ROOKIE MISTAKE I MADE ONLINE “Reading comments. Good or bad or ugly, none of my business!”
THE PERSON WHOSE SOCIAL MEDIA ACCOUNT I’D LIKE TO RUN FOR A DAY Home Depot. “I’d post some funny memes to a Chanel Beads song.”

Three years after the cancellation of her eponymous Showtime talk show, Ziwe went back to her roots by relaunching the series — this time on YouTube. Now branded as You’d Be an Iconic Guest, she’s using her signature confrontational yet deadpan interview style to grill people like Kevin Hart, Law Roach and Hasan Piker in segments that go consistently (and extremely) viral.
CELEBRITY GUEST WHO MOST SURPRISED ME “All of my guests are surprising, please don’t make me choose between icons.”
THE PERSON WHOSE SOCIAL MEDIA ACCOUNT I’D LIKE TO RUN FOR A DAY The Pope. “I would not want to run anyone’s social media, but if I had to choose …”
This story appeared in the Oct. 21 issue of The Hollywood Reporter magazine. Click here to subscribe.

items.title: ‘Nobody Wants This’ Season 3 Review: Kristen Bell and Adam Brody’s Netflix Romance Levels Up but Can’t Ditch Old Habits
items.description: If nothing else, give Nobody Wants This credit for allowing itself a tiny bit of growth: After two seasons of exhaustingly circular conflict about whether a good-boy rabbi like Noah (Adam Brody) could ever really be with an agnostic Gentile sex podcaster like
items.author: Angie Han
paragraphs: If nothing else, give Nobody Wants This credit for allowing itself a tiny bit of growth: After two seasons of exhaustingly circular conflict about whether a good-boy rabbi like Noah (Adam Brody) could ever really be with an agnostic Gentile sex podcaster like Joanne (Kristen Bell), season three begins not only with the couple moving in together, but Joanne starting Jewish conversion classes.

Finally, we’ve graduated from asking if to asking how. For a show whose very dithering had previously seemed to reflect Joanne’s fear that “no one wants to listen to happy,” it’s a welcome step forward. But as lifelong flake Joanne has learned many times over by now, wherever you go, there you are. Nobody Wants This might be on its way to becoming a sweeter, more even-keeled version of itself, but it can’t completely shake the bad habits that have made it nearly as exasperating as it is endearing.
Cast: Adam Brody, Kristen Bell, Justine Lupe, Timothy Simons, Jackie Tohn, Tovah Feldshuh, Paul Ben-Victor, Stephanie Faracy, Michael Hitchcock

Admittedly, it does feel good to bask for once in what feels right about Joanne and Noah’s relationship rather than fret over what might be wrong about it. The lovebirds are so giddy they wake each other up in the middle of the night just to coo: “Hey. We live together.” Nothing can pierce their romantic bliss, not even minor annoyances like Joanne’s inability to ever shut a cabinet door (“It’s like living with a ghost,” Noah complains adorably) or bigger ones like her almost sabotaging their first trip as a couple when she runs into a desperately needy fan (creator Erin Foster) at the airport.

Not, at this point, that there’s anyone or anything trying to ruin them anyway. With Joanne’s no-seriously-this-time decision to convert, previously insurmountable obstacles have melted away. Noah’s old temple is only too relieved to bring him back for a trial run, now that they’ve been reassured his life partner will soon become part of their tribe. His disapproving mother (Tovah Feldshuh) is all too happy to throw herself into turning her possible future daughter-in-law into the perfect rebbetzin (rabbi’s wife). There’s nothing at all standing between them and happily ever after, or so it seems.

Brody continues to excel as a romantic lead, combining the patience of a saint with the goofiness of a guy you could actually imagine meeting and falling for in real life. Bell gets to soften her character’s more abrasive edges; oh-so-kooky Joanne might still do obnoxious things like publicly brag about her and Noah’s sex life in an embarrassing attempt to one-up an ex (Avan Jogia), but at least she’s secure enough to be self-aware about it. And while I remain slightly underwhelmed by their chemistry, it turns out to matter much less when we’re not needing to be convinced every few episodes that theirs is a passion fiery enough to overcome every reasonable objection.

Their newfound sense of chill does not come without narrative cost. Nobody Wants This season three tones down its exploration of Judaism and Jewish culture significantly — like, to the extent that Christmas traditions get a more elaborate episode spotlight than any Jewish holiday does. (It makes some sense in context, but still.) With Noah’s career back on track, the congregation itself mostly fades into the background. Joanne’s conversion classes mainly function as a backdrop for simmering yet undercooked tension with guest stars like Sarah Silverman as Rabbi Eden and Andrew Rannells and Keyla Monterroso Mejia as fellow students.

Perhaps this is a response to critique of the show’s treatment of Jewishness in earlier years, or perhaps it simply reflects the fact that this is no longer a driving issue in the central romance. But given that Joanne’s will-they-won’t-they with Noah has doubled as a will-they-won’t-they with the religion, it comes as a disappointment that we don’t get more insight into her evolving understanding of the faith, the culture and her place within them — give or take a late-season speech about purpose and meaning that’s performed movingly enough by Bell to make you wish she’d had more material like it.

In the absence of any real and obvious issues for Joanne and Noah, the burden of dramatic tension falls more heavily this season on the ensemble around them. Primarily, this means digging into the connection between her chaotically self-absorbed sister, Morgan (Justine Lupe), and his endearing lug of a brother, Sasha (Timothy Simons).

On one hand, the chemistry between Lupe and Simons is undeniable enough (more so than the chemistry between Bell and Brody, for my money) that the show was always going to have to address it eventually. On the other, the series approaches it with a characteristic lack of subtlety, barreling over what should have been a poignant storyline about the very fresh separation between Sasha and his wife (Jackie Tohn, still excellent and still sadly underserved as brusque, brittle Esther).

At least it’s possible to understand what the series is trying to do with this plotline, which is more than can be said for some of the other elements that make up the narrative. Some missteps are deeply silly but easy to forgive — seriously, the absolute carelessness with which the show treats Joanne’s podcasting “career,” which seems to consist of her randomly waving around a microphone while flopping about the couch, has to be a bit at this point.

Others are more grating. I’ve come to understand by now that the writers (led by showrunners Jenni Konner and Bruce Eric Kaplan) and I have vastly different ideas about where the line falls between “endearingly messy” and “off-puttingly toxic.” Where I, for example, see Joanne’s passive-aggressive sniping any time Morgan gets even the tiniest shred of good news as a cruel and unpleasant reaction, they apparently see it as a cute and relatable expression of sibling rivalry.

In fairness, the performances (especially by comic MVP Lupe) are charming enough to almost pass it off as such, and the script so airy it never dwells on any wound long enough for it to fester. With its tight 30-minute episode run times, postcard-pretty L.A. backdrops, and an inherently lovable cast of actors you’ve loved in other things, this series has always gone down as a quick, easy binge, and that hasn’t changed in season three.

But as a romantic like Noah or Joanne would tell you, there’s an ocean of difference between settling for good enough and daring to dream of something magical. Nobody Wants This can certainly offer the former. It’s still got a ways to go before it can deliver the latter.

items.title: Sacha Baron Cohen Gets Real About Backlash, Death Threats and Resurrecting Ali G
items.description: Sacha Baron Cohen insists his new film, Ali G: Who Iz I?, is the last guerrilla comedy of its kind that he’ll make. He’s adamant. No more Borat. No more Bruno. No more Ali G. They’re too hard, he says, too risky. He’s tired of hoodwinking people to expose thei
items.author: Lacey Rose
paragraphs: Sacha Baron Cohen insists his new film, Ali G: Who Iz I?, is the last guerrilla comedy of its kind that he’ll make. He’s adamant. No more Borat. No more Bruno. No more Ali G. They’re too hard, he says, too risky. He’s tired of hoodwinking people to expose their prejudices, and he’s even more tired of the death threats that periodically follow. There are easier ways to make money in this business, and eventually his luck will run out.

The trouble with his declaration, however impassioned, is that he has been making it for years. He’d routinely say he was done before he made the 2020 Borat sequel, which, incidentally, earned two Oscar nominations, and he was even more insistent afterward. And each time he says it, he believes it to be true. He wants it to be true, he tells me. So, why are we here, I ask, discussing an Ali G revival?

“Because I’m terrified of where our society is headed, and the way I can comment on that is through my comedy,” he says. “I wanted to show the extremism on both sides of the political spectrum and the danger of virtuous violence.” There’s a level of seriousness that belies the 90-minute comedy film he’s made, which features an imbecilic white rapper who speaks in Caribbean-British slang and a contraption that shoots bullets out of one’s rear end. Recognizing this, he adds: “And obviously we wanted to make the funniest film that’s ever been made.”

His longtime collaborators have other theories about his return. Anthony “Ant” Hines, who’s been working with Baron Cohen since The 11 O’Clock Show, where the Ali G character originated, believes his pal had missed the adrenaline rush, just as he had. “It’s a visceral buzz you get from making a movie this way,” Hines says, “and nothing comes close to it.”

Dan Mazer, whose friendship with Baron Cohen dates back to secondary school in the U.K., wasn’t particularly surprised to get the call about dusting off Ali G, in part because they’ve never stopped talking about the character. In fact, whenever they got together, they’d often slip into Ali G’s voice, he says, and imagine what patently absurd things he would be saying or doing in different situations.

“I also think it’s a knowledge that Sacha is the Michael Jordan of this sort of filmmaking,” says Mazer. “And yeah, Michael Jordan went off and tried to play baseball, and you go, ‘OK, you’re a pretty good baseball player,’ but he’s not the Michael Jordan of baseball. And Sacha is the Michael Jordan of this, and to an extent, we all are. We invented this genre, and nobody else has matched what we’ve done.”

Whatever the reasoning may be, Ali G is back, rolling into theaters Oct. 23 before landing on Amazon Prime Video soon after. And like plenty else that Baron Cohen has done, it’s already prompted a full-blown meta-outrage cycle, complete with a campaign to boycott the film. With each new trailer or PR stunt posted to social media come fresh accusations of an outdated caricature and of cultural appropriation — the latter a central plot point in the film, in which Ali G’s progressive nemesis (also played by Baron Cohen) attempts to cancel him on those very grounds. Some in his camp have speculated that it’s more of a coordinated attack by pro-Palestinians who are critical of Baron Cohen’s past support of Israel. (Though he’s been quiet about Israeli politics and the conflict in Gaza in recent years, Baron Cohen is a prominent Jew who has sounded the alarm about the surge of antisemitism on social media, reportedly telling TikTok executives in 2023 that what was happening on their platform was “creating the biggest antisemitic movement since the Nazis.”)

Colton Dunn, an Emmy-winning Ali G superfan and one of three Black writers hired on the film, is aware of the cultural appropriation claims. “But we knew where we were coming from, and we dealt with it all in the movie,” he says, “and at the heart of it, Sacha and the movie want to defeat evil and hate. That’s the intention behind it.” Still, the internet has suggested the backlash has Amazon spooked. Courtenay Valenti, Amazon MGM Studios’ head of film, streaming and theatrical, offers this: “We want to be in business with exceptional storytellers who have distinctive creative visions, and Sacha is exactly that. He has always been fearless in his comedy, with a unique ability to tap into the cultural conversation in ways that are both provocative and entertaining.”
Over cappuccinos in the garden of the Chateau Marmont, Baron Cohen lets loose on the mounting backlash, his battles with studios and the $3 million day that nearly derailed his film.
In 2021, you allegedly performed as Ali G at The Comedy Store in Australia. How soon after did you explore the idea of another film, and what did those early conversations entail?

During the pandemic, our family moves to Australia, and when they lock down in Australia, you cannot leave where you are. My ex [Isla Fisher] is from Perth, so we applied to go there. She’s rejected. I find out that you have to show that there’s a financial benefit to Western Australia to be allowed in. You have to apply to the police. So I say, “Listen, I’m doing a stand-up tour. It’s going to create 300 jobs. It’s going to bring tens of millions of dollars into Western Australia.” Obviously I had no intention of doing it. But then the police accept me. We spent 14 days in lockdown, and at the end, a police car turns up, an inspector comes out, and she says, “I am in charge of your stand-up tour.”
So, you had to do a stand-up tour.

I did, and I had the police watching me. I ended up doing a 90-minute show, and what was interesting was that people really loved seeing Borat and Bruno, but when Ali G came out, there was a different response. It was as if people believed he was real. There’s going to be a lot of amateur psychology in this interview, but my observation was that because Ali G existed before I existed as a public figure — for five or six years, I didn’t give an interview [as myself] — people thought Ali was real and therefore there was this different response to him. So, I felt, “Hold on, is there a movie in this character?”

I came back to America at the end of 2021 and started talking with the team about it. We all felt Ali by himself wouldn’t be a satirical movie because he was from a bygone era — this relic from another period who’s unaware that he is deeply problematic. But what if we brought in another character, an ultraprogressive extremist [also played by Baron Cohen] who’s his rival and make it a thriller like The Fugitive? We had in our mind this line that goes, “We have a cultural appropriator on the loose,” from that famous speech in The Fugitive. That felt funny to me.

In the revisionist history of the film, you had ended Da Ali G Show because you couldn’t come to financial terms with HBO. It left me wondering if there were any conversations or interest, from either side, about doing more?

Oh, yes. HBO wanted to carry on. I said no because at that time, in Britain, I think a lot of comedians were snobs about doing multiple seasons. So, there was no expectation or desire to do 15 seasons — to do the American way. I’m very friendly with Larry David, and I’m jealous of him that he can do Curb again and again. I probably would’ve had a much easier life if I just carried on doing Da Ali G Show.

A decade ago, you said of this type of filmmaking: “It’s a young man’s game. You have to be prepared for a small amount of risk, and my philosophy was always: ‘Well, if something bad happens, I’m single and everyone’s going to be all right if I end up in hospital for two weeks.’ Now that I’m married with kids, it’s more difficult to justify.” So, did you find a way to do it differently, or did you just say, “Fuck it”?

I’m never cavalier. These movies are dangerous to make, but we try to limit the risks and keep everybody safe. But even physically, they’re incredibly demanding. So, the final scene of this film is an eight-hour continuous scene that takes place over 12 locations. It’s a continual shot. There’s gunfire in it. There’s a medical procedure. There are drones, there are explosions, and it’s taking place in the desert. On the way to shooting it, I bumped into one of the great stuntmen and he said, “You will go to hospital if you make this movie,” because I explained I’m wearing a prosthetic head in a fat suit. He said, “You’ll be so dehydrated you’ll be in hospital for two weeks.”
You hear that and think what?

That I have to fix the problem. So, I had an endurance specialist who does the Tour de France be by my side during the scene and they’re measuring my weight. I think I had 11 liters of Pedialyte. And listen, a number of people went to the hospital for dehydration, including the bodyguard. There were dangers in the scene as well. One of the people grabbed a gun and almost did something very dangerous. These really are the hardest movies to make, but I suppose I made it because I’m scared of this world of conspiracies and lies that are spread by social media and now by AI. If we don’t have these shared facts, then democracies crumble and we can’t have a tolerant society. And to make people laugh is therapy.
As I read your own quote back to you just now, you were laughing. Why?

Because I’m always surprised at my own idiocy. I’m very bad at looking into the future and imagining how I will feel. So, for example, the naked fight in Borat 1, we get to set and Ken Davitian, who’s not conventionally attractive, is naked, and he’s going to sit on my face. And I say, “I’m not going to do this!” At that point, Larry Charles, the director, said, “So why did you write it?!” I continually make these decisions that are very bad for my own health and sanity.
You are making this film in a very different moment, culturally and comedically. Do you derive some masochistic pleasure from that kind of challenge?

I’ll tell you, in the script, there was a moment where Ali G is canceled, and the way we wanted to do that was that I, Sacha, should be canceled in the real world and the idea was to use the footage of me being canceled and stick it into the movie. And we did actually get some of the second bit, but we didn’t have the money to open up the movie and put the footage in. That was the intention, though.
I’m told you get a fair number of death threats, which now come from both the left and the right. When have you decided something wasn’t worth it?

I was about to do a scene [in Borat 1] and we had a cop who had his gun on his thigh and I said, “Why is your gun on your thigh?” He goes, “Well, I need to be really fast to draw in this area.” I said, “Well, how close are you to me?” And he said, “I’ll be with you within three minutes.” I realized that was not a good thing to do, so I pulled that scene. I will never do a scene if I think I’m actually going to die.
You’ve filmed in a bulletproof vest, so you’ve clearly anticipated the possibility of being shot?
Yes, on Borat 2, there was a scene at a gun rights rally that I knew there was a risk of getting shot. But I felt it was an important film to be made.
Is there anyone who says to you, “Hey, Sacha, I know this seems noble to you, but maybe it’s not necessary”?

I don’t talk about my children. But my brothers tell me that. And my mom and some of my team as well, because there are much easier options. I made a movie called Ladies First. I shot it in three months. It came out. A lot of people saw it [on Netflix]. And it’s as financially beneficial as making something that takes years, and there’s absolutely zero risk. There must be some masochistic nature to me, but I don’t think it’s just that. I want to give the fans who’ve been loyal for the last 28 years something that they’ve never seen before. I want to give them the most ambitious movie I’ve ever made, which is a three-character movie. [Baron Cohen also plays a former Mossad agent.] It is my version of the Avengers.
I’ve always assumed that you were like Tom Cruise, after the same adrenaline rush that he is as he jumps out of planes.
I don’t think that’s the reason I do it.
You don’t? Your collaborators seem to …

No. The first [for-hire] movie I did, Talladega Nights, I walked into my trailer and there was a bed there. I realized I’d never been in a trailer before, and I go, “Hold on, this is a paid job where I can go to sleep?!” I couldn’t comprehend how relatively easy it was, and it was great fun. But as you’ll probably deduce from this interview, I’m not very self-aware.
I don’t know that I buy that.

OK. Do I enjoy it when something works? Yes. Am I upset when something doesn’t work? Yes. So, for example, this final scene is an eight-hour continuous shot over multiple locations and no one had ever done that before. Normally we shoot a scene or two scenes a day. Here, we put probably 40 scenes together and shot them continuously. I had a variety of line producers and assistant directors refuse to schedule it. And there are 400 or so beats that must all go perfectly, because you’re dealing with real people and if anything doesn’t feel quite right, they will stop and say, “Hold on, this isn’t real.”

So gunfire, the squibs have to go off perfectly. A medical procedure happens. That body that we use has to be believable. Then a fire breaks out during the first part of the scene. As we’re driving to the second location to kidnap somebody with these real people, I find out that location four is surrounded by fire, and it’s being evacuated, and we have to pull the scene. And each time we run it, it’s $4 million and we’re insured for $1 million, and I personally have to pay $3 million. So, we shut down production and we have a discussion, which is that it’s completely idiotic that we’re trying this.
And everyone is telling you it’s not possible?
Yes, and I’ve lost $3 million that day. Obviously it was my money, which is a very stupid idea.
But you ultimately got it?

We got it. We had some of the team that worked on the Oscars because I was like, “What is a movie or a TV show where nothing can go wrong? It’s the Oscars.” And even there, sometimes something’s going wrong! I said to them, “OK, this is the Oscars, it’s just taking place over 50 miles in 12 locations. And it has gunfire and blood.” But at the end of all of it, if you look at the behind-the-scenes footage, I’m not jumping up and down. I’m content.
With 2020’s Borat 2, you’ve said that several of the places you pitched were concerned by the political content and the idea of running it before the election. How did this pitch compare?

Well, the desire was always to have this come out a few days before either a presidential election or the midterms. A lot of my movies have come out around those times. Borat 1 came out almost 20 years to the day, on November 3, 2006, just before the midterms. It’s a time for people to think about the choices that they’re about to make. But this movie is more about the dangers of extremism on both sides.
I get that, but you’re also operating in an extremely risk-averse climate. I can’t imagine there weren’t any concerns …
Well, Hollywood is a superficial place.

I know. (Laughter.) But I pitched this after Borat 2 had won two Golden Globes and had Oscar nominations and was the most watched movie ever on Amazon. That’s enough to convince studio heads to buy it. And everyone tried.
It was somewhere else first, no?

Yes. Amazon and Universal were the final contenders. We ended up going with Universal but, in the end, the movie took so long that we went back to Amazon. And it was actually great because we’d had an incredible experience there with the last one. We really did. And that movie [Borat 2] also was at Universal and ended up at Amazon.
So, this one moved because —

It was taking too long. You have to understand the basis of this kind of movie is that we have to find people who don’t know who I am, which becomes harder and harder. I think our research department interviewed 5,000 doctors to get one [for a single scene]. Then we had a number of other things that kept on shutting it down. The fire. The writers strike. I ended up doing another movie in the middle.
Amazon came aboard a third of the way through. What did their notes look like?
For better or worse, maybe for worse, I’m a final-cut producer and director.
So, you’re saying it didn’t much matter what their notes were?
Well, executives can have really fantastic notes. And they can have terrible notes. But I always listen to the audience and I’m really guided by that.

You were once asked about comparisons between you and Andy Kaufman, to which you said, “In a way, he’s more of an artist than I am in that I don’t think he cared what the audience thought — and deep down, I really want to make the audience laugh. And that’s why I fight to get jokes to be funny … I’ll go to war with whatever studio has been stupid enough to pay me money to make a movie.” Again, you’re laughing …
I can’t believe how honest I was.
What did those fights look like on a film like this?

If something is funny, then I will go to war for it. And the studios know that because I make it clear when we do these movies, which makes me not very studio-friendly in some ways because my allegiance is to the audience. And I go to every single screening and I record the laughter and I grade the jokes and I have a few people that I’ve trained to grade them too, and then I cut the jokes within a frame. It’s obsessive and very intricate, but it’s designed to deliver really funny movies. Some people find me incredibly arrogant because they’ll come up and say, “You know that movie, Borat 2, wasn’t funny.” And I’ll say, “You’re entitled to your opinion, but you’re wrong. I have 5,000 people laughing at these jokes and I can show you they are empirically funny.”
You said that you’re not studio-friendly, but, as you noted, this is a superficial business and if your model can put butts in seats …

Yes, it’s about money. But I’m also a great supporter of the Oscars and other awards ceremonies because, however absurd they are, it creates another incentive for studio heads to make quality projects. Because studio heads do want to win Oscars and they want to get nominated. And we’ve been very lucky in that the Academy and the Globes and some other organizations have recognized our work.

In fact, I was sitting at that table [pointing to another table in the Chateau garden] in 2006 having done Borat, and Sean Penn came and sat at the table and he said, “Why don’t you do an Oscar campaign for your performance in Borat?” I said, “That’s absurd. They’ll never give me an Oscar nomination.” And he said, “They will.” So, we went to Fox at the time and they said, “Listen, we’ll pay for one Oscar campaign, but it’s either writing or acting.” At the time, I was actually winning some of the acting awards, to my great surprise, but I spoke to the team and we decided to push the writing. [The 2006 film was nominated for best adapted screenplay.] So, we gave up the acting campaign. Also, I was about to make Bruno and I didn’t want to go on a baby-kissing tour, which would destroy my next movie. Me doing this kind of stuff [an interview as himself] destroys the ability to make another one.
I know, I know. I’m sorry.
There we go. Look what you’ve done. You’ve ruined me.

As you anticipated, it didn’t take long for people to start lodging complaints. One criticism, which mirrors a plotline in the film, is that Ali G uses the character as a cover for enforcing racial stereotypes. What do you say to that?

Well, I’ll repeat what I’ve said for many years, which is that Ali G is a white cultural appropriator who steals from the musical artists that he admires. The reason Ali G says “West Side” is not because the Afro-Caribbean community in London was saying “West Side.” Nobody there was. It’s because Tupac Shakur, who he admires, is saying “West Side.” And so he is funny because he is delusional. He lives this boring, white middle-class life in a suburban town, and he deludes himself that he’s living in Compton, and that is the absurdity of Ali G. The core joke is that a white moron, possibly the stupidest man in the world, is interviewing a white expert or high-status politician, and that white expert or high-status politician believes that this imbecile played by me is real and that leads to comedy. And in my belief, it slightly undermines the power of the establishment. So it was fundamentally an anti-establishment character where we’re pricking the assuredness of the establishment by saying, “Listen, these people aren’t that smart. They believe that Channel 4 or HBO could have sent one of the most stupid people in the world to interview them.”
What do you make of the argument that not everybody recognizes the absurdity and so the stereotypes being presented can have dangerous ramifications?
Everyone is entitled to their own view. And a lot of the stuff on social media is orchestrated, and not necessarily orchestrated by people who really believe in what they’re saying.

But when I did Da Ali G Show in America, the first people who gravitated to it were the Black hip-hop community. The first GQ Award that I was given was given to me by Method Man and Redman. I did a series of adverts for the NBA directed by Spike Lee, who’s not naive about racial issues. They recognized these characters, these white cultural appropriators, and they found them funny. So, this notion of it being problematic hadn’t been raised for 20 years.
OK, but you seemed to know it would be this time around?

Yes. I knew, and I wanted to make sure that this was an anti-racist movie, which is why we were so concerned with having absolutely brilliant Black writers on board and consulting with brilliant Black cultural commentators.
As I believe you were referencing, there was a pretty sizable social media campaign to boycott the movie, and some have speculated that the campaign is tied to your pro-Israel stance —

Well, I haven’t said anything about Israel. [Baron Cohen voiced his support for Israel and the hostages immediately after the Oct. 7 attacks but has been quiet on the Gaza war and Israeli politics in the years since.] I think people are being portrayed as things that they are not on social media and it’s problematic. We are in a world where people can’t distinguish between facts and lies, and that’s something that I’ve spent a lot of the last few years trying to fix. For example, I co-founded a group called Stop Hate for Profit with the NAACP and Color of Change and the ADL and certain other civil rights groups to stop the misinformation and incitement of racism on social media. So, I’m not surprised that prominent Jews are being targeted. I knew that this was going to happen. The level of organization is surprising, but this is a trend of Jews being portrayed in certain ways and trying to be silenced.
You’ve been vocal about the rise of antisemitism, broadly speaking. Have you felt any difference in your own Hollywood career after Oct. 7?
No, not really. I mean, maybe it’s because I don’t do much, but I haven’t.

Well, you’re about to make your West End debut in a Quentin Tarantino play, which feels like a big leap, going from this film, in which you’re in complete control as the writer, director and star, to being a puppet in Tarantino’s theater. How did that come together?

I’ve never had a career plan, but I have this kind of no-brainer rule, which is if one of the best directors in the world asks me to do something, I’ll say yes, even if it’s instinctively the wrong project. So when Martin Scorsese says, “I’m doing a kid’s film, will Sacha play the villain in it?” And I read the book and the character’s not that interesting. I actually had a lot of arguments with [screenwriter John] Logan about it [Hugo]. But I say yes because I want to learn how to make better films. And so if Quentin comes along and says, “I want to do a play,” I say yes. Then I actually read the play and I thought it was fantastic. And I felt, why not? So currently, I’m doing nine hours of sword-fighting training a week. And I would just clarify, rather than be a puppet, Quentin did suggest that there would be some element of collaboration.

A little bit, yes. But Quentin and I have been talking about doing a project for at least 20 years. We talked about doing The Scarlet Pimpernel about 20 years ago. Borat came out and Quentin and I would have dinner monthly and I almost did a part in [his 2012 Western] Django Unchained. In the end, I had to drop out because I ended up doing Les Misérables. But I came very close to doing a scene with Kerry Washington. I even had a prosthetic chin made because Quentin was very adamant that I would resemble this character he’d liked from the ’40s.

Ant Hines, one of your longtime collaborators, suggested you’ve tussled with Amazon in the promotion of this new film. “We’re giving Amazon panic attacks on the daily,” he told me. “They’re used to Timothée Chalamet eating some chicken wings; they’re not used to 300 Timothée Chalamets attempting to take part in the London Marathon, which is a thing they shut down.”

This is why it’s best not to talk to somebody like Ant. (Laughs.) You know, they’ve actually been great in terms of the marketing. But it’s not a traditional process when you work with me and you’re marketing a movie.
You did end up with 300 Ali G look-alikes following you around London. That had to be validating, if a little overwhelming.

The really concerning thing was that these fans were coming out with catchphrases that I’d completely forgotten. I was like, “Wait a minute. I recognize that … What is that from?” And they’d go, “It’s you!” And some of them were doing better Ali G impressions than me. There was one guy there, an Ali G impersonator, and I had to explain, like, “Listen, you’ve been doing this at weddings and bar mitzvahs every week for the last 20 years. I haven’t been doing this.” I’ve actually had that happen before. We did a movie called Bruno, and Jonah Hill was one of the writers. And in the writers room, he was doing impressions of Bruno, and they were better than Bruno. Then when I started shooting the movie, I realized that I was doing an impression of Jonah Hill doing an impression of me.

In any genre, there’s always an “It” person, and at various points, you’ve employed those people shortly before they reached that status: Jonah, Seth Rogen and Evan Goldberg and, most recently, Nathan Fielder, who worked on your Showtime series, Who Is America? What do you think of what Nathan has done in the eight years since you worked together?

Oh, I think he’s a comic genius and he reinvented the genre that I, I suppose, created or developed. And he had a rule, really, which was to not do anything that I had done. But he’s a brilliant, brilliant mind, and absolutely hilarious. I think his documentary [You Can See Everything] is going to be huge, so I’m very excited for him.

But it’s been an honor to have all of these incredible people come and work with me. Seth and Evan, the story with them was, it was the Ali G Show, and they came in with an idea for Bruno — instead of Girls Gone Wild, it was Boys Gone Wild. I said, “OK, you’re hired, but I’ve only got enough money for one writer, so unless you want to share a hotel room and a bed and a wage, I can only hire one of you and it’s going to be Seth.” They came back and said, “We’ll split the wage.” And basically they would write in a double bed in the Best Western hotel we were in. They had beers all around them. They were smoking and they’d write in bed.
That’s fantastic. For you, what do the incoming calls look like these days?
I think they’re kind of what comes in to everyone. I get the traditional comedies, kernels of comedy ideas, and then dramas.
Is one genre more appealing than the other right now?

No. I want to do stuff that challenges me. So again, I’m not doing Borat 3, which also would be incredibly challenging. Again, this movie I just did is the most challenging movie I’ve ever done, but I’m not doing more.
No, no, I really have had enough. I know you don’t believe me.
Oh, I really pray that in six years’ time, you don’t come to me and quote me to myself.
This story appeared in the Oct. 21 issue of The Hollywood Reporter magazine. Click here to subscribe.

items.title: 9 Ways to Remix Your Tux Right Now
items.description: The tuxedo is sacred. It's been around since the 19th century, which is a long time to keep wearing roughly the same thing to a nice dinner. It's remained relatively unchanged in all those years: black jacket, white shirt, bow tie. There are consecrated instru
items.author: Adam Cheung
paragraphs: The tuxedo is sacred. It's been around since the 19th century, which is a long time to keep wearing roughly the same thing to a nice dinner. It's remained relatively unchanged in all those years: black jacket, white shirt, bow tie. There are consecrated instructions about how much cuff should show and what should go around your waist. And naturally, you can spend quite a lot of cash getting all of this exactly right.

At this weekend's Academy Museum Gala in Hollywood, though, some of the best menswear came from guys who switched things up. The trousers got wider. The necklines got lower. And Alexander Skarsgård apparently decided there wasn't nearly enough shirt.
Let's take a gander at the 9 biggest tux swerves that you can keep in mind for your next big black-tie evening.

items.title: The Please Don’t Destroy Boys Are J.Crew Models Now
items.description: The fashion industry has been in a playful mood. Sly slogan tees are back on the menu. Pants are getting so saucily low-rise, they reveal a whiff of butt crack. And a cohort of very funny people—including Ivy Wolk, Benito Skinner, and Cole Escola—have become m
items.author: Savannah Sobrevilla
paragraphs: The fashion industry has been in a playful mood. Sly slogan tees are back on the menu. Pants are getting so saucily low-rise, they reveal a whiff of butt crack. And a cohort of very funny people—including Ivy Wolk, Benito Skinner, and Cole Escola—have become maison darlings. It was only a matter of time before the beloved comedy trio Please Don’t Destroy landed a big-time campaign—and thanks to the good people at J.Crew, that day has finally come.

After meeting at NYU, John Higgins, Ben Marshall, and Martin Herlihy shot to viral fame through a series of pandemic-era TikTok sketches. Not long after, they landed at Saturday Night Live in 2021, injecting the show with a caustic new energy through their surrealist pre-taped bits—many of which starred A-listers like Bad Bunny, Charli XCX, and Timothée Chalamet. Though Higgins and Herlihy have now both left SNL, Please Don’t Destroy remains a going concern—the three spent the back half of the summer touring their live show, before reuniting again for J.Crew’s cameras.

On a steamy Friday last month, Higgins, Marshall, and Herlihy took to the streets of New York in the prep brand’s sharpest fall suits. I stopped by the NoLIta set as Herlihy directed a typically silly, fast-paced video, with the trio running through bit after bit—a James Bond impression one minute, smashing into a display of mannequins the next.
Here, I caught up with the boys about their burgeoning modeling careers, all-time style icons, and the unlikely inspiration behind the new campaign.

Martin Herlihy: It was J.Crew’s idea. They asked if we had any experience or personal knowledge of J.Crew, and we told them that John would go down to J.Crew pretty much every Saturday at SNL and buy something.
John Higgins: I call it retail therapy. Well, I don’t call it that. I think the world calls it that, but I would go there.
Herlihy: That 30 Rock J.Crew was kind of just like a dopamine provider.
Higgins: If you were just bummed about your sketch not going or anything, just getting a new J.Crew sweater just really seemed to spin it up.
Marshall: Is an ice cream store retail? Because Martin did that.

Marshall: No. I got rejected from working at a popsicle stand once. It was the day that my friend, Moss [Perricone]—who now writes for SNL and was my roommate—got his first TV writing job. And I was denied from the popsicle stand.
Higgins: It was easy because the lack of experience guided a lot of the comedy of it, where we kind of were just fucking up over and over again.

Marshall: It was theoretically our first day working there. We wrote the script with our buddy, Brady Lees, and approached it like we would have an SNL sketch—fun and fast. We used a similar format of talking about something like it went really well and then cutting to it not going really well.
Higgins: Don’t give away the secret, dude.
Marshall: We just pulled from our real experience of being dumb guys.
Higgins: That we were born to do, I would say.

Herlihy: It was really strange and uncomfortable... That makes it sound like it was a bad experience and it wasn’t. It was great. Everyone who worked on it was great. Doing it was very strange and uncomfortable, but it was great.

Marshall: You can expect to see us just rising the ranks of the model world, walking in Fashion Week. GQ’s fucking like, “Oh, it’s all about Jack Innanen.” No, it’s not. It’s about Please Don’t Destroy. Look out for us. We’re dressing cool. Everything’s changing.
Herlihy: What was contested about that?

Marshall: I was fucking pissed because it was the coolest picture and it was just you two on a couch clearly big enough for three people. I was boxed out of it for some reason. They literally had me wait in the van. It’s not even like I was doing something else.
Herlihy: I don’t know if I can announce this because it’s pretty far out, but I am doing a runway event for next year’s fashion week. I’m actually walking for Nathan’s Hot Dogs, which is exciting.
Higgins: I’ll be there for Zyn, which is really cool.
Marshall: That’s awesome guys. I’m doing Powerade this year.
Higgins: Yeah, I heard, dude. Congrats, man.
Higgins: That’s a full meal, you’re right. That’s a total meal.
Herlihy: That’s girl dinner.
Higgins: I miss my boys, but it was fun getting back together and it feeling like we had just done this the other week or something. It was kind of just easy to jump right back in.

Marshall: We also, in many ways, had just done it the other week, because we were still touring together all summer and spending a lot of time with each other, which was fun. Now I’m feeling like I really miss you guys, because you guys have been all over the world.
Higgins: I’m in Vancouver right now.
Higgins: Shooting the rest of Scrubs season two.

Herlihy: Yeah, but that’s just because I’m evading law enforcement. You’ll hear about it soon. I don’t know how much of this I’m allowed to talk about. Interpol is up my ass. No, it feels like it’s the same as it always was working together, except the only difference is now we’re not banging our heads on Tuesday at 4 in the morning. We’re doing it at J.Crew at 4 in the evening.

Herlihy: It was pretty similar. Definitely it being a fashion thing felt like we had a little more liberty to take swings with the look. J.Crew had referenced JFK Jr. Me and the DP, Andy Kugler, referenced The Apprentice, the movie. But it was the same as it always is. Like SNL, we were in a rush because the photos went long, but it was awesome.

Marshall: To give Martin a compliment, I think that you did a really good job of making it feel like a more elevated, stylized version of what we normally do. I think it looks artful and cool, while not being too serious.
Herlihy: Thank you, Ben. That’s very, very sweet.
Higgins: I was going to say the exact opposite. No, I love it. I totally agree with that compliment, so we’ll split that compliment.
Marshall: Double compliment?
Higgins: A double compliment, but also shout out to the music underneath.
Marshall: Martin, you wrote and recorded that all yourself.
Herlihy: I taught myself how to play every instrument in a jazz quartet and that’s how I did that.
Herlihy: I’m walking around in jeans and no shirt most days.
Marshall: Fucking sunburned to hell.
Marshall: Style icons. John, who would you say yours is? I feel like yours is like a middle school literature teacher maybe.
Marshall: Cartman? From South Park?

Higgins: I’ll just kind of geek out on a brand for a long time. Recently, I’ve been wearing a lot from this place called 33mm. I started wearing their shirts. A style icon? Flava Flav, I guess. Shirts by 33mm, big clock on my chest by Flava Flav.
Herlihy: It’s hard to beat Flava Flav. Buzz Lightyear?
Herlihy: I wear shirts that I’ve had since I was a child.
Higgins: You do have a lot of Mets shirts that look really cool from when you were a kid.
Marshall: Do you think that we have a future in the fashion industry?
Higgins: Whoa. We are the fashion industry.

items.title: Why This New Hublot Is My Favorite Watch of 2026
items.description: The older I get, the simpler my tastes are becoming. But don’t confuse simple with boring. Simple can be stunning—just look at this new Hublot.
items.author: Mike Christensen
paragraphs: The older I get, the simpler my tastes are becoming. But don’t confuse simple with boring. Simple can be stunning—just look at this new Hublot.

It’s mid-October; I’ve seen a boatload of new watches since the start of the year, and people are already talking unapologetically about Christmas plans, so I feel all right about making some “best of 2026” calls. I know there was a much more fun release from the brand just last month, but this Hublot Classic Fusion Tributo—specifically the one in yellow gold, but the white gold version is also fit—might be that watch for me.

I remember when I first tried on a Classic Fusion. It was in 2018, when Baselworld was still the king of the watch fair scene. I liked it because, unlike many watches, the dial was clean. There was hardly anything going on with the Hublot, and the porthole shape of the case and bezel hit different. There was a bit of AP Royal Oak sniffing around, but it was more stripped back and less showy. The casual nature of a sporty black rubber strap cozying up against the pimping gold case immediately felt quite me; like the horological equivalent of dressing for business up top, party down below.

I reckon this new Classic Fusion is the most complete version of the original ever made. The OG was a 1980 creation by a young Italian gentleman called Carlo Crocco, and the story behind the making of this watch is one of my favorites, and not just because it’s essentially the watch Hublot was founded upon.

When Crocco started working in watches for his family’s company in 1969, he was tasked with “developing entry-level products," he says. But he had greater ambitions: he wanted to create more beautiful things. So in a fitting tribute to his wife Marie-Danielle, he decided to do exactly that.

Crocco's philosophy was simple: “To remove rather than to add.” With that in mind, he came up with a design that used twelve screws to hold it together while also telling the time. Who needs hour markers on a dial? Not Crocco. He wanted to make something innovative that kept the “classicism and know-how of the Swiss industry," he says, while “adding something different and special to it."
Thirty-eight years prior to my first Baselworld, Crocco walked up to that same fair to debut his new creation (the MDM stood for “Marie-Danielle Montre,” montre being watch in French).

Vacheron Constantin’s distributor in Italy told the designer, “You are crazy!” according to Crocco. Meanwhile, Cartier’s director came by and said, "This is the product we should have had," says Crocco. The timing of the watch's release was crucial, though. Many Swiss watchmakers were freaking out about the Quartz Crisis—the arrival of the new more-accurate and easier-to-mass-produce technology in 1969 decimated the luxury industry in the '70s. “We arrived at that moment with a high-end watch equipped with a Swiss quartz movement," says Crocco. "It was the ideal time to introduce a new model.”

Fast forward to 2026, and only one of those directors was correct. Without the Classic Fusion, Hublot wouldn’t be the disruptive powerhouse it is today. Its willingness to combine the precious luxury material with a rubber strap may seem old hat today but it's only because Hublot kickstarted the movement more than four decades ago. And this new tribute version brings back the MDM logo on that polished black onyx dial at 6 o’clock, as well as the 12 screws that hold it together and tell the time. I’m all for the 38mm case (the OG was 36mm) as that size better fits my wrist, especially when a watch has lugs like these. But crucially, it is powered by an in-house movement indicative of how far Hublot has evolved technically in the past 46 years: the HUB1711 Manufacture Self-winding Caliber, with 50 hours of power reserve.

“Minimalism by design” and “horological depth” are two things Hublot CEO Julien Tornare holds in high regard, and this tribute has both in abundance—honoring Crocco’s original not “by freezing it in time, but by keeping it in motion," Tornare says.
My review is in: 10/10 for pure, unadulterated simplicity that's never boring.
This story originally appeared on British GQ.

items.title: Billie Eilish & Finneas Are Collaborating Again—This Time, on a Jewelry Collection
items.description: John Hardy x Billie Eilish & Finneas
items.author: W Staff
paragraphs: John Hardy x Billie Eilish & Finneas

John Hardy is expanding on its relationship with Academy and Grammy Award-winning siblings Billie Eilish and Finneas. The musical duo was announced as John Hardy creative partners last year, but now they’ve surpassed the traditional role of brand ambassador by designing a jewelry collection in collaboration with the house. The Billie Eilish and Finneas collection was created with an emphasis on sustainability. It was designed using more responsible materials, including reclaimed metals, and made in production facilities powered entirely by renewable energy. As far as design, the collection represents a study in the contrast and complement of Eilish and Finneas’s personal styles. It is built around two personas: the understated wildflower and the bold and industrial screwball. The flower motif is represented throughout, rendered in sterling silver, lab-grown diamonds, and pearls. The screwball-inspired pieces, meanwhile, introduce a minimalist edge with sculptural chain links and spherical hardware evocative of piercings. While distinctive, the two styles are meant to be worn together in order to emphasize the tension between the delicate wallflower and the utilitarian screwball. The Billie Eilish and Finneas collection is available now at John Hardy stores, select retail partners, and johnhardy.com.

Henry Zankov is busy. Not only did the designer just present his debut collection for Diane Von Furstenberg alongside the latest for his eponymous brand at New York Fashion Week, but he also designed a collaboration with Banana Republic. Comprised of 27 pieces, the limited-edition, unisex capsule reflects both brands’ approach to craft and detail, offering unexpected pieces made from high-quality materials.

This is Zankov we’re talking about, so of course knits are the cornerstone of the collection. Brushed cashmere and wool yarns create sweaters of vivid stripes and Fair Isle patterns. Zankov looked to the Banana Republic archives when designing the capsule, and one leather and suede-paneled pencil skirt finds its origins in a 1986 style of similar construction. Leather pops up elsewhere in a burgundy bomber jacket and on the collar of a car coat. Accessories round it out with a selection of reversible hats, colorful socks, and scarves. The pieces are simple but exciting, bright and joyous, and inherently grounded in the languages of both Banana Republic and Zankov. The collection ranges in price from $90 to $600 and will be available to the public at select Banana Republic stores and online at bananarepublic.com starting October 20.
Patek Philippe Gondolo Ladies First

Patek Philippe has launched six new Gondolo Ladies First watches. Rendered in bright hues with sophisticated gem settings, the styles recall the original 2009 design while updating it for today. The collection redefines Patek Philippe's relationship with its female clients, offering an easy-to-wear jewelry watch that balances modern and vintage appeal. Set with hundreds of diamonds and offered in white and rose gold cases, the Gondolo watches are rich in detail but free of excess, the perfect accompaniment to a woman’s everyday wardrobe.

Thanks to Ugg and JW Anderson, you won’t have to choose between warmth and style this winter. The two brands have come together to present two of Ugg’s iconic styles—the Classic Boot and Tasman—with a JW Anderson loafer twist. The shoes were designed around JW Anderson’s signature shoe style, and the result toes the line between comfort and class. Motifs from both brands can be seen in the offerings, with JWA’s construction and Ugg’s signature materials both on display.

“Uggs are instantly recognizable, and I was interested in seeing something so familiar through the lens of JW Anderson,” Jonathan Anderson said. “For me, collaboration is about experimentation, bringing two distinct points of view together and seeing where that leads. We’ve explored the loafer extensively at JW Anderson, not only as footwear but also through its details applied to bags and ready-to-wear. I wanted to see how that language could translate into Ugg.”

The offerings are unisex and available in three colorways selected by Anderson: chestnut, khaki, and orange. They are available for purchase in stores and at jwanderson.com and ugg.com beginning October 15.
Christie’s and Boucheron’s Ode to Jewels

The storied jewelry brand Boucheron was founded nearly 100 years after Christie’s held its first auction in 1766. Despite the age gap, however, the two companies both hold rich histories and a sense of legacy within their respective industries. So it only makes sense for them to partner up on a new project—an exhibition created in collaboration between Boucheron and Christie’s called Boucheron: In Focus—A Monograph of a Visionary. On view in New York City from October 9 to 18, the show features over 80 creations drawn from the jewelry house’s heritage, past, and present. In Focus is divided into four sections that speak to Boucheron’s roots, codes, and inspiration: architecture, nature, couture, and innovation. Highlights include Human Being making its American debut, as well as the brand’s newest high jewelry Carte Blanche collection, which will be open to the public as well. “Our history with the United States goes back much further than our physical presence there,” Hélène Poulit-Duquesne, CEO of Maison Boucheron, said in a statement. “The first American clients appeared in Boucheron’s order books as early as 1865, and in 1903, Louis Boucheron opened an office in New York to maintain these close ties. And yet, it was only in 2024 that we opened our first American boutique, on Madison Avenue. This exhibition marks an important new milestone in our American journey.” For more information, click here.
Lady Harcourt’s foliage tiara.
Cartier’s Into the Wild Collection

Cartier is kicking off Tilda Swinton’s tenure as an ambassador for the high jewelry brand by making her the face of its newest collection. The Scottish actor models the over-the-top pieces of Cartier’s new Into the Wild offerings. Swinton shows off five creatures, whose stylized heads are rendered as extravagant rings, necklaces, bracelets, and earrings. A diamond-encrusted tiger gnaws at her finger, while an emerald-eye crocodile eats its tail as a bracelet clasp. The pieces toe the line between realism and abstraction. The animals’ likenesses are clear, but their bodies are distorted and graphic. The Cartier panther, for example, looks to have been stretched from its neck, elongated into a sleek bangle. Elsewhere, it perches on a clock face as the keeper of time. There is a whimsical beauty imbued in the collection, which is likely why Swinton, with her enigmatic grace, was chosen to represent it. She artfully crawls towards the camera like the crocodiles that adorn her neck and finger, embodying the strength of character and freedom of spirit exemplified by the jewels.
Moncler’s Re/Icons 2026 Collection

Moncler is revisiting four iconic styles from the brand’s past and reinterpreting them for a new era. Set around the theme of “Pioneers in Moncler with Extraordinary Dreams,” this year’s Re/Icons collection remains rooted in the mountains and Moncler’s pioneering foundation. Designs from as far back as the 1950s center the brand’s adventurous spirit and connection to iconism, cementing Moncler’s place in alpine history.

The collection features reimagined versions of the Karakorum, Verone, Himalaya, and Tibb. The Karakorum was originally designed in 1954 for Achille Compagnoni and Lino Lacedelli as part of the Italian expedition that achieved the first successful ascent of K2, the world’s second-highest mountain. Fast-forward a few decades for background on the Verone, which gained popularity in Italy in the ’80s when the puffer jacket became part of the metropolitan uniform. But this season, the Re/Icons collection expands beyond outerwear. For the first time, Moncler is also offering a collection of full looks, including windbreakers, T-shirts, pants, and skirts, as well as accessories. Cozy beanies and silk-twill foulards are available, as well as titanium and leather sunglasses inspired by vintage climbing goggles. Every individual piece is updated in a way that makes it feel relevant in the 21st century while maintaining its place in both mountaineering and fashion history.
Rob Roth’s Blondie T-Shirt

Artist and designer Rob Roth has launched a series of limited-edition, one-of-a-kind T-shirts at Dover Street Market New York. The first of the series features images of Debbie Harry, captured by Blondie cofounder Chris Stein. Roth reimagines the photographs through a collage-driven approach that blends art, photography, and fashion with a punk sensibility. The patch-working also acts as an homage to William S. Burroughs, a friend of both Stein’s and Harry’s. Burroughs was known for using “the cut-up method,” a technique in which he snipped and rearranged existing text to create unexpected combinations and meanings. In a similar vein, Roth has brought together two separate images to create a fresh composition: a reinterpretation of Stein’s photography through Roth’s distinct visual perspective. As Roth said in a statement, “Sometimes, you have to turn the frame upside-down.”

Roth sourced vintage T-shirts for the project, which he then sliced up and sewed together in new ways; this makes the garments another extension of the cut-up process. Each piece was finished with minimal embellishments and found objects. All of this means no two tops are alike. “This series of collectible, wearable art is a T-shirt lover’s dream,” said Harry. The shirts are available in limited quantities now at Dover Street Market New York.
Banana Republic x La Ligne

Banana Republic and La Ligne have solved all your fall wardrobe worries. The two brands teamed on a 36-piece collection, which brings a fresh perspective to fall classics. The collaboration centers on functional pieces that can not only build upon each other, but also fit into an existing wardrobe. La Ligne’s three cofounders drew inspiration from the Banana Republic archives, reinterpreting many mainstay elements with contemporary proportions and a rich, fall-adjacent color palette. Of course, La Ligne’s signature stripes are present in an array of shirts, sweaters, and accessories. There is also an emphasis on outerwear, represented by a nubuck barn jacket, belted suede wrap coat, and cape trench. Finally, sweaters—a cornerstone of both brands—are plentiful, with offerings rendered in soft cashmere and chunky cotton. It’s all about the classics done right. The Banana Republic and La Ligne collection is available now at select Banana Republic stores and online at bananarepublic.com.
Givenchy By Sarah Burton’s Shark Pinch Boot

For fall/winter 2026, Sarah Burton reworked (and renamed) Givenchy’s iconic Shark Pinch Boot. The new design elongates the original, bringing it thigh-high, while added “pinch” hardware at the top hearkens back to accessories introduced in Burton’s first season with the brand. Still, the unmistakable boldness of the original shape remains at play. The boot simultaneously embraces the leg while creating a unique and sculptural silhouette. The style has already become a celeb favorite. Anya Taylor-Joy wore the footwear while promoting The Super Mario Galaxy Movie in March, and Ariana Grande donned a custom, embroidered pair on the opening night of her current tour. Finally, you can stick your feet in them, too. The Shark Pinch Boot in its many variations is available now in-store and online at givenchy.com.
Polo Ralph Lauren’s Polo Blaze Bag

Polo Ralph Lauren has launched a new bag just in time for fall. The Polo Blaze bag is named after the white marking on a horse’s face from the forehead to the nose. With sculptural lines and distinctive hardware, the piece represents a bold reimagining of equestrian spirit for the Polo Ralph Lauren woman. The bag is elevated yet effortless, crafted in moto-inspired leathers. The smaller top-handle option is prim and ladylike, while the wider, small-shoulder variety provides a bit of edge. The large shoulder version, finally, balances downtown edge with heritage elegance, providing a new, modern take on a work or travel tote. All three Polo Blaze bags are available now on ralphlauren.com.
Omega Speedmaster 38mm Update

Omega is sharpening up its Speedmaster 38 mm with seven new references that bring the compact chronograph closer to the house’s iconic Moonwatch. The refresh swaps oval subdials for rounded ones, pares back the dial text, and adds a chunkier bezel and Moonwatch-style bracelet. The lineup ranges from classic black-on-steel to icy blue, mother-of-pearl, and two-tone gold versions, with two diamond-set options for a little extra flash. Consider it a cleaner, more polished take on one of watchmaking’s most recognizable silhouettes. For more info visit omegawatches.com.
Dilara Findikoglu’s Bridal Capsule

Alt brides, rejoice. Dilara Findikoglu has released her first-ever bridal capsule. The wedding-ready pieces fit seamlessly in Findikoglu’s Victorian-inspired oeuvre, with the lingerie-adjacent designs mirroring existing signatures from the designer’s collection. Never one to follow rules, Findikoglu said she wanted to take part in the ritual of weddings, but aimed to do so in her own way. The result is a collection comprised of just eight ruffle- and ribbon-covered pieces. There’s a lace-up mini dress, honeymoon-worthy bra-and-panties set, and a sophisticated, tailored look perfect for the courthouse bride. A pink mesh dress adds a girlish touch—ideal for those eschewing white—for the fashionable bridesmaid, while a classic corset can easily be recycled following the nuptials. The collection is available now on dilarafindikoglu.com.

Pearl jeweler Mikimoto and fashion label Chrome Hearts have reunited on another collaboration, two years after their first in 2024. Born from a shared appreciation for craftsmanship, individuality, and timeless design, the collection unites Mikimoto’s pearls with classic Chrome Hearts motifs and metalwork. The five pieces from the first collection, previously rendered in white gold, are now available in 22-karat gold hardware with Akoya pearls and natural diamonds. Two drop earrings, a bracelet, a safety-pin brooch, and a necklace offer traditional jewelry with an added edge, balancing refinement and rebellion in a collection that feels authentic to both brands. Mikimoto x Chrome Hearts is available exclusively at Chrome Hearts Aoyama; Mount Row in London; and the Mikimoto stores in Ginza, New York, and Hong Kong. Also, for a limited time, well-heeled shoppers can peruse the goods via private appointment at Chrome Hearts Cannes and St. Barths.

Now you don’t have to dig through secondhand bins to mimic Hailey Bieber’s laid-back denim style. Any fan of the model knows she loves a vintage Gap jean, and she has officially teamed up with the clothing brand to make her favorite, effortless styles available to all. Introducing: The Hailey Jean, a limited-edition denim capsule that reimagines Gap’s designs through Bieber’s lens. The line is inspired by that effortless ’90s look, as well as the Gap silhouettes Bieber champions in her day-to-day life: the Extra Baggy and Low Rise Loose. Updated fit proportions usher the pieces into the 21st century, while six custom washes allow for an array of styling options. Bieber’s personalization of the jeans continues with the addition of a “1996” design detail referencing Bieber’s birth year, and the model’s signature printed inside the pocket lining. “Gap has been a part of my wardrobe since I was a kid, so this came together very organically,” the model said in a statement. “Nineteen-ninety-six was the year I was born and I get a lot of style inspiration from the ’90s because there was something so effortless about that era and the way people wore denim.” The Hailey Jean launches on July 16 online and in select Gap stores.

Former creative director of Marni, Francesco Risso, is going accessible. The designer just released the fall 2026 collection for Gu, his first as the creative director of the Uniqlo sister brand. The collection marks a turning point for the label, introducing a new design approach built around six lifestyle concepts. Together, these wardrobes—minimal, classic, playful, utility, sport, and cozy —represent the way people live today. Each one outfits a specific character, while encouraging combination in order to create the perfect personal style. The classic line features nostalgic, ’70s-inspired pieces, reinterpreted through a modern lens, while the playful offerings introduce colors and patterns that allow for radical expression. Among all of the pieces, there is truly something for everyone.

“What interests me most about clothing is its ability to accompany life,” Risso said in a statement. “The wardrobe of today needs to feel grounded and accessible, yet also leave space for imagination, individuality, and play. The six lifestyle concepts are an attempt to reflect that reality; everyday dressing can be both practical and expressive, familiar and surprising.” The collection has already started to roll out, and will be available in full in stores and on gu-global.com on July 24.

Pandora is launching a new multiyear creative platform, Pandora Wonders, which will explore a distinct material annually. Up first, freshwater pearls, placed front and center in a whimsical collection co–created by British stylist Harry Lambert. The charms take on the shapes of ice cream cones, mushrooms, squids, and more, all rendered with one-of-a-kind freshwater baroque pearls. That makes each piece a collector’s item, as no two pearls are the exact same. They were chosen distinctly for their shape—because they resembled the body of a rocket ship or the head of a mouse—and are finished with 14-karat gold-plated details and crystals for added sparkle. “I’m such a fan of pearls, so I’m thrilled to bring a renewed sense of childlike delight and nostalgia to Pandora’s unique world of charms,” Lambert said in a statement. Per usual with Pandora, the charms can be worn in a multitude of ways: on necklaces, bracelets, hooked onto hoop earrings, and more. Pandora Wonders will be available in select stores and online at Pandora.net on July 9, 2026.

Balletcore and gorpcore unite in one of the most unexpected footwear collaborations of the summer. Beloved French shoe brand Repetto is transforming classic Birkenstock silhouettes that scream more girly girl than outdoorswoman. Think the classic Boston sandal with its rounded toe, but this time topped with a little bow and finished off with a satin ribbon to be tied up the ankle and calf. The metal buckles of the Arizona, meanwhile, are replaced by oversized rounded ones, and completed in monochrome. Finally, the Opéra offers the most Frankensteined option, melding the two brands together into a rounded, closed-toe shoe with two delicate top straps and a graceful laced bow. All styles are offered in three colors—black, pretty pale pink, and very cherry red—in suede, matte, and patent leather, and boast gingham inserts for an added girly touch. The Birkenstock x Repetto collection will launch on July 16 on 1774.com, repetto.com, and at selected retailers worldwide.

Converse is a classic for a reason, but even classics can stand an update from time to time—and Collina Strada is the perfect brand to inject a little bit of zest into your sneakers for the summer. Converse x Collina Stada reimagines the Chuck 70 with a playful lens, adding texture, embellishment, and color to the high, low, and even knee-high silhouettes. Gems, lace, charms— nothing is off limits in this collab, which features multiple colorways, from cutesy pale yellow and pinks to more Gothic black. The styles already walked the runway—both at Collina Strada’s September 2025 and February 2026 New York Fashion Week shows—but now they’re finally available to buy, at collinastrada.com, converse.com, and in select retailers.

The international retailers continue their quest to make designer brands more accessible, and now, it’s time for Mango and Eckhaus Latta to team up. The two labels have released a summer collection that marries Eckhaus’s experimental nature with Mango’s universality, bringing the cult favorite New York brand to the masses. Denim shines with foil finishes while sheer fabric pops up in dresses, tops, and skirts. Paillettes dangle from the detachable belt of a diaphanous shirt, and braided leather is woven into totes and handbags. Eckhaus Latta’s ethos is absolutely there, guided by the hand of Mango, and the result is a wardrobe that will keep you cool (in both senses of the term) all summer long. Mango x Eckhaus Latta is available now on mango.com.
Bad Bunny and Zara Present Benito Antonio

The budding relationship between Bad Bunny and Zara has finally reached its peak. After wearing custom looks by the retailer to both the Super Bowl and the Met Gala this year, Bad Bunny has switched from customer to designer, creating a 150-piece capsule with the brand. Inspired by Bad Bunny’s identity, the collection is named after the Puerto Rican performer, who was born Benito Antonio Martínez Ocasio. Ocasio worked with his longtime creative director, Janthony Oliveras, on clothes that fit distinctly within the musician’s point of view. Graphic tees in an array of colors, patchwork boxer shorts, zip-up hoodies, and baseball caps comprise the majority of the collection, which is just begging to be worn throughout summer. A double-breasted blazer and an array of more casual button-downs will make going into the office this July a little more bearable. Benito Antonio is comprised of everyday essentials, but with details that make it unique. Patterns clash, pinks shine bright, and the slogan, “The only thing more powerful than hate is love,” which he declared during his historic Grammy win, encapsulates the joy in these clothes. Benito Antonio is available now at zara.com and in select Zara stores worldwide.
Tiffany & Co.’s Sixteen Stone Solitaire Diamond Ring

When Raye wrote the lyrics, “I would like a diamond ring on my wedding finger,” we can only imagine she had Tiffany & Co.’s Sixteen Stone Solitaire Diamond Ring in mind. The piece is the newest expression of Tiffany’s storied Sixteen Stone collection, continuing an evolution started by Jean Schlumberger in 1959. The classic X motif is featured throughout the ring, creating the illusion of diamonds held together by metal threads. In the center sits a solitaire stone, available in 2 to 2.99 carat sizes, and set with a basket of X-shaped prongs. Crafted in platinum and 18k yellow gold, the design is perfect for everyday wear or saved for special occasions.
Louis Vuitton Nicolas Ghesquière Soho Pop-Up

Louis Vuitton is paying homage to its beloved artistic director, Nicolas Ghesquière, with a pop-up-store-slash-exhibition in New York City dedicated to him. Located in Soho, the space features a curated retrospective of Ghesquière’s iconic ready-to-wear looks from throughout the years, all available for purchase. In addition, a separate gallery spotlights various styles of Ghesquière’s Petite Malle, originally introduced in the fall/winter 2014 show. The mini-exhibition aspect is emphasized by large screens in the center of the main space that project archival footage from runway shows of the collections on view, ranging from spring/summer 2019 to fall/winter 2025. It is truly a celebration of Ghesquière’s Louis Vuitton, and it’s open to the public from now through early June.

Your summer footwear solution is here. Isabel Marant and Havaianas have come together as brands from distinct cultural universes to create a limited-edition capsule of two flip-flop styles. First, there’s a reinterpretation of Havaianas’s classic design, now finished in red and tan tie-dye. Those who want something a bit bolder will gravitate toward the all-new Havaianas Puffed, a bold flip-flop that emphasizes volume and comfort alongside style. Black and white designs are finished off with puffer-like straps, studded with metal embellishment for additional edge. Though flip-flops, these shoes will undoubtedly fit in just as well on the city streets as on the beach, allowing for a relaxed, yet elevated addition to your summer wardrobe. Havaianas x Isabel Marant launches on Friday, May 22, at select Havaianas and Isabel Marant stores around the world as well as on both isabelmarant.com and havaianas.com.
Balenciaga x Manolo Blahnik

The heels featured in Balenciaga’s fall 2026 collection—a brainchild between the fashion house and Manolo Blahnik—can finally be yours. Three styles make up the capsule collection, inspired by pieces from the Manolo archives and chosen by Pierpaolo Piccioli. The silk-satin shoes are offered in both slingbacks and mules at 105mm and 55mm. The designs are all rendered in black with injections of butter yellow, emerald, and violet, hues that feel both quintessentially Balenciaga and Manolo Blahnik.
