A hand-embroidered, asymmetric crystal leaf ornament tops every pair, and negates the need for additional jewelry. “This collaboration came to life for very personal reasons,” Piccioli said in a statement, adding matter-of-factly: “I simply like Manolo. That’s it.” The collaboration is available online now at balenciaga.com and in select stores.
Louis Vuitton’s Color Blossom Watch

Louis Vuitton is continuing its expansion of the Color Blossom collection, officially adding timepieces to the fine jewelry line. The new watches capture the design signature and colorful expression of the house’s iconic monogram flower, placing the sun-shaped emblem at the center of the design. The pieces are offered in four versions, including one that boasts a mother-of-pearl dial, steel case, and light beige strap. Other varietals add color in the form of pink gold and yellow gold cases, amazonite dials, and the most glamorous option set with nearly a carat of diamonds. All offer an elegant, refined look, allowing the piece to sit at the crossroads of jewelry and watches.

“We wished to reinterpret an iconic jewelry collection, presenting a women’s timepiece with a jewelry spirit,” said artistic director at La Fabrique du Temps Louis Vuitton, Matthieu Hegi. “With the mother-of-pearl or hardstone dials, or a diamond-set case, there is also an inherently precious essence, which perfectly reflects the Color Blossom collection.”
Audemars Piguet x Swatch Royal Pop Watch

Watch purists, look away. As more and more fashion brands continue to dip their toes in high/low collaborations, it only makes sense for the watch industry to follow suit. And based on the excitement and lines forming outside the Swatch store almost a week ahead of the release, the market is absolutely there for the new Audemars Piguet x Swatch Royal Pop Watch.

Fine watchmaker Audemars Piguet has teamed with Swatch on the Royal Pop, a new collection that combines AP’s iconic Royal Oak design with the modern and colorful Swatch Pop watch. The Royal Pop is a pocket watch, produced in eight eye-catching colors. The piece features design elements of the Royal Oak: an octagon shape and bezel with eight screws. The front of the watch is pretty sleek, but a flip over reveals an explosive back with the “Royal Pop” logo emblazoned in large letters. Three calfskin lanyards of varying length and a small removable strap allow the piece to be worn around your neck, on your wrist, in your pocket, or attached to your bag as another charm next to your decaying Labubu. Basically, however you dream of styling this piece, you can achieve it. That is, if you can get your hands on it. The Royal Pop will be available on May 16 in selected Swatch stores. Likely, they’ll be sold out not long after.
Jacques Marie Mage by Haider Ackermann

Jacques Marie Mage’s commitment to artisanal precision meets Haider Ackermann’s singular vision to bring us a special collection of limited-edition eyewear. The three frames represent Ackermann’s fashion instinct, as well as the polish and sophistication for which he is known. Simple yet resonant, the pieces are made for standing out in the best way possible. Titanium and acetate options offer sleek accessorizing, while leather-wrapped versions of two of the designs add sumptuous texture. “We have a mutual passion for what we do, and a mutual appreciation for a non-compromising approach to design,” JMM founder and creative director Jérôme Mage said about himself and the Tom Ford designer. “We really bonded over that commonality, the idea that design is a presence in every part and phase of your life.” The collection is available now at JMM Galleries, jacquesmariemage.com, and select retailers worldwide.
Givenchy’s Voyou Bucket Bag

There’s a new It bag on the horizon. Givenchy has released the Voyou bucket bag, which takes its name from French slang for a mischief-maker. The Voyou is chic yet practical, with biker-inspired finishes on a leather drawstring bag perfect for daily use. The piece is crafted in calf leather with a fine grain and glossy finish. A top handle as well as adjustable, over-the-shoulder and crossbody straps allow for versatility of wear, while a generous central compartment invites the wearer to toss in all their daily needs. With a pull of the drawstring, the bag’s shape transforms, creating a unique triangular silhouette that fits comfortably on the arm. The Voyou is offered in ivory, light pink, chocolate, or black leather with gold-finish hardware, and in cobalt blue leather with silver-finish hardware. It is avail

items.title: This Startup Is All In on Recursive Self-Improvement. Its Latest Model Is Scary Good
items.description: For the past few days I’ve been testing an impressive open-weight AI coding model called Flint. It suggests that fully recursive self-improvement, or RSI—an exciting and controversial approach that uses AI to build AI—is getting closer.
items.author: Will Knight
paragraphs: For the past few days I’ve been testing an impressive open-weight AI coding model called Flint. It suggests that fully recursive self-improvement, or RSI—an exciting and controversial approach that uses AI to build AI—is getting closer.

Flint is the first offering from Recursive, a company that aims to use RSI to advance both AI itself and other areas of science using AI. “Nearly every aspect of the entire model pipeline was actually done and improved upon by AI,” Recursive CEO and cofounder Richard Socher told me.

Socher says his company used its recursive AI system, dubbed the Eureka Machine, to automate most elements of the model’s development. This enabled a company with a handful of researchers to build a world-class model in just a few months, he says.

Socher told me that the Eureka Machine devised a number of innovations, including a new way of training the base model, new model architectures, and code optimized for specific silicon chips. Recursive shared benchmark scores that suggest Flint outperforms other models of similar size and architecture on coding tasks.

AI is already widely used to help build, test, and improve AI thanks to its amazing coding skills. This can speed up the process of refining a model and testing new ideas without the need for as much input from humans.

It is also possible to create a loop through which AI decides what improvements to make and then begins another round of improvement. For the moment this technique is limited, but if AI can contribute to every aspect of model development, then the process could theoretically continue indefinitely.

Some experts worry that letting AI improve itself in this manner could ultimately lead to disaster. These doomsayers claim that AI capable of improving indefinitely could escape human control and might decide that humans are an impediment to its goals.

Those concerns gained wider notice this September when a researcher quit Anthropic and warned that advances in AI, including recursive self-improvement, could lead to human extinction within a few years—a concern then echoed by a number of other experts. The idea of RSI has become so controversial that several bills in Congress propose to ban it.
Recursive sees these fears as more sci-fi than reality and believes legislation to prevent RSI is an unnecessary impediment to progress.

Socher says Flint was built using a system incapable of escaping human control. He says the goal is for the Eureka Machine itself to achieve full recursive self-improvement, but this would still be overseen by humans who could stop the process if it goes awry. “We hope that this shows people that indeed we have all the steps in place” to build such a system, he says.

Recursive has raised $650 million at a $4.65 billion valuation from Google Ventures, Greycroft, Nvidia, and AMD Ventures. Socher was previously the chief scientist at Salesforce, and his cofounders include Jeff Clune, a professor at the University of British Columbia who researches ways of building AI systems capable of learning indefinitely.

I must say I am impressed with Flint. I tested it on a Mac with 48 GB of RAM—a healthy amount but only enough to run a modest-size AI model like Flint, which has 40 billion parameters. The biggest models out there have several trillions of parameters, and they can only run on racks of industrial servers.

I used Flint to build a bunch of programs and found it to be both fast and very capable. In my experience, models of this size can be annoyingly error-prone or slow compared to Claude or Codex, but Flint nailed my coding requests every time. I used it to create a command line to-do list, then tried having it build a program that scours the web for interesting research related to recursive self-improvement. I also had Flint whip up a simple website that explains how RSI works. You can see that here.

It’s unclear how much progress other US labs have made chasing recursive self-improvement, but some published work suggests fully recursive systems are already feasible. A team from Microsoft, Carnegie Mellon University, and the University of Virginia recently published work, for instance, showing how an AI coding agent can recursively improve itself by modifying the software harness that turns reasoning into useful action and its own model’s weights.

Perhaps there are risks to full RSI if you are close to building a godlike intelligence, but for the time being it seems like a very promising way to improve your own AI models. This is something I’ve dabbled with in previous editions of AI Lab.

Indeed, Socher says the approach used to build Flint could make cutting-edge AI more accessible. “It's the only way this very small team can produce a model that's actually better than any other model in its class,” he told me. “This will hopefully show people that [recursive self-improvement] is actually quite nice and will benefit a lot of people.”
This is an edition of Will Knight’s AI Lab newsletter. Read previous newsletters here.

items.title: Jensen Huang’s Vision for Europe Runs on Plug-In Data Centers
items.description: Jensen Huang outlined his vision of Europe’s future at Nvidia’s global conference in Berlin on Wednesday. It consists of robotics, AI agents, and modular data centers, with Nvidia unsurprisingly powering it all.
items.author: Tom Bristow
paragraphs: Jensen Huang outlined his vision of Europe’s future at Nvidia’s global conference in Berlin on Wednesday. It consists of robotics, AI agents, and modular data centers, with Nvidia unsurprisingly powering it all.
“To be part of this AI economy, you don’t want to just be consuming the AI. You want to be producing the AI,” he told the 4,000-strong crowd at Nvidia’s GTC. “We can do all of that here in Europe.”

The last GTC, held in San Jose, California, in March, was all about AI inference and more efficient compute. Seven months later, the focus has switched to power, agents, and physical AI. There were even some cute little Microduck robots—made by recent Nvidia acquisition Hugging Face—doing Huang’s bidding at the end of his 90-minute pitch.

Huang’s first big announcement was a modular “AI factory” called the DSX Pod. It is a “plug-and-play” option for building AI data centers, with everything arriving already assembled in a large metal container and packed with Nvidia’s latest Vera Rubin compute racks. It can be brought online in 14 days, instead of taking months or years to construct. That may come in especially handy in Europe, where infrastructure projects are notoriously slow. Huang said the DSX Pod would also slash the amount of time compute sits idle in a data center as it will come online quicker. “This is a complete transformation,” he said.

The speech, delivered at Berlin’s Tempodrom, a venue inspired by a circus tent with the lighting of a gamer’s den, veered between selling laptops and sweeping predictions, with Nvidia presented as the fundamental technology provider to every industry. At one point, two Greenpeace protesters stood up and unfurled a banner reading “Clean up your dirty business.” Huang told his security team to “Go easy” as they were marched out.

Humanoid robotics will be the “next great industry,” Huang said, arguing that Europe was well-placed to lead on it due to its manufacturing heritage. But physical AI goes way beyond robotics, Huang pointed out, explaining that even telecom operators are adding Nvidia GPUs to their cell towers. He also announced partnerships with European carmakers VW and Mercedes on AVs.

Nvidia is making a similar move in humanoid robotics, with Huang announcing the launch of a full-stack robotics platform to standardize configuration. It also plans to release a preconfigured reference robot, Agile One, available in the first quarter of next year, to help developers start building physical AI systems. “This is your great opportunity,” he said.

On model usage, Huang predicted: “Every company in the future will use both closed models as well as open models that you customize.” He showcased Nvidia’s own open-source models as hitting frontier performance once customized on an organization’s proprietary data.

He also predicted that agents would mean there will be more users of software tools than ever before, and said agents’ reasoning, iteration, and tool use are pushing token consumption and demand for computing—and Nvidia GPUs—higher.
In case the 90-minute speech was too technical, it ended with an AI-generated Eurovision song summing up what Huang had just announced. The speech was easier to follow, to be fair.

items.title: This Preamp Costs More Than a Fancy Sports Car
items.description: In the world of hi-fi, there’s “high end,” and then there’s Goldmund. Since 1978, the Swiss manufacturer has produced exquisitely designed, astonishingly high-performance and staggeringly expensive audio equipment. As it nears half a century of proudly uncompr
items.author: Simon Lucas
paragraphs: In the world of hi-fi, there’s “high end,” and then there’s Goldmund. Since 1978, the Swiss manufacturer has produced exquisitely designed, astonishingly high-performance and staggeringly expensive audio equipment. As it nears half a century of proudly uncompromised engineering, its determination to position its products as credible alternatives to jewellery, art, or other pricey indulgences for the superrich shows no sign of abating—quite the opposite.

I was recently invited to Goldmund's headquarters in Geneva, Switzerland, to experience the new Mimesis Statement, the company’s flagship analog preamplifier. Goldmund's HQ, incidentally, features the sort of high ceilings, generous use of concrete and glass, and fanatical tidiness that puts me in mind of a Bond villain who's decided to devote their time to audio gratification rather than global tyranny.

In a traditional stereo chain, a preamplifier takes the low-level signals from your source gear, handles volume and input selection, and feeds that clean signal to a power amp to drive your speakers. Most people use an integrated amplifier, one that combines pre-amplification and power amplification in the same box.

Those who want to take things to the next level often separate pre-amplification and power amplification into two boxes—to keep the precious audio signal away from any electrical activity that might compromise its integrity. Goldmund, naturally, is convinced that a preamplifier alone needs to occupy three separate boxes.

The first box, the one with the buttons, dials, and display, houses the pre-amplification electronics. It’s where your source equipment—turntable, network streamer, whatever you fancy—connects using the generous selection of balanced and unbalanced inputs. The other two boxes are external power supplies serving the left and right channels of your stereo signal.

Goldmund reckons this radical separation, along with painstaking internal architecture featuring complete symmetry, voltage regulation stages, and optimized heat dissipation, guarantees signal integrity and utterly consistent operating conditions in all circumstances.

It’s apparently not enough to make a preamplifier with such a low total harmonic distortion figure (0.0002 percent) that it’s extremely difficult to measure in the first place. No, it has to be housed in three chassis with mirrored-glass displays, metal-coated controls, and Goldmund’s signature slender gold-line design flourish to confirm its identity.

In the US, the Goldmund Mimesis Statement analog preamplifier costs $240,000. No, I didn't accidentally add a few zeros. We’re already into “fairly fancy European sports car” territory here, but a preamplifier by itself doesn’t constitute an audio system. For the Mimesis Statement to do its thing, it needs a music input signal, which it will output to a power amplifier. From there, it goes to a pair of speakers.

Thankfully, Goldmund offers plenty of options. During my listen to the Mimesis Statement, it is connected to the company’s Eidos network streamer (yours for $27,000) at one end and a pair of Thelos 9800 power amplifiers (nearly 800 pounds per amplifier, 1,560 watts per channel, an imposing aesthetic, and $500,000 each) at the other. The amplified signal then moves to a pair of Theia Passive four-way floor-standing loudspeakers ($215,000 for two). That’s a total system price of $1,482,000—not so much “sports car” as “very nice apartment, probably with a balcony.” And I haven’t even added in the price of cables.

What does all that money buy you? Well, it most certainly buys a distinctive industrial design language, attention to detail and precision where fit and finish is concerned that’s beyond OCD, hand-soldered circuit boards, military-grade alloys crafted using established Swiss watchmaking techniques, and the sort of overall physical presence that’s more commonly associated with the stuff they build at NASA.

But can a stereo system possibly be worth $1.5 million? The answer has to be “no.” I’ve been a part of the audio equipment appraisal process for over two decades, and I know full well that the law of diminishing returns kicks in long before you’ve spent six figures, let alone seven. But Goldmund isn’t selling you a hi-fi any more than Rolex is selling you a wristwatch—it’s selling you an unmistakable symbol of status, wealth, and success. It’s selling you exclusivity. It’s selling you what it sincerely believes is the pinnacle of artisanal engineering.

And it’s also selling you a serving of detailed, tremendously insightful, and eloquently communicative sound. I am not a prospective Goldmund customer, but if I had the disposable income, I really think I might be.

items.title: Andrew Shue and Marilee Fiebig Are Engaged
items.description: One month after former Good Morning America hosts T.J. Holmes and Amy Robach got married, their ex-spouses announced their own major relationship milestone. On Wednesday, Andrew Shue told People that he and Marilee Fiebig are engaged.
items.author: Olivia Craighead
paragraphs: One month after former Good Morning America hosts T.J. Holmes and Amy Robach got married, their ex-spouses announced their own major relationship milestone. On Wednesday, Andrew Shue told People that he and Marilee Fiebig are engaged.

You remember this drama, right? In 2022, Holmes and Robach developed an HR-nightmare relationship while hosting GMA3 and being legally married to (but separated from) other people. Shue and Fiebig were those other people and, in what I truly believe to be a life-affirming twist of fate, wound up in a relationship of their own.

“You don’t know how you meet the person who’s right for you,” Shue told People. “It just happened. And you can say how it’s just this kind of freak luck that this is how you ended up getting to know that person in a way that would allow you to reveal yourself and for her to reveal herself. And this just happened to be a circumstance that allowed for that.” Shue added that he and Fiebig came together “in a time where we both needed a friend.”

How amazing is it that this actually worked out for everyone involved? I don’t want things to get awkward, but I kind of feel like Holmes and Robach deserve an invitation to the wedding. It’s only polite to invite the people that introduced you to your spouse.

items.title: Unpacking Val Chmerkovskiy’s DWTS Drama
items.description: Last week, Dancing With the Stars pro Jenna Johnson was lightly reprimanded by judge Carrie Ann Inaba for breaking a “no lifts” rule in her samba choreography. Somehow, this mishap kicked off a week of controversy in the DWTS community, mostly focused on Johns
items.author: Olivia Craighead
paragraphs: Last week, Dancing With the Stars pro Jenna Johnson was lightly reprimanded by judge Carrie Ann Inaba for breaking a “no lifts” rule in her samba choreography. Somehow, this mishap kicked off a week of controversy in the DWTS community, mostly focused on Johnson’s husband, fellow DWTS pro Val Chmerkovskiy. After Inaba’s comments, Chmerkovskiy joked (?) to his fans that they “almost saw Fresh Prince enter the ballroom last night,” which was widely interpreted as a threat of physical violence against Inaba. Several apologies later, Chmerkovskiy is on a temporary suspension from the show, and his dance partner, Jenna Dewan, got a new pro for “Dedication Night” on Tuesday. How did we get here? Let’s dive in.
This all started with Harry Shum Jr. and Jenna Johnson dancing the samba.

On the October 13 episode, “Super Bowl Night,” Shum and Johnson performed a samba to Usher’s “Yeah!” Because Shum is literally a professional dancer, they smashed it. However, toward the end of the dance, two male dancers came onstage and lifted him by his arms and launched him into a backflip. It honestly looked pretty cool:

During the judging, Inaba criticized the dance for not being enough of a traditional samba, pointing out toward the end of her feedback that “there was a lift” — which is not allowed based on ballroom and Latin dance competition rules. Inaba doubled down, pulling out a piece of paper and reading the show’s definition of a lift: “Any movement during which one of the dancers has both feet off the floor at the same time with the assistance or support of their partner.” Despite the violation, she ultimately gave the pair an 8 out of 10, which is a very good score.
Chmerkovskiy tried to come to his wife’s defense.

This probably should have just ended there and we could have all moved on to “Dedication Night” in peace, but that was not the case. On October 14, Chmerkovskiy posted a message to his TikTok story that read, “You almost saw Fresh Prince enter the ballroom last night,” referring to when Will Smith slapped Chris Rock at the 2022 Oscars and told him to keep his wife’s name out of his mouth. He also commented on a TikTok about Inaba’s criticisms, writing, “Puts some respect on her name. Shes trippin talking to her like that.”

Inaba didn’t see the initial post, but it came across her desk eventually. In a since-deleted Instagram post on October 15, she shared a screenshot of a “Page Six” story about Chmerkovskiy’s comment and captioned it, “So this is what we are doing now?” She also thanked “Page Six” and Entertainment Weekly for “bringing this to my attention.”

Obviously, DWTS fans were upset by Chmerkovskiy implying that he was going to slap Inaba. On one Reddit thread, viewers called his remark “disgusting” and that it should be a “fireable offense.” “I actually don’t even care if she was being bitchy or doing a bad job, joking about slapping a woman is wrong,” one commenter wrote.
Chmerkovskiy apologized to Inaba.

Following the backlash, Chmerkovskiy shared an apology to his Instagram Story on October 15. “I want to apologize from the bottom of my heart for my recent post,” he wrote. “I have reached out to Carrie Ann to apologize directly and personally, and I also want to apologize publicly as I understand my words affect so many outside of our internal DWTS family.”

Chmerkovskiy wrote that he “should have never made the reference” and that he “deeply” regretted it. “I recognize that I am in a fortunate position to have a platform and to be a role model to some, and I need to treat that with more care by actively pausing to think before I post to ensure what I am sharing aligns with who l am, and who I want to be for you all,” he continued. “I am truly sorry to Carrie Ann, and everyone who I hurt with my careless post. I will do better moving forward.”
But he still got suspended from this week’s episode.

On October 17, Deadline reported that DWTS had given Chmerkovskiy a one-week suspension from the show as a result of his comments. In a statement, DWTS producer BBC Studios said, “The well-being of everyone who works on Dancing with the Stars is non-negotiable. Val’s social media post was inappropriate and does not reflect the values or standards expected of anyone connected with the show. As a result, he will not participate in next week’s show.” People reported that Chmerkovskiy’s suspension was not a result of an HR complaint from Anaba, which some outlets had previously reported.

In response to his suspension, Chmerkovskiy released another statement in which he attempted to clarify his initial comments. “In a moment where my instinct was to defend my wife, I made a poor decision to reference a meme to ‘keep my wife’s name’ out of the conversation, without stopping to think through what else that reference could imply, which was genuinely never my intention,” Chmerkovskiy said. “Carrie Ann certainly didn’t deserve to get caught in the middle of my bad judgment, and I hate that she was.”

“The last thing I want is to become a distraction from an important week or from the incredible work my dance partner Jenna Dewan is putting in,” Chmerkovskiy said. It was, unfortunately, too late for that.
Jenna Dewan did the Viennese Waltz without him.

The show must go on! Tuesday night’s episode opened with co-host Alfonso Ribeiro briefly addressing the situation, saying, “As you can see, Alan Bersten is with Jenna Dewan because Val is not with us this week.” (Bersten, who was previously paired with Giada De Laurentiis, was voted off earlier in the season.) During their rehearsal, Bersten told Dewan, “I know it’s a really unusual situation, but I feel so honored to be able to step in and help you.”

It was “Dedication Night,” so Dewan and Bersten performed a Viennese Waltz set to “Unchained Melody” as an ode to Dewan’s mother. The judges were effusive in their praise, with Inaba calling the dance Dewan’s “ultimate breakthrough.” Dewan and Bersten wound up in second place for the evening, receiving 37 out of 40 points. Inaba gave them a perfect 10.
Chmerkovskiy will be back next week.

What happens then? I don’t know. They have to address it in some capacity, right? Or will they just sweep it under the rug and Inaba will have to judge him and Dewan as if nothing happened? Appropriately, next week is “Horror Movie Night.” What’s scarier than having to address the consequences of your actions head on?

items.title: Cara Delevingne Writes Her Own Story
items.description: All month long, Bustle’s annual The Entertainers Issue is celebrating the performers and creators who lit up our screens and beyond in 2026.
items.author: Jillian Giandurco
paragraphs: All month long, Bustle’s annual The Entertainers Issue is celebrating the performers and creators who lit up our screens and beyond in 2026.

In her decade and a half as a top model and actor, Cara Delevingne has had to embody all kinds of characters. But in 2026, she embraced her most revealing role yet: musician. After years of teasing her talents — like lending backup vocals to Fiona Apple’s “Fetch the Bolt Cutters” — Delevingne finally put her voice front and center with her debut album, Not Normal. “It wasn’t an easy three and a half years, but also it kept me sane. I’m so grateful for music in that way,” Delevingne, 34, says of writing the record. “I’m such a protector of the craft. Why it took me so long to even venture into it is because I wanted to be in the right place to be able to do it.”

The “right place,” she explains, is sobriety — the journey to which she viscerally captures on Not Normal. Even in the streaming era of genre fluidity, the album defies categorization. Co-produced by BJ Burton (Charli XCX, Bon Iver), Not Normal translated Delevingne’s loneliness and disorientation into a controlled cacophony of screeching synths, clanging drums, and unpredictable melodies that start on one plane and end on another entirely.

“It’s basically like having no skin and all the nerves are on the edge of you and you just feel everything,” says Delevingne, who recruited Severance cinematographer Jessica Lee Gagné for some of the album’s tense visuals. But Not Normal is hardly a downer, either: “Crazy, Baby” — a sweet love song to her partner, the musician Minke — has an irresistible hook straight out of ’90s alt-rock radio, while “Looking for You” is a burst of electro-pop delirium with credits from indie duo Sylvan Esso.

Delevingne is headed to the dance floor elsewhere this fall in Club Kid, the new A24 comedy-drama from Jordan Firstman. She plays Sophie, the business partner of Firstman’s Peter, whose hedonistic life as a gay party promoter is upended by the discovery that he has a 10-year-old son. After premiering at the Cannes Film Festival in May, the movie rose to the top of must-see lists and already has awards-season buzz. “I couldn’t be happier for Jordan. He really had a dream and kept pushing it and doing it. It’s a reminder to keep dreaming, to really chase those dreams,” Delevingne says. “Even if they don’t work out, I just think it’s important to chase things in life. Even if mistakes are made, it just teaches you a lot about life.”
On why she waited to start her music career:

Not being a sober person, I was so all over the place, and was on the edge of so much self-hatred, that putting out music and people having judgment on that — I just wouldn’t have been able to handle it. Back then, I could just about cope with people telling me I’m not pretty or ugly or not good at acting, but I couldn’t deal with [scrutiny over my music]. I just wouldn’t have been able to hack it.
On the album’s genre-pushing sound:

I wanted this to sound like nothing else that exists, and I want this to come from a pure place of emotion: This is what I’m going through. Honestly, a lot of these songs were way crazier. We fully set sail, and then we were like, “Maybe we should draw it back in a bit.” But that was important because I felt like I was alone and going through something no one had ever gone through before — that’s a pretty selfish way to think of it, but that was how I wanted it to sound.
On reintroducing herself as a musician:

I 100% worried about [putting myself out there]. I just tried to focus on what I wanted to make and what was an accurate portrayal of that. Nothing like that has ever stopped me before, I suppose. I will never stop making art because of other people’s opinions. Imagine if artists stopped making music because of others’ opinions. It would be so bad. Even if it was going to be bad art to people, I’d rather make bad art than none at all. I have to create — it’s really important for me, for my psyche. If no one sees it, it doesn’t matter.
On the visual world of Not Normal:

I was confused by how the visual side of an album was done because I think a lot of people, specifically after Brat, were like, “What’s your color?” I was like, “I don’t know!” To me, this is multicolored. I just want to feel like I’m floating in space and things are happening around me — but space feels really empty, and this album doesn’t. I made a mood board for it with really abstract-looking photos. One of them was Jessica’s, and it’s a photo of a puddle, and in the puddle are clouds. I was using a lot of things where you don’t know if they’re real or not.

When I first started speaking to Jessica, I didn’t tell her a lot. She was not too keen about making a music video. She was like, “That’s just not something I’m interested in.” I just gave her the album to listen to. I always wanted to make a video of “I Forgot” into “Out of My Head.” They blend seamlessly into each other. She was like, “[What about] making a video of these two songs together?” I was like, “Wow, that’s so crazy. We’re on the same page.”
On working with pal Fiona Apple:

The verses of [“Need It”] were written through us sending pictures of Post-it Notes back and forth to each other, which is now a weird thing to think about. Why did we not just send a Notes app screenshot? But we were like, “I need to write this down on a Post-it Note and send it!” You can’t really hear her as much in the music, but she’s just been an inspiration to me as a person and as an artist. I absolutely adore her.
On getting involved in Club Kid:

Jordan [Firstman] and I met out at parties, I think in LA, which is so cliche. He said to me, “I have an amazing movie I’m making. I want you to play a role.” People say that a lot in LA, so I was like, “Sure.” And then he actually sent it to me, and I was like, “Oh my God, this is sick.” It was so cool and queer and different. Big Daddy was one of my favorite movies growing up, so a queer, druggie Big Daddy? I saw the vision. Jordan’s hysterical. He’s so alive. I was like, “If you can bottle this and put it into a movie, it’s going to be incredible.” And it is. [The opening scene] felt like a perfect capture in time of being in 2016.
On appearing in Taylor Swift’s “Patient Zero” video:

I remember hearing [the song] for the first time and going, “How long is it going to be until this song comes out? I can’t wait to have it on repeat.” I remember her calling me up with the idea for the video when I was driving home. She’s like, “I have an idea.” I was like, “OK!” I love working with friends. It’s the most incredible thing. But the scope of it, the idea, every single detail, the Easter eggs, all of it — it’s unfathomable how someone can do all of those things and do them so well. She’s a genius, she really is.

items.title: I'm The "Luckiest Girl Ever" But Can't Shake My Doubts About My Boyfriend
items.description: Q: I’m starting to think my boyfriend and I aren’t that compatible, but I’m also worried I’m self-sabotaging. We’ve been together for two and a half years and lived together for one. On paper, I should be the luckiest girl ever. He is incredibly kind, caring,
items.author: Sophia Benoit
paragraphs: Q: I’m starting to think my boyfriend and I aren’t that compatible, but I’m also worried I’m self-sabotaging. We’ve been together for two and a half years and lived together for one. On paper, I should be the luckiest girl ever. He is incredibly kind, caring, and funny. I have never been treated this well or felt this secure in a relationship. My friends and family tell me that I’ve hit the jackpot, but sometimes I can’t shake the feeling that something isn’t right.

For example, we disagree heavily on politics. Since we started dating, he has changed a lot of his views and even stated that he would take time to learn more about politics if it would make me happy. But something makes me feel put off and I wonder if he would have the same beliefs if it weren’t for our relationship. His friends share his original beliefs.

Another thing is work. When I met him, he was completing a master’s degree. Now, a year into his career, he often talks about quitting to do blue-collar work. I don’t have anything against that, but I am becoming a doctor, and he makes comments that I will be able to support him. I’d like to be able to take care of my parents and travel a lot, so I worry about him financially.
I’m torn because I do really love him and think he is an amazing person, but I don’t want to rush settling down (we’re 24). I just don’t know how to answer if he is the person for me. Please help!

A: This may not be a great comfort to you, but you are facing a very common problem. A lot of times, we believe we should only break up with someone if things are bad, rather than wrong, or even wrong-ish. That’s not true. You are allowed to leave a good situation, or even a great one. I often think about what author Cheryl Strayed wrote in her Dear Sugar advice column to five women who were considering ending their relationships. Her thesis? "Wanting to leave is enough.”

No matter what your family and friends say, a “perfect situation” may not be perfect for you. Unfortunately, you do not get a letter in the mail from the DMV when your relationship crosses the line and is too much work to be worth it. You won’t get a Partiful invite to leave him when the universe discovers that he is not The One. So, yes, you do have to pay attention.

However, I must tell you that your job in a relationship is not to ferret out whether it will last for eternity as quickly as possible. Your job is simply to understand whether you are sufficiently happy now. (A lot of heavy lifting, of course, is being done by the word “sufficiently.”)

What do you want — and expect — to get out of your time on Earth? In the words of Joan Didion, “Every day is all there is.” If your closest friend or your future child were questioning this relationship, what would you whisper in their ear?

Our happiness is not the responsibility of our partner. But how many days a year of feeling upset — or anxious or miserable or even just “off” — about a relationship are too many? Is it acceptable to experience five? What about 20? 150? (I think we can agree 150 is too much.)
Not all great things that can fit in your life are right for you. You don’t have to stay just because someone is good to you. In fact, that is actually the bare minimum.

Now, let’s get into some specifics. On the subject of politics, someone’s views are actually a direct representation of their values. Even “boring” stuff, like an opinion on where the city should build the new bridge, reveals what they care about. Will people be forced to move if it’s built in a certain neighborhood? Will it be built on the habitat of endangered species? What social services will get cut in order to pay for the bridge?

I think it’s fair to question the legitimacy of his new stances, especially because he’s saying he’ll read up on politics if that would make you happy, but he hasn’t actually done it. Is this same man going to suggest he would load the dishwasher if it would help you out around the house? I sure hope not!
And when it comes to money, it’s more than fair to not want to bring home the bacon for two — especially if this is a preference that he is voicing only through little comments or jokes.

Unfortunately, you do not get a letter in the mail from the DMV when your relationship crosses the line and is too much work to be worth it. You won’t get a Partiful invite to leave him when the universe discovers that he is not The One. So, yes, you do have to pay attention.

You do not need to figure this out now. Or next month. There is no hurry. You can enjoy the good parts of your relationship while continuing to encounter information that will help you decide either way. If you need to go, you will. You do not have to get everything right, certainly not the first time — and almost all of life is the first time.

So, how do you sift out the noise and see your life clearly? My advice to you is this: Make a firm commitment to trusting yourself in every possible situation. Take a jacket or leave it in the car? Trust yourself. Buy the concert tickets or wait until the day of? Trust yourself. Decline to be a bridesmaid to your toxic friend or spend your vacation days on her wedding? You know what to do.

You’re building a muscle. Tell yourself — even if you fear it’s not true — that you believe in your own abilities and insights. Know that even if you make a decision you later regret, you are capable of pivoting, and if necessary, surviving the consequences. You can always run out to the car and get your jacket.
It’s A Pleasure appears here once a month. If you have a sex, dating, or relationship question, fill out this form.

items.title: The Stars Of ‘Paranormal Activity’ Love “Scaring The Sh*t Out Of People”
items.description: The Stars Of Paranormal Activity Love “Scaring The Sh*t Out Of People”
items.author: Christina Amoroso
paragraphs: The Stars Of Paranormal Activity Love “Scaring The Sh*t Out Of People”
Travis A. Knight and Cher Álvarez are making their Broadway debuts in a new play filled with jump scares, and having a blast doing so — even though only one of them is a horror fan.

Broadway’s new thriller Paranormal Activity is the rare theatrical experience in which being surrounded by an audience that shrieks, gasps, and jumps in the middle of a scene doesn’t annoy — it adds to the fun. And its stars, Travis A. Knight and Cher Álvarez, love it. “I fear for my next theater contract because I’m going to be like, ‘Why aren’t you guys reacting?’” says Álvarez. “We love scaring the sh*t out of people.”
“When I put the flashlight on the shower curtain… some guy yelled, ‘Do it,’ as I was about to pull it open,” adds Knight of a recent show. “I was like, ‘I got you, bro. I’m about to do it.’”

Though it lives within the Paranormal Activity universe, Levi Holloway’s play, recently extended through Feb. 28 at the August Wilson Theatre, follows an entirely original plot: A young American couple, Jimmy and Lou (Knight and Álvarez, who shine in their Broadway debuts), have moved to London from Chicago in an effort to put some unsettling experiences behind them. But they, and the audience, soon discover the terror has followed them and is more intense than ever. As the show’s tagline goes, “Places aren’t haunted; people are.”

The excellent performances, sharp writing, inventive direction, and spooky sound and lighting add up to compelling theater, but the production’s unique — and jolting — dimension is the collective reaction of the audience. Along with 1,200 other people, you’ll find yourself gripped by fear one minute, laughing with relief the next. But don’t get too comfortable; the jump scares keep coming.
“It’s a f*cking riot,” says Álvarez. “It’s so dope that horror actually works onstage.”

Álvarez: You’ve got to keep it light. Our dressing rooms are on the same floor, so we’re f*cking with each other all the time, trying to scare each other. Music is also such a way in for me. I think what gets the most exciting is wondering, “What is going to be the personality of this audience that we have?” And that’s really where we go off.

But for me, the signing out is way more crucial — leaving all that stuff at the theater, not taking my work home. There have been times when Travis and I will go out onstage when everyone’s left the theater, and you’re just left with the ghost light. We just thank the space because you never know what kind of portal is out there. We had [famous paranormal investigator] Adam Berry come in and do a ghost tour — that theater’s very haunted, and I don’t need any of those ghosts coming home with me. It’s not what I’m into. But we keep it fun.

Knight: Agreed. As the whole opening monologue is being said into the audience and the curtain is coming up, I’m standing on the other side of the front door waiting for my cue light to turn off. Everything up to that moment is exactly what Cher said — it’s light, there’s a lot of joking around. But the moment I’m putting that key in the door, it’s like all systems go. Especially in that first scene, because you see this couple at their best, and this is the only time in this play that you see them like that. So if I can enter that space with a sense of play, with a sense of wonder, with the goal of trying to make Cher laugh onstage — not Lou — or to surprise her in some way, that to me is so fun.
On their own feelings about horror:

Álvarez: It’s just not for me at all. If I’m going to watch a scary movie, it has to be at, like, 9 a.m. I still have time to recover. Being in it and acting in it is so different from actually watching it and choosing to be scared. I just am a naturally stressed person and have very high cortisol levels, and I would just prefer to stress out with my own thoughts.
Knight: I love horror. I’m a thrill-seeker in that regard.
Álvarez: He wanted to be a ghost hunter — like a legit ghost hunter.

Knight: I was obsessed with ghosts in my late teens, early 20s. We found this old home video, one of the last times I was at my parents’ house in Madison, Wisconsin. It was a video of me, and I had gotten this ghost book on Christmas morning. We were at my grandparents’ house, and I’m sitting next to my sister, and my grandma’s there, and I am explaining the difference between demons and ghosts and all these things as my sister just thousand-yard stares off into the distance — so annoyed that I’m talking about it.

Anyway, I love horror, and especially in October, it’s my jam to get on the streaming services and look at the horror section. I love that feeling of pressure in the chest, chill down the spine, wondering what’s going to happen next. There was a French television series called Marianne that scared the hell out of me last year when I watched it. I also did one of Levi Holloway’s first plays called Grey House in Chicago, and that was my first experience doing a horror stage play. During the whole rehearsal process, I was like, “What the hell are people going to think about this play?” That was my first taste of, like, “Oh, there’s an appetite for this thing.”
On memorable stage-door interactions:

Álvarez: To have two people with no names starring, headlining a show like this on Broadway has been really cool. People are seeing themselves represented onstage, which is really f*cking awesome and dope. Hearing young Latina women who are also in this industry say, “You’ve given me a dream role” — that’s a huge feat for me. That feels like I can die tomorrow, and I’m very happy with that.
Knight: I always get a kick when people are like, “I kept turning to my husband saying, ‘That’s how we talk to each other. That’s how we talk at home.’”

I’ve only had one sort of out-in-the-ether experience that I still think about. This person came to me and said, “This show deeply affected me. Could you sign this box?” And they handed me a small gift box that was empty. It was like a little cube, and I had the Sharpie that they give us at the stage door to sign Playbills. I was going to use that, and then they were like, “No, no, no, use mine.” I was about to write something, and then they said, “Can you write to Jimmy, and then something about demons or heroin?” I said, “Something about demons or heroin? What do you mean?” “Just anything, like bad things,” they said. So I wrote, “To Jimmy, demons, and heroin,” on this box, and I handed it back to them and they said, “Now I need you to sign your name.” So I took it back and kind of scribbled my name — but it wasn’t really my name because I was like, “What in the black magic is this?”

Álvarez: I just started watching New Girl again as a comfort show. You have to be so mindful of how you truly are using your energy when you’re doing a show — any show, but specifically this kind of show, eight times a week, is incredibly demanding. And we’ve all been sick this past week, so you just have to lock in and really take care of you.

It’s also when I feel like I can actually eat. We’ve just ran a marathon, so you feed yourself. And cereal is such a comfort food for me — you get the crunch, you get the sweet milk at the end. Ooh-wee. It’s a whole vibe, specifically the healthy version of Cinnamon Toast Crunch, but I’m sure Travis is pounding back 39 grams of protein or something, I don’t know.
Knight: No, usually 60 to 70 grams.

Knight: That’s the time of day I am eating half of my daily calories. I come home and eat and will watch something or play a video game called Helldivers 2 with two of my friends. And I try to be asleep before 1 a.m., but sometimes it’s tough.

Álvarez: I’m all about self-care, so I’m like, “Where can I get a massage? Who can touch my head? I need my pressure points.” And honestly, watching a movie on a Monday is like, the best for me. God, it restores my faith in humanity. The last thing I saw was that super crazy film with Hannah Einbinder and Gillian Anderson, Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma. I loved it. It was so f*cking weird. The simpler my Mondays are, the better, but you very rarely get that.

Knight: Laundry, grocery shopping. I mean, that’s just it. You pack it all in one day. The number of times I’m like, “It’s 4 o’clock already? F*ck.” I freak out about the time, because how does it go so fast?
On lessons learned from playing a married couple:
Knight: Jimmy has taught me that if you just stop and think for five seconds of your life before you speak, you could save yourself a tremendous amount of problems.
Álvarez: Have you applied it?
Álvarez: Oh. Well, let us know how it goes.
Knight: But truly, there is something to that. I don’t know, be more mindful, bro.
Álvarez: For me, it’s to be honest with the person who you’re going to share your life with. And also finding play, finding laughter within a relationship — that’s absolutely crucial.

items.title: Isamaya Ffrench's Beauty Bag Includes A "Life-Changing" Sleep Essential
items.description: Don't Mess With Isamaya Ffrench's Beauty Sleep
items.author: Emma Stout
paragraphs: Don't Mess With Isamaya Ffrench's Beauty Sleep
The MUA shares her "life-changing" overnight essential, plus a look inside her surprisingly low-key beauty bag.

In Bustle’s Beauty Detail, we dive into the beauty bags of our favorite celebrities and talent for intel on the rituals that keep them glowing. Ahead, makeup artist Isamaya Ffrench shares her drugstore favorites, the one product she can’t stop collecting, and what she does when she’s off the clock.

A few days after speaking with makeup artist extraordinaire Isamaya Ffrench, news broke that caught the beauty world off guard: According to Business of Fashion, she had parted ways with ISAMAYA, the beauty brand she founded in 2022.

It was a tough day for anyone in love with Ffrench’s surrealist, often avant-garde approach to beauty. (After all, where else can you buy a penis-shaped lipstick?) In a sea of sameness, ISAMAYA felt like a world of its own — and it’s hard to imagine the brand without the visionary who defined it.

Then again, Ffrench’s vision has taken on many forms throughout her career. She’s transformed some of the most photographed faces into unrecognizable figures, from an elderly Zendaya to an elf-eared Irina Shayk. She’s turned animal prosthetics and crying Madonnas into high-fashion runway looks, and even ventured beyond beauty altogether with Studio Iron, a concept store devoted to housewares.

“I didn’t study makeup,” she says. “I got into it accidentally through art. I was doing sculpture and dabbling in special effects. Then I got asked to work on a shoot, and I realized there was a world in which you could literally paint faces for a living. I feel like I’ve kind of worked backwards. I started out very colorful and creative, and now I’ve refined my craft.”

As a judge for Instagram Rings — an award celebrating creativity among creators — Ffrench knows how important it is to step away every once in a while and follow your curiosity. “I don’t feel that creativity always comes from seeing something, being inspired by it, and wanting to make something similar,” she says. “It can also come from taking time out of what you do and having new experiences. Inspiration is everywhere.”

Post-fashion month, however, she’s sticking to her tried-and-true routine. “I’m just hanging out with my cats and going to reformer Pilates,” she laughs. “I feel like that’s quite boring, but I love alone time.”
Ahead, Ffrench gives us a peek inside her surprisingly tame beauty bag, from the brow pencil she hoards “like a kleptomaniac” to the drugstore cream that saved her skin.

“Some people love retinol, but I don't really use it. It’s too strong for my skin. Recently, I started using this Sali Hughes toner, and it’s absolutely incredible. It has salicylic acid, AHAs, and BHAs. I think great skin care that works for your specific needs is always worth spending money on.”

“I think a lot of people, myself included, have damaged their skin barrier. But using an emollient cream, like Doublebase or Eucerin, for a couple of weeks back-to-back can really help. Just stick to that and give your skin a break from everything else.”

“You can’t not have lip gloss in your kit. M.A.C.’s Lipglass is sticky as hell, but that’s why it’s so great. It stays put. When I’m doing models backstage, I know it’s not going to move around, and it has a very high-shine finish. I’m always using it on eyelids and as highlighter, too.”

“Brow pencils are another thing I always have in my kit. I feel like a kleptomaniac the way I collect them. I love Anastasia Beverly Hills — I mean, she’s the queen of brows. She has this incredible brow palette that I use every time I do a makeup look. Then, she has these fine-tip pencils that I also use for sculpting and lip lining. They’re just the best brow products out there.”

“Historically, I wore a lot of men’s fragrances because I wanted to smell hot. I thought, if I smell a man who’s hot, surely I’ll smell hot, too. But right now, I’m wearing Musc Miroir by Ormaie. It’s a modern musk, so it’s quite velvety and soft but also warm. It has that unisex quality I find really lovely.”

“Generally, I use all my tools and gadgets first thing in the morning. I’ll wear an LED mask in the evening, but in the morning, I’ll do EMS [Electrical Muscle Stimulation] or gua sha. It helps with the lymphatic system, and I feel a bit more snatched after.”

“If I’m having a bad hair day, I’ll just grease the hell out of it with a leave-in conditioning mask and throw it in a bun. One of my favorite masks is from Arkive, a brand that was set up by hairstylist Adam Reed. He also has a really great styling spray. You just give your hair a light mist before a blowout, and it holds really well.”

items.title: Zendaya, EmRata, & More It Girls Are Already Obsessed With Fall's Top Boot Trends
items.description: This Season’s Buzziest Boot Trends Serve Effortless It-Girl Energy
items.author: Alyssa Lapid
paragraphs: This Season’s Buzziest Boot Trends Serve Effortless It-Girl Energy
Zendaya, EmRata, and Anne Hathaway have already mapped out the playbook for your fall footwear.

Thank the fashion gods: Boot season is finally here. And if your favorite style stars are any indication, the vibe this fall is about the perfect mix of high-drama statements and wearable walk-everywhere shoes. Instead of running the same plain pairs into the ground, the girlies have been swapping them out for footwear that feels a bit sharper and instantly put-together.

Right now, over-the-knee boots are dominating the FYPs. From ultra-loose, slouchy styles to super-fitted, second-skin options, the Anne Hathaway-approved thigh-highs are a chic way to keep wearing minidresses even in the cooler months. Lace-ups are another fave, serving Victorian-era-heroine-meets-modern-cool-girl realness. Then there’s the knife-sharp pointed toe — while it might require a bit of dedication to pull off, it comes in so many options that it’s almost a disservice to your ‘fit to *not* wear it out.

Whether you’re headed to a fancy event or simply off to a pumpkin spice latte run, consider this your sign to lace up, zip up, and strut in this season’s chicest pairs. Your fall wardrobe depends on it.

Lace-up boots are nothing new — combat boots are basically a rite of passage at this point. But this season’s lace-up pairs are trading their classic rock roots for something a little more steampunk-meets-vixen. They come in sleek pointed-toe styles, sky-high platforms, or with lots of metal hardware that practically sparkles. Cynthia Erivo already gave them the red-carpet treatment, while Rosalía wore custom Miista pairs for her LUX Tour (now available to shop in a limited-edition run).

These are surprisingly easy to style, whether you want to lean into a punk look or go a bit more balletcore. The lace-up details aren’t limited to the front, either — look out for subtle side corsetry or ties along the back for a completely unexpected twist.

For anyone who is completely over towering high heels, the latest runway shifts are a welcome relief. Kitten heels have been trending for a hot minute, and they’ve finally made their way onto boots. The Fall/Winter 2026 runways of Prada, Ferragamo, and Celine proved that pretty much every silhouette is getting the low-heel treatment — think knee-high, ankle, slouchy, and embroidered options in just about every color imaginable.

Unlike their stiletto sisters, these are much more comfortable, allowing you to take them from your 9-to-5 to after-work drinks. Beyond the usual skinny heel, low cone shapes are also getting a ton of love among the style set. Emily Ratajkowski, for one, is already sold.

Nothing screams “I’m a baddie” more than over-the-knee boots. Everyone from Hollywood actors to pop stars is embracing the tall style, which made a splash on the Fall/Winter 2026 runways of Balenciaga, Chloé, Stella McCartney, and Valentino.

But don’t be intimidated by the height. The key is to play with proportions. While they pair well with a range of styles, these confidence boosters really shine with teeny tiny skirts or dresses. Hathaway’s billowy ruffled minidress paired perfectly well with her second-skin suede boots. Commit to the boot and own the drama.

A sharp pointed-toe boot is classic for a reason: It instantly makes an outfit more polished and fashion girl-coded. This season, the elongated silhouette gets a fresh spin with equestrian-inspired details, satin finishes, and unexpected textures. Basically, there’s a sharp boot for every aesthetic.
Need inspo? Pair them with a dress to allow the footwear to take center stage like Bella Hadid, or let their pointy ends peek under loose jeans for a more low-key touch.
You don’t need to own a bike to hop on the moto boot trend. The shoe — typically characterized by chunky lug soles and heavy metal accents — is enough to give any outfit an instant edge.

For an easy styling route, try pairing a buckle-clad set with your off-duty jeans-and-T-shirt combo. You can also opt for a chunky-soled pair like Zendaya and rock it with low-key utilitarian pieces for that effortless cool-girl vibe. Too hard-edged? There are pairs in lighter colors or with bedazzled buckles if you want to soften up the look.

items.title: 20 Last-Minute Halloween Costumes On Amazon For All Your Spooky Plans
items.description: 20 Last-Minute Amazon Halloween Costumes For All Your Spooky Plans
items.author: Victoria Montalti
paragraphs: 20 Last-Minute Amazon Halloween Costumes For All Your Spooky Plans
(And you can, of course, re-create Prime Video's Off Campus costumes too!)
13 Going On 30's Jenna Rink

Amazon sells a dupe of Jenna Rink's iconic party dress from everyone's favorite coming-of-age movie 13 Going on 30, and we couldn't be more grateful for the last-minute costume inspo. This Y2K costume is perfect for nostalgic gals, and especially those turning 30 this year! Accessorize with some butterfly clips, a sweet baguette bag, strappy heels, and you're all set to dance to "Thriller" in style.

We've been seeing tons of amazing vintage clown makeup tutorials on our feeds in the lead-up to Halloween, so we had to include a retro clown costume to match. This black-and-white set is spooky and sexy, and even comes with the pom pom hat and striped tights for a full head-to-toe look. Just add face paint and transform into your clown character.

We're expecting lots of Dolly Parton tributes this Halloween for the late, great singer. And while you can throw together any sparkly Western tops with flared pants, we think the most important part of the look is the hair. Luckily, this voluminous blonde wig is available on Amazon as the cherry on top of your diva-approved look.
The Nightmare Before Christmas's Sally

Is it a Halloween movie? Is it a Christmas movie? Also yes. However you classify it, The Nightmare Before Christmas is a classic and Sally is an icon, making this a tried-and-true costume. We especially love this set because of the light blue bodysuit with scar details that replicates Sally's skin (without having to put on body paint all over!).
Off Campus' Allie Hayes As JLo

Okay, we're getting a little meta here. You're not dressing up as JLo, but rather as Off Campus' Allie Hayes dressed as JLo for her own Halloween party. While many dupes of the iconic Versace dress won't arrive before Halloween, this luxe dress is ready to ship on Amazon, and can be re-worn on your next summer vacation.
Off Campus' Dean Di Laurentis as Top Gun's Maverick

Every JLo needs her Maverick... right?! The ultimate couples costume this year will be Allie and Dean dancing in the Prime Video Off Campus Halloween party scene. And this jumpsuit is pretty true to Dean's costume. Wear it with your partner or bestie for the best pop culture reference. Add some aviator sunglasses and combat boots for the full effect.

She was a fairy! Or an elf fairy! This Halloween costume is particularly perfect for romantasy book readers. Pick your favorite boho dress and add on these enchanting wings, flower crown, magic wand, hair tinsel, and elf ears for the most cost-effective and simplest yet impactful look.
Knicks Fan (or Jordyn Woods... or Taylor Swift)

Knicks in five! The Knicks finally took home the 2026 NBA Championship, but before that it was total basketball fan mania last season. Everyone repped their Knicks merch, but if you don't have any yet, here's your chance to cart some up. And to make it even more pop culture-y, add Jordyn Woods's lucky orange handbag or Taylor Swift's kitschy "Stevie Knicks" T-shirt to complete your costume.

If you can't wait to hear "The Dead Dance" this season, you should probably dress as Wednesday Addams for Halloween. This costume kit mimics the Netflix series' viral black tulle dress with a Jenna Ortega-esque wig, black accessories, and even the Thing hand for an extra spooky touch. Even better, it costs under $50!
Zara Larsson's Midnight Sun Era

2026 was Zara Larsson's year as her Midnight Sun era catapulted her career and made us all fans. While you can truly wear your favorite swimsuits and coverups, it may be a bit too chilly, so we recommend a matching skirt set in a sunset ombre. Further get the Midnight Sun look with vibrant and sparkly makeup, like this bold glitter gel.

Another classic costume that you can't go wrong with. Dress as Little Red Riding Hood in this stunning under-$50 dress. To get the full effect, add a woven basket. And to win your costume contest, fill it with Halloween candy and hand it out at your house parties and bar crawls.

One of the biggest films of the year was undoubtedly Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey. While there aren't exact costume replicas of Athena, Calypso, or Queen Penelope, we think any Grecian goddess costume will get the point across, especially if you're paired with your Odysseus.
Pirate (or Renaissance Maiden)

We haven't had a good old-fashioned pirate movie in a while, and we're craving it. So consider dressing as a badass pirate for Halloween with this costume kit. It's not too kitschy and feels more upscale. And if you remove the eye patch, you can re-wear the outfit for a Renaissance fair!
Dallas Cowboys Cheerleader
Even if you're not a football fan, you may be a Dallas Cowboys Cheerleader fan, especially after binge-watching Netflix's America's Sweethearts documentary series.
Pick up your pom poms, slip into white cowboy boots and channel the DCC girls' "Thunderstruck" energy.

Sure, you can be a Disney princess, but dressing as a villain or sidekick is typically more fun to channel. And whether you love the original book or the movie remakes, the Mad Hatter is a character primed for Halloween. This top-rated Amazon costume gives you a quirky head-to-toe look, including a top hat, bow tie, and over-the-knee socks.

Picture it: You're dressed as Anxiety from Inside Out 2 while Doechii's "Anxiety" plays in the background of your TikTok video. Instantly iconic. The character we love to hate makes for a quirky and cute costume for all the anxious gals out there. Just add brown flared pants for the complete look.

When all else fails and you can't put together a totally unique Halloween costume, channel your spiritual and spooky senses, and be a witch. You can quite literally throw on any black dress (we personally like this corseted midi dress) and a pair of fall boots for an effortlessly chic look. Then, add this witch hat, choker, and mesh gloves for a total transformation.

Summer 2026 was defined by the World Cup and sporty style. But one person went beyond the field, and took over our feeds: Erling Haaland. The Norwegian Viking, um, we mean soccer player, became famous for his terrifying height and speed, but mostly for his luscious hair and signature man bun. So if you have long blonde hair, you simply have to do this costume. Add your soccer jersey and you have an easy, funny 'fit.

Spoiler: Fiyero turning into the scarecrow in Wicked: For Good was one of the biggest plot twists for those of us who didn't see the Broadway show. And since we won't have a third November in a row of Wicked mania, we're soaking up our favorite characters this Halloween. To make this a couples costume, have your bestie dress up as Cynthia Erivo's Elphaba and re-create the "As Long As You're Mine" scene!

items.title: My New Fav Charlotte Tilbury Products Are On Sale For Amazon’s Holiday Beauty Event
items.description: My New Fav Charlotte Tilbury Products Are On Sale For Amazon’s Holiday Beauty Event
items.author: Victoria Montalti
paragraphs: My New Fav Charlotte Tilbury Products Are On Sale For Amazon’s Holiday Beauty Event

I recently attended a Charlotte Tilbury masterclass hosted by Amazon, where we got to try tons of OG and new products while re-creating Christina Aguilera's holiday campaign glam, taught by makeup artist Alex Rutkovskiy. While there were so many exciting products that I tried, I wanted to spotlight the ones on sale (so you can get the most bang for your buck and stock up on holiday gifts), plus share Rutkovskiy's application tips to get the prettiest, glowiest glam this season.
And right now, this makeup set is selling for under $25 on Amazon in both Pillow Talk and Super Nude, making it a great beauty kit refresh and even better stocking stuffer.

For the highlighter, which comes in seven shades (all on sale!), Rutkovskiy likes applying it to his hand first and warming it up with a brush. He then adds it to the high points of the face, like the cheekbones, nose, cupid's bow, and chin before applying extra product with his fingertips. "It helps to layer it. It looks very healthy and glowy with more dimension. Charlotte is the queen of the glow, so we love a glowing face." (He also called out how influencers complain about the packaging exploding in their makeup bags and purses, but that there's a simple open-and-close twist applicator. The more you know!)

We also applied the brand's Matte Revolution Lipstick in Pillow Talk with a lip brush, which isn't so much of a requirement for me. While that lip product isn't on sale on Amazon, the creamier K.I.S.S.I.N.G Lipstick is if you want an Aguilera-esque pout.

And the final step was my Holy Grail (aka lip gloss). Speaking on Plumpgasm, Rutkovskiy said: "There’s people who hate plumping glosses and people who are obsessed with them, and there’s no one in the middle." He added: "It’s such a beautiful formula, which combines heat and cool ingredients, so there's pepper and mint. It’s cold and hot at the same time. And it plumps your lips in the first three minutes." Rutkovskiy predominantly keeps the gloss at the center of the lips for extra dimension, but I definitely dowse my lips in the spicy, juicy formula, especially for late-night plans and holiday parties.
Note: If you aren't sold on all three products in the kit, you can find the Beauty Light Wand highlighter and Plumpgasm lip gloss sold separately and on sale too!

items.title: Find sun, surf and Californian modernism at a Ventura Beach house for sale
items.description: Architect Carl Maston completed this exemplary Ventura Beach house in 1984 for a former actress and her partner. The Susman house sits above the shore in the heart of California's surf culture, looking back at the grand sweep of the bay with its Channel Island
items.author: Jonathan Bell
paragraphs: Architect Carl Maston completed this exemplary Ventura Beach house in 1984 for a former actress and her partner. The Susman house sits above the shore in the heart of California's surf culture, looking back at the grand sweep of the bay with its Channel Islands beyond.
Step inside this Ventura Beach house, now on the market

The work of Maston (1915-1992) epitomises the aesthetic and spirit of midcentury California; his own house, completed in 1947, was subsequently owned by Ryan Murphy and then Dakota Johnson, and other local luminaries, including Ray Kappe, worked in his studio.

With Maston’s star riding high, this is a rare opportunity to acquire a late period work that embodies all of his architectural devices, set in an unbeatable location. Back in 1985, the house was extensively photographed by Julius Shulman, adding another layer of historical lustre to an already impressive project.
The ground floor living room
The ground floor dining area
Pacific views from the kitchen sink

This is the Susman House’s first time on the open market. The original owner, Tracy ‘Babs’ Susman, acted and modelled before studying town planning and working in local politics and environmental planning, with the occasional foray into film production.
The house was built on a plot once owned by her sister and brother-in-law, and her brief to Carl Maston was to keep the spirit of the traditional Californian cabin alive in a contemporary structure.

Maston went to town. The Susman House was one of over 40 he completed in the area during his career, but probably most dramatically sited of all of them. Pairing traditional cedar siding on the interior and exterior walls along with exposed brick flooring and fireplaces, Maston integrated large areas of glass for lightness along with hefty concrete foundations to anchor the structure into the coastline.

From the roadside, the 2,640 sq ft house is nestled between mature trees and only hints at the views and space within. A large sitting room adjoins a kitchen with bay views from the sink, with sliding glass doors that open out onto a spectacular terrace with 240 degrees of Pacific views.
Receive our daily digest of inspiration, escapism and design stories from around the world direct to your inbox.
It’s a spot that has long been favoured by surfers, including one of the sport’s pioneers, Mary Monks, who became closely associated with nearby Mondo’s Cove in the late 1950s.
The atrium and galleried landing
The atrium and galleried landing

Upstairs, there are three main bedrooms and a separate sitting area with balcony. All of these incorporate the slope of the roof to achieve high ceilings, walls of glass and Pacific views. A central atrium and landing is arranged around the brick chimney with internal glazed partitions bringing light down into the heart of the house.
The primary bedroom suite, looking back towards the landing
Primary bedroom suite and terrace

The house retains the modesty and feel of the original Faria Beach Colony, one of the classic Californian coastal retreats that began as a stretch of summer cabins in the years before WWII. As the original Shulman photographs attest, very little has changed in the four decades since the house was completed.
The first floor terrace off the primary bedroom
The second of three bedrooms
The family eschewed any extensive remodelling, keeping Maston’s architectural pristine and original as a testament to the fundamental rightness of the original design.
The Susman House is for sale through Shannon and Chuck Menzel at The Menzel Group priced at $5,100,000. More details at MondosCove.com

Jonathan Bell has written for Wallpaper* magazine since 1999, covering everything from architecture and transport design to books, tech and graphic design. He is now the magazine’s Transport and Technology Editor. Jonathan has written and edited 15 books, including Concept Car Design, 21st Century House, and The New Modern House, and co-edits the long-running things magazine weblog.

items.title: JORDAN FIRSTMAN - FANTASTIC MAN
items.description: The first-time director tries to keep his mouth shut
paragraphs: The first-time director tries to keep his mouth shut

Jordan Firstman (American, 35 years old, completely fabulous) might be familiar to readers from his brassy internet memes, or his brilliant leading role in ‘Rotting in the Sun’, 2023’s crime thriller set in sexy Mexico. Or from the news that his debut as a director ‘Club Kid’ (which he also wrote and plays the lead in) was heralded with a seven-minute standing ovation at Cannes earlier this year and triggered a fierce bidding war between the biggest studios in Hollywood. A star was born.

Because he does so much, Jordan often struggles with knowing what to call himself. Luckily, help is at hand from Luca Guadagnino, Jordan’s friend of close to ten years and the director of ‘I Am Love’, ‘Call Me by Your Name’, ‘Queer’, ‘Challengers’ and so many other cinema highs. Here, Jordan gets some handy life advice from his fellow multi-tasking director, who also photographed and interviewed him for this story. The following Q&A has been edited for maximum readability and pleasure. Ready?
From Fantastic Man n° 43 – 2026
Text and photography by LUCA GUADAGNINO
JORDAN — Did I get too sunburnt?

L — A little bit. You’re a bit red, like a lobster. One second, baby, that’s not the beginning of the interview. It should start this way: Okay, Jordan Firstman has always been at the forefront of the most up-to-date things: the most up-to-date behaviour, the most up-to-date public persona. You have been directly and indirectly commenting on the state of the world and making fun of it and finding a way to showcase your personality and individuality. Eventually this has allowed you to be perceived as who you actually are. Not many people succeed in that. How do you see that in the face of the way the world works right now, the way in which authority expresses itself, the way in which parts of the world are in flames but not for the right reason?

J — Well, thank you. That’s a compliment, I think. I’ve always just tried to go from the inside out, and I’ve always known I’ve had a problem with saying everything that was on my mind, and I think it took, from high school, about a decade to figure out how to say that in a way that worked for me and didn’t hinder me. I remember my high school theatre teacher told me that I had special powers, and he said, “But you have to use your powers for good and not evil,” because I think he saw me. He saw that I was capable of both.
L — What kind of evil were you capable of at that stage in your life?

J — I’m able and have since I was a kid been able to see through things and speak honestly about them. He saw that I’ve always felt a strong sense of justice, and when people weren’t treating me or my peers right, I would be outlandish.
L — Is this something that comes out when you deal with power, or people in positions of power?

J — Until very recently this is how I have felt with a lot of people, where I think there is something hidden in their actions. Maybe they feel like I’m going to corrupt the system they have made, so they want to take my voice or my thing away from me, and I often respond very strongly to that.

L — I don’t know anyone, or at least haven’t met anyone in the last ten years, who has been able to express themselves through so many different mediums and through so many different types of performance in the way that you do. Whether that’s movies, or YouTube videos, or TV, or acting as an actor or writing as a writer or directing as a director. Is it possible that it’s a sort of victimisation of the self that helps propel you?
J — I believe I have been very, very lucky, but also, you know, I had to go to the internet because I had eight years of trying to develop ideas for TV that I just kept hitting walls with.
L — But do you agree with me, Jordan, that if you’d had fame and success, let’s say at the age of 22, 23, 24, just after theatre school, you would have become a horrible person?
J — I think it wouldn’t have been great for me. I don’t know if I would have become a horrible person, but I think I would have potentially self-destructed.
L — It’s so important to understand that maturity and success are better allies than success and youth.
J — Well, they say youth is wasted on the young, do they not?
L — I agree. Do you like younger men, men your age, or older men?
J — I usually like my age or older. Young people just end up annoying you in some way or another.
L — Do you despise people that are not fit, particularly men?
J — Of course. I envy you for many, many reasons.
L — No, no, I think the only reason you envy me is my belly and my lack of muscles.
J — I like your belly. I mean, I like a belly. I think it’s a classic gay thing, too, where we like to feel a body with some fluff on it, but we don’t want it for ourselves. I like a bigger guy.

L — One day, many, many years ago – I was very young – I met David LaChapelle, and I shot a tiny little documentary about him that I never edited. It must have been 1994, something like that, and David was super fit, and I was, like, 23 and he said to me, “Listen, as a gay man, I make sure that I’m very fit, because I have to offer something that someone else will recognise as attractive to them.” Do you think these politics are still valid?

J — I think so. It’s not only gay men, though. I mean, maybe it’s not straight men, but I don’t know. I feel we’re at a place in culture where everyone is being objectified. Male movie stars are being objectified purely for their appearance in ways they never have been, which I guess is a good thing. It’s great for women to kind of reclaim that gaze, but then it’s also got some sides that are not so positive. Every- where you look in Hollywood, everyone is bone thin, or every guy is on steroids.
L — What happened to body positivity?
J — I think it ebbs and flows. Everything that was cool in 2019 became not cool in 2022 and then whatever was cool then became not cool in 2025. Things just move very fast now.
L — How many categories of men are there? If you had to take me on a journey through the labyrinth…

J — I’ve never subscribed to the whole “gay animal” thing. I think it’s very weird that we compare ourselves to animals. I don’t really understand that. A lot of people fall in between categories. I’ve always thought of myself as just a normal-looking gay guy.

L — When I met you, I thought you looked like a straight-acting gay guy. For a moment, I actually thought you were straight. Now I would say, first of all, you’re very handsome and very attractive, and it’s interesting because you’ve kept being so throughout the ten years that I’ve known you, which is great, so congratulations.
L — But I have to ask, would you see yourself in the otter category?
J — No! I don’t think I’m an otter, because I think of otters as a little thinner framed than I am. I think I’m a little bit bulky. I think I’m supposed to be… God wants me to be fat.
