items.title: Trump to America: I'll Only Do My Job if Republicans Win
items.description: Donald Trump is a transactional man. If you scratch his back, he’ll scratch yours. This worldview may be understandable for a businessman, which Trump was for many years. It is less understandable for someone who is, ostensibly, a public servant.
items.author: Jack Crosbie
paragraphs: Donald Trump is a transactional man. If you scratch his back, he’ll scratch yours. This worldview may be understandable for a businessman, which Trump was for many years. It is less understandable for someone who is, ostensibly, a public servant.
On the campaign trail recently, Trump has been offering voters a bargain. If they vote for Republicans, he’ll do his job. If they don’t — well, the American people just might be on their own.

The most explicit example of this is the president’s proposed “Trump dividends” program, which boils down to a straight cash gift of $5,000 to every American adult. Trump has been floating this idea, which would cost more than $1 trillion, since the GOP’s emergency midterm convention in a naked attempt to curry favor with reluctant voters. In recent days, however, he’s started applying the same quid pro quo concept to individual states, making open extortion schemes a regular part of his stump speeches.
Two days ago, for instance, at a rally in Kansas to try to buoy the campaign of Republican Senator Roger Marshall, Trump made this bargain explicit.

“With Roger Marshall in the Senate, we will make year-round E-15 permanent,” Trump said. “But if Adam Hamilton is in, I’m not doing it. That’s it. I’m only doing it for him. That’s a big deal for Kansas.”

The program Trump is talking about, E-15, refers to the sale of gasoline diluted with ethanol, a corn-based alcohol that is a major product of Kansas’ corn industry, which is vital to the state’s overall economic health. Usually, the sale of E-15 fuel is regulated by the government for environmental concerns, but the Trump administration has recently eased those regulations in order to bring down gas prices and give struggling corn farmers a boost. In essence, the deal offered here is simple: Trump created a federal program that made some Kansans’ lives easier. Unless they vote for his preferred candidate in the upcoming election, he’ll make it all go away.

This would be shocking if it were a one-time occurrence in a battleground state. Kansas is an unexpectedly close race, with Marshall, the Republican incumbent, facing an extremely stiff challenge from the Reverend Adam Hamilton, a Democrat. Hamilton is ahead in some polls, around 47 percent to 45, and the two candidates are set to debate Wednesday night for the last time ahead of the election. Kansas’ economic future, then, is certainly on the line.

But Kansas isn’t the only state where Trump is pulling this kind of open political extortion. A day later, on Tuesday night, he traveled to North Carolina, where families who live around the Camp Lejeune Marine Corps base have, for decades, been trying to get settlements from the U.S. government after being poisoned by toxic chemicals in their water between 1953 and 1987. There are still thousands of victims who are waiting for payouts from the federal government, with their cases tied up in Department of Justice red tape. Enter Trump’s bargain: if his party wins, those cases get swift resolutions. If his party doesn’t, well, it simply won’t be a priority.

In North Carolina, however, this is an almost impossible ask. Former Democratic Gov. Roy Cooper looks to be beating the pants off former RNC Chair Michael Watley, holding a 13-point lead in the latest polls. There are House races that the Republicans need to compete in there, of course, but there’s only so much the voters of North Carolina can do to preserve Trump’s trifecta in the House, Senate, and White House.

But like any gangster, the details of the extortion rarely matter to Trump. It’s all leverage and threats, carrots and sticks. The job of the president is to protect the people of the United States. Extortion, often, begins with a crook offering their “protection.” And just like any good protection scheme, many American voters may feel they have no choice but to accept.

items.title: Dolly Parton CMA Tribute: Sabrina Carpenter, Julia Roberts, Oprah and More Remember the Country Icon as the ‘Great Unifier’
items.description: Sabrina Carpenter, Julia Roberts and Oprah were among the stars who paid tribute to Dolly Parton during the Country Music Association’s celebration of the late country icon Wednesday night.
items.author: Payton Turkeltaub
paragraphs: Sabrina Carpenter, Julia Roberts and Oprah were among the stars who paid tribute to Dolly Parton during the Country Music Association’s celebration of the late country icon Wednesday night.

Oprah, who appeared in a pre-recorded video at the beginning of the broadcast, shared what Dolly meant to her. “We’re both Tennessee girls, and she represented to me the essence of being 100% who you see yourself to be. Authentic all the time, and I just loved her for it,” she said. “I love that she had such grace and such tenacity. I mean, listen, if she put her mind to something, that was it. And I love that she was so generous of heart and generous of spirit, and her presence here on Earth will be felt for forever because the spirit that is so strong that was hers is actually everlasting.”

Roberts, who starred alongside Parton in 1989’s “Steel Magnolias,” reflected on the experience of filming with the performer. “Dolly came into my life when I was in my early 20s, and it was magical to see someone so alive, so present,” the actress shared in a pre-recorded video. “She really was a shining example of remembering who you are, where you came from, and what it means to be kind. We love her.”

Katy Perry took the stage to remember Parton as a woman who “masterfully toyed with the power of her femininity.” “Devastatingly sharp and equally as sweet, she could read you for filth with a wink and a smile, and then make sure that your children learn to read too. That’s a mother,” she continued. “Beneath the decades of dazzle was an extraordinary generosity of spirit. Some called her the Great Unifier because she had this ability to bring people together from all walks of life, political perspectives and sexual orientations. She saw beyond those labels because she saw the humanity in everyone. For me, Dolly is the blueprint.”

Carpenter, who, before Parton’s passing, had collaborated with her on a remix of “Please Please Please,” said that the “I Will Always Love You” singer “meant lightness” as she began her recorded tribute. “She meant kindness, joy, quick comebacks, rhinestones, big hair, family, radiance, and love. I think Dolly was one of the only people on planet Earth that everyone could universally agree on, which I think is very special in any artist. But there’s nobody like Dolly.”

Carol Burnett, who first met Parton while filming the 1979 CBS television variety special “Dolly & Carol in Nashville,” recalled an early memory of the star while on set. “When I talk about thoughtful, I remember there was one night I was in my hotel room getting ready to go out to dinner to a restaurant, and there was a knock at the door, and I opened it, and there was Dolly with a home-cooked meal for me, so that I wouldn’t have to go out to a restaurant, and to top it off, that home-cooked meal was home-cooked by Dolly herself.”
Bono, Goldie Hawn and other stars also paid tribute to Parton during the show.

The special was a “joyful, emotional celebration of the artist, songwriter, entertainer, humanitarian and entrepreneur whose music and generosity carried her from the mountains of East Tennessee into the hearts of generations around the world, told through performances, archival footage and personal stories that trace her extraordinary journey to becoming one of the most beloved entertainers and philanthropists in American history,” per the evening’s official logline.
The singer-songwriter-actress died in August at the age of 80 following a “brief battle” with cancer.

Over the course of the evening, more than 20 performers took the stage, including Ella Langley, Lainey Wilson, Reba McEntire, Carrie Underwood, Vince Gill, Kristen Bell, Molly Tuttle and Carly Pearce, as well as Kelsea Ballerini, Brad Paisley, Zac Brown, Ashley McBryde, Bela Fleck, Kristin Chenoweth, Lady A, Ricky Skaggs, Sierra Hull, Little Big Town, Lukas Nelson and Darius Rucker.
The special aired live on ABC and Disney+ on Wednesday and will stream on Hulu the following day.

items.title: Netflix Stock Deflates to Two-Year Low. What Will It Take to Revive Revenue Growth?
items.description: Shares of Netflix hit a two-year low after the streamer’s Q3 2026 earnings report revealed an ongoing softening in top-line growth and a miss on advertising revenue for the full year.
items.author: Todd Spangler
paragraphs: Shares of Netflix hit a two-year low after the streamer’s Q3 2026 earnings report revealed an ongoing softening in top-line growth and a miss on advertising revenue for the full year.

The stock was down -7% in premarket trading Wednesday, to under $64/share, a decline of nearly 30% year-to-date to the lowest point since August 2024. It recovered a bit in regular trading but was still down for the day, closing -5.3% to $65.04/share Oct. 21.

Netflix’s Q4 revenue guidance was slightly below Wall Street expectations, and the company said ad sales for 2026 are now expected to be $2.7 billion, $300 million lighter than previously forecast, because of the slower-than-expected rollout of “some ad product capabilities.”
So how does Netflix recharge audience engagement (and therefore keep revenue pointed up) after a drop-off in viewing, particularly in the U.S.?

To Netflix co-CEO Ted Sarandos, the answer is better execution on its core model — that the company needs to crank up its buffet of buzzy, must-watch TV shows and movies. Last week he dismissed content chief Bela Bajaria, who’s being replaced by Peter Rice, as part of a larger overhaul of content leadership. On the Q3 earnings call, Sarandos praised Bajaria but said “I know that we could do better.”
Ahead of its Q3 earnings, Netflix also laid off 1,000 workers, 6% of its headcount, which execs have framed as giving it the ability to invest more into growth areas.

But some on Wall Street believe Netflix needs to do more than churn out TV and movie hits — that it needs a strategy to capture viewing of short-form video content, which is being soaked up by platforms like YouTube, TikTok and Instagram.

“[W[e think the Street should remain skeptical of a long-term strategy that simply sees NFLX double down on its legacy core strength (premium TV, films, and increasingly, live events), while NFLX remains largely absent from the fastest areas video entertainment growth (e.g., mobile, short-form),” New Street Research analyst Dan Salmon wrote in an Oct. 20 research note.

YouTube continues to make significant viewing share gains with an “all content types, all formats” approach on connected TV, Salmon wrote. While it doesn’t make sense for Netflix to adopt a straight user-generated content approach, he said, “we believe bold thinking is increasingly needed to address these long-term threats to NFLX mindshare with younger audiences.”

Pivotal Research Group’s Jeff Wlodarczak similarly cited concerns for Netflix that short-form entertainment “is doing to streaming what streaming has done to traditional Pay TV,” as younger consumers spend an ever-increasing amount of time on social media platforms. Following Netflix’s Q3 earnings report, Wlodarczak reduced his subscriber forecasts and increased programming cost forecasts, leading to a $5 reduction in his year-end 2026 target price on the stock to $65.

Meanwhile, Netflix once touted the addition of videogames as an extension of its core service as a promising growth driver — but games weren’t mentioned at all in its Q3 earnings, except that the company noted in its shareholder letter that it teamed up with Take-Two Interactive to unveil a sneak peek in August of highly anticipated title “Grand Theft Auto VI.”

But all of that said, with over 325 million global subscribers, Netflix remains well positioned to keep its core streaming business humming along nicely, albeit at a somewhat less rapid clip, according to MoffettNathanson analyst Robert Fishman.

“We continue to believe Netflix has significant headspace to push monetization of its leading SVOD scale, which should lead to compounding profits for years to come,” Fishman wrote in a research note. MoffettNathanson forecasts Netflix earnings per share to reach $3.85 in 2027 (down from $4.00 previously), growing by 21% in 2028 to $4.65 (vs. $4.80 previously). The analyst reiterated a “buy” rating on Netflix stock but lowered his 12-month price target by $10 to $90/share.

Also bullish on the long-term strategy was Wedbush Securities analyst Alicia Reese, who wrote in a note that “the details suggest Netflix isn’t beholden to industry headwinds; it is in control.” She noted, “Churn and pricing held up, ad demand is intact, Netflix is expanding its valuable live-events inventory, and it plans to preserve its content strategy rather than duking it out with YouTube on short-form.”

“Importantly, management’s tone underscored its intent to shift toward a platform model as it broadens its licensing partnerships and add-on deals, in addition to reaccelerating its ad rollout,” Reese wrote. Because Netflix still has “significant potential” to expand ad revenue, Wedbush analysts reiterated their “outperform” rating on Netflix but lowered the price target on the stock from $90 to $80/share.

items.title: Los Angeles Film and TV Shoot Days Keep Plunging As Local Officials Scramble for a Turnaround Plan
items.description: Filming in Los Angeles is continuing to slide despite California’s urgent bid to revive production in the region.
items.author: Winston Cho
paragraphs: Filming in Los Angeles is continuing to slide despite California’s urgent bid to revive production in the region.

L.A. saw a nearly 5 percent drop in shoot days from June to September compared to the same period last year and an 11 percent drop compared to the previous quarter, according to the latest report from permitting office FilmLA issued on Wednesday. The total is 36 percent below the five-year average, highlighting the fierce competition between states and other countries to host Hollywood.

The decline comes despite California’s expansion of its film and television tax credit last year, which increased the program’s annual funding from $330 million to $750 million and broadened eligibility to additional types of productions. Projects getting subsidies to shoot in the state accounted for a record 40 percent of on-location filming in L.A.. Since July 2025, 214 projects have been tapped to receive tax incentives under the expanded program, according to the commission.

While the credits are luring individual productions to California — like Tracker, which moved from Canada to L.A. for its fourth season — the latest figures suggest that it hasn’t reversed the region’s production downturn.
“Overall production remains far below where Los Angeles needs it to be, and crews and businesses across the region are feeling it,” said FilmLA CEO Denise Gutches.

Shooting for TV shows, a key source of work for L.A. crews, recorded 1,400 shoot days in the quarter, down roughly three percent from a year earlier. Drama production fell nine percent, to 494 shoot days, even as the number of days logged by dramas getting incentives more than doubled. Comedy production rose sharply, increasing 143 percent to 192 shoot days, with nearly all of the growth coming from productions receiving tax credits. Shows that filmed in the region last quarter include, Shrinking (Warner Bros. TV/Apple TV+), High Potential (ABC) and I Love LA (HBO).

Filming for features also showed a slight uptick, rising two percent year-over-year to 530 shoot days. But commercial production, which isn’t eligible for tax incentives, fell almost 16 percent. The category is more than 41 percent below its five-year average.
In a statement, L.A. mayor Karen Bass said the region is “seeing encouraging signs of progress” but that “we must do more.”

“That’s why I’m calling for an uncapped California film and television tax credit that includes more types of productions, along with passing into law our nation’s first federal film and television tax credit,” she added.

As California loosens its grip as the filming capital of the world, New York is drawing big-name titles at a much faster pace, according to industry tracker ProdPro’s quarterly snapshot released last week. The state saw a 87 percent increase in production spend in the quarter compared with California’s 17 percent uptick.
Next up: Will California ever change its program to allow above-the-line costs to qualify for subsidies, like the majority of regions that offer tax credits?

items.title: Fixer in Hollywood Smear Machine Scandal Spoke of Other Clients: Elon Musk, Jake and Logan Paul
items.description: Jed Wallace is the formerly mysterious Hollywood fixer who this year has been under an increasingly bright legal spotlight for his alleged role as a co-conspirator in a secretive industry smear machine meant to undermine and even destroy the targets of his cli
items.author: Gary Baum
paragraphs: Jed Wallace is the formerly mysterious Hollywood fixer who this year has been under an increasingly bright legal spotlight for his alleged role as a co-conspirator in a secretive industry smear machine meant to undermine and even destroy the targets of his clients.

Court records and other documents have shown that Wallace’s customers appear to have included Travis Scott, Rebel Wilson and Andrew Huberman, as well as the socially prominent Alexander brothers, who’ve since been convicted of sex trafficking. Now, new materials obtained by The Hollywood Reporter reveal additional high-profile names who he’s claimed have been part of his client portfolio: world’s-richest-man Elon Musk, plus Jake and Logan Paul, the influencer-entrepreneurs who are also known for their involvement in combat sports. (It’s unknown if Wallace has produced anonymous smear sites on their behalf as well.)
Neither Wallace nor the newly surfaced clients replied to THR’s inquiries.

In 2025, Blake Lively filed a since-dismissed suit against Wallace, 55, who’s based outside of Austin, for his efforts on behalf of Justin Baldoni, with whom she was then feuding over the director’s conduct during the filming of her starring role in It Ends with Us. She said Wallace’s business serviced “high-profile and high-net worth clients, including by contracting with other public relations and brand management firms to perform discrete work,” and that it specialized in “confidential and ‘untraceable’ campaigns across various social media platforms (including TikTok, Instagram, Reddit, and X) to shape public perception of his clients and their adversaries and to perpetuate those perceptions by, among other things, creating social media accounts with inauthentic users.” Wallace responded in court by describing his work as helping customers “navigate real-life human crisis, threats, trauma and mental health concerns” when they “find themselves unjustly attacked, extorted, doxed, swatted, scammed or need help navigating through the most frightening situations.”

In leaked audio recordings published by THR in September, Wallace counseled the Italian billionaire Leonardo Maria Del Vecchio, who was publicly battling his then-fiancee, the American soap opera actress Jessica Serfaty. To establish his bona fides, Wallace told Del Vecchio that his client list has included “world leaders, celebrities, diplomats, high-profile individuals,” elaborating that “I have to pick and choose who the fuck I work with.” Earlier in his career, Wallace handled communications for companies including VirTra, which sells firearms training simulators to police departments and federal agencies, as well as Sciax Technology, a specialist in tactical remote viewing systems used by SWAT teams in the U.S. and American military personnel engaged in special operations abroad.

THR has since reviewed additional documentation which details more of those names. In a separate voice memo to Del Vecchio, Wallace informed him, “Elon’s a client,” and in a text exchange on Aug. 13, 2024, with Del Vecchio and the crisis publicist Melissa Nathan, Wallace obliquely referenced a separate ongoing work priority, explaining “I’m in this Elon/Trump debrief.” On the previous day, Musk had interviewed the then-presidential candidate on Musk’s social media platform X, although the two-hour discussion was delayed by what Musk characterized as a cyberattack. (Later that year, after Trump won his second presidential term, Robert F. Kennedy Jr. reportedly consulted with Wallace and Nathan as he sought his nomination for health secretary.)

Later in the same text exchange, Wallace informed Del Vecchio, “Just so you know — Logan and Jake have been part of my special client family since 2017.” Logan Paul, a longtime Nathan client, reportedly dated Serfaty between 2014 and 2017.

Paul recently settled a defamation claim against Stephen Findeisen, a YouTuber who published an investigation accusing the influencer of promoting what Findeisen characterized as a bogus crypto venture. Discovery records from the suit include a December 2022 chat history on the encrypted messaging app Signal between Wallace and Paul, who refers to the fixer as “papi.” Wallace, in turn, details multiple ways he can be of assistance in Paul’s attempt to discredit Findeisen: “I have someone that can find anything on anyone,” he explains, detailing a standard private investigation background check (“basic criminal, cases, property, etc.”) before elaborating, “then we can get really nasty from there.”

items.title: ‘Wicker’ Is Less Explicit Than You May Be Expecting: “This Is a Movie to Watch With Your Mom”
items.description: Wicker has had the internet buzzing for months, ever since the first trailer dropped following an ostracized fisherwoman (Olivia Colman) who commissions her rural town’s basketmaker to weave her a wicker husband (Alexander Skarsgård). When the wicker man comes
items.author: Kirsten Chuba
paragraphs: Wicker has had the internet buzzing for months, ever since the first trailer dropped following an ostracized fisherwoman (Olivia Colman) who commissions her rural town’s basketmaker to weave her a wicker husband (Alexander Skarsgård). When the wicker man comes to life, plenty of sex ensues, leading the film to seemingly take the title of horniest movie of the year.
However, at the film‘s Los Angeles premiere on Tuesday, the team was quick to downplay just how explicit the film — which is rated R — gets.

“Don’t be afraid. It’s us two making it and Olivia, we’re kind of prudes,” joked Eleanor Wilson, who wrote and directed the project alongside husband Alex Huston Fischer. “It’s safe to watch with your parents. It’s mostly just funny.” Added Fischer, “This is a movie to watch with your mom, 100 percent. You don’t have to be embarrassed,” confirming that his mom loves the film.
And with plenty of online chatter about the wicker husband’s wicker penis, Colman emphasized, “People have gone mad for the sex scenes but our heads are much dirtier than what’s on camera.”

The Oscar winner produced as well as stars in the film, explaining she was drawn to the out-of-the-box story because she “hadn’t seen anything like this before and that’s exciting. I wanted to play her and I would have been jealous if anyone else had.” Skarsgård — who transformed into the wicker husband in a real suit created by Wētā Workshop — originally thought the movie was a remake of ’70s horror film The Wicker Man — until reading the script and realizing quickly that it was not.
For those looking to experience Wicker in all its glory, a special 4DX screening is being held for one-night-only on Oct. 28 — which Fischer and Wilson have had an active hand in curating.

“I think we all know why people are going to 4DX, so let’s just make sure it’s at the max,” Wilson teased of their strategy, as Skarsgård revealed that the filmmakers have given a number of notes on the immersive experience. A major one was for a scene where Colman’s character throws out a bucket of urine, they asked for the crowd to be splashed (with water, of course).
“The shot is so directly at camera, I was like it’s a missed opportunity to not have a tiny little splash,” Wilson laughed, and Skarsgård promised, “I’m definitely going to catch that screening.”
Wicker hits theaters on Friday.

items.title: Europe Wants Data Centers. Its Climate Goals Are Getting in the Way
items.description: Earlier this year, the German government laid out an ambitious plan: By 2030, it would double the scale of the country’s data center fleet, and quadruple the amount of compute available for running artificial intelligence models. The idea was to minimize Germa
items.author: Joel Khalili
paragraphs: Earlier this year, the German government laid out an ambitious plan: By 2030, it would double the scale of the country’s data center fleet, and quadruple the amount of compute available for running artificial intelligence models. The idea was to minimize Germany’s dependence on the United States for access to AI—a point of concern across Europe—and boost its faltering economy.

However, Germany has found that its AI ambitions are butting up against its climate commitments. EU member states have committed to cutting greenhouse gas emissions by 55 percent by the end of the decade. But policies meant to help meet that target are interfering with attempts to trigger a data center building frenzy.

As part of its broader climate commitments, the previous German administration voted through the Energy Efficiency Act in 2023. Among other things, it required all new data centers to recycle a portion of the waste heat generated by their computer equipment, ideally into nearby municipal heating systems. It seemed like a no-brainer, says Patrick Graichen, who served as a senior official at Germany’s Ministry for Economic Affairs and Energy at the time, before resigning over cronyism allegations.
“We need clean heat, and data centers are a source of clean heat,” Graichen tells WIRED.

In June, a month before the rules were due to finally take effect, the German federal government walked them back. Data center firms had complained that the requirements made it almost impossible to build in the country; the German Data Center Association characterized an early version of the bill as a “data center prevention act.” Under an amended bill, which will be put to the German parliament for ratification imminently, data center operators would no longer be obligated to reuse waste heat, only to scope out the possibility.

Graichen and others have accused the German government of sacrificing climate targets for a chance to ride the AI wave. But countries across Europe find themselves pulled between these same two poles, under simultaneous pressure to cash in on rapid growth in the energy-intensive AI sector—and limit dependence on the US—and to protect the climate.
The German Ministry for Economic Affairs and Energy did not respond to a request for comment.

Among data center developers, the chief objection to the original Energy Efficiency Act was the chance it could land them in an impossible bind, obligated to reuse waste heat even when there was no available offtake—whether a municipal heating system or an industry, like greenhouse agriculture. “Some of the things they had to comply with were outside of their control,” says Barbara Smitten, associate director for critical systems at consulting firm Cundall. “It felt that [the burden] was all on the data center.”

In the last 18 months, multiple data center proposals have fallen through in Germany: Stack Infrastructure canceled a $3 billion facility in Hesse, and state-owned Komm.ONE withdrew from a project in Baden-Württemberg. Though precisely what causes a data center development to fold is rarely clear, Komm.ONE pointed directly to the burdens of the Energy Efficiency Act.

Graichen claims that the industry’s objections are groundless. He says the availability of a heat offtake should become a default criterion for any developer searching for a new site. “Stop complaining,” he says.

When an offtake is available, recycling heat produced by a data center is straightforward. “There is no technical reason why a data center cannot use its waste heat. The technologies and concepts are well known,” says John Booth, managing director at IT consultancy Carbon3IT, who helped to devise EU-wide energy efficiency targets for data centers. “There is absolutely no reason except the will of the organization to do it.”

Nevertheless, under the amended Energy Efficiency Act, data center developers are required only to assess whether recycling heat is economically and technically feasible. If not, they are exempt. “With practical rules for data centers, we are creating the conditions for digital sovereignty and economic growth,” wrote Katherina Reiche, federal minister for economic affairs and energy, when the cabinet approved the change.

The amendment may unlock pent-up demand among data center developers to build in Germany, whose geographic centrality makes it easy to route data efficiently into Western and Eastern Europe. “It lessens the risk of people not seeing the German market as attractive,” says Smitten.

But in a roundabout way, it could also undermine the aim to spark a building frenzy, inviting the type of climate-focused activism that has led to permitting freezes and data center moratoria in the US. Already, in February, the city council of a small German town voted to block the construction of a $2.5 billion data center development, partly over climate concerns.

As policymakers contend with conflicting ambitions to improve domestic AI capabilities and meet climate objectives, some say the swelling public unease about that trade-off will complicate things yet further in Europe. In the last year, the attitude toward data centers “has switched completely,” claims Graichen. “First and foremost in the US, but the same will happen in Europe.”

items.title: French Government Calls Emergency Meetings With Platforms Over Protests
items.description: TikTok and eBay were among six online platforms summoned by the French government this week, as authorities sought to contain widespread rioting and looting and prevent the resale of stolen goods.
items.author: Isabella Ward; Anna Desmarais
paragraphs: TikTok and eBay were among six online platforms summoned by the French government this week, as authorities sought to contain widespread rioting and looting and prevent the resale of stolen goods.

Anne Le Hananff, France’s minister of digital affairs, convened representatives from social media firms on Tuesday for an emergency meeting, after their platforms were blamed for fanning the flames of the worst civil unrest the country has seen in years. The goal of the meeting was to remind platforms that they need to moderate content on their sites, including livestream video, to avoid violent content or anything that could encourage people to break the imposed curfew, according to French TV station BFM.

A review by WIRED of TikTok found that the search term “blocus”—meaning blockade in French— showed videos that were potentially altered or AI-generated, including viral images of a protester in a Pink Panther costume. The search term is also being used to promote “Act II” of the protests for October 24. The platform issued an “evolving situation” tag on the search term that said: “This situation is developing rapidly. Information available now may be unverified, incomplete, inaccurate, or subject to change. Take care when viewing this content, and report anything that may violate our Community Guidelines.”

A separate meeting, confirmed by Serge Papin, minister for small and medium-size enterprises on X, was held on Monday with major online reselling platforms where “an agreement was signed” to crack down on the resale of looted goods. French newspaper Le Monde reported that Vinted, eBay, Amazon, LeBonCoin, Meta, and TikTok were at the meeting. Platforms agreed to forward reports to investigators, monitor ads for goods stolen specifically during the protests, and send the government reports of their actions, with the first one coming within 48 hours, according to Papin.

Peaceful demonstrations against high living costs and strained public services, including schools, erupted into rioting and the looting of more than 1,500 shops and businesses over the weekend. Police “lost control” in some cities, Interior minister Laurent Nuñez admitted, as they responded with tear gas, water cannon, and batons. They have since arrested more than 2,400 people, according to authorities.

French penal law can hand down a five-year sentence and a €375,000 fine to anyone who is concealing, possessing, or transferring an item that they know was obtained through a crime or offense. Police issued a warning in the Netherlands that online ecommerce sites could have a higher number of stolen goods online due to the riots.

The French Alliance of Marketplaces, a nonprofit representing French online retailers such as Back Market, eBay, Etsy, LeBonCoin, ManoMano, and Vinted, said in a press release that its members are relying on user reports, human oversight, and tech tools to monitor ads that resell stolen goods from the riots. When identified, a fake ad is removed and “measures are taken against the accounts involved,” which could include permanent suspension of the seller’s account, according to a statement from eBay. The time it takes for eBay to take action “depends on the nature of the report and the necessary verification process,” the company said. Vinted, Amazon, LeBonCoin, Meta, and TikTok did not respond to WIRED’s request for comment.

items.title: Bose Is Buying Skullcandy. It’s Not as Weird as It Sounds
items.description: Longtime audio giant Bose announced on Wednesday that it's acquiring Skullcandy, the lifestyle brand known for its bass-heavy headphones. Skullcandy will remain a separate company within Bose's Premium Consumer Audio business and will still be based in Park Ci
items.author: Harry Rabinowitz
paragraphs: Longtime audio giant Bose announced on Wednesday that it's acquiring Skullcandy, the lifestyle brand known for its bass-heavy headphones. Skullcandy will remain a separate company within Bose's Premium Consumer Audio business and will still be based in Park City, Utah.

The acquisition isn't out of left field. Bose has lent its audio expertise to Skullcandy over the past year under its Sound by Bose licensing program. Skullcandy designs the headphones and then works with Bose on the audio front. The relationship began with the Skullcandy Method 360 ANC earbuds in 2025 and more recently, with the Crusher 1080 ANC headphones in July.

When WIRED spoke with Skullcandy CEO Brian Garofalow in July about the partnership, Garofalow highlighted the 23-year-old company's ability to build community and culture, specifically around the board sports community (the first Skullcandy product was designed on a ski chairlift). But he admitted the company wasn't “the greatest at the engineering part of innovation with products.”

This is hardly Bose's first audio acquisition (though it may be the most mainstream). Bose acquired McIntosh Group, owners of luxury audio brands McIntosh Laboratory and Sonus Faber, back in 2024. But Bose seems to be after Skullcandy's connection to its community.

“What does the brand stand for? Does it have meaning for consumers? Is it relevant to a group of consumers that, frankly, we otherwise aren’t reaching?" Bose CEO Lila Snyder tells WIRED. "If you think about McIntosh, Sonus Faber, and Skullcandy, they all fit into that realm. Skullcandy gives us access to a customer base that we think we’re largely missing with the Bose brand.”

That's why Bose has no plans to relocate Skullcandy from Park City, Utah, which Snyder says is the epicenter of board sports culture. “We want to make sure we’re right at the heart of it, as they always have been,” she says. Skullcandy products are also affordable, especially compared to other Bose products and Bose-owned brands, which lets Bose compete at both ends of the market.

As WIRED's headphone reviewer, I find Bose and Skullcandy an odd pairing. In consumer audio, Bose pioneered active noise-cancelation (ANC) in headphones, and maintains that legacy with ANC-leading products like the Bose QuietComfort Ultra Headphones (2nd Gen) and Bose QuietComfort Ultra Earbuds (2nd Gen). Skullcandy, on the other hand, has often been viewed as the butt of the joke when it comes to audio quality. It has had a reputation for middling sound, bass-over-everything headphones, and a loud, bold aesthetic.

Recent collaborations have started to change those perceptions—WIRED rated the Method 360 ANC earbuds an 8/10, noting good sound quality and ANC for the money. Snyder says those buds and the recent Crusher collab are just the tip of the iceberg. “It’s the beginning of what we think we can do together,” she says.
I’m very curious about what comes next from Skullcandy, headphones or otherwise. Either way, we’ll see if Bose's acoustic muscle can give the lifestyle brand the permanent glow-up it’s been chasing.

items.title: Don’t be fooled by this summer of AI hype
items.description: It’s been a busy few months for AI hype. At the end of April, Anthropic claimed that its model Claude Mythos is better at finding software vulnerabilities than most security experts. Then we had the OpenAI–Hugging Face hacking incident, after which Anthropic (
items.author: Timnit Gebru
paragraphs: It’s been a busy few months for AI hype. At the end of April, Anthropic claimed that its model Claude Mythos is better at finding software vulnerabilities than most security experts. Then we had the OpenAI–Hugging Face hacking incident, after which Anthropic (proudly) and Meta (reluctantly) disclosed similar incidents involving their models.

This was followed by Anthropic’s claim that one of its models had made a mathematical breakthrough; soon OpenAI claimed a mathematical breakthrough of its own. Most recently, Anthropic engineer Jacob Coxon went viral announcing his departure from the company, claiming that it and OpenAI are “racing straight towards self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.”

Each of these events was mostly covered breathlessly by the press, often repeating the companies’ anthropomorphizing framings—which are designed to portray their software is not only powerful but incipient “artificial general intelligence.” So what is really going on? Are we witnessing a massive, civilization-changing set of technological breakthroughs, or is this marketing?

In all these incidents, massive fanfare from the companies (presented as mea culpas in illicit hacking cases) is accompanied by intense press coverage. Once there is time for experts in the relevant fields to examine what happened, a very different story emerges, but one that gets less media attention.

Regarding the “hacking” incidents, cybersecurity experts say the story is more about OpenAI’s negligence and failure to adopt basic, established security practices than about “models gone rogue” or “AI agents creating civilizations.”

As for the mathematical results, mathematicians who were initially “stunned” by OpenAI’s press release saying that its latest chatbot, Astra, solved problems that “have been open and seen no progress on the main result for at least a decade" later realized that the results weren’t as “novel as first appeared.” Since then, mathematicians have accused the company of research misconduct and plagiarism, and they’ve reiterated that Astra didn’t make a “profound intellectual leap.” Just weeks later, OpenAI claimed its own mathematical breakthrough. Two days before, Tristan Buckmaster, a math professor at New York University’s Courant Institute, published a bombshell statement suggesting that OpenAI had stolen other people’s work and improperly attributed it.

Claims of incipient, dangerous superintelligence are not based in good scientific or engineering practice. Rather, they are narratives based in ideologies of transhumanism, eugenics, and wishful thinking about imagined future digital humans.

It’s worth thinking about why there is so much attention on computer programming and math as fields in which to apply large language models and related technology. Not only are they often elevated as the pinnacle of human intellectual achievement, but they involve problems where answers, once suggested, can be verified. The former property helps AI hype mongers sell the idea that they are building everything machines. The latter makes math and coding problems easier to tune systems for, since system output (sequences of likely words or pieces of computer code) can be evaluated without having to pay data workers to look at and annotate each one.

Mathematicians in particular have warned against corporations using their field in this way. A statement signed by hundreds of them says there is “currently a strong commercial incentive on the part of the technology industry to overstate the capabilities of their products” and asks policymakers to “consult with experts, including mathematicians, in forming policy decisions rather than relying on press releases or popular reporting of mathematical results.”

We echo this call and note that the illusion of speed and urgency promulgated by the tech companies is also a ploy to misdirect both policymakers and the public. Unfortunately, it sometimes works, such as with Senator Bernie Sanders’s well-meaning but ultimately misguided proposed legislation to prevent the development of “artificial superintelligence.”

Describing them as “superintelligence” or “rogue models” ascribes agency to products rather than to the companies building them. This framing markets these companies’ products as “superhuman” and, at the same time, helps the companies evade accountability for their actions.

Instead of OpenAI being prosecuted for creating malware that hacked another company, press releases, news outlets, media personalities, and lawmakers refer to “rogue models” as if they acted on their own. Instead of researchers being questioned about their companies’ habit of plagiarizing academics’ work or using customer data to train models without consent, the public’s imagination is redirected to fears about what the future might hold upon the arrival of fictional superintelligent machines.

The AI industry has even suggested that popular, bipartisan anti-data-center activism is a “distraction” from attempts to regulate the impending, scary, “superhuman” machines these companies are building. According to the AI industry, we should be more worried about a fictional machine god than about the climate catastrophe that these data centers exacerbate, the asthma suffered by those living near them, the rising electricity bills of the public subsidizing them, or the water that is redirected to cooling them.

We know better than to make decisions based on marketing and better than to capitulate to corporate pressure to make those decisions quickly. Wise decision-making, by policymakers and communities, demands time to hear from independent experts and contextualize corporate claims. The best possible outcome from this summer of hype is that policymakers and the public at large learn to take a breath, hold onto our skepticism, and recognize this kind of hype for what it is the next time it comes around.

Timnit Gebru is executive director of DAIR and author of the forthcoming book Deep Unlearning: The Radicalization of a Tech Idealist, which is available for preorders now and set to publish on February 16. Emily M. Bender is professor of linguistics at the University of Washington and coauthor of The AI Con.
