items.title: What life in Denmark shows about the power of emotional safety | Psyche Ideas
items.description: For newcomers to Denmark, many things don’t always make sense. Parents leave sleeping babies outside cafés. Young children cycle to school alone. Primary schools don’t do homework, exams and competition. Success is quietly downplayed rather than celebrated. Me
items.author: Ruth Aharoni Nielsen
paragraphs: For newcomers to Denmark, many things don’t always make sense. Parents leave sleeping babies outside cafés. Young children cycle to school alone. Primary schools don’t do homework, exams and competition. Success is quietly downplayed rather than celebrated. Meetings are spent revisiting the last meeting, planning the current one, eating together and preparing for the next meeting. Decisions are painfully slow, and everything is scheduled and regulated. Nothing is rushed. For me, and for many others who have made Denmark our home, much of everyday life initially seemed to defy the logic by which successful societies are supposed to function.

Marrying into Danish culture, and being a psychologist, I was intrigued by this, but had stopped worrying only when our eldest daughter reached junior high. Until then, I had to reluctantly trust the Danish line of reasoning that appears not only in schools, but across everyday life: you must first feel tryg.

What does it mean to feel tryg? The word is often translated as ‘safe’, but that is not quite right. It does not primarily refer to the absence of threat. Rather, it points to the presence of a particular state: the body at ease – calm, relaxed, with a sense of familiar warmth. Like the relaxed feeling of a child resting in her parents’ arms. In Danish, feeling tryg is not assumed to rise spontaneously. It is rather something that arises as a reaction to specific contexts that are deliberately cultivated. Members of the group implicitly take the responsibility to cultivate settings that promote and foster feeling tryg.

Certain conditions facilitate this emotional stance that allows us to be present, without scanning the environment or anticipating what might go wrong – or what might, suddenly, change. When feeling tryg, attention widens. The world can be met with a quiet, open curiosity. We take in what is happening around us and engage more easily and positively with others. We have the space to review the situation and be free to make the best decisions about what it requires of us.

In Danish culture, feeling tryg is not merely an inherent individual quality, it is rather a cultural and emotional concept that guides how the social world is designed. Predictable environments, well-known surroundings, consistent and trustworthy relationships, friendliness and pleasant spaces are all assumed to promote feeling tryghed – ‘safeness’ – for all.

When tryghed is absent, the body becomes more alert and more prepared. We begin to scan for what might go wrong, and uncertainty is harder to tolerate. We know this from ordinary moments: entering a new group and trying to read the room, sitting in a meeting or a classroom with unclear expectations, or speaking with someone whose tone is harsh or reactions unpredictable. Attention narrows, shifting away from what is being said and toward anticipating what might go wrong. On a basic level, the questions that preoccupy the mind are: friend or foe? Should I engage? Can I leave? Should I protect myself?
Danes extend tryghed everywhere: in classrooms, workplaces and public spaces

In line with decades of psychological research, the neuroscientist Stephen Porges has recently described how states of perceived safeness – a felt sense of being at ease – allow the nervous system to settle, making openness, joyful learning and social engagement possible. In this state of tryghed, tolerance and curiosity flourish, and so does prosocial behaviour. Unlike in traditional psychology, in Denmark, tryghed is not treated as a private matter. Creating environments that are tryg is seen as a shared responsibility and something that Danes take very seriously. This means that attention shifts from how individuals feel to how we structure shared conditions – and to how everyone feels. Physical and social settings are organised around this principle. Danes place a strong emphasis on cultivating environments that convey expectations very clearly – preferably in a friendly way. Actively fostering tryghed helps life feel pleasant and predictable enough for everyone to drop their guard. This is not just ‘safety’ in a physical sense, it’s a set of conditions that allows feelings of safeness to emerge in the group.

In Danish, these conditions are often referred to as ‘rammer’ or the ‘frameworks’ – in which tryghed for everyone is cultivated. Danes value tryghed and seek to extend it everywhere: in classrooms, workplaces and public spaces.

Certain rammer – certain conditions – allow tryghed to emerge. Over time, repeated experiences of feeling tryg accumulate into a form of implicit social knowledge: how to design the very conditions that make tryghed possible.

Cycling to work one morning, I passed an election poster. In large letters it read: Trygge mennesker tør – ‘People who feel tryg dare.’ The message was simple, almost self-evident. When we feel this deep safeness, we are free to engage, to innovate, to act, to move forward. It was not presented as a psychological insight, but as something one could assume people already understood – an election appeal to shared values and what does not need to be justified.

Once you start understanding tryghed in Denmark, it appears everywhere. In how classrooms are organised, in how school curricula are set, in how meetings are run, in how public spaces are designed. The same quiet premise: if people feel tryg, something else becomes possible.
Meetings and schedules are structured to reduce unnecessary uncertainty

In schools, the emphasis is not only on what children learn, but on designing physical and social environments in which they can learn. In family life, there is often a focus on maintaining pleasant and predictable structures and schedules. In neighbourhoods with many children, the streets are empty at 6 pm – everyone is at home having dinner.

In workplaces, meetings and schedules are structured to make expectations explicit and to reduce unnecessary uncertainty. Time is taken to align, to clarify, so that people know what is required of them. In public life, this orientation appears in small, taken-for-granted behaviours: people tend to follow shared rules, and actively maintain a sense of order that others can rely on. Dog poop is picked up, traffic rules are followed, common spaces are designed for safeness, and in turn are highly respected. Individuals intentionally maintain the conditions that foster safeness for everyone every day – and everything that ‘safeness for all’ brings with it. This commitment extends well beyond everyday interactions. It is reflected in the entitlements of society, from paid parental leave for both mothers and fathers to free healthcare and education, all designed to reduce unnecessary uncertainty across the life course.

None of this is absolute, it is not always consistent, and this commitment brings its tensions. For Danes, what is unfamiliar, unpredictable or new can easily be felt as unsettling. Decisions can be painfully lengthy, as more perspectives are considered and alignment is sought. Processes become careful, sometimes to the point of hesitation. Groups move toward consensus – because shared understanding is given high priority. It also affects how difference is experienced: ways of thinking or behaving that fall outside established patterns may feel less tryg, simply because they are unfamiliar. In this sense, tryghed does not only enable openness; it can also limit what is accepted or allowed to emerge.

Rules are designed to allow everyone to feel safeness – but they can make processes slower and heavier. The same conditions that create stability can make quick change more difficult. Over time, tolerance for messiness, ambiguity and rapid adjustment may be less practised, which can, in turn, affect resilience. Can a country that relies so heavily on tryghed be competitive in a rapidly changing world?
Stable relationships and trustworthy frameworks form an infrastructure that supports prosocial behaviour

As a tryg-driven society, Denmark is often described as stable and high-trust, yet it also performs remarkably well across measures such as innovation and economic performance. While liberal democracies are in decline, Denmark also consistently ranks high on the democracy index. Democracies are many things, but they depend heavily on systems of emotional regulation: when institutions and norms foster predictability and shared responsibility, trust and cooperation emerge; when they erode, suspicion and hostility take over.

One way to make sense of this is to shift the focus to everyday life. Stable relationships and trustworthy frameworks – designed to benefit all – form an infrastructure that supports prosocial behaviour. They paradoxically make learning and innovation less risky in an uncertain world.

Often in liberal democracies, political life is framed around concepts like ‘effectiveness’, ‘freedom’ or ‘equality’. In Denmark, the emphasis is more often placed on the felt experience of tryghed – and on whether everyday life promotes feeling safeness – through everyday acts of care performed by individuals and people in office alike. When safeness is not cultivated, a different logic takes hold: under conditions of uncertainty and threat, exclusion can begin to feel rational, and control preferable to openness and trust.

Last spring, I was standing with some of the ‘international’ parents on the grass, watching the annual school football match. These parents – like myself – had settled into life in Denmark, despite having other, sometimes more lucrative, options in the United States, the United Kingdom, Germany or Canada. Among these parents there are CEOs of startup companies, heads of venture capital firms and high-profile consultants. We stood on the sidelines, watching our children run across the field, as one of the parents, Jeff, described something that had become difficult to explain to friends back home: how easy everyday life here felt.

Children cycling alone to school. Wallets returned. Streets kept clean. Systems that work. But also, something less visible – the sense that these conditions are not accidental. That someone, somewhere, has thought about how life should feel, and that this is a shared endeavour.

It is easy to notice the outcomes. It is harder to see the orientation behind them. Not only a commitment to rules or institutions, but to the ongoing work of maintaining conditions in which everyone can let their guard down. Perhaps this is what it means, in practice, to organise a society around care and tryghed – and why it may matter more than we tend to notice.

items.title: A scientist’s search for answers about Amanita muscaria gummies | Aeon Essays
items.description: In late summer 2023, I found myself in a smoke shop looking at a package of ‘magic mushroom’ gummies.
items.author: Eric Leas
paragraphs: In late summer 2023, I found myself in a smoke shop looking at a package of ‘magic mushroom’ gummies.

That phrase, magic mushrooms, usually calls to mind one type of mushroom: those containing psilocybin, the compound showing promise as a therapy for depression, addiction and other psychopathologies. But these gummies were not psilocybin. Instead, the packaging described Amanita muscaria, the red-capped, white-spotted toadstool of fairy-tale forests, iPhone keyboards and Super Mario.

I knew a little about the folklore of Amanita muscaria. I had first seen it discussed in an episode of the show Hamilton’s Pharmacopeia (2016-21), which begins with a claim I now hear often: that Amanita muscaria may be among the oldest human intoxicants. The New York banker-turned-ethnomycologist R Gordon Wasson, whose Life magazine essay from 1957 introduced psilocybin mushrooms to a mass Western audience, certainly took this idea seriously. In his book Soma: Divine Mushroom of Immortality (1968), he argued that the Vedic soma – a ritual drink in ancient Indian religions – was made from Amanita muscaria. The mushroom has also been linked, sometimes carefully and sometimes wildly, to the origins of Santa Claus, Viking berserkers and even Christianity. Some believe its other name, ‘fly agaric’, stems from its use as a natural pesticide for house flies; the word muscaria is also derived from the Latin word musca, meaning fly. Some scholars have linked Amanita muscaria to Lewis Carroll’s mushroom scene in Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland (1865), in which the Caterpillar tells Alice that ‘one side’ of the mushroom will make her taller and the other shorter, though Carroll does not identify a species.

But I wasn’t standing in that smoke shop holding one of these products as a folklorist or looking to lose myself in Carroll’s ‘golden afternoon’. I am a public-health scientist, and my questions were pragmatic: what exactly was in this package? Could it hurt someone? Were these products legal?
The first thing I did was what I usually do. I went to the scientific literature. And down the rabbit hole I tumbled.

Although manufacturers use the term ‘magic mushrooms’, the main psychoactive compound in Amanita muscaria is not pharmacologically interchangeable with psilocybin; the two drugs do not act on the brain in the same way.

The body converts psilocybin into psilocin, the substance that actually produces its psychedelic effects. Psilocin switches on serotonin 5-HT2A receptors, proteins on the surface of brain cells that respond to the chemical messenger serotonin. These receptors are concentrated in the cortex, the brain’s outer layer, and especially in the prefrontal cortex, the region behind the forehead involved in such functions as attention, perception and our sense of self. The receptors sit on the big output neurons that broadcast to the rest of the brain, and switching them on makes those cells fire harder. Brain scans of people on psilocybin show what follows: networks that normally run in step with each other come apart, and regions of the cortex that rarely signal to each other begin to. What people report from the inside is a change in perception rather than false perception – surfaces that appear to move, colours that intensify, time that stops running at a fixed rate.
Muscimol killed mice at a lower dose than nearly all psychotropic drugs we examined, including fentanyl

Amanita muscaria works through a different system. Its principal psychoactive compound, muscimol, acts primarily on GABA-A receptors – part of the brain’s main braking system – quieting neuronal activity rather than amping it up. That puts muscimol broadly on the inhibitory side of brain chemistry, the same signalling system influenced by central nervous system depressants such as benzodiazepines and alcohol. The experience is still ‘psychoactive’, but it can look quite different. Clinical reports of Amanita intoxication describe drowsiness and dream-like states, impaired balance and coordination, confusion and disorientation, sometimes alternating with agitation, as well as visual or auditory hallucinations. In severe cases, people can become profoundly sedated, delirious or lose consciousness. In other words, rather than the characteristic alterations in perception associated with psilocybin, Amanita can produce a much less orderly mixture of sedation, hallucination and confusion.

The risks are different too. When my colleagues and I began looking at the toxicology, the numbers startled me. By the crude measure toxicologists often begin with – the LD50, or the dose required to kill half the test population – published estimates suggested that muscimol administered orally killed mice at a lower dose than nearly all commonly used psychotropic drugs we examined, including fentanyl. As a vegetarian, I found the exercise grim, and translating animal doses to humans is always imperfect. But these were safety signals we took seriously.

That was the first turn in the rabbit hole. The next was dosing. If companies were selling Amanita muscaria gummies and chocolates in ordinary retail settings, then somewhere, implicitly or explicitly, someone had made a decision about dosing. A gummy contains some amount. A package contains some total amount. A label tells a consumer to take one piece, or half a piece, or perhaps more. A certificate of analysis from products submitted to a laboratory can provide an amount per gummy. Those numbers can feel reassuring simply because they are printed on a package. They also imply that someone knew enough to choose a dose for the desired effect.
I wanted to know whether that chain existed.

So, I started with a simple question: are there human studies showing what muscimol does at different doses? The best answer to this would have come from controlled studies in which multiple human participants were given standardised doses under observation, with careful reporting of effects and adverse events. I could not find that literature in the usual places. I could find toxicology estimates, case reports, historical accounts and ethnobotanical discussions. But a modern dosing study, the kind one would want before placing psychoactive candies near a cash register, was not there.

Eventually, I came across the proceedings from a symposium I had not known about: the Ethnopharmacologic Search for Psychoactive Drugs, held at the University of California, San Francisco, from 28 to 30 January 1967. The time and place stood out to me immediately. Two weeks earlier, a couple of miles away in Golden Gate Park, Timothy Leary had told the Human Be-In crowd to ‘turn on, tune in, drop out’, a phrase that would become shorthand for the moral panic that soon surrounded psychedelics and particularly LSD. The symposium also opened with a letter by Albert Hofmann, the Swiss chemist best known for synthesising LSD and who had also led the work identifying psilocybin and psilocin as the active compounds of Psilocybe mexicana. The symposium covered compounds from many psychoactive plants and cultures, including a lecture on nutmeg delivered by Alexander Shulgin – the San Francisco Bay Area biochemist who is remembered most infamously (and perhaps unkindly) for his rediscovery and popularisation of MDMA (aka Ecstasy).
A mid-century scientist, dosing himself, may have produced numbers that later travelled into a marketplace of gummies

Near the end came a session on Amanita muscaria. In the final part of the final lecture, I found what I had been searching for – something resembling a dosing guide. It came from a report of a self-experiment with pure muscimol by Peter G Waser – a Swiss pharmacologist who later served as rector of the University of Zurich – under observation by a Swiss psychiatrist named Jules Angst. Waser repeatedly dosed himself with pure muscimol dissolved in water to establish a range of effects. This was not a modern dosing study. It was stranger than that, and I think it is worth hearing Waser’s language directly because it captures both the scientific seriousness and the unease of the moment:

Curiosity is one of the main qualities of a scientist, and this may be the reason why a pharmacologist watching the behaviour of his animals under certain drugs wants to know more about the emotions and changes in reaction they produce. Another reason is ethical. We have to foresee the accidents and dangerous actions new compounds of general interest may produce on man. My report on some experiments done on myself by ingesting ibotenic acid and muscimol under careful psychiatric control may give you an unauthoritative view on this.

At 5 milligrams taken orally in water, Waser reported little effect beyond a feeling of laziness. At 10 milligrams, however, he described a mild intoxication beginning about 90 minutes later, with dizziness, loss of coordination and elevated mood. He did not experience hallucinations, although he noticed slight changes in taste and colour vision, followed by muscle twitching and then sleep with dreams. Within two to three hours, he reported feeling normal again – rested and able to work – and said he slept deeply the following night.

At 15 milligrams, the effects were stronger and began more quickly, after about 40 minutes. Waser reported dizziness severe enough that he could not walk with his eyes closed, along with slurred speech, diminished appetite and taste, and increasing difficulty concentrating. His visual perception also changed: images of situations he had seen minutes earlier seemed to repeat themselves, and sounds sometimes appeared to echo. Most disturbing to him were repeated involuntary muscle contractions. At times, he wrote, he felt as though he had lost his legs, although he specifically distinguished the experience from the vivid, colourful hallucinations he had experienced with LSD. After falling asleep and awakening several hours later, he felt dull and uncertain rather than refreshed, although the muscle twitching had diminished. His blood pressure rose only slightly during the psychoactive period. In preliminary analyses conducted by the Swiss chemist Conrad H Eugster, muscimol appeared to be detectable in Waser’s urine after the self-experiment, although Waser cautioned, at the time, that the finding still needed confirmation.

What I found was upsetting, but not that surprising. Dosing recommendations from product manufacturers, including the one I found at that smoke shop, appeared to resemble that old self-experiment. While I have no way to confirm it, I have a strange feeling that this mid-century scientist, dosing himself under observation and reporting on it at a famous drug conference, may have produced numbers that later travelled into a marketplace of gummies and chocolates sold to consumers who likely have no idea where the guidance came from.

I wish I had been able to speak with Waser himself, but he died in 2010. In 2024, I did exchange emails with Angst, the psychiatrist who had supervised the experiment. Angst was 97 and not in good health, but he confirmed the point that mattered most to me: Waser had come to Angst for supervision as a precaution. Waser’s own later writing suggests why. Recalling the experiments, Waser described the experiences at high doses as unpleasant and even potentially life-threatening.

Convinced of questionable dosing standards in this marketplace, my line of enquiry returned to the potential harms – were there products on the market that contained enough muscimol to seriously harm someone?

I found a product with a very high reported amount of muscimol. It was a gummy product, one in a benign-looking package that did not have childproofing or clear warnings. I began doing the calculation no one wants to do. If a young child ate the entire package, mistaking it for candy, could they die? I took the reported amount of muscimol, the toxicology estimates (the LD50), a conversion used to translate dosing between species, and the average weight of a small child. The result looked bad. Bad enough that I did not quite trust myself. So, I called a friend, Matthieu Rouffet, a medicinal chemist and the dean of science at a local college, who does toxicology calculations more often than I do. I wanted him to tell me I had made an error. Instead, he was alarmed too.

There is a rare moment as a scientist when you encounter an empirical finding and it becomes emotionally charged. Before, it might just have been intellectual curiosity and your training that drove you to it. After, you feel a sense of responsibility. This was one of those rare moments for me. Perhaps this finding was especially emotionally charged for my friend Matthieu and me because we are fathers of young children. When I made the calculation, my daughter was only a year old. It could have just been the sleep-deprived delirium of early fatherhood, but I felt a moral responsibility to act.
The broader pattern appeared to be permissiveness by omission or legal loophole
Were there policy levers I could pull? It was complex because Amanita muscaria fell into the gap between the categories – not a controlled substance, not a food, not quite a supplement.

Unlike psilocybin, Amanita muscaria and muscimol were not scheduled under the US Controlled Substances Act, and they also did not appear to be controlled under comparable drug laws in most countries, with a few exceptions. The Netherlands treated Amanita muscaria and Amanita pantherina (which also contains muscimol) as controlled substances, and, in the US, manufacturers generally acknowledged Louisiana as a state where sales were restricted. One manufacturer’s legal guidance listed prohibitions in countries including Brazil, Thailand, Australia, Romania, Russia, Sweden and Ukraine. But the broader pattern appeared to be permissiveness by omission or legal loophole.

This was an argument I had seen a few years earlier, when I wrote about the ‘hemp loophole’. It emerged from the 2018 Farm Bill legalising hemp, defined largely by its low level of delta-9-THC, the main intoxicant in cannabis. Some manufacturers saw an opening: if the law restricted just delta-9-THC, they argued, other intoxicating cannabinoids derived from legal hemp could still be sold. One was delta-8-THC, often produced from hemp-derived CBD, a nonintoxicating cannabinoid. Soon delta-8 gummies, vapes and candies were turning up in gas stations, smoke shops and online stores. The industry’s argument was essentially this: if the starting material was legal hemp and the finished product stayed below the federal limit for delta-9-THC, it did not have to be sold through the regulated marijuana market, with safeguards such as age restrictions and testing for potency.

The Amanita muscaria market seemed to be borrowing a similar playbook. The claim was not that Amanita muscaria gummies had been proven safe. It was that they were not psilocybin, not scheduled, and not clearly prohibited.

However, drug scheduling was only one possible policy lever. Food and dietary supplement law was another. Many Amanita muscaria products were being sold as if they were ordinary foods or supplements, but I could not find publicly available notifications showing that Amanita muscaria or muscimol had been accepted as a new dietary ingredient in the US or elsewhere.
Regulators could clarify whether these products could be commercially manufactured and sold at all

Given the toxicology and case reports mentioned above, that absence mattered. The issue, here, was not whether someone could pick a mushroom in the woods and take it home to eat – that’s unambiguously legal. The issue was whether a company could extract, concentrate, flavour, package, advertise, and sell a psychoactive compound in candy-like forms without meeting basic consumer protection standards.

They didn’t appear to be meeting this standard, and so there was legal recourse. Regulators could clarify whether these products could be commercially manufactured and sold at all under dietary supplement and food laws. If sales were not allowed, they could take the products off the shelves. If sales were allowed, they could require product standards such as age restrictions, child-resistant packaging, maximum-dose rules, warning labels, restrictions on cartoons or candy-like marketing, and standardised testing for potency, contaminants and undisclosed drugs. They could also require labels to state what was in the package in units that were interpretable.

Now, with a clear safety concern and a clear pathway for legal recourse, my colleagues and I wrote a paper, published in a peer-reviewed journal, and we began raising awareness on the subject. I issued a press release with my school at the University of California, San Diego, which helped to generate some national media coverage including in The Washington Post and on NPR. I also contacted colleagues at the Department of Justice in my home state of California. They put me in touch with the consumer-safety division that would eventually build an investigation of several brands selling Amanita muscaria-branded products in the state, including one that led to the seizure of more than 95,000 mushroom chocolate bars from a warehouse in San Diego County.

By late 2024, the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) had also reached its own conclusion about Amanita muscaria in food, offering a perspective that confirmed my own. In a scientific memorandum, FDA toxicologists concluded that Amanita muscaria and three of its active constituents, including muscimol, do not meet the criteria for safe use in food in the US.

There’s another side to the story. Some people believe the mushroom helps them. There are books and online communities organised around microdosing Amanita muscaria, often motivated by purported benefits based on, and following dosing information derived from, survey responses or anecdotal reports. The health claims tend to cluster around sleep, anxiety and the possibility of reducing dependence on benzodiazepines or other sedatives. Muscimol’s pharmacology makes some of this plausible in a broad mechanistic sense. A compound acting primarily on the GABA-A receptors could, in theory, have sedating effects that are therapeutic. Even our forerunner Waser alludes to this in his self-experiment. That account also mentions the findings of his colleague Eugster, who held a patent on a method of synthesising muscimol, which is currently assigned to the pharmaceutical company Novartis. Less toxic analogues of muscimol have also been explored as pharmaceuticals; gaboxadol, for instance, was discovered by the Danish chemist Povl Krogsgaard-Larsen. But the benefits and harms of these substances have never been rigorously tested to this day.

A thousand testimonials about the use of Amanita muscaria do not tell you what is in a gummy from a particular batch made by a particular company. They do not establish a safe range for children, older adults, pregnant people, people taking other medications, or anyone who eats more than the label recommends because the product looks harmless.
Once a substance is turned into a consumer good, science and capitalism are already in the room

This is one of the tensions running through the modern conversation about psychedelics and plant medicines like Amanita muscaria. Some proponents of plant medicine argue that science should not be treated as the only legitimate way of evaluating the veracity of therapeutic claims. They point to traditional and Indigenous uses of psychoactive plants and fungi, sometimes over millennia, and ask why randomised controlled trials should outrank lived experience, ritual knowledge or community practice.

I take that argument seriously. Western medicine does not own all wisdom, and therapeutic approval pathways are limited. Many plant medicines will struggle through conventional drug approval because they cannot be easily patented, because no company has an incentive to fund the studies, or because they belong in a ceremonial setting that is not transferable to a randomised trial. If the only knowledge we recognise is knowledge that can be monetised through drug development, we will miss a great deal.

But the Amanita muscaria products sold in smoke shops are not simply traditional plant medicines being used in traditional contexts. They are commercial products in a modern marketplace. They are manufactured, packaged, branded, advertised, and shipped. They borrow the language of science, from microdosing to certificates of analysis, when it helps them. Once a substance is turned into a consumer good, science and capitalism are already in the room. The question is whether they will be used with integrity.

The distinction between plant medicine and a commercial market became painfully clear with the recall of Diamond Shruumz-brand chocolate bars, ice-cream cones and gummies sold by Prophet Premium Blends, based in Santa Ana, California. In 2024, federal agencies investigated 180 cases, including three potential deaths, tied to products marketed with mushroom language and sold in the same broad retail ecosystem of gas stations, smoke shops, hemp-derived cannabinoid stores and online sellers.

In their recall notice, Prophet Premium Blends indicated that the adverse events may have been due to elevated levels of muscimol. But product testing complicated that story. Muscimol did not appear in all products and could not explain all the reported symptoms. Instead, testing found a shifting mixture of substances across products, including psilacetin, a near chemical cousin of psilocin first disclosed in a patent by Albert Hofmann and Franz Troxler in 1961. Unlike psilocin and psilocybin, psilacetin is not always listed by name in controlled-substance schedules, though it may still be regulated under analogue laws or broader drug-control provisions. Some samples also contained psilocin, pregabalin (a prescription medication), and compounds related to the psychoactive root, kava. The result was not a simple story about muscimol toxicity. It was a more troubling story about a marketplace where consumers could not reliably know what psychoactive substances they were consuming.
That, to me, illustrates the central ethical issue I see in the conversation about modern psychedelics and plant medicines.

People can argue about whether adults should be allowed to use psychedelics or plant medicines. My own view is that adults should generally have wide latitude over what they put in their own bodies. But they also have a right to know what they are putting in their bodies, as well as the known benefits and risks. A person cannot meaningfully consent to ingesting one thing while being sold another. They cannot weigh risks that are hidden from them inside of mislabelled gummies. They cannot dose carefully when the dose is uncertain and the active ingredient is undisclosed. The right to alter one’s consciousness does not include a company’s right to deceive.
Psilocybin was creating a halo around other mushrooms, and manufacturers were exploiting it

And while there are many stories about the purported benefits of plant medicines like Amanita muscaria, there are also stories about the harms of this marketplace. The most impactful story I’ve learned about came from Ashley Glover, who contacted me through email in 2024.

Ashley first wrote to me after reading my peer-reviewed article. Her only brother Andrew Davenport died on 23 June 2024, she said, after consuming a Diamond Shruumz mushroom bar. What stood out in Ashley’s emails was not only the grief, but the difficulty of getting the justice system to recognise what might have happened. She wrote that a witness who was with Andrew had insisted that the bars made him sick. She wrote that an opened box of Diamond Shruumz bars was recovered near his body. She also wrote that his initial toxicology report did not show hard drugs or alcohol, and that his prescribed medications were described to the family as being at normal therapeutic levels. But the medical examiner, she said, had not saved the box or bars for testing and the explanation relayed to her was blunt: no one overdoses on magic mushrooms.

That sentence has stayed with me because it captures the potential danger of a category error. If the product had been treated as a psilocybin mushroom, its risk could be dismissed before the relevant chemistry was even known. But these products were not psilocybin mushrooms. They were manufactured psychoactive goods whose contents could vary, whose labels could be incomplete, and whose compounds were difficult for forensic scientists to detect.

Ashley told me that biological samples from Andrew were eventually sent for specialised testing. Whether those results can establish causation is a legal and forensic question, and I do not want to claim more than the evidence can support. But her account shows the public-health problem in human terms. Once a consumer product enters the marketplace without reliable safety evidence, accurate labelling and adequate testing capacity, the uncertainty does not end at the point of sale. It follows the consumer, the family, the medical examiner, the investigator, and anyone trying to reconstruct what happened after an adverse event leaves questions in its wake.

I began this investigation with a question that seemed narrow enough for an academic paper – should unregulated sales of Amanita muscaria products prompt a public-health response? The answer, to me, became an unequivocal yes. But the journey was stranger than the paper could contain.

I did not set out to become the public-health scientist warning people about the fairy-tale mushroom, sounding alarmist or like a teetotaller. I am not opposed to research on psychoactive substances or to responsible use among adults. If anything, the therapeutic promise of psilocybin is part of why Amanita muscaria bothered me; psilocybin was creating a halo around other mushrooms, and manufacturers were exploiting it in ways that I saw as unethical and dangerous.

The lesson I took from Amanita muscaria was not that altered states are inherently dangerous or that science should flatten every human encounter with plants or fungus into a risk calculation. It was simpler than that. If a company sells a psychoactive product to the public, especially in forms that look like candy, it should be transparent about what is in the product, and have evidence that the product can be used without unreasonable harm. This should not be a radical standard. It should be the minimum requirement for sales.

items.title: The Renaissance gun, from diabolical device to popular militias | Aeon Essays
items.description: If you were asked to think of a gun owner, then Lorenzo de’ Medici – the celebrated patron of Renaissance art – would probably not be the first person to come to mind. In fact, however, Lorenzo ‘the Magnificent’ owned five portable firearms, which are listed i
items.author: Catherine Fletcher
paragraphs: If you were asked to think of a gun owner, then Lorenzo de’ Medici – the celebrated patron of Renaissance art – would probably not be the first person to come to mind. In fact, however, Lorenzo ‘the Magnificent’ owned five portable firearms, which are listed in his 1492 postmortem inventory. Guns and gunpowder were controversial. In art and literature, they were labelled the Devil’s work, and were perceived as fundamentally unchivalrous. Yet within half a century, by the early months of 1539, Lorenzo’s descendant Duke Cosimo de’ Medici had 91 firearms in his Florentine storerooms. Somehow, in the courts of late-Renaissance Italy, the gun had become an acceptable, even valued, weapon.

Beyond the palazzi of the peninsula’s towns and cities, guns were also making inroads into more ordinary lives. There were no standing armies in the 16th-century Italian states. Their wars were fought through temporary mobilisations, and with considerable help from companies of mercenaries. Yet as the 1506 provision that established the Florentine militia made clear, ‘little hope’ could be placed ‘in foreign and hired arms’. Far better to establish a new magistracy with ‘full authority and power’ to enlist men from Florentine territory, at least 10,000 of them. One in 10 of these men were to be equipped with firearms, and 500 handguns (schioppetti) should be kept in the Palazzo della Signoria (the city hall, now known as the Palazzo Vecchio) along with ‘such money as should be necessary for the schioppetti’, presumably to purchase gunpowder and shot. Three or four companies (bandiere) entirely of schioppettieri might also be established.

This militia, most often noted for the role of Niccolò Machiavelli in its foundation, was to be organised after the fashion of the Germans, in whose cities there was a centuries-old tradition of civic defence and a duty on every male citizen to maintain suitable arms for the purpose. In fact, one of the Florentine militia’s early constables was German (a Giovanni Tedesco); another (Giliberto Spagnolo) came from Spain, a country making the running in the use of small arms on the battlefield. Giovanni Tedesco arranged target practice for his company, which from 1508 was extended more generally among the militia, with exercises taking place on a monthly basis.

Militias were not new but, by the 1490s, large-scale foreign military intervention on the Italian peninsula was giving a new impetus to their development, as was the growing importance of infantry in the military context. In Friuli, where Venetian lands bordered Ottoman territory, the militia were using handguns from the 1490s, and city guards across the Italian peninsula were soon provided with guns too. The growth of militias was the single most important factor in the proliferation of firearms in 16th-century Italy. This is too early a period for the kind of autobiographical writing that would tell us what these men made of the process, but there was certainly ample encouragement to become familiar with firearms and acquire shooting skills.

The backdrop to these developments was the decades of war in which France and Spain contended for hegemony on the Italian Peninsula. In the 1480s, while pitching his services to the duke of Milan, Leonardo da Vinci, highlighting his potential as a military engineer, wrote:

I have also plans of mortars most convenient and easy to carry with which to hurl small stones in the manner almost of a storm; and with the smoke of this cause great terror to the enemy and great loss and confusion.

By the turn of the century, Spanish arquebusiers – named for the long, wooden-stocked gun with which they were armed – were doing precisely that on the battlefields of Italy. As the conflicts of 1494-1559 rolled on, the rulers of the peninsula’s multiple states promoted shooting in the interests of civic defence and military preparedness and, as they did, their own use of firearms shifted too.

The Medici were not the only leading family of Renaissance Italy to take an interest in this new military technology. In 1538, the duke of another Italian city-state, Urbino, described a novel firearm as ‘very dear to me’. Such appreciation, however, ran counter to the dominant image of guns in the period’s literature. Leonhard Fronsperger, once a captain of the ducal armoury in Munich, wrote of gunpowder as ‘indispensable’, but also as ‘horrible’ and ‘unmanly’. Ludovico Ariosto’s epic poem Orlando Furioso (1532) described guns as a ‘foul and pestilent discovery’, weapons through which ‘no more shall gallantry, no more shall valour prove their prowess’. Only in edgier texts, like the swashbuckling memoirs of the goldsmith and sculptor Benvenuto Cellini, did anyone hint that guns were fun. ‘Frightened’ by a plague that hit Rome in the early 1520s causing thousands of deaths, Cellini ‘began to seek relief in a sport that I found very enjoyable’. In between sketching the city’s ancient ruins, he shot pigeons. He developed his own gunpowder recipe, and boasted of his ‘really good marksmanship’, claiming to be able to shoot ‘200 yards point-blank’. This is probably exaggerated, but just as relevant is Cellini’s explanation that, by getting him out into the fresh air to go hunting, and combating his ‘naturally melancholy disposition’, his gun ‘brought me more gain than loss’.

The textual enthusiasm of both Cellini and the duke of Urbino finds a material counterpart in a growing culture of luxury weapons. The aesthetics of these high-end guns helped firearms fit into a court culture that valued beauty and craftsmanship. They were decorated with classical gods, Christian figures and mottoes, and images of the hunt, while the novelty value of combination weapons such as spears with miniature guns attached appealed to the Renaissance sense of fun.

Records of gun ownership in elite households, too, tell a different story from the literary sources. It is at court that wheellock guns – a groundbreaking technology that allowed concealed carry – first leave traces. Leonardo’s sketches of their mechanisms (probably developed in Germany) can be seen in the Codex Atlanticus. Expensive, convenient and modern, wheellocks seem to have become a status symbol. The standard military firearm of this period, the matchlock, was fired by means of a lighted cord (the match) that ignited the powder when the gun was triggered. But the wheellock was a self-lighting mechanism that avoided the need for a lighted match. It was a more complex and therefore more expensive technology, and could be unreliable (probably especially if produced on the cheap). On the other hand, wheellocks had advantages in hunting, avoiding as they did the glow and smell of the burning match cord which might alert prey to a hunter’s presence.
Designs echoed court imagery: hunting scenes, battles, motifs from ancient history and myth, biblical figures

By the start of 1539, Duke Cosimo de’ Medici owned four wheellock handguns made in the German style that he (or more likely his bodyguards) took with him when he travelled. Not a decade on, a wheellock appeared in the first portrait of a European ruler with a handgun: Titian’s equestrian portrait of the victorious Emperor Charles V after the Battle of Mühlberg, in which Charles is shown ‘in the manner in which he went against the rebels’, that is, in the garb of the wheellock-toting Spanish cavalry.

The aesthetic qualities of high-end firearms helped guns blend into the wider courtly environment. Designs echoed imagery common to the court: hunting scenes, battles, motifs from ancient history and myth, or biblical figures like Judith. A wheellock pistol made in Germany and dated 1548 features a figure of the Roman heroine Lucretia along with a Christian motto and image of the Crucifixion. By this time, guns were finding new uses in Europe’s religious wars: far from the Devil’s weapon, they were a means of asserting true Christianity against the heretics.

Back at court, novelty weapons such as the match-fired combination pollaxe and gun in the Royal Armouries, or the boar-spear with two small guns attached given to Cosimo de’ Medici, engaged with a fashion for wider theatrical and festival machines aimed at provoking wonder in their audience. These firearms functioned as marketing devices, promoting their makers – and perhaps also the cities or states of their makers – as potential providers too of the thousands of weapons that might be commissioned for use in war. A striking indication of their acceptability in elite culture comes in 1553, when Mantuan officials began to make ceremonial presents of firearms to the city’s duke in place of the crossbows they had previously given. That the gun could now appear in these ritual contexts shows it had truly arrived.

In wider society, luxury decoration was out of reach, but other factors favoured an expansion of gun ownership. Florence was not the only state to establish or revive a civic militia. In the context of long-running on-off war, it made sense for rulers across Italy to mobilise citizens and equip them with up-to-date weapons. Alongside requirements for militia drill went contests to incentivise the acquisition of shooting skills. Farmers found guns useful for pest control; hunters used them too. Thus, in the 1520s and beyond, more and more Italian states formalised or expanded their militia. Giovanni Moro, a Venetian official who had previously handled military supplies, proposed in 1525 the formation of a citizen militia of 12,000 men, of whom two-thirds would use firearms; these men would receive powder and lead for practice, and a contest would be held three times a year to encourage them. This would be, said Moro, to the ‘honour and utility’ of Venice, and of ‘great benefit’ when it came to conserving Venetian territory.

Such ambitious plans didn’t always succeed, as two cases from Tuscany show. Jacopo Pessina’s detailed study of military organisation in the Republic of Siena estimates that in the last 30 years of the republic (1525-55), between 20 and 33 per cent of adult men served in the militia, with each 500-strong battalion including 150-200 arquebusiers. A report from 1543, however, suggested that the militia was not fit for purpose, lacking not only sufficient men but also the necessary firearms and helmets. The case of Florence, moreover, where the last republican government of 1527-30 fell to the Spanish-backed Medici party after a long siege, shows the limits of a city militia in the face of a foreign army. Anticipating attack, the republican government issued new ordinances for the militia, instituting training in the use of arquebuses, and shooting contests. During the siege of 1530, artisans from shoemakers to cutlers were equipped with arquebuses. They did not, however, prevail against the much better-resourced Spanish army. Still, governments across Italy continued to expand their militia, which made firearms increasingly available to men of all social ranks.
‘Every low herdsman or shepherd you meet in the countryside today has a wheellock arquebus over his shoulder’

If militia service provided one route to familiarity with firearms, so did the related rise of shooting contests. In 1506, Venice introduced a competition to encourage the development of handgun skills among the archers serving on its naval galleys. In 1518, the first prize was 16 arms-lengths of damask fabric, worth 32 ducats, along with 6 ducats in cash. In 1520, the Republic of Lucca instituted a thrice-yearly shooting contest in order to ensure that its citizens were prepared for defence, the founding decree urging them to prefer ‘death over the loss of dear liberty and the reduction of their fatherland to servitude’. Prizes included a silver cup worth almost 20 ducats, and six arms-lengths of damask worth 5 ducats. Soldiers’ pay could be less than 30 ducats a year, so these were generous rewards. Contests, however, were not only about financial incentives. They were also about establishing an acceptable social image for the firearm, just as the iconography of luxury weapons had done at court. The language of the Lucca decree, for example, offered a new and more positive discourse of the gun, as a weapon for the defence of liberty.

Hunting was another context in which guns became familiar not just for elites but more widely. In 1552, for example, a cowherd named Vincenzo obtained a licence from the Bologna authorities that allowed him to carry arms, including a gun for the purpose of hunting. It came with the standard caveat that the weapon must not be carried in churches, at festivals or in markets. These were busy environments where an accidental misfire had higher risks than out in the countryside, and where a generalised ban on arms-bearing (staff weapons such as pikes were also included) made policing more straightforward. Such wide access to guns, however, was a matter of concern. The anonymous author of a proposition for international gun control observed, probably in the late 1570s, that if the Italian princes did not take action soon, then ‘there will be no place nor state where people are safe, given that every low herdsman or shepherd you meet in the countryside today has a wheellock arquebus over his shoulder’.

As guns became more common, so did their appearance in the criminal records. By 1600, firearms had become the predominant weapon used to commit homicide in Bologna. That said, they still accounted for only a third of offences, and in interpreting the figures we should bear in mind the relative lethality of guns when compared with other weapons. In fact, across the broad range of gun crime, it was still relatively rare to come across cases where guns were directly used in planned homicide. More commonly, they were used to threaten: the ideal outcome for the highwayman who shouts: ‘Your money or your life!’ is to ride away with the money without firing a shot.

Many of the historic investigations feature possession of illegal guns and/or their use to intimidate. In a 1554 case near the northern Italian city of Brescia, Valerio Soncino and a gang of 20 men ‘armed with various weapons, including arquebuses’, scaled the walls of a property belonging to Valerio’s brother Annibale, and ‘with various threats’ forced two of his stewards to bring them carts, which they loaded up with goods, stealing in addition cattle and a horse. The robbers got only five miles, however, before they were halted by some villagers who had got wind of what was happening and sounded the alarm. In the ensuing violence, two men and a woman among the villagers were injured. Here, the primary use of the guns was to frighten people into doing as they were told, not to kill them. That is not to say, however, that the proliferation of firearms was not risky. Criminal records from Bologna describe a case in 1575 in which an elderly woman named Giovanna was killed by a man named Pierantonio Fangarezzo; Fangarezzo had been looking over an arquebus (perhaps an early variety of flintlock) to see how it worked when it accidentally went off.
In some notionally criminal cases there was also a political motivation for gun ownership

People engaged in, or considering, political violence also used firearms. The distinction between criminal and political activity was not always straightforward. The system of exile in the Italian states – in which offenders were banned from their home territory and had their property confiscated – often made banditry an attractive option (hence the overlap between the concepts in Italian, where the word bandito is also used for an exile). Civic authorities were particularly keen to police weapon ownership when it posed a risk to the regime. The early years of Medici ducal rule in Florence (formally established in 1532) saw numerous confiscations of illegal weapons: Girolamo di Filippo Bonciani and Francesco di Piero Serragli, for example, fell foul of the law after an arquebus was found under the straw of their former stable. Some of these weapons were probably planted by city officials, but opponents of the regime might reasonably have decided to arm themselves in case of an uprising (for which there were several precedents).

Dissidents in Brescia (a subject city of Venice) also obtained weapons: testimony from 1539 shows how one alleged firearm offender, Antonio Maria, was accused of saying several times that ‘he desired nothing more than that the Emperor and the King of France should make an accord against our Venetian lords, and that he hoped to come with them to sack Brescia.’ Antonio Maria was further accused of ‘continually keeping in his house exiled men of a bad sort, who go out killing on the streets’; he had in his house around 25 guns of different types. While we typically learn about these cases from regime records, by reading between the lines it becomes clear that at least in some notionally criminal cases there was also a political motivation for gun ownership.

People in northern and central Italy owned guns for several reasons: to participate in militia service, for hunting and livestock control, and for criminal activity. Some of this ownership was purely practical: a gun would more reliably than the alternatives kill the fox eating your chickens. Some of it had political motivations, whether to defend the liberty of one’s own fatherland or to oppose a tyrannical overlord. By the middle of the 16th century, a lot of people had guns. It is challenging to establish quite how many. Based on population estimates and numbers enrolled in the militia, the historians Michael Mallett and John Hale estimated that one in 15 rural households in Venetian territory would have had a firearm following the establishment of the militia in the later 1520s: ‘the government’, they observed in Military Organisation of a Renaissance State (2009), ‘was calculatedly accepting a risk to public order’. By 1540, the ruler of Modena required that one in three countryside households should have a gun. These calculations concern militia service, however, and other people may have bought guns second-hand from soldiers, or won them via gambling.

Later in the century, larger cities had shops where guns might be mended and probably also purchased. A 1559 proclamation issued in Bologna in anticipation of riots declared that ‘shopkeepers, who sell those polearms and arquebuses, must store them in their shops in such a way that they are not ready to use’. There is no reason to think that the anonymous author who complained of wheellock-toting shepherds was greatly exaggerating the extent of proliferation.
Guns had a role to play in changing ideas about gender, both in general and with reference to images of rulership

Certain moments in wartime no doubt accelerated access to firearms. Besides the 1529-30 Siege of Florence, records of the defensive provisions in Ferrara of 1552 (when the city was likewise preparing for a possible siege) show that, out of 520 households equipped with armour, pikes, arquebuses and morions, more than half (270) had a gun. Included in this list are 18 female heads of household, of whom six had guns. This raises the question of how many women were gun-owners more generally. The answer seems to be rather few. Sieges were emergency situations in which gender norms might temporarily be suspended, such as when the women of Siena took responsibility for repairs to the city walls. Outside the wartime context, Joe Tryner’s study of court records in Bologna turned up only a single example of a woman with a firearm, and nothing in my wider survey of source material has suggested that was untypical.

In contrast, guns did come to be associated with masculinity. In The Fruit of Liberty (2013), Nicholas Scott Baker argued that the siege of 1529-30 was a particular turning point for elite identity, redefining notions of masculinity from those associated with practices of civic governance to something more ‘rugged, militaristic’. This was particularly apparent in changing clothing styles, to which the bearing of new types of arms might be added. Focusing on Florence after 1537, in Masculinity, Arms and Armour (2020), Victoria Bartels identifies guns as one factor in shifting performances of masculinity, noting that they increased the danger attached to ‘routine bouts of aggression’ that had traditionally been employed to settle disputes between men. In the context of the Italian Wars (and specific local conflicts within them), guns had a role to play in changing ideas about gender, both in general and with reference to images of rulership. This is confirmed in the account of Benvenuto Cellini, whose self-aggrandising narrative of his participation in the Italian Wars includes a comment he made to a companion, Alessandro del Bene, to persuade him to stick around and shoot back at an invading army during the 1527 Sack of Rome: ‘Now you’ve brought me here, we must show that we’re men.’

Over the course of the 16th century, familiarity with firearms grew. It was increasingly expected that men would be able to use a gun: the expansion of militias was a key factor here alongside direct soldiering experience. The acquisition of skills in shooting was positively encouraged through civic contests with generous prizes. Rhetoric about the importance of guns for civic defence and for the maintenance of honour and liberty offered a counterweight to more negative images of gunpowder weapons as diabolical, unchivalrous or impious. Guns were useful for protection of livestock from predators as well as for hunting more generally. In turn, their ready availability also made them accessible for use by bandits, during vendettas and indeed for political violence. However, their lethality shifted the dynamics of violent encounters: so effective were guns as a threat that in some cases they may have prompted victims to give up without a fight. On the other hand, with increasing proliferation came an increased risk of both accidents and casual use in interpersonal violence. Yet not all gun ownership was enthusiastic. Some applicants for arms licences evidently felt constrained to carry guns in self-defence, and cultural ambivalence about these weapons remained long after they became common objects.
As firearms became more familiar, it was as much a decision not to be a gun owner as to acquire the new technology.

items.title: Róisín Tapponi’s Scene City is a Debut Novel for the Extreme Present
items.description: TikTok hauls from the Chloë Sevigny yard sale. The Mowalola tank top with WET across the front. Nocellara olives at a street-facing table on Broadway Market. People-watching at Allpress Dalston. A Burberry tench coat (gifted). Fines for watching Adam Curtis do
items.author: Thom Waite
paragraphs: TikTok hauls from the Chloë Sevigny yard sale. The Mowalola tank top with WET across the front. Nocellara olives at a street-facing table on Broadway Market. People-watching at Allpress Dalston. A Burberry tench coat (gifted). Fines for watching Adam Curtis documentaries on BBC iPlayer with no TV license. Percy Pigs and a “gash-red stick of Isamaya Ffrench across heavily injected lips”. If any or all of these words make sense to you, you might have spent the last couple of years living in Róisín Tapponi’s debut novel, Scene City.

The novel is set in contemporary London – versions of it, at least. “London is many villages,” the author tells AnOther. “But also you can have a completely different experience of literally the same street, depending on your circumstances.” This version of the city in particular is seen through the eyes of Romy, an art history student who has accepted a writing assignment about the Young British Artists, which involves tipping headlong into night after night of firsthand “research” on the YBAs’ haunts and hedonistic lifestyles. Joining her in this pursuit is a coterie of wealthy friends with careers in the commercial art world, who serve as a counterpoint to her relatively unprivileged upbringing and a constant source of wry humour. “Disclaimer,” she jokes on the very first page: “The art world is a façade for gay men to fuck.”

For anyone familiar with Tapponi’s work, it’s clear the veil between fiction and reality sometimes wears pretty thin in Scene City. For those who aren’t, a brief biography: Tapponi is an Assyrian Iraqi and Irish film programmer and writer, born in 1999. In 2020 she founded the SWANA cinema streamer Shasha Movies, which has landed her (just like Romy) on the Dazed 100 and Forbes 30 Under 30 lists, and she completed a PhD in History of Art at the age of 25.

Tapponi is understandably hesitant to speak about which bits of the book – and especially which characters or institutions – are ‘real’ and which are pure fiction. “Friends, especially the friends who inspired the main characters, were very, very much a part of the process, because these are my real relationships,” she explains. “People probably think it’s a salacious art world exposé, but it’s absolutely not. There’s no gossip.” The more interesting spillover from real life is the constant flood of opinions, she suggests. “There are a lot of opinions in the book, which are also my opinions.”

These opinions are rooted in a hyper-contemporary outlook, delivered in the kind of post-woke, can’t-quite-tell-if-it’s-a-joke register that you might overhear at one of the cooler Frieze parties. The form of the novel itself is similarly of its time – literally composed in Tapponi’s notes app, it’s “a reading experience more akin to scrolling” than the books or films of a bygone era. “I really want to write 21st-century novels,” Tapponi says. “How we experience life and communicate now is so specific, through disassociation, brainrot, doomscrolling, yapping, Instagram captions ... all of those things are in the book as formal devices.”

Similarly, the book embraces the bewildering nature of our fragile reality. This means that there’s no story to follow, as such. Romy – the “marginalised flaneuse” or “Leopold Bloom if he had a 24-inch waist” – drifts from one gallery opening to the next, to a party, to a private members’ club. The next morning is lost to a hangover before the cycle starts all over again. In a world that’s lost the plot, Scene City is a novel of yapping, of vibes.
Thom Waite You work across so many different mediums and worlds. Why a novel, now?

Róisín Tapponi I always wanted to write novels, but life took me on a different path. I ended up a film programmer, and I love Shasha – it’s my baby. But when I finished my PhD, I’d never felt so free ... That coincided with the death of my grandfather. All three of my grandparents died around the same time, but my grandad, who the book is dedicated to, always wanted to write novels, and was always like, “Róisín is going to write”.

I come from a family that doesn’t read books, but is so literary. My family, on both the Iraqi side and the Irish side, are such brilliant storytellers. I grew up in an environment where everyone had a way with words. But perhaps the earliest moment in my life where I realised I was interested in doing this was when I was a child in Ireland and I had a pocket-sized copy of Chamber Music by James Joyce, from 1907. I just loved this little book of poems. Then we moved here [London] and I just always held the memory of being in rural Ireland with this little Joyce book.

TW Joyce looms large in Scene City. He’s mentioned by name, but also present in the style – the stream-of-consciousness and portmanteaus. Do you ever feel as if you’re writing in, or engaging with, a specific literary tradition?

RT There are certainly writers I’m deeply inspired by ... but I guess I was engaging more with specific texts and individuals than whole movements. What’s interesting is that I didn’t actually read a lot of the writers who inspired Scene City until I finished the book. Everyone who’s read it was asking me, “Have you read Bret Easton Ellis?” And I hadn’t. But then I read Glamorama, and I was like, “This makes sense.” Obviously Bret didn’t invent name-dropping as a narrative device but I think he did it best, and that’s something that I used a lot.

Anyway, I’m happy for other people to say [Scene City] belongs to a movement. It would be quite interesting. I’ll join a club. I’ll join a scene. Bret Easton Ellis and Jay McInerney and Tama Janowitz – the ‘Brat Pack’ – they were like, ‘We don’t even hang out’. If I get lumped into something like that, I’ll just accept it. It’s always better to exist within something than in a vacuum, culturally.
“I don’t know if there’s been an interesting movement in the London art world since the 90s” – Róisín Tapponi
TW The YBAs are another movement that’s central to the novel. Why were they important to you, besides being a jumping-off point for all the drinking and partying?

RT The YBAs are also a group of people who hate being called that in retrospect. To be honest, I don’t know if there’s been an interesting movement in the London art world since the 90s, so the YBAs loom large. You can’t really escape them. I mean, so many of them are fantastic, Sarah Lucas, Tracey Emin, but including the lesser-known figures – I loved Hamad Butt and Angus Fairhurst, so many great artists.

TW Both the YBAs and the Brat Pack rejected their labels, but in Scene City it feels like a lot of the characters are actively trying to build or take part in a scene. Do you think our opinion on these cultural dynamics has changed?

RT I think culture right now is obsessed with scenes. You see that most obviously, in London, with Charlie xcx and Brat, that party music scene. Community is such a buzzword, but I think everyone does want to belong to something, and contextualise themselves and their work. Especially when people are becoming increasingly isolated ... you find your family through culture. I think that’s what a scene is, it’s a way of finding family within culture.
TW Could you talk a bit about Romy’s relative otherness, in terms of class and race, and how she relates to her scene in London as a result?

RT Romy’s a character who ... everything’s so foreign to her, and she’s so different. A lot of people in the art world grew up in it, and even if they didn’t grow up within the art world they grew up in upper-middle-class families. We see her in real-time trying to observe as much as possible, to learn the system and make a judgement about how much of herself she wants to sacrifice in order to become the person that she wants to become.
TW Assimilation often also means walking a tightrope between who you want to become and what other people want you to become. How do you navigate that?
“That’s what a scene is ... a way of finding family within culture” – Róisín Tapponi

RT I know exactly what I want. I want to be great. My aspirations aren’t in lifestyle, they’re very focused towards working, to hopefully write decent books. When you’re a very young woman, and from a biracial background or whatever, sometimes people – especially, like, an old white man – have a different imagination for you than they would have for people who are more like them. But if I think something is possible, it is possible, and no amount of incompetence or lack of imagination on another person’s part can tell me that’s not the case.

TW At one point Romy says, “This is a specific moment in my life which is already passing”. Is it partly that awareness that underlies the desire to write fiction? The desire to document or make sense of everything before it disappears?

RT It’s the whole thing. It’s why I wrote the book. I was trying to make sense of what was happening around me. Writing is my way of processing. I was doing an interview with a photographer last week and she said her camera roll was her way of processing her day – if it’s not on her camera roll, her day didn’t exist. My way is writing, and specifically the novel form, because novels are sturdy, they withstand time.
TW Do you think it’s more difficult for such an old, established form to contend with the present?

RT That’s my job, it’s my ultimate task. People write novels for very different reasons, but mine is to ask how the novel can give form to our very specific means of communicating and experiencing life today. How to give the novel a ‘software update’.
TW You’ve described yapping as a device in the book. How do you define “yapping”?

RT Yapping is a synonym of rambling, but I think it’s quite gendered. Girls yap. It’s just a kind of verbal stream of consciousness about one’s day, with so many inconsequential details, of no benefit to anyone who’s listening or even to the speaker themselves. Just kind of speaking for speaking’s sake.

There’s actually so much historical fiction that uses the notion of yapping. It’s so brilliantly done in Wittgenstein’s Mistress by David Markson. I read it and I was like, “Oh my God this is yapping.” But obviously that was predating the internet, predating yapping as a notion. And then there’s Laurence Sterne. It’s funny, there’s books where they’re using formal devices that haven’t even been invented yet.
“I wouldn’t say there’s a plot in the book. Everyone knows what’s going to happen next: it’s the next party” – Róisín Tapponi

TW When you’re yapping, like when you’re scrolling, are you interacting on more of a vibe level, where the actual content is less important? Is that how you envisioned readers engaging with Scene City as well?

RT Yes. Because I wouldn’t say there’s a plot in the book. It’s vibe-based. People keep reading it for the vibe rather than being like, “What’s going to happen next?” Everyone knows what’s going to happen next: it’s the next party. And morally ... there are no morals. No one really changes.

RT Morals don’t guide my decision-making. I try to take everyone at as human a level as possible. I don’t believe in cancel culture. I think it’s so important to give people grace. You especially learn this if you grow up in an environment where people maybe didn’t do the best things around you, but you learn to give them grace and not just shut them out.
TW Are you concerned about the way people might conflate your morality as a person and as a fiction writer, or even a character in the text?
RT I get most upset when I’m misunderstood.
Scene City is out now published by Verso

items.title: A simple wooden shell hides a dramatic waterfront home in Brazil
items.description: On a waterfront site in Delfinópolis in Brazil’s Minas Gerais, this expansive contemporary house uses the luxury of space to create a refined architectural experience. Designed by Filipi and Mariana Oliveira and their team at MF+Arquitetos, Casa Celeiro (Barn
items.author: Jonathan Bell
paragraphs: On a waterfront site in Delfinópolis in Brazil’s Minas Gerais, this expansive contemporary house uses the luxury of space to create a refined architectural experience. Designed by Filipi and Mariana Oliveira and their team at MF+Arquitetos, Casa Celeiro (Barn House) covers some 1,108 m², arranged as two forms set at right angles in the landscape on the shores of a large reservoir.

The simple lines of the upper volume is what gives the house its name. A long, single-storey pitched timber roof structure that runs north-south, it is flanked on all sides by covered verandas. Formed from glue laminated timber frames, the roof structure oversails the built-up area to create the verandas, providing solar shading as well as access to a steel-clad inner core of five ensuite bedrooms, culminating in a principal between suite at the northern end, complete with two walls of sliding glazing that can be opened up to the landscape beyond.

In the centre of the barn element is a grand living room, the only point at which the internal spaces open up to the full height of the pitched roof. The verandas are used for circulation and incorporate glazed and louvred panels that be swung open as required. On the other side is a small kitchen, gym and utility spaces, as well as a generously sized covered terrace.

This space also houses a grand staircase that descends towards the water to the east, leading to the lower level. Half sunk into the hillside, this is the location of the main kitchen and living room, with three sliding glass walls opening onto a pool terrace with the reservoir beyond. The house is therefore divided between public and private, with each component having its own relationship with the landscape and horizon.

On the lower, more public, level, there’s very little perception of the accommodation structure above it. Likewise, when looking out east across the reservoir, the flat concrete roof of the semi-sunken lower level is planted to make it all but invisible. Aside from the internal staircase, one key physical element unites the two components, a cascade of rough-hewn steps that leads down from the upper terrace into the heart of lower pavilion, flanked by mature planting.
Stone steps lead down to the lower level
Stone steps lead down to the lower level

‘Rather than an abrupt connection, this route proposes a gradual transition between architecture and nature,’ the architects explain, ‘For a few moments, the building partially disappears, and movement is guided instead by stone, topography, and vegetation.’ It’s a rare of incursion for nature in a house that prides itself of simplicity and grand structural gestures. The lower level also a sauna and changing areas for the outdoor pool, alongside storage and a wine cellar in the more sheltered, cooler subterranean section.
The lower pavilion adjoins the pool
The lower pavilion adjoins the pool
The lower pavilion adjoins the pool

The architects point to the house’s inherent contradictions – barn-like in form but not in execution, with many layers gradually revealed from within. The monolithic wooden form gives way to multiple materials and textures, as steel, concrete, stone, vegetation, light, and water are brought together under one roof.
Receive our daily digest of inspiration, escapism and design stories from around the world direct to your inbox.
Views out across the pool and reservoir
Views out across the pool and reservoir

‘Casa Celeiro … is simultaneously shelter and openness, form and void, permanence and transformation. The memory of the barn remains present in its most elemental form, while the architecture reinterprets it in response to a different way of living - one that is more open to the climate, to movement, and to the constant presence of the landscape.’
MFmaisArquitetos.com, @MFarquitetos

Jonathan Bell has written for Wallpaper* magazine since 1999, covering everything from architecture and transport design to books, tech and graphic design. He is now the magazine’s Transport and Technology Editor. Jonathan has written and edited 15 books, including Concept Car Design, 21st Century House, and The New Modern House, and co-edits the long-running things magazine weblog.

items.title: Alice Diop and Miu Miu celebrate Black female creativity at Art Basel Paris
items.description: A consideration of the rich and multifaceted lives of women has long shaped Miuccia Prada's Miu Miu, a curiosity that takes shape in both fashion and culture. In 2024, this philosophy was cemented when Miu Miu became the official partner of Art Basel Paris' pu
items.author: Hannah Silver
paragraphs: A consideration of the rich and multifaceted lives of women has long shaped Miuccia Prada's Miu Miu, a curiosity that takes shape in both fashion and culture. In 2024, this philosophy was cemented when Miu Miu became the official partner of Art Basel Paris' public programme, with the partnership uniting a host of creatives, from artists to performers and musicians. The programme debuted with Tales & Tellers, by artist Goshka Macuga, and was followed in 2025 with 30 Blizzards, by artist Helen Marten.

For the third year of the partnership, at Art Basel Paris 2026, Miuccia Prada invited French filmmaker Alice Diop to take the reins, with the presentation of a major project at the Palais d'Iéna HQ of France's Economic, Social and Environmental Council in Paris – which is also the site of Miu Miu's runway shows. For the occasion, Diop is presenting an exhibition, ‘Geste de Consolation’ (Gesture of Consolation), which builds on themes that Diop introduced in her 2025 film Fragments for Venus for Miu Miu's anthology series Women's Tales.
For Diop, who for the first time takes on the role of artist-curator, it is an opportunity to broaden a practice which, to date, has encompassed directing and screenwriting.

‘When Miuccia Prada came to me and offered me this opportunity to create a video installation, I was both surprised and intimidated by the trust she placed in me, to do something I'd never done before,' says Diop. ‘But I have learned to trust women who trust me.'

The works in the space are a celebration of Black female creativity, highlighting a thread that has run throughout Diop's work. Now, she gathers the female artists whom she admires, across a prism of mediums and practices, taking visitors on a scenographic journey to discover their work across four connecting spaces. ‘I have invited Black women artists who have helped me over the years to create, and helped to heal and repair me, not only as an artist but as a Black woman. They have considered the way that we have been building ourselves as Black women, due to the need of having to dissociate because of the fetishising gaze.'
