items.title: Below Deck Recap: Working Out the Kinks
items.description: It’s built into the dramatic structure of Below Deck that the crew hardly has time to get to know each other before the first charter, so that work can be as difficult as possible, as soon as possible. Save for Moe, who works by himself, every crewmember runs
items.author: Rafaela Bassili
paragraphs: It’s built into the dramatic structure of Below Deck that the crew hardly has time to get to know each other before the first charter, so that work can be as difficult as possible, as soon as possible. Save for Moe, who works by himself, every crewmember runs into some kind of adjustment problem this week. Actually, everyone save for Moe and James, who has yet to look alive. The most we get from him this week is a tale about his full-back Thai tattoo, which he got on one of his previous six trips to Thailand, a detail I’m shocked to learn on episode two. Despite not talking much, James’s good looks are enough to make at least one woman cry on the crew’s first night out. Though, to be fair, that’s not the only time Rosa cries this week.

It would take very little to make me cry if there were cameras following me around hoping I mess up on my job, so I sympathize with Rosa. But, as Fraser tells Rainbeau when they’re setting up the beach picnic, first impressions count, and Rosa has unfortunately cried herself into seeming whiny. Her first cry happens after the beach picnic. Kerry is overjoyed to take the guests to a private beach cove with beautiful, dramatic cliffs that remind Fraser of Jurassic Park, but the guests are underwhelmed at best. It doesn’t help that Fraser and Rainbeau set the lunch table only on one side, presumably so the guests can look out at the view, but the effect is that they can’t talk to each other. In fact, slight guest dissatisfaction starts to emerge, coupled with some rationalizations: “I know we didn’t, like, move anywhere since yesterday,” primary Kenny remarks, “but we’re in an epic spot.”

While the guests are on the beach, Rosa tells Kaylee that her first days on the job have felt like “the birth of something great, and birth is ugly.” That’s the mindset with which she receives instructions from Rainbeau upon the latter’s return to the boat. Rosa ostensibly doesn’t appreciate Rainbeau’s lack of manners — she doesn’t say please and thank you — but I imagine what’s really going on is that Rainbeau’s directions are annoying because Rainbeau, younger and less experienced, is the one giving them. Fraser catches Rosa crying. She tells him that she can take direction from “anyone,” but not if they use that tone. Later, with Kaylee, the truth comes out: Rosa says that Rainbeau acts too much the chief stew when she’s only the second.

Kaylee herself has other things on her mind, namely: deckhand Matt, figuring out how to work the juicer (the next day, it takes her 40 minutes with Moe’s help to manage a few glasses of green juice), and learning the difference between a plate and a “charger,” the plate you put plates on. Her flirtationship with Matt begins when he tells Moe, the onboard matchmaker — “pool is too young for me,” Moe explains, “if I can’t swim, I’ll make sure everybody is swimming” — that he likes “Katie” (he means Kaylee). Moe relates the news, and when Kaylee sees Matt, she nearly drops a tray of drinks. Hearing her say that she is a “hopeless romantic” made me want to press a huge red STOP button that would activate sirens and sprinklers on the Azul V. This is not the man, Kaylee. At different points in this episode, Matt tells us that he lost $80,000 trading cryptocurrency and that Rainbeau being taken “doesn’t really mean anything” (as in, he thinks she’s not attractive). It’s giving manosphere. Save yourself, dear girl.

Also, and perhaps most importantly, Matt has an attitude on deck. James likes Alex’s laissez-faire approach to leadership, but Matt thinks he’s too chill; he likes Kerry better, though he admits he has often clashed with captains. It’s an ominous admission, given that Kerry later identifies Matt’s arrogance as a potential problem for the deck crew. Like James, Sen also admires Alex’s approach, though there is more to it than professional respect; she thinks his air of mystery is sexy.

As the second day of the charter winds down, the interior team continues to struggle. Hanging out on the swim platform, the guests ask for chips and dip — Fraser refuses to serve them in the sun because they’ll get “too gross,” but promises to have them on standby once the guests come in. Apparently hungry for chips, they come in right away, like kids ready for their pool-day snack. But the chips never come. Eventually, one of the guests resigns to the fact that they’ll eat dinner soon anyway. I always side with the crew and think guests should demand as little as possible, but if you’re vacationing on a superyacht, you are entitled to have chips with your beer. I mean, it’s only right. These people should speak up!

Like Rosa, who finally speaks up when Rainbeau tries to micromanage her table-setting later that evening. When Rainbeau dismisses the need for gloves to handle cutlery, Rosa puts her foot down and grabs them anyway, “because that’s my standard.” You’d think those would be Rainbeau’s standards, too. At least they manage to set the places all around the table so people can look at each other. Kerry joins for dinner and is gifted a shirt to match the guests’, who have worn matching outfits every. single. day. Also thankfully, Moe nails dinner. His food — tomato and burrata salad; lamb chops with carrot puree; tiramisu — looks delicious, and apparently tastes great, too. When he comes up to talk to the guests, they applaud and cheer. The captain is pleased.

After dinner, the crew puts on a talent show at the guests’ request. Jessenia and Alex do some half cartwheels and backbends or something. Rainbeau yodels horribly (Moe: “I never heard yodeling before and I never want to hear it again), and Matt pulls a condom through his nose and out of his mouth (Moe: “what the fuck?”). It’s all disturbing enough to send the guests right to bed. Earlier, Fraser told Rainbeau to watch her tone with Rosa, who is “sensitive.” He also said that he had an undepicted chat with Kaylee about “sense of urgency.” At first, Rainbeau has no time for Rosa’s “sensitive English girl feelings” and would prefer Rosa to have come to her directly, but, later that night, she asks Rosa if she did anything to “piss [her] off.” Rosa admits to feeling patronized, and Rainbeau tells her briefly about her horrendous experience last season. She apologizes, and they hug. It seems like everything is going to be fine. Rainbeau goes to bed, and Rosa flirts with James for the rest of her shift. James feels some chemistry between them, but then again, he says, he flirts with everyone.

In the morning, Kerry is on edge about the first docking. The current at the marina is strong enough to make whirlpools, and the Azul V doesn’t have a ton of horsepower, so they need to leave early to beat the tide swings. The night before, he makes sure to tell Alex this. Still, Alex only has himself and Sen up early. They need to bring in the NautiBuoys and haul the anchor, a big job for only two people. Though she appreciates his trust, Sen doesn’t feel fully prepared to be in such a high-pressure position. She and Alex fight with the anchor chains long enough for Kerry to come out to the bow. He’s irritated; not only are they behind schedule, but Alex has also gone radio-silent. Kerry fixes the problem in 30 seconds only to realize, once they’re leaving, that Alex and Sen left the anchor ball up.

Before they get to the dock, Sen stops by the wheelhouse to apologize to Kerry for the delay; he doesn’t blame her and even tells her she did great. But he’s not as lenient with Alex, whom he instructs to come up with a better system. Kerry gathers the whole deck team to show them how they’re going to dock the boat. Hoping to redeem himself, Alex goes over the process in painstaking detail with the crew; he even draws a diagram. As he’s talking, Matt interjects and takes the pen from his hand. Still, the docking goes beautifully, with the help of Kaylee and Rosa (a former deck/stew) on the fenders. After the guests leave, Kerry and Alex debrief. Kerry tells Alex that they need to communicate better, and that he needs to keep an eye on Matt’s confidence, which verges on arrogance — the captain noticed Matt’s interruption when they were going through the docking logistics. I’m loving this shrewd, proactive side of Kerry. When Alex retorts that he is happy letting others “take initiative,” Kerry warns him that taking initiative is not taking over; there’s a hierarchy for a reason.

There was nothing in the guests’ manner to suggest they were anything but happy with their experience. At the very last second, Christina tells the crew that though they “bring great energy into their jobs,” it’s clear that they have “never worked together before.” Everyone looks stunned. “That being said, the food — no notes,” she amends. They still leave a decent $25,000 tip, which comes out to $2,083 each, but amazingly, no one brings up Christina’s comment at the tip meeting, not even Kerry. In fact, he congratulates his crew on a great first charter. Instead of discussing the feedback, Kerry has the crew pray for a good season at a Buddhist temple. “I’m praying for money, love, and everyone gets along,” Kaylee says, sounding like Bubbles.

At dinner, Moe continues to matchmake, encouraging Alex to go for it with Sen. Both of them want to tread carefully because of their power imbalance, but by the end of the night, they’re making out in the tuk-tuk. Alex tells Rainbeau that his strategy is to let Sen set the tone. Everyone, including Fraser — who is always puzzlingly encouraging his stews to get involved with crew — pressures Kaylee and Matt to make out, which they do, happily. That’s two Moe-engineered couples exchanging saliva; Moe did advise Rosa to take initiative with James, but she doesn’t like to be the one leading the charge. As far as she’s concerned, anyway, Rainbeau got in the way. She sits next to James at dinner and flirts a little — just because she has a boyfriend, Rainbeau says, it doesn’t mean she can’t flirt — which annoys Rosa. But the real hurt comes when they continue to flirt at the club, even after Rainbeau has encouraged Rosa to go for it in the bathroom.

Rosa’s frustration is understandable; less understandable is the fact that she and James ride back to the boat in a tuk-tuk by themselves and she doesn’t say a word to him. In her cabin, she cries as she tells Sen that she made it “abundantly clear” that she liked him, and only wasted time and energy. Someone — Sen? — needs to gently tell her that she made nothing clear at all, at least not when the cameras were on. I want to be on Rosa’s side, but she’s making it difficult. Meanwhile, Kaylee and Matt are doing things behind the closed doors of a guest cabin. She tells him that they’ll be exclusive for six weeks, which is definitely precocious. It makes me so nervous that this obviously good-spirited, gullible girl is going to put her feelings in the hands of a guy who, in response, can only say: “I have that effect on women.” I need that red button, stat!

items.title: The Real Housewives of Potomac Recap: Love After Lockup
items.description: Last week’s premiere concluded with the revelation that Tia’s husband, Rob, had admitted to maintaining a profile on dating apps for more than a year, insisting that nothing physical happened and that he just “felt lonely in the marriage.” Question for the aud
items.author: Shamira Ibrahim
paragraphs: Last week’s premiere concluded with the revelation that Tia’s husband, Rob, had admitted to maintaining a profile on dating apps for more than a year, insisting that nothing physical happened and that he just “felt lonely in the marriage.” Question for the audience: Is it worse to discover that your husband has been actively cheating on you for a year or that he’s spent 12 months unsuccessfully soliciting strangers on the internet? If the best-case scenario is that you had such poor game that you couldn’t actually close the deal with anyone, I’d argue that you are too far gone to try to come up with reasonable justifications for your indiscretions. Especially since the rub of it all is that he was anything but discreet: Not only did he spend a year advertising himself to prospective romantic partners, but he apparently couldn’t even be bothered to care enough to prevent his wife from finding out through her castmates. And to add insult to injury, Tia had to ask him to take the profile down herself. On a show where the bar for marital fidelity has long been in hell, Rob showed up with a shovel in tow to find even deeper depths sink to.

Tia’s struggle with making sense of her father’s history of infidelity has made Rob’s decision-making here feel especially cruel. We just spent a season watching Tia try to make amends for the siblings she rejected due to feeling betrayed by her dad, only to end up duplicating the life of her mother and repeatedly making excuses about her husband’s selfishness to try to keep the family unit together. With her mother coming to stay for the summer, I’m sure we will continue to see Tia process the painful betrayal of being cheated on by a man with a combover worse than Donald Trump.

But if there’s anything this group of women knows well, it’s how to bounce back from humiliating infidelity, and all of the women gracefully rise to the occasion and offer Tia sound advice. Gizelle urges Tia to slow down and not feel rushed to make any singular decision. Wendy reminds Tia that Rob is the one who violated the marriage, and should be responsible for carrying the burden of explaining his actions to their daughters himself. While it’s sensible advice, the subtext is thick with the reality of Wendy’s admittedly strained relationship with Eddie. At every chance, the former professor is throwing around signs brighter than an air traffic controller that she blames Eddie for the predicament they are in as she tries to convince the audience that everyone is gleefully reveling in her downfall.

Robyn notices this during their one-on-one sit-down, and doesn’t shy away from acknowledging the obvious tension. I’m still trying to figure out exactly how Robyn is going to fit into this cast now, but her willingness to admit to Wendy that she found Ashley and Gizelle gossiping about Tia’s marriage in poor taste is a positive indicator that she won’t just be functioning as Gizelle’s mouthpiece all season. She offers Wendy a clean slate and agrees to try to be more respectful of how they discuss Wendy’s legal affairs on the podcast.

Wendy is in a bit of a tricky position, where she is suffering under the pedestal she built for herself. She has spent years constructing an image of marital and professional achievement, and now that both pillars of that identity are under extraordinary strain, she is asking for empathy that I am doubtful she would offer in return. Her attempts at breadcrumbing financial ignorance aren’t really going over that well after spending seasons insisting she was smarter than all of the other women; Eddie has never really been clear on what he makes for money; and most damningly, Wendy has always presented her marriage as the ideal duo out of the cast. She cannot be surprised that people are not running to comfort her in her low moment, even if it has to hurt; but taking it on the chin and persevering the way Porsha had to rebuild her reputation on camera would go a lot further for her than insisting she is being uniquely victimized. There is a difference between being unfairly abandoned by one’s community and facing professional consequences amid serious allegations of fraud. Wendy is entitled to defend herself, but the narrative that she has been persecuted merely for existing is doing her few favors.

As long as Wendy’s main source of refuge is her mother, Susan, though, I doubt that will change anytime soon. It’s touching to see their bond remain intact during what Wendy describes as the darkest period of her life, but Wendy’s insistence that the entire world has turned its back on her and was waiting for her downfall is becoming increasingly difficult to indulge. The mother-daughter duo finds time to take a (clearly pre-planned) swipe at Karen, with Susan advising her daughter to “go to the library and find another reference.” It’s a cute line, if rehearsed, but the reality is that Karen’s advice, while pointed for entertainment purposes, is correct. The best thing Wendy can do is refuse to talk about the case while everything plays out. If Erika Jayne can remain mum while people are calling her responsible for stealing from grieving families, so can Wendy. The more she talks, the more room she has to let people poke holes in her choices and lifestyle, and no one is more ready to step up to the plate than Gizelle.

Gizelle meets up with Tia with two clear objectives: to smooth over their fight and to call Wendy a scammer on camera. Gizelle might be mainly focused on reputational repair, but I generally believe Gizelle when she says she feels bad for Tia (even if Kal had to walk her through why she was in the wrong). That empathy, however, has a very firm expiration date when the conversation turns to Wendy — and while I am generally inclined to dismiss Gizelle’s moral pronouncements, I actually understand her position here. If Gizelle were the one facing criminal charges, Wendy would not merely throw her under the bus; she would climb into the driver’s seat and reverse over her for good measure. When Tia asks whether Gizelle has personally experienced that kind of treatment from Wendy, Gizelle responds with characteristic bluntness: “I’m not a scammer. I’m not a criminal. I haven’t given that to give.”

At long last, we arrive at Karen’s party, who has decided to celebrate her return home with a Color Purple-themed gathering at a medical spa in Bowie, Maryland. The premise is baffling on several levels, but to be frank, the event is too confusing to be offensive. The women arrive in varying shades of lavender, looking like a bridal party that has been inexplicably redirected to a dermatology appointment. Karen arrives in full Sofia drag, which is a sentence I could never have imagined writing in this lifetime or the next.

Alice Walker’s novel is one about gendered violence and racism with explicit queer undertones, but I imagine Karen hasn’t cracked the book open since it first came to theaters in 1985. I cannot sufficiently explain the absurdity of watching a woman commemorate her release from incarceration by subjecting herself to voluntary pain in a medical spa. The festivities include massages, liquid IV treatments, and what appears to be an extensive menu of cosmetic procedures. At one point, Karen prepares for laser hair removal of her bits and kibbles, prompting the obvious question: Who is the Grand Dame getting ready to fuck?

The Grand Dame’s bizarre event cannot entirely distract from the unresolved tensions among the women, however. Karen begins discussing her experiences with incarcerated women, positioning herself as someone who has gained a newfound understanding of the system’s failures and the people caught within it. Wendy jumps at the opening to nail Karen to the wall about how she feels abandoned by Karen, who chose to punish her last season after Wendy jumped on Stacy’s bandwagon. Karen is no one’s saint — her having the cast eat dinner less than 10 feet from where she had her bootyhole hairs singed off is clear evidence of that — but Wendy needs to learn that at times, the most effective response to a perceived slight is simply to let it pass. She gets in a zinger challenging Karen’s rehab narrative, but her reflexive defensiveness makes it increasingly difficult for Wendy to engage with any discussion of accountability that doesn’t begin and end with her own grievances, and ultimately works against her, whether or not she has a valid point about Karen’s hypocrisy. If Wendy refuses to see that for herself, she will simply have to learn it the hard way.

Next week, Cynthia Bailey makes a guest appearance, and Gizelle discovers that Tia has been relaying details of their discussions to Wendy. This, predictably, does not go over well: the woman who has made a career out of spreading information is now very concerned about the sanctity of confidentiality. See you then!

• I am happy that Thiemo is making an effort to support Stacy’s career on-camera. Unfortunately, Thiemo has all of the charisma of a piece of cardboard. It is likely just a function of German excitement, which tends to register somewhere between mild bemusement and polite acknowledgment. I wish them both the best, but I cannot pretend to be invested in the house-training of a pet while Stacey kisses their dog on the mouth.
• Wendy’s confessional look with the curlicue hairstyle? I don’t know if doubling down on glam is the smart play here, but she is really looking fantastic; I will not lie.

• Courtney freely admitting she and her husband were both cheating on each other and decided it was cheaper to stay married? Move over Will and Jada Pinkett, we have a new bad marriage for life and I am very intrigued.

• Gizelle claiming that Jamal Bryant cheated privately is one of those lies that you just kind of have to let her say. I’m fairly certain it was gossip in the Baltimore and megachurch community for years, but whatever helps her feel more superior, I guess.
• Nothing notable about Robyn’s return just yet, but I am looking forward to her and Karen sparring again. (Although I did find her freely admitting to GLP-1s interesting).

• Tia claims to attempt to broker peace between Gizelle and Wendy, but her revealing that she called Wendy a scammer felt like her being more eager for a moment than looking out for a friend. This is not the first time Tia has done something slippery like this; I have definitely got my eye on her.

• I remain fascinated by the fact that Rob apparently spent time on dating apps 17 years ago. The landscape of online dating back then was completely different and for real horndogs: I’m talking OKCupid/Craigslist days. That is a man who makes cheating a lifestyle.

items.title: The Diplomat Season-Finale Recap: No Fools In This Chain
items.description: The thing about abusive people is that they’re constantly testing everyone around them. They’re pushing buttons; they’re poking at boundaries and psychological sensitivities. They’re blowing past limits and squeezing through loopholes. It’s compulsive and repu
items.author: Sophie Brookover
paragraphs: The thing about abusive people is that they’re constantly testing everyone around them. They’re pushing buttons; they’re poking at boundaries and psychological sensitivities. They’re blowing past limits and squeezing through loopholes. It’s compulsive and repugnant, and can make for great TV, especially when the main abusive character gets what could be (at last!!) something resembling comeuppance. In this corker of a season finale — which caps off a season that’s re-energized The Diplomat top to bottom — Grace turns out to be a victim of her own success, getting behind the wheel while very drunk on power, and taking one autocratic turn too far.

Things start out ordinarily enough for another day in her leadership team. Kate is once again explaining to Hal something very obvious about his own psyche and routine behavior. Yes, my guy, you are an inveterate liar and norm-breaker! The one thing you and I are going to agree on in this episode is that she should have left you long ago! They must work together to prepare Todd for his meeting with Palmer, but Kate will have to do so silently, as she’s been ordered not to speak, lest speaking lead to interference (or, as we used to call it, doing her job).

Holding her tongue is not Kate’s forte in general, and the severity of Todd’s avalanche of blunders in their meeting with the British foreign secretary tests the outer limits of her ability. Should we be laughing at a scene where the First Gentleman/Special Envoy’s incompetence and inadequate preparation to respond to pesky little follow-up questions about whether or not American warships will fire on British and/or Russian vessels as they make their way towards the Russian submarine? Perhaps not, but Bradley Whitford is so good at playing overconfident yet increasingly aware of being far out of his depth that it’s hard not to. (This scene re-created some of the delights of one of my favorite scenes in The West Wing where Josh Lyman had to step in for CJ Cregg at the press room briefing podium as she recovered from a root canal, to hilarious, near-catastrophic results.)

Todd, but a little lost lamb in the woods that he is, manages to suggest several times that the U.S. would engage militarily with Russian vessels, and that shooting at any British ships in the vicinity is not off the table. Upon hearing him say that any British citizens caught between the sides “should make every effort to go somewhere else”, Kate first tells him to stop talking, then stands up to announce that she’s “having unusually sharp womanly pains”. Awkward, yet effective! Great to have that one in your back pocket. I enjoyed those laughs, and also, shame on Grace for putting Todd in a position to end NATO, and a bit of shame on Hal and Kate, too, for not insisting he prepare for Palmer’s predictable follow-up questions.

Fortunately for Kate, she isn’t forced to deal with the immediate fallout of Todd’s debacle, because MI6 has arrived (in the guise of “Rolf”, who would love to introduce her to the German Chancellor’s wife) to extract her to a secondary location for a quick check-in with Vaughn. Sadly, a substantive and enduring friendship between Kate and Vaughn may now be off the table. Vaughn isn’t thrilled by Kate’s initial decision not to inform her of Grace’s ultimatum, and is hopping mad at Todd’s delivery of the details on the U.S. deployment of warships, so much so that now she, too, is deploying ships to follow through on her commitment to provide safe passage to the Russians’ ships.

What’s more, she’s seeing Grace’s bid of warships and raising her the threat of being expelled from the G7 and consequences involving both Articles 4 and 5 of the NATO charter. I looked this up; according to the NATO website, Article 4 allows any NATO member to call for consultation with the North Atlantic Council when “the territorial integrity, political independence or security of any of the parties is threatened”. I’ve heard Article 5 referred to as the mutual defense provision, summarized as “an armed attack against one NATO member shall be considered an attack against them all”. In other words, this could become a gigantic shitshow that would destabilize international relations globally, which is one of the outcomes all responsible diplomats and heads of state, with the glaring exception of Grace Penn, work constantly to prevent.

Hal will be up next with Vaughn, and of course, he’ll deliver Grace’s message with more finesse than Todd did, but it’s hard to imagine it going over well. What could work out better is an idea Stuart floats on Kate’s behalf: at this point, why not just tell the Russians that the Americans have the Poseidon? Hal counters with a reminder that everyone in the U.S. government who weighs in on such things believes the Russians would launch a massive cyberattack on the continental U.S. Kate argues that they would not do so, “because then we’ll tell the world that they had an epic technological fail again; that while they’re getting pantsed by Ukrainian teenagers and homemade drones, we picked their pocket!” (The Diplomat’s timeline differs from ours in a number of ways, but it turns out that the Russians invaded Ukraine in their world, too.) Poor Stuart’s capable and patient efforts come to nothing, because Hal is in a snit and seems to be suffering an acute case of sunk cost fallacy-itis. He’s thrown in his lot with Grace, has a seat at the table, and doesn’t want to risk it, because he still half-believes he can influence Grace for the greater good. Not even Kate’s direct intervention works here, which is quite something. She finds him unrecognizable. She remembers a Hal Wyler who “talked ears off heads until people rethought, who said loyalty, by definition [is] and abdication of judgment”.

Where is that guy now? Off carrying the president’s contaminated water, sadly. His message delivery is no more successful than Todd’s, and now the entire conference is in danger of collapsing. Gannon and Billie’s attempt to convince Grace to back off actually backfires, as they aren’t quite smooth enough to prevent her from deducing that Stuart has filed a cable in the State Department’s Dissent Channel. He’d taken such care to compose a thoughtful, professional alternate perspective on the fuckery he’s been witnessing. It’s such a non-confrontational mechanism that Billie and Eidra laughed at him for doing it, and Kate encouraged him to file so that his perspective would become part of the historical record. Guess who is so thin-skinned and vengeance-minded that she retaliated by punching down and having Stuart recalled from his post? She demands loyalty, and all I can hear ringing in my mind is Kate quoting Hal’s disgust at the notion of abdicating independent judgment.

It’s painful to witness Stuart in particular being punished like this. Kate was right to read him into all of the messy and highly questionable decision-making that’s been going on for the last year and change! He’s got subject-area expertise, a good head on his shoulders, and a strong, finely calibrated moral compass, and should be an ambassador in his own right in the next few years. Instead, he’s being shipped back to D.C., unable to return to the hotel or his home in London, and thanks to her security clearance, Eidra is the one who will have to supervise the whole curtailment of his mission. Everything about this makes my stomach turn, most of all Grace’s smug, cat-that-got-the-cream face when she tells Kate that her DCM undermined her policy in a high-stakes situation, and then tells her to watch herself. Perhaps it’s only metaphorically possible for human blood to run cold in our veins, but I did feel it literally just then.

Kate’s last-ditch effort to get Grace to back off comes to nothing when she learns that if she continues to push back on her “them or us” doctrine, which Grace has neatly swathed in faux-righteousness and magnanimity, the next to lose their jobs will be her and Hal. As Hal puts it the next morning, the chilling effect is very effective. It seems, for a few minutes, as though Grace has this one in the bag. In her remarks to the day’s first full session of G7 nations, she pre-empts Vaughn’s post-session Article 4 consultation by laying out her version of events since the Russian submarine ran aground, and urging her colleagues to consider a bleak future of the group without the U.S. among them. Once again, nobody seems to have the stomach to stand up to her, and the Italian Prime Minister begins to deliver his speech. Kate, bless her, does the exact right thing by resigning in the most public way possible, saying she can no longer support the actions of the Penn administration. She’s followed by Billie, then Gannon, then, yes, it’s him! It’s Hal! Outside the venue, the four of them walk up to the gates, where a scrum of press awaits them, and Hal begins to make a statement. Whew! Let’s go!

As is usual for me at the end of the season, I am overflowing with questions. If four of the most consequential members of Grace’s staff/cabinet quit en masse, what will become of her administration? The U.S. lacks the votes of no confidence and the ability to call a snap election that parliamentary governments operate under, so there can’t be any immediate electoral consequences for her. Will there be more mass resignations? Will we take a time jump to the next in-universe presidential election? Will the title of the series change? Could The Diplomat pivot to being about the British Foreign Office? Or Bethan Vaughn’s unfolding premiership? Can we speed up time to get to the next season by, say, June 2027?

• Just a little smorgasbord of seasonal wrap-up thoughts here: The show seems to have moved on from any thoughts of the investigation into Grace’s assassination attempt, but I would love to see that thread picked up again down the line, preferably bringing Tom Libby back into the story.

• Yes, I did Shazam the song Stuart and Eidra were singing as they got dressed for the musical performance; it’s another Prince song, “Girls and Boys” from his album Parade (most famous for “Kiss”). I love that he’s their artist.

• I really really really hope Stuart gets reinstated at Embassy London ASAP, on both general principles and because I, an avowed sentimentalist, would love for him and Eidra to have some very cute (and tall) babies.

• When Vaughn refers to Todd as “Mr. Pickles”, does she mean the mass-murdering border collie in the Adult Swim series of the same name, former British MP Eric Pickles, or another being altogether, real or fictional?

items.title: Julia Stiles ‘Bawled’ Before Heath Ledger Tribute, Breaks Down ‘10 Things I Hate About You’ Cast Reunion on ‘Dancing With the Stars’
items.description: Julia Stiles paid tribute to the late Heath Ledger on Tuesday night’s episode of “Dancing With the Stars.”
items.author: Emily Longeretta
paragraphs: Julia Stiles paid tribute to the late Heath Ledger on Tuesday night’s episode of “Dancing With the Stars.”

During Dedication Night, she performed a contemporary routine with her partner Ezra Sosa to “Can’t Take My Eyes Off You”; in the 1999 film “10 Things I Hate About You,” Ledger’s character, Patrick, sang the Frankie Valli number to Stiles’ Kat Stratford from the bleachers while she was at soccer practice.

“I said, if we had to have someone with us on stage representing Heath’s legacy or the film, I said it had to be the whole cast. I begged them, each and every one of them, and they all rallied. They really did,” Stiles told Variety after the routine. She said that it was “really trippy” to see herself in the blue dress, similar to what she wore in the film, and her hair done in a similar style. “At 17 years old, I never would have thought that I’d be here at 45, celebrating my body, dancing on the show that I absolutely love and that fans are still interested in this movie and still moved and touched by this movie.”
Earlier in the week, Stiles opened up to Variety about the emotional rehearsals.

“I know that Dedication Night is emotional, but I thought I was distanced from it enough. Like, oh, it was so many years ago. Something about seeing clips from that movie and images and hearing my voice and hearing his voice is bringing back so many memories. It’s a lot,” she said, noting that she started crying while practicing. “One of the things that we really hope to do as performers is to make people feel something and have people care about the work that you do, and his memory lives on because it was such an incredible performance.”
Ledger died in January 2008 at the age of 28.

items.title: Lea Michele in Talks for ‘Glee’ Return in Disney+/Hulu Revival
items.description: The revival of Glee is zeroing in on its first returning castmember.
items.author: Rick Porter
paragraphs: The revival of Glee is zeroing in on its first returning castmember.

Lea Michele is in talks to reprise her role as Rachel Berry in the series, which Disney+ and Hulu announced Wednesday. Where the character will be in the present remains to be seen: There are next to no details about the show other than it has a series order and that 20th Television is producing.

Even the names of Glee creators Ryan Murphy, Brad Falchuk and Ian Brennan weren’t mentioned in Disney’s press release early Wednesday, though sources say that’s likely just a matter of all i’s being dotted.
Reps for Disney and Murphy declined to comment, and messages to Michele’s reps weren’t returned by publication time. Variety first reported Michele’s potential casting.

Michele starred in all six seasons of Glee’s original run from 2009-15 as Rachel, the very talented and occasionally off-putting star vocalist of the McKinley High School show choir, New Directions. Rachel dreamed of Broadway stardom, which she eventually achieved; the 2015 series finale shows her winning a Tony Award.

Michele had appeared in several Broadway productions, notably starring in Spring Awakening before joining Glee. She most recently starred in a revival of Chess on Broadway and had a run in Funny Girl in 2022-23.

Murphy told The Hollywood Reporter in August that he was “considering” returning to Glee: “For many, many people now in their 20s, they grew up on that show and it meant something to them,” he said. “The music meant something. So, let’s kick it around and see what we get.” In September, he said in an interview with Entertainment Tonight that he, Falchuk and Brennan had finished a script for a new version of the series.

items.title: Gaming Can’t Afford More Games the Size of ‘Grand Theft Auto VI’
items.description: Grand Theft Auto VI finally arrives in November. A staggering 13 years and two console generations after the release of its predecessor, the long-awaited sequel has effectively become one of gaming’s holy grails—a title that some thought they’d never actually
items.author: Matt Kamen
paragraphs: Grand Theft Auto VI finally arrives in November. A staggering 13 years and two console generations after the release of its predecessor, the long-awaited sequel has effectively become one of gaming’s holy grails—a title that some thought they’d never actually see, its development cycle so legendarily long that there’s a dedicated “we got [x] before GTA 6” meme.

The latest criminal opus lets players control Jason and Lucia, a modern-day Bonnie and Clyde, and bears all the hallmarks of Rockstar's incredible attention to detail. Leonida, the open-world setting based on Florida, looks almost impossibly vast yet meticulously detailed, with its own weather systems and hundreds of animal species roaming around.
It’s shaping up to be a game of unprecedented scale and ambition—and exactly the sort of experience the wider industry can’t afford to keep chasing.

At launch, it doesn’t matter how good or bad Grand Theft Auto VI actually is. On sheer hype alone, it’s already guaranteed to be the biggest and most successful entertainment product of the year, maybe the decade. Some estimates already put revenue between $1 billion and $4 billion on preorders alone, with eager players clearly not put off by its $80 price (or $100 for the Ultimate Edition).

Although Rockstar hasn’t confirmed the development budget, that would be a healthy return even on the wildest (and debunked) guess of $2 billion, before factoring long-tail sales or the revenue drawn by the ongoing Grand Theft Auto Online. With numbers like those, it’s easy to understand why every publisher and developer wants their own GTA VI–level game.

Yet even if Grand Theft Auto VI is an outlier, the arms race among AAA-tier developers to constantly deliver bigger, more detailed, more ambitious games is a dangerous direction, hurting both game quality and the people who make them.

The games industry is in a paradoxical crisis. It’s the most successful entertainment medium on Earth—generating $200 billion in revenue in 2025, dwarfing the global film industry’s $32.8 billion and even beating the combined sports sector's $174 billion—but the last few years have seen seemingly endless developer layoffs, many at headline AAA studios. Worse, many of these redundancies are coming after successful game launches.

Take 2025’s Battlefield 6 as an example. Despite being the top-selling game of the year, shifting 7 million copies in three days after a reported development budget of $400 million, publisher EA fired workers across at least four studios involved in the game's creation. A spokesperson told IGN that the job losses were made to “better align our teams around what matters most to our community” (the CEO got a nice $8 million bonus, though).

It’s far from the only case—Halo: Campaign Evolved developers Halo Studios faced 268 job losses in September 2026, following Xbox announcing 3,200 cuts in July 2026 as part of a wider “reset” across Xbox, while Ubisoft is hitting at least three of its German studios with a round of “voluntary” layoffs, including its Düsseldorf branch that has worked on the likes of Rainbow Six: Siege, which boasts “more than 100 million registered players.” Smaller studios aren't immune—Refactor Games, behind Netflix’s FIFA World Cup game, lost 85 percent of its staff after a “successful” launch.

With developers facing unemployment threats even after delivering a financially successful game, unionization efforts are unsurprising, though that's seeing pushback. Rockstar is currently embroiled in a UK tribunal hearing over the alleged dismissal of 34 workers in Edinburgh for union activity. (Rockstar says the workers were dismissed for “sharing confidential company information.”)

Beyond a fraught job market and an unpredictable environment to create games, the AAA sector’s endless pursuit of digital perfection is now arguably delivering weaker, blander games. It’s almost understandable from a financial perspective: If you’ve invested millions of dollars, you want the end product to appeal to the largest possible consumer base to maximize your returns.

However, that same impulse can homogenize the gaming experience. Think of all the big-budget shooters that play identically, or the glossy adventure games that signpost every step with yellow paint so players can’t possibly get lost. Look at the likes of Insomniac’s recent Marvel’s Wolverine—rumored to have a development budget in the hundreds of millions—which launched to solid sales (analyst estimates suggest 1.9 million copies sold in its first three days) but tepid reviews and lukewarm player response, with many critiquing its linear progression and repetitive hack-and-slash gameplay.

The bigger games have gotten, the more time they demand from players too, and rarely in meaningful ways. Open-world games in particular feel increasingly crammed with time-eating diversions—Assassin’s Creed Valhalla notoriously needed 150-plus hours to see everything its accurately crafted bleak medieval English settlements had to offer. But much of it felt like busywork to showcase Ubisoft’s investment in creating such realistic environments.

Such virtual spaces are often impressive, yes, but will Grand Theft Auto VI be better with a world map reportedly three times larger than the already colossal Red Dead Redemption 2? Is it worth building something of that size if players don’t have time to experience most of it?
The solution to runaway costs, developer security, and the limited time players have to sink into games should be clear: aim smaller.

That’s not to say the entire industry should pivot toward indie-level games (though there are some absolute greats in that area), but rather that publishers should refocus on games that can still showcase their creators’ talents and offer satisfying but digestible experiences to players, without pouring dangerous sums of money into ever bigger, ever riskier titles. In short, rediscover the “AA”-scale game.

The textbook example of how successful this can be is Clair Obscur: Expedition 33. The debut game from French developer Sandfall Interactive appeared practically out of nowhere in April 2025, and exploded. The RPG earned rapturous reviews and endless fan acclaim, celebrated for its challenging dodge-and-parry twist on turn-based combat, its stunning world—a breathtaking blend of belle epoque and dark fantasy imagery, wrapped in a gorgeous painterly flourish—and its mature and emotionally complex story of explorers battling the inevitability of death.

In technology and production quality terms, it’s no slouch for a “smaller” game, either. Clair Obscur has motion-capture performances, a voice cast featuring Hollywood heavyweights like Charlie Cox and Andy Serkis, a full orchestral score, and dazzling visuals. It even packs a solid 60-odd hours of playtime, making it feel significant and not daunting. It ultimately swept up over 500 Game of the Year Awards and went on to sell 8 million copies as of April 2026.

While that number pales in comparison to Battlefield 6’s 7 million units in mere days, Clair Obscur did it all on a budget of less than $10 million, and with a tiny development staff. The game was hugely successful for its budget, letting the studio continue without resorting to painful layoffs. Sandfall’s success isn’t a one-off. Look at Supergiant Games’ Hades duology, AdHoc Studio’s Dispatch, or Mintrocket’s Dave the Diver for more evidence that studios and labels should focus on smaller but richer gaming experiences.
The Not-Quite Bleeding Edge

Another major benefit of aiming smaller is that it lets companies mitigate rising development costs for themselves and consumers. The memory crisis is forcibly extending the hardware life cycle, delaying new console generations and blocking supplies of powerful PC graphics cards, leaving many players without the means to reap the benefits of the most demanding games.

As Final Fantasy VII Revelation director Naoki Hamaguchi—no stranger to hugely ambitious games with incredibly long development cycles—says, “There isn't a single console that you can say, ‘As long as I have this, I'll be able to play everything, to do everything.’ Personally, I think that over the course of the next 10 years, if someone said, ‘Here's the next generation of consoles,’ the market and the audience are not necessarily going to just jump over.”

Hamaguchi says the industry will still straddle the lower-spec options, like a Steam Deck or Nintendo Switch 2, providing broader experiences to a wider base. It won't be so much about cutting-edge technology, but how developers can compete in game design. "I think we're going to be entering an age where that's really the focus of competition,” he says.

Sadly, this approach has one big problem: Developers are already trying it but failing to draw investment. There’s no easy answer—investors follow the money, and the money points to GTA-scale games, even though AAA development increasingly leaves carnage in its wake.

Even Rockstar appears to realize the current approach is unsustainable, with studio veteran Phil Hooker telling Bloomberg that “the engine, the tools, and the team we've built during the [GTA VI] project will allow us to do things more quickly” in the future. Hopefully, good news for fans who fear another decade-long wait for GTA VII.

Grand Theft Auto VI will be a success, and its longevity is already certain. But when every other publisher sees the inevitable slate of sales records the game will shatter, they’d do well to think twice before chasing it—the games industry might not survive if they do.

items.title: Did My Ambition Cost Me $400,000 — and My Marriage?
items.description: Sitting in an eclectic, art-filled law office in Nashville, I turned off the location services on my phone. I didn’t want my husband — my partner of eight years, six of them married — tracking my movements. The divorce attorney who greeted me in the lobby seem
items.author: April Lockhart
paragraphs: Sitting in an eclectic, art-filled law office in Nashville, I turned off the location services on my phone. I didn’t want my husband — my partner of eight years, six of them married — tracking my movements. The divorce attorney who greeted me in the lobby seemed warm in a way I hadn’t expected. Angry on my behalf, he apologized for what I’d endured, but he was nevertheless honest: I was in a terrible position to negotiate from.

A month earlier, I’d learned my husband, Scott, had been cheating on me for almost a year. We’d never signed a prenup. The vast majority of our household income came from my work as a fashion influencer, but under Tennessee’s equitable-distribution laws, marital assets in a divorce are subject to division regardless of who earned them. I had never before considered that a source for concern. If anything, it’s what seemed most fair: The laws exist in part to protect spouses who step back from wage-based work to focus on unpaid labor that’s no less demanding, like keeping a home or raising children.

Yet I now had a unique vantage point: I belonged to the small but growing percentage of American opposite-sex marriages in which the wife is the couple’s sole or primary breadwinner. And it seemed my husband had come to resent, even envy, the ambition that had drawn him to me in the first place.

I knew I wasn’t alone in this experience. There were other women — many of them also influencers who financially supported their male partners — who shared their private concerns with me over the years, whispered over dinner and at events: how they’d learned to cushion news of the brand deals they secured so their partners didn’t get insecure; how they tried not to seem too happy about a career win lest it stoke jealousy in their marriages. Many of them eased tension by collaborating with their boyfriends and husbands, encouraging the men to step into the spotlight beside them in videos. Others employed their partners behind the scenes, tasking them with filming, managing, or handling the admin. Either way, the women were responsible not only for managing their own careers but for managing the men’s emotions and egos, too.

Finances were, unsurprisingly, the point of tension I heard discussed most frequently. Plenty of the women wanted prenups to protect the careers they’d built, but the topic was an awkward one to discuss, and more often than not they chose to let it go rather than risk conflict. Like me, many of my peers considered themselves responsible for ensuring their partners felt respected and fulfilled. I’ve come to believe that many men — even loving ones, even feminist ones, even the “good ones” — have an instinct to provide, or at least to contribute, and that it wears on them when they can’t. But what do you do, as the woman, when it’s your career that pays the bills?

I had never considered that the standup southern man I’d married might struggle so profoundly with our uneven earnings. The marriage quietly cracked underneath the weight of that imbalance. It’s a phenomenon I hadn’t realized was surprisingly common for sole or primary female breadwinners: They make up around 16 percent of American households yet account for more than 40 percent of divorces.

I left the law firm that afternoon and texted my husband that we’d talk when I got home. I hadn’t told him where I was, but I’d forgotten that he could track my car through the Tesla app. As I crossed the parking lot, I heard him say my name: “April?”

He demanded to know what I was doing — as if he hadn’t followed me here, to my lawyer’s office, where I was trying to divorce him without losing so much of what I’d worked so hard to build. I answered his question with one of my own: “What does it look like?” He knew what was happening. Finally, after many months in the dark, so did I.

I met Scott at a friend’s housewarming party in New York City in 2018. I was 22, just starting out in my career; he was 28. He was, in my estimation, the most handsome man in the room by a wide margin: blue eyes, dark hair, a charming smile. I was genuinely shocked when he walked up to me and offered to make me a drink. We talked for the rest of the party. I couldn’t tell you about what — only that it felt as if everyone else had disappeared. As the tension between us built, he pulled me into one of his friends’ bedrooms and kissed me.
That night, I’d worn a denim jacket with sleeves long enough to hide my limb difference. After we kissed, Scott tugged at the empty sleeve on my left side.

“Wait — where’s your arm?” he asked. I froze, bracing for the reaction I’d come to expect: the one where he’d see me differently and, worse, stop wanting me. After a beat, I stumbled over some version of, “Oh, I was born without it. I’ve always been like this.”
He nodded. “Oh, cool,” he said. And that was it — we moved on to a different subject entirely.

He brought me home in a taxi, and somewhere along the way, he told me I was the most beautiful woman he’d ever seen. We exchanged numbers when he dropped me off. I walked through my door and told my roommates I was pretty sure I’d just met my husband.

Here’s the part I didn’t say out loud back then but will now: I’d always believed I had to date “down” because of my disability. I’d done this math my whole dating life. If I was, for instance, a 9, then my arm probably knocked off a couple of points. That meant I was more like a 7, right? Competing for men who were maybe a 6? Scott, it seemed to me, was an unequivocal 10. I couldn’t quite believe he wanted me. It didn’t occur to me, then, that my math was the problem.

When we first got together, Scott was thriving professionally. He co-owned a small production company and traveled constantly for work. Within a year of our first date, he decided to leave the business and start freelancing instead, hoping to break into narrative film. At the time, I was working in influencer marketing for a clean-makeup brand, climbing toward a senior manager title. Scott seemed drawn to my determination from the start — and to the idea that I was going places.

We were married at the City Clerk’s office on February 28, 2020. About a week later, the world shut down. Scott’s income streams didn’t just slow. They stopped almost overnight. I knew he wasn’t to blame for this, and I was confident he’d find new work eventually. My job was steady and he had savings, so I was happy to carry more of the load for a while.

After we moved from New York to Nashville for a change of pace, I worked remotely while Scott tried to secure freelance jobs — though, with productions shut down industrywide, there wasn’t much work to be found. In my newfound free time, I started posting on Instagram and TikTok again: I needed a hobby to occupy myself with, and the free products were a nice bonus. By that point, I’d already built a small following of around 10,000 on Instagram. At 18, I’d been on an ABC reality show, a singing competition called Rising Star, and though I’d ultimately decided that being a live performer wasn’t for me, I’d still picked up a few fans. After Rising Star, I’d pivoted my page into a beauty account, but now I wanted to focus on fashion instead.

Back then, I was still hiding my limb difference behind sleeves and careful camera angles. It’s hard to admit this now, but I struggled to believe my disability could be beautiful or even baseline attractive. I was proud of my style, my content, the creative choices I made online, and I wanted more than almost anything to be seen as cool, edgy, even. Somewhere inside, I was certain my arm would detract from that effect.

Six months into posting again I landed my first paid deal, and within a year my social platform brought in about 20 percent of my total salary. But when my following soon plateaued, I hit a breaking point: Deep down, I believed I was born this way for a reason, even if I couldn’t yet see my arm as beautiful. So at the start of a new year, I took a creative risk: my own version of a 30-day outfit-styling series, but one in which I’d reveal my limb difference and document how I styled it.

The videos worked. Viewers were engaged and encouraging, and for the first time I felt like I was building a real audience, one that was invested in me and not just my aesthetic. Scott cheered me on through all of it. He always seemed to be the first to comment on every post, and he frequently shared my wins with our friends and family. He was constantly reminding me how hard I worked; it was clear he was proud. Within two years, I was making four times my old salary, and I left a job I loved to build something of my own.

But slowly, Scott became a supporting character in my career. I was a full-time content creator, with a talent manager keeping the brand deals flowing in steadily, and I’d hired two full-time employees to help run the day-to-day of my business. I’d also launched Disabled&, an online community hosting events for other disabled creatives. My husband would show up in my videos sometimes, and the moms in my comments would tell me how sweet he seemed, how lucky I was. I agreed. I was lucky. But, behind the scenes, he seemed listless.

I floated the idea of Scott and I building a real business together, and in the moment the prospect excited him, but that brief thrill never transformed into follow-through. Fashion and beauty content wasn’t for him. I understood and respected that. He tried exploring other career opportunities — building houses, getting his pilot’s license — but nothing stuck, and he never came close to making what he’d made before we married. Instead, what he contributed was mostly logistical: I had developed driving anxiety after a bad accident as a teenager, so he drove me most places and ran my errands. But he’d tell me any of these tasks threw off his entire day. I started to feel as if asking for anything at all risked his ire.

I played the part I thought a wife should play. I listened. I encouraged. I built career plans I genuinely believed might invigorate him. I did my best to never tear him down. But it was clear he was unhappy, and nothing I offered him could substitute the professional fulfillment he sought. I worried that my success had become a kind of ceiling for him. Maybe he even found it emasculating. I was learning what I’d later see reflected in the data: that a woman’s ambition and her marriage can pull her in opposite directions. As a content creator, I was making more money than I’d ever imagined I would in my 20s. Scott didn’t have to work for us to afford our lifestyle. So why would I worry?

That all changed on April 10, 2026. It was a Friday afternoon, and I was working from home while Scott sat on our back porch with his laptop. It seemed to me we were in a good place in our marriage, as if a weight had finally lifted between us. I stepped outside to see how he was doing and noticed his fingers moving across his phone screen. I didn’t recognize the name of the person he was texting.

I had rarely asked to see his phone before — maybe five or six times total throughout our entire relationship. Still, I can’t pretend I didn’t have underlying trust issues. My first serious boyfriend, years earlier, had been repeatedly unfaithful, and he wasn’t the only partner who’d cheated on me. I chose to marry Scott, believing he was nothing like those men. But I wanted the closeness and trust that came with being totally open with each other, having nothing to hide. Giving him permission to look at my phone, and I his, felt like a way to establish that trust.

On those rare occasions, he’d hand his device over begrudgingly with the air of someone being mildly accused. I admittedly knew less about his days than I would have liked, but we were together so constantly that it never really occurred to me that something as serious as infidelity might slip past my notice. Over the years, I had never found anything on his phone that I considered egregious: just conversations with female friends that ran a little long, or an Instagram Explore page that featured more women in bikinis than I would have preferred, but ultimately harmless, I thought. Some warped part of me believed that a man like Scott marrying someone who looked like me meant he had to be one of the “good ones.” He loved the disabled girl.

That afternoon, I asked to see his messages. He told me “sure,” but just give him a second to use the bathroom. He took his phone along with him, which immediately struck me as odd. While he was gone, some instinct in me switched on. I opened Google right there on the porch and typed in: “how to recover deleted messages.” When he returned, he handed over his phone, not quite meeting my eyes. And there in the trash, I discovered multiple threads.

The first one I opened included more than 9,000 messages, the sheer number of which floored me. All 9,000-plus messages had been exchanged within the past month and a half. They were long texts, late-night ones, heartfelt reassurances and obvious flirtation. I felt dizzy, my body reacting before my brain could process what I’d discovered. I knew immediately this wasn’t an isolated incident.

Another thread, another number, from two weeks prior: Scott lamenting to a woman, a stranger, that he hadn’t had as much time to kiss her as he’d wanted. I did some mental math. I’d been in Italy for the Paralympics when that message was sent — a trip I took with my talent manager instead of Scott because I had figured some time apart from my husband would bring us closer. Turns out, it did bring him closer. Just not to me.

After I discovered the secret messages, our marriage unraveled over a blurred ten hours. Scott tried to contain the damage at first. He admitted only to what I’d already found, hoping that was where I’d stop digging. It wasn’t.

Holding his phone, I pulled up the “recently deleted” folder with three separate conversations still sitting in it: one emotional affair, one fling at a bar, one stolen kiss. I hadn’t even gotten to Instagram yet. When I did, I found a message from a woman in New York — someone we had mutual friends with — who called Scott “daddy” and wanted his help covering around $700 of her rent.

That same dizzy feeling came rushing back, now accompanied by rage. I opened his Venmo and saw that between January and April he’d sent her $4,500 via his credit card linked to our joint account, which meant that I had, inadvertently, paid these transactions off. When I showed him the screen, he told me she’d been sending him photos — I never saw these photos, but I assumed they were explicit or at least suggestive — and asking for money in exchange, and that she’d implied his friends would find out if he didn’t pay her. I didn’t buy it. I think he wanted to feel like someone who could carelessly hand over that kind of money. The kind of man who’d wear the Rolex I bought him to pick up women at a bar, then be first to grab the tab with the money I’d made.

There were other confessions that followed: There was a woman he’d met for a drink, then brought back to our rental house, the one with my name on the lease. The emotional affair he’d had with her stung much more than the lost money or even the physical betrayals. Three days before I discovered Scott’s infidelity, I had worked up the nerve to drive myself to an event alone — a real feat, given my anxiety — and my self-driving car swerved to avoid something in the road, nearly running me off the highway. Shaken, I called my husband three times. No answer. I later learned that he was on a rooftop at the W Nashville hotel, having drinks with this woman.

Eventually I saw the text messages exchanged between them later that night. She’d apparently noticed his phone going off while they were at the hotel and asked about it once he’d returned home. He joked that, given how badly he’d wanted to kiss her, he would’ve been happy to make JPMorgan wait.

My friends later pointed out that, perhaps, “JPMorgan” was me. Maybe this wasn’t a random joke; maybe it was a code name. Did my husband refer to me as a metaphorical bank? Funny, if I let myself find it funny.

In the immediate aftermath of discovering Scott’s cheating, I didn’t tell anyone. I knew that once I did, my whole life would change. Infidelity had always been the one thing I considered nonnegotiable, and Scott hadn’t made a onetime mistake. He’d made a year’s worth of calculated choices. Four weeks after that, I was resolute. I was getting a divorce at 31.
Most of the settlement conversations happened in our living room. Across from me, my husband negotiated for money he hadn’t earned while I tried very, very hard not to be sick.

I kept doing this thing during those eight days of negotiations: pricing out what the money could have gone toward, in another life. Renovating my mom’s house. Helping out my grandpa. Hiring more people to grow my business. My lawyer had advised that I file for divorce on the grounds of irreconcilable differences, not adultery, in order to limit how much alimony I might owe and to get an agreement done quickly. (Filing over infidelity, he warned, tends to make the other party less agreeable.) By the time we agreed that Scott would receive $400,000, plus the new Audi I’d already paid off, plus the other $80,000 or so in investments he already had, I felt nauseous in a way that had nothing to do with the number itself and everything to do with how we’d gotten there. I had trusted this man to love me, even when I hadn’t always been convinced I was lovable. I had committed to loving and supporting him in return. And yet here we were, our trust ruined and our marriage a casualty of the very career dreams I’d thought my husband admired.

I’m no longer so surprised when I see stories online about breadwinner women divorcing their husbands or studies like this one, which found that, in a survey of more than half a million opposite-sex couples across 29 countries, those where the wife was the primary earner were 36 percent more likely to separate. What helped me most in the thick of my own mediation process was watching content creators like Jen Hamilton — who similarly discovered her husband was pursuing other women — talk openly about the mess of their own divorces.

In the six months since filing for divorce, showing up online has felt like a difficult performance. It’s also my job — one I don’t take for granted, and one that doesn’t give me the option of going completely silent. I’ve tried not to give in to my anxieties over how my followers might react when I finally share this story: the story of what happened, of why Scott no longer appears in my photos or videos. Would people feel misled? I kept picturing one of the moms who’d called me lucky, phone in hand, hoping her disabled daughter might someday be loved the way I seemed to be loved by Scott. Calling my divorce amicable would have protected the man who’d wronged me. Telling the truth meant shattering the illusion. But I learned once before that hiding myself isn’t a sustainable strategy. And I want to show my community the other side of this ordeal: that it was worth it to choose myself, even if I don’t know what comes next.

Still, there’s a question I can’t stop turning over: How do I avoid this sort of situation again? What do women like me — women who have built something of their own, who have goals they can’t or don’t want to set aside — need to ask of their romantic partners, especially if those partners are men?

An obvious answer is one that’s been discussed ad nauseam on social media this year: Sign a prenup. But I also know the solution isn’t always that simple. Like many women I know, I met my husband when we were in roughly the same income bracket. As one Substack writer argued in a recent piece called “Why So Many Female Influencers End Up Divorced,” many couples like Scott and me marry within their own income and education strata, with the man presumed to be the main character — until the wife unexpectedly becomes one. “And no matter how hard she tries to placate, to share her spotlight, to let him indulge in the fruits of her success,” the writer continues, “it’s never enough.” These words resonated with me deeply. I couldn’t have known how fast my career would grow, or how Scott would feel when it did. You can’t write a prenup for the woman you haven’t become yet.

I’m writing this now from Provence, on a brand trip, doing the very thing that might frighten off whoever comes next. I’m not going to stop being an influencer, and I’m not going to hide my arm again. But I’m more aware than ever that my ambition and my limb difference are two things some men can’t handle. I am, and have always been, beautiful. I know that now. But the voice in my head that wonders if I’m desirable is louder than it’s been in eight years. How do I reconcile that?

I don’t have a tidy answer. Marriage feels distant and unappealing to me right now, but I still love the idea of rebuilding a life with someone. I know exactly what I bring to a relationship. Success, care, intelligence, real substance. And the partner I’d choose now, in my 30s, isn’t who I would have chosen in my 20s. At minimum, I need someone with a firm sense of self, a security that isn’t quietly resting on mine. Someday, I’d like to be on a trip like this one, calling home to someone who’s cheering me on — and has somewhere of their own to be.

items.title: Your Daily Horoscope by Madame Clairevoyant: October 21, 2026
items.description: Dissonance between Venus and Neptune (in Scorpio and Aries, respectively) could make it challenging to make good decisions today. Your insecurities may warp your understanding of what you “deserve” and how you should expect to be treated; your fear of the unkn
items.author: Claire Comstock-Gay
paragraphs: Dissonance between Venus and Neptune (in Scorpio and Aries, respectively) could make it challenging to make good decisions today. Your insecurities may warp your understanding of what you “deserve” and how you should expect to be treated; your fear of the unknown may dissuade you from taking any risks, even entirely reasonable ones. Try to be aware that you’re not your most rational self right now. If you can sleep on any decisions, do so: Your outlook may be completely different tomorrow.

Today, any minor inconveniences you experience will feel like confirmation of your own incompetence. If you fail to meet a goal, you’ll wonder why you were foolish enough even to try; if someone is rude or dishonest with you, you’ll tell yourself you must have done something to invite that behavior. Your challenge right now is to stop blaming yourself for everything. Everyone has an off day sometimes. For the time being, there’s no need to go searching for a deeper meaning to it. And there’s especially no need to make yourself feel terrible for situations outside your control.

You may feel unusually private, even a bit secretive, today. Keeping your true thoughts to yourself could seem like the “right” thing to do. Maybe you imagine it’s more strategic to withhold some details about your life, or maybe you’re trying to avoid burdening your friends with your problems. But right now, the people around you probably know more than they’re letting on. You may think you’re keeping your feelings under wraps, but you’re more transparent than you realize. So instead of stressing yourself out trying to keep secrets, you may as well open up.

If you struggle to assert boundaries with your friends today, don’t be surprised. It’s simple enough to draw the line with people you don’t particularly care about — but it’s harder when it comes to those you actively want in your life. You worry you’ll seem mean or selfish (or worse, boring) when you express your limits. But try to remember that anyone worth your time will respect your boundaries. Don’t talk yourself out of pumping the brakes if that’s what you need.

You tend to value personality over appearance, character over superficial charm. You’re not overly swayed by shiny, glamorous exteriors. You understand that someone can be outwardly appealing but have little to offer on a deeper level. Today, though, your judgment may not be quite as sharp as usual and you’re more likely to be drawn in by charismatic people, even if they clearly aren’t interested in a deep or lasting relationship. There’s nothing wrong with having fun with them — but try to avoid convincing yourself they’re more interesting or profound than they actually are.

There’s a good chance you’ll be disappointed by the people around you today. Your challenge is to figure out whether the problem is their behavior or your expectations. You may find this task surprisingly difficult: You’re liable to think yourself in circles right now. One moment, you’ll resent everyone for failing to live up to your standards; the next, you’ll blame yourself for being so hard to please. If there’s no clear answer, try to go a little easier on everyone — including yourself. Assume people are trying their best, even if the results are imperfect.

If other people’s words seem confusing or contradictory today, you might imagine you must be the problem: Maybe you’re not listening closely enough, or maybe you’re not smart enough to get the point they’re making. In an attempt to avoid embarrassment, you might decide to pretend you understand what’s going on. Really, though, this attitude helps nobody: If something makes no sense to you, chances are good you aren’t the only one who’s confused. Ask questions. You’ll be glad you did.

If you aren’t getting what you need from your relationships lately, you may convince yourself you haven’t earned it yet. Maybe if you were cooler or more interesting, you would be treated with the respect you want. Maybe if you were more selfless or beautiful, people would approach you with more thoughtfulness. But remember that, while self-awareness is important, self-degradation is cruel. You shouldn’t have to earn basic kindness and respect, and you should treat yourself with the same. Don’t listen to anyone who says otherwise.

When you identify problems in your life today, you may feel the need to take action on them immediately. Everything seems incredibly urgent — you’re afraid if you don’t fix things right away, they’ll only get worse. But right now, any hurried or reckless moves will ultimately be counterproductive. When you rush around, you’ll make mistakes that will need to be cleaned up later. Caution and patience will save you time in the long run, so don’t be afraid to slow down.
Sagittarius Daily Horoscope

You try to keep a positive attitude even in less than ideal situations. Convincing yourself that you’re powerless to change your circumstances tends to become a self-fulfilling prophecy: If you’re too pessimistic to even try, it becomes a lot likelier that nothing will improve. But be careful not to let your hopefulness and optimism turn into naïve wishful thinking. You can stay positive while being honest with yourself about the challenges you’re up against. That’s the first step toward actually dealing with them.

Sometimes, you’re wary of offering too much compassion to those who haven’t demonstrated they deserve it. You have limited energy to spare, and you want to be sure you’re using it well; you don’t want to be taken advantage of. But today, it’s better to err on the side of generosity than caution. You may end up helping someone who doesn’t appreciate it the way they should, but right now that’s better than ignoring someone who genuinely does need a bit of extra care.

Be aware you may get jealous of anyone who seems more “successful” than you today. Even if their achievements are in fields you don’t care about, or none of the tangible details of their lives actually appeal to you, you’ll still manage to convince yourself you’re somehow lacking by comparison. But when envy starts to warp your thought processes, take a step back and remember what you actually want and what you’re working toward. You’re running your own race; don’t let other people’s accomplishments distract you.

Focusing your energies on just one task today may strike you as boring. Your ambitions are bigger than that; you want to get to the good stuff. But trying to do everything at once will quickly overwhelm you, increasing the chances that you get so stressed you’ll end up doing nothing at all. Instead, give yourself intentionally modest goals to work toward right now. By making things as simple as possible, you’ll set yourself up for success — and maintain your motivation to keep going.
