items.title: LEGO Icons’ “Venetian Neighborhood” Turns Your Shelf Into a Canal-Side Escape
items.description: LEGO and Marvel have unveiled The Marvel Skyline, an 18+ microscale model that compresses dozens of landmarks from the comics, films and series into a single cityscape
items.author: Sophie Caraan
paragraphs: LEGO and Marvel have unveiled The Marvel Skyline, an 18+ microscale model that compresses dozens of landmarks from the comics, films and series into a single cityscape
Hero headquarters like the Baxter Building and the X-Men Mansion share the skyline with villain hubs including Oscorp Industries and Roxxon Corporation
A Galactus minifigure, Spider-Man and Human Torch trophy figures, and a fleet of miniature vehicles round out the set

LEGO is shrinking the Marvel Universe down to shelf size with The Marvel Skyline, a 1,261-piece microscale set aimed at adult builders and collectors. The display gathers headquarters, labs and corporate towers from across Marvel’s comics, films and series into one continuous city block, splitting its real estate between the heroes and the villains who oppose them.

The skyline’s heroic side stacks up some of Marvel’s most recognizable addresses, with Avengers Tower, the Daily Bugle, the Baxter Building and the X-Men Mansion all rendered in miniature. Deeper-cut locations make the cut too, including the Wakandan Embassy, Rand Enterprises Building and Pym Laboratories, giving longtime readers plenty of landmarks to spot beyond the usual blockbuster sites.

Across town, the villains get their own cluster of buildings. Hammer Industries, Roxxon Corporation, Oscorp Industries and Fisk Tower anchor the darker end of the skyline, setting up a visual standoff between the two halves of the city as the build comes together.

Figures add scale and character to the architecture. A Galactus minifigure looms over the scene, while Spider-Man and Human Torch appear as trophy figures that slot into the display. At street level, the X-Jet, the Fantastic Four Rocket Ship and the Spider-Mobile join other vehicles placed around the roads, turning a static cityscape into something closer to a frozen action shot. The finished model stands over 8 inches (21 cm) tall, stretches 15.5 inches (40 cm) wide and runs 4.5 inches (11 cm) deep, sizing it for a desk, shelf or office display.
LEGO’s The Marvel Skyline is available for pre-order now via LEGO, with shipping set to begin January 1, 2027.

items.title: Фрукты и сладкие напитки могут по-разному влиять на риск депрессии у подростков
items.description: Дополнительная порция фруктов в день может снизить риск депрессии и тревожности у подростков
items.author: Виолетта Ефимова
paragraphs: Дополнительная порция фруктов в день может снизить риск депрессии и тревожности у подростков

Учёные из Сиднейского университета проследили за пищевыми привычками и психическим здоровьем 6537 подростков из 71 школы Австралии. На момент начала исследования участникам было в среднем 12,5 года. В течение нескольких лет они ежегодно заполняли анкеты о питании и самочувствии.

Результаты показали, что каждая дополнительная порция фруктов в день снижала риск появления симптомов депрессии на 13%, а тревожности — на 7%. В то же время употребление сладких напитков, включая газировку, сладкие концентраты и спортивные напитки, повышало риск обоих состояний. Эта закономерность наблюдалась у подростков обоих полов, но особенно выраженной оказалась у мальчиков в отношении тревожности.

«Мы не утверждаем, что яблоко предотвратит депрессию, а газировка вызовет тревожность: психическое здоровье гораздо сложнее», — подчеркнула ведущий автор исследования Лили Дэвидсон из Центра исследований психического здоровья и употребления психоактивных веществ Матильда при Сиднейском университете.

По словам исследовательницы, подростковый возраст особенно важен для изучения этой связи — школьники становятся самостоятельнее в выборе еды и напитков, а в это же время нередко впервые проявляются проблемы с психическим здоровьем.

Для исследования учитывали физическую активность, возраст, пол и социально-экономические условия участников. Учёные считают, что для профилактики важно не только рассказывать подросткам о здоровом питании, но и делать полезные продукты доступнее. В этом могут участвовать школы, семьи и государство.

items.title: Elizabeth Holmes Knows Exactly What She’s Doing
items.description: For a few years, Elizabeth Holmes was everywhere. There she was on the cover of Forbes in 2014, wearing heavy eyeliner and a black turtleneck, holding a vial pinched between her thumb and her index finger. For Inc. magazine, she kept the turtleneck but dropped
items.author: Sarah Jones
paragraphs: For a few years, Elizabeth Holmes was everywhere. There she was on the cover of Forbes in 2014, wearing heavy eyeliner and a black turtleneck, holding a vial pinched between her thumb and her index finger. For Inc. magazine, she kept the turtleneck but dropped the vial, added a faint half-smile, and crossed her arms over her chest. T magazine chose a more artistic vision when it named her one of “The Greats,” in 2015. In its photo, Holmes’s hair looks stylishly wispy as she gazes off into a future that no one else can see. She was 31 years old, the world’s youngest “self-made billionaire,” the celebrated founder of Theranos and inventor of a device that could use a single finger prick to test for hundreds of conditions.

Crucially, she was a woman, a female Steve Jobs in an industry where that was unusual. Most observers knew more about her age or appearance than her scientific credentials or her relationship with Sunny Balwani, the president and chief operating officer of Theranos. The turtlenecks invoked Jobs, her idol, but the red lipstick and mascara set her apart; she stamped femininity on an image she knew the world would recognize. The outfit, her uniform, told us that she was a girl genius. Until she wasn’t. Four days after T published that dreamy photoshoot, reporter John Carreyrou published the first of a series of investigations that ended with Holmes’s image, and company, in tatters. The technology did not work, and Theranos dissolved in 2018. By June 2023, Holmes was in federal prison for fraud.

The black turtleneck does not appear in You Can See Everything, the blockbuster new documentary from Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim. Instead, a softer and more domestic version of Holmes takes over the screen. She wears neutrals and goes barefaced except for mascara; she often holds a baby, the youngest of her two children with partner Billy Evans. They live in a rental on the beach. In this setting, her blonde frizz makes her look more like a busy mom than a prodigy in charge of her own image. We hear a baby gurgle before Holmes ever speaks. But as there was a knowingness to the younger Holmes’s image, there is a knowingness to how she presents herself in the film. This is the real Liz, Evans says, but is it?

Motherhood on Holmes might subvert expectations. Here, she is not Jobs or a criminal but someone personable and more sympathetic. If she’s lying, her opportunism is pathological, and her children are background actors in a production she’s staged. There is, perhaps, a third option, which is that she is so delusional that she’s convinced herself that she never scammed anyone. She does come from an industry rank with unsupported claims about revolutionary tech or the end of civilization, so conceit may feel natural to her. The film allows us to wonder about her relationship to reality, which is one of its strengths. Still, it is clear that she still wants to be taken seriously. Holmes spends much of her last month at home courting new investors for her ideas. Evans is more than her partner; he is her collaborator and watches videos about chemistry when he’s not telling Holmes how to whisk eggs. The children tumble around the edges of things. When the camera closes in on Holmes and her wild blue stare, the effect can be hypnotic. We’re never quite sure who we’re looking at, or what she perceives in turn.

Except for this: Holmes believes she’s a victim. She weeps often, once so hard that snot drips from her nose. Watching The Dropout, the Hulu show starring Amanda Seyfried, causes such acute suffering that she writhes on a bed. Her usual expression is one of bewilderment, as if she can’t grasp the predicament she’s in. The rental is her bunker, and it is claustrophobic to behold. The men around her peddle their own versions of her goodness and victimhood. Evans says he fell in love with her almost instantly, though he can’t explain why. In another scene he tells Fielder that Holmes is not normal and can’t think like other people. Her father, Christian, a former Enron executive, blames a campus rape and the influence of Balwani for her downfall. Their Holmes is not the entrepreneur who appeared on magazine covers and promised to change the world through blood testing but a fragile and misunderstood young mother on the brink of a prison sentence.

To Christian’s point, Holmes met Balwani in 2002, when she was 18 and he was 37. They started dating not long after she dropped out of Stanford at age 19 and hid their relationship while running Theranos together. When Holmes went on trial for fraud, she accused Balwani of psychological and sexual abuse and said he isolated her from her family while she was vulnerable after a sexual assault at Stanford. He misled her about the quality of their labs and the accuracy of their work, so any deficiencies were his fault, she testified. Balwani denied the claims, although the age difference and timing of their relationship suggests an imbalance of some kind. Regardless, it was Holmes, not Balwani, who became the face of Theranos; the company rose on her image and the story of her intellect. Carreyrou, in a review of the film, recalled texts from Holmes to Balwani dismissing worries of her overexposure in the press. “On outside they are jealous,” she wrote.

At times, her façade cracks. When she tells Fielder she’s never told a lie in her life, it’s dumbfounding and revealing. All human beings lie sometimes, Holmes more than most. Theranos told investors, falsely, that its technology had been used “on the battlefield in Afghanistan.” She and Balwani said Theranos conducted patient testing with analyzers that it had produced, when in fact the company relied on machines from a third party. When Theranos’s revenue dropped, she lied, telling investors the company was far more profitable than it was. Prosecutors showed that she “forged reports” to investors and partners, The Wall Street Journal reported. Carreyrou said on Monday that Holmes came after him and his sources, “threatening to sue us out of existence.” She may be a victim, but she is without question a perpetrator too.

That complexity is at odds with the woman Holmes tries to project. Onscreen, she acts like a holy fool, whose eccentricities disguise a humble and giving spirit. Gender is central to her performance, much as it’s been throughout her time in public life. During her trial, she styled her hair in loose waves and brought diaper bags to the courtroom, a look “more at home at a Midwestern insurance office than in a Silicon Valley boardroom,” the Journal sniped. She presents herself to Fielder as a submissive, near-alien creature in thrall to forces and personalities she cannot control. Evans is useful to the argument she makes about herself. While she wanders through scene after scene, Evans is purposeful, with an intensity that often unsettles. He has plans, which he communicates in an emotionless register to Fielder, to Holmes, and to investors. Although he comforts Holmes and seems to believe in her innocence, he also treats her like an asset, as if her notoriety can help him launch his own inventions. Holmes, in turn, gets a zealot in her corner, along with his wealth. Whether or not her love for him is real, she is hardly immune to the optics her new partnership offers. Evans makes her look helpless next to his bravado. Once, he showers in front of the cameras, a full-frontal spectacle that nobody asked to see.

Later, he starts to carry a gun and goes to the range to practice his marksmanship. In one exchange, he insults Fielder’s special guest, telling her that she is just an actress, that he is better read, and that he knows people. Violent people, he implies. His expression never changes, even when he’s issuing threats. He wants Fielder to know that he can take care of business. He’s in control. He is in fact the unaccomplished scion of a hotelier dynasty, but in his head, he knows best — for himself, their family, and Holmes. Days before she goes to prison, she claims that she hated the Forbes cover and disliked the photo shoots and attention she got while she was still on the rise. Evans allows the photo to be plastered all over billboards almost the moment she’s behind bars. He posts for her on X, trolling her critics in her name. At this point I entertained thoughts of a rescue. I didn’t want to break her out of prison, but I did want to get her away from Evans, who disturbed me on a level that I associate with rabid animals in the wild, or strangers who follow me home from the subway. Somehow, I’d started thinking of Holmes as if she were a friend in trouble, not a convicted fraudster. I wondered if that was her goal all along.

items.title: NYC Schools Chancellor Didn’t Impress Nikole Hannah-Jones
items.description: The Knicks home opener against the 76ers wasn’t the only highly anticipated matchup playing out in Manhattan on Tuesday evening. Less than 20 blocks away at the Washington Irving Campus, about 800 education advocates, students, and parents packed an auditorium
items.author: Nia Prater
paragraphs: The Knicks home opener against the 76ers wasn’t the only highly anticipated matchup playing out in Manhattan on Tuesday evening. Less than 20 blocks away at the Washington Irving Campus, about 800 education advocates, students, and parents packed an auditorium to watch journalist Nikole Hannah-Jones face off with New York City schools chancellor Kamar Samuels in a contentious one-on-one. “While they said it’s going to be a conversation, it’s about to be an interrogation,” Hannah-Jones said at the start, drawing applause from the crowd. It was an accurate description of what followed.
The conversation was the marquee event of a town hall co-hosted by the school-integration advocacy group New York Appleseed and the Bell, a student-journalism organization.

A month ago, Hannah-Jones reignited the school-integration debate with a New York Times Magazine essay detailing the challenging aftermath of her decade-old decision to send her daughter to a segregated public school in Brooklyn. When Mayor Zohran Mamdani was later asked about the essay and his plan to address the problems it illustrated, he signaled that his administration was in the process of developing a plan but provided slim details as to what it might be. Samuels didn’t seem to have more news to share at Tuesday’s town hall either — a fact that didn’t go over very well onstage or in the seats.

Hannah-Jones thanked Samuels for agreeing to take part in the event and for his past work tackling segregation when he served as a superintendent, acknowledging that previous mayors likely limited how much he could accomplish. But, she added, “There is no buck to be passed now. You head the system. So while I appreciate the work you have done, today we want to talk about the work you will do.”

When she asked Samuels if he had a “real and substantial” plan for system-wide school integration and when that would be made public, he responded without those specifics. Hannah-Jones interjected: “No, I know you were coached not to actually answer my question. My question is: When will we see a plan to address comprehensive integration across the city?”

Samuels insisted that the outline of the plan can already be seen. “First of all, part of it is making sure that you are engaging and being thoughtful with communities, which is why I’m here,” he said. “And secondly, it’s also making sure that you are building the structures to have those conversations and build the capacity of superintendents who are going to have to lead the work.”

“I don’t believe the best way to integrate schools is by large proclamations,” he added. “We’ve seen that happen before and we’ve seen that that hasn’t necessarily worked because you have an organized resistance against that.”

He continued, “We will have and we will come to you with a more robust conversation. But right now, there are things we are already doing. And so this is not a matter of being coached to not answer your question.”
By this point, it was clear that many members of the audience were not satisfied with what Samuels had to say — or rather, what he hadn’t come prepared to say.

In response, Hannah-Jones pointed to reports put out in 2019 by the School Diversity Advisory Group, a panel of educators, experts, and scholars assembled under former mayor Bill de Blasio who made numerous recommendations about how to tackle school integration, but very few were implemented. “These issues have been studied,” she said. “There was a task force that was very well equipped to study. They came up with recommendations. So why not just adopt the recommendations?” she asked.

Samuels pointed to how screened admissions, which the SDAG recommended getting rid of in elementary and middle schools, went away during the pandemic and how some schools returned to that process in the years that followed, while others did not. “It’s important to me that we engage those communities again to actually see are these screens working for its intended purpose or what is it that our goals are.” Samuels began.
Hannah-Jones volleyed back the chancellor’s response. “What’s the intended purpose of a screen?” she asked to more cheers from the audience.

The crowd also joined in on the interrogation. When the chancellor spoke of having the “necessary conditions” in place to address segregation, one woman shouted, “Create the conditions!” When Samuels, as he has before, raised his recent creation of five district-based community working groups — an effort expected to expand to additional districts down the line, one audience member shouted, “What’s your timeline?”
When Samuels started to respond, saying this was something the administration was working on, there were audible groans throughout the room.

Hannah-Jones chimed in: “So there’s not a timeline. You have to understand kind of the discontentment. It’s ten months in. This is not a surprising conversation. This is not a new issue. So ten months in, when a timeline can’t be offered, you can understand why people feel like that means you are just delayed.”

In brief remarks given onstage prior to his sit-down with Hannah-Jones, Samuels framed the matter of solving school segregation as an ongoing conversation, one he implored parents to be a part of. “We need you to stick with us, even when these conversations get hard, and they certainly will,” he said.

Despite the many tense exchanges, the chancellor also indicated he would be up for another round. “We’ve got to do a part two,” Samuels said after a planned question-and-answer session had to be cut short.
Hannah-Jones quipped, “Oh, you’re a brave man.”

items.title: The Diplomat Recap: What Did Basil Ever Do to You?
items.description: I’m no longer worried about Grace Penn and the maybe-PTSD that seems to be exacerbating her worst qualities. I have set aside all tattered remains of concerns or doubts I’ve been harboring about her fitness to serve as President and Commander-in-Chief, and I w
items.author: Sophie Brookover
paragraphs: I’m no longer worried about Grace Penn and the maybe-PTSD that seems to be exacerbating her worst qualities. I have set aside all tattered remains of concerns or doubts I’ve been harboring about her fitness to serve as President and Commander-in-Chief, and I wish I’d done it sooner. Grace Penn is now coming into what I suspect is her final form as a pure, uncut, pharmaceutical-grade villain. She doesn’t deserve whatever shreds of benefit of the doubt or leeway provided by respect for the office. She’s leveraging norms against her staff (and possibly the world?!), and at the rate she’s going, I won’t be the least bit surprised if she goes full Henry II during the season finale and shouts “Who will rid me of this troublesome ambassador?” leading to Kate getting shanked in her Tuscan villa.

“Phony Negroni” drives home something I had been starting to suspect over the course of the season: Grace may well have PTSD following her attempted assassination, but she’s also devolved into a missing stair. A missing stair is a person in a given community (family, friendship group, workplace) whose behavior consistently violates norms, and for whom everyone adjusts or pre-plans their behavior around so as not to rock the boat. (The metaphor seems to have originated in the BDSM and kink community in response to the presence of a rapist in a specific social circle, but has been in broader use, including psychotherapy, for at least a decade.)

Kate’s painstaking approach (she later describes it as strategic) to Hal to get him to pitch her corpse-retrieval plan to Grace? Seems like a bit of a double missing stair situation to me. Hal and Kate discussing whether to approach Grace before or after dinner and gaming out potential outcomes? Missing stair. Todd doing everything he can not to tell Grace that Kate left him out of her meeting with Vaughn? You guessed it: missing stair. Kate even tells Stuart and Eidra that the reason she lied about having delivered the ultimatum to Vaughn was that she saw Grace nearly tear Gannon’s head off for asking a very reasonable question. She chose to take a fireable-for-cause action rather than inform the President that she exercised her own judgment to tailor her message to Vaughn. Lying to Grace bought Kate some time, sure, but the cost is vertiginously steep. It’s a wonder anything in this administration actually gets done, given how much time and thought everyone puts into managing the President’s mercurial moods and mitigating the effects of her imperious behavior.

Cozied up in their Tuscan villa for the G7 Summit, Grace wants Todd to do as he had been doing in previous episodes, and furnish her with juicy gossip from his job (which is also hugely consequential for statecraft and the relationship between the United States and the United Kingdom, no big deal). Her repeated attempts go from flirty to sincere to demanding, forcing her husband (who is also her employee! cool!) to reveal the shameful truth that Kate left him out of her latest meeting with Vaughn. At this point, both believe that Kate delivered both the request half and the ultimatum half of Grace’s message about the welcome that Russian salvage vessels would receive in British waters, so Todd’s repeated demurrals are not about protecting Kate, but are focused on protecting his own ego and forestalling a huge mood shift from Grace. Naturally, Todd’s worry turns out to be merited when Grace crowbars the truth out of him; she’s like a dog with a bone, wanting to summon Kate and have it out immediately, because she thinks this is a managerial problem. Todd finally — finally! — does what I’ve been imploring him through the screen to do, telling Grace that actually, the problem is not Kate, nor himself, but her. Her behavior has been weird, he says. Her decision-making, too. In the way of loving veteran spouses, he’s incredibly kind about it, making allowances for the effect of the shooting and the pressures of the job. As Todd wends his way towards sharing this analysis, he and Grace go a few rounds in which she belittles his diplomatic knowledge and experience and describes her own reckless behavior as having “decided to jump to the [step on the diplomatic ladder] that works.”

Meanwhile, Kate and Hal are mostly enjoying an interlude that Hal thinks is purely romantic, with a bit of work stuff sprinkled on top, and which Kate has designed as more of a half-and-half experience. She’s orchestrated a state-of-the-relationship conversation in which it becomes clear to Hal for the first time (the first time, how????) that Kate has been thinking he hated her default mode prior to the shift in their relationship that’s been playing out over the season. He’s aghast and deeply apologetic, which is correct, but also: he really did seem, often, to want to punish that version of his wife. He behaved as though he thought she was a real drag and shrewish when she confronted or questioned him. This conversation feels like one they would have had years ago, but it seems helpful and sincere on both sides, and I believe Kate when she later says the substance is real and the timing was strategic.

All of this pillow talk smooths Kate’s path to selling Hal on her idea of extracting the bodies from the Russian sub. He’d have gone for it even without a leisurely, sexy afternoon as an apéritif, because he gets on board right away. The only flaw he highlights is that, having issued an ultimatum to Vaughn, it’ll cost Grace some pride to back off and offer an alternate plan. It only takes Kate’s coming clean with the good news/bad news to throw all their progress out the window, not least because Hal thinks that once Grace finds out about Kate’s lie, it’ll cost both of them their jobs. He can’t bear to lose the access and the role he’s got now, and hates that Kate hits the nail on the head by asking if he’s angry she lied or that his position as Vice President is now in jeopardy. It’s too late to do much about it, though, as they’re about to have dinner with the Penns.

Grace is in full-on shark mode, taking Kate with her to the greenhouse to fetch some basil for the negronis Todd is whipping up (basil is not actually a garnish for a negroni, but nobody is going to say that to Grace). She sets Kate up for a spectacular fall by apologizing for foisting Todd off on her and being fake-disbelieving of all of Kate’s compliments, then asking, well, if Todd is such an asset, why didn’t you take him with you to meet the prime minister?

Things only get worse from here. Grace demands counsel and observation from her innermost circle, then is angry and punitive when they’re honest about their concerns. Hal choosing this moment to pitch Grace on the body-extraction proposal is a bit of a head-scratcher, but by this point everyone is just throwing stuff at the wall to see what sticks. Nothing is effective. Not sincere, caring concern, and not questions about the legality or morality of Grace’s ultimatum. Not even Kate’s last-ditch approach works. Her gentlest possible framing of Grace’s increasing tolerance for international relations risk and threats to human life has come to threaten the collapse of the U.S. and U.K.’s special relationship lands like a lead balloon. She coldly dismisses Kate for the night, saying her increasingly expeditious decision-making is not the result of the shooting, but of her belief that she has a responsibility to the world to move more quickly and decisively. Hal gets barely a minute longer at the table before she sends him away while Billie rummages in her bag for copies of her North Sea situation update materials.

They all should have seen this coming, is the thing. Grace has been leaving an entire loaf’s worth of breadcrumbs all along. Maybe the shooting shook something loose in her and has amplified her worst tendencies. Many of the troubling moments and decisions we’ve seen — biting a staffer’s head off about receiving what turned out to be the correct daily briefing memo; telling Todd to sleep in another room; gleefully congratulating Kate on maneuvering Trowbridge out of office; announcing the Chinese legacy chip ban — could be rationalized or softened just a bit, especially by people who want to believe the best of her. In the aggregate, though, a picture of a very astute leader with an encyclopedic grasp of the rules, an iron grip on the levers of power, and seemingly free from restraint, well on her way to being a ruthless, abusive dictator emerges all too clearly. Most dreadful of all, it seems as if nobody has the rhetorical stamina to argue Grace into a corner and keep her there. She keeps wriggling out of it because they are all operating in good faith that she will do the same, so she keeps turning that against them.

• I have to start with the comic relief of the episode, because the jokes are good and deserve some love. First, Grace hurling the remaining (and wholly superfluous!) basil on the ground, because after all that rigamarole, she doesn’t want any basil in her negroni, because she doesn’t like the smell. The whole thing was a power move, with shades of Logan Roy woven in.

• The poor, sweet, innocent angel of a chef, who was so proud to be able to share his menu with his world leader guests, only for Grace to stalk away mid-recitation? I hope someone hugs and reassures him that none of this was his fault.

• Stuart wielding his State Department-honed delay tactics and feigned incompetence against Billie is funny, and, I was glad to see, ultimately leads to them having the conversation they’ve needed to have since last season when she cautioned him against lawyering up. Who knows if their friendship will survive, but at least the air is clear between them, and she’s heard him say out loud that she bears some responsibility for the mess they’re all in.
• I keep trying not to think this, but Grace’s ability to get away with everything, repeatedly, reminds me ever so slightly of someone else.

items.title: The Diplomat Recap: Advisory Board, Assemble
items.description: The what-could-have-been vibe of “The Dead” is agonizing. If Todd were not so loyal to and trusting of his wife, who is unfortunately also POTUS, he might have been a valued member of the advisory board Kate assembles with Stuart and Eidra. The outcome of Kate
items.author: Sophie Brookover
paragraphs: The what-could-have-been vibe of “The Dead” is agonizing. If Todd were not so loyal to and trusting of his wife, who is unfortunately also POTUS, he might have been a valued member of the advisory board Kate assembles with Stuart and Eidra. The outcome of Kate’s conversation with Vaughn might have been the same, but perhaps if she could have trusted Todd to attend without trumpeting Grace’s warships ultimatum (even one flimsily disguised as an offer of help), he’d have offered an insight that was sufficiently reassuring to get her to accept Kate’s offer of a joint mission to retrieve the bodies of the Russian submariners.

Instead, Kate gets her hopes up for nothing, and the shiny new upgraded security clearance she acquires for Todd may wind up coming back to bite her. Boo! I think another part of what leads Todd to back delivering Grace’s entire message to Vaughn — “tell the Russians to stay out of her yard, or I’ll send warships to do it for her” — over Kate’s preferred plan of only delivering the first half is that he hasn’t seen Grace at her reactive, high-handed worst in one of the high-security Zooms yet. He’s seen enough to make him concerned; he tells Kate what anyone with eyes has already seen many times, that Grace has been different since the shooting and that “there’s a lot less nuance in her perspective and in the way that she talks about things.” This seems to me, a person whose vast medical expertise comes from her decades-long enrollment in such rigorous programs as the full-season runs of ER and Call The Midwife, like a problem that is preventing her from carrying out her duties as the Commander-in-Chief and Chief Executive of the nation. My second bold take of the day is that it’s essential for anyone in those roles to be in command of the facts and capable of working with others to arrive at good solutions to the problems they face. Grace seems to hope for escalation at every turn and is recklessly determined to bring it about. Meanwhile, Hal too often dumps gas on the fire when he ought to be pumping the brakes.

Todd also mentioned feeling shut out from Grace’s thoughts and decision-making process; of course he’s been unsettled and worried as well as resentful. This puts him in good, if uncomfortable, company with Billie, who tells Hal about how the week previous, she was in the middle of a negotiation of the Labor HHS budget, when she received a push notification about the President having approved the $200 billion budget without her. Intentional humiliation? Forgetfulness? Is one any better than the other?

Kate manages to convince Todd to raise the issue of the warships ultimatum with Grace before they meet with Prime Minister Vaughn, and for one tantalizing moment it seems as though reasonableness may prevail. Admittedly, Kate’s (and my) hopes were a little too high to start with. Todd isn’t a seasoned diplomat or political operative, and on top of that, Grace confides that part of why she wants him in London is to show the world that she’s not afraid for him to be in the place where she was nearly murdered. She is afraid, though, and that shared confidence with Todd is a significant one. He can’t bring himself to not do what the President has asked, because she is also his wife.

Once Kate’s Todd hopes are dashed, and she can tell that Stuart told Eidra about her blackmailing Trowbridge, it becomes easier for her to take the big step of reading them both into all of the gory details going back to the attack on HMS Courageous. The levels of shock Stuart experiences…whatever the State Department is paying him, they should triple it immediately. If Kate’s not going to have regular friends, these two, who work alongside and care about her, will make a solidly trustworthy advisory board. Good for her for finally saying out loud that she may be in over her head and incapable of seeing clearly enough to know that she’s working for “a culture of consistent lawlessness”. And good for Stuart and Eidra for confirming her new perception of the situation and facilitating a new plan to circumvent Todd’s participation in her conversation with Vaughn. I love when a plan comes together!

I also love this scene between Kate and Vaughn at the latter’s family home in her constituency. We only see it at nighttime in this episode, but it’s a very impressive old pile, the kind of place you stick with even though it’s impossible to heat or cool consistently and nothing really works anymore. Having opened her home in the middle of the night, Vaughn once again strikes Kate (and me) as the very picture of decency and good faith. The character is written to be very likable and worthy of respect, and Jodie Whittaker brings a really effective extra oomph of warmth and humor to her performance that makes her consistent refusals to accept Kate’s proposals even more striking.

Grace Penn wants Vaughn to revoke her permission to the Russians as a secret-keeping courtesy to the U.S.? It would have been a courtesy for Grace to mention to Trowbridge that she’d ordered the U.S. Navy to remove the Poseidon, but she didn’t. Vaughn hasn’t given up the Americans, though; she has not told the Russians about the Poseidon, largely because it would seem unbelievable that “our closest allies would do that to us without our consent.” She’s so calm, and not in Trowbridge’s usual way of seeming as though he was holding himself back from flying into a rage through force of will. She’s just a very grounded person who is communicating thoughtful decisions.

Kate’s new idea, for a joint mission between the U.S. and Royal Navies to carefully retrieve the bodies of the dead from the submarine and tell the Russians it’s all been entombed in concrete, also fails. Not on its merits, which Vaughn agrees are quite good, but because of the number and scale of betrayals of trust the U.S. has inflicted on the U.K. From her perspective, “The fundamental character of your country has sufficiently changed that we have no idea what you will do next.” She’ll take her chances with the predictable Russians instead, thank you very much. And that’s the end of that. As planned, Kate doesn’t issue the warships ultimatum, and once back at Winfield House, tells Todd he’s welcome to sit in on her conversation with Grace.

Todd is not thrilled that Kate went to speak with Vaughn without him, but there’s no time for him to get into that just yet. Instead, it’s time for Kate to lie her face off by confirming that she issued Grace’s ultimatum, and that Vaughn agreed to call the Kremlin to revoke her permission for Russian ships to enter British waters.

• That final moment with the secure link video call is the first moment that Gannon learns of Todd’s new role as Special Envoy with higher security clearance. The chain of communication in the Penn administration really is something else.

• One tiny glimmer of a good thing for Stuart as he learns one appalling fact after another: he can recover his good opinion of the late President Rayburn, who was not involved in the bombing of HMS Courageous, after all.

• What a sweet relief to see Stuart and Eidra resolve their conflict about the status and future of their relationship. I particularly liked the proposal to discuss from Eidra – all those post-its in the breeze of her desk fan and the legal pad sun held aloft reminded me of Max Cohen’s thousand yellow daisies-based proposal to Lorelai in Gilmore Girls. The song playing on her desk speaker in this scene is Prince’s classic slow jam “Adore”. Solid pick.
• Eidra taking the measure of the young Vaughn who asks for a jammy dodger before delivering a cool “no”. One of my favorite little moments of the season so far.

items.title: ‘Michael’: Golden Globes Reject Submission to Compete in Comedy/Musical Categories
items.description: The music of “Michael” is bringing some drama.
items.author: Clayton Davis
paragraphs: The music of “Michael” is bringing some drama.

Variety has confirmed that Lionsgate’s bid to have its Michael Jackson biopic compete as a comedy or musical at the Golden Globes has been denied. News of the decision was first reported by Gold Derby.

The Golden Globes’ decision means the film, starring Jaafar Jackson as the King of Pop, is currently slated for the drama categories where it would compete for one of the six available slots against Christopher Nolan’s “The Odyssey,” Los Javis’ “La Bola Negra” and more. The supporting actor and actress categories do not separate by genre, so this has no effect on his co-stars Colman Domingo and Nia Long.

Lionsgate can appeal the ruling ahead of the Oct. 31 submission deadline. If the studio moves forward, the organization’s awards committee would evaluate the appeal. According to the Golden Globes rules, it states: “A musical can be a comedy or a drama in which songs are used in addition to spoken dialogue to further the plot.”

Under Globes procedure, when a film submits in a category that goes against the grain, or one in which it would not typically be accepted, a letter from the director is required to proceed. That letter, from “Michael” director Antoine Fuqua, was included with the studio’s submission. The organization reviewed the request and denied it anyway. An appeal may still be possible before the Oct. 31 submission deadline, but sources have shared that it will likely not be pursued. Lionsgate declined to comment.

Musical biopics have long been tricky to classify at the Globes. “Ray” and “Walk the Line” both competed in, and won, the comedy or musical categories in the mid-2000s. Those victories prompted a rule change requiring that songs propel the narrative rather than appear as standalone performances. In other words, music alone is no longer enough to qualify a film as a musical. By that standard, “Bohemian Rhapsody,” “Elvis,” and “A Complete Unknown” were all submitted as dramas in the years since. One notable exception: “Inside Llewyn Davis,” the Coen brothers’ story of a folk singer struggling for success in 1961, was permitted to compete as a comedy during its respective year.

That same distinction appears to have decided the fate of “Michael.” Jackson performs many of his uncle’s biggest hits in the film. Still, the organization evidently viewed those sequences as re-creations of Michael Jackson’s performances rather than as integral storytelling devices.

Fuqua’s film, which opened April 24, became the first biopic in history to surpass $1 billion at the worldwide box office and is Lionsgate’s biggest release ever. It also made a star of Jaafar Jackson, who had never acted professionally before.
The ruling does not affect the Globes’ broader slate of classification decisions. The awards show has accepted both “Obsession” and “Tender Loving Care” as comedies for consideration.
The 84th Golden Globe nominations will be announced Monday, Dec. 7, and the ceremony, hosted by Nikki Glaser, is set for Sunday, Jan. 10.

items.title: ‘Pirates of the Caribbean’ Secret Cinema Immersive Stage Show Casts George Maguire as Jack Sparrow, Extends London Run
items.description: Olivier winner George Maguire will play Captain Jack Sparrow in “Disney’s Pirates of the Caribbean: The Immersive Adventure,” the London stage production from Secret Cinema and TodayTix.
items.author: Naman Ramachandran
paragraphs: Olivier winner George Maguire will play Captain Jack Sparrow in “Disney’s Pirates of the Caribbean: The Immersive Adventure,” the London stage production from Secret Cinema and TodayTix.

Phil Daniels, known for “Quadrophenia,” “EastEnders” and Blur’s “Parklife,” will play Captain Barbossa. Lily Blunsom is Elizabeth Swann, Harrison Wilde is Will Turner and Gleanne Purcell-Brown is Anamaria. The rest of the cast will be named later. Matt Costain, also an Olivier winner, directs.

Previews begin Feb. 16, and the show opens on March 10 at Secret Cinema’s new riverside venue on the Greenwich Peninsula. The production is the first at the site, which the company plans to keep as its home. Strong demand has led the producers to add six weeks to the run.

No earlier stage version of the franchise has been fully immersive, and the show marks a change of approach for Secret Cinema. Live storytelling leads the show. Instead of screening the whole of “Pirates of the Caribbean: The Curse of the Black Pearl,” the production uses selected clips from the film alongside large set pieces. Over two hours, audiences can roam the sets, meet characters and take part in the story, with stunts and a live band.

The creative team includes two-time Emmy winner Jason Sherwood as production designer. His credits include live broadcasts of the Oscars and “Rent Live.” Kait Kerrigan, who wrote the book for Broadway’s “The Great Gatsby,” is the theatrical adaptor. Olivier winner Alan Williams handles music supervision, arrangements and orchestrations. Stuart Burt is casting director, Susan Kulkarni designs costumes, Helen Keane of Campbell Young Associates designs wigs, hair and makeup, and Alex Payne is fight director.

“We’ve taken everything Secret Cinema does best and pushed it further than ever before, creating a new kind of theatrical experience where the story doesn’t just happen in front of you – it happens all around you,” said Merritt Baer, Secret Cinema’s artistic director and producer and president and co-founder of TodayTix Group. “This is exactly the kind of show we’ve been building towards and opening it in our new home at Greenwich Peninsula makes it even more exciting.”

Maguire won his Olivier for playing Dave Davies in the musical “Sunny Afternoon.” His screen credits include “EastEnders,” “Prime Suspect” and “Borgia.” Daniels’ other film work includes “Chicken Run” and “Scum,” and he appears with Olivia Colman in “Wicker,” due out in 2026.

The production is licensed through Disney Theatrical Group. Angelo Desimini, the group’s senior VP of licensed partnerships and brand management, said Disney was excited by the chance to bring the franchise’s spirit to life through theatrical talent and immersive storytelling. “Secret Cinema has assembled a remarkable team to create an experience that is both artistically ambitious and wonderfully entertaining,” Desimini said. “It’s a chance for audiences to experience the world of Tortuga in an entirely new way.”

TodayTix bought Secret Cinema in 2022. Baer took charge of the company in 2024, and since then it has staged “Grease: The Immersive Movie Musical,” its most popular production in 19 years. Its more than 70 shows also include “Stranger Things,” “Guardians of the Galaxy: The Live Experience” and “Star Wars: The Empire Strikes Back.”

items.title: ‘Mayor of Kingstown’ Season 5 Drops Release Date and First Look Photos at Jeremy Renner’s Final Episodes
items.description: “Mayor of Kingstown,” the Taylor Sheridan-created crime series starring Jeremy Renner, will return for its fifth and final season on Jan. 15.
items.author: Selome Hailu
paragraphs: “Mayor of Kingstown,” the Taylor Sheridan-created crime series starring Jeremy Renner, will return for its fifth and final season on Jan. 15.

Accompanying the news, Paramount+ released 15 photos from the season, which picks up “in the wake of Tracy’s murder and the vengeance visited upon Callahan by Mike (Renner) and Kyle McLusky (Taylor Handley),” per the official logline, which continues: “FBI agent Russell Hardy (David Morse) arrives in Kingstown searching for the ‘fugitive’ Callahan. A true lawman, Agent Hardy threatens to unearth all of Mike’s sins and secrets, and disrupt Kingstown’s tenuous balance of power.”

Along with Renner, Handley and Morse, the cast includes Edie Falco as Nina Hobba, Laura Benanti as Cindy Stephens, Hugh Dillon as Ian Ferguson, Tobi Bamtefa as Deverin “Bunny” Washington, Derek Webster as Stevie, Necar Zadegan as Evelyn, Nichole Galicia as Rebecca and Lennie James as Frank Moses.

Sheridan co-created “Mayor of Kingstown” with Hugh Dillon, and both serve as executive producers Antoine Fuqua, David C. Glasser, Ron Burkle, David Hutkin, Bob Yari, Michael Friedman, Dave Erickson, Wendy Riss, Evan Perazzo, Michael Slovis, Regina Corrado, and Keith Cox. Erickson also serves as showrunner for the series, and Sheridan directed the series pilot. Paramount Television Studios, 101 Studios and Bosque Ranch Productions produce the series.
