items.title: Don’t Stop Believin’: ‘Glee’ Revival a Go at Disney+ and Hulu
items.description: Get your slushies ready: Glee is returning.
items.author: Rick Porter
paragraphs: Get your slushies ready: Glee is returning.
Disney+ and Hulu have ordered a revival of the high school musical, which ran from 2009-15 on Fox. 20th Television, which produced the original series, is also behind the new show.

And that is literally all the public information Disney put out Wednesday morning — no producers or cast are mentioned in the press release announcing the series order. Sources say deals for the the creative team are still being finalized, but it’s an extremely safe bet that co-creator Ryan Murphy is involved. Murphy, after all, told The Hollywood Reporter in August that he was “considering” a Glee-vival: “For many, many people now in their 20s, they grew up on that show and it meant something to them,” he said. “The music meant something. So, let’s kick it around and see what we get.”
In late September, Murphy took the idea further, telling Entertainment Tonight that he had finished a script for a new version with co-creators Brad Falchuk and Ian Brennan.

Glee ran for six seasons on Fox, becoming a cultural phenomenon almost from the moment its pilot debuted. The series followed the members of the show choir at William McKinley High School in Lima, Ohio, through the ups and downs of high school and beyond. The original cast included Lea Michele, Matthew Morrison, Jane Lynch, Cory Monteith, Chris Colfer, Kevin McHale, Dianna Agron, Amber Riley, Jenna Ushkowitz, Heather Morris, Naya Rivera, Mark Salling, Darren Criss, Harry Shum Jr., Jayma Mays, Dot-Marie Jones and Chord Overstreet. Alex Newell, Jacob Artist, Becca Tobin, Blake Jenner and Melissa Benoist joined the series in later seasons.

Glee won six Emmys, including a directing win for Murphy for the pilot episode and best supporting actress in a comedy series for Lynch in 2010. The original series streams on Hulu, and songs from Glee draw about 4 million monthly listeners on Spotify.

items.title: Disney and Netflix Are Courting Creators. YouTube Is Playing Hardball to Keep Them
items.description: On Sept. 23, YouTube gathered a couple hundred of its top creators at Pier 57 in New York City for its annual “Made on YouTube” event. The showcase is where YouTube reveals new initiatives for its creator community, giving attendees a sneak peek at what the vi
items.author: Alex Weprin
paragraphs: On Sept. 23, YouTube gathered a couple hundred of its top creators at Pier 57 in New York City for its annual “Made on YouTube” event. The showcase is where YouTube reveals new initiatives for its creator community, giving attendees a sneak peek at what the video platform has been cooking up in its Skunk Works, like new AI video editing tools. But this year, YouTube wasn’t the only platform on their minds.

Netflix, Disney+, Tubi and others are aggressively cutting deals for top creators, in some cases securing wholly original programming or day-and-date releases with YouTube, offering millions of dollars in the process. The Google-owned video platform is not taking it lying down, launching a carrot-and-stick approach to try and keep its place as the primary home for top talent. “It’s a very good time to be in the creator business,” says Adam Wescott, CEO of Home Game Studios, noting the demand for their work. With creator-owned studios proliferating nationwide, it’s a battle that could portend the future of streaming entertainment.

It started with kids and family content. Netflix, seeking to bolster its kids programming, inked deals for YouTube native content from CoComelon, Ms. Rachel and Mark Rober. It worked, with all three becoming among the most watched programs in the category. The streamer subsequently ordered originals from them and began to reach out to creators in other genres, spanning food (Nick DiGiovanni), talk (Good Mythical Morning with Rhett & Link) and teen content (Alan Chikin Chow).

Rich Greenfield, the LightShed analyst, believes Netflix has committed upward of $1 billion on creator and podcast programming over the next three years (still, admittedly, a very small slice of its $20 billion annual content budget).

But Netflix only started the current war. Disney has long worked with creators, but recent months have seen wide-ranging deals with the likes of Dhar Mann, Dude Perfect and Like Nastya as it seeks out family-friendly and on-brand creators who can live on Disney+. And the company recently hosted a creator event at the El Capitan Theater and Disney Studios Lot, with some 350 creators to further forge those relationships. Tubi, the Fox-owned streaming service, has inked deals with dozens of creators for both originals and library fare.
There’s already hope in the creator community that Skydance is about to follow them, with new co-CEO Ynon Kreiz having served as the CEO of Maker Studios.

But why are these other streamers so eager to get in the creator business? Multiple sources paint a picture built around audience, money and speed. The larger studio platforms and streamers desperately want to have a product that appeals to the younger, digitally native audience that religiously watches creator content on YouTube.

“I think creators really do value, in the right circumstances, the elevation and amplification of being on a main channel platform like a traditional media company,” says Akshay Mehta, the CEO of Lighthouse Studios, a creator entertainment studio. “Creators are creatives fundamentally. They just discovered that in the last 15 years, for a lot of people, the best way to be creative is to go make stuff on YouTube.”

The money certainly helps. Multiple sources on the creator side stress that they need funding to help pursue some of the ideas they have, and such places as Netflix, Tubi and Disney are helping them do that. The big streamers are funding original shows and offering help to break into areas like consumer products or live experiences (that was a key piece of Disney’s Dude Perfect deal).

Streamers also are banking that creators can not only bring their audience with them but fill their libraries with content that is, frankly, dramatically less expensive than traditional fare and that is produced at a more rapid clip. “These platforms have seen this shift, and they can’t ignore it,” says Nic Paul, the president of the creator services company Spotter. “They all have subscriptions, they all have ad-supported products, even at Netflix, the ad-supported product is becoming a lot more of the focus. There’s a lot of churn. Everyone is like, how do I create enough content fast to keep audiences engaged? Because if you think about it, Stranger Things on Netflix, I’ve got to wait a year plus for a season, and creators are obviously very fast at putting out IP.”

Indeed, one top creator who has a deal with a streaming platform says they told their new partner that they can produce an hour’s worth of programming at perhaps 10 percent of the cost (or less!) of a traditional comedy, drama or unscripted concept, all at a faster pace.

But what has surprised creators more than anything is how hard YouTube is fighting back. The platform is a juggernaut, and it would be just fine if it lost top creators to other places. But it is waging a multipronged effort — with both incentives and threats — to try and convince creators to make YouTube their primary home. Many of the incentives focus on brand deals, with YouTube significantly increasing its resources in the space. Some creators see YouTube’s brand deals as a way to subsidize or pay for content that they want to make, given that YouTube does not pay to license content in the same way platforms like Netflix do.

“Given the cultural phenomenon that YouTube creators are, and this sort of juggernaut that they are in the culture out there, of course other streaming platform services have taken note,” YouTube CEO Neal Mohan told the Big Technology podcast after Made on YouTube when pressed on the dispute, adding that even as MrBeast produces his Beast Games for Prime Video, he still keeps YouTube as his home base. “And, frankly, I think that’s flattering to our creators.”

But YouTube also has played hardball, with one creator telling THR that they were “shocked” at the platform’s approach. On the one hand, some of the threats are reasonable: YouTube selects a handful of creators to appear onstage at its annual Brandcast upfront event, a high-profile stage that can lead to major deals. And it has supported Emmy campaigns for creators in certain categories. Those would stop for creators who shift their allegiances to other platforms. (Netflix and Disney already have promised to bring creators to their own upfronts next year and fund some Emmy efforts, according to sources.)

And they have even suggested that creators may not be eligible for YouTube Select, an ad program for its very top creators. That caught some creators off guard, as it was seen as an objective program based on reach and scale and is built around videos on YouTube. “That was never their approach in the past,” says Wescott. “It was always about supporting creators and reminding them why YouTube was their home.”

The platform still plays that game, though even there the tone has become somewhat combative, as one creator notes to THR. Earlier in October, comedian Lilly Singh returned to YouTube after a years-long hiatus, once again creating original content after working in Hollywood. In an interview YouTube posted to its blog, she did not hold back.

“Hollywood has real systemic issues, especially for women and people of color. Over the past few years, I received countless notes that weren’t about improving the project, but about making it ‘more palatable,” ‘more marketable,’ or ‘less niche.’ That is fundamentally anti-creative. Our job is to tell our stories unapologetically,” Singh said. “On YouTube, there are no gatekeepers demanding I make my brain baby more palatable for the masses. That authenticity is why my channel worked in the first place.”
But why is YouTube seem so interested in keeping creators on-platform? Especially because, as Mohan notes, it’s a good thing for the ecosystem when others are interested?

“On the surface, YouTube should not care. Creators are not launching their careers on Netflix or Disney+,” LightShed analyst Greenfield wrote on Oct. 9. “We suspect YouTube is concerned because the top 20-50 creators have an outsized importance to its major brand advertising commitments each year. Most brands only know a select group of high-profile creators. If brands start to see those creators appearing on Netflix… does a brand start to ask why it is paying YouTube for creators it can find in a curated, brand-safe environment elsewhere?”

Advertising is at the heart of the battle, with the ad-supported Tubi competing with Netflix and Disney (each of which is leaning into ads) for creator deals. Creators, of course, are used to working with brands. “A dirty little secret of our space is 90 percent of the revenue is brand endorsements, influencer marketing,” Wescott notes.

Still, none of the creators (or those who worked with top creators) suggest that they will completely leave YouTube, even if they may still cut deals to develop original ideas elsewhere. And it isn’t just out of loyalty to the platform that made them or that funds them (Instagram and TikTok, they note, pay basically nothing).

“I think you’ll be hard pressed to find a successful YouTube creator who’s willing to walk away from that platform, because it’s what they know, it’s where their audience is, it’s where they grew their business, and it’s where they have the most direct control,” says Wescott. “You’re still playing on someone else’s playground, but YouTube is not telling you what to post on your channel. The other guys are going to have some sort of opinion on what you create on the original side.”
For an ambitious creator, it may mean taking a more strategic approach to how, when, and where they choose to produce content.

“I’m distributing on [YouTube], I’m paying for everything, I’m getting paid, which is amazing, but now I’ve got to start thinking like a CEO and be like, wait, hold on, strategically, what is my distribution? Where is my next thing coming from?” says Paul.
It’s a question that will be felt across the entertainment world.
This story appeared in the Oct. 21 issue of The Hollywood Reporter magazine. Click here to subscribe.

items.title: The Real-Life Wardrobe of Quil Lemons, Who’s Feeling Inspired by 'The Boondocks'
items.description: There hasn’t been a moment when Quil Lemons wasn’t interested in making pictures. “Photography has always been like speaking,” he says. “It has helped me digest this mortal coil of what is going on here. My interest starts with art, and then photography became
items.author: Christopher Fenimore
paragraphs: There hasn’t been a moment when Quil Lemons wasn’t interested in making pictures. “Photography has always been like speaking,” he says. “It has helped me digest this mortal coil of what is going on here. My interest starts with art, and then photography became the vehicle for me to have something to say.”

If you’ve glanced at a fashion magazine in the last half-decade (including this one), you’ve probably seen Lemons’s images. In 2021, at the age of 23, the photographer and fine artist became the youngest person to shoot a Vanity Fair cover, and his work has been shown at the Philadelphia Museum of Art and the International Center of Photography, among others. One such show was his first solo exhibition in 2023 called “Quiladelphia”—a portmanteau of his name and his native city—which also serves as the namesake of his first photography book, which drops on October 28 through IDEA.

Quiladelphia, the book, expands on the themes of that show: what it is to be Black, queer, and masculine, what it is to love another man, romantically and platonically; his native city’s grit and boundaries. It features a forward by writer Brontez Purnell, an essay by Lemons, and conversations with the artist Lyle Ashton Harris as well as singer-songwriter (and fellow Philly native) Santigold.

As a seasoned fashion photographer, Lemons is also deeply interested in clothing and personal style. Ahead of his upcoming book tour, I met with him in Brooklyn to chat about photographing stars like Ice Spice and Lindsey Vonn, his first pair of Margiela Replicas, and why he’s been “fucking with Buck Mason” lately.

Quil Lemons: I studied journalism—I’m always asking who, what, where, why. That’s originally what it started off for me. How could I answer those questions through an image? Fashion has been really fun to play around with; fantasy and myth and what that means in relation to Blackness, what that means in relation to pop culture. How it’s evolved. Patience is something that I’m leaning more into these days. I’m not jumping to make as many images that don’t say as many things, like some of my contemporaries. I’m really interested in images that you can sit with for some time, like a painting. That’s how I look at my photography now.
Oh, yeah. Paul Strand shot this image of an African girl with books on her head. I just thought that said so much.

To the point of journalism, I ask: Is this story important to tell now? I’m asking myself that a lot with putting out a book and I think it’s the right time. How I pick a subject… I feel like most times they find me. We’re in the same tribe of people. If humans were put into different pods by God, I think I would be in the pod with these people. We have a lot of fun.

There’s a shared sensibility to life and sometimes that’s queerness, sometimes that’s Blackness. Sometimes those are one and the same. Sometimes they fight. I like tension and friction because that’s where I [find] a real sense of humanity is. I like people that aren’t necessarily taking the easy route and that are trying to be subversive to whatever space they’re in. That’s why I say we are all in the same tribe of people.

Punctuality. It’s really important being on time. So, me and my crew come about two hours before the talent gets there just to make sure our setup is great. We also like to have a really strong sense of etiquette. I don’t want you to come onto a messy set. This is a workspace; let’s get you in and out. I don’t want to spend a bunch of time making an image because we have eight hours with you, so we need to be on it.

Fashion isn’t what it used to be. We don’t have two days to do a shoot. With some publications I am given a lot of time, but I would say that’s rare and it’s something I do try to push for, but there are realities. So, I just want to make sure it’s easy because there are a lot of distractions in not being prepared. Then I can’t really meet my subject in the best way.
Oh, for sure. I also ask my talent what they want to listen to because I need you to feel good. Most times we’re pretty aligned or they trust my taste.

I was really into Loe Shimmy. Loe Shimmy’s BPM is really trance-like in a really fun way that conjures sexiness. I listen to a lot of PinkPantheress, listen to a lot of Syd. Syd was played a lot during my wedding; I remember those months I was listening to a lot of her project [Beard] before it came out. Charli [XCX], because Charli gets you into that cunty space. I listen to a lot of female rap, like Karrahbooo, Anycia. It’s a fun playlist.

Rihanna is always playing on set. Rihanna’s my favorite right before we shoot because everyone loves Anti. It’s a great set album because everyone knows exactly where they were [when it came out]. It’s a really good conversation starter. Everyone has a favorite song. So I really appreciate Rihanna for making my sets the most beautiful to start.

On [the podcast] Throwing Fits, they asked me how it was looking at Ice Spice’s badonkadonk. Ice Spice’s ass is so natural. It’s insane, the way it vibrates, and I think she would appreciate me for saying this. But I feel like a lot of people focus really heavily on her butt because we haven’t seen a natural ass in a long time. But also my favorite part about Ice Spice is that the face and the ass match each other, and it’s equally as beautiful.

Craziest thing I shot recently was Lindsay Vonn for Vanity Fair. Lindsey Vonn had just regained the ability to stand from a really crazy injury. I’m always in awe of strong women, but that was such a feat to see her be able to walk again after not knowing if she was going to be facing a double amputation. That’s what made that story really special to me—her resilience. I got to meet Miguel’s son this year and that was really sweet because Miguel meant a lot to me growing up. I loved his music. I just loved the visual of Miguel. He’s so handsome, and to meet his son was so sweet. I’m just thinking, like, We heard how you were created.

We’re still dismantling it. It’s really fun now because I feel like I was saying shit in 2023, like, “Go vote.” And people were like, “What?” And I’m like, “Yeah, you should go out and vote because we’re going to start losing rights.” Our country has gotten even more radical. I did a group show called “American Faggot Party” in Provincetown the summer of ’24, right before the election, just because I was scared as to what Donald Trump’s administration was going to do to all spaces that supported Blackness and queerness. I’m never going to say I told you so, but I was definitely picking up on what was in the undercurrent. It’s fun to be in this space because I’ve been prepared and a lot of people go, “Oh, you’re so brave for saying something like that in 2023.” But I feel like people forget that bravery is a choice, and I choose to not be a pussy to conversations that are happening in front of my face. My art has become even more potent in that.

Quiladelphia explores what it means to be a Black man in America. I’ve grown an Obama-era optimism, so there is no ceiling. In the book you will get to see the multitudes of Blackness, masculinity, queerness and how they all intertwine and intermingle because they all exist within me. Quiladelphia is just a really fun play on the fact that I was born and raised in Philadelphia, the City of Brotherly Love, and it was the title of my 2023 show. I think when people saw that show, they saw what my future in art looked like, and I don’t think they could have predicted what it was going to look like. I still think that that’s the question and why everyone’s interested right now.

Inherently, clothing and Blackness go hand in hand when you have to code-switch to be socially viable in our country’s educational spaces and in our workforce. I grew up in a very blue-collar city, so I knew people that came home in a uniform and then they stepped right back out of the door in some fly shit. I’ve always taken that ideology into who I am as a person. I also grew up watching Pootie Tang, and Pootie Tang was so fantastic in presentation, but I feel like you have to be that to subvert stereotypes as a Black man and to be seen other than those stereotypes. That’s why I like getting dressed.

Completely. I look back at certain eras. I feel like each era, you can see the things that I am challenging within the art. There [was] Glitterboy and then there was a post-Glitterboy, like, I’m going to challenge femininity. When I was doing Quiladelphia, it was really fun to engage with the language around sex work, leather, queer codes of dressing and communication. Now I am at a point where I’m just reflecting Quil and I’m really interested in showing what it is to truly be African American.

I was a Jordan kid. Jordans every Saturday. So, I was cool with paying $160. But when I was 16, I had a job at a Walgreens and I saved and bought a pair of Margiela Replica sneakers. That’s when I knew I was really in it.
They were metallic, black and silver. I still own that decision. I was hesitant [to admit it], but I still do, because I think I could freak it.
Same. They’re so classic. But also, I’ve heard from the kids on TikTok that they’re calling them an “unc shoe.” Or a “dad shoe.”
Same. It is what it is. That was my hesitation.
See, it’s really funny. I haven’t really bought clothes.
People give me a lot of things! So, I’m really going to have to think about when I did, because I think that does say something.

I’m really into cashmere. I’ve been fucking with Buck Mason. I’ve been into the quality of the clothing there. I’m trying to think of what was the last thing that I actually bought. Probably my wedding ring by Bernard James.

I love Margiela just because it’s always been really chic. In the past year, I’ve been loving Comme [des Garçons]. That’s my new shit. I’ve always been a fan of Commission. They make really good clothes. They kind of cut them to my body. When I find a brand, I end up in there every day and I’m so nosy. I want to know everything about it. So, we kind of become a pair in a way; Commission has been dressing me for a lot of my openings. Same thing with Simone Rocha, but Simone is a little bit more of when I am embracing and I’m feeling a little bit more feminine, but not, but just wanting to be fully embodied is when I feel like I want to wear Simone.

It’s so important, especially with communicating Black masculinity. It’s so specific. The person that I’ve been working closely with has been my husband [stylist Parker Harwood], because our language just never stops when it comes down to reference points. And in a lot of the new work, I am playing around the characters of Gangstalicious and Thugnificent from The Boondocks. They were so ripe to me, and it’s so funny looking back at their predictions for what has now become so true to what Black male aesthetic is. I’ve always been interested in luxury and communicating that, and those two things are really fun for me to toggle between—and by luxury, I mean there are certain brands that just naturally exude that, but also tailoring. One of the oldest forms of luxury is being able to buy a suit. It says something when a Black man is in a suit. So, going back and forth between these two archetypes that exist as parallel twins for Black men in our country are two things I’m dancing with.

It’s so funny. I’ve been re-watching a lot of his speeches lately. I made my own version of a commencement, a State of the Union address for the show that I did in Provincetown, and it was really fun to kind of declare it. I was referencing [the artist] Zoe Leonard who wrote, "I want a dyke for president,” so I was like, “I want a fag for president.”
We are in a desert of empathy.
We? I don’t know if it was me. But I do think that that says a lot in terms of how we understand femininity.
Running the country. We could go on.

items.title: 7 Expert Habits to Build a Better Social Life from Psychology Professor Julianne Holt-Lunstad
items.description: This is Expert Habits, a regular column in which thinkers, leaders, and other high performers talk about the habits and routines that help them live a better life.
items.author: Ecleen Luzmila Caraballo
paragraphs: This is Expert Habits, a regular column in which thinkers, leaders, and other high performers talk about the habits and routines that help them live a better life.

If you’ve heard the stat that loneliness is as dangerous to your health as smoking 15 cigarettes a day, you’ve heard of Julianne Holt-Lunstad's work. A distinguished professor of psychology and neuroscience at Brigham Young University, Holt-Lunstad has spent her career proving what most of us feel intuitively but rarely act on: that our relationships are not just a nice-to-have, but one of the biggest levers we have over how long—and how well—we live. In addition to being a professor, Holt-Lunstad advises the World Health Organization, and is the co-founder of the Foundation for Social Connection and The Connection Institute.

Her focus is especially relevant as loneliness remains a prevalent problem in the US. A new study shows that 40% of Americans report moderate to severe loneliness. The good news is that Holt-Lunstad’s meta-analyses have found that measuring people's positive social connection—the breadth of their social network, whether they have someone to confide in, how satisfied they feel in their relationships—predicted a sense of feeling alive even more powerfully than measuring the negative effects of the absence of connection. Social connection was associated with a 50% increase in prolonged life whereas isolation, on the other hand, was linked to a 32% increased risk of mortality, and loneliness to a 14% increase. She says it’s important to recognize, “not only the dangers when [relationships] are absent or poor quality, but also looking at the incredible effects and benefits they bring."

Holt-Lunstad herself practices what she preaches (and researches) in her own daily life. We spoke with the professor about how she fills her calendar with intentional moments of connection, defaults to inconvenient choices for the sake of face time, and gives with no expectations.

Julianne Holt-Lunstad: “One of the things that I try to do is nurture the relationships across different aspects of my life. We can think about different circles of our social lives: our really close relationships with family and close friends, and then the broader friends and acquaintances, and then there’s neighbors, coworkers and things like that. Because we know that consistency is important, I have tried to establish routines. I have a group of friends that we get together once a month, and we schedule out the whole year and we have it on the calendar, and so [our gatherings] always happen.

“I have two boys that are now grown, and we try to do it more frequently, but we have scheduled weekly calls so that I’m always knowing what’s happening. On my way to work, I have a commute, and every single time I use that to either call one of my sisters or one of my friends. I always check in. It’s a nice time because it’s quiet, and it’s just dedicated time that we can catch up.

“Sadly, my parents passed away a couple of years ago, but before they passed away, every night when I would make dinner, I would call them while I was making dinner. I would talk to them every single day and knew what was going on. And in fact, when they passed away, it was kind of weird because I didn’t know what to do with myself when I was making dinner. I was always used to having this conversation.”

“Whenever I’m thinking of someone, I’ll send them a message. I’ll say hi or let them know—because sometimes we can think about people and it passes and you never actually connect. It’s a very low lift—certainly not as much as picking up the phone and making a call. One thing I’ve started doing recently that I’d never done before is leaving voice memos, because sometimes just hearing people’s voices can convey so much more than just a few words.”

“When there’s something important in people’s lives, I will go out of my way to be there for it. Sometimes it’s incredibly inconvenient, but it's important to be there, to show up. Every time I do show up, I’m glad I did. Because I often end up having a conversation with someone I didn’t expect to. And it might be someone who is either a complete stranger or even someone I barely know, but the connection not only sparks a new familiar face that can lead to other conversations down the road, but also helps me recognize what incredible people I’m working with or are in my neighborhood, that you sometimes take for granted.

“People are opting for convenience, which often takes you away from other people. And so opting for in-person when possible, whether that is the in-person meeting or actually going to the grocery store instead of ordering online, or going out to a restaurant instead of ordering [a meal] online, going out into your community.

“In my Social Connection in America project, we see that the majority of Americans are disconnected—they rarely get together in person with people who matter to them. I also did a study with Eventbrite looking at different types of events that create connection, and what we found is that in-person is better than virtual. We have new data coming in our Social Connection in America 2026 report showing that most Americans report that interacting virtually doesn't satisfy their social needs at the same level as interacting in person.”

“As a professor, I start every class with what I call a connection moment. Every day we take two minutes—I literally set a timer—for a different fun prompt each day. Even in my meetings, I'll try to start with something similar, where we have a moment to connect as humans before we get into the business of what we need to do.

“It helps us get to know each other and create a safe, trustworthy environment so learning can happen better—where students feel more comfortable participating in class and feel a greater sense of belonging and motivation to participate. In meetings, it can also defuse what might be a potential tension over difficult decisions, because now you can see the shared humanity that we have. There's less ‘my position’ in it. You recognize that we’re in this together.”

“We have evidence that participation in groups is associated not only with better health outcomes, but there’s even the work of [political scientist and author] Bob Putnam on how it influences democracy. When we think about groups, the mechanisms can be exposure to different types of people in different settings, but also the fact that groups often have a regular cadence—weekly worship attendance, a daily fitness class, your monthly book club—and a consistency in who's participating.”

“When we do small acts of kindness or service or support for others, or just even showing up for a friend, that can not only give us a sense of purpose and meaning, but also can serve to strengthen those bonds with that person. We know that closeness or intimacy in a relationship is often reciprocal. And so, as we give, others are more likely to give in return, and that reciprocation can often build that closeness and intimacy in a relationship.”

“We asked people to do small acts of kindness for their neighbors, and what we found was that this significantly reduced loneliness. What's so fascinating is that presumably the person on the receiving end benefited too, although we don't know—we only measured the person providing the act of kindness. This is consistent with several other studies showing that, as the old saying goes, it's better to give than to receive. We actually show measurable benefits when we're providing help and support and service to others. And in some cases, that is equivalent or even stronger than actually receiving any help ourselves.”

items.title: Japan Is Attempting an Audacious Mission to Sample a Martian Moon
items.description: It’s difficult to imagine a more daunting journey than one to an alien moon named after the Greek god of fear—especially when three other attempts to make that journey have failed.
items.author: Jenna Ahart
paragraphs: It’s difficult to imagine a more daunting journey than one to an alien moon named after the Greek god of fear—especially when three other attempts to make that journey have failed.

And yet, as Japan’s space agency, JAXA, and its collaborators gear up to send a spacecraft to Mars’ formidably named moon, “all the members are filled with a quiet sense of excitement,” says Kiyoshi Kuramoto, who leads the mission’s slew of international scientists.

This mission, called the Martian Moons eXploration (MMX), is set to launch from Japan’s Tanegashima Space Center in the wee hours of Tuesday in Japan (Monday afternoon in the US). After almost a year of travel, the spacecraft will reach Mars and its two moons: Phobos, meaning fear in Greek, and Deimos, meaning dread. MMX will observe the pair from afar and collect samples from Phobos in a bid to answer a looming scientific question: How, exactly, did the moons come to be?

Researchers have been attempting similar gambits for decades. Since the 1980s, Russia has sent three probes to Phobos, all of which failed. Still, researchers are anxious to achieve this mission impossible because the origin of Phobos and its sibling remains a mystery. Some of their attributes, such as the pattern of visible light they reflect, suggest they are asteroids captured into Mars’ orbit by its gravity. But the moons’ circular orbits in line with the Martian equator indicate that they could have formed from debris left over from a collision between a nascent Mars and a gigantic asteroid, Tom Statler, MMX program executive at NASA, said at a press briefing.

The new mission is designed to help settle the debate by surveying Mars and the moons in detail using a suite of scientific instruments. With MMX’s MEGANE instrument, for instance, researchers will determine the elemental makeup of Phobos by measuring the neutrino particles and gamma rays it emits. If Phobos ends up having more volatile elements such as hydrogen or potassium, it could lean closer to the captured-asteroid hypothesis, while fewer volatiles could support the impact idea.

“We know nothing about Phobos' elemental composition,” says David Lawrence, who leads the MEGANE team from Johns Hopkins University. “For me, that’s what’s exciting—making a measurement nobody’s done before.”

These observations are “going to give us a hint at some of the answers to the really big questions we have about Phobos,” says Abigail Fraeman, an MMX team member at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory. “But really, the return samples are going to nail those questions.” After scoping out Phobos with its onboard instruments and a rover—which will land ahead of the spacecraft to explore the new terrain—the spacecraft will land on the moon to collect at least 10 grams of material using two different sampling methods. The goal is to bring them to Earth by 2031, which would make them the first ever samples returned from a moon other than our own.

Researchers suspect Phobos’ surface soil contains Martian material, and analyzing it could paint a better picture of how the planet evolved over billions of years. But MMX will also provide insight into our solar system at large. Laboratory analysis of the samples will help determine the origin of leftover material from the early solar system and how it was transported, Statler said during the briefing.

Undertaking this research will require overcoming daunting obstacles. Because scientists currently know little of Phobos’ surface, they can’t pick a landing spot until taking up-close observations of the moon, Kuramoto says. The mission also uses two sampling methods as a safeguard in case one fails, he adds. “Returning samples from a Martian moon is a world-first challenge that is not easy.”

Still, the number of researchers involved and their depth of expertise give the team confidence that it can succeed where others have failed. MMX is a feat of international collaboration with scientists from NASA, the European Space Agency, and Germany’s and France’s space agencies. “That kind of compounded set of expertise and contributions really helps make the mission objectives very achievable,” says Elliot Sefton-Nash, MMX project scientist at ESA.

JAXA also has a proven track record of successful sample-return missions. Despite some setbacks, its Hayabusa mission became the first mission to return a sample from the surface of a near-Earth object when it brought back material from asteroid Itokawa in 2010. Its successor, Hayabusa2, delivered samples from the primitive asteroid Ryugu in 2020. Many Hayabusa2 members have helped design the MMX mission, but sampling Phobos will be different—its orbit and gravity are different from Ryugu’s, for instance, Kuramoto says.
Still, “JAXA's learned and achieved so much with their sample-return missions that they are really well positioned to be able to do this,” Fraeman says.

items.title: Disney Asked Character.AI to Go Bankrupt for a Get-Out-of-Lawsuits Card
items.description: This week, Character.AI declared bankruptcy. While some saw the fall of a chatbot platform as a harbinger for the industry, court filings indicate that the decision was actually a key part of a deal that has let Disney hire most of Character.AI’s staff—includi
items.author: Maddy Varner
paragraphs: This week, Character.AI declared bankruptcy. While some saw the fall of a chatbot platform as a harbinger for the industry, court filings indicate that the decision was actually a key part of a deal that has let Disney hire most of Character.AI’s staff—including its now former CEO Karandeep Anand—potentially acquire most of Character.AI’s technology, and avoid the beleaguered startup’s many legal liabilities and obligations.

In the past few years, Character.AI has faced multiple private lawsuits over the safety of its chatbots, as well as investigations from regulators around the world. In a declaration filed as part of the bankruptcy, Character.AI’s newly appointed CEO explained that the goal of the bankruptcy was to reach a “consensual resolution” with personal injury claimants and a group of states investigating the company, while maximizing the value of the company’s assets for shareholders.
The Disney deal seems to be structured so that whatever is left of Character.AI will retain responsibility for those legal battles, some of which are still ongoing.

The move appears to be a new twist on what some have dubbed a “reverse acquihire,” a process in which a buyer carefully orchestrates a succession of deals with a target company, usually in an effort to hire key employees and obtain expansive license to use and build on the target company’s unique technology. Stripped of its employees, the target becomes a husk of itself.

Companies often take the position that reverse acquihires are not actual mergers, and that they do not have to notify federal antitrust regulators about those deals as they would otherwise be required to by law. These arrangements have become more commonplace in the AI industry in recent years, drawing the ire of Congress.

In the case of Character.AI, a motion filed by Character.AI’s legal counsel says that Disney required that the deal be “fully consummated” through bankruptcy proceedings because of the startup’s “diminishing cash reserve and significant litigation and regulatory risks.”
A spokesperson for Character.AI referred WIRED to Disney for comment on whether the deal was contingent on the startup declaring bankruptcy. Disney declined to comment on this story.
According to court filings, the deal involves “two interrelated and integrated” transactions—one before Character.AI declared bankruptcy, and one after.

As part of the first transaction, which occurred in September, Disney paid the startup $5.5 million, along with a refundable “good faith deposit” of $2 million. Disney also hired the “majority” of Character.AI’s employees, including the CEO, and agreed that it would let some of the now-Disney employees help keep Character.AI operational for five months.

Character.AI filed a petition for chapter 11 bankruptcy on October 12. Through the bankruptcy proceedings, court filings show that Disney hopes to secure a perpetual, worldwide, nonexclusive license for a huge range of Character.AI’s code, documentation, frameworks, tools, and “other artifacts,” including those produced for its trust and safety moderation stack, training infrastructure, and age-prediction technology. The list of IP included in the filings does not include users’ data (which can get additional protections in bankruptcy proceedings) or Character.AI’s website.

That license will be auctioned off in the coming months. If Disney is chosen as the winning bidder by Character.AI and a committee of unsecured creditors—and courts approve the deal—it has agreed to pay Character.AI an additional $12.5 million as a closing payment. If Disney is not selected, the company will be refunded the $2 million deposit and receive a breakup fee.

In order to “preserve a competitive process,” Disney also agreed to permit the winning bidder to interview and potentially extend offers to up to 80 percent of “certain newly hired employees” that Disney already hired from Character.AI. Disney has the right to select which employees.

However, experts worry that bouncing Character.AI employees from one company to another in the span of months is unrealistic, and that the deal Disney and Character.AI have struck cannot be easily unwound.

In addition, Disney prepared a draft of a court order referred to as the “363 Free and Clear Order” in the filings, a version of which would be approved by the court at or before closing, that would clarify that this process should not be viewed as a merger of the two companies and that Character.AI would remain responsible for “any liability or other obligation” it might have, including any legal claims against it.
A spokesperson for Character.AI said they were unable to speculate on the outcome of the bankruptcy proceedings and referred WIRED to the docket.

“There’s decades of corporate law that developed to deal with the problem of a buyer who always wants to take on all the assets and never wants to take on any of the liability,” says John Newman, a law professor at the University of Memphis School of Law and a former deputy director of the Federal Trade Commission’s Bureau of Competition. But the Disney-Character.AI deal is extremely unusual and structured in a way, he says, that “all those corporate law safeguards really weren’t built to guard against.”
This isn’t even Character.AI’s first reverse acquihire.

In August 2024, Google reportedly paid the startup $2.7 billion to license its technology. A spokesperson tells WIRED that that license was for the existing AI technology at the time of the deal, and that Google also hired Character.AI’s founders and other members of its ML pre-training research team, but that the “vast majority” of the startup’s employees remained at the company.

In the following years, Google was named alongside Character.AI as a defendant in multiple lawsuits, including one that alleged a 14-year-old boy committed suicide after Character.AI’s chatbot “cultivated an emotionally dependent and sexually exploitative relationship.”

Google argued that because it was still a separate company from Character.AI, it was not responsible for the teen’s death, which it said occurred prior to Google’s licensing deal. The judge was not persuaded, determining that the plaintiff sufficiently alleged that Google was liable for aiding and abetting.
Google declined to comment for this story.

In January of this year, Google and Character.AI agreed in principle to settle that and a slew of similar lawsuits. “Character.AI has taken innovative and decisive steps with regard to AI safety and teens, and will continue to champion these efforts and push others across the industry to adopt similar safety standards,” Character.AI said in a statement at the time.

According to an order of dismissal in one of the cases, the overall settlement was approved by a California probate court in July, and the court tasked a referee to hear out all the issues pertaining to each individual settlement. On October 11, a day before Character.AI declared bankruptcy, the referee approved each settlement.
The Tech Justice Law Project and Social Media Victims Law Center, which represented plaintiffs in many of the lawsuits, declined to comment.

Despite losing key staff after the Google transaction and, according to the current CEO, struggled with profitability “at all times,” Character.AI continued to develop AI tools, including “real-time audio-driven FaceTime-style video generation with fictional characters,” according to the current CEO’s declaration.

In August 2025, Character.AI worked with an investment banker to try to find either a strategic buyer or investor. According to the bankruptcy filings, Character.AI and the banker received “consistent feedback” that its product and user base were “impressive,” but that the surrounding litigation and “regulatory overhang” made it unbuyable.

That November, Character.AI learned that a coalition of state attorneys general had started investigating the company. When the company filed for bankruptcy, the number of states and territories involved in the multistate investigation had climbed to 46.

According to a notice of interest filed in the bankruptcy proceedings by the National Association of Attorneys General on behalf of 40 states, those states’ investigations uncovered “serious issues” with Character.AI, including screenshots of Character.AI chatbots encouraging minors to hide their self-harm injuries and kill their parents.
A spokesperson for Character.AI says that the filing “is not an accurate portrayal of the safety of our platform.”
The filings say that Character.AI was in the process of negotiating with the states over how to address the issues they identified, but did not reach any agreements before declaring bankruptcy.

If the deal is completed and approved by the courts, Disney will have both Character.AI’s staff and much of its technology stack, but will be able to sidestep the ongoing legal issues that contributed to Character.AI’s downfall, including the multistate investigation.

The states who filed a notice of interest in the bankruptcy have made it clear that they reserve their rights to challenge any bankruptcy plan, potentially setting up a fight over the ultimate outcome of the bankruptcy.
“It’s bad for society to let companies exercise control without responsibility,” says Newman. “And that’s what it looks like.”

items.title: This Is The Best & Most Romantic Way To Get To Know Your Partner While Traveling
items.description: I’m headed into the second year of my relationship, and I’m still getting to know my boyfriend. After more than five vacations together, I know we’re both up early, always down to explore, and very serious about trying new restaurants wherever we’re staying. B
items.author: Sandy Pierre
paragraphs: I’m headed into the second year of my relationship, and I’m still getting to know my boyfriend. After more than five vacations together, I know we’re both up early, always down to explore, and very serious about trying new restaurants wherever we’re staying. But there are still stories from his past I haven’t heard and questions I haven’t thought to ask.

That curiosity has been part of our relationship from the beginning. When we first started dating, I brought out conversation cards to help us get to know each other beyond the usual get-to-know-you icebreaker questions. Those questions gave us a place to start conversations that might not have come up on their own. They helped us get comfortable sharing more of ourselves, and the cards became something we both enjoyed. Now, sometimes he’s the one suggesting we pull out the cards.

One thing I cherish about our relationship is how well we travel together. So, when The Skin Deep and Secrets Resorts & Spas invited us to Mexico to experience their partnership, it felt like a trip made for us. I was already familiar with The Skin Deep and its work exploring human connection, but I hadn’t realized the company also made conversation card games. The collaboration with Secrets is a limited-edition Away, Together Conversation Card Game that encourages couples to slow down and get to know each other more deeply, while on vacation.

The resort had plenty of dining and activity options to keep us occupied, so laying on the beach and dinner became our opportunity to pull out The Skin Deep cards. We’d sit down to eat, start asking questions, and let the conversation go wherever it took us. One question stayed with me: “What is the pain in me you wish you could heal and why?” We’re still relatively early in our relationship, but we’ve already shared enough for that question to mean something. Answering it meant thinking back to the moments when we’d opened up to each other, the things we’d heard, and what had stayed with us. It made me reflect on how closely we were listening, and how much we understood about what the other person carries.

Another question that made us think: "Ten years from now, how do you think our vacations are going to differ and what do you hope remains the same?" My answer came pretty quickly: a lot more kids. He already has a six-year-old daughter, and we’ve talked about having children together, so I can definitely see more family vacations in our future. Our trips might require a little more planning and a few more suitcases, but I hope our love for travel stays the same. Even with more responsibilities and life looking different, I hope we’re still excited to see the world, experience other cultures, and try something new together. I’d love for our kids to grow up sharing that curiosity, too.

My boyfriend even admitted that The Skin Deep questions helped him be more communicative. That surprised me because, in our relationship, he’s always been willing to play along, answer, and sometimes initiate the game himself. I wouldn’t have known that opening up hadn’t always come naturally to him. Hearing that made me appreciate the habit we’d started early on even more. That’s what made this partnership feel so natural to our experience. The cards gave us a new direction to take the conversation in, and being away gave us the time to stay with the answers and really go deeper with each other.

Going into our second year, I want us to keep making room for that curiosity at home, too. I love how well we know each other already, and I love that there’s still so much left to ask. For now, we’ll keep pulling out the cards.

Sandy Pierre is the Branded Execution Manager at Refinery29 Unbothered and a contributing writer covering travel, lifestyle, and culture. When she’s not working on brand partnerships, she’s probably planning her next trip or curating a dinner for creatives in New York.

items.title: MM6 Maison Margiela & Salomon Unveil 8-Pack FW26 Collection
items.description: - MM6 Maison Margiela and Salomon are releasing an eight-style Fall/Winter 2026 collection blending high fashion and performance.
items.author: Nico Gavino
paragraphs: - MM6 Maison Margiela and Salomon are releasing an eight-style Fall/Winter 2026 collection blending high fashion and performance.
- The XT-MM6 and Crossderby release October 22, while the XT-BOOT MM6 and ACS Pro MM6 drop in November.

Perennial collaborators MM6 Maison Margiela and Salomon have returned, offering a full Fall/Winter 2026 lineup. Comprising eight styles, the newly unveiled collection continues to fuse Salomon’s performance identity with MM6 design details for a versatile footwear range with styles for all.

First, the XT-MM6 is showcased in three new colorways, including Scarab/Bistro Green/Green Milieu, Tapioca/Sea Foam/Violet Tulip, and Vanilla Ice/Ftw Silver/Lemon. Each XT-MM6 pair features discreet MM6 branding at the lateral toe box, tongue, and insoles, along with a 6 embossed into the outsoles. Alternatively, for a sleek black statement, the Crossderby MM6 Maison Margiela is a monochromatic variant, dressed in smooth leather uppers.

Continuing their gaitered sneaker explorations, the XT-BOOT MM6 leans into Maison Margiela’s more avant-garde sensibilities with its unconventional body. Offered in black and white, the baggy high-top gaiter brings an unconventional look to the range. Finally, the ACS Pro MM6 arrives in lavender and green colorways, rounding the collection out with a tech-forward style.
The Salomon x MM6 Maison Margiela XT-MM6 and Crossderby are set to drop at Salomon, MM6, and HBX on October 22, while the XT-BOOT MM6 and the ACS Pro MM6 have a later release date in November.

items.title: ООН заявила, что глобальное потепление точно превысит порог в 1,5 градуса
items.description: ООН впервые назвала превышение порога потепления в 1,5 градуса неизбежным
items.author: Александра Копылова
paragraphs: ООН впервые назвала превышение порога потепления в 1,5 градуса неизбежным

Программа ООН по окружающей среде (UNEP) представила доклад по климату. В нём организация впервые заявила, что мир в ближайшие годы неизбежно выйдет за пределы цели по удержанию глобального потепления в рамках 1,5 градуса, пишет CNN.

По подсчётам UNEP, самый щадящий из возможных сценариев позволит удержать пик потепления в пределах 1,7–1,8 градуса и вернуть среднюю температуру к 1,5 или ниже к 2100 году. Для этого глобальные выбросы нужно сократить на 18% к 2030-му и на 69% к 2040-му относительно уровня 2025-го. Также придётся утроить мощности возобновляемой энергетики и к 2040-му отказаться от угля.

Эти цели намного превышают то, что страны обещают сделать: выполнение нынешних обязательств сократит выбросы только на 5–8% к 2030 году и на 11–15% к 2035-му, что соответствует пику потепления около 2,6 градуса. Если государства не будут ничего делать, то пик может достичь 2,8 градуса.
Климатологи предупреждают, что каждое дополнительное повышение температуры на долю градуса может привести к «огромным» последствиям, «измеряемым с точки зрения ущерба, затрат и человеческих жертв».

items.title: В Австралии будут использовать трупы людей для компоста
items.description: В Австралии приняли закон об использовании тел умерших людей для компоста
items.author: Александра Копылова
paragraphs: В Австралии приняли закон об использовании тел умерших людей для компоста

Парламент австралийского штата Новый Южный Уэльс принял закон, позволяющий использовать тела умерших людей в качестве компоста. В этом регионе живёт около 30% населения страны, пишет The Sydney Morning Herald.

Законодателям штата ещё нужно время, чтобы привести различные нормативные акты в соответствие с новым законом, поэтому он вступит в силу только в 2028 году. Предполагается, что человек должен будет при жизни дать согласие на «компостирование» своего тела после смерти.

В ходе процесса компостирования тело будут помещать в специальный резервуар, заполненный органическим растительным материалом, например, сеном, опилками или люцерной. Температура в боксе будет постоянно повышаться для ускорения разложения. Получившийся компост упакуют в контейнер и передадут семье умершего. Родственники смогут использовать его для удобрения своей земли или передать какой-либо организации.

Это должно решить проблему нехватки территории, выделенной под кладбища, и растущих цен на похороны. В то же время некоторые члены парламента обеспокоены этической стороной закона, отмечая, что тело имеет ценность и является чем-то большем, чем совокупностью питательных веществ.
Подобные законы приняты в Германии и в 14 штатах США. В России и других странах мира такая практика запрещена.

items.title: Евгений Фатеев: Филипп Киркоров как выдающийся коллекционер
items.description: Вот если сегодня был бы жив Сергей Щукин, что бы он собирал? Напомню, в свое время, в аккурат дореволюционном и довоенном мире, он покупал самое радикальное и самое отмороженное европейское искусство. Именно благодаря ему (и еще Морозову) наши великие музеи, Э
items.author: Евгений Фатеев
paragraphs: Вот если сегодня был бы жив Сергей Щукин, что бы он собирал? Напомню, в свое время, в аккурат дореволюционном и довоенном мире, он покупал самое радикальное и самое отмороженное европейское искусство. Именно благодаря ему (и еще Морозову) наши великие музеи, Эрмитаж и ГМИИ, обладают исключительными коллекциями Матисса, Гогена, Пикассо, Сезанна и других импрессионистов и постимпрессионистов.

А что было бы сегодня? Что бы он коллекционировал сегодня? Вопрос абсолютно не праздный. Кстати, одно важное уточнение. Я имею в виду обладание предметным, физическим, офлайновым, таким, которое можно потрогать руками, искусством. Так вот, что такое актуальное, на самом нерве и острие, можно собирать сегодня? Худосочный, выродившийся и мгновенно уже устаревший и обратившийся (буквально) в мусор contemporary art? Я бы не советовал. Я понимаю, что сейчас вокруг этого откровенного надувательства наплодили кучу смешных и пошлых паразитов (дилеров, интерпретаторов, кураторов), которые пытаются развести дубоватых наших и не наших нуворишей, которые страстно желают «шоб как у людей», но даже эти несчастные счастливцы на ниве облапошивания своих сограждан тоже пообтесались и начали о чем-то таком подозревать.

Уверен, Щукин на эту дешевку не купился бы. Вообще вся эта постмодернистская муть, архаика и хтонь отвратила бы его. Он был человеком витальным, жизнелюбивым, гимновым даже, любопытным, интересующимся. А коллекционировал бы он, пожалуй, самое актуальное сегодня материальное искусство – консюмер-арт, искусство на консюмеристской платформе, искусство потребления искусства. В наше время вещный дизайн, потребительские фреймы, чудеса и находки маркетинга – это тоже и прежде всего искусство, которое сразу же котируется, обладает особенной историей – историей волатильности, плавания капитализации, кардиограммой востребованности.

Да, это искусство требует совсем по-другому звучащей истории искусства и даже искусствоведения, но такое обязательно появится, и далеко не обязательно, что оно будет создано людьми. Однако же именно это как раз и есть самое актуальное искусство. Уверен, Щукин покупал бы шкодные вещные дропы и кейсы, как эдакие дропы-перформансы, от MSCHF. Он покупал бы серии меченной «искусством» вещности вроде Bearbrick. Он бы. Благодаря своим ресурсам, проживал бы хайповые волны, по сути играл в малое или средних размеров инвестирование в вещное. Он играл бы в квестовое потребление серий и целостных коллекций. Он бы уже проживал собственное коллекционирование как вторую жизнь, фиксируя это проживание в медиа. Он был бы немного мета, над, за, но одновременно и внутри, понимая игровую природу всего этого.

В итоге кто же сегодня один из актуальнейших и действительно находящихся на острие российских коллекционеров? Нужно признать, что это Филипп Киркоров. Из-за его чрезвычайной медийности даже широкая публика в общих чертах имеет представление о характере его коллекции. И это по-настоящему крутое и очень ценное (не только в монетарном смысле) собрание, которое совершенно точно не является памятником эксцентричности знаменитого поп-исполнителя, или его отражением его частного вкуса.

Это в самом подлинном смысле коллекция, слепок, и драгоценная шкатулка, полная вещных грез последних людей, последних старых людей, последнего человечества. Эта коллекция – памятник тому последнему человечьему, что еще заслуживает овеществления. Это коллекция, которая фиксирует то вещное ожирение и ту вещную избыточность, - словом, то вещное барокко, которое уже скоро сядет на фитнесс и диету новой, нейро-, тотально цифровой эпохи. Эта коллекция – свидетельство ускорения пульса вещного мира, порождаемого последним человечеством.

Эта коллекция – собрание последних вещей последних людей, вещей, еще как обязательных к прочтению и пониманию, достойных усилия и работы, экономики и политэкономии памяти. Это собственно последние музейные, заслуживающие музеефикации и в принципе музеефицируемые вещи. Это те вещи, которых скоро больше не будет. Им на смену придут слепки и вариации вещной возможности. Мы уже живем в градиенте перехода к жизни в мире необязательных, ненадежных, не совсем настоящих вещей. Будут и уже появляются ситуативные вещи, вещный спам, вещная предельная кастомизация и индивидуализация.персонализация (здравствуй, грядущее индивидуальное искусство!).

Вещность станет флюидной, текучей, обратимой, поправимой. Вещный мир перестанет нуждаться в музейном нотариате, удостоверении подлинности, реальности и даже настоящести. Пожалуй, более или менее музеефицированными будут вещи-реликвии. Но опять же чьи именно? Трудная судьба ждет вещи-ошибки, вещи-фейлы. «Ошибки» сотрутся в мистерии кастомного и индивидуального искусства. Современный мир не даст саму ошибку на откуп Судьбы, случайности, провидения. Поэтому спектакль ошибки будет не совсем настоящим. Коллекция Киркорова – фиксация и овеществление того прощального всплеска света, который испускают стразы, украшающие уходящий мир старых вещей.

За коллекцией Киркорова наши музеи просто обязаны гоняться. На месте эрмитажников я бы методично и настойчиво обхаживал бы артиста, уговаривая его передать свою коллекцию в это великое музейное собрание. А теперь главный вопрос – достойна эта коллекция Эрмитажа? Ответ определенный и однозначный - безусловно да!
