This is rare in Florida. “What it usually is,” he says, “is you show up, you go to the rally, they get your information, and then they ask you, like, a day or two later, ‘Can you come back and canvass with us?’ And the difference is, because Angie’s an organizer, she knows that every little hurdle you add in front of someone doing something makes it less likely that they’ll actually volunteer.” Instead, Frost says, people show up to her events as spectators and leave as door-knockers.

Nixon is convinced some Democrats don’t want her in D.C. because they’re lazy. “I would force them to do more work,” she told The Breakfast Club in September. She’s known in Duval County for her hands-on approach to constituent services. Brandon Davis, her senior adviser and media consultant, remembers her once taking time between campaign stops to help someone whose apartment ceiling had collapsed and who couldn’t get a response from their building-management company. Nixon wants to scale this approach if she’s elected, deploying aides across the state for weekly listening sessions and personally hosting town halls in a different part of Florida every month. “We’re going to have community office hours where we go to libraries and coffee shops and small businesses and welcome people to come talk to us about different issues,” she says.

Even Nixon’s opponents have admitted she is uniquely industrious. “Angie was working 24/7,” says Mitchell Berger, the donor, who backed Vindman in the primary. “Not that Alex wasn’t working, but there is something to knocking on doors and showing up at community events as opposed to just working the phones for money and showing up at financial events.”

Nixon’s strong ground game helped make up for an astonishing spending gap. In July, Nixon had a little less than $975,000 on hand. Moody had $11 million, which she has used to fund ads falsely accusing Nixon of being a socialist who wants to abolish the police and prisons. (Nixon’s retort is that she doesn’t want to abolish prisons, she wants to put Moody in one.) This ability to define the opposition is key: A Stetson University poll in September found that 32 percent of Floridians surveyed — close to one-third — still don’t know who Nixon is, compared with just 19 percent for Moody. “Nixon’s not getting anywhere near the resources to run a statewide race,” Susan MacManus, a veteran political analyst who has taught at the University of South Florida, said earlier this year.

That Nixon offset her disadvantages enough to be even slightly competitive with Moody holds lessons for her fellow Democrats — including her skeptics. In the primary, she showed that she could win with less by outworking an Establishment-favored opponent and leveraging relationships unconnected to party leadership. In the general election, she is proving she has the force of personality to bring national attention, and even national money, to a campaign that donors and strategists were inclined to write off. Nixon’s most recent FEC report indicated that she pulled in close to $7.2 million. (Moody, who raised just $1.8 million in the same period, still has a roughly $5 million advantage.) She accomplished it by prodding moderates and galvanizing progressives. Ro Khanna is planning to campaign for Nixon in Florida later this month. Sanders, Chris Murphy, and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez have already done so. Most important, the base has bought in, undeterred by Florida’s red hue.

The last time Democratic voters in Florida were this excited was in 2018. Like today, President Trump was on the defense, and the national spotlight was on a statewide race: the gubernatorial campaign of Andrew Gillum, then the mayor of Tallahassee.

Gillum is an obvious template for Nixon; Davis, her adviser, was Gillum’s campaign manager. Both are Black multigenerational Floridians to the left of their party with a talent for public speaking. Both had a similar projected path to statewide victory: overperforming in Jacksonville and the panhandle while running up the score around college areas in Tallahassee and Gainesville and banking on kitchen-table appeals attracting more South Florida voters than the GOP’s red-baiting scared away. And both share a maximalist campaign philosophy. “Just making sure we go everywhere,” Nixon says. “Making sure we have an aggressive 67-county strategy. Making sure I spend every dollar that I have.” Gillum lost to DeSantis by one of the slimmest margins in Florida gubernatorial history — a 0.4-point, 33,000-vote defeat.

Eight years later, the Gillum moment has become easy to dismiss. After the election, he spiraled into depression and was found inebriated in a motel room with a male escort. He checked himself into rehab, reportedly got sober, and launched a somewhat successful podcast. Then, in July, he was arrested on meth charges in Alabama. The fortunes of Florida Democrats have followed a parallel trajectory. After 2018, they fell into a now familiar pattern, running moderate statewide candidates like Val Demings and Debbie Mucarsel-Powell — and getting clobbered. The party hemorrhaged talent as the people and money that had coalesced around Gillum 2018 disappeared. By 2024, the idea that Kamala Harris could compete in Florida was never seriously considered.

How did things get so bad so quickly? It’s conceivable that a strong state party could run back the Gillum playbook with more success and assimilate internal disagreement without things spilling over. But the reality is that Nixon has had to build most of her own campaign infrastructure because it did not exist. Steve Schale, the longtime strategist who directed Obama’s victorious statewide operation in 2008, scoffs at the idea that Florida’s Democratic Establishment was aligned against Nixon — that would imply some meaningful measure of organization and influence by the party. “You wield power with sticks and carrots, right?” he says. “What happens when you have no sticks and you have no carrots?”

The ability of a state party to exert influence depends entirely on the scope of its electoral power. And Florida Democrats don’t have a senator, a governor, or any statewide officials. Their most influential figure in the House of Representatives is Debbie Wasserman Schultz, who is probably better known for being ousted as chair of the Democratic National Committee months before Hillary Clinton fumbled Florida in 2016. Democrats are a superminority in the state legislature, which is part of the reason Nixon’s weapon of choice has been the bullhorn rather than the backroom deal. The fact that the state party is carrying $6,000 in debt instead of the more than $800,000 deficit it was running in 2020 is arguably its biggest success story of the past ten years. Without electoral power, the board that votes on how the party should proceed is “just a whole bunch of people with opinions,” Schale says. It couldn’t tip the scales of a primary if it wanted to.

Another problem is that, for Florida Democrats, the people and institutions planning, funding, and running elections are extremely transient. “The only partisan infrastructure that’s ever existed here is whatever got built around whatever presidential election was happening at that point,” says Schale. “The other 42 months of that four-year cycle, the party can barely keep the lights on.” Diminishing returns — the last statewide office Democrats won was when Fried was elected commissioner of agriculture in 2018 — has put the party in a kind of death spiral. “I will be 25 years old in less than a month,” says Jackson McMillan, a Tampa-based Democratic strategist who runs a firm called Key Lime Strategies. “And I am considered a veteran strategist here in the state of Florida because I’ve been doing this for, like, eight years.” That’s how you get a campaign like Vindman’s, much of whose staff was chosen and imported by the Washington-based DSCC. The problem is compounded for progressives like Nixon because they have access to so much less money. “The president of Florida’s progressive caucus,” says McMillan, “works multiple jobs and lives with roommates.”

Fried is the eighth FDP chair since 2010 and — at nearly four years into the job — has one of the longest tenures of this century. “We have to acknowledge first and foremost that that job sucks,” says McMillan; you spend a lot of time getting yelled at by activists who think you can do more than you can. People I spoke with credit Fried for being the most productive chair in a long time. From September to October, Democrats outpaced Republicans in month-over-month party registration for the first time in five years. But at this point in the election cycle, that’s like playing catch-up on a hamster wheel. I ask Nixon how this race might look different if the FDP were not “dysfunctional,” as she says. “They would be registering a shit ton of voters and running commercials attacking Ashley Moody left and right, like the Republican Party does,” she says. “My campaign shouldn’t be going negative. I should just be speaking affirmatively about my policies.”

Some of these challenges might be surmountable in a less complicated state. But winning a statewide campaign in Florida is like assembling a “jigsaw puzzle,” says MacManus, the professor and political analyst. It’s the nation’s third most populous and racially diverse state, and within its ethnic blocs are idiosyncrasies that render terms like “the Black vote” (Haitian immigrants or the descendants of sharecroppers?) and “the Hispanic vote” (Mexican Democrats or

items.title: Trump Loyalists Wage ‘Blood Feud’ Over Missing Millions
items.description: In the span of a little more than a week, the Trump administration fired Kimberly Guilfoyle as ambassador to Greece over an alleged pay-to-play scheme, scrapped Pete Hegseth’s plan to livestream an execution, and introduced new press secretary Katia Zacharia b
items.author: Bess Levin
paragraphs: In the span of a little more than a week, the Trump administration fired Kimberly Guilfoyle as ambassador to Greece over an alleged pay-to-play scheme, scrapped Pete Hegseth’s plan to livestream an execution, and introduced new press secretary Katia Zacharia before showing her the door just five days later. With all that going on, you might not have noticed another unfolding Trumpworld scandal or thought it was even possible for a fourth shitshow to simultaneously be occurring. But it is, and it’s a classic, in that it involves two Trump loyalists accusing each other of wrongdoing, an alleged promise of pay-for-access, $17 million that supposedly went missing, and a 29-year-old who claims to be a billionaire but might not actually be either.
The parties: Richard Grenell, Alina Habba Mildon, and Habba Mildon’s new husband

Grenell is Donald Trump’s presidential envoy for special missions. He previously served as U.S. ambassador to Germany, acting director of National Intelligence, and interim director of the Kennedy Center. In another lifetime, he was a foreign-policy advisor to Mitt Romney’s 2012 presidential campaign, and in 2020 he was described by top Obama adviser Susan Rice as “one of the most nasty, dishonest people I’ve ever encountered.”

Alina Habba Mildon joined Trump’s legal team during his first administration, replacing a longtime litigator who had quit. (Per the Washington Post, her previous experience included “being general counsel for a parking garage company.” She also represented a cast member of The Real Housewives of New Jersey in a dispute with Facebook.) In 2024, a judge threatened to send her to jail during the E. Jean Carroll defamation trial. In 2025, she was disqualified from serving as acting U.S. attorney for the District of New Jersey.

Turhan Mildon is a Turkish businessman who Habba met in 2025, and they were married at the Waldorf Astoria last month. (Nelly performed.) According to the New York Times, Mildon “portrays himself as a billionaire,” the suggestion being that he may not actually be one. He has a cement business in Venezuela and “told Forbes Turkey that he produces 4.5 million tons of cement a year” there, though “data seen by the Times shows that Venezuela’s entire annual cement output is about a third of that figure.” The Times also raised questions about Mildon’s comments about his shrimp business; a spokesman for Mildon told the paper he was misquoted by Forbes. And while Mildon says he’s 29, U.S. and British documents list him as 25, per the Times. Mildon and Grenell reportedly first met in late 2024.
The claim: Missing millions that were earmarked for the Kennedy Center

Last Friday, the new Mrs. Mildon, who “has maintained a close relationship with the president,” according to the Times, “stormed into the Oval Office intent on taking down” Grenell. There, according to Axios, she alleged that at Grenell’s urging, her husband wired $17.6 million to a defense company called Texas Armament & Technology, explaining that part of the money would go to a contract with the Democratic Republic of Congo involving software and $5.6 million would go to the Kennedy Center.

Habba Mildon told Trump that she recently learned that the money never made it to the Kennedy Center. Grenell also allegedly sent a text to Mildon promising access to “POTUS,” “VIP events” and Trump officials, according to a text message. “Once the money comes to the company here, I will arrange the donation to Kennedy Centre [sic], and you’ll be joining the VIP events and get close with the administration, even with POTUS,” the text from May 3, 2025, reportedly reads.

Though the wire transfer allegedly occurred some time ago, “Mildon never checked to see if it was deposited” because “he believed it had been credited because he was treated like a VIP donor at the Kennedy Center,” according to Axios.
What Grenell has said about the claims

Speaking to Axios, Grenell called Habba Mildon’s claims “absurd,” adding: “I’ve never asked for one cent to be sent somewhere else pretending it was for the Kennedy Center, and I’ve never received any payment from him at all. Make him give proof to what he is saying, not make these absurd allegations.”
The proof, according to the couple
A lawyer for the Mildons sent the White House a “2025 text that discussed the Kennedy Center donation and Congo ‘software,’” according to Axios.

In the text to Mildon, the sender also says, “There is an e-mail that was sent to you, can you please take a look at it for me ?” That email also was furnished to the White House, as was a May 29, 2025, financial record showing $17.6 million was wired to the company, known by its initials TXAT, sources said.
The weird bits that don’t make any sense

There are many! For starters, while Habba Mildon initially indicated the $17.6 million originated in her husband’s bank account, it actually “was wired to TXAT from Congo’s “Ministère des Finances” in Kinshasa, the capital city, where Mildon has business and access to finances according to a White House official who spoke to Axios. (A spokesman for Mildon declined the site’s request for comment, while representatives for TXAT and the Congolese government could not be reached.)
Meanwhile, Habba Mildon is said to have initially claimed that the full $17.6 million was supposed to go to the Kennedy Center but then said it was $6 million.

Lisa Dale, who was in charge of the Kennedy Center’s finances at the time, told the site that while there was a record showing an outstanding donation of $270,000 from Mildon, “There was nothing about $6 million. I would have heard about that.”
What the White House is saying

One administration official told Axios that “POTUS doesn’t want to deal with this,” but “if there is missing money, this is a big, big problem.” (The White House’s general counsel has reportedly launched an investigation.) Another official noted “these are only allegations,” while a Trumpworld insider summed up the drama: “This is the ultimate MAGA blood feud.”

items.title: Polls Show a Blue Wave Downballot, Too
items.description: Even in an era of increasing partisan polarization and straight-ticket voting, state elections have their own logic and rhythm, in part because salient issues at the state level can be different from those prevailing nationally and also because some state pols
items.author: Ed Kilgore
paragraphs: Even in an era of increasing partisan polarization and straight-ticket voting, state elections have their own logic and rhythm, in part because salient issues at the state level can be different from those prevailing nationally and also because some state pols — notably governors — are news-commanding celebrities in their own right. But the national political environment still affects downballot elections if only by affecting turnout patterns. So Democrats anticipate at least modest gains in the 36 gubernatorial elections being held this year and in the 88 state legislative chambers with some or all of their members facing voters in November.

Exactly half of those 36 gubernatorial elections are for positions currently held by each party, though incumbents (nine Democrats and eight Republicans) are running in only 17 of them, thanks to voluntary retirements and term limits. The Cook Political Report currently rates 12 races as competitive with five leaning Democratic (Alaska, Arizona, Iowa, Michigan, and Oregon), three leaning Republican (Florida, Kansas, and Texas), and four toss-ups (Georgia, Nevada, Ohio, and Wisconsin). If the “leaners” go the way they are leaning, Democrats would net one additional governorship (picking up Alaska and Iowa but losing Kansas). A Democratic sweep of the toss-up races would net three more (Georgia, Nevada, and Ohio). That’s impressive in no small part because 11 of the 12 competitive races (all but Oregon’s) are in states carried by Donald Trump in 2024.

Polling of the gubernatorial races reinforces most of Cook’s analysis. Using the Silver Bulletin polling averages, Democrats have robust leads in four of the five Lean D races. In Alaska, a complicated race because of that state’s top-four primary system with ranked-choice voting in the general election, Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins has 45.6 percent to Republican Bernadette Wilson’s 23.6 percent and Republican Dave Bronson’s 15.7 percent. (Another Democrat who qualified for the general election dropped out.) In Arizona, incumbent Democrat Katie Hobbs leads Republican Andy Biggs by 9.1 percent. In Iowa, Democrat Rob Sand leads Republican Zach Lahn by 7.3 percent. And in Michigan, Democrat Jocelyn Benson leads Republican John James by 8 percent. The closest race of the batch is actually in deep-blue Oregon, where incumbent Democrat Tina Kotek has a 1.6 percent lead over Republican Christine Drazan.

All of the Republican-leaning races, however, are relatively close. In Florida, Republican Byron Donalds was expected to win easily against Democrat David Jolly but leads by only 4.4 percent. So too was Texas incumbent Republican Greg Abbott, but he leads Democrat Gina Hinojosa by just 2.4 percent. Aside from Oregon, the best chance for a GOP flip is in deep-red Kansas, where Republican Ty Masterson leads Democrat Cindy Holscher by 4.3 percent for the office being vacated by term-limited Democrat Laura Kelly.

The four toss-up gubernatorial races are predictably tight, per the Silver Bulletin polling averages. In Georgia, billionaire Republican Rick Jackson leads Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms by one percent. In Nevada, Republican incumbent Joe Lombardo leads Democrat Aaron Ford by 0.8 percent. But in Ohio, Democrat Amy Acton is leading heavily financed Republican Vivek Ramaswamy by 4.4 percent, and in Wisconsin, upset primary-winning Democrat Michael Crowley leads Republican Tom Tiffany by 3.6 percent.

Two other gubernatorial races where the GOP is favored (rated as “likely Republican” by Cook) bear watching for a possible upset. In Nebraska, incumbent Republican Jim Pillen has a relatively narrow 4.4 percent lead over Democrat Lynne Walz, while in Vermont, five-term maverick Republican incumbent Phil Scott has a surprisingly small 2.2 percent lead over Democrat Amanda Janoo.

Let’s say a big blue wave hits gubernatorial races and Democrats win all the competitive contests plus the two “upset specials.” In that unlikely but theoretically possible event, they’d net nine new governorships and hold 33 of 50 overall.

Control of state legislative chambers is harder to predict given the complexities of each state’s elections and sparse relevant public polling. But according to estimates from Larry Sabato’s Crystal Ball, 15 state legislative chambers are in play in November.

Democrats hope to flip the Arizona house and senate, the Georgia house, the Michigan house, the New Hampshire house and senate, the Pennsylania senate, and the Wisconsin assembly. Republicans hope to flip the Maine house, the Michigan senate, and the Minnesota senate. Both parties are battling to control the currently tied Minnesota house. Given the environment for both gubernatorial and legislative races, Democrats are hoping to bust up Republican “trifectas” in Florida, Georgia, Iowa, New Hampshire, Ohio, and Texas while building their own trifectas in Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, Pennsylvania, Vermont, and Wisconsin. Republicans hope to disrupt a Democratic trifecta in Maine and build their own in Kansas.

So once again, a blue wave could significantly reconfigure American politics at the state level (particularly with a new decennial redistricting cycle approaching in four years) as well as in Washington.
- Polls Show a Blue Wave, But Beware All the Close Races
- Trump’s Popularity Is Circling the Drain

items.title: The Knicks Turned New York Into a Party. Can They Keep It Going After an Opening Night Loss?
items.description: During last season’s NBA finals, as Knicks fever swept throughout every corner of New York and beyond, one fan made himself particularly known outside the team’s home arena. In the throng of diehards surrounding Madison Square Garden, he distinguished himself
items.author: Dan Adler
paragraphs: During last season’s NBA finals, as Knicks fever swept throughout every corner of New York and beyond, one fan made himself particularly known outside the team’s home arena. In the throng of diehards surrounding Madison Square Garden, he distinguished himself with a passing resemblance to Knicks superfan Spike Lee.

Come Tuesday night, though, “Sike Lee,” as he calls himself in person and on Instagram, seemed to be in a more measured mood as he returned to MSG for the first game of the Knicks’ title defense. Was he already resigned to losing this year—the inevitable comedown after the best party of your life?
“Hell yeah,” Lee said, predicting a playoff exit before his team could even make it to the finals. “Third round, we get bumped. Second round, that’s it.” (The Knicks lost by six points on Tuesday.)
“See what’s going on with football on the Giants, man.”

A few short months ago, New York transformed. There were makeshift projector screens all across the city, and fire escapes teemed with fans hanging on each play. As The City Reporter reported on Tuesday, a “Jalen” baby name boom is underway in homage to the Knicks’ leader (and recent Saturday Night Live host) Jalen Brunson.

But as sudden as the ascent was, the mood going into the new season has by some measures already soured. In a fast-moving league and city, there were new storylines to follow—LeBron James was in town for his first game as a Philadelphia 76er. The average ticket price for opening night, The New York Times reported on Tuesday, skyrocketed to $1,894, the highest ever for a regular-season NBA game, a sore spot after an outcry last season over longtime fans being priced out of the playoffs. Most of all, much-maligned Knicks owner James Dolan has resumed his media and fan punching-bag status after a passing period of goodwill yielded to contract disputes with key players.

Outside the arena on Tuesday, the crowd thrummed with anticipation. Off to the side, Meekie “Meek” Young, the proprietor of a mobile New York barber shop, had set up a table of hats bearing the Knicks’ name transliterated into Hindi, Arabic, Spanish, Greek, Japanese, Korean, Russian, and Chinese. “I am showing everybody the fabric of New York,” she said. Young saw the stakes of maintaining last year’s atmosphere as high: “A lot of people are lonely and this will allow people to find community.”

“This some AI shit,” one passerby remarked as she passed a Kalshi-branded robot swarmed by content creators. The prediction market has made a significant push into professional sports, and Kalshi mics became a staple of the MSG scene. (“My mayor is Muslim, my bagel is Jewish, my Christian is Dior, Knicks in four,” was uttered into one.) There was now a Kalshi Concourse in the arena, and outside, a content creator wearing a Kalshi tee led a prayer circle before tip-off on Tuesday.

“You just pray with positivity and go step by step,” Tubbycfa, who identified himself by his Instagram handle, said afterwards. “We’re defending champions, everybody can come after us as hard as they can. And guess what? Don’t matter.”

Complaining about New York is one of the great New York traditions, and a pessimistic view may already be taking shape in the eyes of the most cynical fans: a series of Dolan-connected mishaps and a fan atmosphere increasingly dominated by absurd ticket prices alongside inescapable gambling, crypto, and prediction market branding. Like so many bleeding-edge New York bars and restaurants, this phenomenon could always fall away as soon as it was beloved enough to be missed.
Still, as one observer walked past the raucous prayer circle, she noted one aspect of the Knicks experience that could never be taken.
“They don’t do this in Philly.”

items.title: As Art Basel Paris Beckons, Vanity Fair and Four Seasons Convene Two Star Artists
items.description: Art Basel Paris opens this week at the Grand Palais, with 211 galleries filling the massive palace on the Champs-Élysées. At the heart of the fair—beyond the endless dinners and parties, the satellite fairs and local gallery openings, the big-ticket blue-chip
items.author: Nate Freeman
paragraphs: Art Basel Paris opens this week at the Grand Palais, with 211 galleries filling the massive palace on the Champs-Élysées. At the heart of the fair—beyond the endless dinners and parties, the satellite fairs and local gallery openings, the big-ticket blue-chip sales, the fashion crossovers and celeb sightings—are the hundreds of artists behind the work on view and on sale. More than anyone else in Paris, the artists make Art Basel run.

And so, on the first night of a jam-packed week, Vanity Fair teamed up with Four Seasons to throw a party at the Hotel George V, celebrating Camille Henrot and Alvaro Barrington—who are both having huge years. Each has been showing in museums on different continents, with work in the most important art surveys on the globe.

Henrot currently has a new film on view at LUMA Arles, In the Veins, which previously appeared at the New Museum’s inaugural show in its reimagined campus on the Bowery. Barrington currently has one of the most talked-about installations at the Venice Biennale; in November, his Western Beef-High Line will open, where else, on the High Line in New York City.
The two had never met until I convened a conversation between them Monday night at the hotel’s Louis XIII salon, away from the city’s bustling gallery openings.

“What I like about you is you’re ambitious. I want to hear more about what you’re up to,” Barrington said to Henrot in the middle of a wide-ranging conversation about what it’s like to make art in 2026.

Henrot spoke about the process of making her first play, Commedia dell’arte—which premiered in Aspen over the summer before a run in New York—and revealed that she’d like for it to come to Paris. Barrington talked about his standout installation at this year’s Venice Biennale, Labor Day Parade ’91, and how it was born out of a desire to transcend the way art communicates.

As the talk wound down, the party outside the Louis XIII was in full swing. Barrington and Henrot soon joined a crowd snacking on salmon blini and caviar and sipping endless flutes of Champagne. (Every party this week has Champagne; we’re in Paris, of course.) The soiree also featured full-on cocktails. While planning the conversation, I got to talking with Thibault Mequignon, chef de bar at the hotel, about a special themed menu for the bar. We came up with four drinks themed loosely around a diaspora of artists and writers who fled the States—not New York, but smaller American cities—for Paris: a vodka martini inspired by Kenneth Noland, born in Asheville; a rye whiskey long drink inspired by Cy Twombly, born in Lexington, Virginia.

Even amid the swirl of events Monday—including openings at neighborhood galleries such as Gagosian, Skarstedt, White Cube, and Hauser & Wirth—those who came for the conversation stayed for the cocktails after. The guest list included collectors James and Kathryn Murdoch; Karen and Christian Boros; Richard Chang; Komal Shah; and Patrizia Sandretto Re Rebaudengo, along with Eugenio Re Rebaudengo. Artists Claudia Comte, Matt Copson, and Kennedy Yanko were on hand to hear Barrington and Henrot. Art dealers showing in Art Basel and elsewhere this week were out in full force: I spotted Olivia Barrett of LA’s Château Shatto; Mike Egan of New York’s Ramiken; Anton Kern; and Steve Henry and Simone Subal of Paula Cooper Gallery in New York. Morgan Aguiar-Lucander, founder of Morgan Presents in Chelsea, was there, as was his wife, Eva Foundation founder Ecaterina Aguiar-Lucander. Joel Wachs, the president of the Andy Warhol Foundation for the Visual Arts, took a seat in the front row.

While things officially ended at 9 p.m., many stayed to grab one last flute and a final blini well after the set closing time. After all, this is Paris; even with Art Basel opening the next day, for most, dinner wouldn’t start until well after 9:30.

This event is part of an ongoing global series of gatherings and industry conversations hosted by Four Seasons and Vanity Fair across key cultural moments. Spanning major milestones in film, art, and global culture, the series brings together creative leaders to celebrate storytelling, artistic expression, and the distinctive character of Four Seasons destinations worldwide.

items.title: Paul McCartney’s Wife Believes Queen Elizabeth “Fancied” Him. He Likes to Think It Was True
items.description: Paul McCartney met Queen Elizabeth II, who passed away on September 8, 2022, several times throughout his life, beginning with the queen’s first handshake with the Beatles in 1963. But years later, the former Fab Four member added an interesting detail to thos
items.author: Monica Coviello
paragraphs: Paul McCartney met Queen Elizabeth II, who passed away on September 8, 2022, several times throughout his life, beginning with the queen’s first handshake with the Beatles in 1963. But years later, the former Fab Four member added an interesting detail to those memories: According to his wife, Nancy Shevell, the queen had a crush on him.

During an appearance on Good Hang With Amy Poehler, McCartney, 84, answered a question about which famous person, among those he had met, had impressed him the most. “The queen,” he replied. “That’s an autograph you’re not going to get. She’s great. I love the queen.”

When Elizabeth ascended to the throne in 1952, McCartney was just 10 years old. On the day of her coronation, in the Speke neighborhood of Liverpool, families gathered in front of the television to watch the ceremony in black and white. At the same time, McCartney had entered a school essay contest on the monarchy, winning in his category. He would meet the monarch for the first time a little over 10 years later, when the Beatles were already on the road to success. “She was a babe,” he said. “So we kind of liked her in other ways we shouldn’t have liked her,” he recounted, joking about the admiration he and his peers felt for the young queen.

The story of the alleged crush is from the musician’s third wife, who, according to McCartney, told him, “She fancied you.” And he replied, “Now there’s no knowing if there’s any truth to that…but I like to think it’s true.”

McCartney has always remembered the late queen fondly, appreciating her sense of humor above all else. In 1997, when he already had a legendary career behind him, he was knighted by the queen, becoming Sir Paul McCartney. They also met in 1996, at the opening of the Liverpool Institute for Performing Arts, and in 2002, for the queen’s Golden Jubilee, during which McCartney performed alongside other international music stars.

Their last meeting took place in 2018, when McCartney was awarded the title of Companion of Honour. After the queen’s death, the singer recounted the episode on his official website, recalling that he had met her eight or nine times and had been struck each time by the combination of her great sense of humor and her extraordinary composure. “Our last meeting came in 2018. Because of my respect and love for the queen and her fabulous sense of humor, when I was given the Companion of Honour medal I shook her hand, leaned in, and said, ‘We have got to stop meeting like this,’ to which she giggled slightly and got on with the ceremony. I did wonder if I was a bit too cheeky after saying this, after all this was the queen, but I have a feeling she didn’t mind.”
Originally published in Vanity Fair France.

items.title: The Untold Story of Fred Astaire’s Soulmate, Choreographer Hermes Pan
items.description: Glimmery and lavish, racy and absurd in their extravagant Art Deco sumptuousness, the movie musicals that Fred Astaire and Ginger Rogers made for the RKO studio—nine in total, from Top Hat, Swing Time, and The Gay Divorcee, all hits of the Depression era, to T
items.author: David Hajdu
paragraphs: Glimmery and lavish, racy and absurd in their extravagant Art Deco sumptuousness, the movie musicals that Fred Astaire and Ginger Rogers made for the RKO studio—nine in total, from Top Hat, Swing Time, and The Gay Divorcee, all hits of the Depression era, to The Story of Vernon and Irene Castle, made in the last year of 1930s (and not counting the one-shot reunion, The Barkleys of Broadway, produced at MGM in 1949)—were gleeful escapism and something more. They were giddily cogent acts of ideological persuasion—dream visions of capitalism not in crisis, but in perverse triumph through the imagination.

"It's fascinating that at a time of economic catastrophe, America fell in love with these movies about the lives of the very, very, very rich," notes the historian Daniel Okrent, author of Last Call, a narrative history of the Prohibition era. "Audiences identified with Astaire as he went to the Rainbow Room or flew off to Venice. Instead of stirring resentment or scorn, the films inspired people. There was a dream aspect to them." Populated almost entirely by impossibly wealthy characters reveling in penthouse splendor, the Astaire-Rogers movies argued with high style against the proposition that the material and social rewards of wealth were dubious. Fred, Ginger, and the friends and lovers they frolicked with in ballrooms, ocean liners, and French resorts embodied high living as an aspirational ideal—irrational but great fun for 80 minutes.

"Everyone was spectacularly dressed in ermine and silk, and the sets were so magnificent they couldn't exist anywhere except in the fantasies of Thirties Hollywood, and the public flocked to these movies, because they were wish-fulfillment," said Robert Osborne, a longtime host on Turner Classic Movies. “Fred Astaire and Ginger Rogers danced America out of the Depression, at least in America's mind."
They had a third partner, one unseen.

In the 21st century, few people outside of show-business circles still know about the essential role of Astaire's behind-the-scenes collaborator, Hermes Pan. Astaire, whom generations of fans, critics, and dancers (including the ballet master Mikhail Baryshnikov) have recognized as peerless, called Pan "the only person I ever saw who could dance like I could." Pan is most significant, however, not as a performer or a technician, but as a creative spirit, an originator or co-creator of some of the most inventive and influential dances ever put to film, including the Astaire-Rogers numbers—and also Astaire's famous duet with a hat rack (Royal Wedding), his dance with his own shadows (the "Bojangles of Harlem" number from Swing Time), and his ensemble routine with disembodied flying shoes (The Barkleys of Broadway).

As Astaire once explained in an interview, "It's the ideas that are the hardest to get—I mean, getting steps in another thing." Astaire called Pan his "ideas man." Away from Astaire, moreover, Pan happened to be the choreographer on dozens of films including Porgy and Bess, Flower Drum Song, Pal Joey, Kiss Me, Kate, and My Fair Lady. There were Academy Awards for dance direction for only three years, from 1935 to 1937, and Pan was the only choreographer nominated all three times; he won, in '37, for Damsel in Distress, a musical Astaire made at RKO without Ginger Rogers.

Pan was "Fred's alter ego, and he could do everything Fred could do, and he did something which was wonderful, [and that] was come up with the creative things and keep Fred going—that was Hermes," recalled the dancer and actor Marge Champion, who performed on screen with Astaire and Rogers, dancing Pan's choreography in The Story of Vernon and Irene Castle. "It was impossible to know where Hermes left off or Fred left off and the other took over, as far as the choreography. Fred was Hermes, and Hermes was Fred." On the set, Champion once saw one of them, Astaire or Pan, strolling, and, from the back, she couldn't tell which man she was looking at. "Their walk, the posture, was identical—everything about them. To this day, I don't know which one of them that was."

As Audrey Hepburn once remarked in an interview about her experience in the musical Funny Face, "I met [Astaire] when I got to Paramount, on the big, big stage, where there was just a piano and a darling choreographer named Hermes Pan. Hermes was terribly like Fred; it's unbelievable how much of Fred rubbed off on Hermes, and perhaps of Hermes on Fred."

Much the same, the late screenwriter Leonard Gershe, who wrote the scripts to Funny Face and Silk Stockings, told an interviewer, "No one must ever minimize the contribution of Hermes Pan to the legend that is Fred Astaire. Fred rarely worked without Hermes. They were together forever. Both of them were very modest, shy people, so nobody ever said who did what."

Both Astaire and Pan were veterans of brother-and-sister acts—that is, both had begun as performers in sexless theatrical partnerships—and both were struggling when they set out to make careers of their own in the movies. Astaire had grown up on the stages of Broadway and London, working with his older and more celebrated sister, Adele, and he found himself alone when she married an English nobleman, Lord Charles Cavendish, and she moved into his place, Linsmore Castle, retiring from performing. Fred, widely considered the junior and lesser member of the family act, hardly seemed movie material. Indeed, he and Adele had once submitted to a screen test for Paramount Studios but were rejected as unsuitable for film—the specifics are unknown—and Astaire's later test for RKO yielded a response that has (in various tellings) fallen into pop-culture legend: "Can't act. Slightly bald. Also dances."

Pan, born Hermes Panagiotopoulos in 1910, had a privileged early life in Nashville and Memphis as one of three offspring of a Greek consul. He and his older sister Vasso had learned to dance from one of the family's Black maids, and they turned to dancing, the one thing they knew how to do, when their father died suddenly and they needed to work. (According to family lore, a "crazy uncle" held their mother at gunpoint and burned her late husband's stock certificates in rage over being cut out of his will.) Hermes, 13 and educated only to the eighth grade, moved to New York with his mother, his sister, and their young brother, and he and Vasso sang and danced for change in speakeasies. Within a few years, Pan began to drift from performing to choreography, despite his pleasant looks and bright personality, because "that's where he got work, and he needed it bad," according to one of his nieces, Vasso's daughter Mary Ann Johnson.

Astaire and Pan came to Hollywood around the same time, and they met soon afterward, in 1933, on the set of the first movie in which Fred and Ginger were cast together, Flying Down to Rio. Rogers, a rising comic actress at RKO, was billed fourth, behind the one-time stars Dolores Del Rio, Gene Raymond, and Raul Roulien; Astaire, who had appeared briefly (as himself) in only one prior film (Dancing Lady, with Joan Crawford), was fifth in the acting credits. At the time, the Busby Berkeley conception of musical film as outlandish spectacle was the choreographic vogue. In fact, the films that Astaire and Pan choreographed for Astaire and Rogers transformed screen dance so completely that it is almost impossible now to process how different movie musicals were before they started partner-dancing together. Rows of look-alike chorines would position their limbs in formation to create enormous kaleidoscopic designs, functioning in precision like an all-blonde, semi-nude, female Marine troop. In Berkeley's films, the camera did the only dancing.

"When I arrived in Hollywood, it was during the Berkeley era, all of those geometrical designs, top shots and huge numbers," explained Pan to John Kobal, the film historian. "The curtain would go up on a small stage [on screen], and you'd go into a number that seemed to take place on a stage the size of a football field. This was something that was imaginative, but you actually didn't see much dancing on the screen. I think it's true to say that Astaire and Rogers were the first ones to really do a dance routine in its own right.
"I love dancing as such, and I always liked to see the more intimate dancing, a few people rather than a huge number where the dancing gets lost."

Working under a Berkeley acolyte, Dave Gould, Pan was assigned to choreograph Rio's preposterous finale, in which chorus girls do maneuvers on the wings of biplanes in flight. Pan obliged, leveraging the task to persuade Gould to let him do another number his way—a romantic variation of the ballroom style. "I made up another routine to show [Gould] my conception of a dance," Pan would recall, "which we used in the film and called it 'The Carioca.'" The number brought Astaire and Rogers together, dancing on screen for the first time. It initiated a revolution in screen dance and stirred a craze for ballroom dancing.

"Astaire, Rogers Start New Team Vogue," reported The Los Angeles Times in 1935. "The Hollywood scene changed overnight. It was the second step in the evolution of dance-on-film....Team dancing is in!" The revolution was an intimate one, grounded in a simple vision of heaven as a place for dancing cheek to cheek. As cultural historian Richard Barrios has said of the dances Astaire and Pan created for Fred and Ginger, "They [Astaire and Pan] were the ones who developed a new language in dance and in film."

It worked both to Pan's advantage and Astaire's benefit that Pan's "conception of a dance" was wholly compatible with Astaire's. "Fred and I thought alike," Pan said. "This is what I'd always dreamed a dancer should be. This was the sort of dancing I loved, and I think Fred recognized a kindred spirit in me."

Astaire, who disliked interviews in general and was especially reluctant to discuss his craft, was always vague but broadly flattering when asked about his method of working with Pan. "I thought he was a very talented young fellow," Astaire recalled in an unpublished interview for an oral-history project. "Hermes is—he's a very—I call him 'the rock.' You know, the kind of—he's a very fine gentleman to work with, you know....He was very, very helpful in every way."

When they worked in seclusion on their RKO films, the third person in the rehearsal studio was Hal Borne, the house pianist, who later described the sessions to one of Astaire's biographers, Bob Thomas. "Hermes' contribution was always great," Borne told Thomas. "Hermes was a very good dancer, also a singer. His rapport with Fred was sensational. Sometimes they'd walk around in circles, scratching heads. No one would talk and I wouldn't play. I just let them figure out what they were trying to figure out. Fred would say, 'Let's try this: You go over there and you'll be the Ginger part.' And he would start. It was hard to figure who contributed what to the choreography."

Pan himself explained, "[Astaire] would come in before Ginger would come in, and we'd work on things, and I would, often times, be Ginger. We would do the things together, you know, and when Ginger came in, I would show Ginger, because I knew her part.
"With Fred, I was Ginger, and with Ginger, I was Fred."

As Katharine Hepburn famously distilled the formula of Astaire and Rogers, "Fred gave Ginger class, and Rogers gave him sex [appeal]." Although his roles were ostensibly romantic leads, Astaire had an almost radically unorthodox appeal—one that, in its urbanity, cosmopolitanism, elegance, and grace, challenged the prevailing standards for male movie stardom. From the earliest days of his film career, fan magazines and movie columnists fixed on the unconventionality of Astaire's image. "It is Astaire's star—or is it a meteor—that now shines so brightly on Hollywood's celluloid horizon; so brightly that Freddie has stolen all fan mail honors at the RKO studios, by several hundred letters a week," gushed a writer for Picture Show magazine in 1933. "Most of the well wishers are sweet young things. This significant fact indicates to this writer that the affections of the fair fans seem to be switching from those big strong men who rescue them from all sorts of situations, to an esthetic young chap who can give them a dancing thrill. Astaire is the world's foremost exponent of that particular variety of heart throb!"

The following year, from The New Movie Magazine: "His personality caught on right away. No wonder! It's one of the most unusual personalities ever to hit Hollywood. Fred Astaire is Hollywood's first real cosmopolite, you see." And in 1935, from Harriet Parsons, the syndicated columnist, who...actually wrote...like this...in hiccups of ellipses: "He's a gay Lothario...with the accent on the gay...his enchanting nonchalance...and joy-in-life...are his chief charms..."

Parsons didn't mean gay gay…not exactly. In 1934, RKO released The Gay Divorcee, the Fred-and-Ginger adaptation of the Cole Porter musical that Fred and Adele had done on Broadway (originally The Gay Divorce, retitled so as not to imply that dissolving a marriage could be cause for joy), and the studio advertised the film with the slogan, "The nation's gone gay!" The term was then most commonly understood to mean merry, roguish, or carefree (a word that provided the title for another Astaire and Rogers movie); still, "gay" had begun to take on its contemporary meaning among homosexual men and women, and its use in the context of Fred Astaire's image always carried a tinge of the transgressive. "The male ideal in American movies until that time was, typically, tough and a little rough around the edges, probably a country boy, and he proved his worth with his bravery and strength, rather than grace or charm," explained Krin Gabbard, the film scholar. "Astaire was something completely different, and the mise-en-scene of those early Astaire-Rogers films, with their focus on high fashion and society, was thought of as very feminine or stereotypically gay."

These issues are separate from the matter of Astaire's own sexuality, of course. He was known to be straight. Astaire, like everyone else in show business, worked regularly with a great many gay men and women, and the fact of his close collaborative relationship with Hermes Pan tells us nothing in particular about either man's sexual identity. It's not Astaire's private behavior, nor even his public persona, solely, but the larger world of his films—especially the RKO pictures he made with Pan and Ginger Rogers during the Depression years—that is of a piece with certain Thirties-vintage ideas about the gay male sensibility, notions that reinforce stereotypes of effeteness while subverting them through droll parody.

Hermes Pan was an impish, self-effacing man, a much-loved social creature widely known to be homosexual but discreet about it, in the manner of his generation. He had many friends, most of them veteran show folk like Rita Hayworth, David Niven, Randolph Scott, Paulette Goddard, and Ann Miller—a mixed crowd, men and women, straight and gay. "I had the biggest crush on him," Miller once remembered, "then gradually found out he was gay."

Slim and soft-featured, Pan had what balding men like to think of a high forehead, which he, like Astaire, hid with jaunty hats. Most everything about Pan was jaunty—his bouncy gait, his bright eyes, his easy grin. He dressed smartly in cashmere jackets and silk shirts, and he lived in a sweet little cookie-jar house with beveled-glass windows, a homey place cocooned from the rest of Beverly Hills by virtue of high stone yard walls, which Pan topped with shards of broken glass because a robber had once broken in, bound him to a chair with his neckties, and stole a few things. "It didn't seem to faze him," said Mary Ann Johnson. "He wasn't hurt, and the ties weren't damaged."

Pan loved to entertain, cooking Italian meals with herbs he grew in his backyard. "He had wonderful parties with all kinds of food, and celebrities would come and go, and he took it all in stride," said Johnson.

Fond of travel but afraid to fly, Pan would take longish vacations in the Mediterranean, the Middle East, or Mexico, sometimes accompanied by his nieces. "He was far more worldly than my father," recalled Ava Astaire McKenzie, Fred's daughter, who moved in 1975 to County Cork, Ireland, with her husband, Richard McKenzie, a memoirist and painter. She came to Manhattan in June of 2009 to speak at the annual Fred and Adele Astaire Awards, given each year to screen and stage dancers and choreographers in the name of her father and her late aunt. A bubbly, kind-faced woman who seems to have inherited her father's poise and humility, Ava McKenzie had resisted doing interviews for years but was eager to talk about her father's close association with Pan. "Pan was very sophisticated, and that was one of the reasons he and my father were so compatible," she said. "Pan experienced the world through his travels, and my father learned from him."

On a trip to Mexico in 1943, Pan met Frida Kahlo and Diego Rivera, and he and Rivera became lifelong friends. "My uncle loved Mexico, and it was kind of a thing for Hollywood people to go down there," recalled Pan's niece, Michelene Laski, a painter herself. "He and Rivera became really close, because my uncle could engage him in conversations about art and abstract things that my uncle would tell me about—God, the nature of beauty, that kind of thing." In a cafe in Mexico City once in the mid-Fifties, Pan spurred Rivera into a debate that Pan believed to have led Rivera to change the most controversial element in one of his most scandalous works.

"Rivera told him, 'I don't believe in anything I can't see,'" Laski said, recalling her uncle's account. "And Hermes said to him, 'What about beauty? What about love? Can you touch beauty? Can you hold it in your hands?'" Some years earlier, Rivera had painted a mural for the Del Prado Hotel, and it depicted the Mexican writer Ignacio Ramirez Calzada holding a sign that read, "Dios no existe"—"God does not exist." Because of this inscription, the hotel had refused to show the mural. "Rivera and my uncle went back and forth and back and forth, and eventually Rivera said he saw that my uncle had a point, and he went back and painted over the inscription." Blocked from public view for nine years, the mural was finally displayed in 1957.

Around the same time, Rivera painted a full-body portrait of Pan dancing, and Pan hung the painting in the parlor of his house. "It was his prize possession," said Laski, "because he knew that Rivera was a man of very strong passions, and he only painted things he cared a lot about, and he cared a lot about my uncle."

Pan "was not impressed by the trappings of fame or power," according to another of his nieces, Christa Meade. Meanwhile, at least a few members of the powered classes seemed drawn to Pan, with his casual grace, dishy charm, and trunk of Hollywood stories. In the late 1940s, at a Hollywood function, he met a young woman from Iran, Ashraf Pahlavi, and they hit it off so well that she invited him to visit her and her twin brother, the Shah. "He went over there, and he didn't really know who they were," said Laski. "He was invited to visit at their house, so he went, and when he got there, there was this fantastic estate, like a castle." Pan returned nearly every year after that and stayed for a week or so each time.

"He would just go and be himself, and I think they just loved having him around, because everybody loved having him around," said Laski. "He was very cultured and always very down-to-earth at the same time. He was a very likable person, and he always made you feel like you were special, and he was also a special person, and he made you feel like you were likable." On a visit to Princes Pahlavi and the Shah in the early Sixties, Pan brought, as a house gift, the latest Beatles album.

In Hollywood, Pan was a celebrity among the dancers. "If there was a party, Hermes would be there, very charming—everybody would sit at his feet, and he would puff on a cigarette and sip on a glass of wine and make little witty comments," recalled Larri Hoy, who, as Larri Thomas, was a chorus girl in 1955 film of Guys and Dolls and performed with the Hermes Pan Dancers in the Fred Astaire television specials of the Sixties.

"You would meet him at a party, and he was very quiet but delightful, and he had this very sweet face, and he would look at you and smile, and you would say, 'I want to be his best friend,'" recalled the singer and dancer Lee Roy Reams. "Because Fred Astaire was Fred Astaire—you can't get more famous or more revered—Hermes never got the recognition that he deserved, at least not with the general public. But the people who knew him? They loved him, and dancers worshipped him."

No one probably knew Hermes Pan better than Fred Astaire, and no one was closer to Astaire than Pan, outside of Astaire's family. Astaire's daughter Ava said she grew up considering Pan "part of the family," her "favorite uncle"—the man most important to her father, both professionally and personally. "They were inseparable, and I don't mean just on the set," said Ava Astaire McKenzie. "Next to my mother, who also loved Pan very much, and he loved her—they used to garden together and cook—Pan was the best friend my father ever had," said McKenzie. "The leaned on each other. They went to movies together. They talked every day—oh, several times a day, sometimes, all hours of the day and night. It was more than a work association. It was the friendship of a lifetime."

Their friends and family conjure images of close pals sharing the quotidian pleasures meaningful only to them. Since Pan loved to cook and Astaire was not so domestic, Fred would come to Hermes' house, and Pan would make dinner for the two of them—something simple, like white-bean soup and fish, say. If Ava or one of Pan's niece dropped by, they might find the men eating on the patio or just sitting together, having after-dinner smokes. Both of them liked to scour the daily paper for odd bits of news, and they would call each other and read the stories over the phone. "They shared a sense of refinement. They didn't like vulgarity," said Michelene Laski. "But they both had a really keen sense of the absurd, and they loved to people-watch, and they were always laughing, and they loved to pull little practical jokes on each other."

One afternoon in the late Sixties, Pan and Astaire were at Hermes' place, puzzling over the counter-culture, which clearly ran counter to their conception of culture. Together, they hatched a plan to try the hippie experience, and they called a friend, a studio costumer, for help. Pan and Astaire decked themselves out in long wigs, caftans, round sunglasses, and love beads. They rolled down the top of Pan's convertible and drove up Hollywood Boulevard singing Beatles songs. When they found some real hippies gathered on the sidewalk, they got out and chatted them up. On the way back to Pan's, they stopped to see Ava. "I think they really wanted to see what the hippies were all about," she said. "so they went in disguise." What did they learn? "I don't know, but they sure had a good time!"

Astaire and Pan worked together often, though not exclusively with each other through the days of Astaire's final television specials. After their RKO years, Pan took a contract with Paramount, where he created dances for Rita Hayworth and Betty Grable, and Astaire went to MGM. Whenever possible, Astaire brought Pan onto his projects, if only for one showpiece number such as the "Shoes with Wings On." Always Astaire's ideas man, Pan relished the challenge of pushing Astaire to try new things. "Pan always says how precise Fred was about detail," the producer Samuel Goldwyn Jr. once said, "and Fred used to give Pan credit for being a very hard taskmaster."

For Silk Stockings, the romantic Cold War musical that Astaire made at MGM, for instance, Pan persuaded Astaire to try a tricky lift with Cyd Charisse. "If it hadn't been for Pan," Astaire said. "I don't think I ever would have done it. He said, 'Oh, you can do it, you can do it,' and he showed me kind of a way to do it. And I did it. I got her, and I was pleased. He always used to beat me down and get me to do something that I thought I couldn't do, which I was grateful for."

As Pan once explained to the author Sarah Giles, "He took my judgment a lot, but we'd disagree sometimes. I would suggest something, and he would say he didn't want to do it, and I would ask him to try it. When we were rehearsing Let's Dance [with Betty Hutton in 1950], I suggested to him that he step over the back of a chair, or three or four, as an exit. Fred said he wouldn't do it, that he would break a leg. I begged him to try it, and still he insisted he couldn't do it. I held his hand and he did it, and then he said, 'I told you I can't do it.'"

They did only once dance together, as a duo, on film: a stunningly bizarre number for Second Chorus, a musical Astaire made with Paulette Goddard for Paramount in 1940. In the picture, Astaire plays a big-band singer, and one of his numbers is a novelty swing tune called "Waiting for the Ghost Upstairs." After the vocal chorus, Astaire sees an apparition—Pan, costumed in Halloween drag. Pan's legs are bare; he is wearing high heels; a flowing outfit, essentially a sheet, covers his body; and he has a white shroud over his face. In heels, he is a bit taller than Astaire, and he seems, in that outfit, beefier. The two of them dance mostly side by side for a time, until the ghost, Pan, whispers something in Astaire's ear. Astaire rejects whatever he hears, shaking his head. The ghost whispers again. Astaire points to himself and then crosses his arms in front of him, as if to say, "Me? No chance!" The ghost bends a knee and clutches his hands, begging.

Astaire shrugs his shoulder, giving in, and he and the ghost begin a partner dance. At the climax of the number, Astaire does a lindy-hop swing to Pan's right side, then another swing to his left, and then he hops up and straddles Pan, wrapping his legs around Pan's torso. The number was cut from the film but survives on YouTube.
"You can see why it was cut," said Robert Osborne. "It was a distraction, it took you out of the story, and it was really strange."

When Fred Astaire died, at age eighty-eight in 1987, the only person at the burial who was neither a member of the family nor clergy was Hermes Pan, who followed Astaire's ghost upstairs three years later. "My father wanted him there," remembered Ava Astaire McKenzie. "My father always liked to have Pan there."

items.title: The Infamous Stringdusters Are Out to Prove That Bluegrass Is the New Rock & Roll
items.description: During any performance by the Infamous Stringdusters, fans can count on at least a few moments where the members of the jam-grass quintet gather near one another and transform into a melodic ball of kinetic energy. It’s a phenomenon that can only exist because
items.author: Garret K Woodward
paragraphs: During any performance by the Infamous Stringdusters, fans can count on at least a few moments where the members of the jam-grass quintet gather near one another and transform into a melodic ball of kinetic energy. It’s a phenomenon that can only exist because of the brotherhood the players have built over 20 years as a band.

“You can’t learn by yourself and you can’t learn in a practice room or in your bedroom,” Chris Pandolfi, banjo, tells Rolling Stone. “There’s only one way to learn, and that’s to get onstage and try stuff.”

Sitting backstage at the Bear Shadow Festival earlier this year in the Blue Ridge Mountains of Western North Carolina, Pandolfi is joined by Dusters guitarist Andy Falco. The rest of the ensemble, including fiddler Jeremy Garrett, dobroist Andy Hall, and standup bassist Travis Book, are tuning up and readying themselves for the gig. They look relaxed, and they are: They find their zen beneath the stage lights.

“Being in a band is like being in a time warp — one day you feel like you’ve been doing this forever, the next day it feels all brand new,” Pandolfi says. “For 20 years, we’ve truly given all of ourselves to this band, but it also feels like we have a lot more to do. And we just put out this new record that I feel is really the best iteration of the Dusters. It’s two sides of the coin.”

That new record, 20/20, is 20 songs for 20 years together. With titles like “Working Man Blues,” “Up From the Bottom,” “To the End of the Line,” and “Hard Times Ain’t That Hard Anymore,” you can draw a through-line from hardscrabble, hard-working origins to marquee success for the Grammy winners.
“Looking back now, what we went through, and seeing how hard it is for bands to get above the fray and make it,” Pandolfi says. “I’m just glad it all worked out for us the way that it did.
The Dusters are an outfit that’s never learned the word “stop.” They’ve been grinding it out on the road and putting in the time since forming in 2006.

“It’s not easy, it’s a sacrifice,” Falco says. “You have to love the people that you’re out on the road doing this with, and that comes from a high, mutual respect everybody has for each other in our group.”

Since their 2007 debut, Fork in the Road, the Dusters have put out an album pretty much every year. It’s an impressive catalog (there’s also four EPs and live releases), but it came about naturally thanks to five songwriters in the group, each with varied musical tastes: jazz-fusion to heavy metal, honky-tonk country to psychedelic rock. The band’s battle cry? “Bluegrass is the new rock & roll.”

“We have so much music to give and the evolution [of the band] is really what allows you to do it for all these years, and plan on continuing to do it for many more,” Falco says. “We’re allowing ourselves space to evolve as artists and together as people, as musicians, and as collaborators.”

“And that’s indicative of the fact that we’re always trying to push the envelope,” Pandolfi says. “Continuing to reinvent and become better as individuals, and as a band — that’s the energy that’s gotten us here, and that’s the energy that’s going to keep us going.”

Pandolfi, Hall, and founding member Chris Eldridge met as students at the Berklee College of Music in Boston. After graduation, Hall bolted for Nashville, the other two not far behind. It was there they crossed paths with Garrett, who had already been a professional musician for years, starting out in a family bluegrass band, the Greenhoppers, based in Garrett’s native Idaho. Mandolinist Jesse Cobb also joined (only to depart in 2011). Book was found through a 2005 band audition. By 2007, Eldridge would leave to join the Punch Brothers, so Pandolfi called Falco.

“I actually knew Falco before I knew any of these other guys, and we played in a band together. That’s just the way of the bluegrass community, there’s a lot of cross-pollination,” Pandolfi says. “One thing we had in common was that we wanted to be in our own band. It’s a challenge, but it also presents so much opportunity, in terms of being able to play your own music, be your own boss.”

Back in the early 2000s, when jam-grass was in its third wave, contemporaries like Yonder Mountain String Band, Steep Canyon Rangers, and Greensky Bluegrass were carrying the torch lit decades prior by Old & In the Way, New Grass Revival, and Hot Rize. The turn-of-the-century sonic landscape also included String Cheese Incident and Leftover Salmon, who both dominated the festival circuit, and continue to even today.

“We might have been ahead of the curve in recognizing the appeal of bluegrass, but we’re not alone in recognizing that,” Pandolfi says when asked about bluegrass reaching the arena level with artists like Billy Strings and Sierra Ferrell. “And that includes all those other bands and all those fans who are flocking in the door. It doesn’t matter how you got there, the music is the common thread, and the music is real.”
“You feel good about where the music has evolved to and where it’s going,” Falco adds. “When we meet young bands like Mountain Grass Unit or Shadowgrass, the music is in great hands.”

Getting up from their seats backstage at Bear Shadow, Pandolfi and Falco head over to meet up with the other three Dusters who are plucking a few notes on their instruments under a large maple tree behind the stage. They gather in a small circle and start to jam, their eyes making direct contact with one another. They’re entering into that zen zone once again, happily, and together.

“We trust each other, and there’s nobody else we’d rather be playing music with,” Falco says. “We get to create art together, always reaching deeper into our influences and the musical DNA we share together. As we move through our years together, we’re constantly searching for that.”

items.title: The Diplomat Recap: Is She Your Wife or Is She the President?
items.description: Kate Wyler is not having a great week. It’s not enough to have inadvertently prompted the British prime minister to resign. Oh, no; now she must await a new PM’s election, establish and manage a new relationship with a new administration, and process her roili
items.author: Sophie Brookover
paragraphs: Kate Wyler is not having a great week. It’s not enough to have inadvertently prompted the British prime minister to resign. Oh, no; now she must await a new PM’s election, establish and manage a new relationship with a new administration, and process her roiling emotions at having set that whole mess in motion, all while babysitting the Second Gentleman. Bonus first-act plot twist: Said gentleman plans to move into Winfield House and the embassy, has a million questions, and is prone to leaping to wild conclusions. For her part, Bethan Vaughn (the very welcome Jodie Whittaker) steps into Nicol Trowbridge’s shoes at No. 10 with an approach nearly 180 degrees apart from her predecessor. Where he was impulsive (“Ruled by his tempers,” as she puts it), Vaughn is thoughtful and measured, the type of leader who thinks and “consults the graybeards” in her cabinet before making a big decision. What a concept! Are the scales tilting ever so slightly toward measured normalcy? Come on. That’s not what we’re here for.

Both Vaughn and Todd have tremendous potential as maybe-allies for Kate. She’s pretty good at moving Todd where she needs him to go, and he can and does offer insights into Grace’s psyche that nobody else can or will. His suitability for the role is also sharply limited by his understandable loyalty to Grace. Last season, I remarked that Kate is very isolated. She doesn’t really have a trusted chum on this assignment, and she’s stuck confiding in Hal (who is always playing an angle) and unable to do the same with any of the likely candidates in their circle, like Billie. Grace is, at best, her frenemy; Roylin is dead; and Thema Asseidu-Dennison is grieving. Eidra has the best potential — they have a good rapport and she’s read into most of the sticky situations Kate gets herself into — but is a bit too co-worker-y to be Kate’s ride-or-die, and they both know it. Vaughn is bright, warm, funny, capable, self-aware — A+ friend material, if only Kate were not the representative of a government that has attacked a British aircraft carrier, stolen a nuclear superweapon and lied about it, and blackmailed her predecessor.

Kate’s first meeting with Vaughn goes well; they hit it off immediately and part on good terms. It was a strange nothingburger in every other respect, though, as Vaughn spent most of their whopping four minutes together in a funny little song-and-dance with her civil-service secretary, Elaine, who knocks on the door so quietly she can scarcely be heard. It’s a solid time filler and saves Vaughn from having to address anything on Kate’s agenda, especially the content of the congratulatory call she took from her counterpart in Russia. Things get even more alarming when Eidra can’t reach Tom Libby and reports start rolling in that Vaughn is dismissing everyone in Trowbridge’s government who’d had a significant relationship with Kate and her team. Robyn Palmer, while not exactly forthcoming, fills in enough of the gaps in her brief conversation with Kate that the game board comes into sharper focus.

She gets an even crisper twenty-twenty view of the state of play at that evening’s Royal Society gala held in Todd’s honor. In light of recent events, Prime Minister Vaughn has serious concerns about the U.S. relationship with the U.K. and is taking steps to insulate the nation from the unpredictability of its closest ally. She’s permitted the Russians to enter U.K. waters to retrieve the bodies of their dead submariners; when they find that the Poseidon is missing, she says that might put the U.S. in a major security crisis, “and while I do not take that lightly, the last thing I hope to do is make security calculations on your behalf, just as I know you won’t do on mine.”

By my rough calculations, Vaughn is better at her job than Trowbridge was by approximately 82 fafillion percent. She’s calmly, firmly holding up a mirror to Kate, showing her the logical consequences of her actions. Kate keeps saying she’s on the U.K.’s side, but how can she be, when, at the behest of Grace and Hal, she has lied, withheld information, and coerced their government into doing the U.S.’s bidding? That’s actually being the swaggering bully Trowbridge accused the U.S. of being in the previous episode. Kate is more isolated than ever, and more than ever, what she needs is good advice from trustworthy sources. She’s always been a good soldier, doing her best to put the mission first in the name of serving the greater good, but Grace’s orders keep pushing her further and further from anything recognizable as the greater good.

Todd may be Kate’s best bet for a trusted sounding board, especially once they start speaking openly about his likely role as special envoy to the United Kingdom, but he’s also a very mixed bag. He’s clever and kind and seems sincere in his desire to be useful, but he’s also nosy and gossipy, and shares his musings with his wife, who is also the president. Kate sure is throwing up a lot — could she be pregnant? Vaughn stonewalled her about the call she received from Russia — what’s going on there? In fact, what’s going on with Russia in general? Grace is delighted and titillated by Todd’s speculation, and in the middle of a G7 Summit preparation meeting with Billie and Gannon, quietly asks Hal if Kate is pregnant. This little game of highly consequential telephone is a lot to deal with on top of everything else Kate is managing and deciphering. I want to put an extra-fine point on this detail, too: The president of the United States ignored her own chief of staff and secretary of state during a meeting to prepare for their first G7 as a team to have a sidebar conversation about the most personal aspect of her vice-president and British Ambassador’s relationship.

So yes, Grace continues to Grace. She doesn’t just ignore Gannon and Billie; she dismisses their concerns about her planned announcement of a ban on Chinese computer chips, talks over them, and cuts them all off, saying, “Can we stop pretending we’re not in charge? I find it exhausting.” This increasingly frequent defaulting to autocratic behavior combines alarmingly with the almost bloodthirsty pleasure she takes in Trowbridge’s downfall and Kate’s role in it. She actually congratulates Kate and jokes that were it not illegal, she’d appoint Kate to her own post.

Who knows what Grace will think of Todd eventually confirming Hal’s denial of any pregnancy, but Kate has to go to extreme rhetorical lengths to convince him of it, telling him in two separate conversations that her nausea and vomiting are the result of reflux, not morning sickness. Eventually fed up to the back teeth with his refusal to drop the subject, she yells that the real problem is the work she’s doing on behalf of his wife. Sometimes puking is a sign of pregnancy, but in this case, “it’s just the garden variety wave of nausea people get when they’ve overthrown a democratically elected leader!”
If dread-driven nausea is contagious, then poor Frances, unintentionally overhearing this in shocked dismay just outside the door to Kate’s study, is sure to be its next victim.

• Stuart and Eidra have their first big disagreement since getting back together, and it’s a doozy. Eidra pushes her tendency to get glib and sarcastic rather than risk being vulnerable and honest to its farthest limits. Turns out, that pushes Stuart to his limits, too. After she monologues about what a drag it would be to use one of her few individual conversations with the CIA director to request retrofitting Stuart’s house to meet her security needs, concluding with a salty “ew,” Stuart quietly turns away and heads upstairs. Revisit this one tomorrow, lovebirds.

• Turns out Grace asked the head of Todd’s Secret Service detail to plant the special envoy idea. Are we surprised? At all? She needs him out of her hair, and they both need him to feel competent and not an object of Grace’s disdain.

• I recall that early on last season, Hal suggested that Kate shift from her ambassadorship to a brand-new role as special envoy to Europe. It came with tons of potential but no specifics as to budget or brief. What are the odds that these are problems Todd runs into in his own tenure as special envoy?

• Kate Wyler is somewhere between 45 and 55 years old. I get Todd wondering for a few minutes about Kate being pregnant, but a man who fumbled a multimillion-dollar NIH grant and his postmenopausal wife should be capable of a tiny bit of pregnancy-likelihood math before continuing to hang out on the conclusion they jumped to.

• I love the gowns costume designer Jenny Gering has put Keri Russell and Jodie Whittaker in for the gala. Russell always shines in something sleek, and her black column dress makes for a very elegant battle dress. The long sleeves, sweeping A-line skirt, and slightly quilted effect on Whittaker’s black-and-gold number are bold visual reminders of Vaughn’s strategic reserve in her conversations with Kate.

items.title: Outlander: Blood of My Blood Recap: Love Is a Battlefield
items.description: Will anyone on this show ever know peace? Even the people tucked safely away in Castle Leoch are having existential crises. Good lord, give them, like, a cute little festival or something to go to for one episode. But there are no festivals and there is no pea
items.author: Maggie Fremont
paragraphs: Will anyone on this show ever know peace? Even the people tucked safely away in Castle Leoch are having existential crises. Good lord, give them, like, a cute little festival or something to go to for one episode. But there are no festivals and there is no peace; only war and blood and murder!

Much of that war and blood stuff, of course, has to do with the Battle of Sheriffmuir, of which we have people to pay attention to on both sides of the field: Brian, Murtagh, and Dougal are Team Jacobites, and Henry and Arch Bug are standing with Clan Grant, who is standing with the crown. It is a bloody, bloody battle, but admittedly I did find it hilarious that every few minutes we would simply cut back to the fight for like 30 seconds just so that we knew that yep, they’re still trying to kill each other.

Violence aside, there are some important moments within the battle we should discuss. Over on the English side, Henry does, in fact, have the perfect moment to slip away and enact the plan he and Julia had decided upon, but just as he’s going to do it, he sees his new best friend, Arch Bug, about to be killed and opts instead to save his life. If only he knew the grief Arch and his wife would give his daughter in a few decades! But it’s true: Henry and Arch have bonded. Henry makes a cute joke about Arch’s wife; Arch weeps due to the hardships of war. They have each other’s backs.

Speaking of which, there is one moment when Henry and Brian stand across from one another in the field, but instead of fighting, they give each other one of those “I see you” man nods and go about their business. Brian’s too busy to even stop and think about what he should do with his dad’s wife’s secret husband at the moment anyway. First on Brian’s list is to, obviously, keep himself alive so he can return to Ellen and their impending baby. (Although it does give him comfort to know Murtagh promises to take care of them until his last breath should anything happen to Brian, and good lord, you know he means it. Is Murtagh the hottest man on this show? Discuss.)

Brian’s other job is to keep Dougal safe since he promised Ellen after she promised Maura. This specific task on his to-do list proves difficult when Dougal grows dissatisfied by the fight coming to a draw, both sides claiming victory, and both sides being seemingly okay with all of this. Scots died for this, and the people in charge are happy to just walk away. Dougal gathers a group of 20 MacKenzies and sneaks off to attack Argyll, but it’s not long before one of the men comes limping back and informs Brian that they were ambushed and almost everyone was killed. Dougal and Old Angus were taken prisoner by the English. It takes about three seconds for Brian to decide to go and rescue his future brother-in-law, and it takes Murtagh about five seconds to decide to go with him (even if he isn’t exactly jazzed about it). And so they’re off to … Fort William. Did that name send a shiver down your spine?
