Are you also dreading watching Brian walk into the place where in a few decades he’ll witness his son’s flogging and then die from the shock of it all? Cool, me too.

Little does Brian know, he’s about to have an even bigger problem on his hands. While on their way back to Castle Leoch, Ellen and Grace are held hostage by MacKinney’s son. You remember MacKinney, right? The guy who tried to overthrow Colum and take Clan MacKenzie for himself until Ellen went all Die Hard and killed him and his men? We saw his son flee, and now we know he’s been out in the Highlands dreaming of revenge. The only problem — he doesn’t have the lust for blood or the stomach to kill like his father did, and Ellen knows it. She might not be able to fight back physically once MacKinney Jr. has tied her up, but she can use her cunning to save herself and Grace. She really is the best of her ding-dong brothers combined.

Ellen goes all therapist on MacKinney Jr.’s ass. She repeatedly asks him about how it feels to constantly want his father’s approval and not receive it, to know he isn’t like his dad. She knows it must have done a number on him, and if anyone understands what daddy issues can do to people, it’s Ellen. She goads him a little bit — if he really was going to kill them, he would have done it by now. She manipulates him — will killing two women while they’re tied up make him feel like a man his father could be proud of? She plays him perfectly. Before long, he’s crying and cutting the ropes from Grace’s hands and feet. Maybe he could’ve been different if he didn’t have the father he did. And just as he has this epiphany, just before he moves to set Ellen free, he gets slammed in the head with a club and dies. It’s Balloch. And he’s here to kidnap Ellen MacKenzie. Conveniently already tied up, he promptly tosses her on his horse and rides away, leaving Grace there screaming but unable to stop any of this. Oh, you just knew Lovat wasn’t going to let his son reject him without any consequences. Brian is going to be so pissed about this when he finds out.

The employees of Castle Leathers really don’t have any ethical or moral boundaries, do they? Balloch is out there kidnapping women, and let us not forget what Seema is getting up to last we saw her: contemplating how to best kill Julia so she can take her life and make Henry fall in love with her. Castle Leathers is a weird place.

As Seema continues to hold Julia hostage at knifepoint, Julia mostly sits there as the woman discusses why she deserves Henry, how she can easily make the baby forget Julia, how Henry will come to her once Julia’s out of the way. The woman is spiraling. You’d almost feel bad for her, except that she’s holding a knife (and the key to escape the room they’re in) and unlike MacKinney Jr., you know she’ll use it when it comes down to it.

As Seema goes on and on about Single White Female-ing Julia, Julia knows she needs to act. There’s a scuffle for the knife, which flies out of reach. Left with only her hands to fight off Seema, uh … Julia strangles her to death. It’s pretty grisly. I knew Julia was strong and capable, but capable of that? Shaken, she stumbles downstairs to find Davina and baby William together and safe; it doesn’t seem like Davina had any idea what Seema was up to. Julia would have never been safe with Seema around, but still, you have to imagine there is going to be some real fallout going forward.

• Castle Leoch is currently full of MacKenzies having shame spirals. Colum is reeling over what happened to his family on his watch and railing against his dad for making him a man who cannot “love without measuring the cost.” He’s having a real bleak moment these days, and even his wife, Leticia, is like, Please, I beg of you to get your shit together before this baby shows up.

• Jocasta is feeling extra-contemplative, too. She admits to Leticia that her husband is awful and she dreads him coming home. She also sits with Mrs. Fitz and opens up about feeling foolish for having feelings for Murtagh, when he clearly doesn’t reciprocate them. “Foolish hearts are the ones that love the hardest,” she says in an attempt to comfort her. And adds: “There’s no shame in wanting, only in pretending you don’t.” Mrs. Fitz rules.
• Ah! Guess who introduces himself to Henry after being impressed with his battlefield prowess at Sheriffmuir? Captain Lord Gerard Grey — Lord John’s father. Admittedly, I did yelp at the reveal.
• They made us watch Old Angus weep over Old Rupert’s death? The psychological torture of this show on its audience knows no bounds.

items.title: Dark Matter Recap: Safe Haven
items.description: Since “Love and Be Loved,” the stand-alone episode at this season’s midpoint, Dark Matter has been playing with the idea that other versions of characters we’ve come to know are not merely superfluous copies but humans who might have their own separate, dignif
items.author: Scott Tobias
paragraphs: Since “Love and Be Loved,” the stand-alone episode at this season’s midpoint, Dark Matter has been playing with the idea that other versions of characters we’ve come to know are not merely superfluous copies but humans who might have their own separate, dignified destinies to follow. The Jason-pocalypse that ended the first season was framed as a sad-but-necessary bloodbath, in the sense that we’d been following Jason No. 1 in his long, multidimensional journey back home and any other Jasons with a claim to his life could be considered imposters. The show started to question that idea, though, when Daniela was forced to shoot one of the other Jasons who’d found their hideaway in the woods, and she was haunted by the reality that this poor man was her Jason in all but the most technical sense. In doing so, defending their life felt like something akin to murder, despite her justification.

“Love and Be Loved” showed some grace to one of the other Jasons by imagining a path where he lands in a world where he’s welcomed by his mother (who is surprised but open to seeing a son she’d outlived), rehabilitated from his grief and existential malaise, and able to forge a new future with a bookshop owner who is not Daniela. That didn’t end the infinite complications caused by the box — in fact, he’s shown making peace with a couple of other Jasons — but Dark Matter made the crucial point that duplicate characters can have a role to play. The show then immediately followed it up with a pair of episodes in which Daniela, having retreated to the remote family lake house of her youth, winds up interacting with Gabriel, the father of her Analog World equivalent. Once again, the relationship turns out to be meaningful for both parties, despite our Daniela being an imposter to Gabriel’s world.

With all that in mind, this week’s cleverly plotted new episode plays off our assumption that we know the main characters we’re following, only to pull the rug out from under us. It also doubles as a Laurel origin story, which gives the great Margo Martindale a full episode to define a character who has become a one-woman way station for box travelers but has a complicated backstory of her own. With the title card “Two Years Ago” — a disorienting reminder in itself of how much time has passed in this series — the episode marks the moment when the box first crashed into Laurel’s library, well before Charlie landed there while searching for his brother. Jason No. 1 and Amanda No. 2 emerge from the box in a terrible crisis, as a tree branch from a more environmentally hostile world has lodged into Amanda’s chest and she’s fighting for her life. Jason willed their way to Laurel by asking for help, and it turns out he came to the right spot.

Of course, we know now these two really aren’t Jason No. 1 and Amanda No. 2, but the episode is comfortable with letting its viewers hold on to that assumption for as long as possible. In lesser hands, it might feel like a narrative cheat to pull such a bait and switch, but Blake Crouch and Jacquelyn Ben-Zekry, the credited writers for this entire season, use the time to legitimize their separate destinies, much as they did with the random Jason at the center of “Love and Be Loved.” It has long been a philosophical tenet of Dark Matter that human behavior is context dependent — hence Jason No. 1 and Jason No. 2 seeming like completely different people, even though they were literally the same — and the Jason and Amanda of this episode have a context where they make decisions we don’t expect. If you watched last season and ever thought that Jason No. 1 and Amanda No. 2 had some nice chemistry together, then here’s the “what if” scenario you’ve been waiting for.

But first, it’s worth getting to know Laurel, who is truly the focus of the episode and who’s finely etched in the writing and in Martindale’s performance, which carries a nobility that stops short of saintliness. The box has determined that Laurel’s library is the ideal place for people who need help, whether they have a medical emergency like Jason and Amanda or they’re like Charlie and are having trouble with directions. When Jason and Amanda come crashing into her life as her first multidimensional travelers, Laurel is understandably aghast and a little angry (“What the fuck? Did you drive into my house?!”), but she sets those feelings aside in a hurry to handle the emergency. The box seems to realize that Laurel is the ideal EMT for this scenario because she combines the medical know-how of a hospital worker with the discretion of being on her own. In fact, when it’s suggested that she call an ambulance, Laurel refuses to let “those motherfuckers” into her house.

There’s a reason for her hostility, and the show makes subtle allusions to the tensions at play in the America we’re currently living in. In Laurel’s world 20 years earlier, a dirty-bomb attack hit Chicago, and her experience as a corpsman and civilian nurse turned her home into an emergency shelter for critically wounded neighbors. But the “5/20 attack,” much like our 9/11 attack, had the effect of fracturing society and giving rise to bloodthirsty revenge seekers and authoritarians. As she explains it to Jason and Amanda, “I didn’t think turning the other side into dust was any kind of justice for Chicago, and I wasn’t the only one, so we did what we were supposed to do. Protest, march, speak. And they did what they do, made it all illegal.” That’s why she doesn’t allow strangers in her house, because she cannot trust their intentions.

Dark Matter doesn’t necessarily suggest Laurel is correct in bunkering down, however, because she’s essentially given up on the outside world entirely and doesn’t know if it might have changed. In the meantime, the strangers who are slipping into her home through the box have become her part-time companions, starting with Jason and Amanda and continuing with others like Leighton and Blair. After this Jason and Amanda return, after leaving for a stretch, Laurel updates them on the eight visitors she’s had in the meantime, including a Blair, an Alex, a Ryan, one other Jason and Amanda, and two Jasons traveling on their own. The experience has given her unique insight into how best to navigate the box while also turning her into a kind of philosopher for the age of multiple realities.

On that front, the most important takeaway from Laurel in this episode is that the “perfect match” doesn’t matter as much as we might have assumed when Jason No. 1 finally got back to his Daniela and Charlie. Other versions are fine. Other destinies can be fine, too. So when Jason and Amanda are unable to get Jason back to Daniela, and we realize that they are not the Jason No. 1 and the Amanda No. 2 that we assumed they were, it’s okay. They can mourn what they’ve lost and move forward to a future together that might make them equally content. As Laurel philosophizes, “Everything ends. It’s a fact that we somehow never see coming. It will hurt you more than you can stand. It will almost kill you. Then one day, it’s just a chapter.”

From there, the episode can pivot into another touching surprise. In the first episode where Charlie had found his way into Laurel’s care, an unknown third party entered the library, but the show had left that person’s identity as a cliffhanger. Here, it’s revealed that the mystery person is Charlie’s father, Jason. Yet it’s not Jason No. 1 but the Jason who was the first to crash into Laurel’s house, who still knows Charlie as his son, even if he was never able to get back to him. He can help and support Charlie without seeming like an imposter, just as Daniela could feel close to the father of her Analog World version.
The box taketh away. But, in Laurel’s way station, the box giveth, too.
• An amusingly plausible reaction from Laurel to Jason’s story about how he landed in her house: “It’s all too wild and dumb to be fake.”

• A notable moment of self-consciousness from this Jason about not wanting to arouse his inner Jason No. 2: “I want my life and my family back more than anything, but I can’t let it make me into him in the process.” Amanda assures him that he’s “not him,” but can she be so sure? We’ve seen evidence to the contrary with Jason No. 1.

• Asked about why Laurel never lets anyone in her house, she recalls Rory, another former service member who’d become her best friend and the love of her life. Rory spoke out too loudly against the authorities and paid the price. Laurel makes it sound like her world turned into Fahrenheit 451, with Rory getting turned in by a neighbor for possession of banned materials and then dying in his holding cell before he could hear the charges against him. Laurel suspects that maybe some of the books in her library have been banned, but she’s given up trying to find out.

• The literary references on the show continue with Laurel quoting from Ralph Waldo Emerson’s essay “Self-Reliance”: “The voyage of the best ship is a zigzag line of a hundred tacks.” Basically, it was the 1841 version of “I love mess.”

items.title: Ted Sarandos Addresses Netflix Content Exec Purge: ‘I Know That We Could Do Better’
items.description: Netflix, looking to boost its viewing engagement as revenue growth cools off, made a major overhaul of its executive leadership overseeing content.
items.author: Todd Spangler
paragraphs: Netflix, looking to boost its viewing engagement as revenue growth cools off, made a major overhaul of its executive leadership overseeing content.

Last week, amid its layoff of 1,000 employees, Netflix ousted chief content officer Bela Bajaria and has tapped veteran TV exec Peter Rice to replace her. The company also let go head of film Dan Lin and his top lieutenant, Doug Belgrad, as well as director of original series Carolina Garcia.

On the streamer’s Q3 2026 earnings call, co-CEO Ted Sarandos — who had previously led Netflix’s content operations for over 20 years — explained the decision to install a new team overseeing its programming lineup led by Rice.
“I know that we could do better, and we want to build on that momentum,” Sarandos said, when asked about the leadership change on the content side.

Sarandos started by praising Bajaria “for all of her incredible contributions to Netflix. Bela had an incredible decade-long run here. She put a lot of great hits on the board. She led the teams through a lot of expansions of new types of content. She also did the hard work of building this incredible international team, who’s been making local content around the world, which has become a great competitive differentiator for us over the last decade.”

That said, Sarandos continued, “Now we’ve seen an opportunity to take our slate to the next level, especially in the U.S. where we can have an outsized impact when we create a big buzzy show that members love and talk about all over the world.”

Sarandos said he has known Rice, a former Disney and 21st Century Fox television and movie exec, for about 15 years. At Disney, he was chairman of Walt Disney Television before he was ousted by former CEO Bob Chapek in 2022.

“And I’ve got to tell you the outpouring of excitement about him coming to Netflix from across the industry and from the creative community has been nothing short of overwhelming. He’s one of the really rare people in the industry who’s led TV networks, movie studios, streaming services,” Sarandos said. “His creative instinct and his business acumen are remarkable. He’s really an at-scale quality and volume operator, and he does it across every imaginable form of entertainment. You know, network [television], prestige cable, streaming, theatrical and TV films, and live sports.”

Sarandos said, “most importantly… Peter Rice understands talent relations, and in a competitive market, creative talent have choices of where they want to work, and we want Netflix to always be the place that they love to do the best work of their life. Peter is the exact right person to lead those efforts in the U.S. and around the world. Now, that’s a key aspect of what I believe Peter can improve on looking forward.”
A bit later in the call, Sarandos again sang Rice’s praises.

“Peter brings expertise in both art and commerce, television and film. It’s kind of that exact balance skill set that will help guide us through our next chapter,” Sarandos told Wall Street analysts. “Now, there’s a ton to be excited about in our Q4 slate, and a ton to be excited about in 2027. And I believe that Peter will actually be able to have an impact on those projects that are in the works, even in the short term.”

items.title: Christina Applegate Reveals She Was Misdiagnosed With MS: ‘I’m Back at Square One’ and It’s a ‘Mindf—’
items.description: Christina Applegate returned to her podcast, “MeSsy,” on Tuesday with some shocking news: She was misdiagnosed with multiple sclerosis.
items.author: Ellise Shafer
paragraphs: Christina Applegate returned to her podcast, “MeSsy,” on Tuesday with some shocking news: She was misdiagnosed with multiple sclerosis.

After taking a break from the podcast for seven months due to her health, Applegate tearfully shared the revelation in a two-part episode, saying that new technology led to the discovery. “This may come as great news, but to me, I’m back at square one,” she said. “It’s hard to say that [my doctor] came into my room and she said, ‘Congratulations, you don’t have MS.'”

Applegate said that she was “not happy at all” about the news. “You don’t get misdiagnosed and then all of the sudden I’m better. I haven’t gotten better … If anything, I’ve gotten worse in some ways,” she said. “So I’m back at square one, that I don’t know what’s going on with me.”

Applegate originally revealed that she had been diagnosed with MS in 2021, and retired from acting after the finale of her hit series “Dead to Me” the next year. Since then, she has become a fierce advocate for people with the disease — which causes damage to the central nervous system — and started the “MeSsy” podcast alongside “The Sopranos” star Jamie-Lynn Sigler as a way to share her experience and spread awareness.

Despite learning she had been misdiagnosed, Applegate said that her symptoms remain and her illness has now become a mystery. “I have every symptom of someone with MS. Every single one,” she said. “Now, we both know that there are many things that mirror MS — many different things.”

She added that “there’s a pretty damn high number of misdiagnoses with MS,” so this is not a rare occurrence. “It’s clear now that they’re finding something different,” Applegate continued. “Something else is going on.”

Applegate added that “it’s weird because I feel like I let everybody down” after becoming such a big advocate for the MS community. She said that she’s still in a “state of shock,” adding: “It’s a mindfuck, for sure.”

“It’s this weird feeling because I became this — you and I, the poster children for MS,” she said. “I had a reason. I had a fucking reason as to why my day sucked every day. And now I don’t have a reason and it’s very unnerving and it’s really confusing for me.”

In the second part of the episode, Applegate got emotional thinking about the past five years, and how confused she feels now. “I’m still here feeling quite hollow and quite scared and sad. Now, I just feel lost,” she said.

“I’ve gone through a great depression because of it. But, you know, I lost everything. I lost my job,” Applegate continued as she broke down in tears. “God, I’m so sorry, I get really emotional because it stopped my life. I still have to use wheelchairs when I go to the doctor’s office. I can’t walk from the car to the room. I mean, I’m still in this. Nothing magical happened when she said, ‘You don’t have MS.’ Nothing magical happened.”
Listen to the full “MeSsy” episodes below.

items.title: Netflix Stock and Price Targets Drop as Wall Street Debates If the Streamer Can Flip the Script
items.description: Netflix‘s highly anticipated third-quarter earnings report is in, but what does it mean? In co-CEO Ted Sarandos’ telling, it’s all about execution. And how is Wall Street reacting to management commentary about the streaming giant’s outlook and largest layoffs
items.author: Georg Szalai
paragraphs: Netflix‘s highly anticipated third-quarter earnings report is in, but what does it mean? In co-CEO Ted Sarandos’ telling, it’s all about execution. And how is Wall Street reacting to management commentary about the streaming giant’s outlook and largest layoffs in years, including the exit of film head Dan Lin and the replacement of chief content officer Bela Bajaria with Peter Rice?

Sarandos discussed content strategy, with co-CEO Greg Peters addressing a 2026 shortfall in advertising revenue. But the key quote from the call may have been Sarandos’ blunt note about staying the course.

“There is no need for a fundamental shift in the strategy,” he said. “We do need better execution in the U.S.” adding: “It’s just not growing as fast as it could or as fast as we’d like. So we had some really solid doubles and triples this year, but the other territories count on some of those titles being home runs so that they’ll travel around the world.”
In Wednesday pre-market trading, Netflix’s stock was down more than 6 percent at $64.35, signaling a new 52-week low. As of Tuesday’s market close, that low had been at $65.08.
So, what can investors take away from the streamer’s updates? Below, The Hollywood Reporter has compiled analysts’ reactions to Netflix’s latest set of results and outlook.
Analyst: Mark Mahaney, Evercore ISI
Stock rating and price target: outperform, $90, down from $110

Takeaways: “Is A Better Script Coming?” was the key question that the analyst posed in the headline of his report. “For the third quarter in a row, Netflix shares traded off mid-single-digit to high-single-digit percentages in the aftermarket on soft earnings per share results. And this is now the fourth quarter in a row that Netflix guidance has come in lighter on at least one metric. Growth has clearly slowed at Netflix.”

Mahaney reduced his financial estimates and pointed out slowed revenue growth, wondering: “What’s Going Wrong And Is There A Fix?” He then put forward some reasons: “We attribute this to some market maturity, consistent competition from large platforms like YouTube, Amazon, Disney, etc. … potentially a structural challenge from short-form content platforms (TikTok, YouTube again), and content mis-execution (i.e. no major global hits since KPop Demon Hunters).”

What to do? “We believe most of these challenges are addressable, and we view Netflix management as highly capable,” the analyst offered. “By bringing in a new chief content officer, Netflix is at least acknowledging and acting on the challenge. We also believe that Netflix, the global hit machine, will likely have a hit in 2027.”

And Mahaney shared an upbeat conclusion. “This along with an improvement in content delivery and some key live events (Women’s World Cup) may well drive growth again in U.S. viewing hours, changing the engagement narrative. We also see live events and the expansion of the ad-supported plan to 15 new markets in 2027 as potentially accelerating sub ads growth,” he wrote. All in all, “we believe the Netflix long thesis is still intact. Or at least, we are more confident than the market is that it is intact.”
Analyst: Brian Pitz, BMO Capital Markets
Stock rating and price target: outperform, $125
Takeaways: “Advertising faces product delays, but [the] long-term vision [is] still intact,” was the analyst’s post-earnings takeaway, with results leading him to “fine-tune” his financial estimates.

Despite ad momentum running behind expectations, the analyst continues to see advertising as a key growth opportunity for Netflix. “We remain positive on the long-term monetization opportunity and see the near-term advertising slowdown as buildout pain rather than a structural growth challenge,” he wrote.

Content and subscriber momentum are a mixed bag. “Encouragingly, membership growth remains solid, supported by healthy subscriber retention across regions as churn improved year-over-year,” the analyst noted. “We were encouraged that Netflix’s industry-leading churn improved year-over-year globally and in the U.S., better than management expected. However, management acknowledged that U.S. content execution needs improvement, and the incoming chief content officer Peter Rice will focus on it.”

Pitz also addressed the role sports could play in the content strategy. “While Netflix is unlikely to buy expensive season-long premium sports rights, it continues to lean into specific live inventory, adding its first NFL Thanksgiving Eve game,” he said. “Live content accounts for only 1 percent of engagement hours despite representing 5 percent of content spend, but it remains an important lever for improving subscriber acquisition and retention and reducing churn.”
Analyst: Michael Morris, Guggenheim
Stock rating and price target: buy, $78, down from $80

Takeaways: To explain his stock price target reduction, Morris cited “third-quarter results that met guidance but were paired with an outlook modestly short of expectations,” which led him to lower his 2027 revenue estimate to $56.8 billion from $57.1 billion, with his earnings per share forecast down by 9 cents to $3.80.

With Netflix cutting its 2026 advertising revenue target to around $2.7 billion from $3.0 billion also made Morris pare back his 2027 ad estimate to $4.0 billion, which he said compares to a $5.2 billion consensus expectation.

Of course, the recent content leadership changes and what it means for its programming strategy also featured in his report. “Co-CEO Ted Sarandos described the company’s strategy as ‘unchanged’ while acknowledging ‘we could do better,'” he wrote. “Peter Rice’s mandate as chief content officer is to find more home runs across formats and genres and strengthen talent relationships. Returning franchises including Emily in Paris, The Diplomat and Wednesday, and feature films including Narnia, provide a bridge to a lineup developed under Mr. Rice, and we consider a more impactful slate non-negotiable for renewed investor interest.”

He also called content licensing “a silver lining” in content, citing a recent deal with Disney. Concluded Morris: “Netflix is a top platform for licensed product, and in our view more win-win partnerships with underexposed content at attractive terms would be incremental. Bundling with most other major streamers or launching a free service in the U.S. would not sustainably bolster top-line growth.”
Analyst: Ralph Schackart, William Blair
Stock rating and price target: outperform, no price target

Takeaways: The engagement and content debates featured heavily in Schackart’s report. “The company acknowledged the need to accelerate view-hours growth, highlighting India as an example of successful execution, where view hours increased 24 year-over-year and view hours per member grew in the low- to mid-single digits,” he highlighted.

The analyst also weighed in on Rice’s content chief appointment. “Management views the transition as an opportunity to improve content execution, particularly in the United States,” he wrote. “Management stressed that the change does not represent a shift in content strategy, but rather an opportunity to take the slate to the next level.”
Schackart summarized his takeaways from the results and outlook this way: “Unfortunately, this quarter did not give the bears a reason to pull back on their growth concerns.”

What does this mean for investors? “While it may take patience, we believe investors should benefit from accumulating shares on the pullback, recognizing that there is not a near-term catalyst. We believe the company will solve its near-term content concern at some point in 2027.”
Analyst: Laurent Yoon, Bernstein
Stock rating and price target: outperform, $80, down from $95

Takeaways: Patience was a recurring theme in Yoon’s report, which is entitled “When Success Starts Looking Mature.” “New content boss, new content strategy?” it asked. “Perhaps, but not anytime soon,” it offered. “Despite new leadership with deep experience across TV, film, and streaming, the messaging remains firmly centered on traditional content, live events, and licensing. Any meaningful strategic shift – if there’s one – could take years, not quarters, to show up in the slate or the numbers.”

That may also keep weighing on investor sentiment. “Investors will increasingly focus on the durability of ‘double-digit’ growth and the pace of margin expansion as content investment comes back into focus,” the analyst explained. “The risk is not the near-term fundamentals, but perception. A strategy that continues to lean on traditional content, traditional formats, and traditional engagement risks reminding both consumers and investors of the ‘L’ word – legacy. That alone may be enough to keep the stock range-bound near term, even if the underlying business continues to execute well.”

Advertising may not be broken, but also made for a disappointment. “Management discussed slower ad product rollouts rather than demand, suggesting a delay rather than disruption, but it still represents a missed opportunity,” the analyst concluded.

All in all, he reduced its forecasts for Netflix, which also pushed down the stock price target. “Changes in earnings per share estimates are due to slower-than-expected advertising revenue growth, domestic subscriber growth and margin expansion slightly offset by accelerated buybacks,” Yoon noted. “We also reduced our valuation multiple to 20 times (from 25 times) to reflect slower growth and ongoing negative investor sentiment without a near-term positive catalyst.”
Analyst: Rob Fishman, MoffettNathanson
Stock rating and price target: buy, $90, down from $100
Takeaways: MoffettNathanson was among the firms cutting their financial forecasts and Netflix stock price target, in this case by $10, following the latest results and management commentary.
Fishman wondered about the outlook for revenue growth, especially given the ad revenue updates, and the outlook for content spending following the recent executive changes.

“If revenue is slowing, does Netflix need to reaccelerate content spend?” the analyst asked. And he shared that underlying his forecast is 8 percent content spending growth as “management is clearly focused on reining in expenses to invest in high-impact areas, as evidenced by the recent headcount reductions.”

His conclusion is that Netflix can continue to improve the monetization of its reach and scale to grow profits in the future. Wrote Fishman: “After the sell-off, we believe Netflix’s downside is limited, and the stock presents an attractive entry point to capture upside in leveraging the company’s global scale to drive incremental growth above the strength of its core business model.”

items.title: Harrison Ford and Calista Flockhart to Receive First Joint Award as Couple Is Selected for Icon Honors
items.description: Harrison Ford and Calista Flockhart will take a spin in the spotlight at the Stardust Ball, a fundraiser presented by Women’s Guild Cedars-Sinai at the Beverly Wilshire Hotel on Nov. 18. The moment will mark the couple’s first joint award and is coming their w
items.author: Chris Gardner
paragraphs: Harrison Ford and Calista Flockhart will take a spin in the spotlight at the Stardust Ball, a fundraiser presented by Women’s Guild Cedars-Sinai at the Beverly Wilshire Hotel on Nov. 18. The moment will mark the couple’s first joint award and is coming their way to recognize their “extraordinary careers and longstanding commitment to philanthropy,” per the organization.

Ford and Flockhart will be joined on the honoree program by media mogul Byron Allen, who will receive a humanitarian award for a “longstanding commitment to creating opportunity, expanding representation and using his platform to uplift underserved communities.”

Ford has a long history of activism and supporting causes he cares about from environmental conservation to humanitarian service. He joined Conservation International’s board of directors in 1991, and has since become the org’s longest-serving member. Currently a vice chair, Ford received an inaugural E.O. Wilson Legacy Award for “transformative conservation leadership” from the organization. As a well-known pilot, Ford piloted search-and-rescue missions, transported medical professionals and supplies to rescue efforts in Haiti, and supported orgs like Operation Smile, Special Olympics and Wings of Hope.

Flockhart meanwhile has a long history of supporting charitable and philanthropic initiatives with a focus on preventing violence against women and children, animal welfare and good health. She’s specifically pitched in by working with For Goodness Sakes, Peace Over Violence and the Violence Intervention Program.

They’ve been together since around 2002, and maintained a low profile for much of their marriage. They’ve recently stepped out at high profile events in 2026 like the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art opening, the Emmy Awards, the Actor Awards and more. Ford currently stars in Shrinking on Apple TV while Flockhart recently starred in Feud and with a voice role on Invincible.

Allen, who serves as founder, chairman and CEO of Allen Media Group, steers a portfolio that covers TV, film, streaming and broadcast with The Weather Channel, HBCUGO, TheGrio Television Network, BuzzFeed and HuffPost. He’s previously been honored by Harvard Business School, USC, UCLA and Syracuse University’s Newhouse School. Allen created and hosts the long-running Comics Unleashed with Byron Allen, currently celebrating its 20th anniversary and airing weeknights on CBS.

The Women’s Guild Cedars-Sinai fundraiser benefits the Women’s Guild Neurology Project and the Women’s Guild Distinguished Chair in Pediatrics at Cedars-Sinai’s newest expansion, Guerin Children’s. Women’s Guild has raised more than $70 million for the hospital. More info can be found here.

items.title: ‘Doctor Who’ Star Noel Clarke Pleads Not Guilty to Sexual Assault, Voyeurism, Exposure
items.description: Doctor Who star Noel Clarke has pleaded not guilty to multiple sex offenses at Westminster Magistrates Court in London on Wednesday.
items.author: Lily Ford
paragraphs: Doctor Who star Noel Clarke has pleaded not guilty to multiple sex offenses at Westminster Magistrates Court in London on Wednesday.

The British actor best known for playing Mickey Smith, boyfriend to Billie Piper’s Rose Tyler, on the BBC show from 2005 to 2010, was charged last month after detectives received “a file of evidence.”

The 50-year-old faces two charges of sexual assault, three charges of voyeurism and one charge of exposure. Voyeurism refers to when someone secretly watches, photographs or films another person without their consent for sexual gratification. The offenses, said the Met Police, are alleged to have taken place between 2007 and 2016 and relate to five women.

It comes five years after a Guardian exposé published claims from 20 women accusing Clarke of groping, sexual misconduct and bullying, as well as sources alleging they were “sexually harassed or inappropriately” touched on the set of Doctor Who. ITV, Sky and CAA cut ties with the actor soon after, and BAFTA rescinded his Outstanding British Contribution to Cinema award.

He “vehemently” denied the claims at the time, and in 2025 lost a libel case against the Guardian over the report. Over a dozen women testified against Clarke, and he was ordered to pay £3 million ($4m) toward the outlet’s legal costs.

The most recent charges follow an investigation by detectives that began in September 2025. A man, then in his 40s, was arrested in connection with the investigation that same month. Police were photographed at the time leaving Clarke’s house with boxes.
He’ll next appear at Southwark Crown Court, where Russell Brand’s heavily publicized rape and sexual assault trial is ongoing, on Nov. 18.

items.title: Julia Stiles Reunites With ’10 Things I Hate About You’ Cast to Honor Heath Ledger on ‘DWTS’
items.description: It was a night to remember on Dancing with the Stars, as the 10 Things I Hate About You cast reunited on the ABC dance competition show to pay tribute to the late Heath Ledger.
items.author: Carly Thomas
paragraphs: It was a night to remember on Dancing with the Stars, as the 10 Things I Hate About You cast reunited on the ABC dance competition show to pay tribute to the late Heath Ledger.

Ahead of Tuesday’s episode, which was Dedication Night, it was revealed that Julia Stiles and her pro partner Ezra Sosa would be dedicating their dance to Ledger, who starred opposite Stiles in the beloved 1999 rom-com.

The pair danced to “Can’t Take My Eyes Off You” by Frankie Valli, which was the song Ledger’s Patrick Verona serenaded Stiles’ Kat Stratford with during her soccer practice at the high school stadium. In the scene, he runs and dances across the stands as the marching band plays to try and win her over after Joey Donner (Andrew Keegan) pays him to take Kat out.

Following Stiles and Sosa’s emotional dance, which featured some of Ledger’s iconic moves, the poem her character reads in the film about Patrick starts playing in the ballroom. After the actress lays a flower on the ground in honor of Ledger, she is joined by her fellow co-stars, including Keegan, Joseph Gordon-Levitt (Cameron James), Larisa Oleynik (Bianca Stratford), Gabrielle Union (Chastity) and Susan May Pratt (Mandella).
Ahead of the new DWTS episode, Sosa took to Instagram to share how important this dance was for both of them.

“I don’t think we’ve every approached a performance with more care, sensitivity, and intention than this one,” Sosa wrote in the joint post with Stiles. “From the very beginning it was incredibly important to both Julia and I that this tribute be created with the utmost respect, thoughtfulness, and close guidance from those who hold Heath and his memory closest. This isn’t about defining a relationship or telling a story that isn’t ours to tell. It’s about honoring a beautiful moment in time, a film that changed so many lives, and someone whose impact continues to be felt by generations.”

“We’ve poured so much love into this piece, and we’re incredibly grateful for the trust placed in us to bring it to life,” he added. “Our only hope is that it honors his memory with the dignity, love, and respect it deserves.”
Ledger died in 2008 at the age of 28 from an accidental overdose.

10 Things I Hate About You, directed by Gil Junger, follows teen Joey who wants to date Bianca, but she can’t date until her antisocial older sister, Kat, has a boyfriend, per her strict father’s rules. That’s when Joey pays a mysterious boy, Patrick, to ask Kat out.

items.title: America Is Officially Back in the Selvedge Denim Business
items.description: Mike McLachlan, the founder of the Connecticut clothing brand Manresa, has owned many pairs of selvedge denim jeans over the years, but the ones he’s wearing right now are by far the closest to his heart. “Selvedge mills tend to lean more towards more characte
items.author: Jeremy Freed
paragraphs: Mike McLachlan, the founder of the Connecticut clothing brand Manresa, has owned many pairs of selvedge denim jeans over the years, but the ones he’s wearing right now are by far the closest to his heart. “Selvedge mills tend to lean more towards more character-rich neppy, slubby denim,” he says, referencing the textural characteristics prized by many selvedge enthusiasts. “But I've always been more of a fan of what Levi’s would have been using in the middle of the century. It’s fairly flat and uniform, and it’s a style of denim you don’t find very often anymore. It’s as traditional as it gets.”

For McLachlan and many others, selvedge denim—the old-school-style cotton twill woven on antique narrow looms—is both aesthetically and ideologically superior to the stuff most jeans are made of today. Not only does it take on more character as it wears and fades, it represents a direct connection to the authenticity of denim’s golden era, before it was consumed by the modern global fashion industry. McLachlan’s new favorite jeans are a one-of-one prototype, but thanks to the efforts of Trion, Georgia’s Mount Vernon Mills, and a room full of painstakingly restored antique shuttle looms, anyone in search of the kind of no-nonsense dungarees one might have bought at Sears in the 1950s will soon have plenty of options.

In early November last year, Mount Vernon Mills, a 180-year old fabric mill and America’s largest denim producer, posted an Instagram video of a semi truck backed into a loading bay, its cargo shrouded in a white plastic sheet. The video, set to the opening chords of AC/DC’s “Hell’s Bells,” didn’t reveal much, but for those attuned to the fate of American-made selvedge over the last few years, it marked a major milestone. Under that white sheet was one of 40-some Draper X3 looms salvaged from the legendary Cone White Oak denim mill in Greensboro, North Carolina. To those who worship at the altar of 20th century workwear, it represented nothing less than the salvation of American denim. A little less than a year later, that machine and 20 others like it are up and running, fabric samples are being shipped to clothing brands across the country, and a new chapter in a 120-year story is beginning.

“It has been a crazy ride,” says Tim Harris, the director of marketing and specialty sales at Mount Vernon Mills, and the company’s de-facto social media manager. He’s the one who posted the video of the looms arriving last November, and he’s been documenting their progress on TikTok and Instagram in the months since. The equipment, some of which had been in storage for nearly a decade, was in rough shape. “There were some full looms there, but there were also these bins of parts that had 6000 springs and levers in them, things that had not been made since the 1970s,” he says. “It was like, ‘Here we go!’”

The Draper looms’ journey to their current home was long and fraught. The looms—some of which date back to the 1950s—were originally used at the Cone White Oak mill, which opened in 1905 and was the official supplier of selvedge to Levi’s, Wrangler, and many other storied American brands for most of the 20th century. Before White Oak closed in 2017, it had been the last remaining commercial producer of selvedge denim in the United States, and many feared the legacy of American-made selvedge would disappear with it. Enter Vidalia Mills, an ambitious textile startup, which purchased White Oak’s equipment, moved it to Vidalia, Louisiana, and promised a glorious return to form. That never quite came to pass, however, and when Vidalia’s assets went up for auction last year, Mount Vernon Mills bought the lot.

Given its history and its size, Mount Vernon Mills is perhaps the only company with both the resources and the skilled workers necessary to resurrect American selvedge, but restoring the looms to their former glory was no small feat. Pickers scoured barns and warehouses for spare parts, and a crack squad of technicians from Greensboro decamped to Trion to teach Mount Vernon’s staff how to keep the antique machinery running. As of now, Harris says, about 20 of the 45 Draper looms are operational, and each has been christened with the name of a golden-era American cultural icon: Elvis, Aretha, Lucille.

Because antique shuttle looms like the Draper weave at a fraction of the pace of their modern equivalents and require far more maintenance, running a selvedge production line represents a significant investment for a relatively small output. To put it in perspective, Mount Vernon hopes to produce 20,000 yards of selvedge per week at full capacity, the same amount of time it takes its modern looms to churn out millions of yards of conventional denim. Despite this, Harris says, there is no shortage of buyers excited to turn its new selvedge into jeans. “The outpouring we have received for this crazy idea of bringing these old things back to life, and doing this in America, has been amazing,” he says. “Folks are reaching out. They want to be a part of it. We could not have asked for a better reception.”

One of those reaching out is Kyle Moredocks, who recently got his hands on a sample of Mount Vernon Mills selvedge. Moredocks is the founder of an eponymous Portland-based brand that makes customized jeans, jackets, and shirts to order (his Cowboy Jean recently got a shoutout from Derek Guy). Because Moredocks’ concept is based on on-demand production, he doesn’t buy huge quantities of material, and that makes it difficult to meet the minimum orders of large textile mills. “If you can go straight to the mill and meet their volume requirements then obviously that's easier. But if you're someone our size making less than 100 pairs a year, it's more challenging,” Moredocks says. At Mount Vernon, however, the new selvedge program is distinguished by being available to small brands like Moredocks and Manresa at minimums far below the industry standard.

“These [brands] are the ones keeping this thing alive—the romance and the stories behind these jeans, and they look for craftsmanship.” Harris says. “This is not cookie-cutter-every-yard- looks-the-same denim. This is handcrafted by artisans, and it’s different. This is the $300 Pappy Van Winkle, not the $25 Wild Turkey.”

Harris alludes to bigger deals with high-profile clients that he can’t name, but to anyone familiar with the recent surge of special-editions made from White Oak’s remaining American-made selvedge, it’s not hard to guess who the list might include. Mount Vernon is initially offering two standard sanforized (i.e. washed and pre-shrunk) denims: the Revere, a 13-ounce dark indigo, and a heavier 15-ounce Franklin. “We wanted to do old revolutionary names because we were doing something revolutionary,” says Harris. “Mr. Revere came and told us that the revolution was coming.”

At Manresa, McLachlan is working through his last remaining yards of Japanese selvedge, and plans to release his signature 207 jeans in Mount Vernon Mills denim in the coming months. “We'll make Mount Vernon 15-ounce during the colder months, and the 13-ounce during the warmer months,” he says. “Then maybe a field coat, maybe a barn coat, maybe a jean jacket somewhere down the line.”

In the meantime, McLachlan has been wearing his prototype Mount Vernon 207s every day. “They have a little bit more drape than a Japanese counterpart might, and they just feel comfortable as soon as you put them on,” he says. “I feel very lucky to be able to be wearing a pair.” McLachlan also boasts that as one of the first people in the world to have a pair of Mount Vernon selvedge jeans, he’ll have a head start on the fade competition that will inevitably ensue.
“I’m going to wear them every day, so nobody's ever going to catch up to me in terms of my fade,” he says. “So I’m pretty proud of that too.”

items.title: Noah and Timex’s Newest Watch Channels Vintage Patek Philippe
items.description: Want more insider watch coverage? Get Box + Papers, GQ's newsletter devoted to the watch world, sent to your inbox every Friday. Sign up here to get it free.
items.author: Oren Hartov
paragraphs: Want more insider watch coverage? Get Box + Papers, GQ's newsletter devoted to the watch world, sent to your inbox every Friday. Sign up here to get it free.

Ever since their Sun and Moon watch sold out in a snap in 2014, Noah and Timex have nurtured a growing collection of affordable timepieces to cement themselves as one of the most fruitful and popular collaborators in the watch world.

Now, the pair are back with perhaps their most elegant watch yet: the Boatswain. For those of you who didn’t grow up scrubbing the poop deck, a “boatswain”—pronounced “bosun” or “bos’n”—is a senior petty officer on a ship who is in charge of maintenance, operations, crew management, and the like. Like the Anchor watch from earlier this year, the name strikes a nautical to but the Boatswain is cocktail-party ready. The $228 watch is launching October 15th at 11 a.m. EST on Noah's website.

The watch’s Oval shape captures the look of the thin, beloved Golden Ellipse Patek Philippe has made since the 1960s. Noah and Timex have used this shape before, but this dial does away with the lighthouse design and even the moon phase complication for the simplest execution yet. Measuring 31 x 35 mm with an 18mm lug width, the elliptical case comes in steel or gold-tone steel with soft edges, a flat crystal, and a small crown. The dial is pared down to the essentials: an eggshell background is overlaid with black Roman numerals and a black pencil handset. But if you look very closely at what would typically be a railroad-shaped inner minute track on, say, a Cartier Tank, this one is actually shaped like a length of coiled rope, neatly knotting together the watch’s nautical theme.

Powered by a quartz movement and available on a brown leather strap in steel and a black leather strap in gold tone, this is Noah and Timex’s cleanest offering yet—and one of their best-looking. Though 2025’s Lighthouse Watch featured a similar silhouette, this one’s classic dial offers a more restrained take on the partnership’s aesthetic. And at $228, every burgeoning collector fresh to the workforce is almost guaranteed to scoop one up to strap on for work, play, and just about everything else.

The arc of Noah’s Timex projects has been fascinating to watch precisely because they didn’t necessarily resonate widely right off the bat: handsome as the first couple of Weekender-type watches were, they didn’t explode into the popular consciousness with the impact of a sartorial bomb. But ever since the Sun and Moon—followed by the Rectangular Moon Phase Watch, the Lighthouse Watch, Oval Moon Phase Watch, and others—the two brands have been on an absolute tear. Something about the dressier, unisex silhouettes; the playful complications; and the affordability has been right on trend in the watch industry. Plus, it gave younger or more budget-minded collectors the chance to get a taste of the elegant vintage Cartier and Patek Philippe watches that are typically the exclusive province of deep-pocketed buyers.

If Noah founder Brendon Babeznian, a self-professed non-watch guy, has hit upon anything, it seems to be that a great-looking, everyday watch doesn’t need to be a precious heirloom piece that you keep in a safe and only take out for weddings, bar mitzvot, and anniversary dinners. Rather, it can be funky, not too expensive, and nearly perfect.

items.title: 'Hunger Games' Star Joseph Zada Is Learning to Dress the Part
items.description: To say Joseph Zada is on the verge of mega-stardom would be an understatement. The 21-year-old Sydney native beat out a field of contenders to land the role of a young Haymitch Abernathy in The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping, stepping into a franchise wi
items.author: W Staff
paragraphs: To say Joseph Zada is on the verge of mega-stardom would be an understatement. The 21-year-old Sydney native beat out a field of contenders to land the role of a young Haymitch Abernathy in The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping, stepping into a franchise with a proven track record of turning young actors into global superstars (see: Jennifer Lawrence and Josh Hutcherson).

So it was only fitting that, for his first-ever Academy Museum Gala—one of Hollywood’s most glamorous and closely watched red carpets—Zada went with a tried-and-true classic: Giorgio Armani. For the evening, Zada put an elevated spin on the much-debated tan suit, wearing a beige double-breasted tuxedo jacket with satin-trimmed notch lapels, slim-fitting trousers, and a crisp evening shirt. Paired with slicked-back hair, the look felt both relaxed and impeccably polished.

Once inside, Zada connected with his Sunrise on the Reaping costars Elle Fanning and Mckenna Grace both of whom offered their own nods to the Hunger Games universe. Fanning arrived in an ethereal, Effie Trinket-esque Valentino butterfly gown, while Grace paid tribute to Lawrence in a custom red Mônot dress reminiscent of the look the original Katniss wore to the 2011 Oscars.

The cast is about to be seeing a lot more of one another—and so are we—as the press tour ramps up ahead of the film’s November 20 release. But before all that, Zada invited W along as he got ready with Armani, talking personal style, his first memories of the house, and the Hollywood legends he looks to for inspiration.
What’s an early or standout memory you have of Giorgio Armani?
I actually bought my first pair of dress shoes from Armani. It was a last-minute premiere situation, and I love them. I’ve worn them a bunch. Timeless.
What was the vibe you were going for/on the moodboard for your Academy Museum Gala look?

We wanted something classic but with a bit of an edge. Something that feels really cool without trying too hard, which is what Armani does so well. It’s my first time at the gala, so getting to do it in Armani and sit at their table is incredibly special.
What are some of your pre-red carpet rituals?
I usually just put on some music and try not to overthink it. The playlist is a bit of everything depending on the mood—I always have to have some hype-me-up music.
You and McKenna seem to be perfectly in sync style-wise for your events. What sort of outfit coordination do you do with each other?
We both have our own style, and I think that’s what makes it work. I’m always excited to see what she is going to wear.
Who are some of your biggest style inspirations?

Paul Newman. I’ll never match his steez, no one will, but he’s someone I admire in that department. For myself, I look to Timothée [Chalamet], Leo [DiCaprio], and Brad [Pitt] at my age as style inspiration.
Your character Haymitch wears a necklace with a lot of personal significance. What’s the most meaningful fashion item you own?

I’m pretty sentimental about things people have given me, especially when there’s a story behind them. I have a few things from friends and family that mean a lot to me, and I like that they don’t have to mean anything to anyone else for them to be special. I have a bangle from my mum that I never take off.
The Academy Museum Gala is basically a room full of people you’ve grown up watching. Who would leave you genuinely starstruck if you ran into them at the event and why?

There are so many people I’d be over the moon to meet, but Paul Thomas Anderson would be pretty crazy. I’ve grown up watching his films, and he’s one of those people whose career you can’t help but admire. It would be a dream to work with him.
What’s one fashion trend or style of clothing that you never thought you’d wear but have recently come around to?

Honestly, I never really thought about fashion that much before, so a lot of this is new to me. I’ve been having a lot of fun with it, and I’m working with an amazing stylist, Jason Bolden, who’s opening my eyes to all of it. In Jason we trust.
What is the biggest difference between Sydney style and L.A. style?

Sydney style feels a little more laid-back and outdoorsy, whereas L.A. has a bit more of that polished energy. But both places are pretty casual at heart, and I think people in both cities like looking good without making it seem like they tried too hard.

items.title: Maybe Chatbots Shouldn’t Get to Say ‘I’ or ‘Me’
items.description: During four decades of studying the effects of interaction with computers, Sherry Turkle has developed a reputation as a careful if critical social scientist who approaches her work with academic rigor and distance.
items.author: Steven Levy
paragraphs: During four decades of studying the effects of interaction with computers, Sherry Turkle has developed a reputation as a careful if critical social scientist who approaches her work with academic rigor and distance.

Her new book, Artificial Intimacy: Who We Become When We Talk to Machines, breaks this mold. It is a polemic warning that we have reached a state of emergency where our humanity is at risk from overreliance on soulless machines who pose as our tutors, mentors, friends, colleagues, and lovers. Turkle is aiming for the high bar of books —Silent Spring, The Jungle, Unsafe at Any Speed—that awaken the public to impending crises.
Essentially, this diminutive MIT professor is taking on a multitrillion-dollar industry backed by a government eager to accelerate AI into every corner of our personal and professional lives.

STEVEN LEVY: Your previous books reported results of your research as a social scientist, often leading to troubling conclusions about how people, especially children, interact with computers. But this book reads like you’re breaking the glass and pulling the fire alarm. Why the shift?

SHERRY TURKLE: Like I do with all my books, I went in curious. But after 10 or so interviews, conducted during the pandemic, neutral-curious was no longer my state of mind. This was terrible! Here are these people during the pandemic, their families are suffering, reaching out to them, and they're talking to me about how they really want to just hang with their chatbot. When I was able to interview people face to face, I was not happy. People don't want to do anything in politics because they just want to live in chatbot-land. So the arc of the book ended up as—reality needs you. It couldn't be a worse time to give up on reality.
You write that social media set us up for this.

Social media softened us up by getting us used to the idea that if you're feeling sad or blue, open up your computer. Then it made you mad and kept you with your own kind. But now we have this new technology that has no reason to be first-person.
Do you think that we should ban chatbots from using the first person?

Yes! After a career of having credibility as not being Luddite-crazy, I'm not in the mood to give all that away and say all chatbots are toxic all the time. But this is very dangerous, a slippery slope. This is being used to basically say we don't need to pay for psychotherapy, we can use chatbots. In every serious interview I do, people invoke this myth about practice—that you use chatbots to practice for talking to your boss, your lover, your teacher. But when you’re bathing in the warm soup of total acceptance [from LLMs], talking to chatbots becomes the endgame.
You also have a problem with reliance on chatbots in the workplace, and a particular loathing for the term “human in the loop.”

When they use that term, it means the human has been taken out of the productive process and is there to do some sort of cleanup work, to catch the hallucinations or things the AI doesn’t see. That doesn't work, because employers only have a couple of humans in the loop. Those people basically can't change anything. They are there partly to make it sound good when they're litigated, and partly to give people a false sense that the process hasn't been delegated to an AI. But it has been delegated to an AI.

Maybe powerful chatbots are a new form of interaction that isn’t necessarily worse than human conversation, but different, as people report feeling encouraged and empowered by the positive feedback they provide.

An AI won't ever replace human conversation. It’s really not afraid of death, it’s not afraid of illness, it's not afraid of pain, it doesn't love its children, and it doesn't care if you kill yourself or make dinner. So if we raise our kids with it, or have our most intimate conversations with it, we're going to lose contact.
Still, a lot of people have nobody to talk to. They feel that talking to chatbots helps them.
If there's a crisis of loneliness, it's because we're abandoning each other. Give me one data center, and I will turn it into resources for the elderly.

Studies show that most people are skeptical about AI, and there has been considerable pushback. Yet hundreds of millions of people use them. Even people who push back against data centers are using chatbots.
The goal of this book is to expand the terms of the pushback to include this more intimate connection.
Do you really feel that our growing intimacy with AI can be stopped?

I have more hope now than I did six months ago, because of all of this talk about extinction events and Hugging Face and getting into the Australian civil service by mistake. I feel that people will be willing to look at the intimate as well as the non-intimate costs.
This is an edition of Steven Levy’s and Lauren Goode's Backchannel newsletter. Read previous newsletters here.

items.title: How ‘Final Fantasy VII Revelation’ Strikes the Balance Between Old and New
items.description: If you're on the brink of completing one of the most ambitious projects in video game history, you're probably stressed. If said project is the decade-spanning Final Fantasy VII Remake trilogy, a ground-up rebuild and drastic expansion of one of the most influ
items.author: Matt Kamen
paragraphs: If you're on the brink of completing one of the most ambitious projects in video game history, you're probably stressed. If said project is the decade-spanning Final Fantasy VII Remake trilogy, a ground-up rebuild and drastic expansion of one of the most influential games of the last 30 years, you’d probably be even more anxious.

Naoki Hamaguchi doesn’t seem stressed, though. When I ask the Square Enix studio head and game director how he’s feeling as the release of Final Fantasy VII Revelation draws near, capping a series he’s worked on for over a decade, the only reply is a wry “I was just so focused, it really felt like it passed in a flash.”

Hamaguchi’s calm demeanor is all the more surprising given the weight of expectation surrounding the project. The original Final Fantasy VII, released on Sony's PlayStation in 1997, was a pop-cultural phenomenon—not the Japanese-RPG series’ first Western release, but undeniably its breakthrough title; one that arrived right as gaming was growing out of its kids-only niche and into a mainstream medium.

It’s still regarded as one of the best Final Fantasy entries, and its tale of reluctant hero Cloud Strife and his scrappy band of eco-warrior friends battling an all-powerful corporation destroying the planet is more relevant than ever.

A remake has been brewing since the PlayStation 2 era, and even teased with a cinematic tech demo alongside the PS3 reveal. Yet when Final Fantasy VII Remake finally arrived in 2020, toward the end of the PS4’s lifespan, it came with a twist—this wasn’t the same game with modern visuals and mechanics, but rather a glimpse of an alternate reality, one where events could potentially play out differently.

The idea was expanded on in 2024’s second chapter, Final Fantasy VII Rebirth, which saw characters hopping between timelines—but Hamaguchi is keen not to label it his attempt at a Marvel Cinematic Universe–style Final Fantasy VII multiverse.

“When we started approaching these things, seven years or more ago, I don't believe there were so many other pieces of media tackling those same themes at the time,” Hamaguchi laughs. “We don't really tend to use the word ‘multiverse’—we talk about [the story being] ‘multilayered.’ Actually, the word that comes up most often is ‘reunion.’”

That word may resonate with fans of the original, where test subjects experimented on using cells from an alien named Jenova, including Sephiroth, were drawn to each other (and that’s the shortest possible explanation).

Does that hint at where Revelation’s increasingly complex, layered narrative may be heading, with cosmic variations on Final Fantasy VII’s events all merging? Hamaguchi won’t be drawn, but offers that developer Square Enix is “looking at it from the perspective of these layers coming back together and reuniting—quite a unique perspective within the lore that we have.”

Other lore changes include the vastly expanded three-act structure of the Remake trilogy, which allows—or sometimes necessitates—reshuffling characters, locations, and events, placing many out of sequence from the original.

One of the biggest examples is the nation of Wutai, home of Yuffie, a teenage ninja who becomes an ally to Cloud. In the original game, she was an optional recruitable character, and Wutai was two huts on the world map, with only a few screens worth of houses and temples to explore when players entered it. In Revelation, it’s vast. This Wutai is a thriving city with people to talk to and secrets to uncover; you’ll even need to use Chocobos (Final Fantasy’s signature yellow bird mounts) to explore. It’s also somewhere players can actually believe is caught in a war with Midgar, the urban megalopolis where Remake took place. A lot more is going on here than there was back in 1997.

Some may think that holding Wutai (and Rocket Town, another key location) back for the third Remake entry was a way to pad out the equivalent of the original version’s third disc, which mainly left players to mop up side quests and chase down some optional boss battles before the finale. However, Hamaguchi says the opposite was true—even after two 100-plus hour previous games, he was worried about how much was still left to fit into Revelation.

“I did see people online talking about things after Rebirth, saying, ‘Are you going to have enough to fill up another game? What's gonna happen?’” he says. “I was sat there like, ‘No, this is the opposite problem!’ I'm looking at everything we've still got to put in, and how are we going to get it in there? We actually had to be quite careful with what we put in there to avoid having too much content.”

Revelation may still feel crammed, though. It brings in the final two playable characters from the original game, aeronaut Cid Highwind and were-beast gunman Vincent Valentine, expanding party options and battle combos. It also adds its own twist on the memorable Emerald, Ruby, and Ultima Weapon super-boss battles—incredibly challenging fights against literally god-tier foes, often with strict constraints to test players’ skills.

Along with the sizable new areas, the world is far more open, with returning locations from the prior two games promising extra story avenues and battles to pursue when revisited. Players can soar the skies in Cid’s airship, the Highwind (points for personal branding), before parachuting back down to explore further. “I'm not sure if there's anything other than Revelation that is really an open world on a truly ‘world’ scale, on a planetary scale,” Hamaguchi boasts.

On top of that, Hamaguchi has previously said it may take multiple playthroughs to see everything in the game. That might sound like a daunting time sink to some, but Hamaguchi isn’t fazed. “Personally, I don't have any reservations," he says. "I do understand that there were some people who said there's too much content in Rebirth, but I think essentially that boils down to preference.” Variety matters more than volume, though, and Hamaguchi says the scale has expanded with diverse gameplay.

There are a few olive branches for players who like their games big but not all-consuming, though. That multiple-playthrough requirement will take the form of a chapter select, so you can revisit specific scenes and see events from different perspectives. Rebirth's notoriously difficult and often repetitive trophy requirements are also being toned down, but Hamaguchi says “that's not to say that the achievements are easy—not just anyone is going to be able to get all of them.”

If there’s one thing Hamaguchi actively does want to change with Final Fantasy VII Revelation, it’s players’ perspectives on what Final Fantasy fundamentally is. Even though the series has evolved over the years—to the point where 2023’s Final Fantasy XVI was more of an action game than an RPG—outsiders often still see it as staid and formulaic.

“I think that a lot of people have the image or preconception about the Final Fantasy series, that it tends to be quite story-focused,” Hamaguchi says. “That is, of course, fantastic, but I also wanted to really showcase the gameplay and to show that Final Fantasy as a franchise, as a series, could stand alongside other open-world titles that are really celebrated for their gameplay, and I thought that would bring in more fans.”

“Showcase” seems right—although my playtest of Revelation barely scratched the surface, there’s clearly a panoply of stuff to do at every turn, with almost every activity offering a fresh way to engage with the world. Yet for long-term fans, warm nostalgia weaves through, as with the new “Function Integrated Tactical Suitwear” system. This fashion-focused (clock the acronym) tweak to the combat system lets players dress the cast as RPG character classes from the pre-FF7 games—think Knights, White Mages, Summoners, and sundry other Final Fantasy figures—allowing for extraordinary customization over who you bring into battle and how they function. It feels retro but modern, and just one way Revelation writes a love letter to the whole series.

A balance of old and new feels like the perfect capstone for a project like the Remake trilogy, celebrating the industry-shaking original Final Fantasy VII while shaping the franchise's future. More importantly, it’s already attracting the people who will help build it.

“It's been over 10 years since the Remake announcement now, and I’m starting to come across people who are saying ‘Final Fantasy 7 Remake inspired me to get into the games industry,’” Hamaguchi says. “They're coming up now, and they're saying, ‘I want to make Final Fantasy, I have these ideas.’ I think that's wonderful. Nothing could make me happier, and I'll just keep trying my best on the cutting edge to push things forward.”

items.title: This New Food Delivery App Could Be the Antidote to Menu Markups
items.description: Excessively marked-up prices feel inescapable online, even when I’m just trying to grab dinner.
items.author: Reece Rogers
paragraphs: Excessively marked-up prices feel inescapable online, even when I’m just trying to grab dinner.

I’m often hit with eye-popping menu costs and shifting fees when ordering through popular apps like Uber Eats and DoorDash. The major players charge restaurants commissions on each order, and those expenses often pass down to consumers, inflating the price of that chicken Caesar salad wrap.

Apps that initially felt like a convenient way to order food can now seem like a bad deal. But that’s what Olo, a new food-delivery app launching nationwide today on Android and iOS, is trying to avoid.

“Restaurants are paying 20 to 30 percent commissions to the marketplaces and are offsetting that by increasing the price,” says Noah Glass, Olo’s founder and CEO. The core selling point is that it doesn’t use this kind of menu markup.
On Olo, restaurants charge users the same menu price posted in-store, and Olo’s service fee is a flat 5 percent. Yes, you still have to pay a fee for delivery.

While you could save money by ordering directly from the restaurant, Glass sees Olo as a potential middle ground for people who still want the ease of a streamlined food-ordering app without all of the ever-changing fees and menu prices. The app includes 250 brands at launch, with plans to expand that offering.

Olo also eliminates one of the most frustrating problems in modern food-ordering apps: incessant ads. I can’t search for anything without getting bamboozled by sponsored listings. Olo shows a fairly streamlined list of restaurants near you that are available on the app as well as past items you might want to consider reordering.

The name “Olo” may not sound familiar, but there’s a chance you’ve interacted with the company’s software already. The consumer-facing food-delivery app is new, but Glass has worked in the digital ordering space for over two decades. He launched a startup called Mobo in 2005—before the iPhone—which was innovative for facilitating coffee shop orders via text messages.

Mobo was eventually renamed Olo as it slowly morphed into a behind-the-scenes software facilitator for restaurants, helping process their digital menus. Today, Olo claims it assists customers placing more than 3.5 million orders every day. These orders happen through desktop sites, smartphones, and even kiosk touchscreens.

It will be difficult to convince users to switch from their delivery app of choice—an app they’ve likely used for years. Even so, Glass is well positioned as an insurgent, with deep connections in the restaurant industry and a desire to target a core weakness of the major food delivery apps: inflated prices.
The next time I get a chicken Caesar salad wrap delivered for dinner, I’ll check Olo to see if it costs less. A deal is a deal, even when I’m being lazy on my couch.

items.title: How the Xbox’s Disc-to-Digital Program Works
items.description: After Sony announced plans to abandon physical discs by 2028, all eyes turned to Microsoft to see whether its next-gen console, codenamed Project Helix and described as “an open-platform hybrid PC-console,” will continue to support physical media.
items.author: Matt Kamen
paragraphs: After Sony announced plans to abandon physical discs by 2028, all eyes turned to Microsoft to see whether its next-gen console, codenamed Project Helix and described as “an open-platform hybrid PC-console,” will continue to support physical media.

Microsoft has largely stayed silent (though there are plenty of reasons to keep an easily accessible 4K Blu-ray drive for consumers). One big hint that Xbox may be gearing up for a disc-less future, though, is the rollout of a feature called Disc to Digital.

The new tool lets players claim digital copies of their Xbox Series X or Xbox One physical games, making them accessible anywhere they can log into their Xbox account. After a month of beta testing for Xbox Insider users, the feature is now open to everyone, and you don't even need an Xbox Game Pass subscription. In theory, it allows anyone to archive their physical collections—but it’s not without a few complications.

So, how does it work? It’s almost as easy as just popping the disc into your console, but not quite. Microsoft says “playing any supported Xbox One or Xbox Series X game disc while signed in will grant you a digital license of that game.” In my experience, this didn’t happen automatically when I launched a game disc.

Instead, pressing the menu button while hovering over the game tile on the Xbox home screen brings up an option to “Claim Digital License.” If it’s supported (more on that in a moment), you’ll get a pop-up showing “Digital license unlocked.” Disc-to-Digital games are tied to your Xbox account rather than your console, and appear in your library with a new icon on the game tile, a disc “disintegrating” into bits of data.

You can then install the game and any updates, then play without the disc in the drive. This will start automatically if you have “Play disc automatically” enabled in your system settings: Go to Profile & system > Settings > Devices & connections > Disc, and turn that option off to keep on top of storage space.

Thankfully, claiming digital licenses isn’t restricted to the current-gen Xbox Series X—it also works on Xbox One consoles with a disc drive. If you upgraded to the disc-less Xbox Series S or the all-digital Series X but still have an Xbox One, this opens a new path for backward compatibility: redeem physical games on the last-gen model, then install them digitally on the newer console. Overall, it's a remarkably simple and welcome process.

Keep in mind you can play digital Xbox One games from an external HDD if you're limited on storage, but Xbox Series games must be installed on either the Series X or Series S internal SSD or an official expansion drive. All storage is pricey right now (thanks, AI), but these proprietary format cards are especially so, ranging from $200 for Seagate’s 1-terabyte model to $550 for 4 TB.
The main issue? Disc to Digital is far from universal—not every Xbox Series X and Xbox One game disc is supported, and Microsoft doesn't have an official list of which games are.

First-party titles such as Halo, Gears of War, or Forza Horizon are safe bets, but this doesn’t extend to legacy titles—for instance, Fallout 4, released for Xbox One in 2015, can’t be redeemed as a Disc-to-Digital title yet, despite Microsoft acquiring developer Bethesda in 2021. Third-party games are entirely hit and miss. The Warner Bros. Interactive-published The Lego Ninjago Movie Video Game worked, but Capcom’s Dead Rising 3 didn’t.

The language is also confusing about why you might not be able to redeem a game. One disc gave the error “Digital license unavailable: This game is not participating in digital licensing. You can still play with the disc inserted.” Another showed “This disc doesn’t support a digital license: This disc can’t be used to get access to a digital license. This could be because it is an unsupported disc, or because the disc is damaged. You can still play with the disc inserted.” (And I could, putting the damaged disc theory to rest.)

In many cases, this is likely down to Xbox still negotiating with partners to include their titles. As more publishers come on board, expect more compatible discs. Right now though, the lack of clarity on which games can be redeemed, or what happens when they can’t, makes the whole process a crapshoot.

Sadly, this isn’t a golden ticket for all-encompassing backward compatibility, either. It’s strictly limited to Xbox One and Xbox Series games, likely because those consoles have unique identifiers for those discs. Xbox 360 and original Xbox discs didn’t, which could lead to a literal free-for-all of digital licenses if you could ‘rip’ a game and then pass on or sell the disc for someone to do the same.

This does create another point of confusion, though. When you claim the Disc-to-Digital license for a compatible game, you’re told, “Your digital license is linked to your disc. To ensure your digital license stays in your library, keep possession of your game disc.” That sounds contradictory, given the system also removes the need for a disc to play. After all, after claiming the license for Lego Ninjago on my Series X, I installed and played it on my Xbox One without ever inserting the disc.

Microsoft hasn't clarified whether this means the Disc-to-Digital license will need to be renewed by periodically re-inserting the disc. It’s a big “watch this space” for now, but you probably shouldn’t sell off your disc-drive consoles or physical game collections just yet.

The games you can redeem aren’t necessarily accessible across your devices, either.
