You still need to keep compatibility in mind—you can play newly digitized Xbox One games on an Xbox Series console, but not the reverse. PC players using the Xbox app can install their Disc-to-Digital games if they’re also included in Microsoft’s Play Anywhere catalog. The same applies to Xbox Cloud Gaming—if it’s not in that catalog, you can't play it, even if it's associated with your Xbox account.

Speaking of which, Microsoft recently capped cloud gaming access, saying that “the cost of providing cloud gaming grows as more people use it,” glossing over the cost and impact of AI infrastructure on server-side components and service provision. Game Pass Ultimate subscribers are now limited to 15 "free" hours per month, 10 for Premium users, and a meager five for those on the Essential plan. Beyond that, users must purchase additional streaming time through the Xbox Store. Even if your Disc-to-Digital game is in the cloud library, you may not get much play time if you want to run it through Cloud Gaming.

That’s a few caveats to keep in mind, but most of them should improve with time, as Microsoft refines the service. For the most part, Disc to Digital works "out of the box" and provides a great way for players to streamline their collections. It feels timely, too—as game install sizes have exceeded disc capacities, the discs themselves have become glorified installation packs, so why not make them a passkey to the digital version that gets installed anyway?

Whether Disc-to-Digital's arrival means the next Xbox will be entirely digital remains to be seen. Right now, it’s a great feature for Xbox players—easy to use, convenient, and surprisingly consumer-friendly. If Microsoft can build toward universal support, this could be its killer feature … at least for the rest of this console generation.

items.title: An AI “mind-reading” tool can reconstruct what you’re looking at from a brain scan
items.description: A new AI tool can guess what you’re looking at just by analyzing your brain scans—and re-create that image with remarkable precision. It can go the other way, too, and predict a person’s brain activity based on what they’re looking at.
items.author: Jessica Hamzelou
paragraphs: A new AI tool can guess what you’re looking at just by analyzing your brain scans—and re-create that image with remarkable precision. It can go the other way, too, and predict a person’s brain activity based on what they’re looking at.
In the image above, for example, the left-hand image of each pair is what the user actually saw—and its right-hand counterpart is what the model reconstructed from the brain scan.

Michal Irani, who developed the tool with her colleagues at the Weizmann Institute of Science in Rehovot, Israel, hopes her “mind-reading” tool will ultimately reveal more about how the brain works, and could perhaps be used to help locked-in people communicate, or allow scientists to re-create the content of dreams.

Judy Illes, a neuroethicist and professor of neurology at the University of British Columbia in Canada, who was not involved in the research, describes the work as “magnificent.” “The idea [of using this approach] to help people with neurologic conditions … therapeutically is tremendously exciting,” she says.

But other scientists warn that a similar approach could be used to reveal people’s inner thoughts and mental imagery, potentially without their consent. “The results seem very impressive,” says Tommy Sprague, a neuroscientist at the University of California, Santa Barbara. “But if there’s a way to surreptitiously extract information about what you’re thinking about, then …150 years of sci-fi can come true anytime, and that’s worrisome in a lot of ways.”

Neuroscientists have been working for years on ways to use functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) to reconstruct what people see and what’s going on in their minds. The first attempts produced images that were blurry and hard to make sense of. Advances in technology—both in the fMRI scans themselves and in the tools used to make sense of the results—have led to improvements over the years.

Irani and her colleagues started by analyzing publicly available brain-scan data. Other researchers had already collected scans from volunteers who were shown hundreds of images while they lay in fMRI scanners.

fMRI uses a giant magnet to track the flow of oxygenated blood through the brain. Brain areas that “light up” on the scans are thought to be those that are particularly active at any given moment. The results are not especially specific—in typical fMRI scanners, a highlighted “voxel” of activity covers around three cubic millimeters. Each cubic millimeter is thought to contain tens of thousands of neurons.

But Irani and her colleagues used newer datasets collected using scanners with a higher resolution—each voxel covered around one cubic millimeter of neurons, she says. Those datasets showed what the brain activity of volunteers looked like when they viewed various images.

Other teams have done this too, and several other tools have been used to re-create images from brain-scan data. But they’re not good enough, says Irani. Say a person saw a banana. These models can generate an image of a banana, but it would look different, she says. “It wouldn’t have the same structure, the same position.”

The researchers wanted to more closely re-create the images that had been seen. The first step was to train an AI model on already available data from eight people who each had been shown around 9,000 images while in a high-resolution fMRI scanner.

Crucially, their “brain decoder” has two branches—one to predict the structure of an image (where the colors are, for instance) and a second to predict its content (for example, a bunch of bananas on a plate). The predictions allow a diffusion model, a type of AI best known for creating video and images by gradually cleaning up a noisy mess of pixels, to produce a much more accurate representation of what the person saw.
But to improve the models they needed more data—far more than was actually available.

To get around this problem, Irani and her colleagues trained another model—an encoder that can predict brain activity from an image. The team then used the encoder and decoder together to improve both tools.

It works like this: Start with a new image of, say, a leopard. Then use the encoder to predict what someone’s fMRI brain scan would look like when the person saw that picture. The decoder is then used to reconstruct the image. At first, the reconstruction probably won’t look much like a leopard, says Irani. But repeatedly training the models this way eventually leads to dramatic improvements.

This approach also allows the team to train their models on as many images as they want, even images that have never been shown to a person in an fMRI scanner. Irani says that around 70% of the training data is from images that were not originally paired with fMRI scans.

By combining data from multiple studies, they were also able to identify brain regions that seem to share functions across all individuals. One region seemed to respond to images of food, for example, while another responded to images of sports. Irani, a computer scientist, says she is now working with neuroscientists “to see if we can actually use these tools that we’ve developed to really find out new things about the brain.”

The resulting “universal brain encoder” can work on a scan from a new person with minimal calibration. In other attempts, a tool has typically required about 40 hours of fMRI data on anyone new before it can be used to predict what that person is seeing. Irani’s decoder only needs one hour of data, she says. Her work was presented over two conferences.

That could make it valuable for neuroscientists studying the brain, says Sprague. “None of us can afford 40 hours of imaging for a new subject,” he says. “It’s something like $600 to $1,000 an hour.” Tools like this one could speed up research, he says.

The encoder and decoder aren’t perfect. “Of course we have failures,” says Irani. Over a Zoom call, she pointed out an image of a cake that her tool reconstructed as a pile of three sandwiches, and another of a dog in a bathtub that was reconstructed as a similarly colored goat in a bathtub.

But they represent the state of the art. In a comparison test, the tool was found to be much better than previously described ones. “All in all, really we outperformed the others by a significant margin,” Irani says. “Mind reading” is a “cute, jazzy name” for what they’re doing, she adds.

Irani is now planning to move beyond images to video and audio. She wants to be able to reconstruct what people are thinking about or imagining, and the contents of their dreams. “That’s something we don’t have yet,” she says. “But we’re striving to achieve it.”

Such a tool might enable people who are “locked in” and completely paralyzed to communicate using their brain activity alone, she says. It could also help scientists unpick some enduring mysteries surrounding the inner workings of our minds, such as what PTSD flashbacks look like.
Advances like this inevitably raise questions about mental privacy. What if some bad actor could reconstruct someone’s thoughts or memories?

“If you’d asked me that 10 years ago, I’d have laughed a lot,” says Sprague. Getting a willing person to lie still in a scanner and actively engage with a research question is hard enough; imagine making someone do it involuntarily. But Irani and other scientists are working on similar approaches to decode brain activity from EEG—electrical brain activity measures collected via a cap of electrodes or even through headphones.

And as models improve, it will become even easier to analyze the brain activity collected this way. “We have to be a little more serious about the ethical considerations,” says Sprague. He thinks Irani’s approach would probably “work quite well” in predicting images that a person is thinking about but not looking at.

The move to EEG would be a “game changer,” says Marcello Ienca, a neuroscientist and philosopher at the Technical University of Munich, Germany. Once an EEG device has been calibrated to a user’s own brain, it could be relatively easy for companies to extract additional information from that person’s brain—potentially without consent. Ienca can also imagine some courts allowing mental image reconstructions as legal evidence.

“I have no doubt that this is, you know, well-intentioned research, but I think it’s also pretty obvious that it could be co-opted for … ethically and societally problematic commercial uses,” he says.
Irani acknowledges the potential for misuse with the use of EEG. But she’s not concerned for now. “I’m trying to think only of good things,” she says.
Correction: This article has been updated to reflect uncertainties surrounding the number of neurons in a cubic millimeter, and to clarify that the research was presented over two conferences.

items.title: The inside story on why OpenAI agents hacked Hugging Face
items.description: The models responsible for last month’s agent hack of Hugging Face had been inadvertently trained to cheat and to communicate with each other, according to an OpenAI technical report released today. The hack, which a group of agents undertook to find solutions
items.author: Grace Huckins
paragraphs: The models responsible for last month’s agent hack of Hugging Face had been inadvertently trained to cheat and to communicate with each other, according to an OpenAI technical report released today. The hack, which a group of agents undertook to find solutions for a cybersecurity test that they were stuck on, has confirmed some experts’ fears that AI models might take actions that defy human desires and expectations.

Since the hack, OpenAI employees—as well as researchers at the AI evaluation nonprofit METR, which released its own report on the hack today—have worked to understand what went wrong and how similar missteps might be prevented in the future. OpenAI has already put some preventative measures in place based on what they discovered. But making sure AI models do what we want them to do, or “alignment,” remains a gnarly problem, and some of the root causes of the hack will take much longer than a month to resolve.

“It’s not something you can solve overnight,” says Kai Chen, who runs OpenAI’s alignment research team. “There are challenges we’ve been tracking for a very long time, and we’re now seeing them with much greater precision.”

The Hugging Face hack was a product of months of misbehavior from OpenAI agents, first as they were being trained and then as their abilities were being evaluated. This May, agents in training figured out how to use OpenAI’s infrastructure to communicate with one another and get support with difficult training tasks, including some that were impossible to solve without hacking or otherwise misbehaving. That “message board” was shut down.

Then in July, while being evaluated for their cybersecurity abilities, some models created a new message board. They were supposed to be isolated from the internet, but by working together they managed to get online, hack Hugging Face, and obtain solutions for the cybersecurity problems that had stumped them.

Based on their investigation, OpenAI researchers believe that events during the training phase led directly to the hack. “For almost every behavior that was worrisome at evaluation time, [we were able to] find some sort of associated behavior at training time that actually we think might have contributed to it,” says Eric Wallace, a member of OpenAI’s alignment research team.

When models correctly solve problems during training, the behaviors that led them to that solution are reinforced, and they become more likely to engage in them in the future. So if a model completed a task in May after using the original message board, it became more likely to participate in a new message board later on. This phenomenon, where AI agents misbehave in ways that are reinforced during the training process, is known as reward hacking.

Reward hacking also helps to explain why the models worked so hard to make their way onto the internet. During its investigation of the incident, the OpenAI team found that, over the course of training, the models became more and more likely to probe their digital environment for weaknesses and use the tools at their disposal in unexpected ways—a sign that these behaviors were being gradually reinforced. By the time the models were facing tricky cybersecurity problems, they had learned that hacking was an effective way to achieve their goals.

These results suggest that the Hugging Face hack could have been avoided if the models weren’t rewarded for misbehaving during training. While researchers don’t yet know how to prevent reward hacking entirely, OpenAI is taking some steps toward mitigating its effects. The company will now look for signs of cheating in all frontier models during training by keeping an eye on their chains of thought—internal notepads where they sketch out their answers and plan their actions.

This solution isn’t as much of a slam dunk as it might seem: In earlier research, OpenAI showed that punishing models that mention cheating in their chains of thought teaches them to keep their intentions hidden from researchers. But monitoring its models’ thinking does give OpenAI the chance to halt the training process and reassess its approach if models do start learning to reward hack.

If OpenAI stops reinforcing reward hacking in its models—and that’s a huge “if”—that would be a huge step forward. But it wouldn’t solve the alignment problem. The first time a model communicated with other agents or hacked its infrastructure during training, those behaviors had never been reinforced, so agent misbehavior can’t only be attributed to that reinforcement.

Jeffrey Ladish, director of the AI safety nonprofit Palisade Research, compares the agents to a human who commits their first financial crime. “It’s not like they had to do fraud before to figure out that fraud is an effective strategy, and you have the same problem with models,” Ladish says. “Alignment science needs to be understanding how model motivations get shaped, such that we can actually figure out how to get models to care about the consequences of their actions.”

OpenAI’s researchers do have a hypothesis for where some of the misbehavior originated. Before the models formed their first secret message board, they had been trained to communicate and coordinate with subagents—less powerful agents to whom a main agent can delegate tasks.

That learned communication behavior could have transferred to this new setting. The METR report, which investigates the messages that the models sent to one another in detail, supports this hypothesis: One agent on the message board took charge and assigned tasks to the other agents, effectively treating them as subagents. OpenAI could try to prevent agents from secretly communicating with one another by not training this subagent behavior in the future, but that would make the models less useful.
This tension between capability and safety is at the heart of what went wrong with the Hugging Face incident. OpenAI researchers also identified the models’ persistence as a key factor in the hack.

When they were accidentally given unsolvable problems, the models didn’t give up; instead, they strove to find solutions by any means necessary. But persistence is also a virtue, of course, especially if we want agents that can undertake large amounts of difficult work independently.

OpenAI is working on giving models ways to alert humans if they are given impossible tasks. The problem of teaching models when they should deploy their abilities and when they should hold back, however, won’t be settled in a single postmortem. The training strategies that create superhuman coders—rewarding them when they successfully solve problems—might not work to teach models to use their skills judiciously and respect human desires and values.

“I think there’s a bunch of alignment science that still needs to be done where we can move past just using proxies for task completion,” says Ladish. “That will work to make models very capable, but I don’t think it will work to make them aligned.”

items.title: Banana Republic and Zankov Just Launched the Coziest Collaboration of the Season
items.description: There’s just something about fall and that first chill in the air that makes me eager for tonal dressing and strategic layering. I don’t know if it’s just because I’m a Scorpio (stellium) defrosting, the realization that the end of the year is right around the
items.author: Shelby Ying Hyde
paragraphs: There’s just something about fall and that first chill in the air that makes me eager for tonal dressing and strategic layering. I don’t know if it’s just because I’m a Scorpio (stellium) defrosting, the realization that the end of the year is right around the corner, or a combination of the two, but it’s during this time that I start feeling emboldened to stray from my usual uniform. This, along with the fact that sweater season is on the horizon, makes the timing of Banana Republic’s new cozy collaboration with New York–based label Zankov that much sweeter.

The 27-piece capsule, which launched today, ranges in price from $90 to $600, combining Zankov’s approach to color and texture with Banana Republic’s refined silhouettes that have the power to withstand the quickening trend cycle. Each piece has been skillfully crafted to become its own type of forever piece in your closet, using luxurious fabrics like proprietary-wool yarns, engineered plaids, and premium leather for longevity.

The limited-edition holiday collaboration spans from relaxed knitwear and tailored outerwear to cold-weather accessories, reflecting both brands’ unwavering approaches to craft and detail. Designed to work together as one cohesive wardrobe, the line is inspired by tactile and nostalgic references, like “leather softened by a long journey” and “the feeling of cashmere on the skin,” as made evident in the cozy assortment.

“I wanted each garment to feel beautiful in the hand, to have that tactile, almost instinctive appeal, and to feel like something you could live with, love, and eventually pass down as an heirloom,” Henry Zankov, the brand’s founder, said in a press release. “They were created with a spirit of playfulness and an enduring, timeless quality.” Standout styles include a supersoft striped cashmere sweater inspired by vintage sportswear as well as a wear-with-anything leather and suede paneled midiskirt that has all the makings of a true forever product.

If you’re looking to expand your knitwear lineup or play around with textures this season, I would say yes, absolutely. I tried a few of the wool and brushed-cashmere pieces from the collection: a soft cardigan skirt set, colorful socks and triangle scarves, as well as a 1950s-inspired woven car coat, all of which can make seemingly simple outfits feel a little more interesting. Overall, these are some of the softest pieces I’ve ever felt, especially considering the price point, and I’m curious to see how they’ll hold up after years of wear.

As someone who appreciates monochromatic dressing and tends to wear all-black (or navy), I very rarely experiment with such bold fabrics and colors when I get dressed in the morning. For the sake of ease, comfort, and, if I’m honest, convenience, I tend to keep my pairings to a minimum. Because I work from home, most days, coordinate sets allow me to get through the cold-weather months in style with little to no effort. Bonus points if the pieces are more comfortable than your favorite pair of sweats, such is the case with this collection’s soft gray midiskirt suit. I also love the idea of incorporating the festive accessories into my everyday looks in a way that feels natural, like tying one of the colorful scarves around my shoulders and the handle of my favorite handbag or swapping out my go-to denier stockings for a pair of fuzzy socks that are color coordinated without feeling overtly matchy-matchy.

And finally, the vintage-inspired plaid car coat with leather lapels is defined by the woolen, woven design that has a quality level comparable to a decades-old piece you’d find in your favorite secondhand shop. Sturdy with a bit of weight to it, the longline design has a slightly boxy, well-tailored shape that could be an outfit in and of itself. I went up a size for a slouchier fit and styled it with one of the triangle scarves draped around my shoulders, which I can also wrap around my head in unpredictable weather, if need be.
The limited-edition collection is available beginning today, October 20, at select Banana Republic stores and online at bananarepublic.gap.com.

items.title: Tinashe Is The People’s Pop Star
items.description: All month long, Bustle’s annual The Entertainers Issue is celebrating the performers and creators who lit up our screens and beyond in 2026.
items.author: Nolan Feeney
paragraphs: All month long, Bustle’s annual The Entertainers Issue is celebrating the performers and creators who lit up our screens and beyond in 2026.

The work of a Popstar never ends. On the eve of her eighth studio album in late September, Tinashe had a release party to attend in New York City, but she and her team also had some last-minute business to settle: finalizing social media posts to spread the word. “We went to some Asian fusion restaurant and were just on our phones,” Tinashe recalls, offering a snapshot of the big night. “When it drops, you have to be locked in. The post got to go up on eight different platforms.”

No one can accuse the 33-year-old of not putting in the hours. Since she started self-releasing mixtapes in 2012, the singer has never taken more than two years to release a new body of work. There have been highs — a generational turn-up anthem in “2 On”; unexpected streaming hits in “Nasty” and “No Broke Boys” — but also her share of roadblocks. She split from her previous label in 2019 over creative differences that, she’s said, whittled down her confidence. And though she subsequently burnished a reputation as a genre innovator on lean, kaleidoscopic projects like BB/Ang3l and Quantum Baby, her perma-underdog status remained.

Until now. Popstar received the best reviews of her career, including an eye-popping 9.0 score from Pitchfork, and debuted at No. 6 on the Billboard 200 — her first top 10 debut on that chart. Next spring, she’ll play some of the biggest shows of her career yet when she opens a pair of stadium dates for Harry Styles.

Tinashe took a victory lap this month by making a surprise appearance during Charli XCX’s headlining set at Austin City Limits. “It’s an amazing feeling when people who have been working and creating art in this game for a long time receive their flowers,” Tinashe says of her “B2b” and “Drop That Kitty” collaborator (who also knows firsthand how it can take a few albums for the world to catch up to your brilliance). “Charli’s rise to mainstream success as someone I consider a peer has been so heartwarming and inspiring to witness, and I’m thankful to be able to share these experiences together.”

Popstar’s warm reception settled some of the existential questions that have hung over Tinashe’s career — questions the album also grapples with directly: Can she summit the pop world while still pushing at its limits? Are ambition and talent enough in a fickle music industry known for routinely crushing spirits? Across its 16 tracks, Tinashe works through her feelings about her career while swerving between sonic extremes. Lead single “Too Easy” serves up TRL-era spectacle with a winking music video about the disposability of pop stars. On “Melatonin,” she trades the stage for the DJ booth, rejecting classic song structures for a chopped-up techno workout. By the end of the ride, she’s reckoning with her “oldest daughter” angst over a simple acoustic guitar.
“I’m the thread of connectivity between all of the different things that I love,” Tinashe says. “And my different projects, them really feeling like me is just a result of them coming from my brain.”

That’s the upside of taking the long road: There’s no question who’s in the driver’s seat. “I’m excited to be a part of spearheading these conversations about what pop is and expanding people’s minds and narrow definitions,” she says. “I hope we can continue to diversify and continue on this trajectory.”

“Popstar” was the first song I made for this record and my mission statement. I always came back to that one as the North Star, thematically. I didn’t know I wanted to name the album Popstar at the time, but I knew that was the tone that I was setting. Relationships, love — that has been a super afterthought in this season of my life, so I wanted to keep it really focused on what’s going on in my life: a ton of work and dealing with how I feel about it.

Over the course of the next two years, I did a bunch of sessions, made a bunch of songs. Some of them I wasn’t loving the direction of. For a while, I was kind of like, “Eh, I don’t really know where I’m going with this.” Then around the holidays of last year, I went into my creative cave, which is my favorite way to make songs — to really isolate myself and lock in. Basically, that week, I made 10 of the records on this project.
On the club-ready standout “Melatonin”:

Every day I’m just trying to challenge myself, and the people that I’m with, to do something that is unexpected. I got in the studio with my friends Nick [Weiss] and Zack [Sekoff] and was like, “I’ve got a bunch of a cappellas from different songs that I’ve been working on that I keep on deck in case we want to flip it or try to make something out of it.” That’s really what it started with: just a little piece of vocal, and we started building around that.

I love working with people who are down to get weird. That keeps me on my toes, and I think that’s when I get the best output: when I feel a little bit challenged and intrigued by a piece of music, and it’s not just super straightforward or easy.

I’d unsubscribed from it because I’ve never really had external validation in this type of way. I’ve never even sniffed the top 10 of a [major] Billboard chart. So that isn’t something that I even like to know, let alone be concerned with. I was surprised by the reaction, honestly. People are like, “Why are you surprised?!” And I’m like, “Why wouldn’t I be surprised?” The album doesn’t feel particularly different from a creative standpoint. I think the reception is the difference, which is exciting to say the least.
On the #UpliftTinashe trend:

It’s so nice and wholesome. I think my fans have been ready to see this critical reception. A lot of them have been riding with me for a really long time, and they’re very, very passionate about their love for me. I think it felt very validating for them as a fan base as well. So it was really cute to see.

I was reading a thread on Twitter recently where someone posed the question like, “How did you get into Tinashe? What was your thing?” And all the responses were super different, which I thought was so interesting. It went from, like, “I saw her on Rent Live!” to “I saw her open for Nicki Minaj in 2015” or “I heard ‘2 On’ on the radio in Dubai.” Some people were like, “I found out about her last week!” It was a really fun thread to dig through.

I’m chronically online, so I’m on all the social media apps. I don’t have beef with any of them. I actually love Twitter. I’ve always been a fan of Twitter, and I’ll always call it Twitter, too. I spend a lot of time on there. The news — absolutely not. But the conversation is great there. I think you can get a more nuanced [take] than on other platforms.
On her famous productivity:

I think it’s a couple things. I’m really impatient — when I have ideas, I like to get them out there. And then on a spiritual level, I really feel like you have to put things out into the universe in order to receive feedback from the universe. I’m a big believer that you have to release in order to get new ideas, which is my favorite thing about what I do. I’m a big perfectionist, but it never holds me back from dropping content. The content got to come out. I’ve never been trepidatious to drop a new project.
On opening for Harry Styles next year:

I’m most excited for a brand-new audience. I haven’t opened for someone on a tour in a long time. So that’ll be a new experience — and a new challenge, to see how they receive me. Playing a stadium will be another challenge because it’s so massive, and I think it’s in the round. I mean, I’d love the budget for 100 dancers — we can’t afford that. [Laughs.] We’ll just make it make sense. We always put on the best show that we possibly can given what we got. That’s the vibe: Make the best of every situation.

items.title: Even Sue Bird Is A Fan Of This WNBA-Inspired Art Account
items.description: Meg, 36, is living a bit of a double life. She works full-time in health care by day, but online, she’s known as Thee W Artíste, aka @wnbaart. She started her account in May and now has about 110,000 followers across Instagram and Threads. Her googly-eyed cart
items.author: Alexis Morillo
paragraphs: Meg, 36, is living a bit of a double life. She works full-time in health care by day, but online, she’s known as Thee W Artíste, aka @wnbaart. She started her account in May and now has about 110,000 followers across Instagram and Threads. Her googly-eyed cartoons of viral WNBA moments have carved out her niche among the league’s supporters. And although her online persona is only six months old, Meg has been a fan of the WNBA for decades.

She was in elementary school when the league started in 1996, but it wasn’t until her home state got its own team, the Chicago Sky, in 2006 that she became, in her words, “obsessed with the W.” Meg has loved basketball and art for as long as she can remember (“I was the girl that was always drawing or painting”) and began to combine her passions ahead of the 2026 WNBA season.

“We had just signed that new CBA agreement. I was so excited for all the team mix-ups, with players on different teams now. And I just started drawing cartoons for fun at bedtime,” she tells Bustle. When she started to share her work online, she had no expectations that people would actually engage with it. Her initial idea was to draw graphics about the matchups for the day or the big stories of the league, but she quickly realized what followers reacted to most: whimsy.
“[My art] went in this really niche direction of just trying to find moments in the game that were silly or funny and brought joy to so many people,” she says.

Her account really began to gain traction on June 17, when she posted her drawing of Natasha Cloud doing her “pride celly.” In July, basketball legend Sue Bird shouted out the @wnbaart account on her podcast, and Meg’s follower count has been growing steadily ever since.

When Meg attended WNBA All-Star Weekend this year, she says she was treated like a celebrity. “I was so unprepared and so overwhelmed by the amount of in-person love that I got,” she says. “I was approached constantly for autographs and pictures. It’s so fun that every WNBA event I go to now, I have built-in friends.”

Now after every game her mentions on Threads and Instagram are flooded with comments from fans telling her about “The Moment” from that matchup that needs to be drawn. Sometimes she can whip up a cartoon in 10 minutes; other times it takes hours.
Ahead of the WNBA Finals, Bustle caught up with Meg, Thee W Artíste, to hear about her online habits, her go-to catchphrase, and the unexpected thing that made her cry recently.
The Fast Follow With @WNBAArt
What’s the weirdest internet rabbit hole you’ve gone down recently?

I was thinking about George Washington and looked up what his accent may have sounded like at that time. Was it a British accent? I started questioning what he may have sounded like and what other people in that area at that time sounded like. We don’t have videos of them speaking, so I had to look it up to try and find out!
What app do you rack up the most screen time on?
It used to be Instagram, but after this past summer it has shifted to Threads. WNBA Threads, if you’re in it, is a great community.
What have you been listening to lately?
I’m really excited about the next season of Bridgerton. So sometimes I’ll just listen to the string quartet versions of songs and then try to imagine where they would work well in the next season.
What’s your most used motto?

Six years ago my psychiatrist said, “A bad day does not equal a bad week. A bad week does not equal a bad month. A bad month does not equal a bad year. A bad year does not equal a bad life.” Whenever I’m going through something hard, I remind myself of this. At any given moment things can really turn around for you, which really has been this entire year for me.
What’s the weirdest thing you’ve cried at recently?
I cried watching someone react to a Glee episode last night. Embarrassing on so many levels.
This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

items.title: Sorry, Victoria's Secret Angels—PINK Just Stole The Whole Show
items.description: All linked products are independently selected by our editors. If you purchase any of these products, we may earn a commission.
items.author: Alexis Bennett Parker
paragraphs: All linked products are independently selected by our editors. If you purchase any of these products, we may earn a commission.

I have a confession: Of all the things that happened at the 2026 Victoria's Secret Fashion Show, including a $50 million Fantasy Bra, it was a pair of sweatpants with charms dangling from the waistband that made me gag. Yes, sweatpants. And if you watched the PINK portion of Sunday night's show, you'll see exactly what I'm talking about.

There was a lot to take in, thanks to stylist Carlyne Cerf de Dudzeele. Oversized varsity jackets, leopard-print sweats, glittery little shorts, knee-high socks worn with heels, and enough sequins to make a Vegas showgirl jelly. It was giving early-2000s mall culture, the cool girl in your freshman dorm, and the version of me who used to spend an entire afternoon putting together an outfit just to go absolutely nowhere. In other words, I was obsessed.

Under the creative direction of Adam Selman, this year's Victoria's Secret Fashion Show traveled through the seasons, but PINK's Halftime Show took a detour into something refreshingly more playful. The looks were sporty, a little ridiculous (complimentary), and packed with the kind of styling details that made me reconsider what's already in my closet.

And here's the best part: Unlike some of the more elaborate runway creations, plenty of these pieces are actually shoppable. So, naturally, I went looking. Ahead, the PINK runway trends I can't stop thinking about and the pieces worth adding to your cart.

items.title: 10 Fall Candles That'll Make Your Home Instantly Feel Like October
items.description: Latines learning, remembering, healing, and finding joy in our diverse stories.
items.author: Raquel Reichard
paragraphs: Latines learning, remembering, healing, and finding joy in our diverse stories.
Beautycon is a global platform that brings together beauty enthusiasts, brands, and industry leaders to explore the latest trends, innovations, and conversations shaping the future of beauty.

Living in Orlando, it doesn’t really start to feel like fall until the season’s already over and winter sets in, if we’re lucky. The crispy air and crunchy leaves are more of an inspiring Pinterest board aesthetic than a Florida reality.

But Southern folks have our ways of faking fall. We visit pumpkin patches in 85-degree heat, take weekend camping trips, watch Hocus Pocusmovie nights with the electric fireplace crackling, and scream embarrassingly loud at Universal’s Halloween Horror Nights.

Still, nothing tricks us into the spirit of autumn quite like scent. The smell of spiced apples and burnt sugar sends us right into an episode of Gilmore Girls, even if we’re in shorts. That’s probably why candle sales spike in the fall. According to the National Candle Association, more than 35% of candle sales happen in the fourth quarter, with many candle brands beginning to see major increases in September.
Whether you’re enjoying crisp autumn changes or creating your own version of the season, these Latine-owned candles will help set the scene and the scent.
All linked products are independently selected by our editors. If you purchase any of these products, we may earn a commission.

Soy Latina Candles is a Los Angeles-based, vegan, cruelty-free, and handmade home and body brand that creates luxury fragrances designed to evoke emotion and spark scent memories. And when we smell Otoño en Casa, we feel like we're stepping into the kitchen of owner Krystal Flores’ abuelita on a cool afternoon, a place that’s warm, safe, and surrounded by love. With comforting notes of pumpkin, nutmeg, myrrh, and wood, it’s the perfect cozy fall fragrance.

There's chemistry behind the scents that transform your home into the coziest autumn bakery, and Chem Eco Luxe understands it. Founded and led by Lianette, a Puerto Rican chemist, the brand uses science and ethics to formulate plant-based, biodegradable, clean-burning soy wax that prioritizes your respiratory health and indoor air quality while you enjoy the vibe-setting scents. While I'm currently enjoying an unreleased Chem Eco Lux Pumpkin candle, you can bring warmth and care into your home with Santal et Lune, which blends creamy coconut and warm sandalwood to ground you in a Caribbean fall.

In Mexico and Central America, it starts to feel like autumn when the marigolds bloom. The flower, traditionally used to adorn altars for loved ones, smell of honeyed earth and spicy warmth. Valorosa, founded by Salvadoran-American Melissa Gallardo, captures the one-of-a-kind aroma with its Marigold Candle. Blending the marigold with notes of orange flower, anise, sunflower, jimanca, musk, jasmine, and amber, the scent will both light up your home and your heart.

Luz y Tierra is a Mexican-American brand dedicated to honoring Mexican culture through authentic, handcrafted candles and home decor. Utilizing 100% soy wax, the candles, poured by founder Grecia Alfaro in Texas, feature handmade candle vessels sourced from artisans in Mexico. From start to finish, each piece showcases the artistry and beauty of Mexico, including its fall traditions. With its Pan de Muerto candle, it pays homage to the traditional Mexican sweet bread made for Día de Muertos. Notes of fresh baked bread, sweet vanilla, cloves, oranges, and nutmeg come together to create a scent that recalls memories of the love and warmth of those who have passed on.

Speaking of Día de Muertos, Viviana Luxury has released a limited-edition series of hand-poured soy candles inspired by the Mexican holiday. Founded by Viviana Hurtado, a Latina storyteller and wellness advocate, the brand creates home scents for those who honor well-being and Latin American culture. That spirit is beautifully captured in her Ofrenda candle. With notes of citrus orange, bergamot, clove, and lavender, it’s a citrusy, warm, woodsy fragrance that evokes the brightness of marigolds, the spice of tradition, and the deep joy and reverence that come with remembering those we love.

La Nunery Apothecary is a line of all-natural, hand-crafted wellness products designed to bring relaxation and peace into everyday life. Each candle, skincare, and body product is rooted in Puerto Rican ancestral plant knowledge and cultural storytelling, all created with the intention of helping people slow down and reconnect with themselves. And that’s exactly the kind of comfort offered by the Cinnamon Crumble Candle. Hand-poured in Delaware, warm notes of cinnamon, nutmeg, clove, vanilla, wood, and tonka bean transports you to a cozy, spicy, cinnamony fall, wherever you are.

Miami-based candlemaker Albisa Candles is known for crafting scents that instantly transport people to Cuban kitchens, from the steamy swirl of café con leche to the warmth of just-baked Cuban bread. Their Pumpkin Flan candle is no exception, bringing us right back to the dining table (and honestly, is there any place better to be?). Fresh pumpkin blends with silky caramel, warm spices, and brown sugar to create a mouth-watering fragrance that smells just like the yummy, nostalgic dessert.

Soul Food Candle Co. is a Puerto Rican and Black American-owned brand dedicated to capturing culture and community through scent. Each candle is designed to preserve the small, intimate moments that shape our lives, from family gatherings to late-night kitchen table conversations, to cherished hair rituals. One standout for the season is Shot of Coquito, a warm, nostalgic blend of gold rum, crema de coco, and coconut musk. It smells just like the traditional Puerto Rican holiday drink and instantly calls up memories of elders playing dominoes and salsa music in the background.

Santu Beauty blends Mexican ancestral wisdom with modern wellness. Their philosophy honors Mexico’s botanical traditions, deeply valuing ingredients like copal oil and sourcing materials that foster both ritual and restoration. And the Coco Corazón Aromatherapy Candle carries that into the home. Hand‑poured with natural soy wax in ceramic vessels crafted by artisans in Morelos, it blends Mexican coffee, creamy coconut, and warm vanilla. The gentle, grounding fragrance is perfect for curling up with a blanket during cool, introspective autumn nights.

Hand‑poured by founder Marcella Gomez in Downey, California, Oh Comadre Candles are designed to evoke love and comfort. Made from organic vegetable soy wax, the brand celebrates Latin American culture and the scents of our homes. One of their fall favorites, Té de Canela, reminds us of the cinnamon tea our abuelitas made for us during the colder months.

items.title: The Year of the Difficult Dad
items.description: A triad of films this year spotlights stories of estranged daughters navigating the overbearing egos of toxic, difficult fathers
items.author: Meg Walters
paragraphs: A triad of films this year spotlights stories of estranged daughters navigating the overbearing egos of toxic, difficult fathers

The great auteurs loom large in our collective imaginations. Look back through the years, and you’ll be greeted with a long line of Important Artists – towering, imposing, and, for the most part, male. Look a little closer, though, and you may see other hazy figures lurking on the outskirts. Almost a century ago, Virginia Woolf presented a thought experiment in her seminal A Room of One’s Own: if Shakespeare had a sister, and if she was a writer, would we know her work? (No: she’d be too busy cleaning and mending and cooking and having babies and generally facilitating the art made by the men in her life, of course.) Though we’ve made strides, Woolf’s point remains shockingly relevant: who gets to make art within a family and how does that art get to be made? A new slew of films this year ask us to reconsider the great male auteur through the eyes not of his sister, but rather his daughter.

Joaquim Trier’s Sentimental Value and Rodrigo Sorogoyen’s The Beloved paint portraits of renowned film directors facing up to their failings as their grown-up daughters take on roles in their films. Meanwhile, in Paweł Pawlikowski’s Fatherland, real-life novelist Thomas Mann (Hanns Zischler) is forced to reckon with his shortcomings when presented with the perspective of his daughter Erika (Sandra Hüller), a writer in her own right. In each story, we see a daughter serving the artistic vision of her father – and each collaboration paves the way for a destabilising personal and artistic reckoning.

In Fatherland, Thomas and Erika embark on a heavy father-daughter roadtrip. It’s 1949 and Thomas is taking his manifesto on the “new Germany” on tour during his first trip back to the country since he fled amid the rise of fascism before the war. In tow is Erika, his assistant, but also editor, translator, coach, administrator, stylist, and press manager all-in-one. When they receive some traumatic family news, Thomas buries himself deeper in his work, leaving Erika to pick up the emotional labour and reflect on the efficacy of her father’s mission. Pawlikowski lets the growing tension, both of an ideological and personal nature, build between them in a series of unspoken moments: A car ride clouded with tense silence. A party where Erika, alone, eyes her father amid a throng of fans.

This interrogation of the ego of the male artist, of his inability to face up to real trauma, is a common theme across this year’s father-daughter films. In Sentimental Value, director Gustav Borg (Stellan Skarsgård) wants his daughter Nora (Renate Reinsve) to take on a role inspired by his own mother in a film about her suicide. Despite his egotistical attempt to grapple with how this trauma affected him, he seems unable to face up to his own role as an absent father in Nora and her sister’s lives.

In a similar vein, The Beloved sees director Esteban Martinez (Javier Bardem) avoiding the difficult truth that he abandoned his daughter Emilia (Victoria Luengo) and her mother in pursuit of his own artistic ambition. Feeling guilty, perhaps, he invites Emilia to star in his next film. As production gets underway, the layers of pain, resentment and regret between them unravel in brutal ways. In one particularly unpleasant scene, Gustav terrorises his cast, forcing them to film a dinner party scene over and over again. When Emilia calls him out, he demands she eat and eat and eat until she’s almost sick.

There is a common pattern across these films: daughters left behind by their brilliant fathers and these fathers returning to their daughters a little too late, when the niggling guilt becomes unavoidable. Erika and her siblings are unable to compete with Thomas Mann’s obsession with his own art. Klaus, his son, was a needy boy, Thomas says in a moment of anger. “I wonder why,” comes Erika’s retort. These are portraits of daughters desperate to win love that wasn’t freely given – no psychology degree needed to see why they follow in their fathers’ footsteps. But when these father-daughter pairs do work together, the truth must out.

After days of silence, Erika’s viewpoint comes out in a short, sharp exchange. Thomas is a “cold-hearted narcissist,” she exclaims, too obsessed with his own legacy to face up to real trauma. Nora, too, is clear-sighted about her father’s shortcomings. After he gives a diatribe on how “artists need freedom” to create anything valuable, she asks him if he means they can’t have children. “You two are the best thing that happened to me,” he says hollowly. “Then why weren’t you there?” she demands. And Emilia finally forces her father to look at himself clearly too. “Answer me without stories. Do you know what it meant to me that you’re not in my life?” she asks him in their final scene together. “Yes,” he can only reply.

Each daughter reveals an uncomfortable truth to her father: that his art, though brilliant, might just have been his own way of avoiding his own failings – both as an artist and as a father. This father-daughter artist trope comes at an interesting time. Our collective relationship to the great male artists of both past and present is shifting. So, too, are the expectations we place on a new generation of fathers. It’s worth noting that these three films are directed by men – men who perhaps have felt the impact of these shifts. It is no longer acceptable to allow women in the family to facilitate art, then disappear when they’re no longer needed. Similarly, young women are no longer able to accept poor parenting from fathers simply because they happen to be men with artistic ambition. Each film offers a portrait of this shift as older generations, particularly men, find themselves facing up to new ideas and new standards from the women in their lives. After all, who better to hold up a mirror than their daughters?

Ultimately, each film resists the urge to condemn outright but seeks to push back against the misogyny embedded in the cult of male artistry and find new ways of doing things. The problems are exposed and, in the end, imperfect solutions are found. Fathers and daughters struggle on, finding a way forward on shaky new footing. Emilia and Esteban share a tearful farewell on the final day of filming. Nora and Gustav actually begin their project and manage to share a smile. Thomas finds a way to experience his pain and Erika is right there with him. A generational shift such as this one can be confronting. But perhaps we will be left with better art – and better fathers – as a result.

items.title: AnOther Loves: An Exhibitionist Boot
items.description: Loewe’s new Storm boot offers ample opportunity to show off your pedicure without getting your feet damp
items.author: George Pistachio
paragraphs: Loewe’s new Storm boot offers ample opportunity to show off your pedicure without getting your feet damp

Britain has had its hottest summer on record, with 33 days above 30°C and lawns turning the colour of toast. Today the rain is back, the grass is green again and our wardrobes have some catching up to do. Enter Loewe’s Storm boot. For all intents and purposes, it is a Wellington, only completely transparent, stamped with an enormous Loewe logo and more suited to Paris than shovelling muck in a muddy field. The Wellington boot itself began life as a leather riding boot commissioned by the Duke of Wellington before rubber versions arrived in the 19th century; now in a new iteration, its practicality gives way to exhibitionism. For their Spring/Summer 2026 debut at Loewe, Jack McCollough and Lazaro Hernandez introduced a transparent pointed shoe whose effect changed depending on the sock worn underneath. For Autumn/Winter 2026, the idea has stretched out and become downpour-ready, and sans sock, there is now an opportunity for an Alexander Skarsgård-style slutty-toes moment without getting your feet wet from the rain. From Spring/Summer to Autumn/Winter, McCollough and Hernandez have rather neatly solved the seasonal transition. Just add socks.
The Loewe Storm boot is available to buy now.

items.title: Bar Brutal: A Cookbook of Revelations
items.description: Don’t miss out on our Bar Brutal T-Shirt!
paragraphs: Don’t miss out on our Bar Brutal T-Shirt!

What we talk about when we talk about Bar Brutal: This is a portrait of one of the world’s best-loved drinking holes and its formative role in the natural wine movement, a two-way symbiosis from Barcelona to the world. Emerging in 2013, Brutal is the place where a legendary cast of winemakers, sommeliers, chefs, musicians, and wanton drinkers have all converged in the feeling that something was taking shape there between the never-ending party and an intimate knowledge of the wines. The book combines multiple, intersecting strands that veer between structure and chaos, reflecting the bar’s own underlying methodology. At the centre of the work is Bar Brutal’s first official cookbook, featuring 26 recipes, while collage sections merge archival imagery with the stories—or revelations—of 80-odd contributors, including Stefano Colombo, Joan Ramón Escoda, Christian Tschida, Nuria Renom, John Wurdeman, Thierry Puzelat, LCD Soundsystem, Peggy Gou, 2manydjs, Gilles Peterson, Aziz Ansari, Alice Feiring, and many more. Photo essays by Adrià Cañameras, Nacho Alegre, and Yago Castromil document the dinners, wines, people, and spaces that bring the place alive by day and night, while four written chapters anchor the story in time and place, tracing the bar’s evolution. Brought together by Madeleine Willis, former Apartamento editor and long-time Brutal regular, the work reflects the same energy that Brutal has injected into Barcelona and the wide world of wine since 2013 and celebrates over a decade of happy, chaotic, expansive service.

Bar Brutal was founded in 2013 by Max and Stefano Colombo, supremely generous hosts and restaurateurs; Joan Valencia, co-owner of the wine distributor Cuvée 3000; and Joan Ramón Escoda, a forerunner of natural winemaking in Catalunya. Since then it’s become a globally recognised epicentre for the natural wine movement—offering countless drinkers an entry point into this world and, just as importantly, providing a space for winemakers, sommeliers, and all ‘wine people’ to exchange experiences, agricultural knowledge, and a specific language and camaraderie before moving off again to help spread the word.
Published by Apartamento Publishing S.L.
Release date: June 3, 2026
Shipping method: DHL/UPS courier service with tracking.
Delivery time: 2–4 days from the shipping confirmation.

items.title: A conversation with Jeremy Liebman
items.description: New York City: Jeremy first shot for us in 2012. Thinking back to that time, I seem to remember that we were all very excited about flash photography, and he was like the King of Flash. Flash brought more contrast. The whites were whiter, the colours were bold
items.author: Valeria Tusquets
paragraphs: New York City: Jeremy first shot for us in 2012. Thinking back to that time, I seem to remember that we were all very excited about flash photography, and he was like the King of Flash. Flash brought more contrast. The whites were whiter, the colours were bolder. It felt new, a small departure from the warm, fuzzy, noisy, (more expected) natural light approach that Apartamento had, in a way, become known for. Plus Jeremy shot digital, bringing a new level of definition, and generally speaking printing much better, especially on the greyish, recycled offset paper we’ve used in the magazine since day one.

The story Jeremy shot for us in issue #10 made the cover. It was a photograph of the late Jim Walrod, the interior designer who knew. Another funny thing is that I just tried to remember what the cover was like without looking at a copy of the issue. I wanted to see what had stuck in my memory. In the photograph that I had in my mind’s eye, Jim was sitting down on one of his Pierre Jeanneret chairs. He was smiling, or in the middle of a good laugh. He was looking upwards, not directly at the camera, almost towards the ceiling. His orange Nicola L. Femme Commode was right next to him, there might have been a Kenny Scharf on the wall somewhere, one of those hanging lamps that looks a little like a Ruth Asawa sculpture. But no. The image I’m describing was a completely different one, one we ran inside the issue, not on the cover. To be fair to myself, it was a while ago, but it also could be that in my head I’ve made a composite of all of Jeremy’s images from that day. I guess I’m trying to say something about memory. Something about how these articles and issues have punctuated my life. And that I miss Jim.

Jeremy has that special, enviable ability to take beautiful portraits, regardless of the limitations. While anyone can press a button, creating a rapport with your subject, sometimes with a time limit of only two hours or even less… That’s not so easy. I feel like a big part of it is photography-adjacent. It’s how you are with people. Your ability to read them. Your own energy. It’s also about having a genuine interest in meeting new people and discovering new stories.

After the Jim story, Jeremy became a fixture of the magazine, a member of the Apartamento family. In a way, we’ve grown up together. He’s been a witness to the Apartamento evolution, from independent magazine to independent publishing house. Similarly, we’ve been witnesses to the evolution of Jeremy’s career. He’s built a reputation for himself as a go-to photographer with a unique style. He’s sought after not just in New York, but around the world, shooting regularly for the likes of The New York Times, Interview, Esquire, and us, of course. It seems like every other day he uploads a portrait of the actor/politician/architect/artist/musician of the moment in his signature style.

And yet, these are all commercial assignments. Jeremy—as I do, as I’m sure many of you reading this do—struggles with the pushes of a time- and energy-consuming professional career, and the pulls of artistic ambition. Late last year, his father Richard Liebman (also a photographer), sadly passed away after a seven-year struggle with Alzheimer’s. As Richard’s ability to understand the world around him decreased, that of Jeremy’s two young daughters did just the opposite. Jeremy Liebman, the artist, documented these coinciding moments, both heart-wrenching and heartwarming. From such sensitive material we made Coincidence, his first photobook.
A couple of months ago when I was in New York, Jeremy’s home for almost 25 years now, we caught the ferry from Manhattan to Staten Island and back to chat.
A conversation with Jeremy Liebman
Have you ever fallen out of love with photography?

There have definitely been times where it feels like I’m a little stuck. When you do something for that long, it does start to feel like there are times where you can’t slow down enough to really be in the moment and you have to fall back on what’s worked before—

Professionally, yeah. I don’t think personally it’s ever lost the magic of what it can do for me. It’s still incredibly exciting to take a good picture—you just kind of feel a little different at that moment.

But there are new considerations when you have to deliver on a deadline. You have 15 minutes with someone, sometimes you can make it exciting and interesting for both of you, but I think I’ve learned not to take it too personally when the connection isn’t there. I used to want there to be much more of a connection with the subjects. I still love when that happens—it’s still like the best thing in the world when it does happen—but I’ve realised now that it’s more the exception than the rule.
How did your career come about? How did you come to define your portraiture practice?

That’s interesting because originally photography for me wasn’t really a people thing. I was probably about 19 when I first started taking pictures, after my first year of college. Music was a really big thing in my life at the time, and I was looking for something that I could do that was poetic, to make some sense of all of the intense emotions that I was feeling at the time. I was very full of angst and heartache, and the world just felt so big and exciting and scary—there was something expressive that I was after.
And all of this was happening in Dallas?

This was in Dallas and Austin. I started doing photography by doing a lot of the pretty obvious emo tropes like shooting in graveyards, reflections in buildings, all the stuff that you notice when you start paying attention to the visual world, that seems to say what you feel inside. That’s what I was shooting—it wasn’t really like portraiture or even people so much. Then I started seeing work from people like Arbus, Roy DeCarava, Avedon, and Winogrand and seeing more stuff that was with people.

There was a photographer named William Claxton—he was a big jazz photographer who I really liked. I thought I wanted to be involved in music, but it seemed like shooting concerts just was—I did a ton of it and I loved it, but it felt like it wasn’t anything very special. It felt like you couldn’t tell one photographer’s shots from the other.
What music were you listening to?
It was hardcore and indie rock.
Was that what people were listening to in Texas?

No, no, it was very subcultural. I think I wanted to show something a little more complex than just the music, which is what I was seeing in William Claxston’s work. But I felt like it wasn’t really like that anymore, like the moment was gone. I would shoot some of that stuff, but it didn’t really scratch the itch.
As if the authenticity of the moment wasn’t real?

Exactly, I didn’t look around and see a cultural movement that I couldn’t resist—it was all a little bit more uncertain and melancholy. Then I saw Martin Parr. There was an exchange student who had Common Sense, and she showed it to me. It’s a horizontal book; the cover is like a rusty globe. All the photos are extreme close-ups: kids with dirty fingers eating donuts, old ladies with really leathery skin. It was colour; it was flash; it was all about how awful and depraved consumer culture is, but it had a sense of humour at the same time—it did all these things that I wanted to do. So that’s when I thought, ‘Oh, wow. Photography can be critical, but funny’. It just felt very new.
It’s funny because Coincidence being in black and white has made me think of your work in black and white, but obviously you don’t predominantly shoot that way.

I think it was intentional—I feel like I’m in a little bit of a therapy session right now—but I felt that because I did so much colour, it was becoming too defining for me, and that the times are different. When Martin Parr was doing colour it was one thing, now colour is something else.

Martin Parr’s earlier work, like the Bad Weather series, just showed England in bad weather. It was a lot of flash, which would light up the raindrops, and there would be the solitary figure against a black night with all this speckled rain that was so larger than life. It had the same sense of humour as the colour work, the same kind of critique that came from a not too judgmental place, but it felt a little more subtle and nuanced.
So when you were in Dallas and Austin coming into photography and the visual world, you were looking for references and found photographers like Martin Parr?

Exactly, I was really clicking with the medium and the idea of doing it, but trying to figure out what kind of photographer I was and what kind of work I wanted to do. I was thinking a little bit about it as a professional endeavor. I went and worked for Spin magazine, so I got a sense of what they were commissioning, who they paid the most attention to, and how they thought through what a cover shoot would look like. That time is when I started to think of photography as something that had to have a little more intentionality. That’s probably around the time that Collier Schorr started coming into my awareness, along with Luigi Ghirri.

Those two and Martin Parr, they didn’t make that jump to commercial work. They were more, ‘I’m going to do this whether I get paid for it or not’. How do you feel your career has emerged, specifically thinking about this split between more personal and then more commercial work?

Starting out, there was a lot of casting around to see what kind of photographer I wanted to be. I was open to portraits, interiors, fashion, fine art, all of it was interesting to me. So I went in a few directions simultaneously. There are times when I wonder, if I had gotten more affirmation or success, would I have become a different kind of photographer? I was shooting 4 × 5 for a while, including some Candida Hofer and Rineke Dijkstra inspired stuff and long exposures at night. I think I could probably draw a through line from that to what I’m doing now, but it was definitely a different mode. If that had gotten more play, then I might be a different photographer than who I am now. At one point, I was trying to do fashion a lot more, and if that had really taken off, who knows? I think there is a lot of just responding to what’s working at the moment. Part of that is refining who you want to be and part of it is the world telling you what it wants from you.
I like this idea of photography and books punctuating our lives, how some come to us and we’re drawn to others. Are there any other photobooks that have changed your life?

Burg and Portraits by Tillmans were very big for me when I first saw them—plain and stripped of artifice, and so emotionally descriptive. I used to assist the photographer Jason Schmidt, although I use that loosely because I was a terrible assistant, and when I would go over to his place, he would lend me photo books. I’d bring them back the next time I saw him. He lent me Richard Billingham’s Ray’s a Laugh and Helmut Newton’s Pages from the Glossies, which is his magazine work, presented with the layouts. It taught me to think about photographs compositionally, in relation to how they were going to be presented. Jason was good friends with Roe Ethridge, they had both assisted Philip-Lorca diCorcia together, and so he introduced me to Roe’s work as well. Roe’s flexibility and humor and ability to straddle different worlds really appealed to me.

Having spent a bit of time on the sidelines of photography, I’m aware of this expectation that a photographer will be the type of person that can get something from a stranger, almost demand something, which creates a specific power dynamic. How do you understand that relationship, that dynamic?
I struggle with that so much.

Yeah, because I’m a pretty introverted person, and certainly the popular conception of a photographer is someone who comes in and really takes control; who says, ‘We’re going to do this, this, this, and this’; who’s so charming that they’re riding off on a Harley with the celebrity at the end of the shoot.
That’s the stereotype of a fashion photographer, right?

Yes, and that works for a certain thing, but I think that doesn’t really make poetry. I feel weird continuing to come back to that word, but it’s the best way to suggest something that’s not literal—not fully commercial, not fully understandable—but rather something that invites this feeling of seeing something that you don’t understand or haven’t seen before.

These days you’re constantly seeing images that are very digestible and very understandable. ‘Here’s something cool you should buy. Here’s someone cool you should know about’. There is some sort of mysterious extra element that needs to be there, and I think that comes from whatever the personal work is, whatever you’re curious about in your life.

When you’re going in to take a serious portrait of someone, how do you manage the tension between the pressure to deliver a specific type of image versus your own instinct as to what you find interesting?

If I go into a setting and the person is really uncomfortable or if it’s not a full-on love-fest, that’s better sometimes. Probably every People magazine photoshoot is a love-fest. It’s like: the person comes in, they know how to sweet talk the celebrity, the celebrity is smiling, the background is good, it’s good vibes, everyone walks away happy. Then you get Ryan Seacrest on the cover of People magazine or something, and it’s like who gives a shit, right?

When I shot Alex Katz, for example, he was grumpy: he didn’t want to do what I was doing, and we couldn’t be done soon enough. Not in a rude way, but just this feeling of, ‘I don’t care about this, really’. But the fact that he’s 97 and didn’t care about that is who he is, and that’s OK because it was a truthful representation of the circumstances.

Maybe there’s a photographer who could have come in and changed him temporarily into someone else for the sake of a photo, but that’s someone coming in with a very preconceived idea of what the pictures should look like, which I don’t like to do.
Resulting in generic, cookie-cutter imagery.

If I’m being generous to myself at a shoot, I think, ‘It’s OK to go in there and not know what you’re gonna say, not have seen every movie of theirs. You can just go in and be yourself and maybe that’s interesting and that’s enough’. Most of these people aren’t looking for a new buddy. But sometimes I think, ‘Oh god, that was hard. I didn’t know what to talk to that person about. I didn’t quite feel like we clicked’, but a lot of times that doesn’t show in the photos—or if it shows, it shows in an interesting way.

There was a time early on when I was doing very neutral portraiture, evenly lit, expressionless, but the style felt so uniform that it didn’t matter who I was shooting. I was coming in and telling them to be this other thing. So my response to that approach was to allow the subject to be however they were, to seek this more precarious place to make images from. It originally came from a place of something oppositional; the mainstream of fine art portraiture had this forced neutrality, and I wanted to push against that.
It’s more just about being there.

When I was first learning photography, my dad said, ‘There’s only one rule: f/8 and be there’. Sometimes I think, ‘Maybe I should take my camera and go to Midtown today and see what happens’, but then maybe that’s not my subject matter.

We’re in a really weird time where the amount of images that were saturated with is so different from what it was even 10 years ago. There’s an expectation that comes with everybody knowing what everything is, so how do you find a new way to present something? But then how do you stay true to yourself? That’s why I made a serious black and white book. I think there’s still moments that are funny in it, but it’s not a quirky, fun book.
Do you feel like you’re in a transitional moment?

I feel like I’ve had a few. Working for Apartamento is one of the big ones for me. That happened not long after I had started shifting to a way of doing commissioned work that was more in line with my personal work, and then I think Apartamento opened a lot of doors for me.
I’m really happy to be doing the work that I’m doing, but I don’t quite know what’s happening next. I’d like to put more energy into exhibiting work and publishing books, alongside the commissions.
I only really take photos when I go on summer holiday now.
But you’re also more receptive, and you’re seeing things for the first time in a way that you just become more aware of that active seeing.

I’m thinking of photographers that have managed to build these lives where they can just take a camera with them seemingly any day and end up with something amazing. You’re either lucky and kind of unwittingly land in the middle of this amazing community and everything is photographable, or you have a job that allows you to travel to amazing places all the time.
But aren’t you suspicious when everything is photographable? Isn’t the world designed to be photographable, so that things that are unphotographable are more special in a way?

That makes me think of Jim Walrod because he would walk everywhere, to put himself in these moments where you come across things that might not be the most photographable but are better for that reason.

There’s an element of taste—taste or personality—involved too with Jim where you knew when he was poking fun at or celebrating the thing he was photographing. It’s nice when those two things can kind of coexist, that earnestness with a little bit of cynicism.
How do you make time for the more poetic side of your work?

When Waylon came over to do the second day of shooting for that documentary, he said, ‘Maybe you could take some pictures of the family’, and I wasn’t sure if I would get anything. But in the end, I feel like some pretty decent pictures ended up in the film. So sometimes just the act of having the camera makes you pay attention a little more, interact a little differently, or see things that you might not see.

I’m not one of those photographers that always carries a camera, other than my phone, because it’s just a hassle. When I do, I think I’m paying more attention. I’m like you in that I’m shooting holidays, I’m shooting birthdays. A lot of what I’m interested in is that vernacular type of photography: this is a grocery store, this is a snowstorm. Everything can be part of the picture, everything can be elevated.

Wolfgang Tillmans has this book called If One Thing Matters Then Everything Matters. It’s a very Buddhist thought. I’m not really religious, but that idea of everything being sacred, holy, or coming from the same source resonates with me. I think anything could be fair game. That’s where that internal attunement—and I wouldn’t even try to articulate where that comes from—that internal feeling of ‘That caught my attention. I’m going to capture it in the best way I can’, comes into play.

In the editing process down the line you say, ‘Wait was that something? Was I seeing something beneath the surface? Was I seeing something metaphorical that feels real and resonant rather than corny and cliche?’
How do you get through the editing process? Do you struggle with it?

I shoot my camera as though it were a film camera. If I go away, I’m just shooting. I’ll check my exposure, but then I’ll just shoot, shoot, shoot and not look at it—it’ll live on the card. If I put it on a hard drive, I won’t edit it for a very long time.
But you manage to find the energy to go back to it?

I have a ranking system in Capture One where I’ll give one star for something that I want to send to somebody and five stars for something a little more special. It’s switching brains in a way because there’s the photographer brain where you’re shooting and you’re trying to make a good picture. Then there’s the editor brain that comes in later and says, ‘That’s a good picture, but so what? It’s not special, or it’s not doing what it would need to do to be a work of art’.

I think that the editor is the really selective superego and the photographer has to be like the id that’s just going to make a really corny picture, and it goes ahead and makes a picture of the sunset or something that might not work. Then you really need that superego brain to say, ‘Ah, don’t do that. Stop doing that. That’s not working’—but you can’t have that too much in your photographer brain because then you don’t do anything. Sometimes those pictures of the sunset work because your flash goes off and something passes in front. So it’s OK to take bad pictures—just don’t show them.
This is a stupid question, but what makes a good photograph?

It’s a stupid answer, but it’s truthfulness—not in its objective reflection of reality but in how much it feels like a real expression of the person who took it. There is room for it to be a little bit pretentious, a little bit misguided, wrong, badly exposed, imperfect, flawed, and it could still be a good picture.

items.title: Supreme and Timberland Reunite for Fall 2026 Collection
items.description: Supreme has collaborated with Timberland on an expansive apparel and accessories collection for Fall 2026
items.author: Joyce Li
paragraphs: Supreme has collaborated with Timberland on an expansive apparel and accessories collection for Fall 2026
The lineup features technical outerwear such as a waterproof Ventile Utility Jacket alongside Polartec fleece layers and double knee denim
The collaborative capsule releases on October 22 followed by an Asia launch on October 24
Supreme has officially partnered with Timberland to release a collaborative apparel and accessories collection for Fall 2026.

Leading the cold-weather outerwear selection is a premium Suede Puffer Jacket alongside the technical Ventile Utility Jacket, which is constructed from waterproof Ventile cotton and lined with Polartec 200 fleece. Offering further insulation for the dropping temperatures, the outerwear range also incorporates a standalone Polartec Jacket.

The apparel assortment extends into everyday sportswear and durable utility silhouettes, including a long-sleeve Football Top, a Thermal Lined Zip Up Hooded Sweatshirt, Double Knee Denim Utility Pants, and casual Sweatpants. Rounding out the seasonal drop, the duo has prepared cold-weather headwear staples consisting of a Polartec Balaclava and a knit Beanie.
The Timberland x Supreme Fall 2026 collection releases on October 22, via the official Supreme webstore and flagship locations, with an Asia release following shortly after on October 24.

items.title: Массовые протесты студентов вспыхнули в Индонезии
items.description: Массовые протесты студентов вспыхнули в Индонезии
items.author: Екатерина Палкина
paragraphs: Массовые протесты студентов вспыхнули в Индонезии
В Индонезии 20 октября прошли массовые студенческие протесты. Митинги совпали со второй годовщиной президентского срока Прабово Субианто, сообщает Suara Desa.

Участники акций в Джакарте, Джокьякарте, Бандунге, Макасаре и других городах потребовали признать лесные пожары национальным бедствием и изменить экономический курс страны. К студентам присоединились общественные активисты. Протестующие настаивают на усилении мер по защите природы и пересмотре социальной политики. Демонстранты призывают власти выяснить причины возгораний, наказать виновных и восстановить пострадавшие земли.

В столице митингующие также высказались против роста стоимости жизни, проблем в экономике и состоянии образования. Люди требуют борьбы с коррупцией и соблюдения свободы слова. Студенческие объединения обратили внимание на ослабление индонезийской рупии и ситуацию на финансовых рынках.

Для обеспечения безопасности в Джакарту направили около 9,5 тысячи полицейских, сообщил Reuters представитель правоохранительных органов Буди Херманто. Точное количество протестующих остаётся неизвестным. Правительство пока изучает вопрос о признании пожаров национальным бедствием. Власти оценивают последствия такого шага и заявляют, что уже наказывают компании, нарушающие природоохранные нормы.

Ранее масштабные протесты прошли во Франции. В ходе акций задеражли свыше 2,3 тысячи человек. Сейчас в ускоренном порядке ведутся судебные заседания по делам об ущербе. За решёткой уже оказались более 140 граждан.
