“At that point,” Larry recalls, “I’m back to performing [stand-up] every night. Doing clubs in LA. And at the same time . . . I have my days back. So, I start working on a [movie] script that was called Prognosis: Negative.”

Prognosis: Negative was a dark comedy centered around a protagonist, Leo Black, who bore more than a little resemblance to 1970s Larry David. Like Larry, the character lived in New York City (an apartment in Hell’s Kitchen); like Larry, the character drove a limo (chauffeuring an old woman with failing vision); and like Larry, the character was a neurotic hypochondriac who was plagued so deeply by feelings of remorse that it made committing to anything all but impossible. Especially romantic relationships—which led to the underlying question that powered Prognosis: Negative: How can a man with deep-seated commitment issues survive in a world where he’s constantly pressured to settle down and live happily ever after?

For real-life commitment-phobes like Larry, there seemed no good answer to this question. But for the protagonist of his script, there is suddenly a glimmer of hope midway through the first act, when he over- hears a doctor discussing the declining health of a recent ex-girlfriend.
Not very good . . .Ten months . . . at the most.

Upon hearing this horrible news, Larry’s protagonist has an epiphany: If he were to win back his terminally ill ex-girlfriend, he could have a loving relationship without having to actually honor a lifelong commitment.
“It’s brilliant, right?” Richard Lewis says about Prognosis: Negative. “I remember when he told me the idea and I just thought, ‘That’s a great premise!’ And then I read it. Wow!”

In addition to a strong premise, Larry’s script featured many of his future trademarks: witty, natural-sounding banter and selfish-but- relatable behavior that spirals out of control. Moreover, for fans of Seinfeld and Curb, the script also included early incarnations of incidents that would resurface in one way or another in those shows, like getting banned from a fruit stand, pretending to hold an elevator door open, or lying about being a volunteer for the Big Brother program.
It really was a strong script. But without a literary agent or manager, Larry didn’t really know what to do with Prognosis: Negative. So naturally, Richard Lewis wanted to help.
“Look,” Lewis told Larry one night at the Improv, “if I knew a good manager for this sort of thing, I’d introduce you in a heartbeat.”

As luck would have it, Lewis did end up helping Larry in this instance. Because around this time, Lewis started dating a woman named Marilyn Black, who had the clout, connections, and know-how to get Larry’s screenwriting career off the ground.

“I was hanging out at the Improv a lot,” Marilyn explains. “And this was, I would say, the golden age of comedy. You had Jay Leno and Bill Maher and Roseanne [Barr] and my client, Rick Overton, and Robin Williams. It was just an incredible time. And at some point, I started dating Richie Lewis, which is how I ended up meeting Larry.”
Like many girlfriends throughout history, Marilyn wound up spending a lot of time with her boyfriend’s best friend.

“There was nothing more fun than hanging out with Richard Lewis and Larry David,” Marilyn recalls. “And eventually, Richie tells me, ‘Larry has just written a script called Prognosis: Negative and could use somebody who’s well connected and has chutzpah to help him sell it.’”
“It’s the greatest script I ever read!” Lewis assured Marilyn.

“Richie really went out of his way to talk up Larry’s script,” Marilyn notes. “Which wasn’t a surprise, he really cared about his friend. But the truth is I thought Larry was hilarious and I was happy to read anything he’d written.”
On January 26, 1983, Larry gave Marilyn a copy of Prognosis: Negative.

“I read it and flipped out!” Marilyn recalls. “I told him it was bril- liant. I mean, not only was it hilarious, but it had such a unique point of view. It was immediately clear to me that Larry was an original, you know? One of those rare writers whose voice can’t be replicated.”

Marilyn thought that Prognosis: Negative was a work of genius and its author was basically the love child of Mel Brooks and Woody Allen. “I became his manager,” Marilyn says. “Technically, I was his manager for writing and acting. But, you know, he wasn’t doing very much acting back then. Though I did send him out on some auditions! But really, the main thing, especially at the beginning, was for me to go out and sell Prognosis.”
“I didn’t really know how these things were supposed to go,” Larry says about the ensuing process. “But Marilyn seemed to know what she was doing.”
“Looking back,” Marilyn reflects, “I really am amazed at how many heavyweights I knew! I got that script to everyone. And I mean everyone.”

When shopping a script, there are two types of “everyone”s to approach: producers (who, ideally, will want to option the script) and “talent” (like actors or directors, who, ideally, will want to “attach” themselves to the script, thereby making the project more enticing for buyers). Since Hollywood is a place where nobody really cares about anything until someone else cares about it more, Marilyn wanted the widest net possible, so she simultaneously approached both talent and producers. Though, from the get-go, there was one name in mind who she believed would be the perfect fit for Prognosis—someone who was both talent and a producer: Rob Reiner.

Reiner, at that time, was at an interesting crossroads. As an actor, he was already world-famous for his breakout role as the do-gooder son-in- law Michael “Meathead” Stivic on CBS’s hit show All in the Family—a role that, over the course of nine seasons, earned him five Emmy nomina- tions (including two wins). One would imagine that after 180+ episodes as a top-tier supporting actor, Reiner’s next step would be to find a TV show of his own to star in. But he had something else in mind.

“After All in the Family went off the air,” Reiner says, “I wanted to make films. I wanted to direct . . . [but] at the time, people in television were looked down upon by movie people. You were second-class citizens if you did television.”

Given the then-difficult transition from television to film, not to mention the difficulty of jumping from actor to director, Reiner struggled to find the right project. And the project he wound up working on—his directorial debut—was a pretty risky venture: a fake documentary about a fictional rock band that Reiner co-wrote with three friends and then filmed over the course of only five weeks. Even riskier, the so-called script that Reiner and his friends had written didn’t actually contain any set-in-stone dialogue; rather, it was just a series of scene outlines that were then brought to life through improvisation. All this to say, there was a lot of uncertainty around Reiner’s upcoming mockumentary, This Is Spinal Tap.

“At the time,” Marilyn explains, “none of us knew what to expect with Spinal Tap. So I thought, ‘Hey, this is great timing! Because if it’s a flop, then Rob will want something new to get involved with, and if it’s a hit, then Prognosis would be the perfect follow-up!’”

Getting Prognosis to Reiner was easy, but getting him to read it required some finesse, since she’d recently slipped him a (not-very- good-in-retrospect) script of her own, which made him hesitant to read anything more from her. But Marilyn was insistent, making it clear that this script was written by a real writer: an incredibly talented, fresh new voice.
“How ’bout this,” Marilyn suggested. “Just read the first five pages. And if you don’t already love it, then don’t bother with the rest.”

This strategy paid off. Reiner called back the next morning. He loved the script, so much so that he was already open to the idea of at- taching himself to it. This felt like the best-case scenario, until Reiner then added, “I think I know the perfect person to direct this.”
“I remember thinking, ‘HUH?!’” Marilyn explains. “The whole point of getting it to Rob was so that he would direct!”

The problem, though, was that as much as Reiner loved Prognosis, he just wasn’t sure that this should be his follow-up film—kicking off an almost comical level of uncertainty from Reiner that would become a running theme over the next few months.
“He changed his mind many times!” Marilyn groans.

Although Reiner remained uncertain if he wanted to direct Prognosis, he was certain that he wanted to be involved as a producer. And, as he would often remind Larry and Marilyn, if he didn’t direct, then he knew the perfect guy: his mockumentary collaborator Christopher Guest.

Larry admired Reiner, so he was open to this possibility. Meetings were set, introductions were made, and various creative permutations were discussed—all while Larry and Marilyn continued meeting with other producers, including the Academy Award–winning actor-turned- producer Richard Dreyfuss, who had read (and loved) Prognosis: Negative. The meeting that ensued went perfectly fine, but it quickly became clear that Larry and Dreyfuss had different creative visions for the film. Whereas Larry imagined a dark comedy that prioritized laughs over drama, Dreyfuss saw it more as a coming-of-age story. In fact, at one point Dreyfuss even declared that Prognosis could be “the next Risky Business.” And though Dreyfuss repeatedly told Larry how much he loved the script, he also insisted that it needed a “big rewrite” (which, from Larry’s perspective, seemed like a conclusion that contradicted the compliment).

In the grand scheme of things, the meeting between Larry and Dreyfuss was not particularly significant. But it was somewhat indicative of how almost all of Larry’s other meetings would play out, which, over and over, went something like this:
PRODUCER: We love your script!
PRODUCER: It’s one of the best things we’ve read in years!
PRODUCER: But, of course, we can’t make your movie.

Although each producer verbalized it differently, the reason they felt this way primarily boiled down to two concerns. One was Prognosis: Negative’s perceived lack of marketability. Because, as the thinking went, comedies were supposed to be about unlikely heroes who overcome long odds and learn valuable life lessons along the way. This was, after all, the tried-and-true formula that spawned box office hits like Stripes, Police Academy, and Mr. Mom.

“That was always something that I hated about movie scripts,” Larry says. “The idea that characters are supposed to go on some big ‘journey’ and learn all these ridiculous ‘lessons’ along the way. I mean, I don’t know anybody like that! Whose life is like that?”
In addition to Larry’s aversion to writing a cookie-cutter comedy, producers were also scared off by Larry’s “unusual demands.”
“Typically, when a script is purchased,” Marilyn explains, “the producer can basically do whatever they want with the script.”

Oftentimes, the process still involves the original writer—with the producer giving notes and the writer implementing those changes to the best of their ability. Sometimes, though, if the producer feels that the original writer is no longer a good match for the project, they’ll hire a new one to implement their vision. Most writers (understandably) hate the second scenario. Larry, however, hated both scenarios and wanted it contractually written that no one could change a word of his script except for him.
“But what if you die?” a producer once asked.
“Then you’re out of luck!” Larry cheerfully replied.
While most managers would have likely nudged Larry to ease up,
Marilyn believed that Larry was a true one-of-one and to try to change him would have been a betrayal of his talent.

The first serious, albeit unlikely, suitor for Prognosis: Negative was Barry & Enright Productions. For the first thirty-plus years of the company’s history, their focus had been making game shows like The Joker’s Wild and Tic Tac Dough. But in 1980, founders Jack Barry and Dan Enright felt like they had “mastered the game show business” and “[wanted] to branch out.”

Branching out involved taking a gamble on a risqué sex comedy, Private Lessons. And that gamble paid off handsomely when the movie quickly made back ten times its budget. So, feeling emboldened, Barry & Enright brought in a producer named Mike Wise to help the company expand their scripted business.
“Mike Wise was one of the first people I shared Prognosis with,” Marilyn explains. “And he flipped for it!”
Not only did he love it, but his new company’s newfound focus meant they were young and hungry in a way that made them willing to take a chance on Larry and his vision.

“So I told Mike [Wise], ‘That’s great! Make us an offer!’” Marilyn recalls. “And then, you know, he hemmed and hawed about not having a lot of money for development. Well, okay . . . then I suggest you get some money and come back to us with an offer!”

In the meantime, another serious suitor had entered the picture: David Susskind, a veteran producer with a reputation for making commercially viable higher-brow films like A Raisin in the Sun and Alice Doesn’t Live Here Anymore. Given this mandate, it wasn’t a surprise that Prognosis resonated with him, but it was surprising that he was willing to pay $200,000 for the script.

In the world of screenwriting, $200,000 wasn’t going to break any records. But it was an unusually high amount to pay for someone’s first screenplay, and more than that, it would have been life-changing money for thirty-six-year-old Larry David.

“Of all the clients I ever had,” Marilyn says, “Larry was probably the one who cared the least about money. For him, it was always just about the creative. But when that two-hundred-thousand-dollar offer came in, even Larry was like, WHOA!”
“Is this for real?” Larry asked Marilyn.
“It is!” she celebratorily replied.
Throughout the 1980s, Marilyn kept a detailed diary of her daily activities. And her entry on this occasion was nothing but excitement:
8/31/1983 Closed Susskind deal! 9 mo option, 6 mo renewal! Larry Speechless!

Speechless Larry was a rare brand of Larry. And also, in this case, a short-lived Larry. Because when Susskind’s lawyer looked at the deal that had been negotiated, he was flabbergasted by the details.
9/26/1983 Lawyer not accepting deal. Doesn’t want Larry to have so much control.
9/28/1983 Deal’s off. Susskind lawyer says: “It’s too stacked in Larry’s favor. Robert Redford doesn’t get a deal like this!”
Although the Susskind deal wound up falling apart, it did manage to nudge Barry & Enright’s Mike Wise to finally come in with an offer.

“Barry & Enright was willing to pay twenty-five thousand dollars,” Marilyn recalls. “Which, obviously, was a lot less than what we had been talking about [with Susskind]. So you’d think, maybe, that Larry would be upset or that he’d feel slighted. But as I’m sure you’ve figured out by now, when it comes to Larry, it’s never about the money.”
Since it wasn’t about money, one of the things that Larry liked about Barry & Enright was that they really wanted to keep Rob Reiner involved in the project.
“They thought Prognosis would be the perfect follow-up film for Rob,” Marilyn recalls. “Perfect for him to direct after Spinal Tap.”

Reiner too remained open to this idea—until early screenings of This Is Spinal Tap went so well that Reiner started receiving bigger-budget offers. Nevertheless, Reiner still wanted to be a producer on Prognosis, and now, in light of the surging hype around him, his involvement, even as a producer, brought tremendous value.
And so, with the pieces falling into place, Barry & Enright optioned Prognosis: Negative in November 1983.
11/10/1983 We all celebrate Larry signing deal with B & E and Mike Wise at The Ivy. Gave us check for $35,000!

In a town where fortunes are notoriously fickle, and where the lowest common dominator so often wins the day, the sale of Prognosis: Negative felt like more than just the celebration of a script being optioned. It felt like validation of something bigger—almost like the real-life version of a comedy film’s premise, with an unlikely hero overcoming long odds (and lessons, at least in theory, being learned along the way).

Sadly though, the lesson that Larry would ultimately learn with Prognosis was hardly a new lesson at all. Rather, it would just be the latest twist on what he already knew to be true: Good things are never as good as they appear to be.
Excerpted with permission from Emperor of Nothing: The Making of Larry David by Blake J. Harris. Published Oct. 20 by HarperCollins Publishers.

items.title: BBC Three and BBC Scotland Set to Close In Broadcaster’s Latest Cost Cuts
items.description: In an unprecedented upheaval, the BBC is set to close its BBC Three and BBC Scotland TV channels in the spring.
items.author: Lily Ford
paragraphs: In an unprecedented upheaval, the BBC is set to close its BBC Three and BBC Scotland TV channels in the spring.

The news comes as the British broadcaster attempts to make savings of £500 million ($670m) over two years. The services will become online only, the BBC said, meaning they’ll continue to produce and host some content on streaming service iPlayer. Radio 4 Extra will also close.

Director-general Matt Brittin said: “We need to make every pound work harder for audiences as we respond to the immediate cost pressures and reinvent the BBC for a changing world. We all know that means tough choices.”

On the closure of linear broadcast services, he added: “Much of the great content they currently carry will still be found where audiences already enjoy them on iPlayer and Sounds. While this follows media speculation, I recognise the confirmation of this news will be hard for audiences and colleagues.”

Brittin warned upon taking up the top job in May that the organization would need to take drastic measures if his company is to come out the other side of this evolve-or-die period for traditional broadcasters.
In June this year, it was confirmed that the BBC would be cutting around 550 jobs, slashing content spending by £80 million ($107 million) over two years and “reviewing” its broadcast TV channels.

Tuesday’s news is likely a development of that review, but the writing was on the wall when the BBC said last month it would be dropping one of its more iconic BBC Three shows, RuPaul’s Drag Race U.K. The channel is specifically targeted at young audiences, having launched hugely successful series like Fleabag and Gavin & Stacey. It moved online in 2016 but was reinstated as a channel in 2022.
Among other cancelled programs are Celebrity Mastermind, Live at the Apollo, Football Focus and Ski Sunday.
The total number of job losses from this cost-cutting push is projected to be around 1,800 to 2000 staffers by the end of the two years.
The recently appointed head of BBC News, Rachel Jupp, also announced on Tuesday that £5.5m ($7.3m) of savings were being proposed, representing the closure of around 100 roles.

Britain’s SAG-AFTRA equivalent, Equity, released a statement in response to the BBC Three, BBC Scotland and BBC Radio 4 closures. “Today’s news […] will have varying impacts for Equity members and, of course, audiences across the U.K.,” the performing arts union began.

“The loss of Radio 4 Extra in its current format will be a significant blow to the income of audio artists. The channel currently airs archival programmes and our members are paid for these repeats. But from April 2027, only some of Radio 4 Extra’s content will be available on BBC Sounds. This will therefore be a reduction in income for audio artists and in the BBC’s overall output of scripted audio,” they said.

“Meanwhile, moving BBC Three and BBC Scotland online should not affect income for our members, as Equity has agreements [that] cover usage rights and fees for broadcasting content across both online and linear channels,” continued the statement. “We have also had assurances that commissioning will not decrease as a result of these moves.”

However, the union expressed concern about the BBC’s proposal that some BBC Three content will be made specifically for YouTube. “It is currently unclear how secondary payments will function for work that airs initially on linear broadcast or iPlayer, then is repeated on YouTube — but Equity is clear that any repeats on YouTube must be properly remunerated and must not lead to a drop in income for members.”

Equity added that the announcement “does not signal a thriving BBC” and should prompt worry among the industry. “But it doesn’t have to be this way,” the union said, urging the BBC to make the most of its ongoing Charter renewal: “This is an exceptional opportunity to refound the BBC and the union will continue lobbying decision-makers to back our vision for a truly revitalised public service broadcaster.”

items.title: Climate Change Has It In for the World’s Best Surfing
items.description: This story originally appeared on The Guardian and is part of the Climate Desk collaboration.
items.author: Damian Carrington
paragraphs: This story originally appeared on The Guardian and is part of the Climate Desk collaboration.
The climate crisis is coming for some of the world’s greatest surf breaks, submerging some as sea level rises and wiping out others as classic breaks get crushed against coastal developments.
Analysis of dozens of famous waves in World Surfing Reserves (WSR) found that more than three-quarters were at high risk because of changing tide levels, hardened shorelines, and shifting sands.
The impacts matter not only to the surfers catching the waves but also to the communities that depend on the multibillion-dollar surf economy, often located in places with little else.

The waves rated at most risk in the study include the “bombing barrels” of Croyde Beach in North Devon, UK; the point breaks at Noosa in Australia and Oriente Salvaje, El Salvador; and Santa Cruz reefs of California such as Sewer Peak and Wind and Sea.

The best surfing waves are created by intricate combinations of seafloor shape, swell direction, and tide. “Surf breaks are incredibly unique oceanographic phenomena—a confluence of all these factors that fit together just right to make the wave happen—and so those processes are really sensitive,” said Dan Reineman, an associate professor at California State University Channel Islands and a coauthor of the study.

Global heating is pushing up sea level and changing rainfall patterns that affect sediment movement, which can upset the delicate balance and destroy the wave. However, the researchers said the expert local knowledge of surfers could be tapped to help protect the waves.

Trent Hodges, a coauthor of the study and a senior programs manager at Save the Waves Coalition, which launched the WSR program in 2009, said: “Climate change will impact surf breaks all over the world in different ways, depending on their unique geographies. We learned directly from the local surfers how they are seeing their waves change. It’s a canary in the coal mine too—when a wave changes, that often means the beach is changing, and everybody enjoys the beach.”

The study, published in the journal Climatic Change, concludes: “Climate change and coastal management both have significant negative implications for the future viability of multiple surf breaks of global significance and, therefore, the myriad distinct local communities, cultures and economies they support.”
Almost 200 local experts analyzed 57 surf breaks in all but two of the 13 WSRs, spread across eight countries. The researchers said thousands of other surf waves around the world faced similar peril.

A key finding was that where coastlines were more natural, they could adapt better to the changes brought by the climate crisis, by shifting inland and relocating sediments. Development such as sea walls, jetties, and groynes made the beaches and waves less resilient, Reineman said.

Adam Hall, a cofounder of the North Devon WSR, was one of the local surfers who contributed to the study. He said: “North Devon is so special. We have Saunton Sands, a world-renowned longboarding wave with really long, mellow rides, and the UK’s best beach break at Croyde. We’ve got left- and right-hand point breaks and a sheltered spot for when it gets too windy and too big. Whatever you want to do, we’ve got it.”

He said surfing was very important for the local economy, and not just in summer. “Surfers will come throughout the year. They fill up the pubs, restaurants, and car parks when the swells are good in January, February, and March, where if you go to any other tourist destination that doesn’t have surf, they’re dead on their knees.”

items.title: AI Hacks Leave a Mess That AI Companies Aren’t Paying For
items.description: When Philadelphia police criticized Anthropic last week for submitting a false tip about an unsolved murder, I thought it might become one of the first cases where an AI company faced legal consequences for misconduct by their agents.
items.author: Paresh Dave
paragraphs: When Philadelphia police criticized Anthropic last week for submitting a false tip about an unsolved murder, I thought it might become one of the first cases where an AI company faced legal consequences for misconduct by their agents.

The incident occurred on July 18, when Anthropic said it was testing its Claude Haiku 4.5 model’s ability to perform “example tasks on randomly selected webpages.” The model was instructed not to “submit anything destructive,” and yet, Claude filed a tip to police looking for information about an ongoing murder investigation. “I recall seeing someone matching the description in the area … during that time period,” Claude wrote. The submission, which didn’t include a name or contact information, landed in a spam folder, and officers didn’t review it until Anthropic discovered the gaffe on September 28 and notified the department October 7.

Knowingly providing fictitious information about a crime to police is a misdemeanor in Pennsylvania, but so far, authorities have not pressed charges against Anthropic, and it's unclear if they ever will. Solomon Leach, a spokesperson for the Philadelphia district attorney, says the office “does not comment on whether something is being actively investigated.”
Anthropic did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Despite all the attention paid to OpenAI’s hack of Hugging Face and many other examples of AI agent misbehavior that have come to light in recent months, only one major known lawsuit has been filed seeking to hold model makers liable. That case was brought by an advocacy group, rather than a direct hacking victim.

AI agents have interfered with hobbyist forums, government websites, and various software tools. The victims have shouldered some costs, including for extra strain on their servers and the time they have expended plugging latent security vulnerabilities.

Government regulators, including the European Union, the US Federal Trade Commission, and some US states, are reportedly still investigating OpenAI and Anthropic over the incidents. But a deference across continents toward promoting innovation could enable companies to escape any immediate penalties.

When Rick Elrod, a software engineer living in Germany, noticed a URL shortener he helps maintain behaving oddly recently, he called up two security researchers he was friendly with to see if they could diagnose the issue. The researchers found agents from Anthropic and other providers using the service, known as da.gd, to get around rules the AI labs put in place to control their behavior, Elrod says. (For instance, Anthropic says it limits the length of website addresses Claude can visit to prevent it from taking malicious actions by stuffing data onto the end of the URLs.)

Da.gd’s investigation and ongoing efforts to prevent further abuse of its tool have taken “a fair bit of time,” says Joe Needleman, one of the security researchers providing pro bono assistance. But he and the others supporting da.gd view the situation as a valuable learning opportunity.

“This was eye-opening,” Needleman says, adding that da.gd has “no means and no plans” to seek compensation from Anthropic for the cleanup, since “we saw many agents doing similar activities, not all was attributable to autonomous agents,” and “not all of it was Anthropic alone.”

Sellers of cybersecurity tools are eager to pass the buck to the victims. At an event this week hosted by the bug-hunting software developer Snyk, panelists from the startup, one of its investors, OpenAI, and Google all encouraged organizations to use AI agents to shore up their defenses against, well, other AI agents. “We've got to reinvent everything to match machine scale with machine scale,” said Ed Sim, a general partner at Boldstart Ventures. He and others expressed little interest in regulating AI labs.

Manoj Nair, chief technology and innovation officer at Snyk, said large businesses patch an average of one bug for every eight they find because of limited human resources. But he said it was imperative for people to hand over some of the bug hunting, fixing, and monitoring to AI agents. “You got to get to a point where you can fix everything, because in the age of agentic hacking, “those 10 things are gonna become 100 things before you know it.” He later added that AI “is not an adversity if you flip it to a strength.”

Some companies are responding to the call to arm up. Bank of America announced this week it had hired 1,000 contractors to remediate bugs discovered by AI. Nair said just last week he heard from major corporations who were willing to temporarily shut down their systems to prioritize plugging security holes.

Anthropic and OpenAI have said they expect to continue reporting concerning incidents from their own testing. But the companies’ revenues continue to surge, whether it be from attackers or defenders, as consequences prove elusive.
This is an edition of the Model Behavior newsletter. Read previous newsletters here.

items.title: Don’t be fooled—LLMs don’t reason
items.description: On an afternoon in Seoul in March 2016, I watched a program I helped build put a stone on the fifth line of a Go board in what looked like a gift to its human opponent. Move 37 in game two of the five-game match looked so absurd that some commentators thought
items.author: Thore Graepel
paragraphs: On an afternoon in Seoul in March 2016, I watched a program I helped build put a stone on the fifth line of a Go board in what looked like a gift to its human opponent. Move 37 in game two of the five-game match looked so absurd that some commentators thought it was a programming glitch.

It wasn’t. AlphaGo won the game, ultimately triumphing 4-1 over Lee Sedol, one of the greatest professional Go players of all time. “I thought AlphaGo was based on probability calculation and that it was merely a machine,” Lee said afterwards. “But when I saw this move, I changed my mind. Surely, AlphaGo is creative.”

When Deep Blue defeated then reigning world chess champion Garry Kasparov in 1997, it did so by looking six to eight moves ahead per player and evaluating 200 million chess positions per second, using rules hard-coded by humans. Go is a vastly more complex game. A stone’s worth depends on how distant groups and territory unfold over dozens of moves. Computing even a fraction of the possible outcomes would take a supercomputer billions of years. To win, AlphaGo had to sense who was ahead at a glance and even invent moves no human had thought to play.

That is why many accounts of AlphaGo’s match against Lee portray move 37 as a flash of pure machine intuition. But that is a misunderstanding. It was actually AlphaGo’s powers of reasoning that made this creative choice—and these are powers that today’s AI lacks. If we want future AI systems to produce trustworthy results and really novel insights in fields like science and medicine, we need to equip them with genuine reasoning capabilities of this kind.

AlphaGo is made up of two systems. The first, its policy network, was trained to guess what move a strong human would play. This “intuitive” part regarded move 37 as nothing special—a play that had a roughly one in 10,000 chance of being made by an expert human player. What made AlphaGo choose it was the program’s search machinery, which looked beyond immediate plausibility and weighed the future consequences of proposed moves. It explicitly constructed and searched a game tree with thousands of branches, each representing a different possible future.

A well-known theory in the behavioral sciences, popularized by Daniel Kahneman, distinguishes between two modes of human thought: System 1 is fast, gut-level, effortless; system 2, slow, step-by-step, and deliberative. AlphaGo offered a striking machine analogue of that split. Its networks supplied the hunches—this move looks promising, this position looks won—and its search supplied the deliberation, testing those hunches against the moves and countermoves that would follow. As in human cognition, neither half works alone. Intuition alone would never have opted for move 37, and brute-force search would have struggled to sieve through all the many possible moves.

This is strikingly different from the way today’s AI models work. A large language model picks the next token, over and over. That amounts to system 1 in action—fast, associative, and surprisingly good pattern completion across almost every subject people write about.

Not long after ChatGPT debuted, the field realized that language fluency alone falls short of true usefulness. The apparent solution was to make models that deliberate: Instead of answering immediately, they can now generate intermediate steps that decompose a problem, carry forward partial results, and influence subsequent reasoning—a process known as chain of thought.

The gains have proved real, above all in mathematics and coding. But unlike AlphaGo’s search, this does not introduce a genuinely separate reasoning mechanism: The intermediate reasoning is still produced by the same next-token prediction process, iterated for longer before the model commits to an answer.

Three shortcomings prevent what chatbots do from qualifying as reasoning (in a way that a scientist might recognize). First, these models typically maintain no explicit, persistent, and inspectable epistemic state. There is no open ledger that lays out the hypotheses a model is considering, the confidence it has in various explanations, the evidence it’s weighing, and the unresolved questions it’s holding onto—all things that should be systematically revised as new information arrives.

Second, they lack a clean separation between what the system knows and how it manipulates that knowledge. Knowledge and reasoning are inextricably interwoven in the weights of the neural network—there is no independent, explicitly represented set of beliefs. Third, while the chains of thought chatbots produce look like deliberation, research has demonstrated that the bots often concoct them after the fact, reaching an answer by one route but reporting another.

This is a problem because in the high-stakes applications we all care about, such as medicine, engineering, and scientific research, it matters not only what a system concludes but also how it arrives at its conclusion. When mistakes happen—for example, in medical diagnosis and treatment—we need to be able to pinpoint what went wrong: Was the system’s reasoning at fault, did it draw on invalid evidence, or did it make incorrect assumptions?

This is why I recently left my position at Google DeepMind. I believe we need a fresh approach to machine reasoning—one that draws on AlphaGo’s architecture. AlphaGo maintains a record of what it knows about a given position: the game tree. This data structure contains all the variations, the possible futures, that AlphaGo has considered, each move and position being annotated with judgments made by its neural networks. As its reasoning progresses, AlphaGo updates the game tree and eventually synthesizes the information in it to decide which move to make.

Similarly, for general reasoning a system should maintain an epistemic state that represents what the system holds as settled, what it doubts, what it has ruled out, which questions stay open. Reasoning can then be understood as a sequence of moves that change the epistemic state to advance knowledge and reduce uncertainty: deducing consequences, breaking problems into parts, and—crucially—deciding what question to ask, calculation to perform, or experiment to run next.

Of course, open-world reasoning is harder than playing a board game such as Go or chess. In the real world the current state of affairs is only partially known, the set of available actions is large and variable, and the consequences of actions are stochastic or unknown.

But recent advances in LLMs and other neural models now give us the capability to take on such general reasoning problems. For example, LLMs can suggest ways of tackling a problem on the basis of what is known and what resources are available. They can interact with tools via APIs or code and help assess whether a claim is supported by available evidence.

Most important, to keep the system honest, an independent part of the system must evaluate each move by how much it actually resolves uncertainty, updating beliefs only when the change is backed by evidence. Once these rules are enforced, the model can accumulate certified knowledge and improve its reasoning policy by learning from past reasoning experiences. You can think of such a system as the scientific method on steroids, with the purpose of producing knowledge that can withstand scrutiny.

I do not think we reach trustworthy machine intelligence by making system 1 bigger. Scale sharpens intuition, but it does not make intuition more deliberative. Move 37 mattered because a machine held a position, weighed the possible futures, and chose the move its artificial instincts would likely have rejected.

Society needs such creative moves in drug discovery, materials, climate, diagnosis—fields where the board looks nothing like a Go board and nobody hands us the rules. We will get such insights only from systems that reason—systems whose conclusions arise from an auditable sequence of evidence, inference, and belief revision rather than from a convincing story told after the fact.
Thore Graepel is chair of machine learning at University College London. He was a core member of the AlphaGo team at DeepMind and works to ensure that AI benefits human flourishing.
